questions.q: In the Introduction, what setting does Kahneman say he has in mind for readers to benefit from his book?
options: A university seminar where experts debate decision theory
The office water-cooler, where gossip is exchanged
A quiet private study where readers examine their own minds
A corporate boardroom during formal strategy reviews
questions.explain: Kahneman pictures the office water-cooler, where people talk about the judgments and choices of others. He hopes to enrich the vocabulary used in that everyday gossip, not to address specialists or solitary self-examination.

questions.q: A hiring panel rates a tall, confident, articulate candidate's vague answers as unusually insightful. Which diagnostic label from the Introduction fits this error?
options: The availability heuristic
Expert intuition
The illusory certainty of hindsight
The halo effect
questions.explain: Kahneman's example of the halo effect is an audience judging a handsome, confident speaker's comments more favorably than he deserves. The availability heuristic is about judging frequency by ease of recall, which is not what is happening here.

questions.q: In the Introduction's comparison with a physician, what does a diagnostician's large set of disease labels illustrate?
options: That understanding judgment and choice requires a richer vocabulary than everyday language offers
That errors of judgment are illnesses that only trained specialists can cure
That most human judgments are as unhealthy as the diseases physicians treat
That intuition is more reliable in medicine than in business decisions
questions.explain: Just as learning medicine is partly learning the language of medicine, a deeper understanding of judgments and choices needs a richer vocabulary. Each label binds together an idea of a problem, its causes, consequences and possible interventions.

questions.q: How does Kahneman answer the worry that a book about biases of intuition belittles human intelligence?
options: He concedes that human intelligence is unreliable and should be replaced by formulas
He argues that biases affect only people without training in statistics
A focus on error no more denies good judgment than medical texts on disease deny good health
He says errors are rare enough that they can safely be ignored in daily life
questions.explain: Kahneman says the focus on error does not denigrate human intelligence, any more than attention to diseases denies good health. Most of our judgments and actions are appropriate most of the time.

questions.q: True or false: In the Introduction, Kahneman says an objective observer is more likely to detect our errors than we are.
questions.explain: Kahneman notes that we are often confident even when we are wrong, and that “an objective observer is more likely to detect our errors than we are.”

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman argues that New Year resolutions to improve decision making are a more powerful motive for self-criticism than the expectation of intelligent gossip.
questions.explain: He says the reverse: the expectation of intelligent gossip is a more powerful motive for serious self-criticism than New Year resolutions to improve decision making at work and at home.

questions.q: Kahneman explains that systematic errors, which recur predictably in particular circumstances, are known as ____.
questions.explain: The hope for informed gossip rests on distinctive patterns in people's errors; these systematic errors are called biases.

questions.q: When an audience judges a handsome, confident speaker's comments more favorably than he deserves, the diagnostic label Kahneman gives for this bias is the ____.
questions.explain: Kahneman uses the halo effect as his example of how a diagnostic label makes a bias easier to anticipate, recognize, and understand.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give in the Introduction as examples of impressions that arise without your knowing how they got there?
options: Believing there is a lamp on the desk in front of you
Detecting a hint of irritation in your spouse's voice on the telephone
Avoiding a threat on the road before becoming consciously aware of it
Working out a long multiplication step by step
Choosing the wording of a formal letter with care
questions.explain: Kahneman's examples are the lamp, the irritated voice, and the avoided road threat: mental work that goes on in silence. Step-by-step calculation and careful drafting are orderly conscious thought, the kind we can trace.

questions.q: Match each term from the opening of the Introduction to its meaning.
pairs: Water-cooler
Setting where people gossip about the judgments and choices of others
Disease labels
Model for a richer vocabulary for diagnosing errors of judgment
Halo effect
Judging a confident, handsome speaker more favorably than he deserves
Biases
Systematic errors that recur predictably in particular circumstances
questions.explain: The opening links the water-cooler setting, the physician's diagnostic vocabulary, the general term biases, and the halo effect as a sample label.

questions.q: Sort these statements by whether Kahneman affirms or rejects them in the opening of the Introduction.

items.t: Most of our judgments and actions are appropriate most of the time
The confidence we have in our intuitive beliefs is usually justified
We are often confident even when we are wrong
It is easier to label others' mistakes than to recognize our own
Focusing on error implies that human intelligence is poor
Orderly conscious thought is the typical way the mind works
We can usually trace how our impressions came about

questions.explain: Kahneman holds that intuition is usually right but sometimes confidently wrong, and that others spot our errors more easily. He denies that studying errors belittles intelligence and says most impressions arise without our knowing how, so orderly conscious thought is not the typical mode.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman aim his book at water-cooler gossip rather than simply urging readers to examine their own decisions?
questions.a: It is much easier, and more enjoyable, to identify and label the mistakes of others than to recognize our own, and questioning our own beliefs is hardest when we most need to. Because many of us anticipate how friends and colleagues will evaluate our choices, better-informed gossip improves those anticipated judgments. “The expectation of intelligent gossip is a powerful motive for serious self-criticism,” stronger than resolutions to decide better.

questions.q: What is Kahneman's stated aim for watercooler conversations, and what further benefit does he hope might follow?
questions.a: His aim is to improve the ability to identify and understand errors of judgment and choice, in others and eventually in ourselves, by providing a richer and more precise language to discuss them. In at least some cases, an accurate diagnosis may suggest an intervention to limit the damage that bad judgments and choices cause.

questions.q: What does Kahneman say about how the mind usually works, compared with how we believe it works?
questions.a: We believe we know what goes on in our minds, often one conscious thought leading in an orderly way to another, but that is neither the only nor the typical way the mind works. Most impressions and thoughts arise in conscious experience without our knowing how they got there, as with seeing a lamp or sensing irritation in a voice. “The mental work that produces impressions, intuitions, and many decisions goes on in silence in our mind.”

questions.q: According to Kahneman, when and how did the collaboration that shaped the book's central ideas begin?
options: In 1979, when he and Tversky published prospect theory together
In 1974, when Tversky recruited him to a research program at the University of Michigan
In 1969, when he invited Amos Tversky to speak as a guest at his Hebrew University seminar
In 2002, when he and Tversky were both invited to address the Nobel committee
questions.explain: Kahneman traces the central ideas to the lucky day in 1969 when he asked Tversky to speak at a seminar he taught at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. The Michigan program was only the topic Tversky reported on.

questions.q: What question was the University of Michigan research program, as Tversky described it in Kahneman's seminar, trying to answer?
options: Are people good intuitive statisticians?
Are people good intuitive grammarians?
Do emotions explain most departures from rationality?
Can experts learn to trust their intuitions?
questions.explain: Tversky reported on research asking whether people are good intuitive statisticians. Intuitive grammar was the comparison: children follow grammar rules effortlessly without knowing them, so the question was whether statistics works similarly.

questions.q: A researcher finds a striking result in a study of a dozen people and feels sure it would replicate with a similar sample. What did Kahneman and Tversky's survey of expert researchers suggest about this confidence?
options: Experts judge replication odds accurately, so the confidence is probably justified
Experts tend to underestimate how often small-sample results replicate
Only researchers who had not written statistics textbooks made this error
Even experts greatly exaggerate the likelihood that a small-sample result will replicate
questions.explain: Their expert colleagues, including authors of two statistical textbooks, “greatly exaggerated the likelihood that the original result of an experiment would be successfully replicated even with a small sample.”

questions.q: In the conversations Kahneman and Tversky used as research, what was the aim of the many small experiments they ran on themselves?
options: To work out the correct statistical answer to each question they posed
To identify and analyze the intuitive answer that first came to mind, even when they knew it was wrong
To test whether their own answers differed from those of undergraduates
To find the questions on which the two of them disagreed most strongly
questions.explain: They were not seriously looking for the correct answers. They wanted the tempting first intuition, believing that any intuition both shared would be shared by many others.

questions.q: In the Steve problem, why is Steve, described as meek, tidy and shy, more likely to be a farmer than a librarian?
options: There are more than 20 male farmers for each male librarian in the United States
Neighbors more often describe farmers than librarians as meek and tidy
Shy people tend to avoid jobs that bring them into contact with the public
The neighbor's description is unreliable, so it should count for nothing
questions.explain: Because farmers vastly outnumber librarians, more meek and tidy souls are found on tractors than at library desks. The resemblance to a librarian is vivid, but the statistical fact is equally relevant and almost always ignored.

questions.q: In Kahneman and Tversky's experiments with the Steve problem, what did participants rely on to judge Steve's profession?
options: The ease with which examples of each profession came to mind
Feelings of liking or disliking toward each profession
Resemblance of his personality to the stereotype of a profession
The number of men in each profession in the population
questions.explain: Participants ignored the relevant statistical facts and relied exclusively on resemblance, which Kahneman and Tversky proposed was a simplifying heuristic. The proportion of farmers to librarians is exactly what they neglected.

questions.q: In the letter K question, why did Kahneman and Tversky expect people to judge K more likely to be the first letter of a word than the third?
options: K in fact appears more often as the first letter of English words
Words beginning with a letter are much easier to bring to mind than words with it in third place
Scrabble players have learned to favor words that begin with K
People judge a letter by how typical it looks at the start of a word
questions.explain: Retrieving words by their first letter is easier for every letter, so the availability heuristic exaggerates first-position frequency. For K, L, N, R and V, the third position is in fact more common.

questions.q: After reading many news stories about shark attacks, a man concludes that shark attacks are a common cause of death. Which idea from the Introduction best explains his judgment?
options: Judging probability by resemblance to a stereotype
Recognizing familiar cues learned through prolonged practice
Treating problems in isolation instead of together
Judging frequency by the ease with which instances come to mind
questions.explain: This is the availability heuristic: Kahneman notes that the ease of retrieval is largely determined by media coverage, as with his own impression about politicians' adultery. Resemblance to a stereotype is a different heuristic, illustrated by Steve.

questions.q: How did Kahneman and Tversky's Science article challenge the two assumptions about human nature common among social scientists in the 1970s?
options: It argued directly that people are irrational and that emotions are harmless
It showed that fear, affection, and hatred cause most errors of judgment
It showed that only poorly educated people depart from rational thinking
It documented systematic errors in normal people and traced them to the design of cognition, not to emotion
questions.explain: The article challenged both assumptions without discussing them directly, by showing errors in normal people's thinking and locating their source in the machinery of cognition rather than in emotion corrupting thought.

questions.q: What does Kahneman identify as a key reason for the broad appeal of heuristics and biases outside psychology?
options: Their articles framed the findings in the mathematical language favored by economists
Their articles included the full text of their questions, letting readers see their own thinking tripped up
Their findings rested on large conventional experiments with undergraduate participants
They deliberately designed their work to influence philosophers and economists
questions.explain: This incidental feature turned the questions into demonstrations for the reader. Kahneman stresses they chose demonstrations because they were more fun, not to influence philosophers and economists.

questions.q: True or false: When Kahneman and Tversky first met in 1969, Tversky was the older of the two.
questions.explain: Tversky was thirty-two and Kahneman was thirty-five, so Kahneman was the older one.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman came to suspect that his impression of adultery being more common among politicians came from politicians' transgressions being more likely to be reported.
questions.explain: He realized his impression could be due entirely to journalists' choices of topics and to his reliance on the availability heuristic, not to a real difference.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman describes himself as the more logical, theory-oriented partner and Tversky as the more intuitive one rooted in the psychology of perception.
questions.explain: It was the other way round: Tversky was the more logical thinker with an orientation to theory, while Kahneman was more intuitive and rooted in the psychology of perception.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says his 2002 Nobel Prize was for the collaboration on judgment and decision making, and that Tversky would have shared it had he not died.
questions.explain: Kahneman writes that the collaboration was the reason for the prize, which Tversky would have shared had he not died, aged fifty-nine, in 1996.

questions.q: Kahneman and Tversky called the reliance on the ease of memory search the ____ heuristic.
questions.explain: They noticed that judging the divorce rate among professors triggered a search for instances, and that category size was judged by how easily instances came to mind.

questions.q: In the Introduction, Kahneman glosses a heuristic as, roughly, a ____.
questions.explain: He describes resemblance as a simplifying heuristic, roughly a rule of thumb, used to make a difficult judgment.

questions.q: Kahneman and Tversky's article in Science magazine was titled 'Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and ____'.
questions.explain: The article described the shortcuts of intuitive thinking and explained some 20 biases as manifestations of these heuristics.

questions.q: Five years after the Science article, Kahneman and Tversky published ____ theory, a theory of choice that is one of the foundations of behavioral economics.
questions.explain: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision Under Risk came out of their work on simple gambles and is by some counts more influential than their work on judgment.

questions.q: Kahneman and Tversky's first joint study examined the statistical ____ of sophisticated researchers.
questions.explain: Over lunch at Café Rimon they planned a study of the statistical intuitions of sophisticated researchers, to see whether others shared their own deficiency.

questions.q: Kahneman says a recurrent theme of the book is that ____ plays a large role in every story of success.
questions.explain: He applies this to his own work: they were lucky in their choice of demonstrations as a method, and a small change could have made the outcome mediocre.

questions.q: Which of these were assumptions about human nature that Kahneman says social scientists broadly accepted in the 1970s?
options: People are generally rational, and their thinking is normally sound
Emotions such as fear, affection, and hatred explain most departures from rationality
Systematic errors arise from the design of the machinery of cognition
People are poor intuitive statisticians
Most intuitive judgments are produced by simplifying heuristics
questions.explain: The two accepted ideas were general rationality and emotion as the main source of departures from it. Errors rooted in cognitive machinery and poor intuitive statistics are what Kahneman and Tversky's work showed, against those assumptions.

questions.q: Which of these fields does Kahneman list as having used the ideas of heuristics and biases productively?
options: Medical diagnosis
Legal judgment
Intelligence analysis
Architecture
Marine biology
questions.explain: Kahneman lists medical diagnosis, legal judgment, intelligence analysis, philosophy, finance, statistics, and military strategy. Architecture and marine biology are not mentioned.

questions.q: Which of these tasks does Kahneman name as areas in which he and Tversky documented biases of intuitive thinking?
options: Assigning probabilities to events
Forecasting the future
Estimating frequencies
Memorizing lists of words
Recognizing familiar faces
questions.explain: They spent several years documenting biases in assigning probabilities, forecasting, assessing hypotheses, and estimating frequencies. Memory for word lists and face recognition are not among the tasks he names.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give as reasons his collaboration with Tversky worked so well?
options: They were funny together, so long hours of work passed in continuous amusement
Neither ever rejected out of hand anything the other said
They were similar enough to understand each other and different enough to surprise each other
They divided the work so that each could pursue his own projects alone
Neither of them was by nature critical or argumentative
questions.explain: Kahneman stresses shared amusement, checking their critical weapons at the door, and a balance of similarity and difference; they spent much of their working days together. Both were in fact critical and argumentative, Tversky even more so.

questions.q: Put these events from Kahneman and Tversky's story in chronological order.
items: Tversky speaks as a guest at Kahneman's Hebrew University seminar
They plan a study of researchers' statistical intuitions at Café Rimon
They survey experts at a meeting of the Society of Mathematical Psychology
They publish their findings on heuristics and biases in Science
They publish Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision Under Risk
Kahneman receives the Nobel Prize
questions.explain: The seminar in 1969 led to lunch that Friday and the survey of experts; the Science article came in the fifth year of collaboration, prospect theory five years later, and the Nobel Prize in 2002.

questions.q: Put in order the steps of Kahneman's explanation of the Steve problem.
items: A neighbor's description makes Steve sound like a stereotypical librarian
The resemblance to the stereotype strikes the reader immediately
The fact that male farmers far outnumber male librarians is ignored
Resemblance serves as a heuristic to simplify a difficult judgment
Reliance on the heuristic produces a predictable bias
questions.explain: The vivid resemblance crowds out the statistical fact; Kahneman and Tversky proposed that resemblance works as a simplifying heuristic, and reliance on it causes predictable biases.

questions.q: Put in order how Kahneman and Tversky's theory about resemblance in predictions developed.
items: They notice they share silly predictions about toddlers' future professions
They see these predictions follow each child's resemblance to a professional stereotype
The amusing exercise helps them develop a theory about resemblance in predictions
They test and elaborate the theory in dozens of experiments
questions.explain: The toddler game (the argumentative three-year-old lawyer, the nerdy professor) revealed resemblance at work, which fed a theory they then tested in experiments such as the Steve problem.

questions.q: Match each example from Origins to the idea it illustrates.
pairs: Steve, the meek and tidy soul
Resemblance used in place of relevant statistical facts
The letter K
Overestimating first-position frequency because such words are easier to retrieve
Divorce among professors
Judging category size by searching memory for instances
Adultery among politicians
An impression shaped by what journalists choose to report
questions.explain: Steve shows reliance on resemblance; the other three examples show the availability heuristic at work in different ways.

questions.q: Match each name or place from Origins to its role in Kahneman's story.
pairs: Amos Tversky
Rising star in decision research who spoke at the 1969 seminar
Café Rimon
Jerusalem hangout where the first joint study was planned
Society of Mathematical Psychology
Meeting where expert participants answered the survey
University of Michigan
Home of research asking whether people are good intuitive statisticians
Science magazine
Where the main findings on heuristics and biases were published
questions.explain: These are the people and places in the account of how the collaboration began and how its first findings reached a wide readership.

questions.q: Match each work by Kahneman and Tversky to its description in the Introduction.
pairs: Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
Explained some 20 biases as manifestations of heuristics
Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision Under Risk
Theory of choice that is a foundation of behavioral economics
The 1984 article in the second appendix
Summarizes prospect theory and studies of framing effects
questions.explain: The Science article covered judgment, the prospect theory paper covered choice, and the 1984 article reproduced as an appendix summarizes prospect theory along with framing.

questions.q: Sort these examples by whether they belong to Kahneman and Tversky's work on judgment or their later work on decision making.

items.t: Is Steve a librarian or a farmer?
Is K more often the first or the third letter?
How common is divorce among professors?
Would you bet on a coin toss to win $130 or lose $100?
The relative weight given to sure things and uncertain outcomes
Prospect theory

questions.explain: The judgment work studied heuristics in estimating probabilities and frequencies. Immediately afterward they turned to decisions about simple gambles, which led to prospect theory.

questions.q: Sort these traits by whether Kahneman attributes them to himself or to Amos Tversky.

items.t: The more logical thinker
An orientation to theory and an unfailing sense of direction
A perfect memory for jokes
More intuitive
Rooted in the psychology of perception
Aged thirty-five when they met

questions.explain: Kahneman describes Tversky as brilliant, funny, logical and theory-oriented, and himself as more intuitive and grounded in perception; he was thirty-five to Tversky's thirty-two.

questions.q: Sort these by whether Kahneman says they resulted from using demonstrations or would have resulted from reporting only conventional experiments.

items.t: Readers recognized how their own thinking was tripped up
Philosophers and economists saw possible flaws in their own thinking
Scholars became readier to question that the mind is rational and logical
A less noteworthy and less memorable article
Errors blamed on the fecklessness of undergraduates
Skeptical readers distancing themselves from the results

questions.explain: Demonstrations let readers watch themselves fail, which made the dogma of a rational mind harder to hold. Conventional experiments would have let skeptics attribute errors to typical student participants.

questions.q: What did Kahneman and Tversky conclude about their own statistical intuitions, and what did their first study find about other researchers?
questions.a: Despite years of teaching and using statistics, they had no intuitive sense of the reliability of results from small samples: they were too willing to believe findings based on inadequate evidence and collected too few observations. Their survey of experts found the same: colleagues greatly exaggerated the chance that a small-sample result would replicate and gave poor advice about sample size. “Even statisticians were not good intuitive statisticians.”

questions.q: Explain what the Steve problem is designed to show.
questions.a: Steve's description resembles the stereotype of a librarian, and that resemblance strikes everyone immediately. But there are more than 20 male farmers for each male librarian, so a meek and tidy man is more likely a farmer. Participants ignored this statistical fact and relied on resemblance as a simplifying heuristic, which produced predictable biases, showing the power of resemblance as a cue to probability.

questions.q: How does the letter K question illustrate the availability heuristic?
questions.a: It is much easier to think of words that begin with a letter than words with that letter in the third position. Since people judge frequency by the ease with which instances come to mind, they exaggerate how often letters appear first, even letters such as K that occur more often in third position. Reliance on the heuristic produces a predictable bias.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, how does the availability heuristic explain why some public issues seem important while others are neglected?
questions.a: People judge the importance of issues by how easily they are retrieved from memory, and that ease depends largely on media coverage; meanwhile, the media report what they think is on the public's mind. Dramatic events and celebrities trigger feeding frenzies, as after Michael Jackson's death, while critical but unexciting issues get little coverage. Kahneman notes that even his choice of little-covered examples was guided by availability.

questions.q: What did Kahneman and Tversky's research method of conversation involve, and why did they think it would generalize?
questions.a: Their research was a conversation in which they invented questions and examined their own intuitive answers, so each question was a small experiment and they ran many in a day. They were not after the correct answer but the first intuitive answer, the one they were tempted to give even when they knew it was wrong. They believed, correctly, that any intuition the two of them shared would be shared by many others and would be easy to demonstrate.

questions.q: What role does Kahneman say luck played in the success of the heuristics and biases work, and how does this connect to a theme of the book?
questions.a: They chose demonstrations over standard experiments simply because demonstrations were more fun, yet that choice was crucial to the work's impact, so they were lucky in their method as in many other ways. This illustrates a recurrent theme of the book: luck plays a large role in every story of success, and it is almost always easy to find a small change that would have turned a remarkable achievement into a mediocre outcome.

questions.q: How was the heuristics and biases work received, and where does Kahneman say its central idea stands now?
questions.a: The article drew far more attention than expected, became one of the most highly cited works in social science, and was used in many fields. It was also criticized for suggesting an unfairly negative view of the mind, and some researchers refined the ideas while others offered alternatives. By and large, though, the idea that our minds are susceptible to systematic errors is now generally accepted.

questions.q: What does Kahneman say is his main aim in Thinking, Fast and Slow?
options: To give a full exposition of the early research he conducted with Tversky
To offer a step-by-step program for eliminating biases from daily decisions
To present a view of how the mind works drawing on recent cognitive and social psychology
To replace prospect theory with a new economic model of choice
questions.explain: Kahneman says the book is not an exposition of the early research, which others have ably covered. It draws on recent developments, which now show the marvels as well as the flaws of intuitive thought.

questions.q: An intensive-care nurse with many years of experience senses that a patient is deteriorating before the monitors show it. According to the Introduction, what best explains her intuition?
options: Recognition of familiar cues, learned through prolonged practice
The affect heuristic, guided by her liking for the patient
A mysterious sixth sense that some people are born with
Answering an easier question in place of a hard one
questions.explain: Kahneman says the accurate intuitions of experts are better explained by prolonged practice than by heuristics. Following Simon, he treats such intuition as recognition, which involves no magic.

questions.q: In Gary Klein's firefighter story, what turned out to explain the danger the commander sensed?
options: The kitchen fire had spread to the roof above the men
The heart of the fire was in the basement beneath where the men stood
A team member had heard the floor begin to crack
Smoke had begun rising through the kitchen floorboards
questions.explain: The floor collapsed just after the men escaped; the fire was centered in the basement. Only afterward did the commander realize the fire had been unusually quiet and his ears unusually hot.

questions.q: How does Herbert Simon, as quoted in the Introduction, characterize expert intuition?
options: As nothing more and nothing less than recognition
As a sixth sense that only a few gifted experts possess
As an answer to an easier question substituted for a hard one
As judgment guided by feelings of liking and disliking
questions.explain: Simon wrote that a cue gives the expert access to information stored in memory, and “Intuition is nothing more and nothing less than recognition.”

questions.q: Which question does Kahneman say the investment officer failed to consider before buying tens of millions of dollars of Ford stock?
options: Do I like the cars Ford makes?
Does Ford know how to make a car?
Will investors be impressed by Ford's next automobile show?
Is Ford stock currently underpriced?
questions.explain: An economist would call only the underpricing question relevant. Liking Ford's cars is the easier question the executive actually answered.

questions.q: Asked whether a candidate's economic plan will work, a voter answers according to whether she finds the candidate likable. Which idea from the Introduction describes this?
options: Expert intuition based on recognizing familiar cues
Switching to slow, deliberate thinking when intuition fails
Answering an easier question in place of a difficult one, usually without noticing
Judging frequency by the ease of searching memory
questions.explain: Kahneman calls this substitution the essence of intuitive heuristics, as when the Ford executive answered whether he liked Ford cars instead of whether the stock was underpriced. Liking-based answers are also an instance of the affect heuristic.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says emotion now looms much smaller in the understanding of intuitive judgments and choices than it did in the past.
questions.explain: He says the opposite: an important advance is that emotion now looms much larger in our understanding of intuitive judgments and choices than in the past.

questions.q: True or false: According to Kahneman, fast thinking includes the entirely automatic mental activities of perception and memory, as well as expert and heuristic intuition.
questions.explain: Fast thinking covers both variants of intuitive thought, the expert and the heuristic, plus automatic perception and memory, such as knowing there is a lamp on your desk.

questions.q: The investment officer's decision to buy Ford stock would today be described as an example of the ____ heuristic.
questions.explain: In the affect heuristic, judgments and decisions are guided directly by feelings of liking and disliking, with little deliberation or reasoning.

questions.q: Kahneman describes mental life with the metaphor of two agents, System 1 and System 2, which respectively produce fast and ____ thinking.
questions.explain: System 1 produces fast thinking and System 2 slow thinking; Kahneman promises to explain this metaphor more fully in the next chapter.

questions.q: Kahneman says the intuitive System 1 is the secret ____ of many of the choices and judgments you make.
questions.explain: In the picture from recent research, System 1 is more influential than your experience tells you, which is why most of the book is about its workings.

questions.q: In the richer, more balanced picture Kahneman now draws, skill and ____ are alternative sources of intuitive judgments and choices.
questions.explain: The early work did not ask whether all intuitive judgments came from heuristics; it is now clear that expert intuition comes from skill built by prolonged practice.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman offer as everyday feats of intuitive expertise that most of us perform?
options: Detecting anger in the first word of a telephone call
Recognizing on entering a room that we were the subject of the conversation
Reacting quickly to subtle signs that a nearby driver is dangerous
Announcing a forced checkmate while walking past a street chess game
Making a complex diagnosis after a single glance at a patient
questions.explain: Kahneman says our everyday intuitive abilities are no less marvelous than an expert's insights, only more common. The chess master and the physician are his examples of striking expert intuition, not everyday feats.

questions.q: Which of these cues does Kahneman say prompted the firefighter commander's sixth sense of danger in Gary Klein's story?
options: The fire was unusually quiet
His ears were unusually hot
The floor was visibly sagging
He smelled gas from the basement
He heard shouts from below
questions.explain: Only after the fact did the commander realize the fire had been unusually quiet and his ears unusually hot. He had no idea what was wrong at the time, only that something was.

questions.q: Put in order what Kahneman says happens as the machinery of intuitive thought confronts a problem.
items: With relevant expertise, the situation is recognized and the intuitive solution is likely correct
Without a skilled solution, a heuristic may supply a quick answer to an easier question
If neither an expert nor a heuristic answer comes, we switch to slower, effortful thinking
questions.explain: Intuition does the best it can: expertise first, then a heuristic substitute, and only when both fail does the slow, deliberate thinking of the title take over.

questions.q: Match each figure from Where We Are Now to the point Kahneman uses them for.
pairs: Gary Klein
Told the story of a firefighter commander's sense of danger
Herbert Simon
Studied chess masters and called intuition recognition
The investment officer
Bought Ford stock after being impressed at an automobile show
A two-year-old saying doggie
Everyday recognition with the same character as expert intuition
questions.explain: Klein and Simon illustrate valid expert intuition, the child shows that recognition is a familiar miracle, and the executive shows intuition that does not arise from true expertise.

questions.q: Match each term from Where We Are Now to its meaning.
pairs: Affect heuristic
Judgments guided directly by feelings of liking and disliking
System 1
The agent that produces fast, intuitive thinking
System 2
The agent that produces slow, deliberate thinking
Substitution
Answering an easier question in place of a difficult one
questions.explain: These are the core terms Kahneman introduces for describing how intuition works and fails.

questions.q: Sort these examples by whether Kahneman would trace the intuition to true expertise or to a heuristic.

items.t: A chess master's first few candidate moves are all strong
A firefighter commander orders his men out just before the floor collapses
A physician makes a complex diagnosis after a single glance
An executive buys Ford stock because he likes Ford cars
Judging Steve a librarian because he fits the stereotype
Judging how common something is by how easily examples come to mind

questions.explain: Valid intuitions come from experts recognizing familiar elements after prolonged practice. The Ford, Steve and availability cases rest on heuristics, which substitute an easier judgment.

questions.q: Sort these descriptions by whether they apply to System 1 or System 2 as the Introduction presents them.

items.t: Produces fast thinking
The secret author of many of our choices and judgments
Includes automatic perception and memory
Produces slow thinking
Deliberate and effortful
Takes over when neither an expert nor a heuristic answer comes to mind

questions.explain: System 1 is intuitive and automatic and more influential than we realize; System 2 is the slower, effortful mode we switch to when intuitive search fails.

questions.q: How has the picture of intuition changed since Kahneman and Tversky's early work, according to the Introduction?
questions.a: The early work focused on biases, partly because they were interesting and partly because they were evidence for heuristics, and said only that heuristics are useful but sometimes lead to severe errors. It is now clear that not all intuitive judgments come from those heuristics: accurate expert intuitions are better explained by prolonged practice. The result is a richer, more balanced picture in which skill and heuristics are alternative sources of intuitive judgments and choices, and we understand the marvels as well as the flaws of intuition.

questions.q: What is Herbert Simon's account of expert intuition, and how does the example of a child saying doggie illustrate it?
questions.a: Simon held that a situation provides a cue, the cue gives the expert access to information stored in memory, and that information provides the answer, so intuition is simply recognition. We are not surprised when a two-year-old recognizes and names a dog, and expert intuition has the same character. Valid intuitions develop when experts learn to recognize familiar elements in a new situation and act appropriately.

questions.q: A friend invests her savings in a company because she loves its advertisements and products. Using the Introduction's account of the Ford executive, explain what is going on.
questions.a: Like the executive who bought Ford stock because he liked the cars, she has let the affect heuristic guide her: her decision is driven directly by liking, with little deliberation. The hard question, whether the stock is currently underpriced, has been replaced by an easier one, whether she likes the company, usually without her noticing. Kahneman calls this substitution the essence of intuitive heuristics.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say expert intuition strikes us as magical but is not?
questions.a: Stories like the firefighter, the chess master, or the physician who diagnoses at a glance seem magical, but the psychology of accurate intuition involves no magic. Each of us performs such feats many times a day, such as detecting anger in a voice or sensing a dangerous driver. Our everyday intuitive abilities are no less marvelous than an expert's insights, only more common, and both rest on recognition built from experience.

questions.q: What is the slow thinking of the book's title, and what does fast thinking include?
questions.a: When the spontaneous search for an intuitive solution fails, and neither an expert solution nor a heuristic answer comes to mind, we switch to a slower, more deliberate and effortful form of thinking; this is the slow thinking of the title. Fast thinking includes both expert and heuristic intuition, as well as the entirely automatic activities of perception and memory. Kahneman personifies these as System 1 and System 2.

questions.q: According to the Introduction's road map, what major puzzle does Part 2 explore?
options: Why we are so confident in what we believe we know
Why the experiencing and remembering selves disagree
Why it is so difficult for us to think statistically
Why economic agents depart from the rules of rationality
questions.explain: Part 2 updates the study of judgment heuristics around this puzzle. Overconfidence belongs to Part 3, choice and rationality to Part 4, and the two selves to Part 5.

questions.q: Why, according to the road map for Part 2, is statistical thinking hard for System 1?
options: It requires emotional detachment, which System 1 cannot achieve
It requires thinking causally, which System 1 tends to avoid
It requires metaphors, which System 1 is unable to construct
It requires thinking about many things at once, which System 1 is not designed to do
questions.explain: Kahneman says we easily think associatively, metaphorically and causally, but statistics needs many things held at once, which System 1 is not built for.

questions.q: In the example of two painful experiences previewed for Part 5, why might people choose to repeat the worse episode?
options: Their choice is guided by the remembering self, whose memory of the worse episode can be better
Their experiencing self prefers the longer episode because it grows used to the pain
They cannot tell afterward which episode lasted longer
Their System 2 calculates that the longer episode was less painful overall
questions.explain: The automatic formation of memories, a feature of System 1, has rules that can make the strictly worse episode leave a better memory. Guided by the remembering self, people expose their experiencing self to unnecessary pain.

questions.q: Which author does Kahneman say influenced his views on overconfidence and the illusory certainty of hindsight?
options: Herbert Simon, who studied chess masters
Nassim Taleb, the author of The Black Swan
Gary Klein, who studied firefighters' intuitions
Amos Tversky, his longtime collaborator
questions.explain: In previewing Part 3, Kahneman says his views on overconfidence and hindsight have been influenced by Nassim Taleb.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says the observations about choice in Part 4 present a deep challenge to the rationality assumption favored in standard economics.
questions.explain: Part 4 deals with treating problems in isolation and with framing effects; readily explained by System 1, these present a deep challenge to the rationality assumption.

questions.q: Part 5 introduces a distinction between two selves, the experiencing self and the ____ self.
questions.explain: The two selves do not have the same interests, and what makes the experiencing self happy is not quite what satisfies the remembering self.

questions.q: Kahneman describes ____ effects as cases where decisions are shaped by inconsequential features of choice problems.
questions.explain: Framing effects are among the ways human choices deviate from the rules of rationality that Part 4 addresses.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say Part 3 of the book addresses?
options: Excessive confidence in what we believe we know
Underestimating the role of chance in events
The illusory certainty of hindsight
The distinction between the experiencing and remembering selves
How associative memory constructs a coherent interpretation
questions.explain: Part 3 is about overconfidence, our inability to acknowledge ignorance and chance, and hindsight. The two selves are Part 5's topic and associative memory is Part 1's.

questions.q: Which of these distinctions does Kahneman say the concluding chapter explores?
options: The experiencing self versus the remembering self
Agents in classical economics versus agents in behavioral economics
The automatic System 1 versus the effortful System 2
Expert intuition versus heuristic intuition
Gains versus losses in simple gambles
questions.explain: The conclusions take up the three distinctions drawn across the book, in reverse order. The other contrasts appear in the book but are not named as the conclusion's three distinctions.

questions.q: Put the topics of the book's five Parts in the order Kahneman's road map presents them.
items: The basic elements of a two-systems approach
Why statistical thinking is so difficult
Overconfidence and the illusion of understanding the world
A conversation with economics about rational choice
The experiencing self and the remembering self
questions.explain: Part 1 lays out the two systems, Part 2 statistics and heuristics, Part 3 overconfidence, Part 4 choices and prospect theory, and Part 5 the two selves.

questions.q: The concluding chapter takes up the book's three main distinctions in reverse order. Put them in the order the conclusion discusses them.
items: Experiencing self versus remembering self
Classical economics agents versus behavioral economics agents
Automatic System 1 versus effortful System 2
questions.explain: The book introduces the two systems first and the two selves last, so working in reverse, the conclusion starts with the two selves and ends with the two systems.

questions.q: Match each Part of the book to a topic Kahneman previews for it.
pairs: Part 1
Associative memory continually constructing a coherent interpretation
Part 3
Overconfidence fed by the illusory certainty of hindsight
Part 4
Key concepts of prospect theory and framing effects
Part 5
Two selves applied to the measurement of well-being
questions.explain: These previews come from the road map in What Comes Next; Part 2, on statistical thinking, is left out here.

questions.q: Sort these descriptions by whether they fit the experiencing self or the remembering self in Kahneman's preview of Part 5.

items.t: Endures the pain of each episode as it happens
Suffers unnecessary pain when the worse episode is repeated
Guides the choice of which episode to repeat
Can be left with a better impression of the strictly worse episode

questions.explain: People choose by their remembering self, whose memories follow the rules of automatic memory formation, and so expose their experiencing self to more pain than necessary.

questions.q: Explain the example of two painful experiences that Kahneman uses to preview Part 5.
questions.a: One painful experience is strictly worse than the other because it is longer, yet the automatic rules of memory formation, a feature of System 1, can be exploited so that the worse episode leaves a better memory. When people later choose which episode to repeat, they are guided by their remembering self and so expose their experiencing self to unnecessary pain. This shows that the two selves do not have the same interests.

questions.q: What does Part 4 of the book do, according to the road map, and why do its findings matter for economics?
questions.a: Part 4 is a conversation with economics about decision making and the assumption that economic agents are rational. It gives a current view, informed by the two-system model, of prospect theory, and then addresses ways choices deviate from rationality, such as treating problems in isolation and framing effects. Because these deviations are readily explained by System 1, they present a deep challenge to the rationality assumption of standard economics.

questions.q: What does the Introduction set up for Chapter 1, The Characters of the Story?
options: The two agents, System 1 and System 2, whose metaphor Kahneman promises to explain in the next chapter
The history of the collaboration with Tversky, which Chapter 1 continues
The experiencing and remembering selves, whose conflict Chapter 1 resolves
Prospect theory, which Chapter 1 presents in full mathematical form
questions.explain: Kahneman says he will explain more fully in the next chapter why he describes mental life as two characters, System 1 and System 2. The chapter title's characters are those two agents.

questions.q: Where does Kahneman say the Science article Judgment Under Uncertainty appears in the book?
options: As the opening chapter of Part 2, Heuristics and Biases
Reproduced in full as an appendix at the end of the book
As the basis of the book's concluding chapter
Summarized within Chapter 1 alongside prospect theory
questions.explain: The article is reproduced in full at the end of the book; the table of contents lists it as Appendix A, with the 1984 choices article as Appendix B.

questions.q: True or false: According to the Introduction's road map, prospect theory is presented in Part 2 of the book.
questions.explain: Prospect theory belongs to Part 4, Choices, which offers a current view of its key concepts. Part 2 updates the study of judgment heuristics.

questions.q: In the table of contents, Part 4, which Kahneman describes as a conversation with economics about rational decision making, is titled ____.
questions.explain: Part 4, Choices, runs from Bernoulli's Errors through Frames and Reality and contains the chapter on prospect theory.

questions.q: Which of these chapters belong to Part 2, which Kahneman says updates the study of judgment heuristics?
options: The Law of Small Numbers
Anchors
Linda: Less Is More
Prospect Theory
The Illusion of Validity
questions.explain: Part 2, Heuristics and Biases, includes these chapters. Prospect Theory is in Part 4, Choices, and The Illusion of Validity is in Part 3, Overconfidence.

questions.q: Put these Part titles in the order they appear in the book's table of contents.
items: Two Systems
Heuristics and Biases
Overconfidence
Choices
Two Selves
questions.explain: The book moves from the two systems to judgment heuristics, then overconfidence, then choice, and ends with the two selves before the Conclusions.

questions.q: Put the parts of the Introduction in the order they appear.
items: Opening: enriching the vocabulary of water-cooler gossip
Origins: the collaboration with Amos Tversky
Where We Are Now: the marvels and flaws of intuition
What Comes Next: a road map of the five Parts
questions.explain: The Introduction moves from the book's aim, to the history of the ideas, to the present understanding of intuition and the two systems, and then to a guide to what follows.

questions.q: Match each Part of the book to a chapter it contains.
pairs: Two Systems
The Lazy Controller
Overconfidence
The Outside View
Choices
The Endowment Effect
Two Selves
Life as a Story
questions.explain: In the table of contents, The Lazy Controller is in Part 1, The Outside View in Part 3, The Endowment Effect in Part 4, and Life as a Story in Part 5.

questions.q: How does the structure of the Introduction prepare the reader for the rest of the book?
questions.a: The opening states the aim of a richer vocabulary for diagnosing errors, which the conclusion returns to. Origins presents heuristics and biases and prospect theory, the roots of Parts 2 and 4 and of the two appendixes. Where We Are Now introduces the newer picture of intuition, skill versus heuristics and fast versus slow thinking, leading straight into System 1 and System 2 in Chapter 1. What Comes Next then maps the five Parts and the Conclusions.

questions.q: In the opening exercise with the photograph of the angry woman, what does Kahneman say your reaction to the picture illustrates?
options: Fast thinking: you knew her mood and sensed what she would do next without intending to assess anything
Slow thinking: you deliberately inferred her mood from her features in an orderly series of steps
Perception alone: you registered her dark hair, while judging her mood required effortful reasoning
A cognitive illusion: you wrongly believed she was angry even though her expression was neutral
questions.explain: Kahneman says seeing and intuitive thinking combined seamlessly: the judgment of anger and the premonition of unkind words came automatically. “It just happened to you.” It was not a deliberate, step-by-step inference.

questions.q: True or false: Looking at the problem 17 × 24, Kahneman says you would quickly see that 12,609 and 123 are implausible, but without working on it you could not be sure the answer is not 568.
questions.explain: Kahneman says you have a vague intuitive sense of the range of possible results, enough to rule out wild answers, but no precise solution comes to mind without computing.

questions.q: Kahneman calls the deliberate, effortful, and orderly mental work of computing 17 × 24 a prototype of ____ thinking.
questions.explain: The multiplication exercise is contrasted with the angry face: it required retrieving and carrying out a learned program step by step, which Kahneman calls “a prototype of slow thinking.”

questions.q: Put these moments of working on 17 × 24 in the order Kahneman describes them.
items: Recognizing it as a multiplication problem you could probably solve
Retrieving the multiplication program learned in school
Carrying out the program while holding intermediate results in memory
Pupils contracting back to normal on finding the answer or giving up
questions.explain: You first recognize the type of problem, then retrieve the cognitive program, then implement it under strain; the pupils, dilated during the work, contract as soon as the work ends.

questions.q: Sort these features of the two opening exercises by which kind of thinking they belong to.

items.t: Knowing her mood as quickly as seeing her dark hair
A premonition of unkind words came to mind effortlessly
It did not feel like something you did
Feeling you could choose whether to engage
Strain of holding material in memory
Pupils dilating while you work

questions.explain: The face produced an automatic judgment that simply happened to you; the multiplication was a voluntary, strenuous computation with bodily signs of effort such as dilated pupils.

questions.q: What does Kahneman want the reader to notice about their experience of looking at the photograph of the angry woman?
questions.a: Seeing and intuitive thinking were combined seamlessly: you knew she was angry as quickly as you saw her dark hair, and you even sensed she was about to say unkind words. You did not intend to judge her mood or predict her behavior, and it did not feel like something you did. “It just happened to you.” This is fast thinking.

questions.q: How did your body respond while you worked on 17 × 24, according to Kahneman, and what does that show?
questions.a: The computation involved the body as well as the mind: muscles tensed, blood pressure rose, the heart rate increased, and the pupils dilated, contracting back to normal as soon as you found the answer or gave up. These signs show that slow thinking is genuine mental work that is deliberate and effortful.

questions.q: In Thinking, Fast and Slow, whose terms does Kahneman adopt when he speaks of System 1 and System 2?
options: Christopher Chabris and Daniel Simons
Keith Stanovich and Richard West
Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman
Psychologists who study psychopathy
questions.explain: Kahneman says he adopts terms originally proposed by Keith Stanovich and Richard West. Chabris and Simons are the authors of the invisible gorilla study, not of the System 1 and System 2 labels.

questions.q: Although we identify with System 2, which character does Kahneman call the hero of the book?
options: System 2, the conscious reasoning self
The reader, who learns to overcome bias
System 1, the automatic system
The critic who spots other people's errors
questions.explain: Kahneman says System 2 believes it is where the action is, but “the automatic System 1 is the hero of the book,” because its impressions and feelings are the main sources of System 2's beliefs and choices.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what one feature do the highly diverse operations of System 2 have in common?
options: They are innate skills shared with other animals
They become automatic after enough practice
They can run in parallel without limit
They require attention and are disrupted when attention is drawn away
questions.explain: Bracing for a starter gun, filling out a tax form, and checking a logical argument all require attention and suffer when attention is drawn away. Becoming automatic through practice describes skills that have moved to System 1.

questions.q: In the invisible gorilla film, what does Kahneman say causes about half of viewers to miss the gorilla?
options: The counting task, especially the instruction to ignore one of the teams
The gorilla being on screen for only a fraction of a second
The black-and-white shirts making the gorilla blend in
Viewers having seen the film before and expecting nothing new
questions.explain: The gorilla is in view for 9 seconds, and no one who watches without the task misses it; it is the absorbing counting task, and above all the instruction to ignore one team, that causes the blindness.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, which two facts about our minds does the invisible gorilla study illustrate?
options: We see what we expect, and we forget what surprises us
We can be blind to the obvious, and we are also blind to our blindness
Attention is unlimited, but memory is easily distorted
Seeing is effortful, and counting is automatic
questions.explain: Viewers miss a striking event and are then sure it was not there, which shows both blindness to the obvious and blindness to that blindness. The study also shows attention is limited, not unlimited.

questions.q: Priya chats happily with a passenger while driving on an empty highway, but falls silent when she must merge into dense, fast traffic. Which idea from Kahneman's discussion of attention best explains this?
options: System 1 cannot be turned off, so talking always interferes with driving
System 2 is lazy and prefers conversation to driving
Easy tasks can be done together, but effortful activities interfere with each other because attention is a limited budget
Driving is always a System 2 activity, so any conversation is dangerous
questions.explain: Kahneman says you can do several things at once only if they are easy; effortful activities draw on a limited budget of attention and interfere with one another. Driving on an empty road is in his list of System 1 activities, so it is not always effortful.

questions.q: Waiting at a crowded airport arrivals hall, Tom keeps telling himself to watch for a red coat so he will spot his sister quickly. In Kahneman's terms, what is Tom doing?
options: Letting System 1 take over so that System 2 can rest
Experiencing a cognitive illusion about his sister's appearance
Orienting involuntarily to a sudden sound
Using System 2 to program the normally automatic functions of attention, which takes continuous effort
questions.explain: Kahneman's example of looking for a white-haired woman or a bearded man at a train station shows System 2 setting attention to detect a target; maintaining such a set requires continuous exertion of at least some effort.

questions.q: When a driver is overtaking a truck on a narrow road, adult passengers stop talking. What does Kahneman say this shows?
options: Everyone has some awareness of the limited capacity of attention, and social behavior makes allowances for it
Passengers are frightened, and fear switches off System 2
Conversation is a System 2 task that only passengers perform
Drivers cannot hear speech at any time while driving
questions.explain: Kahneman uses the example to show that people know distracting the driver is unwise and suspect he is temporarily deaf; our social behavior allows for the limited capacity of attention.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says the control of attention belongs entirely to System 2.
questions.explain: Kahneman says the control of attention is shared by the two systems: orienting to a loud sound is normally an involuntary operation of System 1, which then mobilizes the voluntary attention of System 2.

questions.q: True or false: In the invisible gorilla study, people who watched the film without the counting task also frequently missed the gorilla.
questions.explain: Kahneman says no one who watches the video without the counting task would miss the gorilla; the blindness comes from the absorbing task and the instruction to ignore one team.

questions.q: Kahneman defines System 1 as operating automatically and quickly, with little or no effort and no sense of ____ control.
questions.explain: The definition reads: System 1 operates automatically and quickly, “with little or no effort and no sense of voluntary control.” System 2, by contrast, is associated with agency, choice, and concentration.

questions.q: Kahneman says his book, with System 1 and System 2 as its two characters, can be read as a ____.
questions.explain: Kahneman says he goes further than most psychologists in using the labels, inviting readers to treat the book as a psychodrama with two characters who act as agents.

questions.q: Kahneman says the phrase "pay attention" is apt because you dispose of a limited ____ of attention that you can allocate to activities.
questions.explain: Attention is like a limited budget: you allocate it among activities, and if you try to go beyond your budget, you will fail.

questions.q: Which of these appear in Kahneman's list of automatic activities attributed to System 1?
options: Detect hostility in a voice
Read words on large billboards
Drive a car on an empty road
Fill out a tax form
Count the occurrences of the letter a in a page of text
questions.explain: Detecting hostility, reading large billboards, and driving on an empty road occur automatically with little effort. Filling out a tax form and counting letters are in the list of System 2 activities that require attention.

questions.q: Which of these appear in Kahneman's list of System 2 activities that require attention?
options: Park in a narrow space
Compare two washing machines for overall value
Orient to the source of a sudden sound
Tell someone your phone number
Make a disgust face when shown a horrible picture
questions.explain: Parking in a narrow space, comparing washing machines, and telling someone your phone number all require attention. Orienting to a sudden sound and making a disgust face are automatic System 1 reactions.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman name as innate System 1 capabilities that we are born prepared for?
options: Avoid losses
Fear spiders
Read words
Find strong chess moves
Orient attention
questions.explain: We are born prepared to perceive the world, recognize objects, orient attention, avoid losses, and fear spiders. Reading is a skill learned through prolonged practice, and strong chess moves are found only by specialized experts.

questions.q: Which of these mental actions does Kahneman describe as completely involuntary?
options: Understanding simple sentences in your own language
Knowing that 2 + 2 = 4
Chewing
Looking for a woman with white hair
questions.explain: You cannot refrain from understanding simple sentences or from knowing that 2 + 2 = 4. Chewing is susceptible to voluntary control though it normally runs on automatic pilot, and looking for a white-haired woman is a System 2 activity.

questions.q: Put the events of the invisible gorilla study in order, as Kahneman describes them.
items: Viewers are told to count the passes made by the white team
Halfway through, a woman in a gorilla suit crosses the court and thumps her chest
The gorilla moves on after 9 seconds in view
About half of viewers report nothing unusual
Viewers who missed it are sure the gorilla was not there
questions.explain: The counting instruction comes first and absorbs attention; the gorilla appears halfway through for 9 seconds; afterward about half have not noticed it, and those who missed it initially cannot believe they did.

questions.q: Match each person or group to their role in Chapter 1 of Thinking, Fast and Slow.
pairs: Keith Stanovich and Richard West
Originally proposed the terms System 1 and System 2
Christopher Chabris and Daniel Simons
Made the film with the gorilla among basketball players
Kahneman's psychotherapy teacher
Warned against a patient whom all previous clinicians had failed
The leading authority on psychopathy
Confirmed that the teacher's advice was sound
questions.explain: Kahneman borrows the system labels from Stanovich and West, the gorilla demonstration from Chabris and Simons, and the clinical warning from his teacher, later confirmed by the leading expert on psychopathy.

questions.q: Match each example of System 2 setting attention or memory to what is being set.
pairs: Waiting for a relative at a busy train station
Watching for a white-haired woman or a bearded man
Searching your memory for a category of names
Capital cities that start with N
Renting a car at London's Heathrow Airport
Remembering to drive on the left side of the road
questions.explain: Each case shows System 2 programming normally automatic attention or memory to do something that does not come naturally, which takes continuous effort to maintain.

questions.q: Sort these activities from Kahneman's lists into System 1 (automatic) and System 2 (effortful).

items.t: Answer to 2 + 2 = ?
Find a strong move in chess (as a chess master)
Understand simple sentences
Complete the phrase bread and ...
Brace for the starter gun in a race
Focus on one voice in a crowded, noisy room
Maintain a faster walking speed than is natural
Check the validity of a complex logical argument

questions.explain: The first group occurs automatically with little or no effort (chess moves only for masters); the second requires attention and suffers if attention is directed elsewhere.

questions.q: Using Kahneman's distinction, sort these everyday activities into those normally handled by System 1 and those that need System 2.

items.t: Turning toward a door that suddenly slams
Sensing irritation in a friend's tone of voice
Recognizing the word on a big road sign
Working out which of two phone plans is cheaper
Squeezing a car into a tight parking spot
Checking a long contract's argument for loopholes

questions.explain: Orienting to a sudden sound, detecting hostility in a voice, and reading large signs are automatic in Kahneman's lists; comparing products for value, parking in a narrow space, and checking a complex argument demand attention.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman make System 1 the hero of the book, even though we identify with System 2?
questions.a: We think of ourselves as System 2, the conscious, reasoning self that has beliefs and makes choices. But System 1 effortlessly originates the impressions and feelings that are the main sources of System 2's explicit beliefs and deliberate choices, and it generates surprisingly complex patterns of ideas. So although System 2 believes itself to be where the action is, most of the action really starts in System 1.

questions.q: How, according to Kahneman, do the capabilities of System 1 arise?
questions.a: Some are innate skills shared with other animals: we are born prepared to perceive the world, recognize objects, orient attention, avoid losses, and fear spiders. Others become fast and automatic through prolonged practice, such as learned associations, reading, and understanding social nuances. Some, like finding strong chess moves, belong only to specialized experts, while others, like matching a personality sketch to a stereotype, are widely shared; the knowledge is accessed without intention or effort.

questions.q: Why could you not compute 17 × 24 while making a left turn into dense traffic, according to Kahneman?
questions.a: Both are effortful activities, and you dispose of a limited budget of attention; if you try to go beyond the budget, you fail. It is the mark of effortful activities that they interfere with each other, so it is difficult or impossible to do several at once. You can do several things at once only if they are easy and undemanding.

questions.q: What does the invisible gorilla study show about attention and about our awareness of it?
questions.a: Seeing and orienting are automatic functions of System 1, but they depend on allocating some attention to the stimulus, so intense focus on counting passes can make people effectively blind to a gorilla in plain view. The viewers who miss it are sure it was not there, and people find the results very surprising. The study shows that we can be blind to the obvious and also blind to our blindness.

questions.q: In Kahneman's plot synopsis of the two systems, what happens when System 2 endorses the suggestions of System 1?
options: Beliefs turn into impressions and actions turn into impulses
Impressions and intuitions turn into beliefs, and impulses turn into voluntary actions
System 1 shuts down until System 2 has finished
The suggestions are stored as biases for later use
questions.explain: System 1 continuously generates impressions, intuitions, intentions, and feelings; if System 2 endorses them, impressions and intuitions become beliefs and impulses become voluntary actions. The tempting reversal gets the direction of the flow backward.

questions.q: Sam is deep in a conversation in a foreign airport, yet when a sign in his own language comes into view, he reads it before he can stop himself. Which limitation of System 1 from Kahneman's plot synopsis does this illustrate?
options: System 1 has little understanding of statistics
System 1 is too slow for routine decisions
System 1 cannot be turned off
System 1 only works when System 2 is resting
questions.explain: Kahneman says one further limitation of System 1 is that it cannot be turned off: shown a word in a language you know, you will read it unless your attention is totally focused elsewhere. Slowness is a feature of System 2, not System 1.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that if you are shown a word on a screen in a language you know, you will read it unless your attention is totally focused elsewhere.
questions.explain: This is his example of the limitation that System 1 cannot be turned off: reading happens automatically even when you do not intend it.

questions.q: True or false: According to Kahneman, System 2 is activated when an event is detected that confirms the model of the world that System 1 maintains.
questions.explain: System 2 is activated when an event violates System 1's model of the world, a world in which lamps do not jump and cats do not bark. Surprise, not confirmation, mobilizes attention.

questions.q: Kahneman says System 1 has ____, systematic errors that it is prone to make in specified circumstances.
questions.explain: Although System 1 is generally very good at what it does, it has biases: systematic errors in specified circumstances, such as answering easier questions than the one asked.

questions.q: Kahneman sums up the plot: most of what you think and do originates in System 1, but System 2 takes over when things get difficult, and it normally has the last ____.
questions.explain: System 2 usually adopts System 1's suggestions with little modification, but when things get difficult it takes over and normally has the last word.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say mobilize System 2?
options: A question for which System 1 offers no answer
An event that violates the model of the world System 1 maintains
Detecting an error that is about to be made
Seeing a familiar word on a screen
Recognizing that a face looks angry
questions.explain: System 2 is mobilized by questions System 1 cannot answer (like 17 × 24), by surprise, and by detecting an error about to be made. Reading a familiar word and recognizing an angry face are automatic System 1 operations.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman list as the suggestions System 1 continuously generates for System 2?
options: Impressions
Feelings
Step-by-step computations
Checks of logical validity
Intentions
questions.explain: System 1 generates impressions, intuitions, intentions, and feelings. Step-by-step computation and checking logical validity are effortful System 2 work.

questions.q: Put the steps of how surprise engages System 2 in the order Kahneman describes.
items: An event violates the model of the world System 1 maintains
Some attention allows the surprising stimulus to be detected
Surprise activates and orients your attention
You stare and search memory for a story that makes sense of the event
questions.explain: Kahneman notes the gorilla experiment shows some attention is needed to detect the surprising stimulus; surprise then orients attention, and you stare and search memory for an explanation.

questions.q: Match each aspect of System 1 to Kahneman's assessment of it in the plot synopsis.
pairs: Its models of familiar situations
Accurate
Its short-term predictions
Usually accurate as well
Its initial reactions to challenges
Swift and generally appropriate
Its grasp of logic and statistics
Little understanding
questions.explain: System 1 is generally very good at what it does, which is why the division of labor works, but it has biases and little understanding of logic and statistics.

questions.q: Sort these roles from Kahneman's plot synopsis by which system performs them.

items.t: Continuously generates impressions and intuitions
Runs automatically and cannot be turned off
Sometimes answers an easier question than the one asked
Continuously monitors your own behavior
Is mobilized to more effort on detecting an error about to be made
Normally has the last word

questions.explain: System 1 supplies automatic suggestions and has biases; System 2 monitors behavior, keeps you polite when angry, steps in when errors loom, and normally has the last word.

questions.q: Describe the normal division of labor between System 1 and System 2 in Kahneman's plot synopsis.
questions.a: Both systems are active whenever we are awake: System 1 runs automatically while System 2 is normally in a comfortable low-effort mode using only a fraction of its capacity. System 1 continuously supplies impressions, intuitions, intentions, and feelings, and when all goes smoothly System 2 adopts them with little or no modification. When System 1 runs into difficulty, it calls on System 2 for more detailed and specific processing.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman call the division of labor between the two systems highly efficient, and what are its weak points?
questions.a: It minimizes effort and optimizes performance, and it works well most of the time because System 1 is generally very good at what it does: its models of familiar situations and short-term predictions are accurate, and its first reactions are swift and appropriate. But System 1 has biases, systematic errors in specified circumstances: it sometimes answers easier questions than the one asked, has little understanding of logic and statistics, and cannot be turned off.

questions.q: In the Figure 2 exercise, why was saying "upper" or "lower" for the words in the second column a strain?
options: The words were printed too small to read quickly
System 2 was not engaged by the task at all
The task required no attention, so people grew careless
The column contained the very words you had set yourself to say, and you could not ignore them
questions.explain: To prepare, you programmed memory so that the relevant words were on the tip of your tongue; the second column contained those words, so an automatic response competed with your intended one and slowed you down.

questions.q: Lena, on a diet, walks past a plate of fresh cookies and has to work hard not to take one. In Kahneman's terms, what is happening?
options: System 2 is overcoming an impulse of System 1, exercising self-control
System 1 is overruling System 2's plan
She is experiencing a visual illusion like the Müller-Lyer lines
System 2 is generating an impulse that System 1 suppresses
questions.explain: Kahneman describes the common conflict between an automatic reaction and an intention to control it, and says one of System 2's tasks is to overcome the impulses of System 1: System 2 is in charge of self-control.

questions.q: Kahneman concludes that one of the tasks of System 2 is to overcome the impulses of System 1; in other words, System 2 is in charge of ____.
questions.explain: After examples like not staring at an oddly dressed couple and not telling someone to go to hell, Kahneman concludes that System 2 is in charge of self-control.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give as everyday examples of conflict between an automatic reaction and an intention to control it?
options: Trying not to stare at an oddly dressed couple in a restaurant
Forcing attention on a boring book
Not telling someone to go to hell
Reading words on a large billboard
Completing the phrase bread and ...
questions.explain: Each of the three conflict examples pits an intention against an automatic pull. Reading billboards and completing a familiar phrase are plain System 1 activities with no struggle involved.

questions.q: Match each everyday conflict Kahneman mentions to the automatic pull being resisted.
pairs: A car skidding on winter ice
The natural urge to touch the brakes
An oddly dressed couple at the next table
The urge to stare at them
A boring book
The mind drifting until the reading loses its meaning
Someone who has provoked you
The impulse to tell them to go to hell
questions.explain: In each case a well-meant intention must overcome an automatic reaction; for the skid, the rehearsed instruction is to steer into it and not touch the brakes, which negates what drivers would naturally do.

questions.q: In the Figure 2 exercise, sort each column by whether Kahneman says it was easy or hard.

items.t: Saying upper or lower case: left-hand column
Saying upper or lower case: right-hand column
Naming the position of words: left-hand column
Naming the position of words: right-hand column

questions.explain: Identifying case, the left column was easy and the right made you stumble; naming position, the left column was difficult and the right much easier. Each hard column contained the very words you were set to say.

questions.q: What does the Figure 2 exercise show about the relationship between the two systems?
