questions.a: The tasks engage System 2, because saying upper/lower or left/right is not what you routinely do with a column of words, so you set yourself by putting the relevant words on the tip of your tongue. When a column contained those very words, you could not ignore them, and overcoming the competing response was a strain that slowed you down. You experienced a conflict between a task you intended to carry out and an automatic response that interfered with it.

questions.q: After measuring the Müller-Lyer lines and learning they are equal, what does Kahneman say you will experience?
options: You will now see the two lines as equal in length
You will still see the bottom line as longer, though you know the lines are equal
You will doubt the ruler and believe the bottom line is longer
You will no longer see the fins attached to the lines
questions.explain: Your System 2 has a new belief, but you cannot prevent System 1 from doing its thing: “you cannot decide to see the lines as equal, although you know they are.”

questions.q: A hiring manager meets a candidate who explains that every previous boss misunderstood him, and she instantly feels she is the one who truly gets him. What would Kahneman's psychotherapy teacher's lesson suggest?
options: Trust the feeling, since strong rapport is a reliable sign of a good fit
Become generally suspicious of all feelings about candidates
Try to stop feeling sympathy, since feelings can be controlled with effort
Treat the strong attraction after a history of repeated failures as a danger sign and not act on it
questions.explain: The teacher did not teach students how to feel or to distrust all their feelings; he taught them to recognize a specific pattern, strong attraction to someone with a repeated history of failed relationships with helpers, as a danger sign, like the fins on the lines.

questions.q: Since cognitive illusions are hard to prevent, what compromise does Kahneman recommend?
options: Learn to recognize situations in which mistakes are likely and try harder to avoid significant mistakes when the stakes are high
Question every thought continuously so no bias slips through
Let System 2 replace System 1 for routine decisions
Accept all intuitions, since System 1 is usually right
questions.explain: Continuous vigilance is impractical and System 2 is too slow to substitute for System 1 in routine decisions, so the best we can do is recognize risky situations and try harder when the stakes are high.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman states that the premise of the book is that it is easier to recognize other people's mistakes than our own.
questions.explain: He ends the discussion of cognitive illusions with this premise, which explains why the book aims to improve how we identify and talk about errors.

questions.q: Kahneman says that not all illusions are visual: there are illusions of thought, which he calls ____ illusions.
questions.explain: The psychotherapy story is his example of a cognitive illusion: the strong sympathy for a certain kind of patient is an impression to be recognized and not believed.

questions.q: The famous figure of two horizontal lines with fins pointing in different directions, which look unequal but are identical in length, is called the ____ illusion.
questions.explain: Kahneman uses the Müller-Lyer illusion to show both the autonomy of System 1 and the difference between an impression and a belief.

questions.q: Put these stages of Kahneman's Müller-Lyer exercise in order.
items: You see the bottom line as obviously longer and believe what you see
You measure the lines with a ruler
Your System 2 holds a new belief that the lines are equal
You learn to mistrust impressions of lines with fins attached
questions.explain: Measuring gives System 2 a new belief, but the impression persists, so the only defense is to recognize the pattern and mistrust your impression of finned lines; even then you still see one line as longer.

questions.q: Sort these items from the Müller-Lyer and psychotherapy examples into impressions that arise from System 1 and beliefs or rules held by System 2.

items.t: The bottom line looks longer
Sympathy for the patient whom all clinicians have failed
The sense that you alone understand this patient
Knowing the lines are equal in length
Mistrusting lengths of lines with fins attached
Treating strong attraction to such a patient as a danger sign

questions.explain: In both cases System 1 produces an impression you cannot switch off, while System 2, the self you call I, can learn to recognize the pattern and refuse to believe or act on it.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what is the only thing you can do to resist the Müller-Lyer illusion, and what does it leave unchanged?
questions.a: You must learn to mistrust your impressions of the length of lines when fins are attached to them, which requires recognizing the illusory pattern and recalling what you know about it. If you can do that, you will never again be fooled by the illusion. But System 1 cannot be stopped from doing its thing, so you will still see one line as longer than the other.

questions.q: Explain how Kahneman's psychotherapy teacher's warning is analogous to the Müller-Lyer illusion.
questions.a: The teacher took for granted that sympathy for the patient would arise from System 1 and not be under the students' control, just as the longer-looking line cannot be unseen. He did not teach them how to feel or to be suspicious of all feelings; he taught them that strong attraction to a patient with a repeated history of failed treatment is a danger sign, like the fins on the lines. It is a cognitive illusion, and System 2 can learn to recognize it and decline to believe or act on it.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say cognitive illusions are hard to overcome, and why is constant vigilance not the solution?
questions.a: System 1 operates automatically and cannot be turned off at will, and System 2 may have no clue that an error is occurring; even with cues, errors are prevented only by enhanced monitoring and effortful System 2 activity. Yet constantly questioning our own thinking would be impossibly tedious, and System 2 is too slow and inefficient to substitute for System 1 in routine decisions. So the best compromise is to recognize situations where mistakes are likely and try harder when the stakes are high.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman prefer the names "System 1" and "System 2" to "automatic system" and "effortful system"?
options: The short names take less space in working memory, and anything occupying working memory reduces your ability to think
The descriptive names would wrongly suggest the systems are located in the brain
Stanovich and West required the numbered names
Numbered names make clear that System 1 is less important
questions.explain: “Automatic system” takes longer to say and so takes more space in working memory, which matters because anything that occupies working memory reduces your ability to think.

questions.q: Kahneman's colleagues compare "System 2 calculates products" to "The butler steals the petty cash." How does he answer their objection?
options: He agrees the systems are little people in the head who really perform the work
He says the sentence is a description, not an explanation, meaningful only because of what you already know about System 2
He says the butler sentence is also not an explanation
He drops agent language and describes only brain regions
questions.explain: Kahneman says the brief active sentence is intended as a description, shorthand for facts such as mental arithmetic being voluntary, effortful, and linked to dilated pupils, not as an explanation of how products are calculated.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that each of the two systems has its home in one specific part of the brain.
questions.explain: He insists they are fictitious characters, not systems in the standard sense of entities with interacting parts, and that there is no one part of the brain either system would call home.

questions.q: Kahneman tells readers to treat "System 1" and "System 2" as ____, like Bob and Joe, identifying characters they will get to know.
questions.explain: The names are shorthand labels for characters, not technical descriptions of real systems, chosen to make the ideas easier to think about.

questions.q: Kahneman says the short name "System 1" is better than "automatic system" because anything that occupies your ____ reduces your ability to think.
questions.explain: A longer label takes more space in working memory, and anything that occupies working memory reduces your ability to think.

questions.q: Which of these reasons does Kahneman give for describing the two systems as agents?
options: A sentence is understood more easily when it describes what an agent does
The mind, especially System 1, has a special aptitude for stories about active agents
Short names take less space in working memory
The two systems correspond to distinct regions of the brain
Agent language is the accepted standard in his professional circles
questions.explain: Kahneman points to quirks of our minds: agent sentences are easier to understand, stories about agents are easy to build and remember, and short names save working memory. He denies the systems have homes in the brain and admits agent language is considered a sin among his colleagues.

questions.q: Match each shorthand sentence about the systems to what Kahneman says it means.
pairs: System 2 calculates products
Mental arithmetic is voluntary, effortful, and linked to dilated pupils
Highway driving under routine conditions is left to System 1
Steering around a bend is automatic, so one can drive and converse
System 2 prevented James from reacting foolishly to the insult
James would have been more aggressive had his effortful control been disrupted
questions.explain: Each sentence with a system as its subject is shorthand for facts about effort, automaticity, and control; for James, Kahneman's example of disrupted control is being drunk.

questions.q: Sort these statements by whether they describe what Kahneman says System 1 and System 2 are, or what he says they are not.

items.t: Fictitious characters
Nicknames, like Bob and Joe
Agents with personalities, abilities, and limitations
Systems in the standard sense of entities with interacting parts
Residents of one particular part of the brain
Explanations of how products are calculated

questions.explain: Kahneman calls the systems useful fictions and descriptive shorthand; he denies that they are real systems with interacting parts, located in a brain region, or explanations in themselves.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman introduce fictitious characters with ugly names into a serious book, even though such language is considered a sin among his colleagues?
questions.a: The characters are useful because of quirks of our minds: a sentence is understood more easily if it describes what an agent does than what something is, so System 2 is a better subject than mental arithmetic. The mind, especially System 1, has a special aptitude for constructing and interpreting stories about active agents with personalities, habits, and abilities, which we readily remember, like the thieving butler. The fictions make it easier for him to think about judgment and choice and for readers to understand.

questions.q: Match each of Kahneman's sample sentences about the two systems to the idea it expresses.
pairs: He had an impression, but some of his impressions are illusions.
Impressions from System 1 can be cognitive illusions
This was a pure System 1 response. She reacted to the threat before she recognized it.
An automatic reaction came before conscious recognition
This is your System 1 talking. Slow down and let your System 2 take control.
A call to engage deliberate, effortful thinking
questions.explain: The closing sentences show how the vocabulary of the two systems can be used in everyday talk to name illusions, automatic responses, and the need for System 2 to take over.

questions.q: What does the title of Chapter 1 of Thinking, Fast and Slow, "The Characters of the Story," signal?
options: That the chapter tells the life stories of famous psychologists
That the book is a novel with fictional human characters
That System 1 and System 2 are introduced as the two agents of a psychodrama the book will follow
That the chapter is about how people judge others' character
questions.explain: Kahneman says the book can be read as a psychodrama with two characters, System 1 and System 2, and invites readers to think of them as agents; the chapter introduces them before the story unfolds.

questions.q: In Chapter 1 of Thinking, Fast and Slow, Kahneman notes that System 1 sometimes answers easier questions than the one it was asked. Which later chapter title in Part I takes up this idea?
options: Attention and Effort
The Lazy Controller
Cognitive Ease
Answering an Easier Question
questions.explain: The remark comes with the phrase “As we shall see,” pointing ahead; Chapter 9, the last chapter of Part I, is titled Answering an Easier Question.

questions.q: True or false: In the book's table of contents, Chapter 1 opens Part I, "Two Systems," which is followed by Part II, "Heuristics and Biases."
questions.explain: Part I, Two Systems, runs from Chapter 1 to Chapter 9, and Part II, Heuristics and Biases, begins with Chapter 10, The Law of Small Numbers.

questions.q: The title of Chapter 1 of Thinking, Fast and Slow presents System 1 and System 2 as the ____ of the story.
questions.explain: The chapter is titled The Characters of the Story because it introduces the two systems as characters, agents with their own abilities, limitations, and functions.

questions.q: Put these opening chapters of Part I of Thinking, Fast and Slow in order.
items: The Characters of the Story
Attention and Effort
The Lazy Controller
The Associative Machine
Cognitive Ease
questions.explain: Part I begins by introducing the two systems, then develops attention and effort, System 2 as a lazy controller, the associative workings of System 1, and cognitive ease.

questions.q: Put the sections of Chapter 1 of Thinking, Fast and Slow in the order they appear.
items: Two Systems
Plot Synopsis
Conflict
Illusions
Useful Fictions
questions.explain: The chapter defines the systems, sketches how they interact, shows them in conflict, uses illusions to separate impression from belief, and finally explains why the systems are presented as fictional agents.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman open Part I of Thinking, Fast and Slow with a chapter introducing System 1 and System 2 as characters?
questions.a: The interaction of the two systems is a recurrent theme of the whole book, so the reader first needs to meet its two characters and a brief synopsis of the plot. Introducing them as agents with abilities and limitations makes later chapters easier to follow, since the mind readily understands stories about agents. The chapter also previews later themes, such as attention and effort in the next chapter and System 1's habit of answering easier questions.

questions.q: In Kahneman's imagined film of Thinking, Fast and Slow, how is System 2 cast?
options: As a supporting character who believes herself to be the hero
As the hero who drives every scene of the story
As a villain who keeps sabotaging System 1's plans
As a narrator who comments but never takes action
questions.explain: Kahneman says System 2 would be “a supporting character who believes herself to be the hero.” The real figure at the center of the story is System 1, which often guides the thoughts System 2 believes it chose.

questions.q: According to the opening of the chapter on attention and effort, what is the defining feature of System 2?
options: It works faster than System 1 on familiar problems
It operates without any awareness or sense of control
Its operations are effortful
It is driven mainly by emotion and impulse
questions.explain: Kahneman states that the defining feature of System 2 is that its operations are effortful. Speed and automatic, unaware operation are features he assigns to System 1.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says one of System 2's main characteristics is laziness, a reluctance to invest more effort than is strictly necessary.
questions.explain: This is how he characterizes System 2 at the start of the chapter. Because of this laziness, the thoughts and actions System 2 believes it chose are often guided by System 1.

questions.q: Kahneman says one of the main characteristics of System 2 is ____, a reluctance to invest more effort than is strictly necessary.
questions.explain: Laziness is named as a main characteristic of System 2 in the chapter's opening. The idea returns at the end of the chapter with the law of least effort.

questions.q: Why, in Kahneman's account, are the thoughts System 2 believes it has chosen often guided by System 1, and what tasks still need System 2?
questions.a: System 2's operations are effortful and it is lazy, reluctant to invest more effort than strictly necessary, so it often goes along with what System 1, the figure at the center of the story, suggests. Yet some vital tasks can only be done by System 2, because they require effort and acts of self-control in which the intuitions and impulses of System 1 are overcome.

questions.q: Put the steps of Kahneman's Add-1 exercise in the order he gives them.
items: Start beating a steady rhythm, about one beat per second
Remove the blank card and read the four digits aloud
Wait for two beats
Report a string with each digit increased by 1, keeping the rhythm
questions.explain: He has you set a rhythm, uncover and read the digits, wait two beats, then report the transformed string. With 5294 on the card, the right response is 6305.

questions.q: In the exercise where you add 1 to each of four digits while keeping time with a metronome, the task is called ____.
questions.explain: Kahneman calls it Add-1 and offers Add-3 as a harder version. He says it should bring you to the limits of your cognitive abilities within 5 seconds.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says few people can cope with more than six digits in the Add-1 task.
questions.explain: He says few people can cope with more than four digits in Add-1. Those wanting a harder challenge are invited to try Add-3.

questions.q: In the Scientific American article that inspired Kahneman's pupil research, how did Eckhard Hess describe the pupil of the eye?
options: As a gauge of hunger and thirst
As a mirror of long-term memory
As a reliable sign of fear
As a window to the soul
questions.explain: Hess described the pupil as a window to the soul. Kahneman and Beatty later teased their participants with the same phrase when they could tell from the pupil that someone had stopped working.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say appeared in Eckhard Hess's article on the pupil?
options: Hess's wife noticing his pupils widen as he watched beautiful nature pictures
Two pictures of the same woman, more attractive when her pupils were dilated
Bazaar shoppers wearing dark glasses to hide their interest from merchants
A finding that pupils constrict when people multiply two-digit numbers
A study showing that hypnosis enlarges the pupils
questions.explain: The article opened with Hess's wife's observation, ended with the two pictures of the woman, and mentioned belladonna and bazaar shoppers. Pupils dilate, not constrict, during multiplication, and Kahneman notes that Hess's work had little to do with hypnosis.

questions.q: What did Hess observe about how the pupil's response to mental effort relates to emotional arousal?
options: It is simply a weaker form of emotional arousal
It is distinct from emotional arousal
It only appears when people are emotionally aroused
It is identical to the response to emotional arousal
questions.explain: Hess found that pupils dilate when people multiply two-digit numbers, more for hard problems, and that this response to mental effort is distinct from emotional arousal. That is why the pupil promised a visible indicator of effort itself.

questions.q: Kahneman's research partner at the University of Michigan, the graduate student ____, later became the leading authority on cognitive pupillometry.
questions.explain: Jackson Beatty shared Kahneman's enthusiasm for Hess's idea, and the two worked together for a year. Kahneman says their collaboration had a large effect on both of their careers.

questions.q: In Kahneman and Beatty's paced digit tasks, what shape did the pupil's response take over the course of a trial?
options: A steady climb that never came down
A flat line with a sudden spike at the end
An inverted V
A U shape, dipping in the middle
questions.explain: Effort built up with every digit heard, peaked as the transformed string was produced, and relaxed as short-term memory was unloaded. The pupil tracked this as an inverted V.

questions.q: Put the phases of effort during an Add-1 or Add-3 trial in the order Kahneman describes them.
items: Effort builds with every added digit you hear
Effort peaks as you rush to produce the transformed string
Effort relaxes gradually as you unload short-term memory
questions.explain: This is the inverted V that the pupil traced. The peak comes during and immediately after the pause, when the transformed string must be produced.

questions.q: Which of these did Kahneman and Beatty's pupil data show in paced digit tasks?
options: Longer strings of digits reliably caused larger dilations
The transformation task added to the effort
The peak of pupil size coincided with maximum effort
Pupil size stayed constant once the task began
Dilation depended mainly on the emotional content of the digits
questions.explain: Kahneman says the pupil data corresponded precisely to subjective experience: longer strings, transformation, and peak effort all showed up in pupil size. The pupil changed second by second, so it did not stay constant.

questions.q: True or false: In Kahneman and Beatty's studies, Add-1 with four digits caused a larger pupil dilation than holding seven digits for immediate recall.
questions.explain: Transforming even four digits was more demanding than simply holding seven. This is one of the findings showing that the transformation compounds the effort.

questions.q: Which task does Kahneman call the most demanding he ever observed in his pupil studies?
options: Add-3
Holding seven digits for immediate recall
Discriminating the pitch of two tones
Inhibiting the reading of distracting words
questions.explain: Add-3 is the most demanding task he observed; people give up if more is asked of them. The other tasks produced smaller dilations.

questions.q: True or false: In the first 5 seconds of Add-3, the pupil dilates by about 50% of its original area and heart rate falls by about 7 beats per minute.
questions.explain: Heart rate increases, not falls, by about 7 beats per minute along with the 50% dilation. Kahneman says this is as hard as people can work.

questions.q: What happened to participants' pupils when Kahneman and Beatty exposed them to more digits than they could remember?
options: Their pupils kept dilating until the trial ended
Their pupils stopped dilating or actually shrank
Their pupils swung rapidly between large and small
Their pupils dilated twice as fast as before
questions.explain: When the load exceeded what they could handle, participants effectively gave up and their pupils stopped dilating or shrank. Likewise, during mental multiplication the pupil contracted immediately when a person found a solution or gave up.

questions.q: Sort these details by whether they come from Hess's Scientific American article or from Kahneman and Beatty's own laboratory.

items.t: Two photos of the same woman, one with dilated pupils
Belladonna used as a cosmetic
Bazaar shoppers in dark glasses
An infrared flash every second triggered by a metronome
A pupil image about a foot wide projected in the corridor
Asking a participant why she stopped working just now

questions.explain: Hess's article supplied the attractive-woman pictures, belladonna and the bazaar shoppers. The camera setup, the projected pupil in the basement corridor and the playful questions came from Kahneman and Beatty's work.

questions.q: What did Kahneman realize when he watched a woman's pupil while she chatted with the experimenter between tasks?
options: That conversation demands more effort than digit tasks
That the pupil cannot be measured during speech
That the tasks he had chosen to study were exceptionally effortful
That talking makes people miss visual targets
questions.explain: Her pupil stayed small during mundane conversation, which demanded no more effort than holding two or three digits. This eureka moment showed him that Add-1 and similar tasks were unusually effortful.

questions.q: Kahneman pictures the pace of mental life as a kind of movement. Put these paces in order from least to most effortful.
items: A comfortable walk
Episodes of jogging
A frantic sprint
questions.explain: Mental life is normally conducted at a comfortable walk, sometimes interrupted by jogging and rarely by a frantic sprint. Add-1 and Add-3 are sprints, while casual chatting is a stroll.

questions.q: Describe the casual observation Kahneman calls a eureka moment in his pupil research, and what it taught him about mental life.
questions.a: While idly watching a woman's pupil during a break, he saw it stay small as she talked and listened in routine conversation, which demanded no more effort than retaining two or three digits. He realized the tasks he had chosen to study were exceptionally effortful. Mental life, the life of System 2, is normally conducted at the pace of a comfortable walk, with occasional jogging and rare sprints like Add-1 and Add-3.

questions.q: In Kahneman and Beatty's version of the gorilla experiment, when were participants most likely to miss the letter K?
options: At the very beginning of the Add-1 task
Near the end of the Add-1 task
When the letter appeared during a pause in the digits
When mental effort was at its peak
questions.explain: Observers almost never missed a K at the beginning or near the end, but missed it almost half the time at peak effort, even with their eyes staring straight at it. Detection failures followed the same inverted V as the pupil.

questions.q: In Kahneman and Beatty's letter-detection version of the gorilla experiment, sort these situations by how the letter K fared.

items.t: K shown at the beginning of the Add-1 task
K shown near the end of the Add-1 task
K shown when the transformation task was less demanding
K shown when mental effort was at its peak
K shown at a time of high demand from the digit task

questions.explain: Participants gave the digit task priority, so a K presented at a time of high demand was simply not seen. Detection was better when the transformation was less demanding.

questions.q: Why did the letter-detection results reassure Kahneman and Beatty that the pupil was a good measure to use?
questions.a: Failures to detect the letter K followed the same inverted-V pattern as the dilating pupil: almost no misses at the start and end of Add-1, but misses almost half the time at peak effort. This similarity showed that the pupil was a good measure of the physical arousal that accompanies mental effort, so they could use it to understand how the mind works.

questions.q: Kahneman compares the pupils to the ____ outside your house, since they index the current rate at which mental energy is used.
questions.explain: Like the electricity meter, the pupils show how fast energy is being used right now. Kahneman says the analogy goes deep: devices draw the energy they need but no more.

questions.q: In Kahneman's example of holding the digits 9462 in memory for 10 seconds when your life depends on it, what point is he making?
options: Strong motivation lets you exert any amount of effort you choose
We decide what to do but have limited control over the effort it takes
Memory for digits fails completely under extreme pressure
Fear of death narrows attention and blocks memory
questions.explain: However much you want to live, you cannot put as much effort into simply holding four digits as an Add-3 transformation would demand. As with an appliance drawing current, the task sets the effort.

questions.q: Explain how Kahneman's comparison between System 2 and the electrical circuits in a home both fits and breaks down.
questions.a: Both have limited capacity, and like an appliance that draws the energy it needs but no more, a mental task sets the effort it takes: we decide what to do but have limited control over the effort. They differ under overload. A breaker trips and all devices on the circuit lose power at once, whereas System 2's response is selective and precise: it protects the most important activity and allocates “spare capacity” second by second to other tasks.

questions.q: Kahneman contrasts how a home's electrical circuit and System 2 respond to threatened overload. Sort these responses.

items.t: A breaker trips when demand is excessive
All devices on the circuit lose power at once
The most important activity is protected
Spare capacity is allocated second by second to other tasks

questions.explain: The circuit's response to overload is all-or-nothing. System 2's response is selective and precise, giving the priority task the attention it needs.

questions.q: How did Kahneman and Beatty know that participants in their letter-detection study really gave priority to the digit task?
options: The timing of the visual letter had no effect on the digit task
Participants said so when interviewed afterwards
Participants detected every letter perfectly
Their heart rates stayed steady throughout the trial
questions.explain: Because the timing of the letter did not affect performance on the main task, the digit task was clearly protected. The cost fell on the letter, which went unseen at times of high demand.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, where does the sophisticated allocation of attention come from, and what happens to it in an emergency such as a car skidding on an oil slick?
questions.a: It has been honed by a long evolutionary history: orienting and responding quickly to the gravest threats or most promising opportunities improved the chance of survival, and the capability is not restricted to humans. In emergencies System 1 takes over and assigns total priority to self-protective actions, so a driver skidding on an oil slick responds to the threat before becoming fully conscious of it.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that when your car skids on an oil slick, System 1 takes over, but only after you have become fully conscious of the threat.
questions.explain: He says you will find you responded to the threat before you became fully conscious of it. System 1 assigns total priority to self-protective actions.

questions.q: Match each person or group to what Kahneman credits them with in the chapter on attention and effort.
pairs: Eckhard Hess
Described the pupil as a window to the soul
Jackson Beatty
Became the leading authority on cognitive pupillometry
Daniel Kahneman
Wrote a book titled Attention and Effort
Authors of The Invisible Gorilla
Kept observers so busy counting passes that a gorilla went unseen
questions.explain: Hess's article sparked the research; Beatty and Kahneman worked together for a year and went in different directions afterwards. The gorilla study is the dramatic case of blindness that the Add-1 letter study echoed.

questions.q: Put these steps in Kahneman's early career in the order he describes them.
items: Visiting a hypnosis laboratory at the University of Michigan
Finding Eckhard Hess's article on the pupil
Measuring pupils with Jackson Beatty
Doing follow-up research at Harvard
Writing the book Attention and Effort
questions.explain: The Hess article came while he was casting about for a topic at Michigan, which led to the year with Beatty. His book drew on that work and on follow-up research at Harvard the following year.

questions.q: A general ____ says that if there are several ways of achieving the same goal, people will eventually gravitate to the least demanding course of action.
questions.explain: Kahneman says this law applies to cognitive as well as physical exertion. In the economy of action, effort is a cost.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman reports that highly intelligent individuals need more effort to solve the same problems, as shown by pupil size and brain activity.
questions.explain: Highly intelligent individuals need less effort for the same problems. Talent, like skill, reduces a task's demand for energy.

questions.q: Mara has two equally reliable ways to reconcile her bank account each month: a quick app summary or a detailed spreadsheet she must think through. Over time she settles on the app. Which idea from Kahneman's chapter on attention and effort best explains this?
options: The inverted-V pattern of mental effort
The adoption of task sets by System 2
The law of least effort
The selective protection of the most important activity
questions.explain: When several ways reach the same goal, people eventually gravitate to the least demanding one. Task sets and selective protection concern how System 2 directs attention, not which route people choose.

questions.q: What does Kahneman mean by the law of least effort, and how do skill and talent affect the effort a task demands?
questions.a: The law of least effort says that if there are several ways of achieving the same goal, people will eventually gravitate to the least demanding course of action; effort is a cost in the economy of action. As skill increases, a task's demand for energy diminishes and fewer brain regions are involved, and highly intelligent individuals need less effort for the same problems. “Laziness is built deep into our nature.”

questions.q: Match each finding about the brain and effort to what Kahneman says about it.
pairs: Becoming skilled at a task
Fewer brain regions are involved and energy demand falls
High intelligence
Smaller pupil dilation and brain activity on the same problems
The prefrontal area
More developed in humans than in other primates; tied to intelligence
An executive region other than the prefrontal area
Involved whenever a conflict must be resolved
questions.explain: Skill and talent both reduce effort. The executive function relies on brain regions including one engaged by conflict and the prefrontal area.

questions.q: Which of these tasks did Kahneman find produced only minuscule pupil effects, about 5% of the increase seen with Add-3?
options: Holding one or two digits in memory
Learning to associate a word with a digit, such as 3 = door
Discriminating between the pitch of two tones
Holding six or seven digits in short-term memory
Mental multiplication of two-digit numbers
questions.explain: Holding one or two digits and learning a word-digit pairing had reliable but tiny effects. Tone discrimination produced significantly larger dilations, six or seven digits were more effortful still, and two-digit multiplication is near the limit of what most people can do.

questions.q: Put these tasks from Kahneman's pupil studies in order from least to most effortful, as he lists them.
items: Holding one or two digits in memory
Discriminating between the pitch of two tones
Holding six or seven digits in short-term memory
Doing the Add-3 task
questions.explain: One or two digits produced only 5% of the Add-3 increase; tone discrimination gave significantly larger dilations; six or seven digits were more effortful; Add-3 is near the limit of what most people can do.

questions.q: Sort these activities by how much mental effort Kahneman's chapter on attention and effort says they demand.

items.t: Add-3
Mental multiplication of two-digit numbers
Storing six digits for immediate recall
Routine conversation with an experimenter
Holding one or two digits in memory
Learning that 3 = door

questions.explain: Add-3 and two-digit multiplication are near the limit of capacity, and six digits for immediate recall is more demanding than most daily tasks. Casual chatting and holding a digit or two barely move the pupil.

questions.q: Which of these everyday acts would Kahneman expect to require a significant mental effort, enough to dilate the pupils?
options: Retrieving and saying aloud your phone number
Mentally multiplying 23 by 47
Chatting casually with a colleague
Holding a single digit in memory
questions.explain: Saying your phone number aloud takes a brief but significant effort because the whole string must be held while the response is organized, and two-digit multiplication is near most people's limit. Casual chat and a single digit demand very little.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say only System 2 can do?
options: Follow rules
Compare objects on several attributes
Make deliberate choices between options
Detect simple relations such as that things are all alike
Integrate information about one thing
questions.explain: Following rules, comparing on several attributes and deliberate choice belong to System 2 alone. Detecting simple relations and integrating information about one thing are things System 1 does well.

questions.q: Sort these capabilities by whether Kahneman assigns them to System 1 or System 2.

items.t: Detecting that the son is much taller than the father
Integrating information about one thing
Noticing that a meek, tidy person resembles a caricature librarian
Taking over in emergencies with self-protective actions
Following rules
Comparing objects on several attributes
Combining the librarian impression with how few librarians there are
Adopting a task set that overrides habitual responses

questions.explain: System 1 detects simple relations, integrates information about one thing and acts first in emergencies. Only System 2 follows rules, makes multi-attribute comparisons, uses statistical information like the small number of librarians, and adopts task sets.

questions.q: Using Kahneman's librarian example, explain what System 1 can and cannot do with a description of a person.
questions.a: System 1 will detect that a person described as meek and tidy, with a need for order and a passion for detail, resembles a caricature librarian, since it excels at integrating information about one thing. But it does not deal with several distinct topics at once and is not adept at purely statistical information. Combining the intuition with knowledge about the small number of librarians is a task only System 2 can perform, and only if it knows how, which is true of few people.

questions.q: Kahneman says a crucial capability of System 2 is the adoption of ____, programming memory to obey an instruction that overrides habitual responses.
questions.explain: Counting every letter f on a page is his example: a new task System 2 can take on with effort. Setting up for it and carrying it out are both effortful.

questions.q: Psychologists speak of ____ to describe the adoption and termination of task sets.
questions.explain: Neuroscientists have identified the main brain regions serving the executive function, including the prefrontal area. Adopting and dropping task sets is what this control does.

questions.q: After counting every letter f on a page, why is counting all the commas on the next page harder, according to Kahneman?
options: Commas are harder to see than letters
You must overcome the newly acquired tendency to focus on f
System 1 has already counted the commas automatically
Counting is easier the first time it is done
questions.explain: Switching from one task to another is effortful, especially under time pressure, because the new task set must override the one just adopted. This is one of the significant discoveries of cognitive psychology he cites.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give as reasons that Add-3 and mental multiplication are so difficult?
options: The need for rapid switching between operations
Time pressure, as memory decay forces the pace
Strong emotional arousal caused by the digits
The digits being presented in an unfamiliar script
Boredom that makes attention drift
questions.explain: Holding digits in different stages of transformation demands rapid switching, and the rate of decay in memory, like a juggler's balls, forces you to hurry. Emotional arousal is a separate response from effort, and boredom is not part of his account.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say Add-3 demands rapid switching, and what do tests built on this kind of switching predict?
questions.a: To perform Add-3 you must hold several digits in working memory at once, each tied to a different operation: some waiting to be transformed, one being transformed, and others already transformed and held for reporting. Modern working-memory tests require repeated switching between two demanding tasks, and people who do well on them tend to do well on tests of general intelligence. Efficiency in controlling attention also predicts the performance of air traffic controllers and Israeli Air Force pilots beyond intelligence.

questions.q: What does Kahneman say measures of efficiency in controlling attention predict, beyond the effects of intelligence?
options: Scores on tests of vocabulary and reading
Success at chess and other strategy games
Recovery from fatigue after demanding work
Performance of air traffic controllers and Israeli Air Force pilots
questions.explain: He uses these jobs to show that the ability to control attention is not simply a measure of intelligence. It predicts performance there over and above intelligence.

questions.q: Kahneman concludes that the most effortful forms of slow thinking are those that require you to think ____.
questions.explain: Time pressure is a driver of effort: memory decay forces the pace, like a juggler who cannot slow down. “The most effortful forms of slow thinking are those that require you to think fast.”

questions.q: Match each image Kahneman uses in his chapter on attention and effort to the point it makes.
pairs: Electricity meter
Pupils index the current rate at which mental energy is used
Circuit breaker
A contrast: System 2 responds to overload selectively, not all at once
Juggler with balls in the air
Memory decay forces you to keep the pace up
Walk, jog and sprint
Most mental life is easy; Add-3 is a rare all-out effort
questions.explain: Each analogy captures one feature of effort: its measurable rate, its selective allocation, the time pressure of holding ideas, and how unusual peak effort is.

questions.q: Why does time pressure make a task like Add-3 so effortful, in Kahneman's account?
questions.a: The rush comes partly from the metronome and partly from the load on memory: like a juggler with several balls in the air, you cannot slow down because material decays in memory, so you must refresh and rehearse it before it is lost. Any task that requires keeping several ideas in mind at once has this hurried character, and unless you have a capacious working memory you must work uncomfortably hard. So the most effortful forms of slow thinking are those that require you to think fast.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say people normally do to avoid mental overload?
options: Divide tasks into multiple easy steps
Commit intermediate results to long-term memory or paper
Hold every intermediate result in working memory
Work faster so material does not decay
Switch rapidly between several tasks
questions.explain: We avoid overload by breaking tasks into easy steps and storing intermediate results outside an easily overloaded working memory. Holding everything in mind, rushing and rapid switching are what make tasks effortful.

questions.q: When planning a complicated trip budget, Dev writes each subtotal on a notepad instead of keeping the figures in his head. In Kahneman's terms, what is Dev doing?
options: Adopting a task set that overrides his habits
Letting System 1 take over to save time
Avoiding overload by committing intermediate results to paper
Increasing time pressure to sharpen his focus
questions.explain: Kahneman says we normally avoid mental overload by dividing tasks into easy steps and committing intermediate results to long-term memory or paper rather than to working memory. That is how we conduct mental life by the law of least effort.

questions.q: Why did Eckhard Hess's observations about the pupil strike Kahneman as a promising research topic?
questions.a: Hess had noticed that the pupils are sensitive indicators of mental effort: they dilate substantially when people multiply two-digit numbers, and more for hard problems than easy ones. His observations also indicated that this response is distinct from emotional arousal. Kahneman concluded that a visible indication of mental effort had promise, and with Jackson Beatty set out to measure it.

questions.q: Match each task from Kahneman and Beatty's pupil studies to the effect it had on the pupil.
pairs: Holding one or two digits
A minuscule dilation, about 5% of that for Add-3
Add-3
Dilation of about 50% of the pupil's area within 5 seconds
Routine conversation
The pupil stayed small and barely dilated
More digits than a person could remember
The pupil stopped dilating or actually shrank
questions.explain: These results show how closely pupil size tracked effort, from trivial loads to tasks so demanding that people gave up.

questions.q: Match each term from Kahneman's chapter on attention and effort to its meaning.
pairs: Task set
Programming memory to obey an instruction that overrides habitual responses
Executive control
The adoption and termination of task sets
Law of least effort
People gravitate to the least demanding way of reaching a goal
Spare capacity
Attention left over, allocated second by second to other tasks
questions.explain: Task sets and executive control describe how System 2 directs attention; the law of least effort describes its laziness; spare capacity is what remains once the priority task is protected.

questions.q: In one of Kahneman's sample remarks, a speaker refuses to solve a problem while driving because it is a ____ task that requires mental effort.
questions.explain: The remark draws on the chapter's finding that pupils dilate in proportion to mental effort. Effortful tasks compete with driving for limited attention.

questions.q: Match each of Kahneman's sample remarks about attention and effort to the idea it applies.
pairs: Refusing to solve a problem while driving
Hard thinking is effortful and competes for limited attention
He will think as little as possible
The law of least effort
She did not forget the meeting; she just didn't hear you
Intense focus can make people effectively blind to other input
A quick idea came from System 1, so I'll search memory deliberately
Switching from intuition to effortful System 2 search
questions.explain: Each remark puts one of the chapter's ideas into everyday words: effort as a limited resource, laziness, attention blindness, and the shift from System 1 to System 2.

questions.q: Kahneman's sample remark says a colleague did not forget a meeting but simply didn't hear about it. Which idea from the chapter does this apply?
options: Fast intuitions come from System 1
Effort fades as a task becomes skilled
Memory decays quickly under time pressure
People intensely focused elsewhere can be effectively blind
questions.explain: She was completely focused on something else when the meeting was set, so the information never got in. This mirrors the participants who missed the letter K during peak effort.

questions.q: A friend misses that their train platform was changed because they were absorbed in a hard work problem on their laptop. Explain this using Kahneman's chapter on attention and effort.
questions.a: When engaged in a mental sprint, people may become effectively blind to other input, as in the Invisible Gorilla study and Kahneman and Beatty's letter-K study, where targets were missed almost half the time at peak effort. System 2 protects the most important activity and allocates only spare capacity to other things, so the announcement went unnoticed rather than forgotten, just like the sample remark about the colleague who did not hear about the meeting.

questions.q: Chapter 2 ends with the law of least effort and System 2's laziness. How does this prepare the next chapter, The Lazy Controller?
options: It sets up a closer look at System 2 as an effortful controller that is reluctant to work
It replaces the two systems with a new model of the self
It begins the heuristics and biases of Part II
It moves on to the choices studied by prospect theory
questions.explain: Chapter 2 establishes effort as System 2's defining feature and laziness as its main trait, which the next chapter's title, The Lazy Controller, takes up directly. Heuristics and biases begin only in Part II, and choices come in Part IV.

questions.q: True or false: Attention and Effort is the second chapter of Part I, Two Systems, coming between The Characters of the Story and The Lazy Controller.
questions.explain: The table of contents lists Part I as The Characters of the Story, Attention and Effort, The Lazy Controller, and so on. Chapter 2 builds on the characters introduced in Chapter 1.

questions.q: The chapter that follows Attention and Effort in Part I is titled The Lazy ____.
questions.explain: Chapter 3, The Lazy Controller, continues the portrait of System 2 whose laziness Chapter 2 introduces through the law of least effort.

questions.q: Put these chapters of Part I, Two Systems, in the order they appear in the book.
items: The Characters of the Story
Attention and Effort
The Lazy Controller
The Associative Machine
questions.explain: Part I first introduces the two systems, then examines System 2's effort and laziness, then turns to the associative workings of System 1.

questions.q: How does the chapter Attention and Effort build on Chapter 1 and set up Chapter 3, and what does its title signal?
questions.a: Chapter 1 introduced System 1 and System 2 as the characters of the story; Chapter 2 develops System 2's defining feature, that its operations are effortful, using Kahneman's pupil research. The title, which is also that of Kahneman's earlier book, signals that attention is a limited resource paid for with effort. Its closing law of least effort and System 2's laziness lead directly into Chapter 3, The Lazy Controller.

questions.q: In the opening of The Lazy Controller, what does Kahneman say happens to his thinking when he speeds up from his strolling pace of about 17 minutes a mile?
options: His ability to think coherently deteriorates sharply as attention goes to keeping up the pace
His thinking becomes sharper because the extra physical arousal spills over into alertness
His thinking is unaffected, since physical and mental effort draw on separate budgets
He can still build intricate arguments, but only if he is walking with a companion
questions.explain: Faster walking draws his attention to the walking itself and demands self-control to resist slowing down, so his train of thought breaks down. The mild arousal that may help alertness belongs to the comfortable stroll, not the fast pace.

questions.q: In Kahneman's walking example, what conclusion does he draw from the fact that he cannot think while walking at his fastest sustainable speed?
options: Physical exercise always blocks mental work
Fast walking uses up the brain's supply of oxygen
Self-control and deliberate thought share one limited budget of effort
System 1 takes over all thinking during physical exertion
questions.explain: At top speed he needs a mental effort of self-control to resist the urge to slow down, which leaves nothing for thinking: “Self-control and deliberate thought apparently draw on the same limited budget of effort.” He does not claim that all exercise blocks thought; he thinks well while strolling.

questions.q: According to the opening of The Lazy Controller, what does the state of flow show about mental effort?
options: That concentration on a task and the deliberate control of attention are two separable forms of effort
That truly effortful activities like racing and chess always require strong willpower
That System 2 switches off entirely whenever people enjoy what they are doing
That effort feels pleasant only when the task is easy and undemanding
questions.explain: Kahneman says flow neatly separates the two forms of effort: in flow, a very demanding activity absorbs attention without any exertion of self-control. Racing and chess are effortful, but in flow they need no willpower, which is why the idea that they always need willpower is wrong.

questions.q: Kahneman suggests a simple experiment: while strolling with a friend, ask him to compute 23 x 78 in his head immediately. What does he predict will happen?
options: The friend will speed up as his arousal rises
The friend will keep walking and answer slowly
The friend will give the intuitive wrong answer
The friend will almost certainly stop in his tracks
questions.explain: Walking and thinking normally coexist, but at the extremes they compete for the limited resources of System 2, so a heavy mental load makes the friend stop walking. The demand on short-term memory is too large to combine with walking.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that the best thinking of his life was done sitting still under time pressure, not on leisurely walks.
questions.explain: He says the reverse: he did the best thinking of his life on leisurely walks with Amos. He prefers sitting still only when he must construct an intricate argument under time pressure, because not all slow thinking requires intense concentration.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman suspects that people avoid frequent switching of tasks and speeded-up mental work when they can, and says this is how the law of least effort comes to be a law.
questions.explain: He suspects such work is not intrinsically pleasurable and that people avoid it when possible: “This is how the law of least effort comes to be a law.”

questions.q: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi named the state of effortless attending, in which people lose their sense of time, of themselves and of their problems, ____.
questions.explain: Csikszentmihalyi called this state flow, a name that has become part of the language. He also called it an optimal experience.

questions.q: Because people in flow describe its joy so compellingly, Csikszentmihalyi called it an ____.
questions.explain: Flow is described as effortless concentration so deep that people lose their sense of time, and its joy led Csikszentmihalyi to call it an optimal experience.

questions.q: Kahneman says that even without time pressure, maintaining a coherent train of thought requires discipline; he infers this from how often he checks e-mail or investigates the ____ during an hour of writing.
questions.explain: An observer counting his trips to e-mail and the refrigerator could infer an urge to escape, showing that keeping at writing takes more self-control than he can readily muster.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman, in the opening of The Lazy Controller, describe as normally taking little effort and no strain, just like a stroll?
options: Making many small decisions while driving a car
Absorbing some information while reading the newspaper
Computing 23 x 78 in one's head immediately
Routine exchanges of pleasantries with a spouse or colleague
Constructing an intricate argument under time pressure
questions.explain: Kahneman lists driving decisions, newspaper reading and routine pleasantries as System 2 at its natural, low-strain speed. Mental multiplication and building an intricate argument under time pressure impose a heavy load and are the opposite of a stroll.

questions.q: Put these walking speeds and their effects on Kahneman's thinking in order from slowest to fastest pace, as described in the opening of The Lazy Controller.
items: Sitting in a recliner: fewer calories burned than walking
About 17 minutes a mile: a stroll with no strain, thinking possible
Faster than the stroll: thinking deteriorates sharply
About 14 minutes a mile: he does not even try to think
questions.explain: Kahneman contrasts the recliner with his stroll, at which he can think and work, then describes how accelerating impairs his train of thought until, at his fastest sustainable pace, he gives up thinking altogether.

questions.q: Match each element of the opening of The Lazy Controller to what Kahneman uses it to show.
pairs: The 17-minute-a-mile stroll
System 2 has a natural speed that involves little strain
The 14-minute-a-mile pace
Self-control and deliberate thought share a limited budget
The friend asked to compute 23 x 78
Walking and heavy thinking compete at the extremes
Trips to e-mail and the refrigerator
A coherent train of thought requires discipline
Flow
Effort can be sustained without exerting willpower
questions.explain: Each image supports one step of the opening: System 2 has an easy natural pace, extreme demands compete for limited resources, sustained thinking requires self-control, and flow shows that this self-control is not always needed.

questions.q: Sort these activities, from the opening of The Lazy Controller, by whether Kahneman says they let him think freely or interfere with thinking.

items.t: Strolling at about 17 minutes a mile
Leisurely walks with Amos
Walking at about 14 minutes a mile
Accelerating beyond his strolling speed
Mental work that loads short-term memory while walking
Monitoring the environment in a non-wary situation

questions.explain: Low-demand activities like strolling and routine monitoring leave room for thought. Fast walking and heavy short-term memory loads compete for the limited resources of System 2.

questions.q: Sort these descriptions by whether they fit the state of flow or ordinary effortful work that needs willpower, as Kahneman describes them in The Lazy Controller.

items.t: Effortless concentration so deep one loses track of time
Absorption in a competitive chess game with no exertion of self-control
Resources freed to be directed to the task at hand
Keeping at writing despite urges to check e-mail
Resisting the urge to slow down on a fast walk
Maintaining a coherent train of thought by discipline

questions.explain: In flow, focused attention requires no self-control, so resources go to the task itself. The other activities require deliberate control of attention, the second form of effort that flow removes.

questions.q: In The Lazy Controller, how does Kahneman use his walks in the Berkeley hills to argue that self-control and deliberate thought draw on the same resource?
questions.a: At about 17 minutes a mile he strolls without strain and can think and work. When he accelerates, attention is drawn to walking and to maintaining the pace, and his train of thought falls apart; at about 14 minutes a mile he does not even try to think, because a mental effort of self-control is needed to resist slowing down. He concludes that “Self-control and deliberate thought apparently draw on the same limited budget of effort.”

questions.q: According to The Lazy Controller, what are the two forms of effort that flow separates, and why does flow free resources for the task?
questions.a: The two forms of effort are concentration on the task and the deliberate control of attention. Activities like riding a motorcycle very fast or playing competitive chess are very effortful, but in a state of flow, maintaining focused attention on them requires no exertion of self-control. Because no willpower is spent keeping attention in place, those resources can be directed to the task itself.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say, in the opening of The Lazy Controller, that maintaining a coherent train of thought requires self-control even when there is no time pressure?
questions.a: He suspects that task switching and speeded-up mental work are not intrinsically pleasurable, so people avoid them, which is how the law of least effort becomes a law. Even without time pressure, staying on a line of thought takes discipline. His own frequent checks of e-mail and the refrigerator during an hour of writing reveal an urge to escape, showing that keeping at it takes more self-control than he can readily muster.

questions.q: In the dessert study described in The Lazy Controller, people holding seven digits in memory are offered chocolate cake or fruit salad. What does the evidence suggest they do?
options: They choose the fruit salad more often, because effort makes them health-conscious
They become more likely to choose the tempting chocolate cake
They refuse both desserts so they can concentrate on the digits
They choose no differently from people who carry no memory load
questions.explain: When System 2 is busy, System 1 has more influence on behavior: “System 1 has more influence on behavior when System 2 is busy, and it has a sweet tooth.”

questions.q: According to The Lazy Controller, what is the straightforward conclusion Kahneman draws from findings that cognitive load, drink and sleeplessness all weaken self-control?
options: Self-control is a fixed personality trait unaffected by circumstances
Self-control is an automatic function of System 1
Only physical fatigue can reduce self-control
Self-control requires attention and effort, and is a task of System 2
questions.explain: Because anything that loads or tires System 2 loosens control of behavior, Kahneman concludes that self-control requires attention and effort; controlling thoughts and behaviors is one of the tasks System 2 performs, not a System 1 automatism.

questions.q: What did Roy Baumeister's experiments, as reported in The Lazy Controller, show about voluntary effort?
options: All variants of voluntary effort, cognitive, emotional or physical, draw at least partly on a shared pool of mental energy
Emotional effort and physical effort draw on completely separate pools of energy
Effort of will makes people more willing to exert self-control on the next challenge
Only simultaneous tasks, never successive ones, reduce self-control
questions.explain: Baumeister's group, using successive rather than simultaneous tasks, found that an effort of will is tiring and reduces self-control on the next challenge, showing a shared pool of mental energy. That is the opposite of the idea that effort strengthens later self-control.

questions.q: In The Lazy Controller, how does Kahneman distinguish ego depletion from cognitive load?
options: Ego depletion can be overcome only by glucose, while cognitive load can be overcome by incentives
Ego depletion affects only emotions, while cognitive load affects only reasoning
Ego depletion is at least in part a loss of motivation that a strong incentive can overcome, while extra effort cannot remove a memory load
Ego depletion and cognitive busyness are two names for the same mental state
questions.explain: After self-control, people do not feel like making an effort but could if they really had to, and strong incentives overcame depletion; in contrast, keeping six digits in memory is not something extra effort can fix. As the book says, “Ego depletion is not the same mental state as cognitive busyness.”

questions.q: According to The Lazy Controller, what did Baumeister's group find about blood glucose and mental effort?
options: Blood glucose rises during difficult reasoning, giving a burst of energy
Blood glucose drops during difficult reasoning or self-control, and ingesting glucose can undo ego depletion
Blood glucose is unaffected by mental work, so mental energy is only a metaphor
Glucose helps physical stamina but has no effect on judgment
questions.explain: Effortful mental activity is especially expensive in glucose, like a runner drawing down muscle glucose in a sprint, and the group confirmed that ingesting glucose undoes depletion. This is why Kahneman says mental energy is more than a mere metaphor.

questions.q: In the study of eight Israeli parole judges described in The Lazy Controller, how did the approval rate change across the time between food breaks?
options: It stayed near 35% all day, unaffected by meals
It was lowest just after each meal and rose steadily before the next one
It rose steadily during the morning and fell only after lunch
It spiked to about 65% after each meal and dropped to about zero just before the next
questions.explain: Approvals spike after each meal and fall steadily over the next two hours or so. The 35% figure is the overall approval rate, not a constant rate across the day.

questions.q: What is the best account, according to The Lazy Controller, of why the Israeli parole judges approved fewer requests as time passed since their last meal?
options: Tired and hungry judges fall back on the easier default of denying parole
The hardest cases were scheduled just before meals
Judges became more skeptical as they learned more about the prisoners
Judges deliberately saved approvals for after their breaks
questions.explain: The cases were presented in random order, and the authors checked many alternative explanations; the best account is that tired and hungry judges fall back on the default position of denial. Both fatigue and hunger probably play a role.

questions.q: True or false: In Baumeister's lemonade study described in The Lazy Controller, ego-depleted volunteers who drank glucose-sweetened lemonade made more intuitive errors than those who drank lemonade sweetened with Splenda.
questions.explain: It was the reverse: the Splenda drinkers showed the expected depletion effect, while the glucose drinkers were not depleted. Restoring sugar in the brain prevented the deterioration of performance.

questions.q: True or false: According to The Lazy Controller, the self-control of morning people is impaired at night, and the reverse is true of night people.
questions.explain: Kahneman lists this, with a few drinks and a sleepless night, as causes of weakened self-control other than cognitive load.

questions.q: Baumeister's group named the phenomenon in which an effort of will or self-control leaves people less willing or able to exert self-control on the next challenge ____.
questions.explain: The finding that self-control is tiring, so that forcing yourself to do something weakens later self-control, is called ego depletion.

questions.q: In a typical ego-depletion demonstration, people who stifled their emotional reaction to a charged film later performed poorly on a test of physical stamina: how long they could keep a strong grip on a ____.
questions.explain: The emotional effort reduced the ability to withstand sustained muscle contraction, so depleted people quit the dynamometer grip sooner.

questions.q: Kahneman says that too much concern about how well one is doing in a task can disrupt performance by loading short-term memory with pointless ____ thoughts.
questions.explain: Worry about performance acts like a cognitive load, filling short-term memory and weakening System 2's control.

questions.q: In the parole study, the default decision for the Israeli judges was denial; only about ____ percent of requests were approved overall.
questions.explain: Only 35% of requests were approved overall, which makes denial the easy default that tired and hungry judges fall back on.

questions.q: Which of these does The Lazy Controller list as situations or tasks known to deplete self-control?
options: Avoiding the thought of white bears
Trying to impress others
Eating a meal or snack
Responding kindly to a partner's bad behavior
Watching a film without any instructions
questions.explain: All the depleting tasks involve conflict and the need to suppress a natural tendency. Eating is what restores the parole judges, and merely watching a film is not depleting; it was inhibiting the emotional response to a film that depleted people.

questions.q: Which of these does The Lazy Controller say people who are cognitively busy are more likely to do?
options: Make selfish choices
Use sexist language
Solve logic puzzles more carefully
Make superficial judgments in social situations
Resist tempting foods
questions.explain: Memorizing and repeating digits loosens the hold of System 2 on behavior, so busy people make more selfish choices, use sexist language and judge superficially. They resist temptation less, not more.

questions.q: Which of these does The Lazy Controller name as causes of weakened self-control?
options: A few drinks
A sleepless night
Drinking glucose-sweetened lemonade
Memorizing and repeating digits
A recent meal
questions.explain: Cognitive load, a few drinks and a sleepless night all weaken self-control. Glucose and food work the other way: glucose undid depletion, and the parole judges were most lenient just after eating.

questions.q: Put the steps of Baumeister's lemonade study, as described in The Lazy Controller, in the order they happened.
items: Volunteers interpret a woman's body language in a silent film
They ignore words crossing the screen, refocusing on the woman
All volunteers drink lemonade sweetened with glucose or Splenda
All do a task requiring them to overcome an intuitive response
Splenda drinkers show depletion; glucose drinkers do not
questions.explain: The self-control of ignoring the words caused depletion; the lemonade came before the second task; only those who received glucose avoided the usual rise in intuitive errors.

questions.q: Put these points in the order Kahneman presents them when describing how parole approvals change through a judge's day in the Israeli study.
items: A food break is taken
About 65% of requests are granted
Approvals drop steadily over about two hours
Approvals fall to about zero
The next food break is taken
questions.explain: The proportion of approvals spikes after each meal to about 65%, then drops steadily until it reaches about zero just before the next meal.

questions.q: Match each ego-depletion study in The Lazy Controller to its result.
pairs: Stifling emotion during a charged film
Poorer stamina later in a handgrip test
Eating radishes while resisting chocolate
Giving up earlier on a difficult cognitive task
Ignoring words while judging body language, then glucose
No rise in intuitive errors
Ignoring words while judging body language, then Splenda
The expected rise in intuitive errors
Parole judges far from their last meal
Falling back on denying parole
questions.explain: Each study shows that exerting self-control reduces later self-control or effort, and that glucose or food can restore it.

questions.q: Sort these items from The Lazy Controller into tasks that deplete self-control and indications that a person is depleted.

items.t: Avoiding the thought of white bears
Inhibiting the emotional response to a stirring film
Making a series of choices that involve conflict
Responding kindly to a partner's bad behavior
Deviating from one's diet
Overspending on impulsive purchases
Reacting aggressively to provocation
Persisting less time in a handgrip task

questions.explain: Kahneman gives two lists: depleting tasks all involve conflict and suppressing a natural tendency, while the signs of depletion are failures of control that follow.

questions.q: Sort these statements from The Lazy Controller by whether they describe ego depletion or cognitive busyness (cognitive load).

items.t: At least in part a loss of motivation
Can be resisted when a strong incentive is offered
Follows an earlier, successive act of self-control
Undone in experiments by ingesting glucose
Keeping six digits in memory while doing a task
Increasing effort is not an option to escape it
Choosing chocolate cake while holding seven digits in mind

questions.explain: Ego depletion is a lingering after-effect of self-control that incentives or glucose can overcome; cognitive busyness is a simultaneous load that extra effort cannot remove.

questions.q: In The Lazy Controller, what does Kahneman mean by saying that System 1 has more influence on behavior when System 2 is busy? Use the dessert study as an example.
questions.a: Self-control is a task of System 2 that requires attention and effort, so when System 2 is occupied, its hold on behavior loosens and System 1's impulses get through. In the dessert study, people told to keep seven digits in memory as their top priority were more likely to choose the sinful chocolate cake over the virtuous fruit salad. In the book's words, System 1 “has a sweet tooth.”

questions.q: What is ego depletion, according to The Lazy Controller, and how does it differ from cognitive busyness?
questions.a: Ego depletion is the finding by Baumeister's group that an effort of will or self-control is tiring, so that after forcing yourself to do something you are less willing or able to exert self-control on the next challenge. It is at least in part a loss of motivation: people could make the effort if they really had to, and strong incentives let them resist the effect. Cognitive busyness is different, because when you must keep digits in short-term memory, increasing effort is not an option.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman, in The Lazy Controller, say that Baumeister's glucose findings show that mental energy is more than a mere metaphor?
questions.a: The nervous system consumes more glucose than most other parts of the body, and difficult reasoning or self-control lowers blood glucose, much as a sprinter draws down glucose in her muscles. If depletion is really a drop in available fuel, then restoring glucose should undo it, and Baumeister's experiments confirmed this: in the lemonade study, depleted volunteers who drank glucose avoided the rise in intuitive errors that Splenda drinkers showed.

questions.q: Explain the Israeli parole judges study described in The Lazy Controller and what it shows about depletion in real judgments.
questions.a: Eight parole judges reviewed cases in random order, spending about 6 minutes on each, with denial as the default. Approvals spiked to about 65% after each meal and fell steadily to about zero just before the next. After checking alternative explanations, the best account is that tired and hungry judges fall back on the easier default of denying parole, showing that depletion affects serious, real-world decisions.

questions.q: In the bat-and-ball puzzle (a bat and ball cost $1.10, the bat costs one dollar more than the ball), what is the correct price of the ball?
options: 10 cents
5 cents
1 cent
55 cents
questions.explain: If the ball cost 10 cents, the bat would cost $1.10 and the total $1.20. The intuitive answer of 10 cents is appealing and wrong; the correct answer is 5 cents.

questions.q: According to The Lazy Controller, what did Shane Frederick conclude about anyone who answers 10 cents in the bat-and-ball puzzle?
options: The person lacks the mathematical ability to solve the puzzle
The person never had the intuitive answer come to mind
The person did not actively check, and System 2 endorsed an intuition it could easily have rejected
The person was deliberately trying to mislead the researcher
questions.explain: Frederick reasoned that a person who says 10 cents did not check, though a few seconds of mental work would have caught the mistake. Ability is not the issue, since such students can solve much harder problems.

questions.q: According to The Lazy Controller, what share of students at Harvard, MIT and Princeton gave the intuitive, incorrect answer to the bat-and-ball puzzle?
options: More than 50%
About 10%
Under 25%
More than 80%
questions.explain: More than 50% of students at these elite universities gave the intuitive answer. The figure above 80% applies to less selective universities.

questions.q: Why, according to The Lazy Controller, do most college students wrongly accept the syllogism that all roses are flowers, some flowers fade quickly, therefore some roses fade quickly?
options: They have never been taught the rules of logic
They misread the premises because of time pressure alone
They know nothing about how quickly roses fade
A plausible conclusion comes to mind at once, and overriding it requires hard work
questions.explain: As with the bat and ball, a plausible answer comes to mind immediately, and the insistent sense that it is true makes checking the logic hard, so most people do not take the trouble. The argument is invalid because no roses need be among the flowers that fade quickly.

questions.q: In Shane Frederick's Michigan murder question described in The Lazy Controller, why did people asked about Michigan give lower estimates than a similar group asked about Detroit?
options: They did not know that Detroit is a high-crime city
Most did not think of Detroit when asked about the state, though they knew it is in Michigan
They assumed rural states have no murders at all
They were asked to answer more slowly than the Detroit group
questions.explain: College students know Detroit is Michigan's largest city, but facts we know do not always come to mind when we need them, and most respondents did not think of Detroit when asked about the state.

questions.q: According to The Lazy Controller, what do failures on the bat-and-ball problem, the flowers syllogism and the Michigan question have in common?
options: They reflect a lack of basic intelligence
They arise only when people are under severe time pressure
They are, at least in part, a matter of insufficient motivation, not trying hard enough
They are caused by ego depletion from earlier tasks
questions.explain: Anyone admitted to a good university can reason through these problems; they fail because they are satisfied with a superficially plausible answer and stop thinking, which is why Kahneman calls their System 2 lazy rather than incapable.

questions.q: True or false: According to The Lazy Controller, at less selective universities the rate of failure to check on the bat-and-ball puzzle was lower than at Harvard, MIT and Princeton.
questions.explain: The rate was higher, not lower: in excess of 80% at less selective universities, compared with more than 50% at Harvard, MIT and Princeton.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that people who gave the correct answer to the bat-and-ball puzzle probably also had the intuitive answer of 10 cents come to mind, but managed to resist it.
questions.explain: He says it is safe to assume the intuitive answer also came to the mind of those who ended up correct; they somehow resisted the intuition.

questions.q: Kahneman says that people who answer 10 cents in the bat-and-ball puzzle appear to be ardent followers of the law of ____.
questions.explain: They accepted an answer that a small investment of effort could have rejected, so they appear to follow the law of least effort.

questions.q: Kahneman says people who avoid the sin of intellectual sloth could be called ____: more alert, more intellectually active and more skeptical about their intuitions.
questions.explain: He contrasts lazy thinkers with engaged ones, and notes that Keith Stanovich would call the engaged more rational.

questions.q: The bat-and-ball problem introduces a recurrent theme of the book: many people are ____, prone to place too much faith in their intuitions.
questions.explain: Kahneman says this is the first encounter with the theme that many people are overconfident and find cognitive effort at least mildly unpleasant.

questions.q: Which of these does The Lazy Controller say are true of people who give the intuitive answer of 10 cents in the bat-and-ball puzzle?
