options: They did not actively check whether the answer was correct
They missed an obvious social cue about why such an easy puzzle would be asked
They lacked the ability to do the arithmetic
They appear to follow the law of least effort
They had been depleted by an earlier self-control task
questions.explain: Frederick reasoned that such people did not check, should have wondered why a questionnaire would include such an obvious puzzle, and followed the law of least effort. Kahneman stresses lack of motivation, not lack of ability, and the puzzle involves no prior depleting task.

questions.q: Which of these does The Lazy Controller say determine whether Detroit comes to mind when someone is asked about murders in Michigan?
options: The automatic function of memory, a System 1 attribute
How detailed the person's representation of Michigan is
Whether the person deliberately slows down to search memory
The amount of glucose the person has just consumed
Whether the person is a morning or a night person
questions.explain: Kahneman lays the blame on both systems: automatic memory and the richness of one's representation of the state belong to System 1, while the extent of deliberate search is a System 2 characteristic that varies among individuals.

questions.q: Put the minitests in The Lazy Controller in the order Kahneman presents them.
items: The bat-and-ball puzzle
The roses and flowers syllogism
The Michigan murders question
questions.explain: He starts with the bat and ball, then the flowers syllogism, then the Michigan question, and finally draws out what the three have in common: insufficient motivation.

questions.q: Match each minitest from The Lazy Controller to the intuitive response it tempts.
pairs: Bat-and-ball puzzle
The ball costs 10 cents
Roses syllogism
The argument is valid
Michigan murders question
A low estimate that leaves out Detroit
questions.explain: Each problem evokes a superficially plausible answer that comes readily to mind; checking would reveal 5 cents, an invalid argument, and Detroit's crime problem.

questions.q: Match each person in The Lazy Controller to the contribution Kahneman attributes to them.
pairs: Shane Frederick
Devised the bat-and-ball and Michigan questions
Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi
Named and studied the state of flow
Roy Baumeister
Showed that self-control draws on a shared pool of energy
Keith Stanovich
Distinguished rationality from intelligence
Walter Mischel
Tested four-year-olds' ability to wait for two cookies
questions.explain: These researchers supply the chapter's main evidence: flow, ego depletion, the lazy-System-2 puzzles, delay of gratification, and the rationality versus intelligence distinction.

questions.q: Sort these elements of the Michigan murders problem, as Kahneman analyzes it in The Lazy Controller, by which system they belong to.

items.t: Whether Detroit automatically comes to mind with Michigan
Memory function in general
A richer representation of the state in residents' minds
Slowing down to actively search memory for relevant facts
The extent of deliberate checking, which varies among individuals
Checking the intuitive answer before accepting it

questions.explain: Kahneman says “Memory function is an attribute of System 1.” Deliberate checking and active search are characteristics of System 2.

questions.q: In The Lazy Controller, what question did Shane Frederick use the bat-and-ball puzzle to study, and why is failure to check remarkable?
questions.a: Frederick used the puzzle to study how closely System 2 monitors the suggestions of System 1. Anyone who says 10 cents did not check, so their System 2 endorsed an intuitive answer it could have rejected with a small investment of effort. The failure is remarkable because checking is so cheap: a few seconds of mental work with slightly tensed muscles and dilated pupils would avoid an embarrassing mistake.

questions.q: What does the roses syllogism in The Lazy Controller suggest about reasoning in everyday life?
questions.a: Most college students endorse the invalid syllogism because a plausible conclusion comes to mind immediately, and the insistent feeling that it is true makes checking the logic hard. This suggests that when people believe a conclusion is true, they are also very likely to believe arguments that appear to support it, even unsound ones. In the book's words, “If System 1 is involved, the conclusion comes first and the arguments follow.”

questions.q: Why does Kahneman, in The Lazy Controller, say that calling the System 2 of students who fail his minitests lazy is harsh but not unfair?
questions.a: These students are certainly able to reason through the problems and could remember Detroit's crime problem if they reflected; they solve much harder problems when not tempted by an easy answer. Their failures are a matter of insufficient motivation, of being satisfied enough to stop thinking. So the problem lies in their self-monitoring, not their ability, which is what the word lazy describes.

questions.q: Apply The Lazy Controller: a shopper sees a coat at 40% off and a matching scarf, and quickly decides the deal is great without adding up the totals; later she finds an arithmetic error. How would Kahneman explain this?
questions.a: A plausible answer came readily to mind from System 1, and her System 2 endorsed it without checking, even though a few seconds of mental work would have caught the mistake. As with the bat-and-ball puzzle, the failure is not one of ability but of motivation: she followed the law of least effort and was satisfied enough to stop thinking. An engaged System 2 would have been more skeptical of the intuition.

questions.q: In Walter Mischel's experiment described in The Lazy Controller, how did most of the children who managed to wait 15 minutes for the larger reward succeed?
options: By being promised extra toys if they waited
By talking with the experimenter during the wait
By ringing the bell to check the time
Mainly by keeping their attention away from the tempting reward
questions.explain: The room had no toys or distractions and the experimenter left; about half the children waited, mainly by directing attention away from the cookie, an early sign of the attention control linked to later outcomes.

questions.q: According to The Lazy Controller, what did ten or fifteen years of follow-up reveal about the children in Mischel's experiment who had resisted temptation?
options: They had higher executive control, were less likely to take drugs, and scored substantially higher on intelligence tests
They scored no differently on intelligence tests but were more popular
They were more likely to take risks and seek immediate rewards
They had better memory but weaker control of attention
questions.explain: The resisters had higher measures of executive control, especially the ability to reallocate attention, were less likely to take drugs as young adults, and had substantially higher intelligence scores, linking self-control to cognitive aptitude.

questions.q: What did the University of Oregon team described in The Lazy Controller find when children aged four to six played computer games designed to demand attention and control?
options: Executive control improved, but intelligence scores did not change
Training attention improved executive control and nonverbal intelligence scores, with gains lasting several months
Intelligence improved only for a few days and then vanished
The games reduced the children's ability to control their emotions
questions.explain: Training attention improved both executive control and nonverbal intelligence scores, and the improvement was maintained for several months. The group also found a close connection between control of attention and control of emotions.

questions.q: According to The Lazy Controller, how did students who score low on Shane Frederick's Cognitive Reflection Test answer a question about money now versus later?
options: Only 37% preferred $3,400 this month over $3,800 next month
Almost none would accept a smaller amount immediately
63% preferred $3,400 this month over $3,800 next month
They were willing to pay half as much for overnight delivery of a book
questions.explain: 63% of intuitive respondents preferred the smaller immediate sum, compared with only 37% of those who solved all three puzzles. Low scorers would also pay twice as much, not half as much, for overnight delivery.

questions.q: In Keith Stanovich's view, as presented in The Lazy Controller, what is superficial or lazy thinking?
options: A flaw in the algorithmic mind caused by low intelligence
An unavoidable result of cognitive load
A sign of ego depletion after self-control
A flaw in the reflective mind, a failure of rationality
questions.explain: Stanovich separates the algorithmic mind, which handles demanding computation and is measured by intelligence tests, from rationality. Lazy thinking is a failure of rationality, so high intelligence does not make people immune to biases.

questions.q: True or false: According to The Lazy Controller, Keith Stanovich and Richard West originally introduced the terms System 1 and System 2, though they now prefer to speak of Type 1 and Type 2 processes.
questions.explain: Kahneman credits Stanovich and West with originally introducing the terms, and notes their current preference for Type 1 and Type 2 processes.

questions.q: True or false: Stanovich and his colleagues found that conventional measures of intelligence such as IQ tests are better indicators of susceptibility to cognitive errors than the bat-and-ball question.
questions.explain: They found the reverse: the bat-and-ball question and others like it are somewhat better indicators of susceptibility to cognitive errors than IQ tests, which supports distinguishing rationality from intelligence.

questions.q: Shane Frederick's ____, made up of the bat-and-ball problem and two other questions, has emerged as one of the better predictors of lazy thinking.
questions.explain: Frederick chose questions that invite a compelling but wrong intuitive answer; low scorers have a weak supervisory System 2.

questions.q: Stanovich calls the part of System 2 that deals with slow thinking and demanding computation, and that intelligence tests measure, the ____ mind.
questions.explain: Stanovich divides System 2 into an algorithmic mind, measured by intelligence tests, and a reflective mind whose failures are failures of rationality.

questions.q: Stanovich's book on why some people are more susceptible to biases than others is titled Rationality and the ____ Mind.
questions.explain: The book, Rationality and the Reflective Mind, argues that rationality should be distinguished from intelligence.

questions.q: Which of these traits does The Lazy Controller attribute to people who score very low on the Cognitive Reflection Test?
options: Prone to answer with the first idea that comes to mind
Impulsive, impatient and keen on immediate gratification
Willing to pay twice as much for overnight delivery of a book
Unusually skeptical of their intuitions
Less susceptible to biases than high scorers
questions.explain: Frederick found that low scorers accept System 1's suggestions uncritically, both on puzzles and in choices about money and waiting. Skepticism about intuitions describes the engaged, not the low scorers.

questions.q: Which of these did the University of Oregon research group, as described in The Lazy Controller, report about children's control of attention?
options: Specific genes are involved in the control of attention
Parenting techniques affect this ability
Control of attention is closely connected to control of emotions
Attention training lowered nonverbal intelligence scores
Control of attention cannot be improved by training
questions.explain: The group identified genes involved in attention control, showed that parenting techniques matter, and found a close link between controlling attention and controlling emotions. Their training raised, not lowered, nonverbal intelligence scores.

questions.q: Put the events of Walter Mischel's delay experiment, as described in The Lazy Controller, in order.
items: A four-year-old is offered one cookie now or two after a wait
The child is left alone with a cookie and a bell
The child waits 15 minutes or rings the bell
Ten or fifteen years later, the children are compared
Resisters show higher executive control and intelligence
questions.explain: The children faced the choice, waited alone in a bare room watched through a one-way mirror, and were followed up years later, when a large gap had opened between those who had resisted and those who had not.

questions.q: Put the steps of Stanovich's argument, as Kahneman presents it in The Lazy Controller, in logical order.
items: System 2 has two parts, which he calls separate minds
The algorithmic mind handles demanding computation and is measured by intelligence tests
High intelligence does not make people immune to biases
So rationality must be distinguished from intelligence
Lazy thinking is then a failure of rationality in the reflective mind
questions.explain: Stanovich splits System 2, assigns intelligence to the algorithmic mind, observes that intelligence does not prevent bias, and so locates lazy thinking in a separate ability, rationality.

questions.q: Match each finding about Shane Frederick's Cognitive Reflection Test in The Lazy Controller to its figure.
pairs: Low scorers preferring $3,400 now over $3,800 next month
Perfect scorers with the same shortsighted preference
Low scorers' payment for overnight book delivery vs high scorers
Twice as much
Number of questions in the test
Three
questions.explain: Low scorers are more impatient and keen on immediate gratification than those who solve all three puzzles, showing that uncritical acceptance of intuition extends beyond puzzles.

questions.q: Sort these descriptions by whether they fit what Stanovich, as presented in The Lazy Controller, calls the algorithmic mind or rationality.

items.t: Slow thinking and demanding computation
Measured by conventional intelligence tests
Switching from one task to another quickly and efficiently
Similar to what Kahneman calls engaged
Its failure produces superficial or lazy thinking
Better indicated by the bat-and-ball question than by IQ tests

questions.explain: Stanovich's core point is that rationality should be distinguished from intelligence: brain power belongs to the algorithmic mind, while the reflective mind's engagement guards against biases.

questions.q: Sort these traits by which character of Kahneman's psychodrama they describe, according to Frederick's findings in The Lazy Controller.

items.t: Impulsive
Intuitive
Keen to receive immediate gratification
Capable of reasoning
Cautious
Lazy, at least for some people

questions.explain: Kahneman says System 1 is impulsive and intuitive, while System 2 is capable of reasoning and cautious but, at least for some people, lazy.

questions.q: What does Walter Mischel's cookie experiment, as described in The Lazy Controller, suggest about the link between self-control and intelligence?
questions.a: About half of the four-year-olds waited 15 minutes for two cookies, mainly by keeping their attention away from the reward. Ten or fifteen years later, the resisters had higher executive control, especially in reallocating attention, were less likely to take drugs, and scored substantially higher on intelligence tests. This suggests that people's rankings on self-control and on cognitive aptitude are linked.

questions.q: In The Lazy Controller, what does Kahneman mean by saying that Frederick's findings show the characters of the psychodrama have different personalities?
questions.a: Low scorers on the Cognitive Reflection Test accept System 1's suggestions not only on puzzles but also in life, being impulsive, impatient and keen on immediate gratification. This fits System 1 being impulsive and intuitive, and System 2 being capable of reasoning and cautious but, for some people, lazy. People differ accordingly: some are more like their System 2, others closer to their System 1.

questions.q: Apply The Lazy Controller: two job candidates have the same high IQ score, but one routinely double-checks first impressions and the other goes with whatever answer comes to mind. Using Stanovich's distinction, which is more likely to avoid biases, and why?
questions.a: The one who double-checks. Stanovich argues that high intelligence, the algorithmic mind, does not make people immune to biases; another ability, rationality, is involved. The candidate who accepts the first answer shows lazy thinking, which Stanovich treats as a flaw in the reflective mind, while the checker resembles what Kahneman calls engaged.

questions.q: In the Speaking of Control phrases, a colleague who just turned to standard operating procedures after a long day of meetings is described as having his ego ____.
questions.explain: After a day of effortful meetings his self-control is depleted, so he falls back on the easy default rather than thinking the problem through, like the hungry parole judges.

questions.q: True or false: In the Speaking of Control phrases, a person who tends to say the first thing that comes into her mind is predicted to have trouble delaying gratification, a sign of a weak System 2.
questions.explain: This applies Frederick's finding that people who uncritically follow their intuitions are also impulsive and keen on immediate gratification.

questions.q: Match each Speaking of Control remark to the concept it applies.
pairs: She did not have to struggle to stay on task for hours
Flow
He turned to standard operating procedures after many meetings
Ego depletion
Does he usually have a lazy System 2 or was he unusually tired?
Lazy System 2 versus depletion
She says the first thing that comes into her mind
Weak System 2 and impulsivity
questions.explain: Each remark turns one of the chapter's ideas into everyday language: flow, ego depletion, the lazy controller, and the link between intuitive answers and impatience.

questions.q: What does the title The Lazy Controller signal about System 2?
options: That System 2 is too weak to control anything
That System 1 secretly controls System 2
That control is entirely automatic and effortless
That System 2 monitors and controls behavior but often avoids the effort of doing so
questions.explain: One of System 2's main functions is to monitor and control the suggestions of System 1, but people find effort unpleasant and often fail to check. The controller is capable; it is lazy, not powerless.

questions.q: Which of these ideas does The Lazy Controller build on from Chapter 2, Attention and Effort?
options: The law of least effort
Effort shown by dilated pupils
The limited budget of attention
Prospect theory's treatment of losses
The endowment effect
questions.explain: The Lazy Controller extends the law of least effort, the pupil as a sign of effort, and the limited budget of System 2 to self-control. Prospect theory and the endowment effect belong to the later part on choices.

questions.q: Put the sections of Chapter 3, The Lazy Controller, in the order they appear.
items: The walk in the Berkeley hills and flow
The Busy and Depleted System 2
The Lazy System 2
Intelligence, Control, Rationality
Speaking of Control
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the shared budget of effort, to how load and depletion weaken control, to System 2's laziness in checking intuitions, to individual differences in control and rationality, ending with everyday phrases.

questions.q: Put these chapters of Part 1, Two Systems, in their order in the book.
items: Attention and Effort
The Lazy Controller
The Associative Machine
Cognitive Ease
questions.explain: In the table of contents, Attention and Effort is chapter 2, The Lazy Controller chapter 3, The Associative Machine chapter 4, and Cognitive Ease chapter 5.

questions.q: Match each item from The Lazy Controller to how it links to other parts of the book.
pairs: The bat-and-ball puzzle
First encounter with the recurrent theme of overconfidence
The other two Cognitive Reflection Test questions
Shown in chapter 5
The terms System 1 and System 2
Originally introduced by Stanovich and West
Memory as an attribute of System 1
Leads into The Associative Machine
questions.explain: Kahneman flags the bat and ball as the first instance of a theme that recurs throughout the book, defers the other CRT questions to chapter 5, and credits the two-systems terms to Stanovich and West; the next chapter turns to System 1's associative memory.

questions.q: Why does The Lazy Controller come right after Attention and Effort in Part 1 of the book?
questions.a: Attention and Effort establishes that System 2's effort is limited and that people follow a law of least effort. The Lazy Controller extends this to self-control: self-control and deliberate thought draw on the same limited budget, so when System 2 is busy, depleted or simply lazy, it fails to monitor and correct System 1. This sets up the following chapters on System 1's automatic workings, such as The Associative Machine.

questions.q: How does The Lazy Controller prepare the ground for the rest of Thinking, Fast and Slow?
questions.a: It shows that System 2 often endorses System 1's suggestions without checking, so intuitive errors pass uncorrected. Kahneman calls the bat-and-ball problem the first encounter with a recurrent theme of the book: many people are overconfident, placing too much faith in their intuitions. Later parts on heuristics, biases and overconfidence depend on this picture of a capable but lazy controller.

questions.q: In the 'Bananas Vomit' demonstration that opens The Associative Machine, what does Kahneman say your mind automatically did with the two words?
options: It assumed a temporal sequence and a causal link, with bananas causing the sickness
It treated the words as unrelated and stored each one separately in memory
It deliberately searched memory for a past occasion when bananas made you ill
It flagged the pairing as nonsense and suppressed any emotional reaction to it
questions.explain: Kahneman says the mind formed a sketchy scenario in which bananas caused the sickness, with no particular reason to do so. The reaction was automatic, not a deliberate memory search, and it produced emotion rather than suppressing it.

questions.q: True or false: In the 'Bananas Vomit' demonstration, Kahneman says the reader's responses to the words were completely automatic and beyond the reader's control.
questions.explain: He describes the facial expression, heart rate and recoil as an attenuated version of reacting to the real event, all of it “completely automatic, beyond your control.” He attributes it to System 1.

questions.q: In The Associative Machine, the process by which evoked ideas trigger many other ideas in a spreading cascade of brain activity is called ____.
questions.explain: Kahneman names the process behind the 'Bananas Vomit' reaction associative activation: “ideas that have been evoked trigger many other ideas,” spreading in a cascade.

questions.q: Kahneman says the self-reinforcing pattern of cognitive, emotional and physical responses to 'Bananas Vomit', diverse yet integrated, has been called associatively ____.
questions.explain: The essential feature of associative activation is coherence: each element supports and strengthens the others, so the whole pattern is called associatively coherent.

questions.q: Which of these are the three principles of association that David Hume set out in 1748, according to Kahneman?
options: Resemblance
Contiguity in time and place
Causality
Frequency of repetition
Emotional intensity
questions.explain: In An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Hume reduced the principles of association to resemblance, contiguity in time and place, and causality. Repetition and emotional intensity are not on his list.

questions.q: Using the 'Bananas Vomit' example, Kahneman says cognitive scientists now emphasize that cognition is ____: you think with your body, not only with your brain.
questions.explain: The physical recoil and emotional response were part of how the mind interpreted the two words, which is why Kahneman says “cognition is embodied.”

questions.q: In Kahneman's account of associative memory, match each example link to the type of link it illustrates.
pairs: virus to cold
A cause linked to its effect
lime to green
A thing linked to its property
banana to fruit
A thing linked to the category it belongs to
questions.explain: Kahneman lists these three kinds of links in associative memory: causes to effects, things to properties, and things to their categories.

questions.q: In The Associative Machine, sort each statement into the older view of association from Hume's day or the current view of associative memory.

items.t: The mind goes through a sequence of conscious ideas, one at a time
Association reduces to resemblance, contiguity and causality
A great deal happens at once
Most associative work is silent, hidden from consciousness
An activated idea activates many ideas, which activate others

questions.explain: Kahneman says we have advanced beyond Hume by no longer picturing a one-at-a-time sequence of conscious ideas. Now many ideas are activated at once and most of the activity is silent, though Hume's three principles are still a good start.

questions.q: True or false: According to Kahneman's account of associative memory, most of the ideas activated by associative thinking register in consciousness.
questions.explain: It is the reverse: only a few activated ideas register in consciousness. Kahneman says most of the work of associative thinking is silent and hidden from our conscious selves.

questions.q: Using the 'Bananas Vomit' example, explain what Kahneman means by associative activation and why he says its essential feature is coherence.
questions.a: Seeing the words evoked memories, which evoked emotions, which evoked facial expressions and an avoidance tendency, all in a spreading cascade that Kahneman calls associative activation. Each element is connected to the others and strengthens them: the expression and recoil intensify the feelings, and the feelings reinforce compatible ideas. The result is a self-reinforcing pattern of thought, emotion and bodily response that is both diverse and integrated, which is why it is called associatively coherent.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what did System 1 accomplish in the second or so after you read the words 'Bananas Vomit'?
questions.a: Starting from a completely unexpected event, System 1 made as much sense as it could of two oddly paired words by linking them in a causal story. It judged the possible threat as mild to moderate and prepared you for events that had just become more likely. It also evaluated how surprising the pairing was, so you ended up as informed about the past and as prepared for the future as you could be.

questions.q: What does Kahneman call 'an odd feature' of how System 1 responded to the words 'Bananas Vomit'?
options: It ignored the words until System 2 had finished reading them
It reacted only to the first word and ignored the second
It treated the mere conjunction of two words as a representation of reality
It produced a strong reaction that was larger than reacting to the real event
questions.explain: System 1 treated the mere pairing of two words as if it represented something real, and the body reacted with a toned-down replica of a reaction to the real thing. The reaction was weaker, not stronger, than the real event would produce.

questions.q: In the 'Bananas Vomit' demonstration, sort each word by whether Kahneman says you became readier to recognize it through its link to 'vomit' or through its link to 'bananas'.

items.t: sick
stink
nausea
yellow
fruit
berries

questions.explain: Kahneman says you became unusually ready to recognize words linked to vomit, such as sick, stink and nausea, and words linked to bananas, such as yellow and fruit, and perhaps apple and berries.

questions.q: Psychologists think of ideas as nodes in a vast network, called associative ____, in which each idea is linked to many others.
questions.explain: Kahneman describes associative memory as a vast network of nodes in which each idea links to many others through causal, property and category links.

questions.q: In the 'Bananas Vomit' example, put the links of Kahneman's chain of responses in order, starting with the word.
items: The word evokes memories
The memories evoke emotions
The emotions evoke facial expressions and an avoidance tendency
The expression and avoidance intensify the linked feelings
questions.explain: Kahneman traces a chain from word to memories to emotions to facial expressions and other reactions. Those reactions then intensify the feelings, which makes the pattern self-reinforcing.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman argues that the notion of limited access to the workings of our minds is true, even though it is alien to our experience.
questions.explain: He grants that the idea is hard to accept because it does not match our experience, but insists it is true: “you know far less about yourself than you feel you do.”

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say happened to you as a result of reading the words 'Bananas Vomit'?
options: A temporary aversion to bananas
Readiness to recognize words such as sick, stink and nausea
Mild surprise at an unusual pairing of words
A lasting dislike of bananas that will need effort to undo
A conscious decision to push the book away
questions.explain: Kahneman lists a temporary aversion to bananas (he says it will pass), readiness for related words, and mild surprise at the odd pairing. The aversion is not lasting, and any pushing away of the book was automatic and imperceptible, not a decision.

questions.q: Maya scrolls past a headline that pairs the words 'oysters' and 'hospital'. At dinner that night she finds herself oddly reluctant to order oysters, though she cannot say why. Which idea from The Associative Machine best explains this?
options: System 2 weighed the medical evidence and decided oysters were risky
Associative activation linked the words in a causal story and left a temporary aversion
Ego depletion from the workday reduced her appetite for unfamiliar food
Hume's principle of resemblance made oysters look like hospital food
questions.explain: As with 'Bananas Vomit', System 1 automatically joins two juxtaposed words into a causal story, leaving a temporary aversion. No deliberate weighing of evidence by System 2 is involved.

questions.q: What does Kahneman mean when he says that 'cognition is embodied', and how does the 'Bananas Vomit' example show it?
questions.a: He means that we think with our bodies, not only with our brains. When you read 'Bananas Vomit', your face twisted, your heart rate rose and you recoiled slightly, an attenuated replica of reacting to the real thing. Kahneman says this emotional response and physical recoil were part of how System 1 interpreted the event, not just a side effect of it.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say can count as an 'idea' under his expansive view in The Associative Machine?
options: A verb
A noun
A clenched fist
Only a thought that has reached consciousness
Only a concrete, never an abstract, concept
questions.explain: Kahneman says an idea can be concrete or abstract and can be expressed as a verb, a noun, an adjective, or a clenched fist. He also says most activated ideas never reach consciousness, so consciousness is not required.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say the claim that we have limited access to the workings of our minds is hard to accept, and why does he insist it is true anyway?
questions.a: It is hard to accept because it is alien to our experience: we do not feel that most of our mental activity is hidden. But in the current view of associative memory, an activated idea sets off many others at once and only a few of them register in consciousness. Most associative work is silent, so “you know far less about yourself than you feel you do.”

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what was the first big breakthrough in understanding the mechanism of association?
options: Hume's reduction of association to three principles
Brain scans that showed ideas lighting up as nodes
Asking people for the first word that comes to mind
An improvement in a method of measurement
questions.explain: Kahneman says that, as is common in science, the breakthrough was a better method of measurement: the 1980s finding that exposure to a word produces measurable changes in how easily related words are evoked. Asking for the first word that comes to mind was the older method it improved on.

questions.q: In Kahneman's example of a priming effect, someone who has recently seen the word EAT is more likely to complete the fragment SO_P as ____.
questions.explain: EAT primes SOUP, so the fragment is more likely to be completed as SOUP than as SOAP. Seeing WASH would have the opposite effect.

questions.q: True or false: In Kahneman's word-fragment example, having just seen the word WASH makes a person more likely to complete SO_P as SOUP.
questions.explain: WASH primes SOAP, not SOUP. It is EAT that primes SOUP; Kahneman says the opposite would happen after seeing WASH.

questions.q: When exposure to EAT makes SOUP easier to evoke, Kahneman says we call this a ____ and say that EAT primes SOUP.
questions.explain: He names the measurable change in how easily related words are evoked a priming effect.

questions.q: In The Associative Machine, what does Kahneman's image of 'ripples on a pond' describe?
options: Activation spreading through a small part of the network, with primed ideas weakly priming others
Conscious thoughts following one another in an orderly sequence
The way a priming effect grows stronger the farther it spreads
The way System 2 calms the emotional reactions produced by System 1
questions.explain: Primed ideas can prime other ideas, though more weakly, so activation spreads like ripples through a small part of the vast network. The effect weakens rather than strengthens as it spreads.

questions.q: Put the steps of John Bargh's 'Florida effect' experiment at New York University in order.
items: Students assemble four-word sentences, some built from elderly-themed words
Students are sent to another experiment in an office down the hall
Researchers unobtrusively time the walk along the corridor
Students are questioned and report noticing no common theme
questions.explain: The scrambled-sentence task came first; the short walk to another office was what the experiment was really about. Afterward none of the students reported noticing that the words had a common theme.

questions.q: Kahneman says the priming phenomenon in the Florida effect, the influencing of an action by an idea, is known as the ____ effect.
questions.explain: In the Florida effect the idea of old age changed how fast students walked. Kahneman names this influence of an idea on an action the ideomotor effect.

questions.q: Which of these words does Kahneman list as elderly-themed words used in Bargh's 'Florida effect' sentences?
options: Florida
wrinkle
bald
old
slow
questions.explain: The listed words were Florida, forgetful, bald, gray and wrinkle. Kahneman stresses that the word old was never mentioned, which is part of what makes the effect striking.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what are the two stages of priming in the 'Florida effect'?
options: The word old primes slow walking, and slow walking primes thoughts of Florida
Slow walking primes thoughts of age, and those thoughts prime elderly words
The words prime thoughts of old age, and those thoughts prime walking slowly
The words prime conscious images of the elderly, which students then imitate
questions.explain: First the set of words primes thoughts of old age without the word old ever appearing; then those thoughts prime a behavior associated with old age, walking slowly. All of this happens without awareness, so there is no conscious imitation.

questions.q: True or false: After Bargh's 'Florida effect' experiment, none of the students reported noticing that the scrambled words had a common theme.
questions.explain: When questioned, none of the students noticed the theme, and all insisted that the words could not have influenced what they did next.

questions.q: True or false: In the German study that mirrored Bargh's experiment, students who walked at about one-third of their normal pace were slower to recognize words related to old age.
questions.explain: They were quicker, not slower, to recognize words such as forgetful, old and lonely. The study showed that the ideomotor link also works in reverse.

questions.q: In The Associative Machine, match each study to its finding.
pairs: Bargh's scrambled sentences at NYU
Elderly-themed words made students walk more slowly
The German slow-walking study
Walking slowly sped up recognition of old-age words
Pencil held in the mouth
Students made to 'smile' found Far Side cartoons funnier
Headphone test with head movements
Nodders tended to accept radio editorials
Eyebrows squeezed into a frown
Stronger emotional response to upsetting pictures
questions.explain: Each study shows priming beyond words: ideas prime actions, and actions and gestures prime ideas and feelings, all without awareness.

questions.q: In the study where students rated cartoons from Gary Larson's The Far Side while holding a pencil in their mouths, what did Kahneman report?
options: Students who were 'frowning' found the cartoons funnier
Students who were 'smiling' found the cartoons funnier
Students noticed the pencil's effect and adjusted their ratings
The pencil position made no difference to humor ratings
questions.explain: Those whose faces were shaped into a smile, without being aware of it, rated the cartoons funnier than those shaped into a frown. It illustrates a reciprocal link: being amused makes you smile, and smiling makes you feel amused.

questions.q: In The Associative Machine, sort each finding by the direction of the priming link it shows.
groups: An action or gesture primes a thought or feeling

items.t: Elderly-themed sentences make students walk more slowly
Reading about the elderly makes you slower to rise from a chair
Walking at a third of normal pace speeds recognition of old-age words
A pencil-forced smile makes cartoons seem funnier
Nodding while listening increases acceptance of a message

questions.explain: The ideomotor effect runs from idea to action, as in the Florida effect. Kahneman shows that the link also runs in reverse, with bodily actions and gestures shaping thoughts and feelings.

questions.q: What does Kahneman mean by reciprocal links in the associative network, and why do they tend to produce a coherent reaction?
questions.a: Reciprocal links run both ways: thinking of old age makes you act old, and acting old (walking slowly) makes thoughts of old age more accessible; being amused makes you smile, and smiling makes you feel amused. Because each side reinforces the other, a primed thought produces a matching action, and the action in turn strengthens the thought. The result is a coherent reaction rather than a single isolated response.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say the common admonition to 'act calm and kind regardless of how you feel' is very good advice?
questions.a: Priming studies show that simple gestures and expressions shape thoughts and feelings without awareness: smiling makes cartoons seem funnier, and nodding makes people accept a message. Because there is a habitual link between a feeling and its physical expression, acting out calm and kindness tends to produce the feeling itself. So, he says, you are likely to be rewarded by actually feeling calm and kind.

questions.q: Before a stressful phone call, Dev deliberately holds a smile for a minute and then notices he feels somewhat more cheerful. Which idea from The Associative Machine best explains this?
options: The Lady Macbeth effect, in which a stained conscience seeks physical cleansing
Hume's principle of contiguity, which links events close in time
Money priming, which makes people more self-reliant
A reciprocal link in which smiling tends to make you feel amused
questions.explain: Kahneman notes that being amused tends to make you smile, and smiling tends to make you feel amused. Dev's deliberate smile works through that reciprocal link, much like the pencil and cartoon study.

questions.q: Put these stages in the study of association, as Kahneman describes them, in chronological order.
items: Hume reduces association to three principles
Researchers tally the first words people give in response to a cue word
Psychologists find that exposure to a word measurably eases related words
Priming is found to reach actions and emotions, not only words
questions.explain: Hume wrote in 1748. Until a few decades ago, associations were studied by tallying word responses; the 1980s brought measurable priming effects, and a further advance showed that actions and emotions can be primed too.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what was the 'major advance' that followed the discovery of priming with words?
options: Showing that priming happens only when people attend to the prime
Showing that priming works only for concepts closely related to the prime
Showing that primed ideas never spread to other ideas
Showing that actions and emotions can be primed by events we are not aware of
questions.explain: Kahneman says priming is not restricted to concepts and words: your actions and emotions can be primed by events of which you are not even aware. He calls this an alien idea that conscious experience cannot reveal.

questions.q: In The Associative Machine, match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Priming effect
Exposure to a word makes related words easier to evoke
Ideomotor effect
An idea influences an action
Florida effect
Elderly-themed words make young people walk more slowly
Reciprocal link
Smiling makes you feel amused, and amusement makes you smile
questions.explain: Kahneman defines a priming effect with EAT and SOUP, names the influence of an idea on an action the ideomotor effect, illustrates it with Bargh's Florida effect, and notes that many links in the associative network run both ways.

questions.q: In the study of Arizona precincts in 2000, what did Kahneman report about votes on propositions to increase school funding?
options: Support was greater when the polling station was in a school
Support was lower when the polling station was in a school
Polling station location had no measurable effect on support
Only parents were affected by the polling station location
questions.explain: Support for school funding was significantly greater when the polling station was in a school than at a nearby location. This challenges the view of voting as a deliberate act untouched by irrelevancies.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman reports that the effect of showing people images of classrooms and school lockers on support for a school initiative was smaller than the difference between parents and other voters.
questions.explain: The effect of the images was larger, not smaller, than the difference between parents and other voters, a result Kahneman marks with an exclamation point.

questions.q: Kahneman says the general theme of Kathleen Vohs's money-priming findings is that the idea of money primes ____.
questions.explain: Money primes individualism: a reluctance to be involved with others, to depend on others, or to accept demands from others.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman report about people primed with reminders of money?
options: They persevered almost twice as long on a hard problem before asking for help
They picked up fewer of the pencils an experimenter dropped
They placed two chairs farther apart for a get-acquainted conversation
They spent more time helping a confused fellow student
They showed a greater preference for working in groups
questions.explain: Money-primed people were more self-reliant, more selfish and more distant: they persisted longer alone, helped less, and set the chairs farther apart. The ideas that they helped more or preferred company get the findings backward: they were less willing to help and preferred being alone.

questions.q: In The Associative Machine, match each person to what Kahneman credits them with.
pairs: John Bargh
The 'Florida effect' study of elderly words and walking speed
Kathleen Vohs
Experiments showing that reminders of money prime individualism
David Hume
Reducing the principles of association to three
Timothy Wilson
A book titled Strangers to Ourselves
questions.explain: Bargh ran the NYU walking study, Vohs the money-priming research, Hume wrote the 1748 Enquiry on association, and Wilson wrote Strangers to Ourselves, which Kahneman uses to introduce the hidden System 1.

questions.q: Kahneman says the feeling that one's soul is stained appears to trigger a desire to cleanse one's body, an impulse dubbed the '____ effect'.
questions.explain: The impulse has been dubbed the “Lady Macbeth effect.” For example, thinking about stabbing a coworker in the back makes people more inclined to buy soap or disinfectant.

questions.q: In the experiment where participants were induced to 'lie' to an imaginary person, which products did they prefer afterward?
options: Phone liars preferred soap; e-mail liars preferred mouthwash
Both groups preferred soap over mouthwash
Phone liars preferred mouthwash; e-mail liars preferred soap
Neither group showed any product preference
questions.explain: The cleansing urge was specific to the body part involved in the sin: those who lied with their mouths on the phone wanted mouthwash, and those who lied with their hands by e-mail wanted soap.

questions.q: True or false: According to Kahneman, people recently asked to think of an action they are ashamed of are more likely to complete the fragments W_ _ H and S_ _ P as WASH and SOAP.
questions.explain: Shame makes WASH and SOAP more likely and WISH and SOUP less likely. Kahneman presents this as confirming Freudian insights about symbols and metaphors in unconscious associations.

questions.q: According to the priming studies Kahneman cites, what does reminding people of their mortality do?
options: It makes them more generous toward strangers
It makes them more resistant to any form of authority
It reduces their interest in cleansing products
It increases the appeal of authoritarian ideas
questions.explain: Reminders of mortality increase the appeal of authoritarian ideas, which may become reassuring in the context of the terror of death. Resistance to authority is the opposite of what the studies suggest.

questions.q: When audiences ask whether priming studies show we are completely at the mercy of whatever primes the environment provides, how does Kahneman answer?
questions.a: He says, of course not: the effects of primes are robust but not necessarily large. In the school-voting example, only a few voters out of a hundred, those whose preferences were uncertain, would vote differently because their precinct is in a school rather than a church. But he adds that a few percent could tip an election, so small effects still matter.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say that 'disbelief is not an option' about priming results, and why do people still tend not to believe the results apply to them?
questions.a: The results are not made up or statistical flukes, so we must accept the major conclusions and accept that they are true about ourselves. We resist because the results correspond to nothing in our subjective experience. But that experience is largely the story System 2 tells itself, while priming arises in System 1, to which we have no conscious access.

questions.q: Put the events of the 'honesty box' experiment in a British university office kitchen in order.
items: Staff pay for tea or coffee by dropping money into an honesty box
A banner poster appears above the price list without explanation
For ten weeks the image alternates weekly between eyes and flowers
Contributions are compared: almost three times as much in eye weeks
questions.explain: Staff had long paid by honesty box. A poster was then put up without warning, with a new image of eyes or flowers each week for ten weeks, and contributions changed significantly though no one commented on the decorations.

questions.q: In the British university office kitchen experiment, staff paid for tea or coffee by dropping money into an '____ box'.
questions.explain: Members of the office paid into an “honesty box,” and contributions per liter of milk were tracked while the poster above the price list changed weekly.

questions.q: In the honesty-box experiment, what did Kahneman report about contributions during weeks with a poster of eyes compared with weeks with a poster of flowers?
options: Contributions were about the same in both kinds of weeks
Contributions were almost three times as high in eye weeks
Contributions were higher in flower weeks
Contributions rose only after people commented on the eyes
questions.explain: Users contributed almost three times as much in eye weeks, starting at 70 pence per liter of milk in week 1 against about 15 pence in week 2. No one commented on the posters, so the effect occurred without awareness.

questions.q: Sort each prime from Primes That Guide Us by the effect Kahneman reports for it.

items.t: A screen saver of dollar bills floating in water
A stack of Monopoly money on a table
Building a money-themed phrase from scrambled words
Recalling an action one is ashamed of
Thinking about stabbing a coworker in the back
Lying to an imaginary person by e-mail

questions.explain: Vohs's money primes made people more self-reliant, selfish and distant. Moral primes such as shame, betrayal or lying produced the Lady Macbeth urge to cleanse, including WASH and SOAP completions and a preference for soap.

questions.q: What does Kahneman suggest Kathleen Vohs's money-priming findings imply about the cultures we live in?
questions.a: Living in a culture full of reminders of money may shape our behavior and attitudes in ways we do not know about and of which we may not be proud. Other cultures prime other things, such as respect, God, or obedience through huge images of the Dear Leader. Kahneman asks whether there can be any doubt that ubiquitous portraits of a national leader in dictatorial societies not only convey that 'Big Brother Is Watching' but also reduce spontaneous thought and independent action.

questions.q: In closing The Associative Machine with Timothy Wilson's phrase 'strangers to ourselves', what does Kahneman say System 1 does for us?
questions.a: System 1 is the stranger in you that may control much of what you do without your awareness. It provides the impressions that often turn into beliefs and the impulses that often become choices and actions, and it offers a tacit interpretation linking the present with the recent past and expectations about the near future. It holds the model of the world that instantly judges events as normal or surprising and is the source of rapid, often precise intuitions, as well as many systematic errors.

questions.q: A charity worried about honesty at an unstaffed snack stand hangs a picture of a pair of eyes above the payment jar, without any written message. Based on the honesty-box experiment, what should it expect?
options: No change, since a picture cannot affect behavior without a written warning
Higher payments, because a symbolic reminder of being watched prods better behavior
Lower payments, because people resent being watched and pay less
Higher payments only from customers who consciously notice the picture
questions.explain: Kahneman concludes that “a purely symbolic reminder of being watched prodded people into improved behavior.” The effect occurred without awareness, so conscious noticing is not required.

questions.q: A town holds a vote on a new tax to fund schools, and some precincts vote inside school buildings. Based on the Arizona study Kahneman describes, what is the most likely result?
options: Support is somewhat higher in precincts that vote inside schools
Support is identical everywhere, because voting reflects settled values
Support is lower inside schools, because voters resent the setting
Only voters who notice the setting are affected by it
questions.explain: The Arizona study found significantly more support for school funding when the polling station was in a school. Voters are not aware of the influence, and the effect is robust but not necessarily large.

questions.q: Using Kahneman's account of why audiences doubt priming results, sort each item by the system it belongs to.

items.t: The source of priming phenomena
The model of the world that judges events normal or surprising
The source of impulses that often become choices
Believes it is in charge and knows the reasons for its choices
Tells the story that makes up most of subjective experience

questions.explain: Kahneman says priming arises in System 1, which also holds our model of the world and generates impulses. System 2 believes it is in charge, and our subjective experience is largely the story it tells itself, which is why primes feel unbelievable.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman list as roles of System 1 at the close of The Associative Machine?
options: Providing the impressions that often turn into beliefs
Holding the model of the world that evaluates events as normal or surprising
Being the source of rapid and often precise intuitive judgments
Checking intuitions and correcting them before they become choices
Knowing the reasons behind each of our choices
questions.explain: Kahneman credits System 1 with impressions, the model of the world, and rapid intuitions, mostly without our awareness. Checking intuitions is not on his list, and the belief that we know our reasons belongs to System 2's story.

questions.q: Kahneman closes his discussion of priming by citing the psychologist Timothy Wilson's book '____ to Ourselves'.
questions.explain: Wilson's book is titled Strangers to Ourselves. Kahneman uses it to introduce System 1 as the stranger in you that may control much of what you do.

questions.q: In Kahneman's account of the Lady Macbeth effect and related studies, match each situation to the result it produced.
pairs: Lying to someone on the phone
Preferring mouthwash over soap
Lying to someone by e-mail
Preferring soap over mouthwash
Thinking about stabbing a coworker in the back
Leaning toward disinfectant or detergent over juice or candy
Recalling an action one is ashamed of
Completing word fragments as WASH and SOAP
questions.explain: A stained conscience triggers a wish to cleanse, and the wish is specific to the body part involved: the mouth for spoken lies, the hands for written ones.

questions.q: What is the Lady Macbeth effect, and what did the lying experiment add to it?
questions.a: The Lady Macbeth effect is the impulse to cleanse one's body when one's soul feels stained: thinking of a shameful act or of betraying a coworker makes people more drawn to washing words and cleansing products. The lying experiment showed that the cleansing is highly specific to the body parts involved in the sin. People who lied on the phone preferred mouthwash, while those who lied in e-mail preferred soap.

questions.q: Which of these primes does Kahneman describe being used in the money-priming experiments?
options: Building a money-themed phrase from five scrambled words
A stack of Monopoly money on a table in the background
A screen saver of dollar bills floating in water
Paying participants in cash before the task
Showing images of classrooms and school lockers
questions.explain: Kahneman lists the scrambled money phrase and subtler primes such as Monopoly money and a dollar-bill screen saver. Classroom images came from the school-voting research, and cash payment is not mentioned.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, why do audiences so often react with disbelief when he describes priming studies?
options: Because System 2 believes it is in charge and knows the reasons for its choices
Because the studies have small samples that make the results uncertain
Because the effects of primes are too large to be credible
Because people consciously notice the primes and discount them
questions.explain: He says disbelief is no surprise since System 2 believes it is in charge and knows why it chooses as it does. He insists the results are not flukes, and the primes work without awareness.

questions.q: A reviewer says of a committee: 'They were primed to find flaws, and this is exactly what they found.' What point from The Associative Machine does the remark apply?
options: Careful System 2 checking reliably uncovers real flaws
Money reminders make people more critical of others
A primed idea shapes what people notice and conclude, without their awareness
Priming effects disappear once people are warned about them
questions.explain: Priming makes associated ideas more accessible and guides judgment from outside awareness. The remark suggests the flaws the committee found reflect the prime, not a neutral review.

questions.q: Match each remark from Speaking of Priming in The Associative Machine to the idea it applies.
pairs: "The sight of all these people in uniforms does not prime creativity."
Surroundings prime behavior and thought
"The coherence comes mostly from the way your mind works."
Associative coherence is made by the mind, not found in the world
"His System 1 constructed a story, and his System 2 believed it."
System 2 accepts the stories System 1 builds
"I made myself smile and I'm actually feeling better!"
Reciprocal links: expressions can produce feelings
questions.explain: Each remark carries an idea from the chapter into everyday speech: environmental priming, associative coherence, System 1 storytelling, and the reciprocal link between smiling and feeling good.

questions.q: One remark in Speaking of Priming reads: 'The world makes much less sense than you think. The ____ comes mostly from the way your mind works.'
questions.explain: The remark applies the chapter's point that associative activation is coherent: System 1 links events into causal stories, so much of the sense we find is supplied by the mind.

questions.q: Explain the remark 'His System 1 constructed a story, and his System 2 believed it. It happens to all of us' using ideas from The Associative Machine.
questions.a: System 1 automatically links what it encounters into a causal story, as it did with 'Bananas Vomit', and it is the source of impressions that often turn into beliefs. System 2 believes it is in charge, yet our subjective experience is largely the story System 2 tells itself, without access to the System 1 processes behind it. So the story gets accepted as one's own reasoned view, and since priming affects everyone, it happens to all of us.

questions.q: Put these chapters from Part I, Two Systems, of Thinking, Fast and Slow in the order they appear.
items: The Lazy Controller
The Associative Machine
Cognitive Ease
Norms, Surprises, and Causes
questions.explain: The Associative Machine is Chapter 4, after The Lazy Controller (Chapter 3) and before Cognitive Ease (Chapter 5) and Norms, Surprises, and Causes (Chapter 6).

questions.q: How does Kahneman frame the opening of The Associative Machine within Part I, Two Systems?
options: As a summary of the heuristics covered in Part II
As the start of an exploration of the surprising workings of System 1
As a defense of System 2 as the true author of our choices
As an introduction to the choices studied in prospect theory
questions.explain: The chapter begins, “To begin your exploration of the surprising workings of System 1,” and moves from the effortful System 2 to the automatic associative network.

questions.q: Put the parts of The Associative Machine in the order they appear in the chapter.
items: The 'Bananas Vomit' demonstration and associative memory
The Marvels of Priming
Primes That Guide Us
Speaking of Priming
questions.explain: The chapter opens with the 'Bananas Vomit' demonstration and the idea of associative memory, then shows priming of words, actions and emotions, then priming in real life, and ends with the Speaking of Priming remarks.

questions.q: What does the title The Associative Machine signal about Kahneman's subject in Chapter 4?
options: System 2's effortful search through memory for related facts
A computer model that Kahneman built to simulate memory
System 1 as an automatic mechanism that spreads activation through linked ideas
Hume's philosophy of the mind as a sequence of conscious ideas
questions.explain: The chapter presents System 1 as working by association: evoked ideas automatically activate many others, quickly and without control. That automatic spread, not effortful search or a conscious sequence, is what makes it a machine.

questions.q: Which of these show how The Associative Machine connects to other parts of Thinking, Fast and Slow?
options: It ends by noting that System 1 is the origin of many systematic errors to be shown in later chapters
It follows The Lazy Controller and is followed by Cognitive Ease in Part I
It closes Part I, leading directly into Heuristics and Biases
It introduces the two characters, System 1 and System 2, for the first time
questions.explain: Chapter 4 sits between The Lazy Controller and Cognitive Ease and closes by promising that later chapters will show System 1 as the origin of many systematic errors. Part I continues to Chapter 9, and the two systems were introduced in Chapter 1.

questions.q: Why does it make sense for The Associative Machine to come after the chapters on System 2's effort and laziness and before the later chapters on errors of intuition?
questions.a: The earlier chapters show System 2 as effortful and often lazy, so much of our thinking is left to System 1. This chapter then explains how System 1 works: associative activation and priming shape impressions, beliefs and actions without awareness. Having introduced System 1 as the hidden source of beliefs and choices, Kahneman notes it is also “the origin of many of the systematic errors in your intuitions,” setting up the chapters that follow.

questions.q: In Kahneman's cockpit image of cognitive ease, match each element to its role.
pairs: The "Easy" reading
Things are going well: no threats, no major news, no need for effort
The "Strained" reading
A problem exists that will need more mobilization of System 2
System 1
Carries out the dial assessments automatically
System 2
Supplies the extra effort when the dial signals a problem
questions.explain: Kahneman pictures a cockpit of dials that System 1 updates automatically; one function of these assessments is to decide whether extra effort is needed from System 2.

questions.q: In Kahneman's cockpit image, the cognitive ease dial ranges between "Easy" and "____."
questions.explain: The dial runs from Easy, a sign that things are going well, to Strained, a sign that a problem exists and System 2 must be mobilized.

questions.q: In Kahneman's account of cognitive ease, sort each tendency by the state it goes with.

items.t: Being in a good mood
Believing what you hear
Trusting your intuitions
Thinking in a casual, superficial way
Being vigilant and suspicious
Investing more effort in the task
Making fewer errors
Being less creative than usual

questions.explain: Ease goes with good mood, belief, trust in intuition and superficial thinking; strain goes with vigilance, effort and fewer errors, but also less intuition and creativity.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman, describing Figure 5, list as things that make a sentence processed with cognitive ease?
options: Being printed in a clear font
Having been repeated
Having been primed
Being printed in washed-out gray type
Being heard while in a sad mood
questions.explain: Figure 5 shows a clear font, repetition and priming as causes of ease; a poor font and a bad mood work in the opposite direction, toward strain.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says the various causes of cognitive ease or strain have interchangeable effects.
questions.explain: This is the central lesson of Figure 5: a clear font, repetition, priming and good mood all produce the same feeling of ease, so one cause can stand in for another.

questions.q: In Kahneman's chapter on cognitive ease, what do the "Easy" and "Strained" readings of the cognitive ease dial signal, and who reads the dial?
questions.a: The dial is one of several assessments that System 1 carries out automatically. Easy is a sign that things are going well, with no threats, no major news and no need to redirect attention or mobilize effort. Strained indicates that a problem exists, which will require increased mobilization of System 2. So the dial helps decide whether extra effort is required from System 2.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what is the cost of being in a state of cognitive strain?
options: You are more likely to accept what you hear
You make more errors than usual
You are less intuitive and less creative than usual
You feel that the situation is comfortably familiar
questions.explain: Strain makes people vigilant and careful, so they make fewer errors, but they are also less intuitive and less creative. The idea that strain causes more errors reverses the finding.

questions.q: Kahneman says cognitive strain is affected by both the current level of effort and the presence of unmet ____.
questions.explain: Strain reflects not only how hard you are working right now but also demands that have not yet been met.

questions.q: Who first demonstrated in the laboratory the memory illusion in which a made-up name like David Stenbill comes to seem famous?
options: Robert Zajonc
Larry Jacoby
Danny Oppenheimer
Sarnoff Mednick
questions.explain: Larry Jacoby demonstrated the illusion. Zajonc is linked to the mere exposure effect, Oppenheimer to needlessly long words, and Mednick to the Remote Association Test.

questions.q: Larry Jacoby titled his article on how made-up names come to seem famous "Becoming Famous ____."
questions.explain: The title captures how a single earlier exposure can make an unknown name seem like a celebrity's.

questions.q: Jacoby said the experience of familiarity has a simple but powerful quality of "____" that seems to reflect prior experience.
questions.explain: Kahneman calls this quality of pastness an illusion: the feeling actually comes from the ease of seeing a word again.

questions.q: Put in order the steps by which a made-up name like David Stenbill comes to seem famous.
items: You see the made-up name once
Days later, the name is easier to see than new names
Seeing it easily produces cognitive ease
The ease gives an impression of familiarity
You judge the person to be a celebrity
questions.explain: Words seen before become easier to see again; this ease of perception is felt as familiarity, and familiarity without a file of information is taken as fame.

questions.q: True or false: In the false-fame illusion, people who judge David Stenbill to be well known can usually say whether they know him from movies, sports, or politics.
questions.explain: They cannot: they have no mental file about him, only a sense of familiarity, so they do not know in what context they met the name.

questions.q: In Kahneman's discussion of how you know whether someone is famous, sort each name by what you would have in mind when you see it.
groups: A rich mental file of information

items.t: Albert Einstein
Bono
Hillary Clinton
David Stenbill
Monica Bigoutski
Shana Tirana

questions.explain: For truly famous people you have a rich file of information; for the names Kahneman just made up, all you would have later is the feeling that you have seen the name somewhere.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say make a completely new word more likely to be recognized as familiar?
options: Unconsciously priming it for a few milliseconds before the test
Showing it in sharper contrast than other words in the list
Showing it more severely blurred than other words
Printing it in a fainter font than other words
questions.explain: Anything that makes a new word easier to see, such as unconscious priming or sharper contrast, gives it the quality of pastness; blurring or fading it would add strain instead.

questions.q: True or false: In the task of picking out the more clearly shown words from a list of blurred words, a word you have seen recently appears clearer than unfamiliar words.
questions.explain: This is the link working in the other direction: familiarity makes a word seem easier to see, just as ease of seeing makes a word seem familiar.

questions.q: In Kahneman's account of illusions of remembering, how does the illusion of familiarity come about?
questions.a: A word you have seen before is easier to see again, and this cognitive ease is what gives the impression of familiarity. Because the various ways of inducing ease or strain are interchangeable, you may not know what made something easy. So ease produced by other causes, such as priming or sharper contrast, is also felt as familiarity, and a new word can seem to have been seen before.

questions.q: A week after skimming a list of invented company names, Priya sees one of them in a quiz and feels sure it is a real, well-known firm. Which idea from Kahneman best explains her error?
options: She retrieved a rich mental file about the company
Strain from the quiz mobilized her System 2
The ease of seeing a name again felt like familiarity
Rhyming names are judged more insightful than others
questions.explain: As with David Stenbill, a name seen before is processed more easily, and that ease feels like familiarity and fame. She has no file of information about the firm.

questions.q: In Kahneman's illusions of truth discussion, why is "A chicken has four legs" judged false more slowly than "A chicken has three legs"?
options: Associative memory supplies that many animals have four legs
System 2 refuses to judge statements about animals
Chickens are more often pictured with four legs than three
The first sentence is printed in a harder font to read
questions.explain: The associative machinery delivers the facts that many animals have four legs, and perhaps that chicken legs are sold in packs of four, which slows the judgment.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that when he took driving tests in a new state, he assumed that an answer that felt familiar was probably true.
questions.explain: Where no good answer came to mind, all he had was cognitive ease: familiar answers were taken as true, and new or improbably extreme ones were rejected.

questions.q: Kahneman says a reliable way to make people believe in falsehoods is frequent ____, because familiarity is not easily distinguished from truth.
questions.explain: Repetition creates familiarity, and familiarity is easily mistaken for truth.

questions.q: What did the experiment with the phrase "the body temperature of a chicken" show?
options: Statements about animals are judged more slowly than others
Repeating one phrase made a whole statement more believable
People reject arbitrary numbers once they hear them repeated
Only a full statement repeated many times gains belief
questions.explain: People repeatedly exposed to the phrase were more likely to accept as true that a chicken's body temperature is 144 degrees; the familiarity of one phrase made the whole statement feel familiar and true.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say leave you with no option but to go with the sense of cognitive ease when judging a statement?
options: You cannot remember the source of the statement
You have no way to relate it to other things you know
The statement contradicts facts you know well
You studied the topic and recall the logic behind it
questions.explain: Without a remembered source or links to other knowledge, ease is the only cue left. When you know contradicting facts or the underlying logic, you are not forced to rely on ease.

questions.q: In Kahneman's driving-test story, how did System 1 and System 2 share the work of judging an answer when no good answer came to mind?
questions.a: System 1 produced an impression of familiarity, which is a form of cognitive ease. System 2 then relied on that impression to make the true or false judgment. If the answer felt familiar, Kahneman assumed it was probably true; if it looked new or improbably extreme, he rejected it.

questions.q: In Kahneman's illusions of truth discussion, match each statement to how people respond to it.
pairs: "New York is a large city in the United States"
Quickly known to be true
"A chicken has three legs"
Obviously false
"A chicken has four legs"
False, but judged more slowly
"The body temperature of a chicken is 144°"
Believed more after exposure to part of it
questions.explain: Related information arrives quickly for each statement, but associations about four-legged animals slow the chicken judgment, and repeated exposure to a phrase lends belief to an arbitrary number.

questions.q: Kahneman says authoritarian institutions and marketers have always known something about repetition. What did psychologists add to this?
questions.a: Authoritarian institutions and marketers have long known that frequent repetition makes people believe falsehoods, because familiarity is not easily distinguished from truth. Psychologists discovered that you do not have to repeat the entire statement to make it appear true. Repeated exposure to just one phrase, such as the body temperature of a chicken, made the whole statement feel familiar and therefore true.

questions.q: What does Kahneman call the lesson of Figure 5 for judgments of truth?
questions.a: Predictable illusions inevitably occur if a judgment is based on an impression of cognitive ease or strain. Anything that makes it easier for the associative machine to run smoothly will also bias beliefs. So repetition, partial familiarity or other sources of ease can make a statement feel true even when it is not.

questions.q: Marco has heard a claim about a miracle diet so many times that he now insists it is common knowledge. He cannot recall where he heard it. What does Kahneman's account of illusions of truth suggest?
options: His System 2 has checked the claim against what he knows
Repetition made the claim familiar, and familiarity feels true
Hearing it often has made him suspicious and vigilant
He believes it because it was printed in a pale color
questions.explain: Familiarity from repetition is not easily distinguished from truth, and when the source is forgotten there is little to go on except the sense of ease.

questions.section: How to Write a Persuasive Message
questions.q: In Kahneman's advice on writing a persuasive message, what general advice does the example of two false birth years for Adolf Hitler illustrate?
options: Choose sources with easy names
Put your ideas in verse
Avoid needlessly long words
Maximize legibility
questions.explain: Kahneman introduces the Hitler statements right after saying you should first maximize legibility; experiments showed the more legible version is more likely to be believed.

questions.section: How to Write a Persuasive Message
questions.q: Kahneman's general principle for a persuasive message is that anything you can do to reduce cognitive ____ will help.
questions.explain: All of his specific tips, from legible print to easy names, are ways of reducing strain so that the message feels easy and therefore true.

questions.section: How to Write a Persuasive Message
questions.q: What general principle lies behind Kahneman's advice on how to write a persuasive message, and what practical steps follow from it?
questions.a: The general principle is that anything you can do to reduce cognitive strain will help a true message be believed. So you should maximize legibility, for example with high-quality paper and bright blue or red rather than middling colors. You should use simple rather than complex language, make the message memorable, ideally in verse, and quote a source whose name is easy to pronounce.

questions.section: How to Write a Persuasive Message
questions.q: Danny Oppenheimer showed that couching familiar ideas in ____ language is taken as a sign of poor intelligence and low credibility.
questions.explain: His article, with its deliberately long-winded title, refuted the undergraduate myth that professors are impressed by complex vocabulary.

questions.section: How to Write a Persuasive Message
questions.q: Put Kahneman's tips for writing a persuasive message in the order he presents them.
items: Maximize legibility
Use simple rather than complex language
Make it memorable, ideally in verse
Quote a source with an easy-to-pronounce name
questions.explain: Kahneman moves from legibility (font, paper, color) to simple language, then rhyme, and finally the choice of an easily pronounced source.

questions.section: How to Write a Persuasive Message
questions.q: Which of these are the rhyming versions of aphorisms in the experiment Kahneman describes?
options: Woes unite foes
Little strokes will tumble great oaks
A fault admitted is half redressed
Woes unite enemies
A fault confessed is half redressed
Little strokes will tumble great trees
questions.explain: The rhyming originals end in foes, oaks and confessed; the transformed versions swap in enemies, trees and admitted, which break the rhyme.

questions.section: How to Write a Persuasive Message
questions.q: In Kahneman's advice on persuasion, match each example to the lesson it teaches.
pairs: Two false birth years for Hitler
Make the message legible
"Woes unite foes" versus "Woes unite enemies"
Rhyming sayings are judged more insightful
Brokerage reports from Artan and Taahhut
Easy-to-pronounce sources get more weight
Oppenheimer's article on long words
Pretentious language lowers credibility
questions.explain: Each study shows a different way of reducing strain that makes a message more believable or its author more credible.

questions.section: How to Write a Persuasive Message
questions.q: In the experiment on fictitious Turkish companies, what would have been the best procedure for observers given two disagreeing brokerage reports?
options: Trust the report from the firm with the easier name
Average the two reports
Trust the report that was read first
Ignore both reports and guess
questions.explain: Kahneman says averaging was the best procedure, but observers instead gave much more weight to the report from Artan than to the one from Taahhut.

questions.section: How to Write a Persuasive Message
questions.q: In the brokerage-report experiment, why did observers give more weight to the report from Artan than to the report from Taahhut?
questions.a: Kahneman explains that System 2 is lazy and that mental effort is aversive. The recipients of a message want to stay away from anything that reminds them of effort, including a source with a complicated name. So the easily pronounced name, which caused less strain, was trusted more, even though averaging the two reports would have been better.

questions.section: How to Write a Persuasive Message
questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says high-quality paper, bright colors, and rhyming language can make even an obviously nonsensical message believable.
