questions.explain: He warns against getting carried away: these devices will not be much help if a message is obviously nonsensical or contradicts facts the audience knows.

questions.section: How to Write a Persuasive Message
questions.q: What limits does Kahneman place on his advice about using cognitive ease to persuade, and what do psychologists actually believe about people?
questions.a: Kahneman says the tricks will not help much if a message is obviously nonsensical or contradicts facts the audience knows to be true. Psychologists do not believe people are stupid or infinitely gullible. They believe we live much of our life guided by System 1's impressions without knowing their source, and although people can overcome superficial causes of truth illusions when strongly motivated, on most occasions the lazy System 2 adopts the suggestions of System 1.

questions.section: How to Write a Persuasive Message
questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give as reasons a statement can feel true because of how it fits what you already believe or trust, rather than because of superficial features?
options: It is strongly linked by logic or association to beliefs you hold
It comes from a source you trust and like
It is printed in a high-quality font
Its prose has an appealing rhythm
questions.explain: Links to your other beliefs and a trusted, liked source are genuine reasons for ease. The font and the rhythm of the prose are the other, superficial causes that you cannot easily tell apart from the genuine ones.

questions.section: How to Write a Persuasive Message
questions.q: In Kahneman's advice on persuasion, sort each feature by its effect on whether a message is believed.

items.t: High-quality paper with strong contrast
Text in bright blue or red
A rhyming phrasing
A source with an easily pronounced name
Text in middling green, yellow, or pale blue
Needlessly long, pretentious words
A source with a hard-to-pronounce name

questions.explain: Features that reduce strain help belief; middling colors, pretentious vocabulary and tongue-twisting source names add strain and reduce credibility.

questions.section: How to Write a Persuasive Message
questions.q: A student rewrites a scholarship essay, replacing plain words with obscure synonyms to sound brilliant. According to the Oppenheimer study Kahneman describes, what is the likely effect?
options: Readers will find the essay more insightful
Readers will judge the writer more intelligent
Readers will judge the writer less intelligent
Readers will not notice the change in wording
questions.explain: Oppenheimer showed that couching familiar ideas in pretentious language is taken as a sign of poor intelligence and low credibility, the opposite of the student's hope.

questions.q: In the study where 40 Princeton students took the Cognitive Reflection Test, what share made at least one mistake?
options: 35% with the normal font and 90% with the bad font
90% with the normal font and 35% with the bad font
50% with the normal font and 35% with the bad font
90% with both the normal and the bad font
questions.explain: Performance was better with the bad font: 90% erred with normal print, but only 35% when the print was barely legible.

questions.q: Shane Frederick's test made of the bat-and-ball problem and two other puzzles is called the Cognitive ____ Test.
questions.explain: The Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) uses puzzles that invite an immediate intuitive answer that is wrong.

questions.q: In the Princeton study of the Cognitive Reflection Test, sort each description by the group it fits.

items.t: Read the puzzles in clear, ordinary print
90% made at least one mistake
More likely to accept System 1's intuitive answer
Read the puzzles in small, washed-out gray print
35% made at least one mistake
Experienced cognitive strain while reading

questions.explain: The barely legible font induced strain, which mobilized System 2 and led to fewer mistakes; the normal-font group went with the intuitive answers more often.

questions.q: Why were the three puzzles in Shane Frederick's Cognitive Reflection Test chosen?
options: They each evoke an immediate intuitive answer that is incorrect
They are too hard for most students to solve
They require arithmetic that System 1 cannot do
They have no single correct answer
questions.explain: All three items, including the widgets and lily pad problems, were chosen because a quick, wrong intuitive answer comes to mind, testing whether people check their first idea.

questions.q: In Kahneman's discussion of strain and effort, what is the self-reinforcing reciprocity between cognitive strain and System 2?
questions.a: On one hand, cognitive strain is experienced when the effortful operations of System 2 are engaged. On the other hand, the experience of strain, whatever its source, tends to mobilize System 2. This shifts people's approach to problems from a casual intuitive mode to a more engaged and analytic mode, just as smiling and feeling happy reinforce each other in associative coherence.

questions.q: Put in order the steps and logic of the Princeton study on the Cognitive Reflection Test and font.
items: 40 Princeton students are recruited to take the CRT
Half see the puzzles in a small, washed-out gray font
The poor font induces cognitive strain
Strain mobilizes System 2
Fewer students give the intuitive wrong answers
questions.explain: Kahneman concludes that strain, whatever its source, mobilizes System 2, which is more likely to reject the intuitive answer suggested by System 1.

questions.q: A team wants reviewers to catch tempting but wrong conclusions in a report. Based on the Cognitive Reflection Test font study, which change would most likely help?
options: Printing the report in a large, very clear font
Having reviewers read it while in a cheerful mood
Repeating the key conclusions several times
Printing the report in a font that is harder to read
questions.explain: The bad font induced strain, which mobilized System 2 and reduced intuitive errors. Clear print, good mood and repetition all increase ease and would encourage acceptance instead.

questions.q: Which of these puzzles does Kahneman say make up Shane Frederick's Cognitive Reflection Test?
options: The bat-and-ball problem
The 5 machines making 5 widgets problem
The lily pads doubling in a lake problem
The triad dive, light, rocket
The aphorism "Woes unite foes"
questions.explain: The CRT consists of the bat-and-ball problem and the widgets and lily pad problems. The word triad belongs to the Remote Association Test, and the aphorism to a study of rhyme.

questions.q: In the experiment described in "Mind at Ease Puts a Smile on the Face," how were participants' emotional reactions measured?
options: By asking them to rate how much they liked each picture
By measuring the size of their pupils
By trained observers watching their facial expressions
By recording electrical impulses from facial muscles
questions.explain: Facial muscle recordings picked up changes too slight and too brief for observers to detect, revealing a faint smile when pictures were easier to see.

questions.q: From the "Mind at Ease" experiment, Kahneman concludes it is a feature of System 1 that cognitive ease is associated with good ____.
questions.explain: People showed a faint smile and relaxed brows when pictures were made easier to see, linking ease to positive emotion.

questions.q: Which of these findings about pronounceable names does Kahneman report?
options: Companies with pronounceable names do better in the first week after the stock is issued
Stocks with pronounceable tickers like KAR outperform those with tickers like PXG
The first-week advantage of pronounceable company names grows over time
Swiss investors expect clunky names like Ypsomed to earn higher returns
questions.explain: The first-week advantage of pronounceable company names disappears over time, and Swiss investors expected fluent names like Emmi and Comet, not clunky ones, to earn more.

questions.q: Robert Zajonc called the link between repetition of an arbitrary stimulus and the mild affection people develop for it the mere ____ effect.
questions.explain: The mere exposure effect: repeated exposure alone, with no other reason, makes people like a stimulus more.

questions.q: Put in order the steps of the mere exposure study run in the Michigan student newspapers.
items: Ad-like boxes with Turkish-sounding words appear on the front page
Each word appears a different number of times, from once to 25 times
The series of ads ends
Questionnaires ask whether each word means something good or bad
More frequently shown words are rated more favorably
questions.explain: The words were repeated with different frequencies for some weeks, then readers rated them, and frequency predicted favorability.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman reports that the mere exposure effect is actually stronger for stimuli that the individual never consciously sees.
questions.explain: The effect does not depend on consciousness at all; it occurs, and is even stronger, when words or pictures are flashed too quickly to be noticed.

questions.q: According to Zajonc, why does the mere exposure effect occur?
options: Familiar stimuli are easier for System 2 to analyze
Repeated stimuli become associated with rewards
A repeated stimulus is followed by nothing bad and becomes a safety signal
People consciously remember liking what they have seen before
questions.explain: Zajonc argued that caution toward novelty fades when repeated exposure brings nothing bad, so the stimulus becomes a signal of safety, and safety is good.

questions.q: In Kahneman's discussion of the pleasure of cognitive ease, match each study to its finding.
pairs: Chinese ideographs, faces, and random polygons
Confirmed that repeated exposure increases liking
Tones played to fertile chicken eggs
Hatched chicks gave fewer distress calls to the familiar tone
Swiss stock names like Emmi and Comet
Investors expected them to earn higher returns
Outlines flashed before pictures of objects
Viewers smiled faintly when pictures were easier to see
questions.explain: Each study links ease or familiarity to good feelings: liking, reduced distress, optimism about returns, and a faint smile.

questions.q: Why did Zajonc argue that the mere exposure effect is a profoundly important biological fact that extends to all animals?
questions.a: To survive in a dangerous world, an organism should react cautiously to a novel stimulus, with withdrawal and fear. But it is also adaptive for that caution to fade if the stimulus is actually safe; repeated exposure followed by nothing bad turns the stimulus into a safety signal, and safety is good. To show this is not restricted to humans, an associate exposed chicken eggs to tones, and the hatched chicks gave fewer distress calls to the familiar tone.

questions.q: Which of these kinds of stimuli does Kahneman say have been used in experiments confirming the mere exposure effect?
options: Chinese ideographs
Faces
Randomly shaped polygons
Rhyming aphorisms
Brokerage reports
questions.explain: The Michigan newspaper finding was confirmed with Chinese ideographs, faces and random polygons. Aphorisms and brokerage reports belong to studies of truth and persuasion.

questions.q: Zajonc wrote that the consequences of repeated exposures are the most primitive basis of social ____.
questions.explain: Zajonc argued that repeated exposure lets an organism tell safe objects from unsafe ones and so forms the basis of social organization and cohesion.

questions.q: A café plays the same unfamiliar song every day. Regulars come to like it, though few remember noticing it. Which idea from Kahneman best explains this?
options: The mere exposure effect
The illusion of truth
The Cognitive Reflection Test
The Remote Association Test
questions.explain: Repetition of an arbitrary stimulus produces mild affection for it, and the mere exposure effect does not require conscious awareness of the exposures.

questions.q: How does the mere exposure effect show that System 1 can respond to events that System 2 is unaware of?
questions.a: The mere exposure effect does not depend on the conscious experience of familiarity, or on consciousness at all. It occurs even when repeated words or pictures are shown so quickly that observers never become aware of seeing them, and they still end up liking the ones shown more often. The effect is actually stronger for stimuli that are never consciously seen, so System 1 is responding to impressions that System 2 never registers.

questions.q: In Kahneman's discussion of pronounceable names in the stock market, sort each name or ticker.

items.t: Emmi
Swissfirst
Comet
KAR
Geberit
Ypsomed
PXG
RDO

questions.explain: Kahneman contrasts fluent names and tickers like Emmi, Swissfirst, Comet and KAR with clunky or tongue-twisting ones like Geberit, Ypsomed, PXG and RDO.

questions.q: What did Sarnoff Mednick believe was the essence of creativity?
options: Associative memory that works exceptionally well
The effortful control of System 2 over impulses
A good mood that loosens vigilance
The ability to reject intuitive answers
questions.explain: Mednick's simple but powerful idea was that creativity is associative memory working exceptionally well, which he measured with the Remote Association Test.

questions.q: Mednick's test of creativity, in which people find a word linked to three others, is called the Remote ____ Test.
questions.explain: The Remote Association Test (RAT) asks for a word associated with all three words of a triad.

questions.q: In Kahneman's examples from the Remote Association Test, match each triad to its solution.
pairs: cottage Swiss cake
cheese
dive light rocket
sky
salt deep foam
sea
dream ball book
No shared association
questions.explain: Cheese is the easy example, sky the hard one that fewer than 20% of students found in 15 seconds, sea the coherent triad that brings a slight smile, and dream, ball, book has no solution.

questions.q: In the German study of mood and the Remote Association Test, why were subjects given only 2 seconds to guess whether a triad was linked?
options: To keep them in the mood they had been put in
Because longer times made them lose interest
So that the actual solution could not come to mind
To prevent them from smiling at coherent triads
questions.explain: Two seconds was much too short for anyone to retrieve the solution, so accurate guesses had to rest on a feeling that a solution existed.

questions.q: True or false: In the German study of the Remote Association Test, people's 2-second guesses about whether a triad was linked were no better than chance.
questions.explain: The first surprise was that guesses were much more accurate than chance, apparently guided by a faint signal of cognitive ease from the associative machine.

questions.q: Which of these manipulations did a German team find increase the tendency to see a word triad as linked?
options: Priming
A clear font
Pre-exposing the words
Putting subjects in a sad mood
Telling subjects that music influences their emotions
questions.explain: Priming, a clear font and pre-exposure all increase cognitive ease, confirming its role. A sad mood destroyed intuitive accuracy, and the music cover story eliminated the intuition of coherence.

questions.q: In the German study, how did mood affect the "intuition index" of accuracy on linked and unlinked triads?
options: Sad subjects were more accurate than happy ones
Mood had no measurable effect on accuracy
Both moods improved accuracy by about the same amount
Happy thoughts more than doubled accuracy
questions.explain: A good mood more than doubled accuracy, while unhappy subjects were completely unable to perform the task; their guesses were no better than random.

questions.q: Kahneman describes two clusters of states that go together. Sort each item into its cluster.

items.t: Intuition
Creativity
Gullibility
Reliance on System 1
Vigilance
Suspicion
An analytic approach
Increased effort

questions.explain: Good mood, intuition, creativity, gullibility and reliance on System 1 form one cluster; sadness, vigilance, suspicion, an analytic approach and effort form the other.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say the link between mood and the control of System 2 makes biological sense?
questions.a: A good mood is a signal that things are generally going well, the environment is safe, and it is all right to let one's guard down; so a happy mood loosens System 2's control and people become more intuitive and creative but less vigilant. A bad mood indicates that things are not going well and there may be a threat, so vigilance is required. As in the mere exposure effect, the connection makes biological sense.

questions.q: Put in order the steps of the German study of mood and the Remote Association Test.
items: Subjects think about happy or sad episodes in their lives
They see a series of triads, half linked and half unlinked
They press a key within 2 seconds to guess whether each is linked
Accuracy is scored with an intuition index
questions.explain: Mood was induced first, then subjects made rapid guesses on linked and unlinked triads, and their accuracy was computed as an intuition index.

questions.q: What does the slight smile people show when reading a coherent triad such as "salt deep foam" reveal about cognitive ease?
questions.a: Measurements of facial muscles show a slight smile when people read a coherent triad, even when they are told nothing about common associates and are merely asked to press the space bar after reading. This suggests that the impression of cognitive ease that comes with a coherent triad is mildly pleasurable in itself.

questions.q: How did the music cover-story experiment show that good feelings actually cause intuitions of coherence, not merely occur alongside them?
questions.a: Some participants were told that music in their earphones influences emotional reactions, giving them another explanation for their good feeling. This completely eliminated the intuition of coherence. So the brief emotional response to a triad, pleasant if coherent, is the basis of the coherence judgment; once the feeling is expected and blamed on the music, it is no longer linked to the words.

questions.q: Kahneman concludes that cognitive ease is both a cause and a ____ of a pleasant feeling.
questions.explain: Ease produces good feelings, as the faint smile shows, and a good mood in turn increases ease and reliance on intuition.

questions.q: True or false: When participants in the Remote Association Test study were told that music in their earphones influences emotional reactions, their intuition of coherence became stronger.
questions.explain: The cover story completely eliminated the intuition of coherence, because the pleasant feeling was now attributed to the music rather than to the words.

questions.q: Elena gets wonderful news in the morning and that afternoon agrees to an investment pitch without reading the fine print. What does Kahneman's account of ease and mood suggest?
options: Her good mood mobilized System 2 to check the offer
Her good mood has no bearing on how carefully she thinks
Her good mood made her more suspicious of novelty
Her good mood loosened System 2's control and vigilance
questions.explain: A happy mood loosens the control of System 2: people become more intuitive and creative but also less vigilant and more prone to logical errors.

questions.q: Someone says, "I'm in a very good mood today, and my System 2 is weaker than usual. I should be extra careful." Which finding from Kahneman's chapter on cognitive ease does this apply?
options: A happy mood makes people less vigilant
Repetition makes statements feel true
A poor font improves reasoning
Repeated exposure breeds liking
questions.explain: A good mood loosens System 2's control over performance, making people less vigilant and more prone to logical errors, so extra care is warranted.

questions.q: Match each remark from Kahneman's "Speaking of Cognitive Ease" examples to the idea behind it.
pairs: "Let's not dismiss their business plan just because the font makes it hard to read."
A poor font causes strain that should not decide a judgment
"We must be inclined to believe it because it has been repeated so often."
Repetition creates familiarity that is mistaken for truth
"Familiarity breeds liking."
The mere exposure effect
"My System 2 is weaker than usual."
A good mood loosens System 2's vigilance
questions.explain: Each remark applies one of the chapter's findings: strain from a font, illusions of truth from repetition, mere exposure, and the effect of mood on System 2.

questions.q: How does Kahneman link "Cognitive Ease" to the preceding chapter, "The Associative Machine"?
options: It shows how the ease with which the associative machine runs shapes judgments of truth and liking
It abandons associative memory to focus on statistical reasoning
It introduces System 1 and System 2 for the first time
It shows that associative links work in only one direction
questions.explain: The chapter builds on associative coherence: anything that makes it easier for the associative machine to run smoothly also biases beliefs, and the same two-way links, like the pencil smile, appear in cognitive ease.

questions.q: In Part I of Thinking, Fast and Slow, which chapter comes immediately after "Cognitive Ease"?
options: The Associative Machine
A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
The Lazy Controller
Norms, Surprises, and Causes
questions.explain: Chapter 5, Cognitive Ease, is followed by chapter 6, Norms, Surprises, and Causes; The Associative Machine comes just before it.

questions.q: Put the sections of Kahneman's chapter "Cognitive Ease" in the order they appear.
items: Illusions of Remembering
Illusions of Truth
How to Write a Persuasive Message
Strain and Effort
The Pleasure of Cognitive Ease
Ease, Mood, and Intuition
questions.explain: The chapter moves from memory and truth illusions to persuasion, then to how strain mobilizes System 2, and finally to the links between ease, good feeling, mood and intuition.

questions.q: What does the title "Cognitive Ease" signal about this chapter's role in Part I, "Two Systems"?
questions.a: The title names the dial that System 1 automatically reads, running from Easy to Strained, which helps decide whether System 2 must be mobilized. The chapter shows that this single feeling has many interchangeable causes, such as repetition, clear fonts, priming and good mood, and many consequences, including familiarity, belief, liking and trust in intuition. It thus connects the workings of the associative System 1 to when the lazy System 2 steps in.

questions.q: Put these chapters of Part I, "Two Systems," of Thinking, Fast and Slow in order.
items: The Lazy Controller
The Associative Machine
Cognitive Ease
Norms, Surprises, and Causes
A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.explain: Cognitive Ease is chapter 5, after The Lazy Controller (3) and The Associative Machine (4), and before Norms, Surprises, and Causes (6) and A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions (7).

questions.q: Kahneman's chapter "Cognitive Ease" draws on ideas from earlier chapters. Match each earlier idea to how this chapter uses it.
pairs: Smiling with a pencil held in the mouth
Shows associative links run in both directions, as ease and strain do
The bat-and-ball problem
Part of the test showing a bad font improves performance
The lazy System 2
Explains why readers avoid sources with hard names
questions.explain: Kahneman explicitly recalls the pencil studies of associative coherence, the bat-and-ball problem, and the laziness of System 2 to explain cognitive ease findings.

questions.q: At the start of Chapter 6, Kahneman says the spreading of activation in the associative machine is ____, although System 2 has some ability to control the search of memory.
questions.explain: The opening recaps that activation spreads automatically, while we (System 2) can partly steer memory search and program attention to detect events.

questions.q: How does the opening of Chapter 6 describe the mental 'computer' we carry in our heads?
questions.a: Kahneman describes a remarkably powerful computer that is not fast by conventional hardware standards but can represent the structure of our world through associative links in a vast network of ideas. Activation spreads through this associative machine automatically, while System 2 can partly control memory search and program it to notice events. The chapter then goes into more detail about what System 1 can and cannot do.

questions.q: According to its opening paragraph, what is Chapter 6 meant to do within Part 1 of Thinking, Fast and Slow?
options: Introduce System 1 and System 2 for the first time
Argue that System 2 is the main source of judgment errors
Present the book's first experiments on choices between gambles
Go into more detail on the wonders and limitations of System 1
questions.explain: The opening says the central features of both systems have already been introduced and that the chapter will go into more detail of what System 1 can do. The idea that the systems are introduced here for the first time is wrong because that happened in earlier chapters.

questions.q: True or false: In Chapter 6, Kahneman links the Moses illusion back to the triads that produce cognitive ease, the topic of the previous chapter.
questions.explain: He says that, as with the triads that produce cognitive ease, you unconsciously detect associative coherence between Moses and the ark and accept the question.

questions.q: Which of these links to other parts of the book does Chapter 6 make?
options: It compares the Moses illusion to the triads that produce cognitive ease
It says the misuse of causal thinking where statistics are needed is a recurrent theme of the book
It says the chapter introduces System 1 and System 2 for the first time
It says the chapter closes the discussion of System 1 for the rest of the book
questions.explain: The chapter ties the Moses illusion to cognitive ease and calls the prominence of causal intuitions a recurrent theme. It does not introduce the two systems, which its opening says were already introduced.

questions.q: Put the parts of Chapter 6, Norms, Surprises, and Causes, in the order they appear.
items: Recap of System 1 as a powerful associative machine
Assessing normality
Seeing causes and intentions
Speaking of norms and causes
questions.explain: The chapter recaps the associative machine, then shows how System 1 maintains norms and detects surprises, then how it sees causes and intentions, and ends with example sentences.

questions.q: Why does Chapter 6, Norms, Surprises, and Causes, fit between Cognitive Ease (Chapter 5) and A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions (Chapter 7)?
questions.a: Chapter 5 shows how associative coherence produces a feeling of ease, and Chapter 6 extends this by showing how System 1 maintains a model of what is normal, detects surprises, and automatically constructs coherent causal stories. That automatic readiness to link fragments into a causal story prepares the next chapter, whose title presents System 1 as a machine for jumping to conclusions.

questions.q: In Chapter 6, what does Kahneman call the main function of System 1?
options: To check the logic of the conclusions System 2 proposes
To store an exact record of everything that has happened
To maintain and update a model of your personal world that represents what is normal in it
To compute the probability of every event before it happens
questions.explain: Kahneman says the main function of System 1 is to maintain and update a model of the personal world representing what is normal. The model is built from associations among events that co-occur regularly, not from computed probabilities.

questions.q: Kahneman writes that ____ itself is the most sensitive indication of how we understand our world and what we expect from it.
questions.explain: A capacity for surprise is called an essential aspect of mental life, and surprise is the most sensitive sign of our expectations.

questions.q: True or false: Passively expected events are ones you do not wait for, yet you are not surprised when they happen.
questions.explain: Kahneman describes a large category of events expected passively: they are normal in a situation though not probable enough to be actively expected.

questions.q: Match each term from Chapter 6 to its meaning.
pairs: Active expectation
A conscious wait for a particular event, such as the door opening
Passive expectation
An event you do not wait for but are not surprised by
Norm for a category
The typical case plus the range of plausible values
Norm theory
Kahneman and Miller's account of how events come to seem normal or abnormal
questions.explain: These are the chapter's core terms: two varieties of expectation, norms that include both average and range, and the theory written with Dale Miller.

questions.q: What are the two main varieties of surprise that Kahneman describes in Chapter 6?
questions.a: Some expectations are active and conscious, as when you wait for the sound of the door as your child returns from school, and you are surprised if the expected event does not occur. A much larger category of events is expected passively: you do not wait for them, but you are not surprised when they happen because they are normal in the situation, though not probable enough to be actively expected.

questions.q: In the story of meeting Jon in a London theater, why were Kahneman and his wife less surprised the second time?
options: The first meeting had changed the idea of Jon into someone who shows up when they travel abroad
They had calculated that meeting Jon a second time was actually quite probable
Jon had told them in advance that he would be in London
They were too tired after the theater to feel any surprise
questions.explain: The first meeting made Jon “the psychologist who shows up when we travel abroad,” so System 1 made meeting him seem almost normal. They knew the second meeting was actually the more remarkable coincidence.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman and his wife were more surprised to meet Jon in the London theater than they had been to meet him on the Great Barrier Reef island.
questions.explain: They were distinctly less surprised the second time, even though they knew it was the more remarkable coincidence, because the first meeting had changed their idea of Jon.

questions.q: Put the events of Kahneman's story about his acquaintance Jon in order.
items: Kahneman and his wife meet Jon at dinner on a small island resort
Jon leaves the resort the next day
About two weeks later a latecomer sits next to Kahneman in a London theater
At the intermission Kahneman sees that his neighbor is Jon
questions.explain: The island meeting came first; two weeks later in London the latecomer turned out to be Jon, which surprised them less than the first meeting.

questions.q: In the story of the burning cars on the road from New York City to Princeton, what turned a passive expectation into an active one?
options: A news report warned them about fires on that road
The second fire happened in the same circumstances, on the same weekly drive
They saw a third burning car the following week
They worked out the statistical rate of car fires on that road
questions.explain: Because the second fire happened at the same spot on the same weekly drive, it made the spot “the place where cars catch fire,” and they were ready to see another for a long time afterward (they never did).

questions.q: After seeing a second burning car at the same spot, Kahneman and his wife came to think of that stretch of road as the place where cars catch ____.
questions.explain: The label shows how a single recurrence under the same circumstances created a new norm and an active expectation.

questions.q: Kahneman and psychologist Dale Miller described how events come to be perceived as normal or abnormal in what they called ____ theory.
questions.explain: Norm theory is the source of the restaurant example about the guest who winces at the soup.

questions.q: Put the steps of the restaurant example from norm theory in order, as the observer experiences them.
items: The first guest to taste the soup winces
The same guest startles violently when touched by a waiter
The second odd event retrieves the first from memory
Both events are read as showing that the guest is an exceptionally tense person
questions.explain: Kahneman says the second abnormal event retrieves the first from memory and the two fit into a pattern of a tense guest.

questions.q: According to norm theory, why do later events seem normal after an observer sees a restaurant guest wince at the soup?
questions.a: The wincing changes the normality of many related events, such as the guest startling at a waiter's touch or another guest stifling a cry over the same soup. These events seem normal not necessarily because they confirm advance expectations, but because they recruit the original episode, retrieve it from memory, and are interpreted in conjunction with it, so the events fit together into a coherent pattern.

questions.q: How does Kahneman explain the Moses illusion, in which few people notice the error in "How many animals of each kind did Moses take into the ark?"
options: People do not know the story of Noah's ark well enough
The question is too long for System 2 to read carefully
People notice the error but answer politely anyway
The biblical context makes Moses not abnormal, so associative coherence leads people to accept the question
questions.explain: The ark sets up a biblical context in which Moses is not surprising, and Moses and Noah share a vowel sound and syllable count. The idea that people simply do not know the Noah story is not the explanation Kahneman gives.

questions.q: In the brain study where people heard "Earth revolves around the trouble every year," how quickly did a distinctive brain response appear after the odd word began?
options: Within about two seconds
Within about half a minute
Within two-tenths of a second
Only after the whole sentence ended
questions.explain: The distinctive pattern of brain activity started within two-tenths of a second of the onset of the odd word, showing how fast violations of normality are detected.

questions.q: Which of these does Chapter 6 say produce the same fast brain response as a semantically odd word in a sentence?
options: A male voice saying "I believe I am pregnant because I feel sick every morning"
An upper-class voice saying "I have a large tattoo on my back"
A familiar voice saying a familiar greeting
A child's voice reading a list of numbers aloud
questions.explain: Both mismatches between speaker and content triggered the same response at the same speed, which requires a vast amount of world knowledge to be brought to bear instantly.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman find it remarkable that the brain reacts quickly when an upper-class voice says "I have a large tattoo on my back"?
questions.a: To detect the incongruity, the voice must be identified as upper-class English and then confronted with the generalization that large tattoos are uncommon in the upper class. A vast amount of world knowledge has to be brought to bear instantly, yet the brain responds as fast as it does to a plain semantic error, showing that violations of normality are detected with astonishing speed and subtlety.

questions.q: What does the sentence "The large mouse climbed over the trunk of the very small elephant" show about our norms for categories?
options: Norms specify a typical size and also the range of variability within the category
Norms are private, so each listener pictures something completely different
Words like large and small refer to absolute sizes regardless of the category
System 2 must calculate sizes before the sentence can be understood
questions.explain: Both writer and reader picture a mouse smaller than a shoe and an elephant larger than a sofa, because shared norms carry typical values and plausible ranges. The idea that norms are private contradicts his point that shared norms make communication possible.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say a norm for a category contains?
options: A typical or average case
Information about the range or variability within the category
The exact value for every member of the category
The cause that produced each member's features
questions.explain: He says norms specify a typical or average size and also contain information about the range within the category; System 1 has access to both.

questions.q: How do norms make communication possible, according to Kahneman?
questions.a: We can communicate because our knowledge of the world and our use of words are largely shared. When someone mentions a table, you understand a normal table with a roughly level surface and far fewer than 25 legs. System 1 has access to norms of categories that specify the range of plausible values and the most typical cases, and these norms also provide the background for immediately detecting anomalies such as pregnant men and tattooed aristocrats.

questions.q: Sort these examples from Chapter 6 by whether the mind readily accepts them or detects them as abnormal.

items.t: Moses taking animals into the ark
A mouse smaller than a shoe climbing an elephant larger than a sofa
A table with a roughly level surface
Earth revolves around the trouble every year
A man saying he is pregnant
George W. Bush taking animals into the ark

questions.explain: Items that fit the context or the category norm pass unnoticed, while items that violate a norm, including the Bush version of the ark question, are spotted at once.

questions.q: Match each example from Chapter 6 to the idea it illustrates.
pairs: Meeting Jon again in London
One incident can make a recurrence less surprising
The second burning car
A passive expectation can quickly turn active
Moses and the ark
Associative coherence can hide an error
The large mouse and the small elephant
Shared norms include typical cases and ranges
Earth revolves around the trouble
Violations of normality are detected very fast
questions.explain: Each anecdote or study in the assessing-normality discussion supports a distinct claim about how System 1 represents what is normal.

questions.q: Maya's neighbor's dog barked at midnight last Tuesday. This Tuesday it barks again at midnight, and Maya feels hardly surprised and half expects it next week. Which idea from Chapter 6 best explains this?
options: Statistical thinking based on a careful count of barking nights
A single recurrence under the same circumstances can create a new norm and an active expectation
Michotte's illusion of physical causality
The Moses illusion produced by similar-sounding names
questions.explain: Like the second burning car at the same spot, a repeat in identical circumstances makes the event feel normal and turns a passive expectation active. Maya has not counted anything, so statistical thinking is not involved.

questions.q: Reading "Fred's parents arrived late. The caterers were expected soon. Fred was angry," you know why Fred was angry. According to Kahneman, how is that cause found?
options: System 2 carefully weighs both possible causes
You recall a similar party from your own life
You guess at random between the two facts
System 1 automatically builds a coherent causal story, which System 2 accepts
questions.explain: Anger and lateness are linked in the associative network as effect and possible cause, so System 1 instantly constructs the story. System 2 is offered the causal interpretation and accepts it rather than working it out.

questions.q: In Taleb's story of the bond market on the day Saddam Hussein was captured, what lesson does Kahneman draw from the two opposite headlines?
options: Investors react rationally to major news
Bond prices are predictable from the day's top event
A statement that can explain two contradictory outcomes explains nothing at all
Financial news services are usually biased toward risky assets
questions.explain: Both rising and falling prices were explained by the capture, so the headlines only satisfy our need for coherence. The idea that prices are predictable from the top event is the illusion the story exposes.

questions.q: Put the events of the bond market story from The Black Swan in order.
items: Saddam Hussein is captured in his hiding place
Bond prices rise and a headline says the capture may not curb terrorism
Half an hour later bond prices fall back
A revised headline says the capture boosts the allure of risky assets
questions.explain: The same event was used to explain both the rise and the fall, illustrating the automatic search for causes.

questions.q: What does the story of the Hussein capture headlines show about the automatic search for causes?
questions.a: The capture was the major event of the day, so it was destined to explain whatever happened in the market, whether bonds rose or fell. A statement that can explain two contradictory outcomes explains nothing at all; the headlines merely satisfy our need for coherence, since a large event is supposed to have consequences and consequences need causes. System 1 is adept at finding a coherent causal story that links the limited fragments of knowledge at its disposal.

questions.q: In the story of Jane in the crowded streets of New York, the ideas of a lost wallet, New York, and crowds jointly evoke the explanation that a ____ caused the loss.
questions.explain: Associative coherence picks one cause out of many possibilities, such as the wallet slipping out or being left in a restaurant.

questions.q: What was Albert Michotte's challenge to the long-accepted view of causality going back to Hume?
options: We see causality directly, just as we see color
We infer causality from many repeated observations of correlations
Causality is a concept invented by philosophers and not perceived at all
Only adults who have learned physics can perceive causality
questions.explain: The accepted wisdom was that we infer physical causality from repeated correlations; Michotte argued that we see causality directly. That correlation view is exactly what he overturned.

questions.q: Observers of Michotte's moving squares know there is no physical contact, yet they have a powerful "illusion of ____."
questions.explain: When the second square moves instantly after contact, people say it was launched by the first, even though they know nothing really touched it.

questions.q: In Michotte's demonstrations, if the second square starts moving instantly, observers describe it as having been ____ by the first.
questions.explain: The immediate launching impression shows that causality is perceived directly by System 1 rather than reasoned out.

questions.q: True or false: Experiments show that six-month-old infants see Michotte-style sequences as cause-and-effect scenarios and show surprise when the sequence is altered.
questions.explain: Kahneman concludes that we are ready from birth to have impressions of causality, which are products of System 1 rather than reasoning.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say viewers see in Heider and Simmel's film?
options: An aggressive large triangle bullying a smaller triangle
A terrified circle
The circle and the small triangle joining forces to defeat the bully
A black square launching another square
A car catching fire by the road
questions.explain: These are the agents and intentions viewers read into the film's simple shapes. The launching square belongs to Michotte's demonstrations of physical causality.

questions.q: Which of these does Chapter 6 say about infants and causality?
options: Six-month-olds see a launching sequence as cause and effect
Infants under one year old identify bullies and victims
Infants expect a pursuer to take the most direct path to its target
Infants perceive causes only after many repeated observations of correlations
questions.explain: The evidence shows we are born prepared for both physical and intentional attributions. Learning from repeated correlations is the older view Michotte overturned.

questions.q: Match each person to the idea or story Chapter 6 attributes to them.
pairs: Albert Michotte
We see physical causality as directly as we see color
Fritz Heider and Mary-Ann Simmel
A film of moving shapes shows the perception of intentional causality
Paul Bloom
Separating physical and intentional causality explains religious belief
Nassim Taleb
Bond headlines on the day Saddam Hussein was captured
Dale Miller
Co-author with Kahneman of an essay on norm theory
questions.explain: Each name is tied to one study, story, or claim in the chapter.

questions.q: Sort these examples by the kind of causality Chapter 6 says we perceive in them.

items.t: One billiard ball hitting another
A black square launching another square
Knocking over a vase by brushing against it
A large triangle bullying a small one
Picking up the salt because you want salt
A pursuer taking the direct path to catch its target

questions.explain: Physical causality concerns objects moving objects; intentional causality concerns agents acting on wants, traits, and goals, including your own freely willed actions.

questions.q: True or false: Paul Bloom argued that our inborn tendency to merge physical and intentional causality into one concept explains the near universality of religious beliefs.
questions.explain: Bloom's claim is about our readiness to separate the two kinds of causality, which makes it natural to imagine soulless bodies and bodiless souls.

questions.q: Which of these beliefs does Paul Bloom say our two modes of perceiving causation make natural to accept?
options: An immaterial divinity is the ultimate cause of the physical world
Immortal souls temporarily control our bodies and leave them when we die
All events in the world happen by pure chance
Physical causes can only be known through repeated correlations
questions.explain: These are the two central beliefs of many religions that Bloom links to the separate concepts of physical and intentional causality built into System 1.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say the prominence of causal intuitions is a recurrent theme of the book?
options: Causal thinking is always more accurate than statistical thinking
People apply causal thinking inappropriately to situations that require statistical reasoning
System 1 is skilled at statistical reasoning but not at causal stories
Most people receive training in statistics but ignore it
questions.explain: System 1 cannot reason statistically, and although System 2 can learn to, few people get the training. The idea that most people are trained in statistics reverses what he says.

questions.q: Kahneman writes that ____ thinking derives conclusions about individual cases from properties of categories and ensembles, a mode System 1 lacks.
questions.explain: System 2 can learn to think statistically, but few people receive the necessary training, so causal intuitions dominate.

questions.q: How did Michotte's demonstrations change the understanding of how we perceive causality?
questions.a: The accepted view, going back to Hume, was that we infer physical causality from repeated observations of correlations, like one billiard ball hitting another. Michotte showed observers drawn squares where one seems to launch another; they knew there was no real contact but still had a powerful illusion of causality. With evidence that six-month-old infants also see cause and effect, this suggests impressions of causality are present from birth and are products of System 1, not reasoning.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman describe System 1 and System 2 as agents with traits and preferences, even though he calls them fictions?
options: Brain scans have located the two systems as separate agents
He wants readers to believe the systems are real little people in the head
Readers are expected to reason statistically about the mind
Thinking in terms of agents and intentions fits the way we think about causes and is easier on the mind
questions.explain: He calls it a matter of mental economy, like Heider's shapes that are easy to see as agents. He explicitly does not intend to convince readers that the systems are real.

questions.q: Kahneman says that the two systems and the associative machine are ____, used because they fit the way we think about causes.
questions.explain: He uses metaphors of agency for mental economy and does not intend to convince readers that the systems are real.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman use metaphors of agency, such as the two systems, to describe the mind?
questions.a: The psychology of causality led him to describe mental processes as agents with traits and intentions, and sometimes as an associative machine of mechanical regularities. He admits the system and the machine are fictions, but they fit the way we think about causes, so they offer mental economy. Just as Heider did not intend viewers to believe the large triangle is really a bully, he does not intend to convince readers that the systems are real.

questions.q: Sort these activities by which system Chapter 6 assigns them to.

items.t: Maintaining a model of what is normal
Instantly finding the cause of Fred's anger
Detecting an odd word within a fraction of a second
Seeing causality from birth
Knowing the idea of Jon always showing up is ludicrous
Learning, with training, to think statistically
Partly controlling the search of memory

questions.explain: System 1 builds norms, causal stories, and anomaly detection automatically; System 2 can see that an intuition is silly, steer memory, and learn statistical reasoning.

questions.q: Match each example from Chapter 6 to what it shows about seeing causes and intentions.
pairs: Fred's angry reaction
Causal links are found automatically while reading a story
Jane's missing wallet
A coherent cause is remembered even though it was never stated
Reaching for the salt
Willed action feels caused by a decision, not by physical forces
Heider's moving triangles
The mind is eager to see agents with traits and intentions
questions.explain: Each example illustrates a distinct way System 1 supplies causes or intentions to what it observes.

questions.q: On a day when the biggest news is a celebrity scandal, a TV anchor says the stock market fell 'as investors reacted to the scandal'; the next morning, when the market rises, another anchor says investors 'shrugged off the scandal.' Which idea from Chapter 6 best fits?
options: The automatic search for causes makes the big event explain whatever happens
Norm theory's account of passive expectations
Statistical thinking applied to market data
The perception of physical causality in launching
questions.explain: As with the Hussein headlines, the day's major event is destined to explain any market move, and an explanation that fits opposite outcomes explains nothing.

questions.q: Put these works discussed in Chapter 6 in chronological order.
items: Heider and Simmel's film of moving triangles and a circle (1944)
Michotte's book on the perception of causality (1945)
The English translation of Michotte's book (1963)
Paul Bloom's essay in The Atlantic on causality and religion (2005)
questions.explain: Heider and Simmel's film came in 1944, at about the same time as Michotte's 1945 book, which was translated into English in 1963; Bloom wrote in The Atlantic in 2005.

questions.q: Match each sentence from the end of Chapter 6 to the idea it applies.
pairs: The second applicant was also an old friend, and I was less surprised
Very little repetition makes a new experience feel normal
Survey the reactions without focusing only on the average
Norms include the whole range of normal reactions
She cannot accept that she was just unlucky
People need a causal story and may invent intentions
questions.explain: The three closing sentences turn the chapter's ideas about recurrence, norms with ranges, and the need for causes into everyday speech.

questions.q: Sort these examples by whether they mainly illustrate norms and surprise or causes and intentions.

items.t: Feeling little surprise when a second applicant is also an old friend
Considering the whole range of normal reactions to a product
Expecting another burning car at the same spot
Thinking someone sabotaged her work instead of accepting bad luck
Explaining a market move by the day's biggest news
Knowing instantly why Fred was angry

questions.explain: The first group shows how norms form and shape surprise; the second shows the automatic hunger for causes and intentions.

questions.q: After a project fails, a colleague insists a coworker must have deliberately undermined her, although nothing points to that and bad luck is plausible. Which closing example from Chapter 6 matches this?
options: Very little repetition is needed for a new experience to feel normal
We should consider the entire range of normal reactions
She needs a causal story and will end up thinking someone sabotaged her work
Violations of normality are detected with astonishing speed
questions.explain: The closing example describes someone who cannot accept that she was just unlucky and needs a causal story involving intentional sabotage, the tendency to see causes and intentions where chance is enough.

questions.q: True or false: One closing example in Chapter 6 advises that, when surveying reactions to products, the team should focus mainly on the average reaction.
questions.explain: The example warns against focusing exclusively on the average and says to consider the entire range of normal reactions, since norms include range as well as typical values.

questions.q: What does the closing remark "Very little repetition is needed for a new experience to feel normal" draw on from Chapter 6?
questions.a: It applies the lesson of the Jon and burning-car stories: a single incident can make a recurrence less surprising. System 1 updates its model of what is normal after one occurrence, so a second similar event, like a second applicant who is an old friend, feels much less surprising than the first.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: In the opening of A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions, when does Kahneman say jumping to conclusions is efficient?
options: When the situation is unfamiliar and there is no time to gather more information
When conclusions are likely correct, occasional mistakes are affordable, and the jump saves effort
When System 2 has already checked the evidence and found it complete and reliable
When the stakes are high and a fast decision is needed to avoid a costly delay
questions.explain: Kahneman says jumping is efficient if the conclusions are likely to be correct, an occasional mistake is acceptable, and the jump saves much time and effort. Unfamiliar, high-stakes situations with no time to collect information are exactly the ones he calls risky.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Whose line does Kahneman quote at the start of A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions, about a woman whose favorite sport is jumping to conclusions?
options: Amos Tversky
Daniel Gilbert
Solomon Asch
Danny Kaye
questions.explain: The line comes from the comedian Danny Kaye and has stayed with Kahneman since adolescence. Tversky is mentioned only because the line came up in their first conversation about statistical intuitions.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman name, in the opening of A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions, as circumstances that make jumping to conclusions risky?
options: The situation is unfamiliar
The stakes are high
There is no time to collect more information
The conclusions are likely to be correct
The cost of an occasional mistake is acceptable
questions.explain: Kahneman says jumping is risky when the situation is unfamiliar, the stakes are high, and there is no time to collect more information. Likely-correct conclusions and acceptable mistakes are the conditions under which jumping is efficient.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Sort these conditions by what they do to jumping to conclusions, according to the opening of A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions.

items.t: The conclusions are likely to be correct
An occasional mistake costs little
The jump saves much time and effort
The situation is unfamiliar
The stakes are high
There is no time to collect more information

questions.explain: Kahneman pairs likely-correct conclusions, acceptable errors and saved effort with efficiency. Unfamiliar situations, high stakes and no time for more information are where intuitive errors are probable.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Why does Kahneman think Danny Kaye's joke about jumping to conclusions describes System 1, and what role does he give System 2 when the jump is risky?
questions.a: Kahneman believes jumping to conclusions is how System 1 normally works. It pays off when conclusions are likely to be right, mistakes are cheap and the jump saves time and effort. When the situation is unfamiliar, the stakes are high and there is no time for more information, intuitive errors are probable, and they “may be prevented by a deliberate intervention of System 2.”

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: Neglect of Ambiguity and Suppression of Doubt
questions.q: In Kahneman's figure 6, why do readers see the identical middle shape as B in one display and as 13 in the other?
options: Because the shape is drawn slightly differently in each of the two displays
Because System 2 deliberately compares both readings and picks the likelier one
Because the surrounding letters or numbers determine how the shape is read
Because people read letters more readily than numbers in any kind of display
questions.explain: The middle items are identical; the same shape is read as a letter among letters and as a number among numbers, because the whole context determines each element. There is no deliberate comparison: readers never notice the ambiguity at all.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: Neglect of Ambiguity and Suppression of Doubt
questions.q: In Kahneman's discussion of the sentence about Ann and the bank, how does System 1 resolve the word bank when no explicit context is given?
options: It generates a likely context on its own, guided by experience such as frequent visits to banks
It keeps both meanings active until a later sentence settles which one is intended
It flags the word as ambiguous and passes the decision to System 2 for review
It picks one meaning at random, so readers split evenly between the two readings
questions.explain: Without explicit context, System 1 generated a likely context itself, and since most people go to banks more often than they float on rivers, the money meaning wins. It does not keep alternatives active or alert System 2; the reader is unaware a choice was made.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: Neglect of Ambiguity and Suppression of Doubt
questions.q: According to Kahneman's account of ambiguity, why is conscious doubt not part of what System 1 can do?
options: Because System 1 has no access to memories of past experiences
Because doubt means holding incompatible readings in mind at once, which takes effort
Because System 1 works only on visual inputs such as letters and numbers
Because doubt arises only from emotions, which System 2 normally suppresses
questions.explain: Kahneman says doubt requires keeping incompatible interpretations in mind at the same time, which demands mental effort, so “Uncertainty and doubt are the domain of System 2.” System 1 does draw on experience, so the idea that it lacks memory is wrong.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: Neglect of Ambiguity and Suppression of Doubt
questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that when no recent event comes to mind, more distant memories, such as having sung your ABCs, govern how System 1 resolves an ambiguity.
questions.explain: Recent events and current context carry the most weight, but when nothing recent comes to mind, more distant memories take over. That is why the figure 6 letters read as A B C: you sang your ABCs, not your A13Cs.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: Neglect of Ambiguity and Suppression of Doubt
questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say about how System 1 handles an ambiguous input such as the word bank?
options: It makes a definite choice without your knowing it
It does not keep track of the alternatives it rejects
Recent events and the current context carry the most weight
It keeps a record of rejected readings for later review
It alerts you whenever a second reading is possible
questions.explain: A definite choice is made without awareness, rejected alternatives are not tracked, and recent events and context weigh most. The ideas that System 1 keeps rejected readings or warns you of a second reading contradict his point that you are never aware of the ambiguity.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: Neglect of Ambiguity and Suppression of Doubt
questions.q: In Kahneman's account of ambiguity, uncertainty and doubt are the domain of ____.
questions.explain: Doubt requires holding incompatible interpretations in mind at once, which demands effort, so it belongs to System 2 rather than the automatic System 1.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: Neglect of Ambiguity and Suppression of Doubt
questions.q: Kahneman says that when uncertain, System 1 ____ on an answer, and its choices are guided by experience.
questions.explain: He describes System 1's handling of ambiguity as betting: it commits to one answer, with recent events and current context weighing most.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: Neglect of Ambiguity and Suppression of Doubt
questions.q: Put in order what happens, in Kahneman's account, when you read the middle shape in the letter display of figure 6.
items: The shape appears between the letters A and C
The context of letters shapes the interpretation
A single reading, the letter B, comes to mind
You remain unaware that 13 was also possible
questions.explain: The context comes first and determines the reading; only one interpretation reaches awareness, and the ambiguity that was resolved is never noticed.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: Neglect of Ambiguity and Suppression of Doubt
questions.q: Match each ambiguous item from Kahneman's discussion of ambiguity to how it is usually read.
pairs: Middle shape between A and C
Read as the letter B
Middle shape between 12 and 14
Read as the number 13
Bank, just after a sentence about floating down a river
Taken as a riverbank, with no thought of money
Bank, with no explicit context
Taken as a place with tellers and vaults, based on experience
questions.explain: In each case the context, or experience when context is missing, selects one reading. Thinking of a river makes bank lose its money association; without context, everyday experience with banks decides.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: Neglect of Ambiguity and Suppression of Doubt
questions.q: Sort these by which system Kahneman assigns them to in his discussion of ambiguity and doubt.

items.t: Resolving an ambiguity without awareness
Betting on an answer guided by experience
Losing track of rejected alternatives
Holding incompatible interpretations at once
Experiencing uncertainty and doubt
Spending mental effort to keep options open

questions.explain: System 1 silently picks one reading and forgets the rest. Keeping incompatible readings in mind takes effort, so doubt and uncertainty belong to System 2.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: Neglect of Ambiguity and Suppression of Doubt
questions.q: What does Kahneman call the most important aspect of the figure 6 letters-and-numbers display and the sentence about Ann and the bank?
questions.a: In both examples a definite choice was made, but you did not know it. Only one interpretation came to mind and you were never aware of the ambiguity, because System 1 does not keep track of the alternatives it rejects, or even of the fact that there were alternatives. Doubt would require holding incompatible readings at once, which takes effort and belongs to System 2.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: Neglect of Ambiguity and Suppression of Doubt
questions.q: Kahneman says the rules by which System 1 bets on an interpretation are intelligent. What are those rules, and how do they explain the bank example?
questions.a: Recent events and the current context have the most weight in determining an interpretation, and when no recent event comes to mind, more distant memories govern. If you had just read about floating down a river, bank would not suggest money. Without such context, most people resolve it toward money because they go to banks far more often than they float on rivers.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: A Bias to Believe and Confirm
questions.q: According to Daniel Gilbert's theory of believing, what must happen before you can decide that a statement is false?
options: System 2 must search memory for evidence that contradicts the statement
You must hear the statement repeated several times before judging it
You must hold the statement in mind without forming any interpretation
You must first try to believe it, to know what it would mean if true
questions.explain: Gilbert proposed that understanding begins with an attempt to believe: you must know what the idea would mean if it were true, and only then can you unbelieve it. This first step is automatic and belongs to System 1, not a deliberate memory search.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: A Bias to Believe and Confirm
questions.q: In Gilbert's experiment with nonsense assertions such as a dinca is a flame, what did holding digits in memory do to participants?
options: It made them doubt even the sentences that had been labeled true
It had no measurable effect on their memory for the true and false labels
It made false sentences hard to unbelieve, so many were later recalled as true
It improved their memory for the labels by keeping them more alert
questions.explain: Disrupting System 2 had a selective effect: it made it difficult to unbelieve false sentences, and depleted participants later thought many false sentences were true. The effect ran toward believing, not toward extra doubt.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: A Bias to Believe and Confirm
questions.q: A viewer comes home exhausted after a long day and watches a string of commercials making empty claims. Based on Kahneman's discussion of Gilbert, what is most likely?
options: She is more likely to be swayed by the empty messages than when she is rested
She is less likely to be swayed because tiredness makes her ignore the ads
Her tiredness makes no difference, since persuasion depends only on content
She will reject the messages because fatigue makes System 2 more suspicious
questions.explain: Kahneman notes evidence that people are more influenced by empty persuasive messages, such as commercials, when tired and depleted. Doubting is System 2's job, and a depleted System 2 leaves gullible System 1 in charge.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: A Bias to Believe and Confirm
questions.q: True or false: Gilbert sees unbelieving a statement as an automatic operation of System 1.
questions.explain: Gilbert treats the initial attempt to believe as automatic System 1 work, but unbelieving as an operation of System 2. That is why loading System 2 with digits made false sentences harder to reject.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: A Bias to Believe and Confirm
questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that someone asked about the probability of a tsunami hitting California in the next thirty years is prone to overestimate it, because images of tsunamis come to mind.
questions.explain: The confirmatory bias of System 1 brings to mind instances that fit the question, as with whitefish eat candy, so the person is prone to overestimate the probability of the disaster.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: A Bias to Believe and Confirm
questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman attribute to the confirmatory bias of System 1?
options: Uncritical acceptance of suggestions
Exaggerating the likelihood of extreme and improbable events
Systematic attempts to refute one's own hypotheses
Greater accuracy when judging rare disasters
A habit of automatically unbelieving nonsense statements
questions.explain: Kahneman says the confirmatory bias of System 1 favors uncritical acceptance of suggestions and exaggeration of the likelihood of extreme and improbable events. Trying to refute hypotheses is what philosophers of science advise, and unbelieving is System 2's job.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: A Bias to Believe and Confirm
questions.q: A deliberate search for confirming evidence, which is also how System 2 tests a hypothesis, is known as ____.
questions.explain: Kahneman names this the positive test strategy: people, and often scientists, seek data compatible with what they already believe instead of trying to refute it.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: A Bias to Believe and Confirm
questions.q: Kahneman says the operations of associative memory contribute to a general ____ bias.
questions.explain: Asking whether Sam is friendly calls up different memories of Sam than asking whether he is unfriendly; this is how associative memory feeds confirmation bias.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: A Bias to Believe and Confirm
questions.q: Put the steps of Gilbert's experiment on believing and unbelieving in order.
items: Participants saw a nonsensical assertion such as a dinca is a flame
A few seconds later a single word, true or false, appeared
Later, their memory for which sentences had been labeled true was tested
questions.explain: Each nonsense assertion was followed after a few seconds by its label, and the memory test came later; in one condition participants also held digits in memory throughout the task.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: A Bias to Believe and Confirm
questions.q: Match each name or term from Kahneman's discussion of believing and confirming to its role.
pairs: Daniel Gilbert
Proposed that understanding a statement begins with an attempt to believe it
Baruch Spinoza
Seventeenth-century philosopher to whom Gilbert traced his theory
Philosophers of science
Advise testing hypotheses by trying to refute them
Positive test strategy
Seeking data compatible with beliefs one already holds
questions.explain: Gilbert built his theory of believing and unbelieving on Spinoza. The philosophers' rule of refutation is the standard that the positive test strategy violates.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: A Bias to Believe and Confirm
questions.q: Sort these by the system that Gilbert and Kahneman assign them to.

items.t: The initial attempt to believe a statement
Constructing the best interpretation of a situation
Linking fish and candy to make sense of nonsense
Unbelieving a false statement
Being in charge of doubting
Being disrupted by holding digits in memory

questions.explain: Believing is automatic and belongs to System 1, which searches associative memory for sense. Doubting and unbelieving belong to System 2, which is what the digit load disrupted.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: A Bias to Believe and Confirm
questions.q: What moral does Kahneman draw from Gilbert's experiment in which participants held digits in memory?
questions.a: When System 2 is otherwise engaged, we will believe almost anything. “System 1 is gullible and biased to believe,” while System 2 is in charge of doubting and unbelieving, but System 2 is sometimes busy and often lazy. Indeed, there is evidence that tired, depleted people are more influenced by empty persuasive messages such as commercials.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: A Bias to Believe and Confirm
questions.q: How does the question Is Sam friendly? illustrate confirmation bias, and how does people's usual way of testing hypotheses differ from the philosophers' advice?
questions.a: Asking whether Sam is friendly brings to mind different instances of his behavior than asking whether he is unfriendly, so associative memory supplies confirming evidence. System 2 also tests hypotheses by a positive test strategy, deliberately searching for confirming data. Philosophers of science advise trying to refute hypotheses, but people, and often scientists, seek data compatible with what they already believe.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: What does Kahneman mean by the halo effect?
options: The tendency to remember first impressions more clearly than later ones
The tendency to like or dislike everything about a person, even unobserved things
The tendency to rate attractive people as less competent than they are
The tendency to believe empty statements more readily when tired
questions.explain: The halo effect is the tendency to like or dislike everything about a person, including things you have not observed. It does give first impressions extra weight, but the term names the spreading of a global feeling, not a memory effect.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: In Kahneman's example of Joan, whom you found personable at a party, what do you actually know about her generosity?
options: That she is probably generous, since agreeable people tend to give
That she is probably stingy, since charm often hides selfishness
That she is about as generous as the average guest at the party
Virtually nothing, since being agreeable says little about giving
questions.explain: Kahneman says you know virtually nothing, because there is little reason to believe that people agreeable in social situations are generous to charities. The belief that she is generous is a gap filled by your liking for her.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: In Solomon Asch's study of Alan and Ben, why do most people view Alan more favorably?
options: Alan is described with more positive traits than Ben is
Ben's list includes the trait envious, which Alan's lacks
The first traits change the meaning of the traits that follow
People simply prefer the name Alan to the name Ben
questions.explain: Both men have the same six traits in reverse order. “The initial traits in the list change the very meaning of the traits that appear later.”

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: In a variation on Asch's study, participants considered Alan's first three adjectives and then the last three as describing another person. What did most say when asked if all six could describe one person?
options: That it was impossible
That it was quite likely
That it depended on the order
That they needed more facts
questions.explain: Having imagined two distinct individuals, most participants thought it was impossible for all six adjectives to describe the same person, showing how strongly early traits shape the whole picture.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: When Kahneman switched to grading all students' answers to one question before moving to the next, what happened to his confidence in his grades?
options: It rose, because his grades became more consistent across essays
It fell, and he took that as a sign the new procedure was better
It fell, and that convinced him to return to his old method
It stayed the same, although individual grades shifted slightly
questions.explain: His confidence dropped because he now saw that a student's essays could vary widely, which was uncomfortable. He recognized this as a good sign: the earlier consistency had been produced by the halo effect.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: A manager wants her committee's best judgment on a proposal. Following Kahneman's advice on decorrelating error, what should she do?
options: Let the most experienced member speak first to guide the discussion
Hold an open discussion and then take a simple show-of-hands vote
Ask members to agree on one shared estimate before the meeting
Have each member write a brief summary of their position first
questions.explain: Kahneman recommends that all members write a very brief summary of their position before the issue is discussed. Open discussion gives too much weight to those who speak early and assertively, causing others to line up behind them.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: True or false: In Kahneman's original way of grading essays, a high score on a student's first essay made him stricter with vague or ambiguous statements in that student's later essays.
questions.explain: It was the opposite: after a high first score he gave the student the benefit of the doubt on vague or ambiguous statements later, which is how the halo effect entered his grading.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that allowing observers to influence each other effectively reduces the size of the sample, and with it the precision of the group estimate.
questions.explain: Pooling judgments reduces error only when the observations are independent. Observers who influence each other make correlated errors, which is like having fewer observers.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Which of these were part of the grading procedure Kahneman adopted to tame the halo effect?
options: Reading all students' answers to the first question before moving on
Writing scores on the inside back page of the booklet
Reading each student's booklet straight through in one sitting
Adjusting grades to reduce discrepancies between a student's essays
Letting the first essay set the standard for the later ones
questions.explain: He scored one question across all students at a time and hid the scores on the inside back page so they would not bias him. Reading booklets straight through was his old method, and changing grades to reduce discrepancies was the temptation he resisted.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say are needed for averaging many judgments, as in estimating the pennies in a jar, to reduce error?
options: The observations are independent of each other
The individuals' errors are uncorrelated
The observers share a common bias
The observers discuss the jar before estimating
There is no systematic bias in the judgments
