questions.explain: Errors average toward zero only when observations are independent, errors uncorrelated, and there is no systematic bias. A shared bias is not reduced by aggregation, and discussion makes errors correlated.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: The general principle behind Kahneman's new grading procedure and the police rule for witnesses is: ____ error!
questions.explain: Kahneman calls the principle decorrelate error: make sources of evidence independent so their errors do not move together.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: The tendency to like or dislike everything about a person, including things you have not observed, is known as the ____.
questions.explain: Kahneman says the term has been used in psychology for a century and is a good name for a common bias that makes System 1's picture of the world simpler and more coherent than reality.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: In Asch's study, the ambiguous adjective ____ is seen as likely justified in an intelligent person but makes an envious person seem more dangerous.
questions.explain: Kahneman uses stubborn to show that the halo effect is also a case of suppressed ambiguity: like the word bank, it is read to fit its context.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Kahneman cites James Surowiecki's book The ____ of Crowds to explain why pooled guesses of pennies in a jar are accurate.
questions.explain: In The Wisdom of Crowds, individuals estimate poorly but the average of many independent judgments is remarkably accurate.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Put the events of Kahneman's essay-grading story in order.
items: He read each student's booklet straight through, grading as he went
He noticed his grades within each booklet were strikingly homogeneous
He suspected a halo effect from the first question he scored
He switched to scoring all answers to one question before the next
His confidence in his grades dropped, which he saw as a good sign
questions.explain: The homogeneous grades led him to suspect a halo effect, the new procedure followed, and the lower confidence it produced came last and convinced him the new method was superior.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Put Alan's traits in the order in which Asch listed them.
items: intelligent
industrious
impulsive
critical
stubborn
envious
questions.explain: Alan's list starts with intelligent and ends with envious; Ben's is the same list reversed, which is why Alan is seen more favorably.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Match each example from Kahneman's discussion of the halo effect to the idea it shows.
pairs: Liking the president's politics
You probably like his voice and appearance as well
Joan at a party
Liking fills a gap where evidence of generosity is missing
Alan and Ben
Early traits change the meaning of later ones
Alan's six traits split between two people
Most judged it impossible for one person to have all six
Grading booklets in sequence
The first essay swayed the student's whole grade
questions.explain: Each example shows the halo effect spreading an early or global impression to things not observed or later encountered.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Match each situation in Kahneman's discussion of decorrelating error to the remedy he describes.
pairs: Halo effect in grading essays
Score one question for all students before the next
Several witnesses to an event
Do not let them discuss it before testifying
Committee meetings
Have members write brief position summaries before discussion
Estimating pennies in a jar
Average many independent individual judgments
questions.explain: Each remedy keeps judgments independent so that errors do not become correlated and redundant.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Sort these by which of Kahneman's two essay-grading methods they belong to.

items.t: Reading one student's booklet straight through
Grades within a booklet were strikingly homogeneous
Giving the benefit of the doubt after a strong first essay
Feeling confident in the grades
Scoring all answers to one question first
Writing scores on the inside back page
Finding one student's grades varied widely
Feeling uncertain and frustrated

questions.explain: The old method felt comfortable because the halo effect made grades consistent. The new method exposed real inconsistency and so produced discomfort and lower confidence.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Using Kahneman's example of Joan, explain how the halo effect leads you to believe a person is generous and why it then makes you like her even more.
questions.a: You found Joan personable, but there is little reason to think social agreeableness predicts generosity, so you know virtually nothing about it. Because you like Joan and also like generous people, association predisposes you to believe she is generous, filling the gap with a guess that fits your emotional response. Having added generosity to her pleasant attributes, you now like her even better.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Why did Kahneman conclude that his loss of confidence after changing his grading method was a good sign?
questions.a: Under the old method, a strong first essay led him to give the benefit of the doubt later, so grades looked consistent and he felt cognitive ease. “The consistency I had enjoyed earlier was spurious”: it spared him the dissonance of seeing a student do well on some questions and badly on others. The inconsistency the new method revealed was real, reflecting both the inadequacy of any single question and the unreliability of his own grading.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Explain Kahneman's principle of decorrelating error using the pennies-in-a-jar task, and say when it fails.
questions.a: Individuals estimate the number of pennies poorly, but all look at the same jar while their errors are independent, so when many judgments are averaged the errors tend to cancel and the average is quite accurate. The magic works only when observations are independent and errors uncorrelated. If observers share a bias, aggregation does not reduce it, and letting them influence each other effectively shrinks the sample and the precision of the estimate.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: On a hiring panel, the first interviewer praises a candidate loudly before the others have given their ratings. Using Kahneman's argument, what is the problem and what should the panel do?
questions.a: The others' judgments are no longer independent: they are likely to line up behind the early, assertive speaker, so their errors become correlated and the panel yields less information than its size suggests. Following the principle of decorrelating error, each member should write down a brief rating or position before any discussion, just as witnesses are kept from talking before testifying.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: What does Kahneman say is the measure of success for System 1?
options: The amount of data on which its judgment is based
The accuracy of its predictions over the long run
The coherence of the story it manages to create
The speed with which it passes problems to System 2
questions.explain: Kahneman says the measure of success for System 1 is the coherence of its story, while the amount and quality of the data are largely irrelevant. That is why it jumps to conclusions when information is scarce.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: In the study by Amos and his Stanford students using the Thornton false-arrest case, how did participants who heard only one lawyer compare with those who heard both?
options: They were more confident in their judgments
They were less confident, knowing half was missing
They were equally confident but less accurate
They routinely built the other side's case themselves
questions.explain: Participants knew the setup and could easily have generated the other side's argument, yet one-sided evidence strongly affected their judgments and made them more confident than those who heard both sides.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: In Kahneman's example Will Mindik be a good leader? She is intelligent and strong, what did the reader fail to do?
options: Notice that intelligence and strength are positive traits
Ask what would need to be known before judging leadership
Combine the two adjectives into a single quick impression
Feel that the answer came easily and without discomfort
questions.explain: Kahneman points out that you did not start by asking what you would need to know before forming an opinion about someone's leadership. Instead System 1 combined the two positive adjectives into a quick yes with great cognitive ease.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: A shopper picks a yogurt labeled 95% fat-free over an identical one labeled 5% fat. Which bias that Kahneman explains with WYSIATI does this show?
options: Base-rate neglect
The halo effect
Confirmation bias
A framing effect
questions.explain: Framing effects arise because different presentations of the same information evoke different emotions, and a person normally sees only one formulation, as with cold cuts described as 90% fat-free versus 10% fat.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: How does Kahneman use WYSIATI to explain base-rate neglect in the case of Steve, the meek and tidy soul?
options: People know there are more librarians than farmers and weigh it heavily
People deliberately decide that statistics are irrelevant to Steve
The vivid description comes to mind while the farmer statistic does not
People lack any knowledge of how many farmers and librarians exist
questions.explain: The personality description is salient and vivid, and although you know there are more male farmers than male librarians, that fact almost certainly did not come to mind. The problem is not missing knowledge or a deliberate choice; what you saw was all there was.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: True or false: According to Kahneman, System 1 is highly sensitive to the quantity and quality of the information that gives rise to its impressions.
questions.explain: Kahneman says the reverse: “System 1 is radically insensitive to both the quality and the quantity of the information” behind its impressions and intuitions.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that knowing little often makes it easier to fit everything you know into a coherent pattern.
questions.explain: Because confidence depends on the coherence of the story rather than its completeness, having little information can make a coherent story easier to build.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: Which of these biases does Kahneman list, in A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions, as examples that WYSIATI helps explain?
options: Overconfidence
Framing effects
Base-rate neglect
The endowment effect
Regression to the mean
questions.explain: Kahneman's list here gives overconfidence, framing effects and base-rate neglect, among many others. The endowment effect and regression to the mean are topics of later chapters and are not given here as WYSIATI examples.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say WYSIATI does?
options: It facilitates coherence and the cognitive ease that makes us accept a statement as true
It explains why we can think fast
It explains how we make sense of partial information in a complex world
It guarantees that the coherent story matches reality
It makes System 1 wait for more data before concluding
questions.explain: WYSIATI supports coherence, cognitive ease and fast thinking with partial information, and much of the time the story is close enough to reality. It guarantees nothing, and System 1 does not wait; that is the problem.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: Which of these were true of the Thornton false-arrest study reported by Amos and his students?
options: All participants read the same background story
The lawyers added no useful information beyond that story
Participants did not realize they had heard only one side
One-sided evidence had a very pronounced effect on judgments
Hearing both sides made participants more confident
questions.explain: Everyone read the background, and the lawyers added nothing that could not be inferred from it. Participants were fully aware of the setup, yet one-sided evidence strongly swayed them and made them more, not less, confident.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: Kahneman's abbreviation WYSIATI stands for what you see is ____.
questions.explain: WYSIATI names jumping to conclusions on limited evidence, an idea Kahneman says comes up so often in the book that it deserves an abbreviation.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: In Amos Tversky's comedy routine, his old philosophy professor would growl, You must never forget the Primat of the ____.
questions.explain: The phrase reminded Kahneman and Tversky of the asymmetry between how the mind treats information that is available and information it does not have.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: Kahneman says an essential design feature of the associative machine is that it represents only ____ ideas.
questions.explain: Information that is not retrieved from memory, even unconsciously, might as well not exist for System 1.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: Explaining the Thornton study, Kahneman says it is the ____ of the information that matters for a good story, not its completeness.
questions.explain: Confidence follows the coherence of the story built from available information, so a one-sided but consistent account feels more convincing.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: Put in order what happens in Kahneman's example of judging whether Mindik will be a good leader.
items: Reading intelligent, System 1 registers something good
Adding strong makes the story very good
The answer yes comes quickly to mind
Learning she is corrupt would revise the story, leaving a bias toward the first impression
questions.explain: System 1 starts from the first adjective and builds the best story it can; revision comes only if new information arrives, and even then the first impression keeps some weight.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: Match each bias to how Kahneman explains it with WYSIATI.
pairs: Overconfidence
Confidence depends on the story's quality, not the amount of evidence
Framing effects
A person normally sees only one of two equivalent formulations
Base-rate neglect
A vivid description crowds out a statistical fact that never comes to mind
questions.explain: In each case judgment is built from whatever is in view, and missing information is not allowed for.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: Match each item from Kahneman's discussion of WYSIATI to what it illustrates.
pairs: The Primat of the Is
The asymmetry between available and missing information
90% survival versus 10% mortality after surgery
Equivalent statements that evoke different emotions
Mindik is intelligent and strong
A quick verdict formed from two adjectives
Buying a home
System 2 deliberately seeking information it does not have
questions.explain: Most of these show System 1 working from what is present; buying a home is Kahneman's example of System 2's more careful, checklist approach.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: Sort these by whether, according to Kahneman, subjective confidence depends on them or largely ignores them.

items.t: The coherence of the story
The consistency of the information
How good a story one can tell about what one sees
The quantity of the evidence
The quality of the evidence
The completeness of the information
Information not retrieved from memory

questions.explain: Kahneman says confidence depends mostly on the quality of the story one can tell, while the quantity, quality and completeness of evidence count for little, and unretrieved information might as well not exist.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: Sort these by which system Kahneman links them to in his discussion of WYSIATI.

items.t: Building the best story from currently activated ideas
Delivering a verdict with no waiting and no discomfort
Being insensitive to the quantity of information
Lazily endorsing intuitive beliefs
Following a list of boxes to check before deciding
Deliberately seeking missing information when buying a home

questions.explain: System 1 seeks coherence from what is active. System 2 can be systematic, but because it is lazy it often endorses the impressions System 1 generates.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: What does WYSIATI mean, and why does Kahneman think it is so important for understanding intuitive thinking?
questions.a: WYSIATI, what you see is all there is, names jumping to conclusions on limited evidence. The associative machine represents only activated ideas, and System 1 builds the most coherent story it can from them without allowing for information it does not have. Because coherence, not the quantity or quality of data, is its measure of success, WYSIATI explains fast thinking with partial information and also a long list of biases, such as overconfidence, framing effects and base-rate neglect.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: In the Thornton false-arrest study, why were participants who heard only one side more confident than those who heard both, according to Kahneman?
questions.a: Confidence is determined by the coherence of the story people can build from the available information. One-sided evidence makes a tidier story, so even though participants knew the setup and could have generated the other side's argument, they did not. “It is the consistency of the information that matters for a good story, not its completeness.”

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: Kahneman says System 2 will endorse many intuitive beliefs. Why, and does careful deliberation escape System 1's influence?
questions.a: A coherence-seeking System 1 combined with a lazy System 2 means System 2 often accepts beliefs that closely reflect System 1's impressions. System 2 can take a systematic approach, such as working through a checklist and seeking missing information when buying a home. But System 1 is expected to influence even careful decisions, because its input never ceases.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.section: What You See is All There is (wysiati)
questions.q: A friend reads one glowing review of a new restaurant and is sure it is the best in town. Explain her certainty using Kahneman's WYSIATI and his account of overconfidence.
questions.a: Her System 1 built a coherent story from the one review in view and did not allow for the many reviews and experiences she has not seen. Under WYSIATI, neither the quantity nor the quality of evidence counts for much in subjective confidence, which depends mostly on how good a story she can tell. She fails to allow for missing evidence that should be critical: what she sees is all there is.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Someone says, They made that big decision on the basis of a good report from one consultant. Which idea from A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions does Kahneman attach to this remark?
options: WYSIATI
The halo effect
Decorrelating errors
The positive test strategy
questions.explain: Kahneman's example remark continues that they did not seem to realize how little information they had, which is WYSIATI: what you see is all there is.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Kahneman's sample remark reads: Let's ____ errors by obtaining separate judgments on the issue before any discussion.
questions.explain: Separate judgments before discussion keep errors independent, so the group gets more information from independent assessments.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: What is wrong with a judgment described as She knows nothing about this person's management skills; all she is going by is a good presentation?
questions.a: Kahneman labels this the halo effect. A favorable impression from one presentation spreads to qualities she has not observed, such as management skill, just as liking Joan at a party led to believing she was generous. The gap in real evidence is filled by a guess that fits her emotional response.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Which chapter immediately follows A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions in Part 1, Two Systems?
options: How Judgments Happen
Answering an Easier Question
Norms, Surprises, and Causes
The Law of Small Numbers
questions.explain: The table of contents places How Judgments Happen as chapter 8, right after chapter 7. Norms, Surprises, and Causes comes just before, and The Law of Small Numbers opens Part 2.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: True or false: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions is the first chapter of Part 2, Heuristics and Biases.
questions.explain: It is chapter 7 in Part 1, Two Systems, between Norms, Surprises, and Causes and How Judgments Happen. Part 2 begins with The Law of Small Numbers.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Which of these does the title metaphor of A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions describe?
options: System 1 working with scarce information
The associative machine building the best story from activated ideas
System 2 checking boxes before buying a home
System 2 unbelieving false statements
System 1 seeking coherence rather than complete data
questions.explain: Kahneman says that when information is scarce, System 1 operates as a machine for jumping to conclusions, building the most coherent story from activated ideas. The careful checklist and the act of unbelieving are System 2's contributions, not the machine of the title.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Put these sections of A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions in the order they appear.
items: Neglect of Ambiguity and Suppression of Doubt
A Bias to Believe and Confirm
Exaggerated Emotional Coherence (Halo Effect)
What You See Is All There Is (WYSIATI)
Speaking of Jumping to Conclusions
questions.explain: The chapter moves from silent resolution of ambiguity, to believing and confirming, to the halo effect, and ends with WYSIATI, which ties these together.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Put these chapters of Part 1, Two Systems, in the order they appear.
items: The Associative Machine
Cognitive Ease
Norms, Surprises, and Causes
A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
How Judgments Happen
questions.explain: In the table of contents these are chapters 4 to 8; A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions sits between Norms, Surprises, and Causes and How Judgments Happen.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: Match each section of A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions to its central idea.
pairs: Neglect of Ambiguity and Suppression of Doubt
System 1 picks one reading without your awareness
A Bias to Believe and Confirm
Understanding begins with believing; doubting takes System 2
Exaggerated Emotional Coherence (Halo Effect)
Liking or disliking spreads to traits not observed
What You See Is All There Is (WYSIATI)
Only activated information counts in building a story
questions.explain: Each section shows a different way System 1 produces a simpler and more coherent picture than the evidence supports.

questions.unitTitle: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
questions.q: How do the sections of A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions build toward WYSIATI, and how does Kahneman signal that the idea matters for the rest of the book?
questions.a: The chapter first shows System 1 resolving ambiguity without awareness, then its bias to believe and confirm, then the halo effect, which Kahneman calls another case of suppressed ambiguity. WYSIATI gathers these into one rule: System 1 builds the most coherent story from what is activated and ignores what is missing. Kahneman says this comes up so often in the book that it earns an abbreviation, and he will invoke it to explain a long list of biases, including overconfidence, framing effects and base-rate neglect.

questions.q: In Kahneman's opening to How Judgments Happen, what does he call the essential idea of the heuristics and biases approach?
options: Basic assessments of System 1 are easily substituted for more difficult questions
System 2 always checks and corrects the answers proposed by System 1
People judge probability by how easily examples come to mind
Intuitive judgments are reliable only when the environment is regular
questions.explain: Kahneman says System 1's continuous basic assessments matter for intuitive judgment because “they are easily substituted for more difficult questions”. The idea that System 2 reliably corrects System 1 runs against the book's picture of a lazy System 2.

questions.q: Kahneman's question "If Sam were as tall as he is intelligent, how tall would he be?" shows System 1's ability to translate values across ____.
questions.explain: The opening lists translating values across dimensions as one of the System 1 features that supports substituting one judgment for another; the Sam question is its example.

questions.q: In the opening of How Judgments Happen, what three features of System 1 does Kahneman say support the substitution of one judgment for another?
questions.a: First, System 1 continuously generates basic assessments of the situation without intention and with little effort, and these are easily substituted for harder questions. Second, it can translate values across dimensions, as in matching Sam's height to his intelligence. Third, there is the mental shotgun: an intention of System 2 to answer one question automatically triggers other computations, including basic assessments.

questions.q: Match each term from How Judgments Happen to its meaning.
pairs: Basic assessment
An evaluation System 1 makes continuously, without intention and with little effort
Intensity matching
Translating a value on one scale to an equally extreme value on another scale
Mental shotgun
Computing more than System 2 asked for when it intends one judgment
Prototype
A typical exemplar by which System 1 represents a category
questions.explain: These are the chapter's core terms: basic assessments are automatic, intensity matching works across dimensions, the mental shotgun is excess computation, and prototypes are how System 1 represents sets.

questions.q: According to Alex Todorov's research in Thinking, Fast and Slow, which two facts can people evaluate from a single glance at a stranger's face?
options: How intelligent and how honest the stranger is
How dominant and how trustworthy the stranger is
How old and how wealthy the stranger is
How happy and how healthy the stranger is
questions.explain: Todorov showed that a glance reveals how dominant (and so potentially threatening) a stranger is and how trustworthy, meaning whether his intentions are friendly or hostile. Intelligence is not one of the two dimensions Kahneman names.

questions.q: In Todorov's research on reading faces, what provides the cues for assessing a stranger's dominance?
options: Facial expression, such as a smile or a frown
The direction and steadiness of the eyes
The shape of the face, such as a strong square chin
The tone of voice that accompanies the face
questions.explain: Kahneman says face shape cues dominance, with a strong square chin as one cue, while facial expression (smile or frown) cues the stranger's intentions. Mixing these up confuses dominance with trustworthiness.

questions.q: In Todorov's study using campaign portraits, in about what share of races for senator, congressman, and governor did the winner have the face rated as more competent?
options: About 30%
About 50%
About 90%
About 70%
questions.explain: In about 70% of the races the winner was the candidate whose face had earned the higher competence rating from Princeton students who saw the photos briefly and without political context.

questions.q: In Todorov's research on faces and elections, which ratings did Kahneman find surprisingly better at predicting voting outcomes?
options: Ratings of competence
Ratings of likability
Ratings of attractiveness
Ratings of age and experience
questions.explain: Kahneman notes, to his own surprise, that “ratings of competence were far more predictive of voting outcomes in Todorov’s study than ratings of likability”.

questions.q: A judge feels uneasy giving a ten-year sentence for shoplifting, because the punishment seems to sound far louder than the crime. Which idea from How Judgments Happen best explains this feeling?
options: The mental shotgun
Intensity matching
Neglect of sum-like variables
Judging competence from faces
questions.explain: Kahneman describes people matching the intensity of crimes and punishments on a common scale, even matching both to the loudness of a sound; a punishment much louder than the crime feels unjust. The mental shotgun concerns excess computation, not a mismatch of intensities.

questions.q: Walking at night, you instantly feel wary of a stranger with a square jaw and a turned-down mouth, before thinking about it at all. How would Kahneman describe this reaction?
options: A deliberate System 2 judgment based on past experience
An example of the mental shotgun disrupting a task
A basic assessment by System 1 of dominance and intentions
A sum-like judgment that ignores the size of a category
questions.explain: Judging a stranger's dominance from face shape and intentions from expression is the chapter's main example of a basic assessment, made at a glance by System 1; Kahneman says a square chin with a turned-down mouth may spell trouble.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman reports that there is no evidence that the facial features that exude competence actually predict how well politicians will perform in office.
questions.explain: Kahneman states plainly that there is no evidence these features predict performance in office; voters fall back on them because they are quick and automatic, not because they are valid.

questions.q: True or false: In the brain studies Kahneman cites, winning candidates evoked stronger indications of negative emotional response than losing candidates.
questions.explain: It was the losers who evoked stronger indications of negative emotional response, suggesting we are biologically predisposed to reject candidates who lack the attributes we value.

questions.q: Kahneman says good mood and ____ are the human equivalents of assessments of safety and familiarity.
questions.explain: System 1 evolved to assess threats continuously; in humans these basic evaluations show up as good mood and cognitive ease, signalling safety and familiarity.

questions.q: Voters who judge candidates by facial competence fall back on a simpler, automatic assessment instead of judging how good a candidate will be in office; Kahneman calls this an example of a judgment ____.
questions.explain: Kahneman says the voting case is an example of what he will call a judgment heuristic: a hard question is answered with a simpler assessment that is available when System 2 must decide.

questions.q: According to Todorov, people judge competence from a face by combining the two dimensions of strength and ____.
questions.explain: Competent-looking faces combine a strong chin (strength) with a slight confident-appearing smile (trustworthiness).

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman list as basic assessments routinely carried out as part of perceiving events and understanding messages?
options: Computations of similarity and representativeness
Attributions of causality
Evaluations of the availability of associations and exemplars
Computations of the total size of a set
Counts of the syllables in every word heard
questions.explain: Kahneman names similarity and representativeness, causality, and availability as basic assessments performed even without a task. Totals of sets and syllable counts are not computed automatically; they need intention or System 2.

questions.q: Which of these questions does Kahneman say System 1 was shaped by evolution to assess continuously?
options: Is there a threat or a major opportunity?
Should I approach or avoid?
How many objects are in front of me in total?
Is everything normal?
How happy am I with my life as a whole?
questions.explain: The survival questions Kahneman lists include whether there is a threat or opportunity, whether things are normal, and whether to approach or avoid. Overall happiness is not continuously evaluated, and totals are a weakness of System 1.

questions.q: Which of these features does Todorov find in faces that exude competence?
options: A strong chin
A slight confident-appearing smile
A round chin
A turned-down mouth
A broad, open-mouthed grin
questions.explain: Competent-looking faces combine strength (a strong chin) with trustworthiness (a slight confident-appearing smile). A turned-down mouth with a square chin is the combination Kahneman says may spell trouble.

questions.q: In Todorov's face-reading research, sort each facial cue by what it is used to assess.

items.t: A strong square chin
A round chin
A smile
A frown
A turned-down mouth

questions.explain: Kahneman says the shape of the face, such as the chin, cues dominance, while facial expression such as a smile or frown cues whether the stranger's intentions are friendly or hostile.

questions.q: Put the steps of Todorov's study of faces and elections in the order Kahneman describes them.
items: Students saw politicians' faces, sometimes for a tenth of a second
Students rated the faces on attributes such as competence
The ratings were compared with the results of the elections
Winners had the more competent-looking face in about 70% of races
The finding was confirmed in elections in other countries
questions.explain: Students first rated brief photos without political context; only then were ratings compared with election results, revealing the 70% figure, which was quickly confirmed in Finland, England, Australia, Germany, and Mexico.

questions.q: How does Todorov's research on faces and elections illustrate what Kahneman calls a judgment heuristic?
questions.a: Voters face a hard question: how good will this candidate be in office? Instead they fall back on a simpler assessment, the competence they read in a face, which System 1 makes quickly and automatically and which is available when System 2 must decide. Faces rated more competent won about 70% of races, even though there is no evidence these features predict performance in office.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, which voters are most influenced by facial competence, and what does this show about System 1?
questions.a: Political scientists found that the effect of facial competence on voting is about three times larger for politically uninformed voters who watch a great deal of television than for better-informed voters who watch less. This shows that the relative importance of System 1 in determining choices differs between people; it is an example of individual differences.

questions.q: What does Kahneman's figure of two block towers and an array of blocks show about the limits of basic assessments?
questions.a: A glance tells you at once that the two towers are equally tall and more similar to each other than to the blocks on the floor. But you get no immediate impression that the left tower has the same number of blocks as the floor array, or of how tall a tower built from them would be. Confirming the numbers requires counting and comparing, which only System 2 can do, so not every attribute is assessed automatically.

questions.q: In the Exxon Valdez study, groups stated how much they would pay to save 2,000, 20,000, or 200,000 birds. What did the results show?
options: Willingness to pay rose roughly in proportion to the number of birds
The number of birds made very little difference to what people would pay
People would pay more to save fewer birds, because the cause felt more personal
People refused to put a price on saving birds at all
questions.explain: Average contributions were $80, $78, and $88, so quantity was almost ignored. Participants reacted to a prototype, the image of a single helpless bird drowning in oil, not to a sum.

questions.q: Why, according to Kahneman, does System 1 deal well with averages but poorly with sums?
options: Because sums require memory, which System 1 lacks entirely
Because System 1 can only judge things it has seen many times before
Because System 1 represents categories by a prototype or a set of typical exemplars
Because System 2 suppresses System 1 whenever numbers are involved
questions.explain: Kahneman explains that since System 1 represents categories by prototypes or typical exemplars, “it deals well with averages but poorly with sums”, so the size of a category tends to be ignored.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman reports that people's judgments of the average length of an array of lines become much less accurate when they are cognitively busy with a memory task.
questions.explain: The accuracy of these judgments is not impaired by a concurrent memory task, which shows that System 1 computes averages automatically and System 2 is not needed.

questions.q: Kahneman says System 1 represents categories by a ____ or a set of typical exemplars.
questions.explain: Representing a set by a prototype is why System 1 handles averages well and neglects the number of instances in a category.

questions.q: Kahneman says the size of a category tends to be ignored in judgments of what he calls ____ variables.
questions.explain: Sum-like variables depend on how many instances there are, such as the total value of saving many birds, and System 1's prototype-based view neglects that quantity.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say System 1 registers automatically and effortlessly when looking at an array of lines?
options: The average length of the lines
The color of the lines
The fact that the lines are not parallel
The total length of all the lines
The average length expressed in centimeters
questions.explain: System 1 forms an impression of the norm of length just as it registers color and that the lines are not parallel. The total needs System 2, and people cannot necessarily state the average in inches or centimeters even though they can match it.

questions.q: Sort each task from How Judgments Happen by which system Kahneman says handles it.

items.t: Registering the average length of an array of lines
Seeing that two towers are equally tall
Knowing the number of objects when there are four or fewer
Finding the total length of an array of lines
Confirming two sets of blocks have the same number
Multiplying an average length by the number of lines

questions.explain: System 1 gives immediate impressions of averages, similarities, and small numbers of objects; totals and exact counts of sets require System 2 to count, estimate, and multiply.

questions.q: Using Kahneman's idea of prototypes, sort each judgment by whether System 1 handles it well or tends to neglect its size.

items.t: The average height of players in a team photo
The image of a typical bird drowning in oil
The average length of lines in a figure
The value of saving 200,000 birds rather than 2,000
The total calories in a plate of ten snacks
The total length of lines in a figure

questions.explain: System 1 represents sets by typical members, so averages and prototypes come easily, while anything that depends on how many instances there are is a sum-like variable whose quantity tends to be ignored.

questions.q: Put in order the steps Kahneman says System 2 must take to find the total length of the lines in a figure.
items: Estimate the average length of the lines
Estimate or count the number of lines
Multiply the average length by the number of lines
questions.explain: System 1 has no suggestion for a total, so System 2 laboriously estimates the average, estimates or counts the lines, and multiplies the two.

questions.q: Using the Exxon Valdez bird study, explain what Kahneman means when he says System 1 neglects sum-like variables.
questions.a: If saving birds is an economic good, saving 200,000 should be worth far more than saving 2,000, yet groups offered about $80, $78, and $88. Participants reacted to a prototype, the awful image of one helpless bird drowning in oil, because System 1 represents categories by typical exemplars and deals well with averages but poorly with sums. The number of instances, a sum-like quantity, was almost completely neglected.

questions.q: In Kahneman's example of Julie, who read fluently at age four, how does he say people predict her college GPA?
options: By recalling how often early readers they know did well in college
By starting from the average GPA and adjusting a little for her early reading
By refusing to predict, since reading age says nothing about GPA
By translating from one scale to another and picking the matching GPA
questions.explain: People match intensities across scales, picking a GPA as impressive as reading at four. Kahneman warns that “this mode of prediction by matching is statistically wrong”, although it feels natural to System 1.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that people's intensity matches for Julie's reading prowess will be quite close to those of other people in their cultural milieu.
questions.explain: Kahneman assures readers their matches for height, income, crime, and GPA will be quite close to those of others in their culture, showing that intensity matching is easy and shared.

questions.q: Kahneman says an underlying scale of ____ allows System 1 to match across diverse dimensions, such as crimes and colors.
questions.explain: Questions about happiness, popularity, or punishment all refer to a dimension of intensity or amount, which lets System 1 translate a value on one scale into another.

questions.q: Which of these intensity-matching tasks does Kahneman describe from classic experiments?
options: Adjusting the loudness of a sound to the severity of crimes
Adjusting the loudness of a sound to the severity of legal punishments
Adjusting the temperature of water to the severity of crimes
Adjusting the size of a fine to the color of a crime scene
questions.explain: In the classic experiments people matched loudness to the severity of crimes, and other people matched loudness to the severity of punishments; hearing mismatched tones would feel unjust.

questions.q: In Kahneman's exercise matching Julie's early reading to a man's height, match each item to how Kahneman describes it.
pairs: Reading fluently at age four
Fairly remarkable, but not extraordinary
Reading at fifteen months
Extraordinary, perhaps like a man who is 7 feet 8 inches
A man 6 feet tall
Obviously too little to match Julie
A man 7 feet tall
Probably too much to match Julie
questions.explain: The task is to find a height as remarkable as Julie's achievement; Kahneman rejects 6 feet as too little and 7 feet as probably too much, and links reading at fifteen months to a man of 7 feet 8 inches.

questions.q: What is intensity matching, and what problem does Kahneman flag with using it for predictions like Julie's GPA?
questions.a: Many questions refer to an underlying dimension of intensity or amount, and System 1 can match values across very different dimensions, such as finding a height as remarkable as reading at age four. People predict Julie's GPA by translating from the reading scale to the GPA scale and picking the matching value. Kahneman says this prediction by matching is statistically wrong, though it is natural to System 1 and, for most people except statisticians, acceptable to System 2.

questions.q: In the rhyme-detection experiment Kahneman describes, what slowed participants down when deciding whether pairs like VOTE and GOAT rhymed?
options: Not knowing the meaning of one of the words
Hearing the words spoken by different voices
Discrepant spelling, though only sound mattered
Having to remember the previous pair of words
questions.explain: Participants only heard the words, yet they also compared spelling; the mismatch on this irrelevant dimension made them distinctly slower, showing that an intention to answer one question evoked another.

questions.q: In the sentence-verification experiment, why were "Some roads are snakes" and "Some jobs are jails" harder to reject than "Some jobs are snakes"?
options: They can be metaphorically true, which conflicts with the literal answer
They are literally true, unlike the sentence about jobs being snakes
They contain more familiar words, which slows down reading
They were presented later in the session, when people were tired
questions.explain: All three sentences are literally false, but the two difficult ones can be metaphorically true; computing the metaphor was not asked for, yet it ran anyway and disrupted performance. The idea that they are literally true is wrong.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that, like perceiving objects in three dimensions, you maintain a continuous evaluation of how happy and how wealthy you are.
questions.explain: Kahneman contrasts routine continuous assessments, such as building a three-dimensional representation of what you see, with occasional, voluntary judgments like how happy or wealthy you are, which occur only when you intend them.

questions.q: Kahneman calls the excess computation that happens when System 1 does more than System 2 asks of it the ____.
questions.explain: Kahneman writes, “I call this excess computation the mental shotgun.” A shotgun's scattering pellets make it impossible to aim at a single point.

questions.q: Which of these statements about the sentence-verification experiment in How Judgments Happen are correct?
options: All three sentences, about roads, jobs, snakes, and jails, are literally false
"Some jobs are snakes" is more obviously false than the other two
Most participants gave the wrong answer to the metaphorical sentences
Reaction times confirmed a substantial difference between the sentences
Participants were instructed to judge whether sentences were metaphorically true
questions.explain: The task asked only about literal truth; the correct answer prevailed, but the conflict with the irrelevant metaphorical reading slowed responses, as reaction times showed.

questions.q: Sort each computation by whether Kahneman says it is a routine assessment or an occasional, voluntary judgment.

items.t: A three-dimensional representation of what you see
Monitoring for violated expectations
Whether a situation is a threat or an opportunity
How happy you are
The president's prospects
The number of syllables in each word you read

questions.explain: Kahneman says no intention is needed for routine perception and monitoring, which run whenever your eyes are open, while judgments about happiness, wealth, a president's prospects, or syllable counts happen only when you intend them.

questions.q: Match each study in How Judgments Happen to what it showed.
pairs: Rhyme detection with VOTE and GOAT
Irrelevant spelling slowed judgments of sound
Judging sentences like Some jobs are jails
Metaphorical truth slowed the literal answer
Judging the average length of lines
System 1 registers a set's norm in a fraction of a second
Paying to save oil-soaked birds
The number of instances barely changed what people offered
questions.explain: The first two studies inspired the mental shotgun image; the line and bird studies show that System 1 handles averages and prototypes but neglects sums.

questions.q: A friend is asked whether a restaurant serves healthy food, but her answer keeps drifting to how friendly the waiter was. Using Kahneman's image of the mental shotgun, explain what is happening.
questions.a: Her System 2 intends to answer one specific question, but control over intended computations is far from precise, so System 1 computes much more than was asked, including a basic assessment of the waiter's friendliness. Like a shotgun whose pellets scatter, the intention evokes other, irrelevant computations, and these can intrude on and disrupt the main judgment, as spelling disrupted judgments of rhyme.

questions.q: Match each remark from Speaking of Judgment to the idea from How Judgments Happen that it illustrates.
pairs: Evaluating people as attractive or not, whether or not you want to
A basic assessment made automatically
Circuits evaluate dominance from face shape; he looks the part
Reading leadership from the shape of the face
The punishment won't feel just unless it matches the crime
Intensity matching across dimensions
Asked if a company is sound, he couldn't forget he likes its product
The mental shotgun
questions.explain: Each closing remark applies one chapter idea: automatic basic assessments, face-based judgments of dominance, matching intensities of crime and punishment, and excess computation intruding on a question.

questions.q: In Speaking of Judgment, a man asked whether a company was financially sound could not forget that he likes their product. Why does Kahneman call this a clear instance of a mental shotgun?
questions.a: The intended question was about financial soundness, but the intention to answer it also triggered other computations, including his evaluation of how much he likes the product. Because System 1 computes more than System 2 charges it to do, that irrelevant answer intruded on the judgment he was trying to make.

questions.q: At the end of How Judgments Happen, what does Kahneman say the next chapter will show the combination of the mental shotgun and intensity matching explains?
options: Why people are more sensitive to losses than to gains
Why we have intuitive judgments about many things we know little about
Why experts become overconfident in unpredictable environments
Why small samples produce extreme results more often
questions.explain: Kahneman closes by saying that in the next chapter, Answering an Easier Question, these two features explain why we have intuitive judgments about many things we know little about. Loss aversion and small samples belong to later parts of the book.

questions.q: Put the sections of How Judgments Happen in the order they appear.
items: Basic Assessments
Sets and Prototypes
Intensity Matching
The Mental Shotgun
Speaking of Judgment
questions.explain: The chapter moves from System 1's automatic assessments, through its handling of sets and its matching of intensities, to the mental shotgun, and ends with everyday remarks.

questions.q: Put these chapters of Thinking, Fast and Slow in the order they appear in the book.
items: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
How Judgments Happen
Answering an Easier Question
The Law of Small Numbers
questions.explain: How Judgments Happen is chapter 8, between chapter 7 and chapter 9, the last chapter of Part I; The Law of Small Numbers opens Part II, Heuristics and Biases.

questions.q: How does How Judgments Happen prepare the ground for the next chapter, Answering an Easier Question, at the close of Part I?
questions.a: The chapter lays out the System 1 features that make substitution possible: basic assessments that are easily substituted for harder questions, intensity matching across dimensions, and the mental shotgun that computes more than is asked. Kahneman says the combination of the mental shotgun with intensity matching explains why we have intuitive judgments about things we know little about, which the next chapter develops as answering an easier question. It also introduces the term judgment heuristic, used in the chapters that follow.

questions.q: In the opening of Kahneman's chapter on answering an easier question, what does he call a remarkable aspect of your mental life?
options: You are rarely stumped, because intuitive opinions come to mind about almost everything
You usually notice when a question is hard and stop to reason it through
You form opinions of people only after learning a good deal about them
You can nearly always explain and defend the evidence behind your intuitions
questions.explain: Kahneman says dumbfounded moments like facing 17 × 24 are rare: “The normal state of your mind is that you have intuitive feelings and opinions about almost everything.” The other options reverse his point that we like, trust and predict without knowing why.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says you often have answers to questions you do not completely understand, relying on evidence you can neither explain nor defend.
questions.explain: This is how the chapter opens: whether stated or not, we hold answers to questions we only partly understand, resting on evidence we cannot explain or defend. The chapter then sets out to explain how this happens.

questions.q: Kahneman calls the operation of answering one question in place of another ____.
questions.explain: He proposes that when no satisfactory answer to a hard question is found quickly, System 1 finds a related, easier question and answers it. He names this operation substitution.

questions.q: Match each term from Kahneman's account of substitution to its meaning.
pairs: Target question
The assessment you intend to produce
Heuristic question
The simpler question you answer instead
Heuristic
A simple procedure that finds adequate, though often imperfect, answers to hard questions
Substitution
Answering one question in place of another
questions.explain: Kahneman defines the target question as the assessment you intend to produce and the heuristic question as the simpler one you answer instead. A heuristic, technically, is a simple procedure giving adequate but often imperfect answers.

questions.q: In Kahneman's technical definition, a ____ is a simple procedure that helps find adequate, though often imperfect, answers to difficult questions.
questions.explain: This is the technical definition of heuristic given in the chapter. Kahneman adds that the word comes from the same root as eureka.

questions.q: How did Kahneman and Amos Tversky's puzzle about judgments of probability lead to the idea of substitution?
questions.a: They asked how people manage to judge probability without knowing precisely what probability is, and concluded that people must somehow simplify that impossible task. Their answer was that people asked to judge probability actually judge something else and believe they have judged probability. This idea of substitution became the core of the heuristics and biases approach.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, how do George Pólya's heuristics in How to Solve It differ from the heuristics discussed in the chapter on answering an easier question?
options: Pólya's are automatic shortcuts of System 1, while Kahneman's are chosen by System 2
Pólya's usually produce errors, while Kahneman's usually produce correct answers
Pólya's are deliberate strategies of System 2, while Kahneman's are not chosen at all
Pólya's apply only to perception, while Kahneman's apply only to emotions
questions.explain: Pólya's heuristics are “strategic procedures that are deliberately implemented by System 2.” The heuristics in this chapter are not chosen; they are a consequence of the mental shotgun. The idea that Pólya's heuristics are automatic System 1 shortcuts reverses the two.

questions.q: Kahneman says the heuristics he discusses are not chosen but are a consequence of the ____, the imprecise control we have over targeting our responses to questions.
questions.explain: The mental shotgun, introduced in the previous chapter, means System 1 computes more than intended. It readily evokes easy heuristic questions alongside hard target ones.

questions.q: In Kahneman's Table 1, match each difficult target question to the heuristic question people answer instead.
pairs: How much would you contribute to save an endangered species?
How much emotion do I feel when I think of dying dolphins?
How happy are you with your life these days?
What is my mood right now?
How popular will the president be six months from now?
How popular is the president right now?
How should financial advisers who prey on the elderly be punished?
How much anger do I feel when I think of financial predators?
How far will this primary candidate go in politics?
Does this woman look like a political winner?
questions.explain: Each heuristic question in Table 1 is easy to answer from current feelings or impressions and provides an off-the-shelf answer to the harder target question beside it.

questions.q: To express feelings about dying dolphins as a dollar contribution, System 1 uses ____, finding the amount that matches the strength of the feeling.
questions.explain: Both feelings and contribution dollars are intensity scales, so System 1 maps one onto the other. “The dollar amount that will come to my mind is the matching amount.”

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say can happen when a lazy System 2 endorses a heuristic answer?
options: You are not stumped by the question
You may not notice that you did not answer the question you were asked
You may not realize that the target question was difficult
You become aware that you answered an easier question
You check carefully whether the heuristic answer is appropriate
questions.explain: Kahneman says you will not be stumped, will not work hard, and may not notice the switch or even that the target question was hard, because an intuitive answer came readily. A lazy System 2 endorses the answer without much scrutiny, so the ideas that you become aware of the switch or check the heuristic answer carefully are wrong.

questions.q: What part does System 2 play after the mental shotgun and intensity matching supply an answer to an easier question?
questions.a: System 2 has the opportunity to reject the intuitive answer or to modify it by incorporating other information. However, a lazy System 2 often follows the path of least effort and endorses the heuristic answer without much scrutiny of whether it is truly appropriate. When it does, substitution occurs.

questions.q: Put in order the steps by which, in Kahneman's account, an intuitive answer to a hard target question is produced.
items: A hard target question gets no quick satisfactory answer
The mental shotgun evokes a related, easier heuristic question
The heuristic question is answered readily
Intensity matching fits that answer to the target question's scale
A lazy System 2 endorses the heuristic answer
questions.explain: System 1 first finds an easier related question and answers it, then intensity matching fits the answer to the original question. Finally System 2 could reject or modify the answer but often simply endorses it.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says the heuristic alternative to careful reasoning always leads to serious errors.
questions.explain: He says the heuristic alternative “sometimes works fairly well and sometimes leads to serious errors.” It is not always wrong.

questions.q: Which of these are issues Kahneman says you would first have to deal with before giving a reasoned answer to the target questions in Table 1?
options: What is the meaning of happiness?
How many dates did I have last month?
What are the likely political developments in the next six months?
How strong is the competition that the candidate faces?
How tall are the people in the corridor drawing?
questions.explain: Kahneman lists the meaning of happiness, likely political developments, sentences for other financial crimes, the candidate's competition and other environmental causes. Dealing with these seriously is impractical, which is why heuristic answers take over.

questions.q: Priya is asked whether a new local startup will still be in business in five years. She answers at once, based on how excited she felt during the founder's pitch. In Kahneman's terms, what has she done?
options: She deliberately used a Pólya-style strategy chosen by System 2
She answered an easier heuristic question in place of the target question
She misunderstood what question she was being asked
She reasoned carefully through the startup's competition and market
questions.explain: The hard target question is about the firm's future; the easy heuristic question is how she feels about the pitch. As with Kahneman's examples, she need not be confused about the question for substitution to occur.

questions.q: Dana reads a moving story about families stranded by a flood and immediately feels that 50 dollars is the right donation. Which System 1 capability, as Kahneman describes it, turns her feeling into a dollar figure?
options: The 3-D heuristic
Deliberate memory search
The mood heuristic for happiness
Intensity matching
questions.explain: Kahneman explains that feelings and contribution dollars are both intensity scales, and System 1 supplies the amount that matches the strength of the feeling, as with the dying dolphins.

questions.q: Put in order the steps of Kahneman and Amos Tversky's reasoning that led to the idea of substitution.
items: They asked how people judge probability without knowing what it is
They concluded that people must simplify that impossible task
They set out to find how people do it
They answered that people judge something else and think it is probability
questions.explain: Kahneman describes this sequence as the early origin of substitution, which became the core of the heuristics and biases approach.

questions.q: Sort each question into a target question or a likely heuristic question that might replace it, following Kahneman's account of substitution.

items.t: Will this restaurant still be thriving in five years?
How much did I enjoy my meal there tonight?
How happy are you with your life these days?
What is my mood right now?
How should financial advisers who prey on the elderly be punished?
How much anger do I feel when I think of financial predators?

questions.explain: A target question is the hard assessment you intend to make; a heuristic question is an easier, related one that comes readily to mind, such as a current feeling or impression.

questions.q: In Kahneman's picture of three men in a corridor, what does measuring the figures with a ruler reveal?
options: The figure on the right is indeed larger on the page
The figures are exactly the same size on the page
The figure on the left is actually larger on the page
The figure on the right is slightly smaller on the page
questions.explain: The obvious answer is that the figure on the right is larger, but a ruler shows the figures are exactly the same size. The impression comes from a powerful illusion that illustrates substitution.

questions.q: In Kahneman's corridor picture, why does the figure on the right look larger than the figure on the left?
questions.a: The corridor is drawn in perspective, so your perceptual system automatically interprets the picture as a three-dimensional scene rather than a flat image. In that 3-D interpretation the person on the right is both farther away and much larger. Substitution occurs: the dominant impression of 3-D size dictates the judgment of 2-D size, an illusion due to a 3-D heuristic.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says the corridor illusion of the three men is a misunderstanding of the question rather than a true illusion.
questions.explain: He says “What happens here is a true illusion, not a misunderstanding of the question.” You knew the question was about the figures as printed on the page.

questions.q: In discussing the corridor illusion, what evidence does Kahneman give that people are not confused about the question they were asked?
options: They judge the figures as equal when given more time to look
They can match the figures correctly once the corridor is erased
Asked to estimate the figures' size, they answer in inches, not feet
Asked to estimate the figures' size, they answer in feet, not inches
questions.explain: Experiments show that people estimating the size of the figures give answers in inches, so they understand the question is about the page. Answering in feet would reverse this detail.

questions.q: In the corridor illusion, Kahneman says you were influenced by the answer to a question you were not asked: How ____ are the three people?
questions.explain: You were asked about the size of the figures on the page but were swayed by the answer to an unasked question about the people's real height, which is the 3-D substitution.

questions.q: True or false: According to Kahneman, the bias associated with the 3-D heuristic is that objects that appear more distant also appear larger on the page.
questions.explain: Kahneman states this bias directly and adds that a judgment based on substitution “will inevitably be biased in predictable ways.”

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say about the 3-D heuristic in the corridor picture?
options: The substitution of 3-D for 2-D size occurs automatically
The 3-D cues are irrelevant to the task but cannot be ignored
Careful attention from System 2 makes the illusion disappear
The illusion mainly affects people who misread the question
Visual artists and experienced photographers can see the drawing as an object on the page
questions.explain: The substitution happens so deep in the perceptual system that you cannot help it, and only artists and photographers have learned to see the flat drawing. It is a true illusion, not a misreading of the question.

questions.q: Put in order the steps of Kahneman's corridor demonstration of the 3-D heuristic.
items: Look at the drawing of three men in a corridor
Judge whether the right figure is larger as printed on the page
Feel strongly that the figure on the right is larger
Measure with a ruler and find the figures the same size
questions.explain: Kahneman asks the reader to look and judge, notes that the obvious answer comes quickly, and then reveals that a ruler shows the figures are equal.

questions.q: In the survey of German students, what happened when the question about dates last month came before the question about happiness?
options: The correlation was about as high as correlations between psychological measures get
The correlation between dates and happiness stayed about zero
Students with more dates reported being less happy overall
Students refused to answer the happiness question at all
questions.explain: When happiness was asked first, the correlation was about zero. Reversing the order made it about as high as correlations between psychological measures can get.

questions.q: True or false: From the first German student survey, Kahneman concludes that dating was the center of these students' lives.
questions.explain: When happiness was asked first, happiness and dating were uncorrelated, so Kahneman concludes dating was apparently not the center of their lives. Dating only mattered when it was brought to mind first.

questions.q: In the survey of German students, sort each result or interpretation by the question order it belongs to.

items.t: Correlation between dates and happiness was about zero
Dating was not what first came to mind when judging happiness
Correlation was about as high as psychological measures can get
Emotion from the previous question was still on students' minds
Students with no dates were reminded of loneliness and rejection

questions.explain: Asked first, happiness did not track dating. Asked after dating, students substituted the emotion just aroused by their love life for an assessment of life as a whole.

questions.q: In the German student survey, why did asking about dates first make reported happiness track the number of dates?
questions.a: The dating question aroused an emotional reaction: students with many dates were reminded of a happy part of their life, and those with none of loneliness and rejection. Happiness these days is not a natural or easy assessment, but these students already had a ready-made answer to a related question, how happy they were with their love life. They substituted that answer for the question they were asked.

questions.q: In the German student survey, does Kahneman think students who answer the happiness question with their love life in mind are confused about the question?
options: Yes; they treat romantic life and life as a whole as the same thing
Yes; they misread the happiness question as one about dating
No; they deliberately chose dating as the best measure of happiness
No; they can tell the two apart, but System 1 has a ready answer
questions.explain: Students do not lose the ability to distinguish romantic life from life as a whole and would say the concepts differ if asked. They were asked how happy they were, and System 1 had a ready answer.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman name as questions that, asked just before a question about general happiness, produce the same pattern as the dating question?
options: A question about the students' relations with their parents
A question about the students' finances
A question about the students' favourite films
A question about the students' exam grades
questions.explain: Kahneman says the same pattern appears with questions about parents or finances; satisfaction in that particular domain dominates happiness reports. Any emotionally significant question that alters mood has the same effect.

questions.q: Kahneman ties the mood heuristic for happiness to the acronym ____: the present state of mind looms very large when people evaluate their happiness.
accept: what you see is all there is
questions.explain: WYSIATI, what you see is all there is, means the judgment uses whatever is currently in mind. Here the mood just aroused dominates the happiness report.

questions.q: Ravi is asked about a job he was just turned down for, and then asked how satisfied he is with his life as a whole. Based on Kahneman's mood heuristic for happiness, what is most likely?
options: His answer will be a careful average across all areas of his life
The rejection will weigh heavily and lower his reported satisfaction
The job question will have no effect, since he knows the topics differ
He will report higher satisfaction to make up for the bad news
questions.explain: Any emotionally significant question that alters mood carries over, and the present state of mind looms very large in happiness judgments. Knowing the questions differ does not stop the substitution.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says the psychology of the German dating survey is precisely analogous to the psychology of the corridor size illusion.
questions.explain: In both, people are not confused about the question but are swayed by a ready answer to a related, easier question: 3-D size for page size, and love-life happiness for happiness overall.

questions.q: The psychologist Paul Slovic proposed the ____ heuristic, in which people let their likes and dislikes determine their beliefs about the world.
questions.explain: Kahneman presents the affect heuristic as the case where the dominance of conclusions over arguments is most pronounced, because emotions are involved.

questions.q: According to Kahneman's account of the affect heuristic, what does a hawk in attitudes toward other nations tend to believe about them?
options: They are strong and will not be easily coerced
They are as strong as one's own country
They are relatively weak and likely to submit
They are friendly and unlikely to cause conflict
questions.explain: The hawk's attitude shapes the belief that other nations are weak and will submit. Believing other nations are strong and not easily coerced is what Kahneman says a dove probably thinks.

questions.q: Under the affect heuristic, what happens when you learn that an activity you disliked is less risky than you thought?
options: Your view of its benefits improves, even if nothing was said about benefits
Your view of its benefits gets worse, to balance the lower risk
Only your belief about its risk changes, not your view of its benefits
Nothing changes, because your opinion is wholly immune to information
questions.explain: Kahneman says your beliefs may change a little, and the news about lower risks “will also change your view of the benefits (for the better).” The mind is not completely closed, so the idea that opinion is immune to information is wrong.

questions.q: Sort each description of System 2 by whether Kahneman gives it in earlier chapters or for the context of attitudes in his discussion of the affect heuristic.
groups: System 2 in the context of attitudes

items.t: Resists System 1's suggestions and imposes logical analysis
Active in complex computations, comparisons and planning
Seems ultimately in charge, as in the bat-and-ball problem
An apologist for the emotions of System 1
An endorser rather than an enforcer
Searches mostly for information consistent with existing beliefs

questions.explain: Earlier System 2 appeared to be in charge, able to slow things down and criticize. With attitudes, it mostly defends System 1's emotions and seeks confirming information.

questions.q: In discussing the affect heuristic, what does Kahneman mean by the primacy of conclusions, and does it mean the mind is closed?
questions.a: Our likes and dislikes come first and determine which arguments we find compelling: if you like a policy you believe its benefits are substantial and its costs manageable. This does not mean the mind is completely closed; beliefs and even emotional attitude may change a little when you learn a disliked activity is less risky. But that information also improves your view of its benefits, even though nothing was said about them.

questions.q: Which of these beliefs would Kahneman's affect heuristic predict for Sam, who strongly dislikes nuclear power?
options: Its risks are high
Its benefits are negligible
Its benefits are substantial
Its risks are lower than those of the alternatives
questions.explain: Kahneman says that if you dislike something such as nuclear power, you probably believe “its risks are high and its benefits negligible.” Liking it would produce the opposite beliefs.

questions.q: Maya loves her electric scooter. Asked about it, she says its dangers are small and its benefits are huge, though she has never looked into either. Which idea from Kahneman's chapter on answering an easier question best explains her view?
options: The 3-D heuristic
The mood heuristic for happiness
Pólya's deliberate substitution strategy
The affect heuristic
questions.explain: In the affect heuristic, liking something drives beliefs that its risks are low and its benefits high, as Kahneman says of attitudes toward things like motorcycles.

questions.q: In the context of attitudes, Kahneman says System 2 is an endorser rather than an ____ of the emotions of System 1.
questions.explain: Kahneman describes System 2 here as “more of an apologist for the emotions of System 1 than a critic of those emotions.” It endorses rather than enforces.

questions.q: A hiring committee must decide whether a candidate can succeed in the job, but spends its meeting discussing how well she interviewed. In Kahneman's terms, what has happened?
options: They answered the target question of how well she interviews
They substituted how well she interviews for whether she can succeed
They substituted whether she can succeed for how well she interviews
They used the affect heuristic to judge her interview skills
questions.explain: Kahneman's example says the question faced is whether the candidate can succeed, while the question seemingly answered is whether she interviews well. The idea that they substituted whether she can succeed for how well she interviews reverses target and heuristic.

questions.q: A team predicts a firm's value several years from now by looking at last year's performance. Following Kahneman's advice on substitution, how should they challenge this?
questions.a: They should recognize that last year's performance is serving as a heuristic for the harder target question of the firm's future value. Kahneman suggests asking whether this heuristic is good enough and what other information is needed. More generally, they should ask whether they still remember the question they are trying to answer or have substituted an easier one.

questions.q: In Kahneman's table of System 1 characteristics, match each feature to the label he gives it.
pairs: Exaggerates emotional consistency
Halo effect
Focuses on existing evidence and ignores absent evidence
WYSIATI
Computes more than intended
Mental shotgun
Sometimes substitutes an easier question for a difficult one
Heuristics
Responds more strongly to losses than to gains
Loss aversion
questions.explain: The table attaches these labels in parentheses to each characteristic, gathering ideas from Part 1 and previewing loss aversion from Part 4.

questions.q: Which of these System 1 characteristics does Kahneman mark as introduced in detail in Part 4?
options: Responds more strongly to losses than to gains
Infers and invents causes and intentions
Overweights low probabilities
Neglects ambiguity and suppresses doubt
Frames decision problems narrowly, in isolation from one another
