questions.q: What did Kahneman advise his negotiation students to do when the other side makes an outrageous proposal, and why?
questions.a: He advised against coming back with an equally outrageous counteroffer, because that creates a gap that is hard to bridge later. Instead they should make a scene, storm out or threaten to, and make clear to themselves and the other side that they will not continue with that number on the table. The point is to deny the initial anchor its powerful effect.

questions.q: Explain why capping personal injury damages at $1 million might not be good for all potential defendants.
questions.a: A cap would eliminate awards larger than $1 million, but the cap itself becomes an anchor. It would pull up the size of many awards that would otherwise be much smaller. As a result it would almost certainly benefit serious offenders and large firms much more than small ones.

questions.q: Why, according to Kahneman, is System 2 susceptible to anchors even though anchoring tasks are completed by System 2?
options: System 2 deliberately chooses to trust the anchor because it saves effort
System 2 works on data retrieved from memory by an automatic System 1 operation, and anchors make some information easier to retrieve
System 2 is never involved in judgments of quantity
System 2 detects the anchor's influence but decides it is harmless
questions.explain: Retrieval is automatic and involuntary, so anchors bias what System 2 has to work with; System 2 has no control over the effect and no knowledge of it.

questions.q: Before estimating the cost of a renovation, a homeowner hears a contractor casually mention $90,000. What does Kahneman say she should assume?
options: That the number cannot affect her as long as she knows it was mentioned casually
That the number is useful because the contractor knows the true cost
That the number has had an anchoring effect on her, and if the stakes are high she should mobilize System 2 to combat it
That she can undo its effect simply by noticing she heard it
questions.explain: Kahneman advises assuming any number on the table has had an anchoring effect. You are aware of the anchor but cannot imagine how you would have thought without it, so noticing it is not enough.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman reports that people exposed to absurd anchors, such as Gandhi dying at 144, readily acknowledge that the anchor influenced their estimate.
questions.explain: They confidently deny that such obviously useless information could have influenced them, and they are wrong; System 2 has no knowledge of the effect.

questions.q: Kahneman links anchoring to the idea that the gist of a message is a story built from whatever information is available, however slight or poor, an idea he abbreviates as ____.
accept: what you see is all there is
questions.explain: A message affects the associative system regardless of its reliability, and a random anchor is the extreme case because it carries no information at all.

questions.q: Which of these explain why Kahneman says anchoring threatens our sense of autonomy?
options: We are aware of the anchor but do not know how it guides and constrains our thinking
We are usually unaware that any anchor was presented
We cannot imagine how we would have thought had the anchor been different or absent
Anchors only affect us when we believe they are informative
questions.explain: Unlike unnoticed primes, anchors are seen and attended to, yet their influence is hidden because we cannot picture the alternative. Their power does not depend on believing them.

questions.q: Sort these parts of anchoring by whether Kahneman assigns them to System 1 or System 2.

items.t: Automatically retrieving information from memory
Making anchor-compatible ideas easier to retrieve
Generating an impression of a very old Gandhi
Completing the final judgment or choice
Deliberately adjusting away from an anchor
Being mobilized to combat an anchor when stakes are high

questions.explain: System 1 supplies the biased associations automatically; System 2 completes the task and adjusts deliberately, but has no control over or knowledge of the System 1 bias.

questions.q: Why does System 2 fail to protect us from random anchors, according to Kahneman?
questions.a: Anchoring tasks are completed by System 2, but System 2 works on data retrieved from memory by an automatic and involuntary operation of System 1. Anchors make some information easier to retrieve, so System 2 works from a biased sample. It has no control over the effect and no knowledge of it, which is why people confidently deny being influenced by absurd anchors.

questions.q: What practical advice does Kahneman draw from the fact that we cannot see how an anchor shapes our thinking?
questions.a: We are always aware of the anchor, but we cannot imagine how we would have thought if it had been different or absent, so we cannot detect its influence. Kahneman says you should assume that any number on the table has had an anchoring effect on you. If the stakes are high, you should mobilize your System 2 to combat it, for example by thinking the opposite.

questions.q: Match each remark from the end of the anchors chapter to the idea it applies.
pairs: The acquired firm's expected revenue: set it aside
Refusing to let a received number shape judgment
Plans are best-case scenarios
Avoid anchoring on a plan by imagining how it could go wrong
Our aim is to get them anchored on this number
Using a first offer as an anchor in negotiation
If that is their proposal, the negotiations are over
Refusing to negotiate from an outrageous anchor
The defendant's lawyers mentioned a ridiculously low amount
A frivolous number anchored the judge's damages
questions.explain: The remarks cover defending against anchors (setting numbers aside, thinking of what could go wrong, refusing an outrageous start) and exploiting them in negotiation and court.

questions.q: A team forecasting a project's actual results wants to avoid anchoring on its own plan. Which approach does the anchors chapter suggest?
options: Average the plan's figures with last year's results
Ask the plan's authors how confident they feel
Adjust the plan's figures downward by a fixed percentage
Think about ways the plan could go wrong
questions.explain: Plans are best-case scenarios, and thinking about how the plan could fail is a form of thinking the opposite that counters the anchor. A fixed downward adjustment is still anchored on the plan.

questions.q: Why does the chapter on anchors belong in Part II, "Heuristics and Biases"?
options: It describes a systematic bias in estimation produced by adjustment and by automatic priming
It introduces the two systems for the first time
It explains how people choose between risky gambles
It shows how experts make reliable intuitive judgments
questions.explain: Part II examines heuristics and the biases they produce, and anchoring is a classic bias of judgment. The two systems were introduced in Part I, and risky choice belongs to Part IV.

questions.q: In the section on anchoring and the two systems, which earlier chapter's discussion does Kahneman recall to argue that a message affects the associative system regardless of its reliability?
options: The science of availability
The law of small numbers
Regression to the mean
Linda: less is more
questions.explain: He refers back to the discussion of the law of small numbers, the chapter just before. Availability comes next, and regression and Linda appear later in Part II.

questions.q: Put the main sections of the anchors chapter in the order they appear.
items: Anchoring as Adjustment
Anchoring as Priming Effect
The Anchoring Index
Uses and Abuses of Anchors
Anchoring and the Two Systems
questions.explain: The chapter first explains the two mechanisms, then measures the effect, then shows real-world uses, and finally draws the lesson about the two systems.

questions.q: Put these chapters from Part II of the book in order.
items: The Law of Small Numbers
Anchors
The Science of Availability
Availability, Emotion, and Risk
questions.explain: Anchors (Chapter 11) sits between the law of small numbers (Chapter 10) and the two availability chapters (12 and 13).

questions.q: Match each idea from Part I of the book to the role it plays in the anchors chapter.
pairs: Priming
Explains suggestion and the System 1 form of anchoring
Associative coherence
System 1 builds a world where the anchor is true
A lazy System 2
Explains why adjustment stops too soon
WYSIATI
A story is built from whatever information is present
questions.explain: The chapter applies Part I's account of the two systems: the anchor's System 1 effects come from priming and coherence, and the System 2 effect from lazy adjustment.

questions.q: Which of these ideas from earlier in the book does Kahneman draw on to explain anchoring?
options: Priming effects
Associative coherence
A weak or lazy System 2
Regression to the mean
The availability heuristic
questions.explain: Priming, associative coherence and the lazy controller all come from Part I. Regression to the mean and availability are discussed in later chapters, not used here.

questions.q: How does the anchors chapter connect the book's Part I account of the two systems to the heuristics and biases of Part II?
questions.a: Kahneman shows that anchoring has two sources, one for each system: deliberate but insufficient adjustment by a lazy System 2, and automatic priming by System 1 through associative coherence. It also echoes the previous chapter on the law of small numbers, where a message affects the associative system regardless of its reliability. So a bias in Part II is explained by the machinery described in Part I.

questions.q: Judging the frequency of a category by the ease with which instances come to mind is called the ____ heuristic.
questions.explain: Kahneman and Tversky named this process the availability heuristic while working in Eugene, Oregon.

questions.q: True or false: When Kahneman and Tversky first studied availability, they determined that the heuristic is an automatic operation rather than a deliberate strategy.
questions.explain: The two-system approach did not yet exist, and they did not attempt to decide whether the heuristic was deliberate or automatic. Kahneman says we now know that both systems are involved.

questions.q: In the two sets of letters XUZONLCJM and TAPCERHOB, how many words must you construct before you sense which set offers more possibilities?
options: None
At least three
About six
As many as twelve
questions.explain: Kahneman says the answer is none: you know almost immediately, without generating any instances, that one set offers far more possibilities. An impression of ease does not require retrieving examples.

questions.q: What does the example of the two letter sets (XUZONLCJM and TAPCERHOB), together with the countries in the news, show about how the availability heuristic works?
questions.a: It shows that an impression of how easily instances come to mind does not require actually retrieving any instances. You know almost immediately that one letter set allows far more words, perhaps by a factor of 10, and you can sense how often countries such as Belgium or Nicaragua appeared in the news without recalling specific stories. The feeling of ease is available before any instance is produced.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, which substitution does the availability heuristic perform?
options: It replaces a question about what is likely with one about what is typical
It replaces a judgment of value with a judgment of how much one would pay
It replaces the size of a category with how easily instances come to mind
It replaces an estimate of a number with an anchor seen just before
questions.explain: You wish to estimate the size of a category or the frequency of an event, but you report an impression of the ease with which instances come to mind. Swapping in an anchor is the mechanism of the previous chapter, not availability.

questions.q: Kahneman says that ____ of questions, as in the availability heuristic, inevitably produces systematic errors.
questions.explain: Like other heuristics of judgment, availability answers an easier question in place of the one asked, and “Substitution of questions inevitably produces systematic errors.”

questions.q: Why does the availability heuristic produce systematic errors, and what simple procedure does Kahneman offer for discovering its biases?
questions.a: The heuristic substitutes one question for another: instead of estimating the size of a category or the frequency of an event, you report how easily instances come to mind. Because ease depends on more than frequency, the substitution produces systematic errors. To find the biases, list factors other than frequency that make it easy to come up with instances; each factor on the list is a potential source of bias.

questions.q: What procedure does Kahneman recommend for discovering how the availability heuristic leads to biases?
options: Compare your estimate with the estimate of an expert
Count how many instances you can recall in one minute
Ask a friend to list instances and compare the totals
List factors other than frequency that make instances easy to recall
questions.explain: Each factor other than frequency that makes instances easy to come up with is a potential source of bias. The other procedures are not ones Kahneman proposes.

questions.q: A ____ event that attracts your attention, such as a Hollywood celebrity divorce, is easily retrieved from memory, so its frequency is likely to be exaggerated.
questions.explain: Salient events attract attention and come easily to mind, which is why people overestimate Hollywood divorces and political sex scandals.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman list as factors, other than frequency, that make instances easy to come to mind?
options: A salient event that attracts attention
A recent dramatic event such as a plane crash
Personal experiences and vivid examples
Statistics presented in a newspaper table
Incidents that happened to other people
questions.explain: Salience, dramatic events and personal or vivid experiences all raise availability. Statistics and incidents that happened to others are named as less available than personal experiences and vivid examples.

questions.q: Match each idea to Kahneman’s example of it.
pairs: A salient event
Hollywood divorces and political sex scandals seem more frequent
A dramatic event
A plane crash in the news alters feelings about the safety of flying
A personal experience
A judicial error affecting you undermines faith in the justice system
Ease without retrieval
Sensing which letter set allows more words without forming any
questions.explain: Three of these are factors other than true frequency that make instances come easily to mind, and so inflate judged frequency or risk. The letter sets show that ease can be sensed without retrieving any instances.

questions.q: Sort each kind of information by how available Kahneman says it tends to be.

items.t: Personal experiences
Pictures
Vivid examples
Your own household efforts
Incidents that happened to others
Mere words
Statistics
Your spouse's household efforts

questions.explain: Personal experiences, pictures and vivid examples are more available than incidents that happened to others, mere words or statistics. In the spouses study, each partner remembers his or her own efforts more clearly than the other's.

questions.q: Which of these questions does Kahneman offer as examples of reconsidering an impression to resist availability bias?
options: Is our belief that thefts by teenagers are a major problem due to a few recent instances in our neighborhood?
Could it be that I feel no need to get a flu shot because none of my acquaintances got the flu last year?
How many experts on the subject would agree with my estimate?
What was the first number I saw before I made this estimate?
questions.explain: Both of Kahneman's examples ask whether a few easily recalled cases, or their absence, are driving the impression. The question about a first number concerns anchoring, the topic of the previous chapter.

questions.q: In the spouses study, the self-assessed contributions to household tasks added up to more than ____.
questions.explain: Each spouse's own efforts are more available in memory, so both overestimate their share and the total exceeds 100%.

questions.q: How does Kahneman explain why spouses' self-estimated contributions exceed the possible total?
options: Each spouse remembers their own efforts more clearly than the other's
Each spouse wants to appear more helpful to the researchers
Each spouse counts shared tasks twice when estimating
Each spouse anchors on the first chore that is mentioned
questions.explain: The explanation is a simple availability bias: own contributions are remembered more clearly, and the difference in availability becomes a difference in judged frequency. The idea that spouses simply want to look good is ruled out because they also overestimated their part in causing quarrels.

questions.q: True or false: In the spouses study, partners also overestimated their own contribution to causing quarrels, though to a smaller extent than for desirable outcomes.
questions.explain: This is why Kahneman says the bias is not necessarily self-serving: it reflects what is available in memory, not only what flatters the self.

questions.q: What does the spouses' contribution study show, and why is this one of the rare cases where Kahneman is optimistic about controlling a bias?
questions.a: Spouses' self-estimated contributions to household tasks added up to more than 100% because each remembers their own efforts more clearly than the other's; the bias is not simply self-serving, since they also overestimated their part in quarrels. Kahneman is usually not optimistic about personal control of biases, but here the situations where credit allocation comes up are easy to identify, especially when tensions arise. Merely observing that there is usually more than 100% credit to go around is sometimes enough to defuse the situation.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman consider the bias in allocating credit for joint work an exception to his usual pessimism about debiasing?
options: Because the bias is weak and fades with experience
Because the situations where credit is allocated are easy to identify
Because people are rewarded for being modest about credit
Because experts in teamwork are immune to the bias
questions.explain: The opportunity for debiasing exists because circumstances involving credit allocation are easy to recognize, especially when several people at once feel unrecognized. Nothing in the chapter says the bias fades or that some people are immune.

questions.q: Maya and three colleagues finish a group report, and each privately feels they did more than a quarter of the work. Based on the availability account of the spouses study, what is the most useful thing for Maya to remember?
options: Her colleagues are probably exaggerating to win credit
She should insist that the work be recorded more precisely
Each member likely feels the same, because one's own efforts are more available
She probably did less than her share and should do more
questions.explain: Kahneman advises remembering that you are likely to feel you did more than your share even when every member of the team feels the same way. The idea that colleagues are lying misreads a memory bias as a deliberate one.

questions.q: Match each item from the opening of the chapter to its description.
pairs: 1971–72 in Eugene, Oregon
Kahneman and Tversky's most productive year together
Paul Slovic
Their main host, later the leading psychologist among scholars of risk
Attention and Effort
The book Kahneman wrote at night during that year
The two-system approach
Not yet developed when availability was first studied
questions.explain: The chapter opens with the Eugene year at the Oregon Research Institute, where the availability heuristic was studied before the two-system framework existed.

questions.q: In the early 1990s, a group of German psychologists led by Norbert ____ asked how listing a specified number of instances affects judgments of frequency.
questions.explain: Norbert Schwarz's group produced what Kahneman calls a major advance in understanding the availability heuristic.

questions.q: In Schwarz's assertiveness experiment, why does asking people for twelve instances rather than six pit two determinants of judgment against each other, and which one wins?
questions.a: Listing instances can affect the judgment through the number of instances retrieved and through the ease with which they come to mind. Twelve instances give an impressive number of cases, but the last few are hard to find, so fluency is low. The ease won: people who listed twelve rated themselves as less assertive than those who listed six, because “The experience of fluent retrieval of instances trumped the number retrieved.”

questions.q: In Schwarz's study, how did people who listed twelve instances of their own assertive behavior rate themselves, compared with people who listed six?
options: As more assertive, since they had found more examples
As equally assertive, since both lists were complete
As more assertive, but only if the task felt easy
As less assertive, since the last instances were hard to find
questions.explain: Self-ratings were dominated by ease of retrieval: struggling to finish a list of twelve signaled low assertiveness. The idea that more examples would raise the rating is exactly what the result overturned.

questions.q: True or false: Participants asked to list twelve cases in which they had not behaved assertively ended up thinking of themselves as quite assertive.
questions.explain: If you cannot easily come up with instances of meek behavior, you are likely to conclude that you are not meek at all.

questions.q: In the smiling and frowning version of the assertiveness study, "smilers" were told to contract the ____ muscle, which produces a light smile.
questions.explain: Smilers contracted the zygomaticus muscle, while frowners were told to furrow their brow.

questions.q: In the assertiveness study in which participants held a facial expression while listing six instances, what happened to the frowners?
options: They rated themselves as more assertive than the smilers
They rated themselves as relatively lacking in assertiveness
They listed more instances than the smilers in the time allowed
They were unaffected, since all listed the same number
questions.explain: Frowning accompanies and increases cognitive strain, so frowners had more difficulty retrieving assertive examples and rated themselves as relatively lacking in assertiveness, just as predicted.

questions.q: Which of these paradoxical results of listing instances does Kahneman report?
options: People believe they use their bicycles less often after recalling many instances
People are less confident in a choice after producing more arguments for it
People are less impressed by a car after listing many of its advantages
People are more confident an event was avoidable after listing many ways to avoid it
People are more eager to buy a car after listing many of its advantages
questions.explain: In each reported case, being asked for many instances makes retrieval hard and lowers the judgment. Listing more ways an event could have been avoided made people less, not more, confident that it was avoidable.

questions.q: Sort each result reported in Schwarz-style listing studies by the direction of the judgment after people listed many instances.

items.t: Self-rated assertiveness after listing twelve nonassertive acts
Course rating after listing many ways to improve it
Self-rated assertiveness after listing twelve assertive acts
Belief in how often one rides a bicycle
Confidence in a choice after many supporting arguments
Impression of a car after listing many advantages

questions.explain: Difficulty in retrieving many instances is read as evidence against the category retrieved. So listing many nonassertive acts or many course improvements produced the opposite of what the content alone suggests.

questions.q: How did a UCLA professor exploit the availability bias when he asked students to list ways to improve his course?
options: Students who listed more improvements rated the course higher
Students who listed more improvements rated the course lower
Students who listed more improvements dropped the course
Students who listed more improvements were more critical later
questions.explain: Struggling to come up with many improvements suggested the course had few flaws, so the students who listed more ways to improve the class rated it higher.

questions.q: Match each experimental condition to its reported result.
pairs: Listed twelve assertive acts rather than six
Rated themselves as less assertive
Furrowed their brow while listing
Rated themselves as relatively lacking in assertiveness
Told music would make retrieval harder
Rated themselves equally assertive after twelve as after six
Listed many ways to improve a course
Rated the course higher
questions.explain: Each result follows from how easy or hard retrieval felt, and the music condition shows that the effect disappears when the difficulty has an explanation.

questions.q: Because the judgment rests on fluency being worse than expected, Kahneman says the heuristic is better described as an "unexplained ____" heuristic.
questions.explain: Participants infer that they cannot be very assertive only because the drop in fluency surprises them; when the difficulty is explained, the effect disappears.

questions.q: What did Schwarz and his colleagues do to disrupt the availability heuristic, and what did this reveal?
questions.a: They gave participants an explanation for their fluency of retrieval, for example by saying background music would affect memory performance. Those told the music would make retrieval harder rated themselves as equally assertive after twelve instances as after six. Similar cover stories, such as curved or straight text boxes or the screen's background color, had the same effect, showing that ease affects judgment only when the low fluency is unexpected and unexplained.

questions.q: Which of these spurious explanations for retrieval fluency removed the effect of ease of retrieval in Schwarz-style studies?
options: Background music said to affect memory
Curved or straight text boxes
The background color of the screen
A cash reward for each instance listed
A warning that the task was being timed
questions.explain: Kahneman lists music, curved or straight text boxes and screen color among the irrelevant factors experimenters used. Rewards and time warnings are not mentioned in the chapter.

questions.q: Put the steps of the reasoning that leads people asked for twelve instances to call themselves unassertive in order.
items: Produce instances with diminishing fluency
Find the drop in fluency steeper than expected
Feel surprised by the unexpectedly low fluency
Conclude that one cannot be very assertive
questions.explain: Kahneman describes a chain: diminishing fluency, wrong expectations about its rate, a surprise, and the inference that one must not be very assertive. Remove the surprise and low fluency no longer affects the judgment.

questions.q: Which of these features of System 1 does Kahneman cite to show that the unexplained unavailability effect needs no complex reasoning?
options: It sets expectations and is surprised when they are violated
It looks for a possible cause of a surprise among recent surprises
It calculates exactly how fast fluency should decline
It deliberately weighs the number of instances against their ease
questions.explain: System 1 sets expectations, is surprised by violations and retrieves possible causes from recent surprises. Exact calculation and deliberate weighing are not what the automatic system does.

questions.q: Using the example of the neighbor's three-year-old in a top hat, explain how the music cover story can work without any complex reasoning.
questions.a: System 1 sets expectations and is surprised when they are violated, and it looks for causes of a surprise among recent surprises. System 2 can reset System 1's expectations on the fly: if you are told the boy next door often wears a top hat, you are far less surprised to see it. In the same way, mentioning the music as a cause of retrieval problems makes the difficulty of finding twelve instances no longer a surprise, so it does not enter the judgment of assertiveness.

questions.q: In the study of risks to cardiac health, how did students with a family history of heart disease respond after retrieving many instances of safe behavior?
options: They felt more at risk, because retrieval was difficult
They felt no different, because the task was casual for them
They felt more at risk, because they thought about heart disease
They felt safer, because they went by the content retrieved
questions.explain: Personally involved students focused on the number of instances, the opposite of the availability pattern shown by students without such a history. The idea that difficulty made them feel at risk describes the casual students.

questions.q: In Schwarz's cardiac health study, sort each student by how the student felt after the recall task.

items.t: No family history; struggled to find eight risky behaviors
Family history; retrieved many safe behaviors
No family history; struggled to find safe behaviors
Family history; retrieved many risky behaviors

questions.explain: Students without a family history followed ease of retrieval, while students with a family history went by the content they retrieved.

questions.q: True or false: In the cardiac health study, the students with no family history of heart disease focused on the number of instances they retrieved rather than on ease of retrieval.
questions.explain: It was the other way round: students without a family history were casual and followed the availability heuristic, while those with a family history attended to the number of instances.

questions.q: What does the cardiac health study show about when people rely on ease of retrieval and when they rely on content?
questions.a: Students with no family history of heart disease were casual and followed the availability heuristic, feeling safe when risky behaviors were hard to recall. Students with a family history, who were personally involved, showed the opposite pattern and went by the number of instances retrieved. Kahneman concludes that ease of retrieval is a System 1 heuristic that is replaced by a focus on content when System 2 is more engaged.

questions.q: Kahneman concludes that ease of retrieval is a System 1 heuristic, replaced by a focus on ____ when System 2 is more engaged.
questions.explain: People who are vigilant or personally involved attend to what they retrieved rather than to how easily it came.

questions.q: Sort each kind of person by whether Kahneman reports they are guided more by ease of retrieval or by the content retrieved.

items.t: Someone busy with another effortful task
Someone in a good mood after recalling a happy episode
Someone high on a scale of faith in intuition
Someone made to feel powerful
A true expert on the topic
A student with a family history of heart disease judging cardiac risk

questions.explain: People who go with the flow of System 1 are more affected by ease of retrieval. True experts, as opposed to knowledgeable novices, and personally involved students attended more to content.

questions.q: Which of these conditions make people more strongly affected by ease of retrieval than by the content retrieved?
options: Being engaged in another effortful task at the same time
Scoring low on a depression scale
Being made to feel powerful
Scoring high on a depression scale
Being a true expert on the topic
questions.explain: Kahneman lists a concurrent effortful task, a low depression score and feeling powerful among conditions in which people go with the flow. True experts are contrasted with knowledgeable novices, who rely more on ease.

questions.q: True or false: People are more strongly affected by ease of retrieval when they score low on a depression scale.
questions.explain: A low score on a depression scale appears in Kahneman's list of conditions in which people go with the flow and are guided more by ease than by content.

questions.q: What finding about power does Kahneman find particularly intriguing?
options: Powerful people rely less on intuition than others
Reminding people of a time they had power increases trust in their intuition
Trust in intuition is a fixed trait that power cannot change
Powerful people retrieve more instances before judging
questions.explain: The authors show that reliance on intuition is only in part a personality trait, since merely recalling a time of having power increases trust in one's own intuition. The idea that it is a fixed trait is what the finding contradicts.

questions.q: Lena is asked to write down ten reasons she likes her new apartment. She struggles after the first four and afterward feels less sure she made a good choice. Which idea from Schwarz's research best explains this?
options: Ease of retrieval trumped the number of reasons retrieved
Her mood improved, so she relied more on content
She anchored on the first reason that came to mind
She weighed the content of her reasons carefully
questions.explain: As with people who are less confident in a choice after producing more arguments for it, her unexpected difficulty in finding reasons was read as evidence against the apartment. Careful weighing of content would have made her more sure, not less.

questions.q: Put these studies in the order Kahneman presents them in the section on the psychology of availability.
items: Listing six versus twelve assertive acts
Smilers and frowners listing six instances
Background music given as a cause of difficulty
Students judging their cardiac risk
Conditions in which people go with the flow
questions.explain: The section moves from the basic paradox, to a direct test of fluency, to explaining away fluency, to personal involvement, and finally to the general conditions favoring ease over content.

questions.q: Match each everyday remark from the chapter's closing examples to the bias it describes.
pairs: Two planes crashed last month
She now prefers the train though the risk has not changed
Few media stories on indoor pollution
He underestimates its risks
Too many spy movies
She sees conspiracies everywhere
Several successes in a row
Failure does not come easily to the CEO's mind
questions.explain: Each remark traces a judgment of frequency or risk to what happens to be easy to bring to mind rather than to the actual statistics.

questions.q: In the chapter's closing remark about a CEO who has had several successes in a row, what does the availability bias produce?
options: Excessive caution, since she fears her luck will run out
Overconfidence, since failure does not easily come to mind
Indifference, since successes no longer feel like news
Accurate forecasts, since her experience is recent
questions.explain: Because failure does not come easily to her mind, “The availability bias is making her overconfident.”

questions.q: A friend refuses to fly after two widely reported plane crashes last month and takes the train instead. How would Kahneman explain her choice, and what would he advise?
questions.a: Kahneman would call this an availability bias: a dramatic event that attracts media coverage temporarily makes its category more available and alters feelings about the safety of flying. The actual risk has not changed, only the ease with which crashes come to mind. He would advise reconsidering the impression by asking whether it rests on a few recent instances and checking the statistics instead.

questions.q: Put these chapters of Part II, Heuristics and Biases, in the order they appear in the book.
items: Anchors
The Science of Availability
Availability, Emotion, and Risk
Tom W's Specialty
questions.explain: The Science of Availability is chapter 12, after Anchors and before Availability, Emotion, and Risk, which is followed by Tom W's Specialty.

questions.q: True or false: The Science of Availability is the first chapter of Part II, Heuristics and Biases.
questions.explain: Part II opens with The Law of Small Numbers, followed by Anchors; The Science of Availability is the third chapter of the part.

questions.q: Put these parts of the chapter The Science of Availability in the order they appear.
items: The productive year in Eugene with Paul Slovic
The definition of the availability heuristic
The spouses' contributions study
Schwarz's experiments on listing instances
Everyday remarks about availability
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the origin story to the definition and its biases, then to Schwarz's refinement under The Psychology of Availability, and closes with Speaking of Availability.

questions.q: Which statement best describes how The Science of Availability refines the original idea of the availability heuristic?
options: It abandons the idea that ease of retrieval affects judgments
It shows that availability applies only to judgments of risk
It finds that both systems are involved, with content replacing ease as System 2 engages
It shows that availability is the same mechanism as anchoring
questions.explain: The two-system approach did not exist when availability was first studied; the chapter concludes that ease of retrieval is a System 1 heuristic replaced by a focus on content when System 2 is more engaged.

questions.q: How does The Science of Availability connect to the ideas of Part I and prepare for the next chapter, Availability, Emotion, and Risk?
questions.a: The chapter treats availability as a case of the substitution described earlier: an easier question about ease of retrieval replaces a question about frequency. It explains Schwarz's results with Part I ideas such as cognitive strain, System 1's expectations and surprises, and System 2's ability to engage and reset them. Its examples of dramatic events, media coverage and perceived risk, and its host Paul Slovic as a scholar of risk, set up the next chapter's focus on how availability shapes judgments of risk.

questions.q: In the opening of the chapter on availability, emotion, and risk, what pattern did Howard Kunreuther notice in how Californians respond to significant earthquakes?
options: They buy little insurance at first, then steadily more as the years go by
They are diligent about insurance and protection for a while, then grow complacent as memories dim
They stay equally careful indefinitely once they have lived through one quake
They prepare carefully only for disasters they have read about but never experienced
questions.explain: Kunreuther saw that worry and diligence peak right after a disaster and fade as the memory dims, producing cycles of disaster, concern, and complacency. The idea of steady or permanent caution misses how availability decays with memory.

questions.q: A town builds its new flood wall exactly as high as the worst flood in its records and no higher. Which observation by Kunreuther does this illustrate?
options: People overprepare for disasters that the media have covered heavily
Governments protect against average floods rather than unusual ones
Insurance purchases rise right before a disaster is expected
Protective actions are designed to be adequate to the worst disaster actually experienced
questions.explain: Kunreuther observed that individuals and governments prepare for the worst disaster they have actually seen, as societies since pharaonic Egypt did with river high-water marks. “Images of a worse disaster do not come easily to mind.”

questions.q: Since pharaonic Egypt, societies have tracked the ____ of rivers that periodically flood, assuming floods will not rise higher than it.
questions.explain: Societies prepared for floods up to the existing high-water mark, apparently assuming no flood would exceed it. This shows protection pegged to the worst disaster actually experienced.

questions.q: Put in order the recurring cycle that Kunreuther described around disasters such as earthquakes.
items: A significant disaster strikes
Victims and near victims become very concerned
People diligently buy insurance and take protective measures
Memories of the disaster dim
Worry and diligence fade into complacency
questions.explain: Kahneman says the dynamics of memory explain the recurrent cycles of disaster, concern, and growing complacency. Diligence follows the disaster and fades as the memory loses its availability.

questions.q: How does availability explain the pattern of insurance purchase and protective action that Kunreuther observed after disasters?
questions.a: Right after a disaster, images of it come easily to mind, so people worry and buy insurance and take protective measures. As memories of the disaster dim, so do worry and diligence, producing recurrent cycles of disaster, concern, and growing complacency. Protection is also pegged to the worst disaster actually experienced, because “Images of a worse disaster do not come easily to mind.”

questions.q: In the survey on causes of death by Slovic, Lichtenstein, and Fischhoff, what did respondents conclude about strokes and accidents?
options: 80% judged accidental death to be more likely, though strokes cause almost twice as many deaths
80% judged strokes to be more likely, though accidents cause almost twice as many deaths
Most judged the two about equally likely, though strokes cause 18 times as many deaths
Most judged strokes more likely, which matched the health statistics of the time
questions.explain: Strokes cause almost twice as many deaths as all accidents combined, yet 80% of respondents picked accidents. The roughly equal judgment with an 18-to-1 ratio belongs to the comparison of disease with accidents.

questions.q: Which of these were findings of the causes-of-death survey by Slovic and his colleagues?
options: Tornadoes were seen as more frequent killers than asthma, though asthma causes 20 times more deaths
Death by disease and accidental death were judged about equally likely, though disease is 18 times as likely
Death by diabetes was judged far more likely than death by accidents
Death by lightning was judged more likely than death from botulism, matching the true ratio
Respondents' judgments closely matched the health statistics of the time
questions.explain: The tornado and disease findings both show dramatic causes overestimated. In fact accidents were judged more than 300 times as likely as diabetes deaths (true ratio 1:4), and lightning was judged less likely than botulism though it is 52 times more frequent.

questions.q: True or false: In the causes-of-death survey, death by lightning was judged less likely than death from botulism, even though lightning is 52 times more frequent.
questions.explain: This is one of the sample findings. Kahneman notes that unusual events such as botulism attract disproportionate attention and so seem less unusual than they really are.

questions.q: Match each comparison from the causes-of-death survey to the true frequency relationship reported.
pairs: Strokes vs. all accidents
Strokes cause almost twice as many deaths
Asthma vs. tornadoes
Asthma causes 20 times more deaths
Lightning vs. botulism
Lightning is 52 times more frequent
Disease vs. accidents
Disease is 18 times as likely
Accidents vs. diabetes
True ratio is 1:4, not 300 to 1
questions.explain: In each case, the cause that is vivid or newsworthy was overestimated relative to the duller but more common cause. Kahneman concludes that such estimates are warped by media coverage.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what is the clear lesson of the survey on causes of death?
options: People underestimate all causes of death to avoid feeling anxious
Respondents lacked access to accurate health statistics
Estimates of causes of death are warped by media coverage, which is biased toward novelty and poignancy
People overestimate causes of death that are common in their own families
questions.explain: Kahneman writes that “estimates of causes of death are warped by media coverage,” and that the coverage itself favors novelty and poignancy. The judgments track how often and how vividly risks are presented, not ignorance of statistics.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says the media shape what the public is interested in but are not themselves shaped by the public's interests.
questions.explain: Kahneman says the media are shaped by the public as well: editors cannot ignore the public's demands that certain topics and viewpoints receive extensive coverage. The influence runs both ways.

questions.q: Kahneman says the estimates of causes of death directly represent the activation of ideas in associative memory and are a good example of ____.
questions.explain: People answer the hard question of frequency with the easier question of how readily instances come to mind. This replacement of one question by another is what Kahneman calls substitution.

questions.q: What deeper insight did Slovic and his colleagues draw from the causes-of-death studies about availability and emotion?
questions.a: They saw that the ease with which ideas of risks come to mind and the emotional reactions to those risks are inextricably linked. Frightening thoughts and images come to mind with particular ease, and fluent, vivid thoughts of danger in turn intensify fear. Availability and emotion therefore reinforce each other in judgments of risk.

questions.q: Paul Slovic developed the notion of the ____ heuristic, in which people make judgments and decisions by consulting their emotions.
questions.explain: In the affect heuristic people ask: Do I like it? Do I hate it? How strongly do I feel about it? Their opinions and choices then express those feelings, often without their knowing it.

questions.q: Explain the affect heuristic and why Kahneman calls it an instance of substitution.
questions.a: In the affect heuristic, people make judgments and decisions by consulting their emotions: do I like it, do I hate it, how strongly do I feel? Their opinions and choices directly express their feelings and their tendency to approach or avoid, often without their knowing it. It is substitution because the answer to an easy question (How do I feel about it?) serves as the answer to a much harder one (What do I think about it?).

questions.q: Citing Antonio Damasio's work, Kahneman says that an inability to be guided by a “healthy ____” of bad consequences is a disastrous flaw.
questions.explain: Damasio observed that people who do not show appropriate emotions before deciding, sometimes because of brain damage, make worse decisions. Emotion plays a central role in guiding good decision making.

questions.q: Match each person to the contribution described in the chapter on availability, emotion, and risk.
pairs: Howard Kunreuther
Linked availability to insurance buying after disasters
Antonio Damasio
Proposed that emotional evaluations and bodily states guide decision making
Jonathan Haidt
Said the emotional tail wags the rational dog
Timur Kuran
Named the availability cascade together with Cass Sunstein
Lois Gibbs
Worked to sustain interest in the Love Canal problem
questions.explain: Each person appears at a distinct point in the chapter. Kunreuther opens it, Damasio and Haidt support the affect heuristic, and Kuran and Gibbs belong to the discussion of availability cascades.

questions.q: In Slovic's survey of technologies such as water fluoridation, chemical plants, food preservatives, and cars, what relationship appeared between respondents' estimates?
options: A strong positive correlation between perceived benefits and perceived risks
An implausibly high negative correlation between perceived benefits and perceived risks
No relationship between how people rated benefits and how they rated risks
A close match between perceived risks and the actual safety record of each technology
questions.explain: People who liked a technology saw large benefits and little risk, and people who disliked it saw the reverse. Because technologies lined up neatly from good to bad, no painful tradeoffs needed to be faced.

questions.q: In Slovic's technology survey, sort each judgment by whether it was typical of respondents who liked a technology or respondents who disliked it.

items.t: Rated it as offering large benefits
Saw it as imposing little risk
Could think only of its disadvantages
Found few advantages coming to mind

questions.explain: Feelings toward a technology set both estimates at once. Liked technologies seemed beneficial and safe, and disliked ones seemed risky and useless.

questions.q: True or false: In Slovic's technology survey, estimates of risk and benefit corresponded less closely when people rated them under time pressure.
questions.explain: Under time pressure the estimates corresponded even more closely. With less time for deliberate thought, affect governed the ratings even more.

questions.q: True or false: Members of the British Toxicology Society showed no link between how risky they thought a substance was and how beneficial they found it.
questions.explain: Kahneman says the toxicologists responded similarly to lay respondents: they found little benefit in substances or technologies they thought risky, and vice versa. Expertise did not remove the pattern.

questions.q: Kahneman says that consistent affect, as in the matching risk and benefit ratings for technologies, is a central element of what he calls associative ____.
questions.explain: When feelings line up, good things seem good in every respect and bad things bad in every respect. This tidy consistency is what Kahneman means by associative coherence.

questions.q: Put in order the steps of Slovic's experiment on the affect heuristic and technologies.
items: Respondents rate the benefits and risks of various technologies
Respondents read brief passages arguing in favor of a technology
The passages change the technology's emotional appeal
Beliefs shift even on the dimension the message never addressed
questions.explain: After the initial survey, some respondents read about benefits and others about low risks. The striking result was that a message about one dimension also changed beliefs about the other.

questions.q: A company's ad campaign stresses only the many health benefits of its new sweetener and says nothing about safety. What does Slovic's research predict about people who see the ad?
options: They will rate its benefits higher but leave their view of its risks unchanged
They will become more suspicious of its risks because the ad avoids the topic
They will also come to see it as less risky, though they received no evidence about risk
They will rate it as both more beneficial and more risky than before
questions.explain: People who read only about a technology's benefits also changed their beliefs about its risks, judging what they now liked more as less risky. The idea that risk judgments stay put ignores how a single feeling drives both.

questions.q: What did the second stage of Slovic's technology experiment show, and why does Kahneman find it striking?
questions.a: Respondents read passages arguing for technologies, stressing either their benefits or their low risks, which changed the technologies' emotional appeal. Those told about benefits also judged the technology less risky, and those told the risks were mild saw more benefits, though they received no relevant evidence. As Haidt put it, “The emotional tail wags the rational dog.”

questions.q: Which of these describe the imaginary world that, according to Kahneman, the affect heuristic creates?
options: Good technologies have few costs
Bad technologies have no benefits
All decisions are easy
Painful tradeoffs between benefits and costs must constantly be faced
Risks and benefits are judged independently of each other
questions.explain: The affect heuristic creates a world much tidier than reality, in which good things are good in every respect and bad things bad. In the real world, by contrast, we often face painful tradeoffs between benefits and costs.

questions.q: Match each term from the chapter on availability, emotion, and risk to its meaning.
pairs: Affect heuristic
Judging and deciding by consulting one's feelings of liking or disliking
Availability cascade
Self-sustaining chain from media reports to public panic and government action
Availability entrepreneurs
People or groups who keep a flow of worrying news going
Probability neglect
Concern that is not adequately sensitive to the probability of harm
questions.explain: These four terms carry the chapter's argument from individual emotion to social amplification of risk. The affect heuristic is Slovic's; the other three come from Sunstein and Kuran.

questions.q: Which of these features belong to Slovic's unflattering picture of Mr. and Ms. Citizen as judges of risk?
options: Guided by emotion rather than by reason
Easily swayed by trivial details
Inadequately sensitive to differences between low and negligibly low probabilities
Overly deferential to experts' numerical estimates
Unmoved by vivid stories in the media
questions.explain: Slovic describes citizens as emotional, swayed by trivial details, and insensitive to small differences in probability. Deference to experts and indifference to vivid stories run against everything else in the chapter.

questions.q: According to Slovic, how do experts compare with the public in their judgments of risk?
options: Experts are better with numbers and show many of the same biases in attenuated form
Experts are free of the biases that distort the public's judgments of risk
Experts are worse with numbers but make better value judgments than the public
Experts and the public show identical biases with identical strength
questions.explain: Slovic finds experts clearly superior with numbers and amounts, yet they show many of the same biases in attenuated form. The idea that experts are immune ignores that weaker version of the same biases.

questions.q: Sort each way of thinking about risk by whether Slovic attributes it mainly to experts or to the public.

items.t: Counting the number of lives lost
Counting life-years lost
Distinguishing good deaths from bad deaths
Separating random accidents from deaths in voluntary activities like skiing

questions.explain: Experts often measure risk by lives or life-years lost, while the public draws finer distinctions. Slovic argues these distinctions are legitimate and ignored by statistics that merely count cases.

questions.q: Which of these distinctions does Slovic say the public draws but statistics that merely count cases tend to ignore?
options: Between good deaths and bad deaths
Between random accidental fatalities and deaths during voluntary activities such as skiing
Between deaths per million people and deaths per million dollars of product
Between lives saved and dollars spent by regulators
questions.explain: These finer distinctions lead Slovic to argue that the public has a richer conception of risk than the experts do. Measures such as deaths per million dollars of product are among the nine expert-style definitions he lists, not public distinctions.

questions.q: Why does Slovic argue that risk is not objective, and what does he conclude from this?
questions.a: Slovic holds that risk does not exist out there waiting to be measured; humans invented the concept to cope with danger and uncertainty. He lists nine ways of defining the mortality risk of a toxic release, from deaths per million people to deaths per million dollars of product, so the evaluation depends on which measure is chosen. He concludes that “defining risk is thus an exercise in power,” and resists letting experts rule unchallenged.

questions.q: In Cass Sunstein's view of risk regulation, what are the natural units for analyzing policy?
options: The intensity of public concern and the media coverage a risk receives
The number of lives (or life-years) saved and the dollar cost to the economy
The number of distinct ways a risk can be defined and measured
The share of citizens who voluntarily accept a given risk
questions.explain: Sunstein wants regulation guided by rational weighting of costs and benefits measured in lives or life-years saved and dollars. Life-years give more weight to saving the young; public concern is exactly what he thinks distorts priorities.

questions.q: Which of these reasons does Sunstein give for why lawmakers and regulators may be overly responsive to citizens' irrational concerns about risk?
options: Political sensitivity
They are prone to the same cognitive biases as other citizens
They are paid by availability entrepreneurs
They lack access to any health statistics
They are legally required to follow opinion polls
questions.explain: Sunstein names political sensitivity and shared cognitive biases. Biased reactions to risks thus become an important source of erratic and misplaced priorities in public policy.

questions.q: What is Cass Sunstein's position on the roles of experts and the public in risk policy?
questions.a: Sunstein defends experts as a bulwark against “populist” excesses and thinks United States regulation sets priorities poorly because it reacts to public pressure. He wants risk regulation guided by rational weighting of costs and benefits, measured in lives or life-years saved and dollars. Unlike Slovic, he believes science, expertise, and careful deliberation can achieve objectivity about risk.

questions.q: Sunstein and Timur Kuran named the mechanism through which biases flow into policy the availability ____.
questions.explain: An availability cascade is a self-sustaining chain of events that can run from media reports of a minor event to public panic and large-scale government action.

questions.q: When Kuran and Sunstein say “availability is more equal than the others,” what expanded notion of the availability heuristic do they have in mind?
options: Availability is the only heuristic that affects experts as well as the public
Availability determines how often people read the news
The importance of an idea is judged by the fluency and emotional charge with which it comes to mind
Availability makes people judge rare events as rarer than they are
questions.explain: In the social context, availability supports judgments other than frequency, notably judgments of how important an idea is. The idea that rare events seem rarer reverses the botulism finding, where unusual events seemed less unusual.

questions.q: Individuals or organizations who work to ensure a continuous flow of worrying news, speeding along an availability cascade, are called availability ____.
questions.explain: Availability entrepreneurs deliberately keep a risk in the news, feeding the cycle of coverage and concern. Lois Gibbs's efforts at Love Canal show the role in action.

questions.q: Put in order the stages of an availability cascade as Kahneman describes them.
items: A media story about a risk catches the attention of part of the public
That public becomes aroused and worried
The emotional reaction becomes a story itself, prompting more coverage
The issue becomes politically important because it is on everyone's mind
Priorities are reset and other risks fade into the background
questions.explain: Coverage and concern feed each other in a self-sustaining loop until the political response follows the intensity of public sentiment. The end state is that the cascade has reset priorities.

questions.q: Which of these are features of an availability cascade as Kahneman describes it?
options: Scientists who try to dampen the fear attract little attention, most of it hostile
The emotional reaction of the public becomes a news story in itself
The danger is increasingly exaggerated as the media compete for headlines
The political response is guided by careful analysis of all risks
Media coverage fades as public concern grows
questions.explain: In a cascade, coverage and concern amplify each other, and anyone who says the danger is overstated is suspected of a cover-up. The response is guided by the intensity of public sentiment, not by careful analysis of all risks.

questions.q: A local news report about a single rare illness at a school sparks parent worry, the worry becomes its own story, coverage grows, and the town council funds an expensive response. What concept from Kuran and Sunstein fits best?
options: Probability neglect without any social amplification
The affect heuristic applied to new technologies
Associative coherence among expert judgments
An availability cascade
questions.explain: The chain runs from a minor media report through rising concern and more coverage to government action, the standard script of an availability cascade. Probability neglect alone would not explain the self-reinforcing social cycle.

questions.q: Which of these events were part of the Love Canal availability cascade as Kahneman recounts it?
options: Daily stories about Love Canal at the peak of the affair
ABC News airing a program titled The Killing Ground
Empty baby-size coffins paraded in front of the legislature
The testimony of the actress Meryl Streep before Congress
The FDA banning the offending chemical
questions.explain: These three events belong to Love Canal, which began when buried toxic waste was exposed in 1979. Meryl Streep's testimony and the FDA ban belong to the Alar incident.

questions.q: The legislation passed after Love Canal, called CERCLA, established a ____ for cleaning up toxic sites.
questions.explain: CERCLA established a Superfund and is considered a significant achievement of environmental legislation. It was also expensive, and some claim the money could have saved more lives elsewhere.

questions.q: Using the Love Canal affair, explain how an availability cascade works.
questions.a: An availability cascade is a self-sustaining chain in which media reports of a risk arouse public worry, the worry becomes news itself, and coverage and concern feed each other until government acts. At Love Canal, exposed toxic waste in 1979 led to daily stories, activism by Lois Gibbs, a program called The Killing Ground, and scientists who said the danger was overstated being ignored or shouted down. Residents were relocated and CERCLA's Superfund followed, though claims of actual health damage appear not to have been substantiated.

questions.q: Put in order the events of the Alar incident as Kahneman recounts them.
items: Press stories report tumors in rats and mice given gigantic doses
Frightened public prompts more media coverage
Meryl Streep testifies before Congress
The manufacturer withdraws Alar and the FDA bans it
Later research suggests a very small possible risk
questions.explain: Fear and coverage fed each other, the basic mechanism of a cascade, leading to the product's withdrawal and ban. Subsequent research showed the incident was an enormous overreaction to a minor problem.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what was the probable net effect of the Alar incident on public health?
options: Probably detrimental, because fewer good apples were consumed
Strongly beneficial, because a dangerous carcinogen was removed from apples
Neutral, because the chemical had no effect and apple consumption was unchanged
Beneficial, because it raised the priority of food safety research
questions.explain: Kahneman judges Alar “an enormous overreaction to a minor problem” and says its net effect on public health was probably detrimental because people ate fewer good apples.

questions.q: Sort each detail by whether it belongs to the Love Canal affair or the Alar incident.

items.t: Buried toxic waste exposed during a rainy season
Lois Gibbs works to sustain interest
Empty baby-size coffins paraded before the legislature
A chemical sprayed on apples to improve their appearance
Meryl Streep testifies before Congress
A caller asks whether to pour apple juice down the drain

questions.explain: Kuran and Sunstein used both cases to illustrate availability cascades. Love Canal concerned toxic waste near a community; Alar concerned a growth regulator sprayed on apples.

questions.q: Sunstein coined the phrase “____” for the pattern in which concern is not adequately sensitive to the probability of harm.
questions.explain: With small risks we either ignore them or give them far too much weight. Combined with availability cascades, probability neglect leads to gross exaggeration of minor threats.

questions.q: Lena reads about a one-in-a-million side effect of a vaccine, cannot stop picturing it, and refuses the shot. Which idea from the chapter best explains her reaction?
options: The affect heuristic making her see large benefits and small risks
Expert judgment showing biases in attenuated form
Associative coherence among unrelated technologies
Probability neglect: she imagines the numerator and ignores the denominator
questions.explain: Kahneman says that with small risks we either ignore them or give them far too much weight, because we imagine the tragic story (the numerator) and not the denominator. Seeing large benefits and small risks would push her toward the shot, not away from it.

questions.q: What basic limitation in dealing with small risks does the Alar tale illustrate, and how does Kahneman explain it?
questions.a: With small risks we either ignore them altogether or give them far too much weight, with nothing in between. As with a parent waiting up for a teenager late from a party, images of disaster come to mind even when there is almost nothing to worry about. We imagine the numerator, the tragic story on the news, and not the denominator; Sunstein calls this “probability neglect.”

questions.q: Why does Kahneman call terrorists the most significant practitioners of inducing availability cascades?
options: Because terror attacks usually cause more deaths than traffic accidents
Because gruesome, endlessly repeated images make a small risk highly available
Because experts consistently underestimate the number of terror casualties
Because governments deliberately hide the frequency of terror attacks
questions.explain: Even in Israel, weekly terror casualties almost never approached traffic deaths; the difference lies in how easily and often the risks come to mind. “Terrorism speaks directly to System 1.”

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says Paul Slovic trusts the experts less and the public somewhat more than Cass Sunstein does.
questions.explain: Slovic points out that insulating experts from public emotion produces policies the public will reject, which is impossible in a democracy. Sunstein instead seeks mechanisms that insulate decision makers from public pressure.

questions.q: Match each thinker to the view on risk policy given in the chapter.
pairs: Paul Slovic
Risk is not objective; defining it is an exercise in power
Cass Sunstein
Experts should be a bulwark against populist excesses
Kuran and Sunstein
In society, availability is more equal than other heuristics
Daniel Kahneman
Policy should combine experts' knowledge with the public's emotions
questions.explain: Slovic and Sunstein disagree sharply about experts, Kuran and Sunstein coined the availability cascade, and Kahneman agrees with both friends in part.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it reflects Slovic's side or Sunstein's side of the debate on risk policy.

items.t: The public has a richer conception of risk than experts
There is no such thing as objective risk
Insulating experts produces policies the public will reject
Regulation should rationally weigh costs and benefits
Decision makers should be insulated from public pressure
Science and careful deliberation can achieve objectivity

questions.explain: Slovic trusts the public more and denies that risk is objective. Sunstein trusts expert cost-benefit analysis and wants decisions shielded from public pressure.

questions.q: Where does Kahneman come down in the debate between Slovic and Sunstein?
options: He sides with Sunstein that public fears should be ignored when they are irrational
He sides with Slovic that availability cascades do not really distort priorities
He agrees with both, and says policy makers must protect the public from fear, not only real dangers
He agrees with neither and proposes that risk policy be left to the courts
questions.explain: Kahneman shares Sunstein's discomfort with irrational fears shaping policy and Slovic's belief that widespread fears should not be ignored. Fear is painful and debilitating whether rational or not.

questions.q: Sort each consequence of availability cascades by whether Kahneman presents it as a cost or as a possible long-term benefit.

items.t: Distorting priorities in the allocation of public resources
Money that might have saved more lives elsewhere
Gross exaggeration of minor threats
Calling attention to whole classes of risks
Increasing the overall size of the risk-reduction budget
Raising the priority of environmental concerns

questions.explain: Kahneman grants that cascades distort priorities, yet notes that Love Canal, though it may have drawn excessive resources to toxic waste, raised the general priority of environmental concerns.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman think policy makers should not ignore widespread public fears, even unreasonable ones?
questions.a: Kahneman shares Slovic's belief that widespread fears should not be ignored, because rational or not, fear is painful and debilitating. Policy makers must therefore protect the public from fear, not only from real dangers. He also notes the public resists decisions by unelected, unaccountable experts, so psychology should inform risk policies that combine experts' knowledge with the public's emotions and intuitions.

questions.q: Match each example from the chapter to the idea it illustrates.
pairs: River high-water marks in pharaonic Egypt
Preparing only for the worst disaster actually experienced
Parent waiting up for a late teenager
Imagining the numerator and not the denominator
Terror attacks in Israel vs. traffic deaths
A small risk made highly available by vivid images
Liked technologies rated low in risk
Feelings driving both benefit and risk judgments
questions.explain: Each example ties a concrete case to one mechanism: availability tied to memory, probability neglect, availability cascades driven by images, and the affect heuristic.

questions.q: A colleague is raving about a new software tool that, she insists, has large benefits and no costs at all. Which diagnosis does Kahneman offer for such talk?
options: The affect heuristic is at work
An availability cascade is under way
Probability neglect is distorting her view
She is anchoring on the price of the tool
questions.explain: Kahneman's sample remark reads: “She’s raving about an innovation that has large benefits and no costs. I suspect the affect heuristic.” Liking something makes its benefits seem large and its costs small.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman's sample remark describes an availability cascade as a nonevent inflated by the media and the public until it becomes all anyone is talking about.
questions.explain: The closing remark calls an availability cascade “a nonevent that is inflated by the media and the public until it fills our TV screens.” It captures the self-sustaining loop of coverage and concern.

questions.q: Someone tells you a new diet pill is wonderful and totally safe because they love how it makes them feel. Using the chapter's ideas, how would you respond?
questions.a: This sounds like the affect heuristic: liking the pill makes its benefits seem large and its risks small, even without evidence about risk. Slovic found that when people favor a technology, they rate its benefits high and its risks low, a world tidier than reality. Real choices usually involve painful tradeoffs, so the risks deserve separate, evidence-based scrutiny.

questions.q: What does the title “Availability, Emotion, and Risk” signal about how this chapter builds on the previous chapter, “The Science of Availability”?
options: It drops availability in favor of a new theory of emotion
It argues that availability matters only in laboratory tasks
It shows that experts are immune to the availability heuristic
It extends availability by linking it to emotion and applying it to judgments of risk and policy
questions.explain: The chapter takes the availability heuristic from Chapter 12 and connects it to the affect heuristic, then follows it into public perceptions of risk and risk policy. Experts, it notes, share the biases in attenuated form.

questions.q: Put in order the parts of the chapter on availability, emotion, and risk.
items: Kunreuther on insurance and protection after disasters
Availability and Affect
The Public and the Experts
Speaking of Availability Cascades
questions.explain: The chapter moves from individual responses to disasters, to the link between availability and emotion, to the social and policy debate, and ends with sample remarks.

questions.q: The chapter on availability, emotion, and risk belongs to Part 2 of the book, titled “____.”
questions.explain: Part 2 runs from The Law of Small Numbers through chapters on anchors and availability. This chapter sits between The Science of Availability and Tom W's Specialty.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter on availability, emotion, and risk is where the affect heuristic is first mentioned in the book.
questions.explain: Kahneman introduces it with the words “As mentioned earlier,” signaling that the affect heuristic appeared before. This chapter develops it further in the context of risk.

questions.q: How does the chapter on availability, emotion, and risk fit into the book's argument about heuristics, coming after The Science of Availability and before Tom W's Specialty?
questions.a: It carries the availability heuristic beyond frequency judgments to show how ease of recall and emotion together shape perceptions of risk, and how social mechanisms such as availability cascades turn these biases into public policy. Like earlier chapters, it treats both availability and the affect heuristic as instances of substitution. The next chapter, Tom W's Specialty, continues Part 2 with a further problem of judgment.

questions.q: In the first version of Kahneman's Tom W puzzle, where Tom is picked at random from a university's graduate students and nothing else is known, what should guide your ranking of the nine fields?
options: The base rates, meaning the relative size of enrollment in each field
How closely Tom fits the stereotype of a student in each field
Which fields you personally find most interesting or prestigious
Which fields come most easily to mind as examples of graduate study
questions.explain: Kahneman says you knew immediately that the relative size of enrollment in the different fields is the key, just as the share of red and green marbles decides a draw from an urn. Stereotype fit cannot apply because nothing is known about Tom yet.

questions.q: In the Tom W chapter, Kahneman says the proportion of marbles of a particular kind in an urn is called a ____.
questions.explain: He introduces the term with the urn analogy, then applies it: the base rate of humanities and education is the proportion of all graduate students enrolled in that field.

questions.q: In the second Tom W task, after reading the personality sketch, what were people asked to rank the nine fields by?
options: The likelihood that Tom W is now a student in each field
The number of graduate students enrolled in each field
How similar Tom W's description is to the typical student in each field
How much each field would benefit from someone like Tom W
questions.explain: The second task is a similarity task: compare the description of Tom W with the typical graduate student in each field. The likelihood ranking is the third, critical task given to the prediction group.

questions.q: Which of these traits are part of the personality sketch of Tom W in Kahneman's puzzle?
options: High intelligence, although lacking in true creativity
A need for order, clarity, and neat and tidy systems
Little feel and little sympathy for other people
A great enjoyment of interacting with others
Highly original writing praised by his teachers
Indifference to questions of right and wrong
questions.explain: The sketch describes Tom as intelligent but not truly creative, needing order and tidy systems, and having little sympathy for others. It says he does not enjoy interacting with others, that his writing is dull and mechanical, and that he has a deep moral sense.

questions.q: Match each hint planted in the Tom W description to the stereotype judgment Kahneman says it prompts.
pairs: Corny puns
Hints of nerdiness that make computer science fit well
Neat and tidy systems
A good fit with engineering
Little feel and little sympathy for other people
A poor fit with social science and social work
questions.explain: Kahneman says the description was written to fit the computer science stereotype, with engineering also ranked high. The lack of sympathy for people makes Tom seem a poor match for social science and social work.

questions.q: In Kahneman's Tom W similarity task, sort each item by whether it is relevant or irrelevant to judging how similar Tom is to students in a field.

items.t: How well the sketch matches the stereotype of each field
Hints in the sketch such as corny puns
Your image of a typical library science student
The number of students enrolled in each field
Whether the sketch is a true portrait of Tom
Whether the university even has a library science department

questions.explain: For a similarity task only the fit between the description and each stereotype matters. Kahneman notes that the accuracy of the description and the base rates are irrelevant, since the similarity of an individual to a group's stereotype is unaffected by the size of the group.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says ranking nine careers by similarity needs the sequential organization of System 2, while the hints planted in the Tom W description were meant to activate a stereotype automatically through System 1.
questions.explain: He says the ranking task requires the discipline of which only System 2 is capable, but the hints such as corny puns were intended to activate an association with a stereotype, an automatic activity of System 1.

questions.q: Kahneman says Tom W was intentionally designed as an “____” character: a good fit to small fields and a poor fit to the most populated specialties.
questions.explain: The description fits computer scientists, librarians and engineers, which are small groups, and fits poorly with the largest groups, humanities and education and social science and social work. That design pits representativeness against base rates.

questions.q: Sort these graduate fields by how Kahneman says the Tom W description fits them.

items.t: Computer science
Library science
Engineering
Humanities and education
Social science and social work

questions.explain: Tom W fits the stereotypes of small groups such as computer scientists, librarians and engineers, and fits poorly with the two largest fields, which participants almost always ranked very low.

questions.q: Put these fields in the order of the average similarity ranking for Tom W when the experiment was first run in the early 1970s, from best fit to worst fit.
