items: Computer science
Engineering
Physical and life sciences
Law
Social science and social work
questions.explain: The average ordering put computer science first and engineering second, physical and life sciences fourth, law sixth, and social science and social work last. Kahneman adds that professional stereotypes have changed little in the nearly forty years since.

questions.q: Put the tasks of Kahneman's Tom W study in the order they are presented.
items: Rank the fields by likelihood with no information about Tom
Read a personality sketch of Tom of uncertain validity
Rank the fields by how similar Tom is to their typical students
Rank the fields by the likelihood that Tom is a student in each
questions.explain: The first puzzle relies on base rates alone, the second introduces the sketch and asks for a similarity ranking, and the third, critical task asks the prediction group for a likelihood ranking given the sketch.

questions.q: In the Tom W chapter, why is the size of a group irrelevant when you judge how similar Tom is to that group's students?
questions.a: Similarity compares an individual with the stereotype of a group, and that stereotype is the same however many people belong to the group. Kahneman notes that you could compare Tom with an image of library science students even if the university had no such department. Base rates and the accuracy of the description therefore play no part in a similarity judgment.

questions.q: Using Kahneman's urn analogy, explain why base rates are the right guide in the first Tom W puzzle.
questions.a: With no specific information, Tom is like a single marble drawn at random from an urn, and the chance of a colour depends on how many marbles of each colour there are. In the same way, the probability that Tom is in a field is the proportion of graduate students in that field, its base rate. So you would guess humanities and education over computer science or library science, because more students are enrolled there.

questions.q: Kahneman and Tversky called the focus on how similar Tom W's description is to the stereotypes of the fields ____.
questions.explain: They expected the prediction group to focus exclusively on the similarity of the description to the stereotypes, which they called representativeness, and to ignore base rates and doubts about the description.

questions.q: Which of these did the psychology graduate students in Kahneman's Tom W prediction group know?
options: The base rates of the different fields
That the source of Tom W's description was not highly trustworthy
Statistics, from having taken several courses in it
Which field Tom W was actually enrolled in
That the description was designed as an anti-base-rate character
questions.explain: The prediction group knew the relevant statistical facts and the weakness of the source, and all had taken several statistics courses. They did not know Tom's real field or how the description had been designed, which is why their answers were a fair test of representativeness.

questions.q: In Kahneman's Tom W study, how did the prediction group's rankings by probability compare with rankings by similarity to the stereotype?
options: They were a compromise between similarity and the base rates
They did not differ from the similarity rankings
They followed the base rates closely and ignored similarity
They differed sharply because the students knew statistics
questions.explain: Kahneman says substitution was perfect: the 114 students' probability rankings did not differ from similarity rankings, with no sign that they did anything but judge representativeness. Their training in statistics did not lead them to weigh the base rates.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman call Robyn Dawes's tentative guess “computer scientist?” a happy moment?
options: Dawes was a sophisticated statistician, so even an expert had neglected the base rate
Dawes guessed Tom's real field, which proved the description was accurate
Dawes refused to guess, showing the puzzle was too hard for experts
Dawes immediately cited the base rate, showing that experts are immune
questions.explain: Dawes was a statistician and a skeptic about intuitive judgment, so if anyone would see the relevance of the base rate it would be him. When he still guessed computer scientist, Kahneman felt that “even the mighty had fallen”.

questions.q: Put the events of Kahneman's story about Robyn Dawes and the Tom W description in order.
items: Kahneman finishes the Tom W description in the early morning
Robyn Dawes is the first person to arrive at work
Dawes guesses that Tom W is a computer scientist
Kahneman mentions the base rate
Dawes immediately recognizes his mistake
questions.explain: Kahneman wrote the description overnight in Eugene, showed it to Dawes when he arrived, and heard him guess computer scientist. Dawes saw his error as soon as the base rate was mentioned, but had not thought of it spontaneously.

questions.q: What statistical background did the 114 psychology graduate students in Kahneman's Tom W prediction task have?
options: None, since they were chosen for having no statistical training
A single short lecture on base rates given before the task
Training as professional baseball statisticians
Several courses in statistics, taken by all of them
questions.explain: All 114 students, from three major universities, had taken several statistics courses. Even so, their probability rankings matched the similarity rankings, showing that statistical knowledge did not stop the substitution.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman call it a serious mistake to answer a question about Tom W's probability with a judgment of similarity?
questions.a: Judgments of similarity and probability are not constrained by the same logical rules. It is fine for a similarity judgment to ignore base rates and the chance that the description is inaccurate, but a probability judgment that ignores base rates and the quality of evidence will certainly make mistakes. Substituting the easier similarity question for the hard probability question imports that error.

questions.q: How did Kahneman come to write the Tom W description, and what was it meant to do?
questions.a: During the year he and Amos spent in Eugene, Kahneman stayed in the office through the night and made up a description that would pit representativeness and base rates against each other. He finished Tom W in the early morning hours. The sketch was designed so that the most representative fields were small ones, letting the experiment show whether people would ignore the base rates.

questions.q: Kahneman says that for many experts, “the probability that Tom W studies computer science” is a measure of subjective ____ of belief.
questions.explain: Events you are sure of and events you think impossible sit at the extremes, and for many events you hold an intermediate degree of belief, which is your probability of that event.

questions.q: Match each of Kahneman's examples to the degree of belief he assigns it when explaining subjective probability.
pairs: That the sun rose this morning
An event you are sure of
The Pacific Ocean freezing all at once
An event you consider impossible
Your next-door neighbor being a computer scientist
An event given an intermediate degree of belief
questions.explain: Kahneman uses these three examples to show probability as subjective degree of belief, ranging from certainty through intermediate belief to impossibility.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say the vague lay notion of probability is related to?
options: Uncertainty
Plausibility
Surprise
Precise mathematical frequency
Logical necessity
questions.explain: For laypeople, he says, probability is a vague notion related to uncertainty, propensity, plausibility and surprise. Precise definitions are what logicians and statisticians have developed, not what ordinary people use.

questions.q: When Kahneman notes that no one ever asked him what he meant by probability, what does he contrast this with?
options: Statisticians, who always demanded a precise definition first
A strange concept such as globability, which people would have asked about
Questions about base rates, which people found impossible to answer
Questions about similarity, which people refused to attempt
questions.explain: People acted as if they knew how to answer probability questions, unlike an invented concept such as globability, about which they would have raised a hand. Probability is vague in the way words like democracy or beauty are, yet usable.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, why are people not stumped when asked to assess probability?
questions.a: They do not try to judge probability as statisticians and philosophers use the word. A question about probability or likelihood activates a mental shotgun that evokes answers to easier questions. One of these easy answers is an automatic assessment of representativeness, which is routine in understanding language.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says System 1 generates an impression of similarity only when a person deliberately sets out to compare two things.
questions.explain: He says “System 1 generates an impression of similarity without intending to do so”, which is why the idea of Elvis Presley's parents wanting him to be a dentist strikes us as mildly funny.

questions.q: Match each person to their role in Kahneman's discussion of prediction by representativeness.
pairs: Robyn Dawes
Statistician who still guessed Tom W was a computer scientist
Michael Lewis
Author of a bestseller about the inefficiency of predicting by representativeness
Billy Beane
Manager who overruled scouts and picked players by past statistics
questions.explain: Dawes shows that even experts substitute representativeness for probability. Lewis's Moneyball tells how Beane, manager of the Oakland A's, beat the scouts' habit of judging players by build and look.

questions.q: In Kahneman's account of Moneyball, why were the players chosen by the Oakland A's inexpensive?
options: They had poor statistics of past performance
They were young players with no record at all
Other teams had rejected them for not looking the part
Scouts had rated them highly but they had been injured
questions.explain: Billy Beane selected players by the statistics of past performance, while other teams' scouts judged partly by build and look. Players who did not look the part were cheap, and the team soon achieved excellent results at low cost.

questions.q: A hiring panel prefers a candidate because he just looks like a leader, without checking his record. Which idea from Kahneman's Tom W chapter best describes this?
options: Base-rate reasoning
Regression to the mean
The availability heuristic
Prediction by representativeness
questions.explain: Kahneman says we rely on representativeness when we judge leadership potential by the shape of a chin or the force of speeches. Judging by fit to a stereotype, rather than by statistics or base rates, is prediction by representativeness.

questions.q: Sort each prediction by whether it relies on representativeness or on statistics, in the sense of Kahneman's Tom W chapter.

items.t: A scout rates a player by his build and look
“He won’t go far as an academic; too many tattoos.”
Judging a candidate's leadership by the shape of his chin
Choosing players by the statistics of past performance
Guessing Tom's field from enrollment proportions
Forecasting a start-up from the industry's success rate

questions.explain: Representativeness judges by fit to a stereotype, as with tattoos or a candidate's chin. Billy Beane's player statistics and base rates for enrollment or industry success are statistical information that Kahneman contrasts with it.

questions.q: What virtue does Kahneman grant to judging probability by representativeness?
options: It always respects the base rates of the categories involved
It is immune to bias when the evidence is vivid
It works only for people trained in statistics
Its intuitive impressions are usually more accurate than chance guesses
questions.explain: He says the impressions it produces are often, indeed usually, more accurate than chance, because many stereotypes contain some truth. The trouble comes from relying on it exclusively and neglecting base rates.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give as examples where the stereotypes behind representativeness have some truth?
options: People who act friendly are usually in fact friendly
A very tall, thin professional athlete is more likely to play basketball than football
Young men are more likely than elderly women to drive aggressively
A shy poetry lover is more likely to study Chinese literature than business
A New York Times reader on the subway is more likely to have a PhD than no degree
questions.explain: These are among his examples of stereotypes with some truth. The shy poetry lover and the subway reader are his examples of the opposite: cases where representativeness misleads because it neglects base rates.

questions.q: Kahneman says one sin of representativeness is an excessive willingness to predict the occurrence of unlikely, low ____ events.
questions.explain: Representativeness pushes people to predict rare outcomes when an individual fits their stereotype, even though such outcomes are uncommon in the population.

questions.q: In Kahneman's example of a woman reading The New York Times on the New York subway, why is “she has a PhD” not necessarily the wiser bet?
options: Many more nongraduates than PhDs ride New York subways
PhDs rarely read The New York Times on the subway
The description of her reading is not trustworthy
Representativeness always gives the wrong answer
questions.explain: Representativeness suggests the PhD, but the base rate points the other way: far more people without a college degree ride the subway. Kahneman does not say the heuristic is always wrong, only that it neglects this base rate.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman advises that a woman described as “a shy poetry lover” should be guessed to study Chinese literature rather than business administration.
questions.explain: He advises the opposite: opt for business administration. Even if every female student of Chinese literature were shy and loved poetry, the much larger population of business students almost certainly contains more of them.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say you should guess business administration rather than Chinese literature for a woman described as a shy poetry lover?
questions.a: The description fits the stereotype of a Chinese literature student, but that field is small and business administration is much larger. Even if every female student of Chinese literature were shy and loved poetry, there are almost certainly more bashful poetry lovers among the many business students. Following representativeness here commits the sin of predicting a low base-rate event.

questions.q: Sort each piece of information from Kahneman's examples into base-rate information or information about the individual case.

items.t: The share of graduate students enrolled in humanities and education
Many more nongraduates than PhDs ride New York subways
A belief that 3% of graduate students are in computer science
Tom W's writing is enlivened by corny puns
A woman is described as a shy poetry lover
A stranger is reading The New York Times

questions.explain: Base rates are proportions in the whole population. Descriptions of a particular person activate stereotypes and tend to be weighted more than mere statistics.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says his and Tversky's early conclusion, that base-rate information will always be neglected when information about the specific instance is available, was too strong.
questions.explain: Later experiments that explicitly provided base rates found many participants were influenced by them, although information about the individual case was almost always weighted more than mere statistics.

questions.q: Match each instruction or condition to its effect on the use of base rates, as Kahneman reports.
pairs: Told to “think like a statistician”
Enhanced use of base-rate information
Told to “think like a clinician”
Reduced use of base-rate information
Frowning during the Tom W task
Some sensitivity to the base rates
Puffing out the cheeks during the task
Exclusive reliance on representativeness
questions.explain: Norbert Schwarz and colleagues found the statistician instruction helped and the clinician instruction had the opposite effect. In the Harvard study, frowners showed some sensitivity to base rates, while cheek-puffers replicated the original results.

questions.q: In the Harvard experiment on the Tom W problem, why did frowning improve predictive accuracy?
options: Frowning put students in a bad mood that made them doubt the sketch
Frowning increases the vigilance of System 2 and reduces reliance on intuition
Frowning made the base rates easier to read and remember
Frowning is an emotionally neutral expression, unlike puffing the cheeks
questions.explain: Kahneman says frowning generally increases System 2 vigilance and reduces overconfidence and reliance on intuition. Puffing the cheeks was the emotionally neutral condition, and those students ignored the base rates.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman name as the two possible reasons for the failure of System 2 when base rates are neglected?
options: Ignorance
Laziness
Excessive trust in statistics
Lack of arithmetic skill
Strong emotional arousal
questions.explain: Some people ignore base rates because they believe them irrelevant once individual information is given, which is ignorance. Others make the same mistake because they are not focused on the task, which is laziness.

questions.q: Kahneman concludes that if frowning makes a difference, ____ seems to be the proper explanation of base-rate neglect, at least among Harvard undergraduates.
questions.explain: Their System 2 knows that base rates are relevant but applies that knowledge only when it invests special effort, which frowning encourages. Ignorance would not be cured by a frown.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say both System 1 and System 2 should be indicted when an incorrect intuitive judgment is made?
questions.a: System 1 suggests the incorrect intuition, and System 2 endorses it and expresses it in a judgment. System 2 can fail through ignorance, believing base rates irrelevant, or through laziness, not focusing on the task. The frowning study suggests that laziness is the explanation, at least for the Harvard students tested, since System 2 knows base rates matter but uses that knowledge only with special effort.

questions.q: Kahneman says the second sin of representativeness is insensitivity to the ____ of evidence.
questions.explain: In the Tom W example the description may or may not be accurate, and readers were told it should not be trusted, yet it still drove their judgments.

questions.q: Kahneman links insensitivity to the quality of evidence to the System 1 rule known by the acronym ____.
accept: what you see is all there is
questions.explain: WYSIATI, what you see is all there is, means System 1 works with the information at hand as if it were true, so a description of doubtful accuracy still activates the associative machinery.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say about evidence of doubtful quality, such as the Tom W sketch?
options: In principle, worthless information should be treated no differently from a lack of information
Unless you reject evidence immediately, System 1 processes it as if it were true
The statement that Tom has little sympathy for people probably convinced most readers he is unlikely to study social work
Once you are warned that a source is unreliable, System 1 automatically discounts it
An untrustworthy description has little effect on most readers' judgments
questions.explain: Kahneman says you understand the principle that worthless information equals no information, but WYSIATI makes it hard to apply because System 1 treats the available information as true. That is why the warning did not stop readers from ruling out social work.

questions.q: What does Kahneman say you can do when you have doubts about the quality of the evidence?
options: Ignore the base rate and rely on your strongest impression
Seek out a more vivid description of the case
Let your judgments of probability stay close to the base rate
Reject all the evidence and give no estimate at all
questions.explain: His advice is to keep probability judgments close to the base rate. He warns that this discipline is not easy, since it requires significant self-monitoring and self-control.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that keeping your probability judgments close to the base rate when evidence is doubtful is easy once you understand the principle.
questions.explain: He warns, “Don’t expect this exercise of discipline to be easy”, because it requires a significant effort of self-monitoring and self-control.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what is the correct answer to the Tom W puzzle?
options: Rank computer science first, since the description fits it best
Stay close to the base rates, slightly lowering populous fields and slightly raising rare ones
Ignore the description completely and use only the base rates
Give every field an equal chance, since the description is unreliable
questions.explain: You should stay very close to your prior beliefs, adjusting them only slightly toward the description. You are not exactly where you would be with no information, but because the evidence is untrustworthy, the base rates should dominate.

questions.q: Explain Kahneman's correct answer to the Tom W puzzle and why it is correct.
questions.a: You should stay very close to your prior beliefs, slightly reducing the high probabilities of well-populated fields such as humanities and education and social science and social work, and slightly raising the low probabilities of rare fields such as library science and computer science. The description gives a little evidence, so you do not end exactly where you would with no information. But that evidence is not trustworthy, so the base rates should dominate your estimates.

questions.q: A coworker known for spreading false gossip tells you a colleague is about to quit, and you suddenly feel sure it is true. What would Kahneman advise?
options: Keep your estimate close to the base rate of colleagues quitting
Trust the feeling, since a vivid story is usually diagnostic
Treat the rumor as certain until it is proved false
Assume the opposite, since the source is unreliable
questions.explain: When you doubt the quality of evidence, Kahneman says to let probability judgments stay close to the base rate. WYSIATI makes the story feel convincing, but weak evidence should move you only a little.

questions.q: Sort each judgment into the sin of representativeness it mainly shows, following Kahneman.
groups: Insensitivity to the quality of evidence

items.t: Betting that a subway Times reader has a PhD
Guessing that a shy poetry lover studies Chinese literature
Ranking small computer science above much larger fields for Tom
Ruling out social work from a sketch you were told not to trust
Treating a psychological test of uncertain validity as a true portrait

questions.explain: The first sin bets on rare categories because the case fits their stereotype. The second sin lets evidence of poor or unknown quality drive judgments as if it were accurate.

questions.q: In Kahneman's rain example, if you believe there is a 40% chance it will rain sometime tomorrow, which belief does the logic of probability forbid?
options: A 60% chance it will not rain tomorrow
A 40% chance it will rain sometime tomorrow
A 50% chance it will rain tomorrow morning
A belief that rain tomorrow is uncertain
questions.explain: Rain in the morning is only part of rain sometime tomorrow, so it cannot be more likely than 40%. You must also believe there is a 60% chance of no rain, because beliefs should be constrained by the logic of probability.

questions.q: In Kahneman's election example, if you believe candidate X has a 30% chance of being elected and an 80% chance of reelection if he wins, you must believe his chance of being elected twice in a row is ____.
questions.explain: The chance of both events is 30% times 80%, which is 24%. Kahneman uses this to show that subjective beliefs should still obey the logic of probability.

questions.q: Kahneman says the relevant rules for cases such as the Tom W problem are provided by ____ statistics.
questions.explain: He calls Bayesian statistics an influential modern approach, named after the Reverend Thomas Bayes.

questions.q: Who does Kahneman say Thomas Bayes was?
options: An English minister of the eighteenth century credited with the logic of changing one's mind in light of evidence
A colleague of Kahneman's in Eugene who helped design the Tom W study
A nineteenth-century statistician who first measured enrollment base rates
A modern psychologist who showed that frowning improves base-rate use
questions.explain: Bayes is credited with the first major contribution to the problem of how people should change their mind in the light of evidence. The frowning study and the Tom W design involved other people.

questions.q: Bayes's rule, as Kahneman describes it, specifies how prior beliefs should be combined with the ____ of the evidence, the degree to which it favors the hypothesis over the alternative.
questions.explain: In this chapter the prior beliefs are base rates, and diagnosticity is how strongly the evidence points to one hypothesis rather than another.

questions.q: In Kahneman's Bayes example, if 3% of graduate students are in computer science and Tom W's description is 4 times more likely for a computer science student, what probability should you assign to Tom being a computer scientist?
questions.explain: Bayes's rule combines the 3% base rate with the 4-to-1 diagnosticity of the evidence to give 11%. Simply multiplying 3% by 4 to get 12% is not how the rule works.

questions.q: True or false: In Kahneman's Bayes example, if the base rate for computer science had been 80% instead of 3%, the same description would raise the probability to 94.1%.
questions.explain: Kahneman gives this figure to show that the same evidence produces very different conclusions depending on the base rate it is combined with.

questions.q: Put the steps of Kahneman's argument in his discussion of how to discipline intuition in order.
items: Subjective beliefs should be constrained by the logic of probability
Bayesian statistics supplies the rules for problems like Tom W
Bayes's rule combines base rates with the diagnosticity of evidence
Two ideas to keep in mind about how we mess up Bayesian reasoning
Two keys: anchor on a base rate and question the diagnosticity
questions.explain: Kahneman starts with the rain and election examples, introduces Bayes and a numerical example, states the two ideas about where we go wrong, and ends with the two practical keys.

questions.q: Which of these are the two ideas Kahneman says to keep in mind about Bayesian reasoning and how we tend to mess it up?
options: Base rates matter even in the presence of evidence about the case at hand
Intuitive impressions of the diagnosticity of evidence are often exaggerated
Base rates can be ignored once a vivid description is available
We usually underestimate how diagnostic our evidence is
The mathematical details must be mastered before any judgment
questions.explain: Kahneman says base rates matter even with evidence, which is often not intuitively obvious, and that we tend to exaggerate diagnosticity. He says the mathematical details are not relevant in his book.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, why do our intuitive impressions of the diagnosticity of evidence tend to be exaggerated?
questions.a: The combination of WYSIATI and associative coherence tends to make us believe in the stories we spin for ourselves. We treat the information in front of us as all there is and build a coherent story from it. That coherence makes the evidence feel more telling about the case than it really is.

questions.q: What are Kahneman's two essential keys to disciplined Bayesian reasoning, and what does he admit about them?
questions.a: The first is to anchor your judgment of the probability of an outcome on a plausible base rate. The second is to question the diagnosticity of your evidence. Kahneman says both ideas are straightforward, yet he was shocked to realize he was never taught how to implement them and still finds it unnatural to do so.

questions.q: Match each term from Kahneman's discussion of Bayesian reasoning to its meaning.
pairs: Prior beliefs
In this chapter's examples, the base rates
Diagnosticity
The degree to which evidence favors the hypothesis over the alternative
Bayes's rule
How prior beliefs should be combined with the diagnosticity of evidence
Subjective probability
Your degree of belief, which should obey the logic of probability
questions.explain: Kahneman defines these terms in the section on disciplining intuition, using base rates as the priors for problems like Tom W.

questions.q: In Kahneman's example remark about a company with a well-trimmed lawn, a competent-looking receptionist and attractive furniture, what is the speaker warning against?
options: Ignoring the base rate of company failures in the industry
Trusting a damning report based on weak evidence
Judging how well the company is managed by representativeness
Predicting rare events from vivid personal stories
questions.explain: The speaker hopes “the board does not go by representativeness”: surface signs that look like a well-run firm do not show that it is well managed.

questions.q: True or false: One of Kahneman's example remarks says that when the evidence is weak, one should stick with the base rates.
questions.explain: The remark criticizes people who keep predicting rare events from weak evidence and concludes that weak evidence calls for staying with the base rates.

questions.q: Match each of Kahneman's example remarks about representativeness to the lesson it applies.
pairs: The lawn is well trimmed and the furniture is attractive
Appearances that fit a stereotype do not show good management
This start-up looks as if it could not fail
Ask how this case differs from a very low industry success rate
They keep making the same mistake
When evidence is weak, stay close to the base rate
This report is absolutely damning
Allow for uncertainty about the quality of evidence
questions.explain: Each remark applies an idea from the chapter: avoid judging by appearance, respect base rates and ask how a case differs, stay close to base rates when evidence is weak, and allow for the quality of evidence.

questions.q: A colleague says a new start-up “looks as if it could not fail”. Using Kahneman's reasoning, what should be asked and why?
questions.a: One should ask what the base rate of success is in the industry and how we know this case is different. The start-up's appearance is a judgment of representativeness, and Kahneman's first key is to anchor the prediction on a plausible base rate, which here is extremely low. The impression should then move the estimate only as far as its diagnosticity justifies.

questions.q: Why does Tom W's Specialty fit where it does in Part 2 of Thinking, Fast and Slow?
options: It ends the book's discussion of the two systems before heuristics are introduced
After two chapters on availability, it introduces another heuristic, representativeness
It opens the part on overconfidence by showing the illusion of validity
It introduces prospect theory before the chapters on choices
questions.explain: Part 2, Heuristics and Biases, follows The Science of Availability and Availability, Emotion, and Risk with this chapter on representativeness. Overconfidence and choices are the subjects of Parts 3 and 4.

questions.q: Put these chapters of Part 2 of Thinking, Fast and Slow in their order in the book.
items: The Science of Availability
Availability, Emotion, and Risk
Tom W’s Specialty
Linda: Less is More
Causes Trump Statistics
questions.explain: Chapters 12 and 13 cover availability, chapter 14 introduces representativeness through Tom W, and chapters 15 and 16 continue with the Linda problem and the weight of causal versus statistical information.

questions.q: How does the Tom W chapter apply the idea of substitution from the earlier chapter Answering an Easier Question?
questions.a: Asked a hard question about the probability that Tom W is in each field, people answer an easier one instead: how similar Tom is to the stereotype of each field. Kahneman says the prediction group's substitution was perfect, and that a probability question activates a mental shotgun that evokes easier answers such as an automatic assessment of representativeness. The chapter thus shows substitution producing a specific heuristic and its biases.

questions.q: Which of these chapters belong with Tom W’s Specialty in Part 2, Heuristics and Biases?
options: The Law of Small Numbers
Anchors
Linda: Less is More
The Illusion of Validity
The Lazy Controller
questions.explain: Part 2 runs from The Law of Small Numbers to Taming Intuitive Predictions. The Lazy Controller belongs to Part 1, Two Systems, and The Illusion of Validity to Part 3, Overconfidence.

questions.q: What does the title Tom W’s Specialty signal about the chapter?
questions.a: It names the puzzle at the center of the chapter: guessing which field of graduate specialization Tom W is in. Kahneman designed the puzzle to pit representativeness, Tom's fit to stereotypes of small fields, against base rates. The title therefore points to the chapter's lesson about how people predict from a description and neglect base rates.

questions.q: Put the parts of Kahneman's chapter Tom W’s Specialty in order.
items: The three Tom W tasks: base rates, similarity, and the anti-base-rate design
Predicting by representativeness
The sins of representativeness
How to discipline intuition
Speaking of representativeness
questions.explain: The chapter sets up the puzzle, shows people predicting by similarity, names the two sins, offers Bayesian discipline as the remedy, and closes with example remarks.

questions.q: In the within-subject Linda questionnaire, what did Kahneman find when he glanced at the first ten or so forms in the tray on his assistant's desk?
options: Every subject had ranked feminist bank teller as more probable than bank teller
Most subjects had ranked bank teller above feminist bank teller, as logic requires
About half the subjects had noticed the logical relation between the two items
Subjects had ranked the eight scenarios at random, ignoring the description
questions.explain: All of the accumulated forms ranked the conjunction higher, which so surprised Kahneman that he called Tversky at once. He summed it up: “we had pitted logic against representativeness, and representativeness had won!”

questions.q: In the Linda problem, how did doctoral students in Stanford's decision-science program, all trained in probability and statistics, perform?
options: Almost all of them avoided the error because of their training
85% of them still ranked feminist bank teller as more likely than bank teller
They did slightly better than chance but worse than ordinary undergraduates
They refused to rank the items, calling the question meaningless
questions.explain: Kahneman expected statistical sophistication to protect them, but 85% made the same error, close to the 89% of undergraduates. Training did not stop representativeness from overriding logic.

questions.q: In Kahneman and Tversky's terms, what is the conjunction fallacy?
options: Judging an event to be likely because examples of it come easily to mind
Ignoring the base rate of a category when judging a single case
Judging a conjunction of two events to be more probable than one of those events in a direct comparison
Believing that a small sample reflects the population it was drawn from
questions.explain: The conjunction fallacy is judging a combination, such as bank teller and feminist, to be more probable than one of its parts, bank teller. The other descriptions fit availability, base-rate neglect and the law of small numbers, which are different biases.

questions.q: In the Linda studies, why did 64% of social-science graduate students answer correctly in the short two-alternative version, but only 15% of a similar group in the eight-item version?
options: The short version used simpler words that the students understood better
The eight-item version was given under time pressure
The short version mentioned Venn diagrams in its instructions
The short version forced an explicit comparison that mobilized System 2, while the long list let readers judge each item on its own
questions.explain: In the long list an intervening item (insurance salesperson) separated the two critical outcomes, so readers judged each independently. The stark version required a direct comparison, which mobilized System 2 for most of these statistically sophisticated students.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, why do the questions 'Mark has hair vs. Mark has blond hair' and 'Jane is a teacher vs. Jane is a teacher and walks to work' produce no conjunction fallacy?
options: People are more familiar with hair color and jobs than with feminism
The more detailed outcome is only more detailed, not more plausible or a better story
The questions were shown only to statistically trained respondents
The names Mark and Jane carry no stereotype at all
questions.explain: These questions have the same logical structure as Linda, but the added detail does not make a more coherent story, so no competing intuition arises. As Kahneman puts it, “In the absence of a competing intuition, logic prevails.”

questions.q: A consultant tells a client: 'A recession next year, triggered by a banking collapse in Europe that spreads to US lenders, is a serious threat.' Based on Kahneman's flood and earthquake study, what is the main risk in how the client will judge this scenario?
options: The added causal detail will make it seem more probable even though each detail makes it less likely
The client will dismiss it because detailed scenarios sound less credible
The client will judge it correctly because it names a specific cause
The client will underweight it because recessions are rarely in the news
questions.explain: In the study, people rated a California earthquake causing a deadly flood as more probable than any deadly flood in North America. Kahneman warns that “adding detail to scenarios makes them more persuasive, but less likely to come true.”

questions.q: In Stephen Jay Gould's account of the Linda problem, what does the 'little homunculus' in his head represent, according to Kahneman?
options: His knowledge of probability theory
A critic who thought the problem was badly worded
His memory of radical students at Berkeley
His System 1, insisting that Linda cannot just be a bank teller
questions.explain: Gould knew the right answer, yet the homunculus kept shouting that she cannot just be a bank teller. Kahneman identifies that insistent voice as System 1, showing that the fallacy stays attractive even when recognized.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: In Christopher Hsee's dinnerware study, what did people in joint evaluation, who saw both sets side by side, pay for the 40-piece Set A and the 24-piece Set B?
options: $23 for Set A and $33 for Set B
$30 for Set A and $32 for Set B
$32 for Set A and $30 for Set B
$40 for Set A and $24 for Set B
questions.explain: Seeing both sets, people recognized that Set A contains everything in Set B plus seven intact dishes, and paid a little more for it: $32 versus $30. The $23 versus $33 figures are from single evaluation, where the result reversed.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: In Hsee's dinnerware study, why was Set B (24 intact pieces) priced much higher than Set A (40 pieces, some broken) when each set was seen alone?
options: People counted the pieces and preferred a smaller, easier-to-store set
Sets are represented by norms and prototypes, so the average value of the dishes dominated and broken dishes pulled Set A down
People assumed the larger set must be of lower quality overall
People anchored on the store's $30 to $60 price range
questions.explain: Kahneman explains that sets are represented by norms and prototypes, and nobody wants to pay for broken dishes, so Set A's average value is lower. If the average dominates the evaluation rather than the total, Set B wins.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: How did the experimental economist John List extend Hsee's less-is-more finding?
options: He found that experts in a real market were immune to the effect
He showed that the effect disappears when real money is at stake
He found the effect only in joint evaluation, not single evaluation
He replicated it in a real market for baseball cards, where sets with three added modest cards were valued less in single evaluation
questions.explain: List auctioned sets of ten high-value cards and identical sets with three modest cards added. As with dinnerware, the larger sets were worth more in joint evaluation but less in single evaluation, which Kahneman calls troubling for economic theory.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: According to Kahneman, why does joint evaluation remove the less-is-more error in Hsee's dinnerware study but not in the Linda problem?
options: The sum-like nature of the variable is less obvious for probability than for money
The Linda problem used undergraduates while the dinnerware study used shoppers
People care more about money than about probability judgments
The Linda problem has a different logical structure from the dinnerware problem
questions.explain: Kahneman says the two problems have exactly the same structure, since both value and probability are sum-like. The difference is that people see the adding-up nature of money more easily than that of probability.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: In the Wimbledon problem about Björn Borg, what did 72% of participants do?
options: Correctly ranked 'Borg will lose the first set' above 'Borg will lose the first set but win the match'
Ranked 'Borg will win the first set but lose the match' as most probable
Assigned 'Borg will lose the first set' a lower probability than 'Borg will lose the first set but win the match'
Refused to rank outcomes involving a single player
questions.explain: Losing the first set is the more inclusive event and must be at least as probable as losing it but winning the match. Yet 72% judged the narrower outcome more likely, because it fit better with what was known about the dominant player.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: Why did Kahneman and Tversky build the die problem, with sequences of green and red faces and no use of the word probability?
options: To show that people understand dice better than words
To head off the objection that the conjunction fallacy comes from misinterpreting the word probability
To measure how much money people would bet on a sure thing
To test whether frequency formats remove the error
questions.explain: Critics might say people read 'probable' as something else. The die problem required a probability judgment without words or the term itself, yet almost two-thirds still bet on the longer, more representative sequence.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: A teacher wants students to avoid the conjunction fallacy on a health-survey question. Following the British Columbia study, which wording should she use?
options: What percentage of the men surveyed are over 55 and have had a heart attack?
What is the probability that a man surveyed is over 55 and has had a heart attack?
How likely is it that a typical man surveyed has had a heart attack after 55?
How many of the 100 participants are over 55 and have had a heart attack?
questions.explain: Errors fell from 65% with the percentage wording to 25% with the 'how many of the 100' wording. Thinking of individuals brings a frequency representation to mind that makes it easy to see one group is included in the other.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: According to Kahneman, what was the net effect of the Linda problem on the reputation of his and Tversky's work?
options: It settled the debate about heuristics in their favor among scholars
It made their work less known to the public but more respected by scholars
It increased their visibility to the general public but put a small dent in their credibility among scholars
It had little effect either way, since few people noticed it
questions.explain: They expected the Linda results to persuade doubters, but the problem became a magnet for critics. The outcome was more public visibility and “a small dent in the credibility of our approach among scholars in the field.”

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: When Kahneman asked Ralph Hertwig why critics focused only on the conjunction fallacy rather than on stronger findings, what did Hertwig answer?
options: That the Linda problem was the weakest part of the evidence
That it was more interesting
That the between-subjects studies had been refuted
That reviewers had demanded it
questions.explain: Hertwig smiled and said “It was more interesting,” adding that Linda had brought so much attention that Kahneman had no reason to complain. The between-subjects evidence was never refuted; it was simply not addressed.

questions.q: A shop adds a cheap plastic keychain to an expensive leather wallet, and shoppers who see only the bundle value it less than the wallet alone. Which idea from the Linda chapter does this illustrate?
options: The frequency representation
Regression to the mean
The anchoring effect
Less is more
questions.explain: This mirrors a chapter remark about a cheap gift making a whole deal less attractive. Judged alone, the bundle is valued by its average, so the low-value item drags it down, as in Hsee's dinnerware study.

questions.q: Kahneman says the Linda problem is similar to the Tom W problem of Chapter 14, but with a twist. What is the twist?
options: There is a logical relation between two of the scenarios, since every feminist bank teller is a bank teller
Linda's description is based on a real person
Participants were given base rates for each occupation
Linda's scenarios were judged only by similarity, never by probability
questions.explain: As in Tom W, people ranked scenarios by representativeness or by probability. The twist is that one outcome is wholly included in another, which pits the intuition of representativeness directly against the logic of probability.

questions.q: Kahneman concludes that the laziness of System 2 is part of the conjunction fallacy story. Which earlier chapter of Part I introduced this idea of System 2 as a lazy monitor?
options: The Associative Machine
The Lazy Controller
Cognitive Ease
Anchors
questions.explain: Chapter 3, The Lazy Controller, introduced System 2's reluctance to invest effort. Chapter 15 applies it: subjects knew the logic of Venn diagrams but did not apply it reliably. Anchors is a Part II chapter, not Part I.

questions.q: Why does the Linda problem set up a conflict between representativeness and the logic of probability?
questions.a: Linda's description fits a feminist bank teller better than the stereotype of a bank teller, because adding the feminist detail makes a more coherent story. But the set of feminist bank tellers is wholly included in the set of bank tellers, so the conjunction must be less probable. “When you specify a possible event in greater detail you can only lower its probability.”

questions.q: Why does Kahneman describe the result of the within-subject Linda experiment as a failure of System 2?
questions.a: Both critical outcomes appeared in the same ranking, so participants had a fair opportunity to notice that the logical rule applied. They did not take that opportunity; 89% of undergraduates and even 85% of trained decision-science doctoral students ranked feminist bank teller above bank teller. System 2 failed to check the intuitive answer.

questions.q: In the Linda studies, what does the difference between 64% correct answers in the short version and 15% in the eight-item version teach?
questions.a: In the long version the two critical outcomes were separated by another item, so readers judged each outcome independently without comparing them. The short version demanded an explicit comparison, which mobilized System 2 and let most statistically sophisticated students avoid the fallacy. Whether a direct comparison is forced matters a great deal.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say the uncritical substitution of plausibility for probability is dangerous in forecasting?
questions.a: Detailed scenarios form coherent stories, and coherent stories feel plausible, which people confuse with probable. In the flood study, an earthquake in California causing a deadly flood was rated more probable than any deadly flood in North America, contrary to logic. Forecasters and clients are trapped because detail makes scenarios more persuasive but less likely to come true.

questions.q: Why do questions like 'Mark has hair or Mark has blond hair' fail to produce the conjunction fallacy, even though they share the Linda problem's logical structure?
questions.a: The more detailed outcome is only more detailed: it is not more plausible, more coherent, or a better story. So the evaluation of plausibility does not suggest an answer to the probability question, and no intuition competes with logic. “In the absence of a competing intuition, logic prevails.”

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: Explain Hsee's 'less is more' pattern in the dinnerware study.
questions.a: In single evaluation, the 24-piece intact Set B was priced at $33 and the 40-piece Set A, which had some broken pieces, at $23. Sets are represented by norms and prototypes, so people judged the average value of the dishes, and broken dishes lowered Set A's average. Removing 16 items from Set A, 7 of them intact, would actually raise its value.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: What does Kahneman mean by a sum-like variable, and why does it give the Linda and dinnerware problems the same structure?
questions.a: A sum-like variable is one where the whole equals the sum of its parts, so adding a positively valued item can only increase it. The economic value of a set of dishes is sum-like, and so is probability: the probability that Linda is a teller equals the probability she is a feminist teller plus the probability she is a non-feminist teller. In both cases System 1 averages instead of adding, which produces less is more.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: Why did joint evaluation fix the error in Hsee's dinnerware study but not in the Linda problem?
questions.a: In the dinnerware study, people who saw both sets applied the logical rule that more dishes can only add value. In the Linda problem, intuition often overcame logic even in direct comparison, because the sum-like nature of probability is less obvious than that of money. “Intuition governs judgments in the between-subjects condition; logic rules in joint evaluation” only for the dishes.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: Why is the question 'How many of the 100 participants...' so much easier than 'What percentage...' in the British Columbia health survey?
questions.a: Asking how many of 100 people makes you think of individuals and brings a spatial picture to mind, like people sorting themselves into a corner of a room. This frequency representation makes it easy to see that men over 55 with heart attacks are a subset of all men with heart attacks. Errors fell from 65% to 25%.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: What do the conjunction-fallacy studies teach about System 2, according to Kahneman?
questions.a: System 2 is not impressively alert: participants knew the logic of Venn diagrams but did not apply it reliably even when everything was in front of them. System 2 is also lazy; with a real stake, unlimited time, and orders to follow logic, most would probably have avoided the error, but they answered quickly as if just giving an opinion. Representativeness can block the use of an obvious logical rule.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: How did the Linda problem become, in Kahneman's words, a case study in the norms of controversy?
questions.a: Critics focused on the conjunction fallacy, found hints that reduced it, and argued that people read probability as plausibility, then suggested the whole heuristics approach was misguided. Kahneman compares this to lawyers discrediting a witness by attacking the weakest part of the testimony, a political style he thinks inappropriate in science. The stronger between-subjects evidence was not challenged, simply ignored.

questions.q: Explain the remark: 'In most situations, a direct comparison makes people more careful and more logical. But not always.'
questions.a: Joint evaluation usually lets System 2 apply logic, as when people seeing both dinnerware sets valued the larger set more. But in the Linda, Borg and die problems the conjunction error survived a direct comparison, because the coherent story felt plausible. “Sometimes intuition beats logic even when the correct answer stares you in the face.”

questions.q: How does Chapter 15, Linda: Less is More, build on the previous chapter on Tom W, and what does its title signal?
questions.a: Chapter 14 showed that judgments of probability follow representativeness when people ignore base rates. Chapter 15 adds a sharper test, putting representativeness against an elementary rule of logic, and shows that representativeness often wins even in direct comparison. The title signals the less-is-more pattern: removing items from a set, or detail from a scenario, can raise its judged value or probability.

questions.q: Kahneman and Tversky named the error of judging 'bank teller and feminist' more probable than 'bank teller' the ____.
questions.explain: People commit the conjunction fallacy when they judge a conjunction of two events to be more probable than one of the events in a direct comparison.

questions.q: In the Linda problem, people's judgments of probability corresponded precisely to judgments of ____, that is, similarity to stereotypes.
questions.explain: In both the Tom W and Linda problems, probability rankings matched resemblance rankings. Kahneman defines representativeness here as similarity to stereotypes.

questions.q: Kahneman was so surprised by the first Linda questionnaires that he still retains a ____ of the gray metal desk where he found them.
questions.explain: He finds the forms all ranked feminist bank teller above bank teller, a discovery vivid enough to leave a flashbulb memory of the desk and of where everyone was.

questions.q: To see why feminist bank teller must be less probable than bank teller, Kahneman suggests thinking in terms of ____, where one set is wholly included in another.
questions.explain: Every feminist bank teller is a bank teller, so that set sits inside the bank-teller set. Later he notes that subjects knew the logic of Venn diagrams but did not apply it.

questions.q: Kahneman warns that the uncritical substitution of ____ for probability has pernicious effects when scenarios are used for forecasting.
questions.explain: Coherent stories feel plausible, and people easily confuse plausibility with probability, which makes detailed scenarios seem more likely than they are.

questions.q: Kahneman compares the conjunction fallacy to the ____ illusion, because it remains attractive even when you recognize it for what it is.
questions.explain: Just as the lines of the Muller-Lyer illusion still look unequal after you measure them, Gould still felt the pull of the wrong Linda answer while knowing the right one.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: Hsee calls the condition in which a group sees both dinnerware sets side by side ____, as opposed to single evaluation.
questions.explain: Joint evaluation allows a comparison of the two sets and is a within-subject design; single evaluation shows each group only one set and is between-subjects.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: Kahneman explains that economic value and probability are both ____ variables, so adding a positively valued item can only increase the total.
questions.explain: The value of a set is the sum of its parts, and so is probability: Linda being a teller equals her being a feminist teller plus a non-feminist teller.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: A question phrased as 'how many of the 100 participants' brings to mind what is known as the ____, which makes it easy to see that one group is wholly included in another.
questions.explain: Thinking of individuals, rather than percentages, helps people see the inclusion relation, and errors in the health survey fell from 65% to 25%.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: Hsee called the pattern in which removing items from a dinnerware set raised its price in single evaluation ____.
questions.explain: Removing 16 items from Set A, 7 of them intact, would improve its value in single evaluation, because the average value of the dishes dominates.

questions.q: Chapter 15, Linda: Less is More, belongs to Part II of the book, titled ____.
questions.explain: Part II runs from The Law of Small Numbers to Taming Intuitive Predictions, and the Linda chapter is its sharpest demonstration of a heuristic, representativeness, overriding logic.

questions.q: Which of these were responses Kahneman reports from students after they learned they had violated an elementary logical rule in the Linda problem?
options: A student in the back row shouted, 'So what?'
A graduate student said she thought she had just been asked for her opinion
The class demanded that the question be removed from the exam
A student said the problem was a trick about Berkeley
questions.explain: Kahneman notes that the sinners seemed to have no shame: one shouted “So what?” and a graduate student said she thought she was just being asked for her opinion. The other reactions are not in the book.

questions.q: Which of these details are part of Kahneman and Tversky's description of Linda?
options: She majored in philosophy
She took part in antinuclear demonstrations
She works in a bookstore and takes yoga classes
She is outspoken and very bright
She is a member of the League of Women Voters
questions.explain: The description says Linda is thirty-one, single, outspoken, very bright, a philosophy major, and concerned with discrimination and social justice, with antinuclear protests. The bookstore and League of Women Voters items are among the eight scenarios to be ranked, not the description.

questions.q: Which of these notions does Kahneman say are easily confused by the unwary when judging scenarios like Linda's?
options: Coherence
Base rates
Plausibility
Probability
Regression
questions.explain: The most representative outcomes make the most coherent stories, which are plausible but not necessarily probable. Kahneman says “the notions of coherence, plausibility, and probability are easily confused by the unwary.”

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: Which of these studies showed the conjunction error or a less-is-more pattern surviving a direct comparison of the critical items?
options: The short two-alternative Linda question given to undergraduates
The Wimbledon problem about Björn Borg
The die problem with green and red sequences
Hsee's dinnerware study in joint evaluation
The 'how many of the 100 participants' health survey
questions.explain: Errors persisted for 85% to 90% of undergraduates on the stark Linda question, 72% in the Borg problem, and almost two-thirds in the die problem. In joint evaluation of dinnerware people valued the larger set more, and the frequency wording cut errors to 25%.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman treat as sum-like variables?
options: The economic value of a dinnerware set
The probability that Linda is a bank teller
The value of a collection of baseball cards
The average value of the dishes in a set
questions.explain: A set's value and a probability both add up from their parts, so adding a positive item can only increase them. The average value is exactly what System 1 uses instead of the sum, and it can fall when items are added.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: Which of these conditions much reduced the conjunction fallacy in Kahneman and Tversky's studies?
options: Asking 'how many of the 100 participants' instead of 'what percentage'
Giving the short direct-comparison Linda question to social-science graduate students at Stanford and Berkeley
Using doctoral students in decision science on the eight-item Linda list
Removing the word probability and using a die with colored faces
questions.explain: The frequency wording cut errors from 65% to 25%, and 64% of the graduate students answered the short version correctly. Decision-science doctoral students still erred 85% of the time, and in the die problem almost two-thirds still chose the wrong sequence.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: Which of these did critics of the Linda problem do, according to Kahneman?
options: Found combinations of instructions and hints that reduced the fallacy
Argued that subjects could reasonably read 'probability' as meaning 'plausibility'
Refuted the between-subjects evidence for heuristics
Showed that the fallacy never occurs among statisticians
questions.explain: Critics reduced the fallacy with hints and argued that probability was being read as plausibility, then extended this to doubt the whole enterprise. The between-subjects evidence was not challenged but “simply not addressed.”

questions.q: Which of these chapters belong to the same part of the book as Chapter 15, Linda: Less is More?
options: The Law of Small Numbers
The Illusion of Validity
Anchors
Regression to the Mean
The Lazy Controller
questions.explain: Part II, Heuristics and Biases, includes The Law of Small Numbers, Anchors and Regression to the Mean. The Illusion of Validity is in Part III and The Lazy Controller in Part I.

questions.q: True or false: In Kahneman and Tversky's initial between-subjects Linda experiment, feminist bank teller ranked higher than bank teller both in rankings by resemblance and in rankings by likelihood.
questions.explain: Each participant saw only one of the critical items, and as with Tom W the average rankings by resemblance and by likelihood were identical, with feminist bank teller ranked higher.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman ran a carefully designed special experiment for the within-subject Linda questionnaire because he expected most subjects to fall for the fallacy.
questions.explain: He was so sure subjects would notice the logical relation that he did not think a special experiment worthwhile; his assistant simply had subjects fill it in while signing out. The result surprised him.

questions.q: True or false: According to Kahneman, the set of bank tellers is wholly included in the set of feminist bank tellers.
questions.explain: It is the other way around: every feminist bank teller is a bank teller, so feminist bank tellers are a subset of bank tellers. That is why the conjunction must be less probable.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: True or false: In John List's baseball card auction, sets with three modest cards added were valued less than the smaller sets in single evaluation.
questions.explain: As with dinnerware, the larger sets were valued more in joint evaluation but less in single evaluation, a less-is-more result Kahneman calls troubling for economic theory.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: True or false: In the British Columbia health survey, the group asked 'what percentage' made fewer conjunction errors than the group asked 'how many of the 100 participants'.
questions.explain: The direction is reversed: errors were 65% with the percentage wording and only 25% with the 'how many of 100' wording, which brings individuals to mind.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: True or false: In the die problem, although almost two-thirds bet on the longer sequence, a large majority found the argument for the shorter sequence more convincing when shown arguments for both.
questions.explain: Representativeness dominated the bets, but when presented with the arguments, most people recognized that the sequence favoring the shorter, included pattern was correct.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman concludes that a direct comparison always makes people careful and logical enough to avoid the conjunction fallacy.
questions.explain: He says a direct comparison usually helps but not always: “Sometimes intuition beats logic even when the correct answer stares you in the face.”

questions.q: Put Kahneman and Tversky's Linda studies in the order the chapter describes them.
items: Between-subjects study with one critical item per participant
Within-subject eight-item list filled in by subjects signing out
Extension showing 89% of undergraduates violated logic
Same questionnaire given to Stanford decision-science doctoral students
Stark two-alternative question put to large groups
questions.explain: The researchers moved from a between-subjects design to a within-subject list, then to undergraduates and trained doctoral students, and finally to the stark version in “increasingly desperate” attempts to eliminate the error.

questions.q: Put the steps of Kahneman's argument before the first sub-heading of the Linda chapter in order.
items: Linda's description and the eight scenarios
The consensus that Linda fits feminist better than bank teller
The Venn-diagram logic of the two critical items
The experiments showing representativeness beating logic
Plausibility substituted for probability in forecasting
Mark and Jane questions where logic prevails
questions.explain: The opening sets up Linda, establishes the logical rule, shows it being violated, generalizes to plausibility in forecasting, and ends with cases where no competing intuition arises.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: Put these studies in the order they appear in the section on less is more in joint evaluation.
items: Hsee's dinnerware sets
List's baseball cards
Borg at Wimbledon
The green and red die
The British Columbia health survey
questions.explain: The section starts with Hsee and List on value, ties them to probability, then gives further conjunction errors (Borg, die) before the breakthrough with the health survey's frequency wording.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: Order the steps of Kahneman's explanation for why Set A was priced lower than Set B in single evaluation.
items: Sets are represented by norms and prototypes
Broken dishes lower the average value of Set A
The average dominates the evaluation
Set B is priced higher despite having fewer items
questions.explain: Because sets are judged by their prototypes, the average value matters more than the total, so the broken dishes drag Set A down and less becomes more.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: Put these parts of the chapter's closing discussion in the order Kahneman presents them.
items: System 2 is not impressively alert
The laziness of System 2 is part of the story
The contrast between Linda and the broken-dishes study
Critics focus on the conjunction fallacy
Lawyers' two styles of criticism
The conversation with Ralph Hertwig
questions.explain: Kahneman first draws lessons about System 2, contrasts Linda with the dinnerware result, then turns to the controversy, the courtroom analogy, and ends with Hertwig's answer.

questions.q: Put these chapters of Part II in the book's order.
items: Availability, Emotion, and Risk
Tom W's Specialty
Linda: Less is More
Causes Trump Statistics
Regression to the Mean
questions.explain: Chapter 15 sits between Tom W's Specialty (14) and Causes Trump Statistics (16), continuing the treatment of representativeness after the availability chapters.

questions.q: Match each group in the Linda studies to its result.
pairs: Undergraduates, within-subject list
89% violated the logic of probability
Stanford decision-science doctoral students
85% ranked feminist bank teller as more likely
Social-science graduate students, short version
64% answered correctly
Similar graduate students, eight-item version
Only 15% answered correctly
questions.explain: Statistical training alone did little, but a forced direct comparison helped sophisticated students: 64% correct in the short version versus 15% in the long one.

questions.q: Match each example from the opening of the Linda chapter to the idea it illustrates.
pairs: Mark has blond hair
Extra detail that is not more plausible causes no fallacy
California earthquake causing a flood
A more plausible scenario judged more probable despite lower probability
Linda as a feminist bank teller
A coherent story beating the logic of probability
Gould's homunculus
The fallacy stays attractive even when recognized
questions.explain: Each example isolates one part of the argument: detail alone is harmless, plausibility misleads forecasts, coherence overrides logic, and the error keeps its pull, like the Muller-Lyer illusion.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: Match each person to their role in the Linda chapter.
pairs: Christopher Hsee
Priced dinnerware sets and named the less-is-more pattern
John List
Replicated less is more with baseball cards in a real market
Björn Borg
Dominant tennis player in a Wimbledon probability problem
Ralph Hertwig
Persistent critic who said Linda was more interesting
questions.explain: Hsee and List supply the value studies, Borg is the subject of a conjunction problem, and Hertwig explains why critics focused on Linda.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: Match each conjunction study to its reported rate of error.
pairs: Borg at Wimbledon
72% ranked the narrower outcome as more probable
Die with four green faces
Almost two-thirds bet on the longer sequence
Health survey, 'what percentage'
65% made the error
Health survey, 'how many of the 100'
Only 25% made the error
questions.explain: The Borg and die problems show the error surviving direct comparison; only the frequency wording of the health survey cut it sharply.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: Match each term from the Linda chapter to its meaning.
pairs: Joint evaluation
Seeing both options at once, a within-subject design
Single evaluation
Seeing only one option, a between-subjects design
Sum-like variable
A total that can only grow when a positive item is added
Frequency representation
Thinking of counts of individuals, which reveals inclusion
questions.explain: These terms explain why less is more appears in single evaluation, why it should not given sum-like variables, and why 'how many' wording helps.

questions.q: Match each remark from Speaking of Less is More to the idea it expresses.
pairs: A very complicated scenario called highly probable
It is only a plausible story, not a probable one
A cheap gift added to an expensive product
The whole deal became less attractive
A direct comparison usually makes people careful
Intuition can still beat logic in plain view
questions.explain: The three remarks restate the chapter's lessons: plausibility is not probability, averaging produces less is more, and joint evaluation does not always rescue logic.

questions.q: Sort these Linda scenarios by how well readers agree they fit her description.

items.t: Active in the feminist movement
Works in a bookstore and takes yoga classes
Bank teller
Insurance salesperson

questions.explain: The near-perfect consensus is that Linda is a very good fit for an active feminist, a fairly good fit for the bookstore and yoga scenario, and a very poor fit for bank teller or insurance salesperson.

questions.q: Sort these studies by their experimental design.

items.t: Initial Linda study with only one critical item per participant
Eight-item Linda list with both critical items
Stark two-alternative Linda question
Flood and earthquake scenarios shown to different groups
Mark has hair versus Mark has blond hair

questions.explain: Between-subjects designs show each person only one of the critical outcomes; within-subject designs put both in front of the same person, giving System 2 a fair chance to notice the logic.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: Sort these outcomes from the less-is-more studies by the kind of event.

items.t: Borg will lose the first set
Borg will lose the first set but win the match
Die sequence RGRRR
Die sequence GRGRRR
Men who have had a heart attack
Men over 55 who have had a heart attack

questions.explain: Each narrower event is contained in the inclusive one, so it can only be less probable; GRGRRR contains RGRRR with a G added in front. People often judged the narrower, more representative event as more likely.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: Sort these judgments by whether they reflect a rule of intuition or the rule of logic.

items.t: Pricing the set with broken dishes low when seen alone
Valuing Set A above Set B when both are shown
Averaging instead of adding
Betting on GRGRRR over RGRRR
Seeing older heart-attack victims as a subset of all victims

questions.explain: Kahneman says “System 1 averages instead of adding,” which drives low prices for the broken-dish set and bets on representative sequences. Joint evaluation of dishes and the frequency wording let logic rule.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: Sort these results from Hsee's and List's studies by evaluation condition.

items.t: Set A priced at $32 and Set B at $30
Set B priced at $33 and Set A at $23
Larger baseball card sets valued more
Larger baseball card sets valued less

questions.explain: Seeing both options, people apply the rule that more items add value; seeing one alone, they judge by the average and less becomes more.

questions.q: In the cab problem (85% of cabs Green, 15% Blue, a witness who is right 80% of the time says the cab was Blue), what is the correct probability that the cab was Blue?
questions.explain: Combining the base rate and the witness’s reliability by Bayes’s rule gives 41%. The figure of 15% uses only the base rate, and 80% uses only the witness.

questions.q: In the original cab problem, what is the most common answer people give for the probability that the cab was Blue?
options: 15%, the base rate of Blue cabs
41%, the Bayesian solution
80%, the witness’s reliability
50%, an even split
questions.explain: People ignore the base rate and go with the witness, so the most common answer is 80%. The correct Bayesian answer is 41%.

questions.q: In the second version of the cab problem, how is the base rate presented?
options: The companies have equal fleets, but Green cabs are in 85% of accidents
85% of the cabs in the city are Green and 15% are Blue
The witness is shown to be right about Green cabs 85% of the time
Blue cabs are on the road far less often at night than Green cabs
questions.explain: Only the presentation of the base rate changes: the fleets are equal, but Green cabs cause 85% of accidents. The two versions are mathematically indistinguishable.

questions.q: In the second version of the cab problem, why do people give considerable weight to the base rate?
options: It is stated as a larger and more striking number
It contradicts the witness and so draws attention
It is presented after the witness information rather than before
It supports a causal story that Green drivers are reckless
questions.explain: The accident figures suggest Green drivers are reckless, a causally relevant fact about individual drivers. A statistical fact about fleet sizes gives a mind “hungry for causal stories” nothing to chew on.

questions.q: How does Kahneman define stereotypes in the chapter on causal base rates?
options: Hostile beliefs about a social group that are always factually false
Statements about a group that are tentatively accepted as facts about every member
Statistical facts about a population that say nothing about individuals
Prototypes of objects such as horses or refrigerators held in memory
questions.explain: Stereotypes are statements about the group that are (at least tentatively) accepted as facts about every member. Kahneman stresses that stereotypes can be correct or false, not only hostile and wrong.

questions.q: An insurer tells a driver that owners of one sports-car model cause four times as many crashes as other owners. According to Kahneman’s account of causal base rates, how will the driver most likely treat this figure when judging a particular owner?
options: As a statistical fact about the group, largely ignored for the individual
As irrelevant, because only a witness’s report counts for individuals
As a fact about that owner’s recklessness, readily combined with other information
As useful only if the driver first applies Bayes’s rule deliberately
questions.explain: Like Green cabs causing more accidents, the figure invites a causal stereotype about the drivers. Causal base rates are treated as information about the individual case and easily combined with other case-specific information.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, which basic characteristic of System 1 gives rise to stereotypes?
options: It computes averages of a category rather than sums
It suppresses doubt and ambiguity about categories
It substitutes an easier question for a harder one
It represents categories as norms and prototypical exemplars
questions.explain: System 1 holds in memory one or more “normal” members of each category; when the categories are social, these representations are called stereotypes.

questions.q: What is Kahneman’s position on the cost of resisting stereotypes?
options: Neglecting valid stereotypes has real costs, but they are worth paying
Resisting stereotypes is costless because stereotypes are always false
The costs of resistance are so high that stereotyping should be allowed
