Resistance has costs only in legal settings such as hiring and profiling
questions.explain: He calls resistance to stereotyping a laudable moral position whose costs are worth paying for a better society, but says denying that the costs exist is not scientifically defensible.

questions.q: In Ajzen’s experiment, how was a causal base rate created?
options: By telling participants an investigator built a sample in which 75% had failed
By telling participants the students came from a class in which 75% or 25% passed
By showing participants videos of the students describing their study habits
By telling participants how many hours each student had studied
questions.explain: A class in which only 25% passed implies a brutally difficult test, and test difficulty is a causal factor in every student’s outcome.

questions.q: In Ajzen’s experiment, how was a noncausal (purely statistical) base rate suggested?
options: Participants were told the exam had been unusually hard that year
Participants were told about the national pass rate for all Yale exams
Participants were told an investigator had built a sample selected by pass or fail
Participants were given the base rate after making their first judgment
questions.explain: An investigator interested in the causes of failure selected a sample in which 75% had failed. This is a fact about the ensemble the cases were drawn from and has no bearing on any individual student.

questions.q: In the helping experiment described by Nisbett and Borgida, how many of the fifteen participants responded immediately to the seizure victim’s appeal?
options: Six
Eleven
Fifteen
Four
questions.explain: Only four of the fifteen responded immediately; six never left their booths and five came out only well after the victim apparently choked.

questions.q: A friend has just learned that in a study most bystanders failed to help, then meets a pleasant, ordinary neighbor who took part in that study. Based on the Nisbett-Borgida findings, what is the friend most likely to assume?
options: The neighbor was one of the few who rushed to help
The neighbor probably did not help, as most did not
The neighbor’s behavior cannot be guessed at all
The neighbor was the stooge who staged the seizure
questions.explain: Students who knew the dismal base rate still predicted that the nice, normal people in the videos had been quick to help; they “quietly exempt themselves” and people like them from surprising results.

questions.q: What teaching method did Nisbett and Borgida find made students appreciate the point of the helping experiment?
options: Repeating the group statistics until students could recite them
Telling students that two individuals they had seen had not helped
Explaining the official interpretation of diffusion of responsibility
Having students take part in a new version of the experiment
questions.explain: When students were told that the two nice people in the videos had not helped and then guessed the global results, their guesses were extremely accurate. Surprising individual cases taught what statistics did not.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what is the test of having learned psychology?
options: Whether you can recite the details of a surprising experiment
Whether you tell friends about the surprising facts you heard
Whether your understanding of situations you encounter has changed
Whether you can state the official interpretation of a result
questions.explain: Students could recite the experiment and its interpretation without changing their beliefs. Kahneman says the test is whether your understanding of situations has changed, “not whether you have learned a new fact.”

questions.q: A manager wants new staff to grasp how often a common workplace accident happens. Following the advice at the end of the chapter on causes and statistics, what should she do?
options: Present the full accident rate table and trust them to use it
Ask staff to calculate the accident rate themselves from records
Remind staff that statistics apply only to other people
Show one or two representative individual cases of the accident
questions.explain: The chapter’s closing advice is that people cannot be assumed to learn from mere statistics, so representative individual cases should be used to influence System 1.

questions.q: How does the chapter Causes Trump Statistics build on the earlier treatment of base rates in Part II?
options: It shows base rates are used when they are causal, though statistical ones are neglected
It shows that base rates are always used correctly once people are warned
It replaces base rates with regression to the mean as the main topic
It argues base-rate neglect occurs only in problems about professions
questions.explain: The chapter refines the picture of base-rate neglect: statistical base rates are underweighted, while causal base rates are treated as information about the individual case.

questions.q: True or false: In the cab problem, if the two cab companies had been equally large, the probability that the cab was Blue would be 80%.
questions.explain: With equal-sized companies the base rate is uninformative, so only the witness’s 80% reliability matters.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says statistical base rates are generally overweighted when specific information about the case at hand is available.
questions.explain: Statistical base rates are generally underweighted, and sometimes neglected altogether, when case-specific information is available. It is causal base rates that are readily used.

questions.q: True or false: In the causal version of the cab problem, stereotyping the Green drivers improves the accuracy of judgment.
questions.explain: In the cab problem relying on the causal base rate is desirable and brings judgments close to the Bayesian solution; Kahneman notes the irony that elsewhere stereotyping is rightly rejected.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman and Tversky invented the notion of causal base rates.
questions.explain: They constructed the variants of the cab problem but borrowed the notion of causal base rates from the psychologist Icek Ajzen.

questions.q: True or false: The helping experiment that Nisbett and Borgida taught their students had been conducted at the University of Michigan.
questions.explain: Nisbett and Borgida worked at the University of Michigan, but the helping experiment they described had been conducted at New York University.

questions.q: True or false: Students who were told only that two interviewees had not helped, and then guessed the global results of the helping experiment, guessed extremely accurately.
questions.explain: This was the method that worked: surprised by two individual cases, students immediately generalized and inferred that helping is harder than they thought.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that even compelling causal statistics will not change long-held beliefs or beliefs rooted in personal experience.
questions.explain: Causal statistics affect thinking more than noncausal ones, but they still fail against long-held beliefs; surprising individual cases have a more powerful impact.

questions.q: Kahneman calls the cab problem a standard problem of ____ inference.
questions.explain: It combines a base rate with the imperfectly reliable testimony of a witness, the classic setting for Bayesian inference.

questions.q: In the cab problem, the base rate and the witness’s reliability can be combined by ____.
questions.explain: Bayes’s rule combines the two sources of information and gives the correct answer of 41%.

questions.q: ____ base rates are facts about a population to which a case belongs, but they are not relevant to the individual case.
questions.explain: Statistical base rates, such as the share of Green cabs in the city, are generally underweighted when case information is available.

questions.q: ____ base rates change your view of how the individual case came to be.
questions.explain: Causal base rates, such as Green cabs causing 85% of accidents, are treated as information about the individual case.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, when the categories that System 1 represents by normal members are social, these representations are called ____.
questions.explain: System 1 represents categories by norms and prototypical exemplars; for social categories these are stereotypes, which can be correct or false.

questions.q: Kahneman says that in politically charged arguments people commonly rely on the ____, so the positions they favor seem to have no cost.
questions.explain: Under the affect heuristic, “The positions we favor have no cost and those we oppose have no benefits.”

questions.q: Kahneman and Tversky borrowed the notion of causal base rates from the psychologist Icek ____.
questions.explain: Icek Ajzen’s experiment on students taking an exam at Yale showed the power of causal base rates.

questions.q: The lesson of the helping experiment is that a potent feature of the situation, the diffusion of ____, makes decent people behave unhelpfully.
questions.explain: Individuals feel relieved of responsibility when they know others have heard the same request for help.

questions.q: Nisbett and Borgida wrote that students quietly ____ themselves from the conclusions of experiments that surprise them.
questions.explain: Students “quietly exempt themselves” (and their friends) from surprising findings, so their predictions about individuals do not change.

questions.q: Nisbett and Borgida concluded that subjects’ unwillingness to deduce the particular from the general was matched only by their willingness to infer the ____ from the particular.
questions.explain: Students ignored the group statistic when judging individuals, but generalized at once from two surprising individual cases.

questions.q: Which of these are the two items of information given in the cab problem?
options: A base rate of Green and Blue cabs
The testimony of an imperfectly reliable witness
The cab driver’s past accident record
The lighting on the street that night
A police report on the cab’s speed
questions.explain: The problem combines a base rate and the witness’s imperfectly reliable testimony; nothing is given about the driver’s record, lighting or speed.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman present as stereotypes that fit a causal story?
options: Most of the graduates of an inner-city school go to college
Interest in cycling is widespread in France
Green drivers are dangerous
85% of the cabs in the city are Green
An investigator built a sample in which 75% had failed
questions.explain: The school, France and Green-driver statements suggest a propensity in individual members. The fleet share and the investigator’s sample are purely statistical facts.

questions.q: Which of these are contexts where Kahneman says there is a strong social norm against stereotyping?
options: Hiring
Profiling
Judging the color of the cab in a hit-and-run
Thinking about what a normal horse looks like
questions.explain: In hiring and profiling, base rates should be treated as facts about the group, not about individuals. In the cab problem relying on the causal base rate is desirable.

questions.q: Which of these were features of the helping experiment at New York University?
options: Participants spoke from individual booths over an intercom
Only one microphone was active at any one time
A stooge said he was prone to seizures
Participants could see one another through glass
An experimenter appeared in person to ask for help
questions.explain: Participants sat in separate booths and spoke in turn over an intercom; the stooge followed a script and feigned a seizure. They could not see each other.

questions.q: Which of these describe the videos Nisbett and Borgida showed their students?
options: The interviewees appeared to be nice, normal, decent people
The videos were designed to be uninformative about helpfulness
The interviewees described conventional hobbies and plans
The interviewees admitted on camera that they had not helped
The interviews were long and probed each person’s character
questions.explain: The interviews were short and bland and gave no reason to think the two were more or less helpful than anyone else. In one condition students were told separately that they had not helped.

questions.q: Which of these are the two inferences Kahneman says people can draw from causal base rates?
options: A stereotypical trait attributed to an individual
A significant feature of the situation that affects an individual’s outcome
An estimate of how reliable a witness is
A rule for combining two probabilities
questions.explain: The reckless cabdrivers illustrate a trait attributed to an individual; the impossibly difficult exam illustrates a feature of the situation.

questions.q: Which of these chapters belong, with Causes Trump Statistics, to Part II, Heuristics and Biases?
options: Tom W’s Specialty
Linda: Less is More
Regression to the Mean
The Illusion of Validity
The Outside View
questions.explain: Part II runs from The Law of Small Numbers to Taming Intuitive Predictions. The Illusion of Validity and The Outside View belong to Part III, Overconfidence.

questions.q: Put the events of the helping experiment in the order they happened.
items: Participants are led to individual booths
The stooge describes his problems and his seizures
Each other participant takes a turn to talk
The stooge becomes agitated and asks for help
The next participant’s microphone becomes active
questions.explain: The stooge spoke first, then everyone took turns; when his turn came again he feigned a seizure, and the next microphone switched on so nothing more was heard from him.

questions.q: Put the steps of Nisbett and Borgida’s successful teaching method in order.
items: Teach the procedure of the helping experiment without the results
Show videos of two interviewees
Tell students the two individuals had not helped
Ask students to guess the global results
questions.explain: Students learned the procedure without the group results, saw the two videos, were told the two had not helped, and then guessed the overall results accurately.

questions.q: Put the steps of the Bayesian approach to predicting an interviewee’s helpfulness in order.
items: Consult the base rate: 4 of 15 helped immediately
Form a prior that the person did not rush to help
Look for relevant information about the individual
Finding none in the bland video, stay with the base rate
questions.explain: Bayesian logic starts from the base rate, then adjusts for relevant individual information; because the videos were uninformative, the answer stays with the base rate.

questions.q: Put the parts of the chapter Causes Trump Statistics in the order they appear.
items: The cab problem
Causal Stereotypes
Causal Situations
Can Psychology Be Taught?
Speaking of Causes and Statistics
questions.explain: The chapter opens with the cab problem, explains causal stereotypes and causal situations, turns to whether psychology can be taught, and closes with sample quotations.

questions.q: Put these Part II chapters in the order they appear in the book.
items: Tom W’s Specialty
Linda: Less is More
Causes Trump Statistics
Regression to the Mean
Taming Intuitive Predictions
questions.explain: In the table of contents, chapter 16 comes after Tom W’s Specialty (14) and Linda (15) and before Regression to the Mean (17) and Taming Intuitive Predictions (18).

questions.q: Match each person or people with their role in the chapter on causes and statistics.
pairs: Icek Ajzen
Showed the power of causal base rates with Yale exam vignettes
Nisbett and Borgida
Tested whether students learned from the helping experiment
Kahneman and Tversky
Constructed the variants of the cab problem
The stooge
Followed a script and feigned a seizure
questions.explain: Ajzen originated causal base rates, Nisbett and Borgida studied teaching, Kahneman and Amos built the cab variants, and the stooge played the seizure victim.

questions.q: Match each term with its meaning in the chapter on causes and statistics.
pairs: Statistical base rate
A fact about a population, not relevant to the individual case
Causal base rate
Information that changes your view of how the individual case came to be
Stereotype
A statement about a group accepted as a fact about every member
Bayesian solution with uninformative evidence
Stay with the base rate
questions.explain: These are Kahneman’s definitions; when new evidence, such as a bland video, tells nothing, Bayesian logic stays with the base rate.

questions.q: Match each number with what it stands for in the chapter on causes and statistics.
pairs: Share of Green cabs in the first version of the cab problem
How often the witness correctly identified each color
Correct Bayesian probability that the cab was Blue
Probability that an unidentified helping-experiment participant helped at once
questions.explain: 85% and 80% are the cab problem’s inputs and 41% is the Bayesian answer; 27% comes from 4 of the 15 helping-experiment participants.

questions.q: Match each example with the idea it illustrates in the chapter on causes and statistics.
pairs: Green cabs are in 85% of accidents
A stereotypical trait attributed to individuals
Only 25% of the class passed the exam
A feature of the situation that affects each outcome
An investigator built a sample where 75% failed
A purely statistical base rate
Two nice interviewees who did not help
Surprising individual cases that teach a general lesson
questions.explain: Recklessness and test difficulty are causal inferences; the investigator’s sample says nothing about any student; the two cases taught students what statistics could not.

questions.q: Match each number of participants with what they did in the helping experiment (fifteen participants in all).
pairs: Four
Responded immediately to the appeal for help
Six
Never got out of their booth
Five
Came out only well after the victim apparently choked
questions.explain: Only four of fifteen helped at once; six never left their booths and five came out late.

questions.q: Sort each base rate into statistical or causal, as Kahneman uses the terms.

items.t: 85% of the cabs in the city are Green
Green cabs are involved in 85% of accidents
The students came from a class in which only 25% passed
An investigator built a sample in which 75% had failed
The students came from a class in which 75% passed
15% of the cabs in the city are Blue

questions.explain: Fleet sizes and the investigator’s sample say nothing about how an individual case came to be; accident rates and class pass rates suggest reckless drivers or an easy or hard test.

questions.q: Sort each feature into the version of the cab problem it belongs to.

items.t: The base rate is a statistical fact about cabs in the city
The most common answer is 80%
The base rate is often ignored
A stereotype of reckless Green drivers forms
Two causal stories must be reconciled
The average judgment is close to the Bayesian solution

questions.explain: The two versions are mathematically identical, but only the second gives the mind a causal story, so its base rate is used.

questions.q: Sort each kind of information by its effect on students in the Nisbett-Borgida studies and Kahneman’s conclusions.

items.t: Learning that only 4 of 15 participants helped at once
Being told two nice interviewees had not helped
A surprising statistical fact about behavior
Surprising individual cases
Learning the official interpretation of the experiment
Finding surprises in one’s own behavior

questions.explain: Students learned nothing from statistics or the official interpretation, but generalized at once from surprising individual cases; Kahneman adds that surprises in your own behavior teach best.

questions.q: Sort each situation by how Kahneman says group base rates should be treated in it.
groups: Relying on causal base rates is desirable
Social norm rejects causal base rates

items.t: Judging which cab was in the hit-and-run
Hiring a new employee
Profiling
Inferring a test was hard because only 25% passed

questions.explain: In the cab problem and Ajzen’s study, causal base rates improved judgment; in hiring and profiling we want base rates treated as statistical facts about the group, not presumptive facts about individuals.

questions.q: Sort each task by whether, according to the chapter, System 1 handles it readily or does it poorly.

items.t: Following a story whose elements are causally linked
Reasoning with purely statistical facts
Representing a category by a normal, prototypical member
Combining a fleet-size base rate with a witness’s reliability
Being moved by one or two representative individual cases

questions.explain: “System 1 can deal with stories in which the elements are causally linked, but it is weak in statistical reasoning.”

questions.q: In the cab problem, why is the correct answer 41% rather than the 80% most people give?
questions.a: There are two items of information: the 15% base rate of Blue cabs and the 80% reliability of the witness. Bayes’s rule combines them into 41%. People ignore the base rate and go with the witness, which gives 80%.

questions.q: Why do people use the base rate in the second version of the cab problem but ignore it in the first, even though the two are mathematically the same?
questions.a: In the first version the base rate is a statistical fact about fleet sizes, and nothing explains how the number of cabs would cause this driver to hit and run. In the second, Green cabs causing 85% of accidents creates a stereotype of reckless Green drivers, a causally relevant fact about individual drivers. That causal story is combined with the witness’s testimony, and judgments come close to the Bayesian answer.

questions.q: What is the difference between statistical and causal base rates, and how is each treated?
questions.a: Statistical base rates are facts about a population to which a case belongs but are not relevant to the individual case; they are generally underweighted, and sometimes neglected, when case-specific information is available. Causal base rates change your view of how the individual case came to be; they are treated as information about the individual case and easily combined with other case-specific information.

questions.q: What irony does Kahneman note about stereotyping in the cab problem compared with hiring or profiling?
questions.a: In the cab problem, neglecting the base rate is a failure of Bayesian reasoning, and stereotyping the Green drivers improves accuracy. In hiring or profiling there is a strong social and legal norm against stereotyping, and rightly so: we want base rates treated as statistical facts about the group rather than presumptive facts about individuals. In those contexts we deliberately reject causal base rates.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say resistance to stereotyping is not costless, and what does this have to do with the affect heuristic?
questions.a: Neglecting valid stereotypes inevitably produces suboptimal judgments, so resistance has real costs, even though they are worth paying for a more civilized and equal society. Denying the costs is not scientifically defensible. It reflects the affect heuristic common in politically charged arguments, where the positions we favor seem to have no cost and those we oppose no benefits.

questions.q: How did Ajzen’s experiment distinguish causal from statistical base rates, and what did it find?
questions.a: Participants judged whether Yale students had passed an exam. Being told a class had a 75% or 25% pass rate implied an easy or brutally hard test, a causal factor, and participants were highly sensitive to it. Being told an investigator had built a sample in which 75% failed was purely statistical, and it had much less impact, because System 1 handles causal stories but is weak in statistical reasoning.

questions.q: What did the helping experiment show, and why do its results surprise most people?
questions.a: Only four of fifteen participants responded at once to a fellow participant’s apparent seizure; when people know others have heard the request, they feel relieved of responsibility. It surprises us because we think of ourselves and other decent people as quick to help. The point is that even normal, decent people do not rush to help when they expect others to deal with it.

questions.q: What did Nisbett and Borgida find when students who knew the results of the helping experiment predicted how two interviewees behaved?
questions.a: Their predictions were indistinguishable from those of students who knew only the procedure: both groups thought the nice people in the videos had been quick to help. They knew the base rate but did not apply it to individuals. In the authors’ words, students “quietly exempt themselves” and people like them from conclusions that surprise them.

questions.q: How did Nisbett and Borgida finally succeed in teaching the lesson of the helping experiment, and what general conclusion does Kahneman draw?
questions.a: They taught the procedure without the results, showed the two videos, and told students the two individuals had not helped; students then guessed the global results very accurately. Surprising individual cases must be resolved and embedded in a causal story, so people readily infer the general from the particular but are unwilling to deduce the particular from the general. Surprising individual cases are therefore a more effective tool for teaching psychology than surprising statistics.

questions.q: Why, according to Kahneman, does Thinking, Fast and Slow contain questions addressed personally to the reader?
questions.a: Because statistical facts about people in general rarely change how we think, while surprising individual cases do. Readers are more likely to learn something by finding surprises in their own behavior than by hearing surprising facts about people in general. The test of learning is whether your understanding of situations has changed, not whether you learned a new fact.

questions.q: What does the title Causes Trump Statistics signal, and how does the chapter fit into Part II’s discussion of base rates?
questions.a: The title states the chapter’s claim: information with a causal interpretation outweighs merely statistical information. After the Tom W and Linda chapters show people neglecting base rates in favor of representativeness, this chapter refines the picture: statistical base rates are neglected, but causal base rates are used. It also shows the limit of that rule, since even causal statistics fail to change beliefs that conflict with how people see themselves.

questions.q: In Kahneman's story of the Israeli Air Force flight instructors, what principle of skill training was he teaching when a seasoned instructor objected?
options: Punishment of mistakes works better than rewards for improvement
Rewards for improved performance work better than punishment of mistakes
Praise and punishment have no effect at all on skill learning
Training works best when feedback is delayed until the end
questions.explain: Kahneman was explaining that rewards for improved performance work better than punishment of mistakes, a principle backed by research on pigeons, rats, humans and other animals. The instructor claimed the opposite was true for flight cadets.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what explains the flight instructor's observation that cadets usually did worse after being praised for a clean maneuver?
options: Praise made the cadets overconfident and careless on the next try
Cadets resented being singled out in front of their peers
Instructors praised cadets only when the maneuver was easy
Praise was given only after unusually good, probably lucky, performances
questions.explain: The instructor praised only performances far better than average, which were probably partly lucky, so the next attempt was likely to be worse whether or not praise was given. The idea that praise caused overconfidence is the kind of causal story the chapter warns against.

questions.q: In the flight instructor episode, what did Kahneman do instead of giving a lesson in the algebra of prediction?
options: He asked the officers to throw two coins at a chalk target without looking
He showed a film of cadets performing aerobatic maneuvers
He had the instructors stop praising and punishing for one week
He asked each instructor to rate cadets before and after feedback
questions.explain: He marked a target on the floor with chalk and had every officer turn his back and throw two coins at it in succession. Ranking the first throws showed the best mostly got worse and the worst mostly improved, with no praise or punishment involved.

questions.q: What does Kahneman mean when he says the flight instructors were trapped in an unfortunate contingency?
options: They could not tell which cadets were talented and which were lucky
They were punished by their superiors whenever their cadets performed poorly
They were rewarded by later improvement after punishing poor performance, even though punishment was ineffective
They had to choose between praising everyone or praising no one
questions.explain: Because they punished cadets after poor performance, the improvement that regression made likely felt like a reward for punishing. The trap is that this feedback came even if punishment did nothing.

questions.q: Kahneman says that the flight instructor had attached a causal interpretation to the inevitable fluctuations of a ____ process.
questions.explain: The quality of each maneuver fluctuated randomly, and the instructor read cause into it: “The instructor had attached a causal interpretation to the inevitable fluctuations of a random process.”

questions.q: Kahneman concludes from the flight instructor episode that the feedback to which life exposes us is ____.
questions.explain: Because we are nice when others please us and nasty when they do not, regression makes it look as if niceness is punished and nastiness rewarded. He calls this feedback perverse.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says the flight instructor's observation was correct but the inference he drew from it about reward and punishment was wrong.
questions.explain: Kahneman writes that the instructor was right and also completely wrong: praised performances really were followed by worse ones, but this did not show that punishment works better than reward.

questions.q: True or false: In Kahneman's coin-throwing demonstration, every officer who did best on the first throw did worse on the second.
questions.explain: Kahneman says most, but not all, of those who did best the first time deteriorated on their second try. Regression describes a tendency, not a rule that holds for every person.

questions.q: Which of these are lessons Kahneman draws from the flight instructor episode?
options: Good performance tends to be followed by deterioration even without any feedback
Because we are nice when others please us, we are statistically punished for being nice
Punishment is in fact more effective than reward for flight cadets
Research on animals does not apply to human skill training
The instructor's improvement after shouting was largely regression to the mean
questions.explain: The coin demonstration showed deterioration after good results and improvement after bad ones with no praise or punishment, which is regression to the mean. Kahneman does not concede that punishment works better, and he does not reject the animal research.

questions.q: Put the events of Kahneman's flight instructor story in the order they happened.
items: Kahneman teaches that reward works better than punishment
A seasoned instructor says praise is followed by worse performance
Officers throw two coins at a chalk target without looking
Results are ranked from best to worst on the first throw
Kahneman points out that the best first throws mostly got worse
questions.explain: The objection came after his speech on reward, and he answered it with the coin demonstration rather than algebra. Ranking by first throw revealed the same pattern the instructor had seen, without praise or punishment.

questions.q: Match each part of Kahneman's flight instructor story to what it shows.
pairs: Praise after a clean maneuver
Usually followed by a worse attempt because the good one was partly luck
Shouting after a bad maneuver
Usually followed by improvement that would have come anyway
Two coins thrown at a chalk target
Shows regression with no praise or punishment at all
The instructor's conclusion
A causal story imposed on random fluctuation
questions.explain: Each piece illustrates regression to the mean: extreme performances, good or bad, tend to be followed by more average ones, and the coin game shows this happens without any feedback.

questions.q: In Kahneman's flight instructor story, sort each statement by whether it is the instructor's claim or Kahneman's explanation.

items.t: Praise makes cadets do worse next time
Screaming at a cadet makes him do better
Reward works for birds but not for flight cadets
Praised performances were probably lucky ones
Bad performances were likely to improve whatever the instructor did
The pattern is regression to the mean

questions.explain: The instructor read his observations as proof that punishment beats reward. Kahneman accepts the observations but explains them as regression from unusually good or bad attempts.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say that, because of regression to the mean, we are statistically punished for being nice and rewarded for being nasty?
questions.a: We tend to be nice to people when they have just pleased us and nasty when they have not. Since unusually good behavior is likely to be followed by something more ordinary, and unusually bad behavior by improvement, niceness tends to be followed by worse results and nastiness by better ones. This is why Kahneman says “the feedback to which life exposes us is perverse.”

questions.q: In the flight instructor story, how could the instructor be both right and completely wrong at once?
questions.a: He was right that praised maneuvers were usually followed by worse ones and that shouting was usually followed by improvement. He was wrong to infer that praise hurts and punishment helps, because he praised only unusually good, probably lucky attempts and shouted only after unusually bad ones. Those performances would have regressed toward the average whatever he did.

questions.q: What were the two 'favorite equations' Kahneman offered when John Brockman of Edge asked scientists for one?
options: success = talent + effort, and great success = talent + a lot of effort
success = talent + luck, and great success = a little more talent + a lot of luck
success = luck, and great success = a lot of luck
success = talent x luck, and great success = talent squared
questions.explain: Kahneman offered success = talent + luck and great success = a little more talent + a lot of luck. The point is that extreme success leans heavily on luck, which will not reliably repeat.

questions.q: In Kahneman's golf tournament example, what may you reasonably infer about a player who scored 66 on day 1 when the average was par 72?
options: He will certainly score 66 or better again on day 2
He is more talented than average and his luck was irrelevant
He probably had average talent and an extremely lucky day
He is more talented than average and probably had better-than-average luck that day
questions.explain: If talent and luck both contribute to success, the conclusion that the player was lucky is as warranted as the conclusion that he is talented. Neither inference is certain, but both will be right more often than wrong.

questions.q: In Kahneman's golf example, what is the best prediction for the day 2 score of a golfer who scored well above average on day 1?
options: Above average but less so than on day 1
Below average, because good luck is followed by bad luck
The same score as on day 1, since talent is stable
Exactly average, since day 2 luck is unknown
questions.explain: Talent is expected to stay the same while luck is expected to be average, so the golfer should still do well but less well than on day 1. The idea that good luck is followed by bad luck is wrong: the best guess for luck is simply average.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say the best guess about a golfer's luck on day 2 must be that it will be average?
options: Because luck always balances out over two days
Because lucky players get nervous on the second day
Because there is no way to predict anyone's luck on any day
Because tournament organizers adjust course difficulty
questions.explain: Since luck cannot be predicted, the only reasonable guess is that it will be neither good nor bad. That is why the day 2 prediction should not repeat the day 1 performance.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, why does a more extreme day 1 golf score call for more regression in the day 2 prediction?
options: Extreme scores are usually caused by measurement error
An extremely good score suggests a very lucky day
Extreme scores make players change their strategy
Extreme scores show that the course was unusually easy
questions.explain: The more extreme the original score, the more regression we expect, because an extremely good score suggests a very lucky day. That extra luck is unlikely to hold.

questions.q: What is Kahneman's simpler account of the 'Sports Illustrated jinx'?
options: Athletes on the cover become overconfident and stop training hard
The pressure of high expectations makes cover athletes tense
The magazine chooses athletes who are near the end of their careers
Cover athletes had an exceptional season, probably helped by luck, and luck is fickle
questions.explain: To make the cover an athlete must have performed exceptionally well, probably with a nudge from luck, so a poorer next season is expected. Overconfidence and pressure are the causal stories Kahneman calls unnecessary.

questions.q: Kahneman says that the best predicted golf score on day 2 is closer to the average than the day 1 score, which is why the pattern is called regression to the ____.
questions.explain: The predicted performance is more moderate than the evidence it is based on, pulling back toward the mean.

questions.q: In Kahneman's account of the Olympic ski jump, the sportscaster detected regression to the mean and invented a ____ story for which there was no evidence.
questions.explain: The commentator said a skier with a great first jump would be tense and one with a bad first jump would be relaxed. Kahneman says the change needs no causal explanation.

questions.q: Kahneman's formula says great success = a little more talent + a lot of ____.
questions.explain: His offering to Edge was “great success = a little more talent + a lot of luck,” which implies extreme success depends heavily on something that will not repeat.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that if you rank golfers by their day 2 scores and look back at day 1, you find no regression to the mean.
questions.explain: Going against the time arrow gives precisely the same pattern: the best day 2 golfers probably did less well on day 1. Kahneman uses this to show regression has no causal explanation.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says the regressive prediction for golfers is reasonable but not guaranteed to be accurate, since a few who scored 66 on day 1 will do even better on day 2.
questions.explain: A few golfers whose luck improves will beat their day 1 score, but most will do worse because their luck will no longer be above average.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman predict for two golfers, one well above and one well below average on day 1?
options: The strong golfer will probably still be above average on day 2
The weak golfer will probably improve on day 2
The gap between the two golfers will probably shrink
The weak golfer will probably overtake the strong golfer
Both golfers will probably repeat their day 1 scores
questions.explain: Talent carries over but luck is expected to be average, so both scores move toward the mean and the gap shrinks. The best guess is still that the first player does better, so overtaking is not predicted.

questions.q: Which of these are causal stories that Kahneman says are offered for regression effects in sport but are not needed?
options: A cover athlete is overconfident after appearing in Sports Illustrated
A ski jumper with a great first jump will be tense protecting his lead
A ski jumper with a bad first jump will be relaxed with nothing to lose
A golfer who scored 66 probably had a lucky day
A cover athlete probably had help from luck in the previous season
questions.explain: Overconfidence, tension and relaxation are invented causes. Luck on day 1 or in the previous season is Kahneman's own non-causal account of the pattern.

questions.q: Put the steps of Kahneman's reasoning about predicting a golfer's day 2 score in order.
items: A high day 1 score suggests both talent and good luck
Talent is expected to stay the same on day 2
Luck on day 2 is expected to be average
So the day 2 score should be good but closer to the mean
questions.explain: He first splits the day 1 score into talent and luck, then carries over talent while setting luck to average. The result is a regressive prediction.

questions.q: Put the examples in Kahneman's Talent and Luck section in the order he presents them.
items: The favorite equations for Edge
The two days of a golf tournament
The Sports Illustrated jinx
The Olympic ski jump commentary
questions.explain: He starts with the success equations, applies them to golf, then turns to two sports examples where people invent causes for regression.

questions.q: Match each example from Kahneman's Talent and Luck section to its point.
pairs: Golfer who scored 66 on day 1
Probably talented and probably lucky that day
Golfer who scored 77 on day 1
Probably weaker than average and had a bad day
Ranking by day 2 and looking back at day 1
Regression runs backward too, so it has no cause
Sports Illustrated cover
Selected after a lucky peak, and luck is fickle
questions.explain: Each example shows that extreme results combine talent with luck, and the luck part does not carry over.

questions.q: Match each statement from Kahneman's Olympic ski jump example to its role in his argument.
pairs: Norway had a great first jump and will be tense
The commentator's invented cause for a decline
Sweden had a bad first jump and will be relaxed
The commentator's invented cause for an improvement
Measuring the athletes' pulse
A way the story might be tested, true or not
Luck played a role in the first jump
Why the change is mathematically inevitable
questions.explain: Kahneman allows that the commentator's story could even be true, but the change needs no cause: it follows from luck in the first jump.

questions.q: In Kahneman's golf example, sort each feature by whether it is expected to carry over from day 1 to day 2.

items.t: A golfer's level of talent
Being above average if talented
Being below average if weak
Unusually good luck on day 1
Unusually bad luck on day 1
The exact day 1 score

questions.explain: You expect the golfer to retain the same talent, but luck cannot be predicted and is best guessed as average. So the exact score should not be repeated.

questions.q: Sort these accounts of sports results by whether Kahneman treats them as invented causal stories or as the regression explanation.

items.t: Cover athletes crack under the pressure of high expectations
A leading ski jumper is tense protecting his lead
A trailing ski jumper relaxes with nothing to lose
The cover athlete's great season had a nudge from luck
The first jump's result was partly luck
The day 1 leader was probably lucky that day

questions.explain: Kahneman says regression effects are ubiquitous and so are misguided causal stories for them. The simpler account is always that luck in the first result does not repeat.

questions.q: Using Kahneman's golf example, explain why the best prediction for day 2 should not repeat a golfer's day 1 score.
questions.a: A day 1 score reflects both talent and luck, so a very good score suggests both above-average talent and good luck that day. Talent will carry over, but luck cannot be predicted, so the best guess is that it will be average on day 2. The prediction should therefore be good but closer to the mean, and the more extreme the day 1 score, the more regression to expect.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman think looking at golf scores 'against the time arrow' shows that regression has no causal explanation?
questions.a: If you rank golfers by their day 2 scores and look back at day 1, you find precisely the same regression: the best day 2 players probably did less well on day 1. A later event cannot cause an earlier one, so the pattern cannot come from anything like pressure or complacency. It comes from luck playing a part in each score.

questions.q: What is Kahneman's point about the sportscaster's comments at the Olympic ski jump?
questions.a: The commentator saw regression to the mean and explained it with tension after a great jump and relaxation after a bad one. Kahneman grants that the story might even be true, but says the change from first to second jump needs no causal explanation. It is a mathematically inevitable consequence of luck playing a role in the first jump, even if we would all prefer a causal account.

questions.q: How does Kahneman explain the 'Sports Illustrated jinx' without any appeal to overconfidence or pressure?
questions.a: To get onto the cover an athlete must have performed exceptionally well in the preceding season, probably helped by some luck. Since luck does not persist, a poorer next season is what regression to the mean predicts. In his words, “luck is fickle.”

questions.q: Who discovered and named regression to the mean, according to Kahneman?
options: Sir Francis Galton
Charles Darwin
David Freedman
Howard Wainer
questions.explain: Galton, a half cousin of Darwin and a renowned polymath, discovered and named it late in the nineteenth century. Freedman and Wainer are later statisticians Kahneman cites about how hard regression is to explain.

questions.q: What did Galton's experiments on seeds, reported in his 1886 article, show about offspring?
options: Offspring were always the same size as their parent seeds
Offspring of large seeds grew even larger in each generation
Offspring tended to be more mediocre than their parents, smaller if parents were large and larger if parents were small
Offspring size was unrelated to parent size
questions.explain: Galton found offspring did not tend to resemble their parent seeds but to be always more mediocre than them, and the regression was proportional to the parental deviation.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what general rule did Galton eventually reach about when regression occurs?
options: Regression occurs only in inherited traits such as height
Regression occurs whenever the correlation between two measures is less than perfect
Regression occurs only when measurements contain errors
Regression occurs only when two measures use the same scale
questions.explain: It took Galton several years to move from filial regression in size to the broader idea that regression inevitably occurs when correlation is imperfect. Kahneman states the rule as “whenever the correlation between two scores is imperfect, there will be regression to the mean.”

questions.q: In Kahneman's example, why is the correlation between aptitude tests and success in graduate school much lower than between SAT scores and college GPA?
options: Graduate school grades are assigned randomly
Graduate students stop caring about their grades
Aptitude tests for graduate school are poorly designed
Measured aptitude varies little among the selected group of graduate students
questions.explain: If everyone has similar aptitude, differences in it are unlikely to play a large role in success. Kahneman puts the SAT and college GPA correlation at about .60.

questions.q: In Kahneman's example 'Highly intelligent women tend to marry men who are less intelligent than they are,' what is the correct explanation?
options: The correlation between spouses' intelligence is less than perfect
Intelligent men do not want to marry intelligent women
Intelligent women avoid competition from equally intelligent men
Intelligent women marry earlier, before men's intelligence is known
questions.explain: Kahneman says the interesting statement and the trivial one about imperfect correlation are algebraically equivalent, given that men and women do not differ in intelligence on average. The stories about competition are the causal explanations people invent at parties.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what is the main reason regression is so hard for people to understand?
options: The mathematics of regression requires advanced calculus
Regression effects are rare and seldom encountered in daily life
Our mind is strongly biased toward causal explanations and does not deal well with mere statistics
Most people are never taught about averages
questions.explain: He calls this a recurrent theme of the book: associative memory looks for a cause when an event draws attention. Regression is common, so rarity is not the problem.

questions.q: In Bazerman's sales forecasting problem that Kahneman adapts, how should you forecast 2012 sales for each store when overall sales are expected to rise 10%?
options: Add exactly 10% to each store's 2011 sales
Add more than 10% to the low-performing stores and less, or even subtract, for the others
Add more than 10% to the high-performing stores and less to the others
Give every store the same dollar amount of sales
questions.explain: Store sales differ partly because of random factors, so forecasts should be regressive. Adding 10% to each store is the obvious answer Kahneman says is wrong.

questions.q: Galton's 1886 article was titled 'Regression towards ____ in Hereditary Stature.'
questions.explain: The title reflects his finding that offspring were more mediocre than their parents. The chapter's final section borrows the phrase in its heading.

questions.q: Kahneman says it took Galton several years to figure out that correlation and ____ are not two concepts but different perspectives on the same concept.
questions.explain: In Kahneman's words, “correlation and regression are not two concepts—they are different perspectives on the same concept.”

questions.q: Kahneman says the correlation between family income and the last four digits of their phone number is ____.
questions.explain: No factor is shared between the two measures, so the correlation is zero. At the other end, the size of objects measured in English or metric units has a correlation of 1.

questions.q: Kahneman says that to conclude a treatment for depressed children is effective, you must compare treated patients with a ____ that receives no treatment or a placebo.
questions.explain: The control group is expected to improve by regression alone, so the experiment asks whether the treated patients improve more than regression can explain.

questions.q: Kahneman says regression to the mean has an explanation but does not have a ____.
questions.explain: Causal explanations will be evoked when regression is detected, but they will be wrong: “regression to the mean has an explanation but does not have a cause.”

questions.q: Kahneman says regression effects can be found wherever we look, but we do not recognize them; they hide in plain ____.
questions.explain: He makes this point about Galton's surprise at a statistical regularity as common as the air we breathe: “They hide in plain sight.”

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says regression to the mean was identified about two hundred years before the theory of gravitation and differential calculus.
questions.explain: It was the other way round: regression was first identified and understood two hundred years after gravitation and calculus, which shows how strange it is to the human mind.

questions.q: True or false: According to Kahneman, depressed children given an energy drink would show a clinically significant improvement, but so would depressed children who hug a cat for twenty minutes a day.
questions.explain: Depressed children are an extreme group and extreme groups regress to the mean over time, so they improve whatever is done. Only a comparison with a control group can show that a treatment works.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says the correlation between self-reported height and weight among adult American males would be lower if women and children were included.
questions.explain: He says it would be much higher, because gender and age influence both height and weight, which increases the relative weight of shared factors. The figure for adult American males is .41.

questions.q: Which of these correlation examples does Kahneman give correctly?
options: SAT scores and college GPA: approximately .60
Income and education level in the United States: approximately .40
Size of objects measured in English or metric units: 1
Self-reported height and weight among adult American males: .90
Family income and last four digits of the phone number: .50
questions.explain: Kahneman gives .60, .40 and 1 for these pairs. Height and weight among adult American males is .41, and income and phone digits is 0.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say follow from the simplified model in which weight = age + ice cream consumption and piano playing = age + weekly hours of practice?
options: There will be regression to the mean when predicting piano playing from weight
Tom, who ranks twelfth in weight, is probably older than average
Barbara, eighty-fifth in piano, is likely to practice less than most children
Children who eat more ice cream practice the piano more
Weight and piano playing are perfectly correlated
questions.explain: Age is the only shared factor, so the correlation is imperfect and regression follows. The model assumes ice cream and practice are unrelated, so the claim that ice cream eaters practice more is wrong.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give as signs of how hard regression is to grasp?
options: It took one of the best minds of nineteenth-century Britain, with great difficulty, to make sense of it
David Freedman said the side that must explain regression to a jury will lose
Eminent researchers have confused correlation with causation in regression effects
Only people with no statistical training misunderstand it
Galton understood it fully the first time he saw his seed data
questions.explain: Kahneman cites Galton's struggle, Freedman's remark, and Howard Wainer's list of eminent researchers. He says the confusion persists even after some statistical instruction, and Galton took several years to reach the general idea.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say about the roles of System 1 and System 2 in our difficulty with regression?
options: The difficulty originates with both System 1 and System 2
System 2 finds the relationship between correlation and regression hard to understand and learn
The insistent demand for causal interpretations is a feature of System 1
System 2 easily corrects System 1 once a regression effect is noticed
Only System 1 is involved, so statistical training removes the problem
questions.explain: Kahneman says the trouble comes from both systems: System 2 finds regression hard to learn, partly because of System 1's insistent demand for causes. He says the problem often survives statistical instruction.

questions.q: Put these points in the order Kahneman presents them in his Understanding Regression section.
items: Galton discovers regression in seeds and heights
Correlation measured with ranks: weight and piano playing
Intelligent women marry less intelligent men
Depressed children and the energy drink
Sales forecasting for a department store chain
questions.explain: He moves from Galton's discovery and the link between correlation and regression to examples of mistaken causal readings, and closes with a forecasting problem.

questions.q: Order these pairs by the size of the correlation Kahneman reports, from highest to lowest.
items: Size in English and metric units
SAT scores and college GPA
Self-reported height and weight of adult American males
Family income and last four digits of the phone number
questions.explain: The figures are 1, about .60, .41 and 0. A higher correlation means a larger share of determining factors is shared by the two measures.

questions.q: Match each person to Kahneman's mention of them in the chapter on regression.
pairs: Francis Galton
Discovered and named regression to the mean
David Freedman
Said the side that must explain regression to a jury will lose
Howard Wainer
Listed eminent researchers who mistook regression for causation
Max Bazerman
Wrote the text from which the sales forecasting problem is adapted
questions.explain: Galton is the discoverer; Freedman and Wainer show how hard regression is even for experts; Bazerman's Judgment in Managerial Decision Making supplies the forecasting example.

questions.q: Match each correlation coefficient to the pair of measures Kahneman gives it for.
pairs: Size of objects measured in English or metric units
About .60
SAT scores and college GPA
About .40
Income and education level in the United States
Family income and last four digits of the phone number
questions.explain: The correlation coefficient measures the relative weight of the factors two measures share, from 0 for none to 1 for all.

questions.q: Sort these statements about intelligent spouses by whether Kahneman calls them interesting or trivial, though they are algebraically equivalent.
groups: Seems trivial with nothing to explain

items.t: Highly intelligent women tend to marry less intelligent men
Intelligent women avoid competing with equally intelligent men
Intelligent men do not want to compete with intelligent women
The correlation between spouses' intelligence scores is imperfect
Nobody would expect spouses' intelligence to correlate perfectly

questions.explain: People readily invent causal stories for the first statement, but it follows mathematically from the obvious second one. Regression cannot be more interesting or explainable than the imperfect correlation.

questions.q: In the case of depressed children treated with an energy drink, sort each statement by whether Kahneman calls it a justified or unjustified conclusion.

items.t: The treated children will probably improve over three months
Depressed children are an extreme group and will tend to regress
A treatment works only if it beats a control group
The energy drink caused the improvement
Hugging a cat cures depression in children
Any group that improves after a treatment proves it works

questions.explain: Improvement is expected from regression alone because depressed children are an extreme group. Inferring that the drink or cat hugging caused it is completely unjustified without a control group.

questions.q: What did Galton find in his seed experiments, and what broader idea did he later reach with help from statisticians?
questions.a: Galton found that offspring seeds did not resemble their parents but were more mediocre, smaller if the parents were large and larger if they were very small, with regression proportional to the parents' deviation. Over several years he worked out the broader notion that regression inevitably occurs whenever the correlation between two measures is less than perfect. He also saw that correlation and regression are different perspectives on the same concept.

questions.q: Explain why Kahneman says the statement that highly intelligent women tend to marry less intelligent men needs no causal explanation.
questions.a: If the correlation between spouses' intelligence is less than perfect and men and women do not differ in intelligence on average, it is a mathematical inevitability that very intelligent women will have husbands who are on average less intelligent. That is just regression to the mean. The interesting statement is algebraically equivalent to the trivial one about imperfect correlation, so it cannot be any more explainable.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say a control group is needed to judge a treatment for depressed children?
questions.a: Depressed children are an extreme group, and because depression scores on successive tests are imperfectly correlated, they will get somewhat better over time whatever is done. A treated group will therefore improve even if the treatment is useless. Comparing it with an untreated or placebo control group shows whether the treatment produces more improvement than regression alone can explain.

questions.q: What does Kahneman mean by saying that regression to the mean has an explanation but not a cause, and why do our minds struggle with this?
questions.a: Regression is explained by luck or other uncorrelated factors in an extreme result, not by any force acting on the next result. Our mind is strongly biased toward causal explanations: when an event draws attention, associative memory automatically looks for a cause already stored in memory. So causal stories are evoked when regression is detected, but they are wrong, and System 2 finds the statistical account hard to learn.

questions.q: In the sales forecasting problem Kahneman adapts from Bazerman, why is adding 10% to each store's sales the wrong forecast?
questions.a: Store sales differ partly because of location and competition but also because of random factors, so this year's high sellers were probably helped by luck and low sellers hurt by it. Forecasts should be regressive, adding more than 10% to the weak stores and less, or even subtracting, for the strong ones, while keeping the overall 10% increase. Most people find the uniform 10% answer obvious, which shows that the concept of regression is far from obvious.

questions.q: A manager tells Kahneman that experience has taught her criticism works better than praise. What does Kahneman's sample remark say she fails to understand?
options: That praise works better with experienced employees
That her employees are more talented than she thinks
That criticism works only when given in private
That it is all due to regression to the mean
questions.explain: Like the flight instructor, she sees improvement after criticism and decline after praise, but that pattern is regression to the mean, not proof that criticism works.

questions.q: Kahneman's sample remark about hiring says that because a screening procedure is good but not perfect, we should anticipate ____.
questions.explain: An imperfect screen means an imperfect correlation with later performance, so the very best candidates will often fail to meet expectations.

questions.q: True or false: In a sample remark, Kahneman suggests a candidate's second interview was probably less impressive because his first interview was unusually good.
questions.explain: The remark grants he may have feared disappointing the interviewers, but says it is more likely that the first was unusually good, a regression explanation rather than a causal one.

questions.q: Match each everyday situation from Kahneman's sample remarks to the regression point it makes.
pairs: A manager who believes criticism beats praise
Her experience reflects regression, not the power of criticism
A second interview weaker than the first
The first was probably unusually good
Top candidates who disappoint after hiring
An imperfect screen means we should expect regression
questions.explain: Each remark replaces a tempting causal story with the expectation that extreme first impressions will be followed by more average ones.

questions.q: According to Kahneman's sample remark about screening, why shouldn't we be surprised when the very best candidates fail to meet our expectations?
questions.a: A screening procedure that is good but not perfect is imperfectly correlated with later performance, so there will be regression to the mean. The candidates who score highest were probably helped by some luck in the screening, which will not repeat on the job. Their later performance will tend to be closer to average than their scores suggested.

questions.q: Chapter 17, 'Regression to the Mean,' comes right after 'Causes Trump Statistics.' What theme links them?
options: Both show how the mind prefers causal stories to statistical facts
Both describe how anchors distort numerical estimates
Both explain how losses loom larger than gains
Both contrast the experiencing self with the remembering self
questions.explain: Kahneman calls the bias toward causal explanations over mere statistics a recurrent theme of the book. Regression is a statistical fact that people insist on explaining with causes.

questions.q: How does Chapter 17, 'Regression to the Mean,' prepare for the next chapter, 'Taming Intuitive Predictions'?
options: It introduces the idea of loss aversion that the next chapter applies to prediction
It argues that intuitive predictions are always accurate for experts
It shows that predictions should be regressive, ending with a forecasting problem people get wrong
It shows that the remembering self controls our predictions
questions.explain: The chapter closes with Bazerman's sales forecasting problem, where the right forecasts are regressive. Kahneman even mentions he and Amos were writing about intuitive prediction, which the next chapter takes up.

questions.q: Which of these chapters belong to the same part of the book, 'Heuristics and Biases,' as Chapter 17, 'Regression to the Mean'?
options: The Law of Small Numbers
Linda: Less Is More
Causes Trump Statistics
The Illusion of Validity
Prospect Theory
questions.explain: Part II runs from The Law of Small Numbers to Taming Intuitive Predictions. The Illusion of Validity belongs to Part III, Overconfidence, and Prospect Theory to Part IV, Choices.

questions.q: Put these chapters of Part II, 'Heuristics and Biases,' in book order.
items: Linda: Less Is More
Causes Trump Statistics
Regression to the Mean
Taming Intuitive Predictions
questions.explain: These are chapters 15 to 18. Regression to the Mean sits between the chapter on causal versus statistical thinking and the chapter on correcting intuitive predictions.

questions.q: Sort these chapters by whether they come before or after Chapter 17, 'Regression to the Mean.'

items.t: The Law of Small Numbers
Tom W's Specialty
Causes Trump Statistics
Taming Intuitive Predictions
The Illusion of Understanding
Intuitions vs. Formulas

questions.explain: Chapters 10, 14 and 16 come before it; chapter 18 directly follows, and chapters 19 and 21 open Part III, Overconfidence.

questions.q: Why does the chapter 'Regression to the Mean' open with the flight instructor story rather than with Galton's statistics?
questions.a: The story shows regression as a lived experience that fools even seasoned experts, who read cause into random fluctuations. Starting there makes the stakes clear before the history and statistics: we are misled by perverse feedback in everyday life. Galton's discovery then explains why the pattern exists and why it was so hard to see.

questions.q: What does the title of the chapter's final section, 'Speaking of Regression to Mediocrity,' signal, and how does it tie back to the chapter?
questions.a: It echoes the title of Galton's 1886 article, 'Regression towards Mediocrity in Hereditary Stature,' linking everyday talk to the original discovery. Like the book's other closing sections, it offers sample remarks for spotting the bias in daily life, here about criticism and praise, interviews, and screening candidates. Each remark replaces a causal story with the expectation of regression.

questions.q: In the opening of Kahneman's chapter on taming intuitive predictions, which forecasters are said to rely largely on look-up tables, precise calculations and explicit analyses of similar past cases?
options: Engineers estimating the concrete needed for a building
Fireground commanders judging how many trucks a fire needs
Venture capitalists assessing a start-up's profitability
Spouses forecasting a partner's reaction to a move
questions.explain: Kahneman sets engineers apart as forecasters whose predictions rest on calculation and look-up tables. Fireground commanders, by contrast, are his example of skilled intuition, not explicit analysis.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, drawing on Gary Klein's work, why does a solution come to mind quickly for a chess master or experienced physician?
options: Because they substitute an easier question for the hard one
Because familiar cues are recognized from repeated experience
Because they carefully compute the base rate for the case
Because they are more confident than other people
questions.explain: Skilled intuitions arise from expertise acquired by repeated experience, so the answer comes quickly because familiar cues are recognized. Substituting an easier question describes the other, heuristic kind of intuition.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says intuitions produced by heuristics always feel clearly different from skilled intuitions based on expertise.
questions.explain: He says heuristic intuitions are “sometimes subjectively indistinguishable from the first,” meaning from skilled intuitions. That is why confident intuition is no guarantee of skill.

questions.q: In Kahneman's account of intuitive forecasting, some intuitions arise from heuristics that often ____ an easy question for the harder one that was asked.
questions.explain: The second variety of intuition comes from heuristics that substitute an easy question for a hard one. Such judgments can be made with high confidence even on weak evidence.

questions.q: Sort these judgments by the variety of intuition Kahneman describes at the start of the chapter on taming intuitive predictions.

items.t: A chess master instantly seeing a strong move
A physician rapidly recognizing a familiar pattern of symptoms
A fireground commander recognizing familiar cues at a fire
Guessing a senior's GPA from the fact that she read early
A confident forecast built on a nonregressive reading of weak evidence
Answering an easy question in place of the hard one that was asked

questions.explain: Klein's chess masters, physicians and fireground commanders show intuition based on recognizing familiar cues. Predicting Julie's GPA from her early reading shows the heuristic kind, which substitutes an easier question and ignores how weak the evidence is.

questions.q: In opening the chapter on taming intuitive predictions, what two main varieties of intuitive prediction does Kahneman distinguish, and why does the distinction matter?
questions.a: One variety draws on skill and expertise built by repeated experience, as in Klein's chess masters, fireground commanders and physicians, where familiar cues are recognized. The other comes from heuristics that substitute an easy question for the harder one asked. The distinction matters because the two can feel the same from the inside, and heuristic intuitions can be held with high confidence even when they rest on nonregressive assessments of weak evidence.

questions.q: In the Julie problem (a university senior who read fluently at age four), what GPA do people familiar with American education typically give?
options: About 3.0, the average GPA
About 2.5, below the average
About 3.7 or 3.8
Exactly 4.0, the maximum
questions.explain: Kahneman reports that people quickly come up with a number often in the vicinity of 3.7 or 3.8. The average would be the regressive baseline, which intuition does not supply.

questions.q: In the Julie problem, why would System 2 probably reject a report that Julie won a fly-fishing competition as evidence about her GPA?
options: Because no causal link to academic performance can be found
Because the report comes from an unreliable source
Because the event happened too long ago to matter
Because the base rate of fly-fishing winners is unknown
questions.explain: The first step of intuitive prediction is a search for a causal link between the evidence and the target. Early reading connects to GPA through academic talent; fly-fishing has no such link, so it is rejected as irrelevant.

questions.q: In the Julie problem, which task does Kahneman say System 1 cannot do?
options: Reject evidence as irrelevant or false
Construct a coherent story from available information
Compare evidence with a norm for a reference group
Adjust for smaller weaknesses in the evidence
questions.explain: The process is effectively dichotomous: System 1 can reject information as irrelevant or false, but it cannot adjust for smaller weaknesses. As a result, “intuitive predictions are almost completely insensitive to the actual predictive quality of the evidence.”

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says intuitive predictions are almost completely insensitive to the actual predictive quality of the evidence.
questions.explain: Because System 1 either accepts or rejects evidence and cannot adjust for its smaller weaknesses, intuitive predictions barely change with how predictive the evidence really is.

questions.q: In the Julie problem, the group to which the child is compared when judging how precocious she is goes unspecified; Kahneman calls it a ____.
questions.explain: The evidence is evaluated against a norm for a reference group. Kahneman notes it is rarely specified, just as in normal speech when someone is called quite clever.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, ____ yields predictions that are as extreme as the evidence on which they are based.
questions.explain: Intensity matching assigns Julie the same percentile for GPA as for reading precocity, so the prediction is just as extreme as the evidence. That leads people to answer two quite different questions identically.

questions.q: Put in order the System 1 operations Kahneman lists for predicting Julie's GPA from her early reading.
items: Seek a causal link between early reading and GPA
Evaluate the early reading against a norm for a reference group
Substitute that evaluation and assign the same percentile to GPA
Translate the percentile into a number on the GPA scale
questions.explain: Kahneman describes a link search, then evaluation against a norm, then substitution and intensity matching, and finally translation into GPA units. He adds that the real process is spreading activation rather than tidy steps.

questions.q: After listing the steps behind the intuitive prediction of Julie's GPA as an orderly sequence, what caveat does Kahneman add?
options: System 2 checks each step before moving to the next one
Associative memory works by spreading activation that settles on the most coherent solution
The steps occur only in people unfamiliar with American education
The final step is always rejected by System 2 as implausible
questions.explain: He warns that associative memory does not work as an orderly sequence. Activation spreads from the evidence and question, feeds back on itself, and settles on the most coherent solution possible.

questions.q: Which of these operations does Kahneman include in the System 1 process that produces a GPA for Julie?
options: Searching for a causal link between the evidence and the GPA
Evaluating the evidence against a norm
Intensity matching from an impression to the GPA scale
Starting from the average GPA as a baseline
Estimating the correlation between reading age and GPA
questions.explain: The intuitive process seeks a link, evaluates the evidence against a norm, and matches intensity onto the GPA scale. Starting from the average and estimating the correlation belong to the corrective procedure, which is work for System 2.

questions.q: In the study of counselor descriptions of college freshmen, the description 'intelligent, self-confident, well-read, hardworking, inquisitive' was judged very likely to place the student in the top ____ but unlikely in the top 3%.
questions.explain: Readers sense the counselor thinks the student is good but not spectacularly good, since stronger adjectives were available. The verdict was likely top 15%, unlikely top 3%, with impressive consensus.

questions.q: In Kahneman and Tversky's study of five-adjective descriptions of college freshmen, what did the comparison between the evaluation group and the prediction group show?
options: Predictions of GPA were much more moderate than evaluations
Predictions of GPA were more extreme than evaluations
The percentile judgments of the two groups were identical
Only the evaluation group reached a consensus
questions.explain: The judgments were identical: participants treated the prediction of future GPA as if it were the same as evaluating the description. Correctly regressive predictions would have been more moderate.

questions.q: True or false: In the study of counselor descriptions of college freshmen, participants who predicted GPA gave more moderate percentile judgments than participants who only evaluated the descriptions.
questions.explain: The two groups gave identical percentile judgments. Showing no extra moderation for the uncertainty of the future is exactly what reveals substitution.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman call the study of counselor descriptions of college freshmen perhaps the best evidence for the role of substitution?
questions.a: One group evaluated how impressive each description was, while another predicted the student's GPA at the end of the freshman year, a far more uncertain question. The percentile judgments of the two groups were identical, so people asked for a prediction answered with an evaluation of the evidence without noticing the switch. As Kahneman puts it, “the prediction of the future is not distinguished from an evaluation of current evidence,” which guarantees predictions that ignore regression to the mean.

questions.q: Match each element of the study of counselor descriptions of college freshmen with what it was.
pairs: The descriptions
Five adjectives allegedly written by a counselor after interviews
First group's task
Judge how impressive each description was for academic ability
Second group's task
Estimate the GPA each student would obtain
The result
The two groups' percentile judgments were identical
questions.explain: The study compared evaluation of evidence with prediction of an outcome. Identical answers showed that prediction was simply matched to evaluation.

questions.q: Summing up the freshman-description study, Kahneman says that prediction matches ____.
questions.explain: People asked for a prediction substituted an evaluation of the evidence. Because evaluation has no uncertainty about the future built in, the resulting predictions completely ignore regression to the mean.

questions.q: In Kahneman's study at the Israeli army unit that selected officer candidates, what did he ask the officers to provide in addition to their usual ratings?
options: Their confidence in each of their own ratings
Their best guess of each candidate's grade in officer school
The base rate of candidates who fail officer school
A ranking of candidates by leadership style
questions.explain: He asked for their best guess of the grade each future cadet would obtain in officer school, and they collected a few hundred such forecasts. The question was about a real prediction rather than their usual evaluation.

questions.q: True or false: In Kahneman's army study, the relative frequency of A's and B's in the officers' forecasts was almost identical to the frequencies in the officer school's final grades.
