questions.explain: The results were striking because the ratings were known to have rather poor validity. Predictions with poor validity should have been regressive, not a copy of the actual grade distribution.

questions.q: Why were the officers' forecasts of officer-school grades a compelling example of nonregressive prediction?
options: Because the officers had never seen the school's grading system
Because the forecasts were wildly more optimistic than the actual grades
Because the officers refused to give forecasts for weak candidates
Because their low-validity forecasts were spread out just like the actual grades
questions.explain: Given the considerable uncertainty, good forecasts would have clustered more toward the middle. Instead the officers translated their own grades onto the school's scale by intensity matching, producing a spread as wide as the real outcomes.

questions.q: Which of these were the two tasks that the officers in Kahneman's army study failed to tell apart?
options: Evaluating a candidate's performance during the stay at the unit
Predicting a cadet's future grade in officer school
Estimating the base rate of A grades among all soldiers
Ranking the instructors at officer school
questions.explain: Kahneman says the officers completely failed to discriminate between their usual mission of evaluating performance at the unit and the actual prediction of a future grade he requested.

questions.q: Put in order the course of Kahneman's study of the army unit that selected officer candidates.
items: The unit rated candidates through interviews and field tests
Kahneman asked the officers for their best guess of each cadet's officer-school grade
A few hundred forecasts were collected
The forecast grade frequencies were found to match the school's actual grade frequencies
questions.explain: The study added a prediction request to the usual evaluation, collected the forecasts, and compared their distribution with real grades. The near-identical frequencies showed substitution and intensity matching.

questions.q: Sort these questions from Kahneman's discussion of nonregressive intuitions into evaluations of current evidence and predictions of a future outcome.

items.t: How much does this description impress you with respect to academic ability?
What percentage of descriptions of freshmen would impress you more?
What is your estimate of the GPA the student will obtain?
What is the percentage of freshmen who obtain a higher GPA?
How well did this candidate perform during his stay at the unit?
What grade will this cadet obtain in officer school?

questions.explain: Evaluation questions ask only about the evidence in hand; prediction questions ask about a future outcome and carry much more uncertainty. Kahneman's point is that people answer both kinds the same way.

questions.q: Using the Julie problem, explain what intensity matching is and why it leads people to give the same answer to two quite different questions.
questions.a: Intensity matching takes an impression on one dimension and finds the matching level on another, so Julie's percentile for reading precocity becomes her percentile for GPA and is then translated onto the GPA scale. Because the match is one-for-one, “Intensity matching yields predictions that are as extreme as the evidence on which they are based.” People therefore answer the question about reading precocity and the question about GPA with the same percentile, ignoring how weakly the two are related.

questions.q: What does Kahneman mean when he says System 1's treatment of evidence in the Julie problem is effectively dichotomous, and what follows from it?
questions.a: System 1 can either reject information as irrelevant or false, like a fly-fishing win, or accept it once a causal link is found, like early reading. It cannot adjust for smaller weaknesses in evidence that is relevant but only weakly predictive. As a result intuitive predictions are almost completely insensitive to the predictive quality of the evidence, and WYSIATI builds the best possible story from whatever was accepted.

questions.q: Maya hears that a new colleague gave a dazzling job interview and immediately predicts that within a year he will be the best performer in the department. In Kahneman's terms, what is Maya doing?
options: Applying a base rate drawn from the department's history
Using skilled intuition built from years of hiring feedback
Deliberately regressing her forecast toward the department average
Matching her prediction to her evaluation of the interview and ignoring regression
questions.explain: Like the officers and the participants in the freshman study, Maya substitutes her evaluation of current evidence for a prediction and matches its intensity. An interview is weak evidence of future performance, so a regressive forecast would be more moderate.

questions.q: In Kahneman's schematic formula, the correlation between reading age and GPA is equal to the proportion of ____ among their determinants.
questions.explain: Both reading age and GPA are made up of shared factors and factors specific to each. The share of common causes, such as aptitude and family support, sets the correlation.

questions.q: What is Kahneman's most optimistic guess of the correlation between reading age and college GPA in the Julie example?
options: About 30%
About 70%
About 10%
About 50%
questions.explain: He says his most optimistic guess of the proportion of shared factors is about 30%. That figure is then used to move only 30% of the way from the average GPA to the intuitive GPA.

questions.q: Put in order Kahneman's four steps for an unbiased prediction of Julie's GPA.
items: Start with an estimate of average GPA
Determine the GPA that matches your impression of the evidence
Estimate the correlation between your evidence and GPA
Move that fraction of the distance from the average toward the matching GPA
questions.explain: The baseline comes first, then the intuitive prediction, then the correlation that decides how far to move, and finally the moderate prediction between the two.

questions.q: Using Kahneman's four-step correction, suppose the average GPA is 3.0, the GPA matching your impression of a student is 3.8, and the correlation is .30. What should you predict?
questions.explain: You move 30% of the distance from the average (3.0) toward the matching GPA (3.8): 0.3 times 0.8 is 0.24, giving 3.24. Predicting 3.8 is the uncorrected intuition, and 3.56 moves 70% of the way instead of 30%.

questions.q: Match each step of Kahneman's corrective procedure for predicting Julie's GPA with its role.
pairs: Step 1: average GPA
The baseline you would predict knowing nothing about Julie
Step 2: matching GPA
Your intuitive prediction, matching your evaluation of the evidence
Step 3: correlation estimate
Sets how far you may move from the baseline toward intuition
Step 4: move part of the distance
A prediction influenced by intuition but far more moderate
questions.explain: Kahneman explains that step 1 gives the baseline, step 2 is the intuition, step 3 governs the distance moved, and step 4 yields the moderated prediction.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman compares step 1 of his GPA correction, starting from the average, to assigning the base-rate probability of business administration graduates when told nothing about Tom W.
questions.explain: In both cases the baseline is what you would predict with no information about the individual. For GPA that is the average; for Tom W it was the base rate.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, how large should the adjustment of an intuitive prediction be when there is a strong correlation between the evidence and the outcome?
options: Large, because strong evidence tends to be overrated
Small, because the intuition can be largely trusted
Zero in every case, because intuition is then perfect
Equal to the full distance back to the average
questions.explain: “The approach builds on your intuition, but it moderates it, regresses it toward the mean.” When the correlation is strong, the adjustment will be small; only a perfect correlation would justify no adjustment at all.

questions.q: Kahneman says his four-step approach applies whenever you need to predict a ____ variable, such as GPA, profit from an investment or a company's growth.
questions.explain: The procedure is general for quantities measured on a scale. Discrete outcomes, like Tom W's field, are handled by the parallel procedure built on base rates.

questions.q: Predicting that each golfer's score on day 2 of a tournament will equal his day-1 score is biased because it does not allow for ____ to the mean.
questions.explain: Golfers who did well on day 1 will on average do less well on day 2, and those who did poorly will mostly improve. Predictions that ignore this are as extreme as the evidence.

questions.q: If you predict each golfer's day-2 score to equal his day-1 score, how will those predictions turn out to be biased, according to Kahneman?
options: Too pessimistic for the leaders and too optimistic for those who started badly
Too optimistic for every golfer, regardless of the first day
Too optimistic for the leaders and too pessimistic for those who started badly
Unbiased overall, because day-1 scores are real evidence
questions.explain: Nonregressive predictions are on average overly optimistic for those who did best on day 1 and overly pessimistic for those with a bad start. Reversing these directions gets regression backward.

questions.q: True or false: According to Kahneman, corrected predictions still contain errors, but the errors are smaller and do not favor either high or low outcomes.
questions.explain: Corrected predictions are about equally likely to overestimate and underestimate the true value. Errors remain, but they are smaller and no longer biased in one direction.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say are true of corrected, regressive predictions?
options: High and low predictions are about equally likely to overestimate and underestimate the true value
Their errors are smaller than those of uncorrected intuitive predictions
They contain no errors at all
They are as extreme as the evidence on which they are based
They ignore the evidence and always equal the average
questions.explain: Corrected predictions remove the bias and shrink the errors but do not eliminate them. Being as extreme as the evidence is the mark of the uncorrected intuition, and the average is used only when the evidence is useless.

questions.q: Why, according to Kahneman, do intuitive predictions need to be corrected at all?
questions.a: Intuitive predictions are not regressive: they are as extreme as the evidence, so they ignore regression to the mean. When compared with actual outcomes they are found to be biased, too optimistic for cases with extreme favorable evidence and too pessimistic for cases with extreme unfavorable evidence. Correcting them makes predictions equally likely to err in either direction and makes the errors smaller.

questions.q: If you predict college grades from childhood reading without regressing toward the mean, what pattern of surprises does Kahneman say you will experience, and why?
questions.a: You will more often than not be disappointed by the grades of early readers and happily surprised by the grades of those who learned to read relatively late. Early reading and GPA share only part of their causes, so an extreme score on one predicts a less extreme score on the other. Predictions matched to the evidence are therefore too high at the top and too low at the bottom.

questions.q: In Kahneman's corrective procedure, why does the distance you move from the baseline toward your intuitive prediction depend on the estimated correlation?
questions.a: The correlation measures how much the evidence and the outcome share their determinants, and so how much the evidence really tells you. With no useful evidence you stay at the baseline; with a perfect correlation you could keep the intuitive prediction; in between you move the matching fraction, such as 30% for a correlation of .30. This builds on intuition but moderates it, regressing it toward the mean.

questions.q: Sort these determinants of reading age and college GPA, from Kahneman's schematic formula, into shared factors and factors affecting only one outcome.

items.t: Genetically determined aptitude
Family support for academic interests
Anything that makes the same people early readers and successful students
Overly ambitious parents pushing a child to read early
An unhappy love affair that depresses college grades
A skiing accident in adolescence causing slight impairment

questions.explain: Shared factors make the same people both precocious readers and good students, so they create the correlation. Specific factors move one outcome and not the other, which is why the correlation is far from perfect.

questions.q: Sort these forecasts, drawn from Kahneman's discussion of prediction, into nonregressive intuitive predictions and regressive corrected predictions.

items.t: Predicting each golfer's day-2 score to equal his day-1 score
Giving Julie the same percentile for GPA as for reading precocity
Officers translating their unit grades onto the officer-school scale
Moving 30% of the way from average GPA toward the GPA matching the evidence
Predicting Kim's future performance closer to the mean than her impression suggests
Staying with the average when the evidence is useless

questions.explain: Nonregressive predictions copy the extremeness of the evidence. Corrected predictions start from the baseline and move toward intuition only as far as the evidence's validity allows.

questions.q: A sales manager must forecast next quarter's results for a rep who just had a record quarter, knowing that quarterly results are only weakly correlated. Following Kahneman's correction, what should the manager forecast?
options: A figure between the team average and the record, closer to the average
Another record quarter, since the evidence is clear
Exactly the team average, ignoring the record entirely
A figure below the team average, to offset the luck
questions.explain: With a weak correlation, the corrected forecast moves only a short distance from the baseline toward the intuitive figure. Ignoring the record entirely is right only when the evidence is useless, and predicting below average overshoots the mean.

questions.q: In Kahneman's corrective procedure, put these outcomes in order as your confidence in the evidence rises from none to complete.
items: Stay with the baseline prediction
End somewhere between, nearer the baseline
End somewhere between, nearer your intuitive prediction
Stay with your initial intuitive prediction
questions.explain: With no useful evidence you stay at the baseline; only after a critical review leaves you completely confident do you keep the intuition. Most cases fall between the two poles.

questions.q: Match each element of Kahneman's corrective procedures with what it is in the categorical (Tom W) or numerical (GPA) case.
pairs: Baseline in the categorical case
The base rate
Baseline in the numerical case
The average outcome in the relevant category
Intuitive prediction
The number that comes to mind, a probability or a GPA
Target prediction
Intermediate between the baseline and the intuitive response
questions.explain: Kahneman stresses that the two procedures share the same structure: a baseline, an intuition, and a final answer between them. Both address the bias that intuitive predictions are overconfident and too extreme.

questions.q: Which two biases of discrete prediction did the procedure introduced with Tom W counter, according to Kahneman?
options: Anchoring and the availability of vivid examples
Loss aversion and the endowment effect
Overconfidence and the planning fallacy
Neglect of base rates and insensitivity to the quality of information
questions.explain: Kahneman recalls that the Tom W procedure countered neglect of base rates and insensitivity to the quality of information, and that predictions on a scale show similar biases.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says correcting intuitive predictions is a task for System 1.
questions.explain: “Correcting your intuitive predictions is a task for System 2.” Finding the reference category, estimating the baseline and judging the evidence all take significant effort.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, when is the effort of correcting intuitive predictions justified?
options: When the stakes are high and you are keen not to make mistakes
Whenever any prediction at all is being made
Only when the evidence is extremely strong
Only when no base rate can be found
questions.explain: “The effort is justified only when the stakes are high and when you are particularly keen not to make mistakes.” For everyday forecasts the work of System 2 is not worth it.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say require significant effort when correcting intuitive predictions?
options: Finding the relevant reference category
Estimating the baseline prediction
Evaluating the quality of the evidence
Constructing a coherent story from the evidence
Recognizing familiar cues from experience
questions.explain: These three tasks are the System 2 work of correction. Building a coherent story and recognizing familiar cues are things System 1 does automatically.

questions.q: Kahneman notes that unbiased predictions permit the prediction of rare or extreme events only when the ____ is very good.
questions.explain: If your predictions have modest validity, you will never guess an outcome that is rare or far from the mean. That is a built-in cost of being unbiased.

questions.q: What does Kahneman say you give up if your predictions are unbiased?
options: The ability to make any predictions about individuals
The use of base rates in your judgments
The satisfying experience of correctly calling an extreme case
Any chance of your predictions being accurate
questions.explain: You will never be able to say “I thought so!” when your best law student becomes a Supreme Court justice. Unbiased predictions are still useful and usually more accurate overall.

questions.q: When, according to Kahneman, is a preference for unbiased predictions justified, and when might extreme predictions have some justification?
questions.a: Unbiased predictions are best if all errors are treated alike regardless of their direction. When one kind of error is much worse, absence of bias is not what matters most: a venture capitalist fears missing the next Google more than a modest failed investment, and a conservative banker fears a single bankruptcy more than turning away good clients. In such cases extreme language may have some justification for the comfort it provides, even on evidence of modest validity.

questions.q: Sort these statements according to whether they describe Kahneman's venture capitalist or his conservative banker.

items.t: Missing the next Google or Facebook is the costlier error
Aims to call extreme cases correctly, even at the cost of overestimating many ventures
Might use the phrase 'very good prospect'
The risk of a single borrower going bankrupt looms largest
Accepts turning down several would-be clients who would have paid
Might use the phrase 'serious risk of default'

questions.explain: Each fears a different error. The venture capitalist dreads missing a huge winner, while the banker making large loans dreads a default, so each leans toward a different kind of extreme judgment.

questions.q: How does Kahneman's rational venture capitalist view her job?
options: As picking the most promising bets available, knowing even the best have only a moderate chance
As finding start-ups that are certain to succeed
As avoiding every start-up that is more likely to fail than succeed
As matching her forecasts to the founders' enthusiasm
questions.explain: She knows that “even the most promising start-ups have only a moderate chance of success” and does not need to delude herself. She still invests in the best bets available.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says a rational person will never invest a large sum in an enterprise that is most likely to fail.
questions.explain: He says the opposite: a rational person will invest a large sum in an enterprise most likely to fail if the rewards of success are large enough, without deluding herself about the chances.

questions.q: Kahneman says that if you choose to delude yourself by accepting extreme predictions, you will do well to remain aware of your ____.
questions.explain: He allows that some people may need distorted estimates to avoid paralysis, but asks them to know they are indulging themselves rather than predicting accurately.

questions.q: In Kahneman's choice between job candidates Kim and Jane, why should the prediction for Kim be regressed more deeply toward the mean?
options: Because her interviews were less impressive than Jane's
Because recommendations are always exaggerated
Because there is less information about her, and small samples contain more luck
Because she is younger and therefore less reliable
questions.explain: Kim has a brilliant talk and recommendations but no track record, so her sample of information is smaller. “There is more luck in the outcomes of small samples,” so her impression should be regressed more than Jane's.

questions.q: Match each element of Kahneman's Kim and Jane hiring example with its description.
pairs: Kim
Spectacular recommendations and a brilliant talk, but no track record
Jane
Three productive postdoc years and an excellent record, but less sparkling interviews
The intuitive choice
Kim, because she left the stronger impression
Kahneman's own vote
Jane, after allowing for Kim's greater regression
questions.explain: The intuitive choice favors the stronger impression, but more information about Jane means her record needs less regression. Kahneman says he would vote for Jane, though it would be a struggle.

questions.q: Kahneman says the Kim and Jane hiring choice brings us back to the law of ____, because there is a smaller sample of information about Kim.
questions.explain: Extreme outcomes are much more likely in small samples, as the law of small numbers taught. A dazzling impression from little information deserves more regression.

questions.q: What does Kahneman see as perhaps the most valuable contribution of his corrective procedures, and how does the Kim and Jane example illustrate it?
questions.a: The procedures “will require you to think about how much you know.” Intuition favors Kim because she left a stronger impression, and WYSIATI ignores that there is much less information about her than about Jane. Asking how much the evidence is worth reveals that Kim's small sample contains more luck, so her prediction should be regressed more, and Jane may be the better choice.

questions.q: Which of these statements match Kahneman's account of the Kim and Jane hiring choice?
options: There is much less information about Kim than about Jane
Extreme outcomes are more likely to be observed in small samples
Kahneman admits it would be a struggle to overcome his impression that Kim is more promising
Jane's talk and interviews were more impressive than Kim's
Kahneman says his intuition clearly favored Jane from the start
questions.explain: Kim made the stronger impression but with less information, so Kahneman would vote for Jane only with difficulty. It was Kim's talk, not Jane's, that sparkled.

questions.q: Put in order the steps of Kahneman's reasoning about whether to hire Kim or Jane.
items: Kim leaves the stronger impression, so intuition favors her
There is much less information about Kim than about Jane
Extreme outcomes and luck are more common in small samples
Kim's prediction should be regressed more deeply toward the mean
Jane may be the better choice despite the weaker impression
questions.explain: The argument moves from impression, to the amount of information, to the law of small numbers, to deeper regression for Kim, and finally to a possible choice of Jane.

questions.q: In Kahneman's example of a venture capitalist choosing between two start-ups in different markets, what question deserves careful consideration, and why?
questions.a: One start-up has a product whose demand can be estimated with fair precision; the other is more exciting and intuitively promising but less certain. The question is whether the best guess for the exciting start-up is still superior once its uncertainty is factored in. As with Kim and Jane, the less certain option should be regressed more toward the mean, so its intuitive appeal may overstate its prospects.

questions.q: In Kahneman's two-systems view of regression, System 1 generates overconfident judgments because confidence is determined by the ____ of the best story you can tell from the evidence at hand.
questions.explain: Confidence tracks how coherent the story is, not how good the evidence is. So System 1 produces predictions that are both too extreme and held with too much faith.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give as reasons regression to the mean is a problem for System 2?
options: The idea is alien and difficult to communicate and comprehend
Even Galton had a hard time before he understood it
Matching predictions to the evidence seems a reasonable thing to do
People learn regression readily from everyday experience
Once noticed, regression is usually given the correct statistical interpretation
questions.explain: “We will not learn to understand regression from experience,” and when it is noticed, as with the flight instructors, it is given a causal interpretation that is almost always wrong.

questions.q: Sort these, from Kahneman's discussion of prediction and regression, by which system they belong to.

items.t: Matching the extremeness of a prediction to the extremeness of the evidence
Generating confidence from the coherence of the best available story
Predicting rare events from weak evidence
Finding the relevant reference category and baseline
Evaluating the quality of the evidence
Needing special training to understand regression

questions.explain: Extreme, overconfident predictions are manifestations of System 1's associative machinery. Correction, and the understanding of regression itself, fall to System 2, which needs effort and training.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, why does System 1 produce predictions that are too extreme and held with too much faith?
questions.a: The associative machinery naturally matches the extremeness of a prediction to the perceived extremeness of the evidence, which is how substitution works. Confidence, meanwhile, is set by the coherence of the best story that can be told from the evidence at hand, not by its quality. So intuitions deliver predictions that are too extreme, and we are inclined to put far too much faith in them.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say regression to the mean is a problem for System 2 as well as System 1?
questions.a: The idea of regression is alien and difficult to communicate and comprehend: Galton struggled with it, and statistics teachers dread teaching it. Matching predictions to evidence feels not only intuitive but reasonable, and “We will not learn to understand regression from experience.” Even when regression is noticed, as with the flight instructors, it gets a causal interpretation that is almost always wrong, so System 2 needs special training.

questions.q: Match each figure or example with the point Kahneman makes about it in his two-systems view of regression.
pairs: Galton
Had a hard time before he understood regression
Statistics teachers
Dread the class in which regression comes up
The flight instructors
Gave an observed regression a wrong causal interpretation
System 1's associative machinery
Matches the extremeness of predictions to the evidence
questions.explain: Kahneman uses these to show that regression is hard for everyone: intuition ignores it, and even trained minds misunderstand or misexplain it.

questions.q: Match each remark from Kahneman's 'Speaking of Intuitive Predictions' with the idea it applies.
pairs: The start-up's outstanding proof of concept may not last
There is a lot of room for regression
Our favorable intuitive forecast is probably too high
Weigh the strength of evidence and regress toward the mean
The investment may be good even if it will probably fail
Do not pretend to believe it is the next Google
One excellent review could be a fluke
Prefer brands with many reviews, a larger sample
questions.explain: Each remark puts a chapter idea into everyday language: regression after extreme results, correcting a favorable intuition, investing without self-delusion, and distrusting small samples.

questions.q: Which of these remarks reflect the advice of Kahneman's chapter on taming intuitive predictions?
options: That start-up had an outstanding proof of concept, but we shouldn't expect them to do as well in the future
Our intuitive prediction is very favorable but probably too high, so let's regress it toward the mean
One review of this brand was excellent, so it must be the best brand available
The investment looks promising, so let's tell everyone it is the next Google
questions.explain: Kahneman's remarks call for expecting regression and moderating favorable intuitions. Trusting a single review ignores the small-sample problem, and he explicitly advises against claiming an investment is the next Google.

questions.q: Explain, in terms of Kahneman's chapter on taming intuitive predictions, the remark: 'I read one review of that brand and it was excellent. Still, that could have been a fluke.'
questions.a: A single review is a tiny sample, and extreme results are much more likely in small samples, as in the case of Kim. An excellent single review should therefore be regressed strongly toward the mean. The sensible choice is to consider only brands with a large number of reviews and pick the one that looks best, because its rating reflects much less luck.

questions.q: Put the sections of Kahneman's chapter 'Taming Intuitive Predictions' in the order they appear.
items: Nonregressive Intuitions
A Correction for Intuitive Predictions
A Defense of Extreme Predictions?
A Two-systems View of Regression
Speaking of Intuitive Predictions
questions.explain: The chapter first shows that intuitive predictions are nonregressive, then offers a correction, weighs objections to it, explains the problem in two-systems terms, and closes with everyday remarks.

questions.q: Put these chapters of 'Thinking, Fast and Slow' in book order.
items: Linda: Less Is More
Causes Trump Statistics
Regression to the Mean
Taming Intuitive Predictions
The Illusion of Understanding
questions.explain: Chapters 15 to 18 close Part II, with Taming Intuitive Predictions last; The Illusion of Understanding, chapter 19, opens Part III on overconfidence.

questions.q: Match each chapter of 'Thinking, Fast and Slow' with how the chapter 'Taming Intuitive Predictions' connects to it.
pairs: Regression to the Mean (ch. 17)
Introduced the shared-factor formula and the golf example used for correction
Tom W's Specialty (ch. 14)
Supplied the base-rate procedure that parallels the numerical correction
The Law of Small Numbers (ch. 10)
Explains why Kim's thin record deserves more regression
The Illusion of Understanding (ch. 19)
Comes next, opening Part III on overconfidence
questions.explain: Kahneman explicitly says the correct way to predict Julie's GPA was introduced in the preceding chapter, recalls Tom W for discrete predictions, and returns to the law of small numbers for Kim and Jane.

questions.q: 'Taming Intuitive Predictions' is the last chapter of Part II of 'Thinking, Fast and Slow', titled ____ and Biases.
questions.explain: Part II, Heuristics and Biases, runs from The Law of Small Numbers to Taming Intuitive Predictions. Part III, Overconfidence, follows.

questions.q: What does the word 'taming' in the chapter title 'Taming Intuitive Predictions' signal about Kahneman's approach?
options: Intuitive predictions should be thrown out and replaced by the average
Intuitive predictions are kept but moderated by regressing them toward the mean
Intuitive predictions are reliable once people feel confident in them
Intuitive predictions can be trained by experience to become regressive
questions.explain: The correction “builds on your intuition, but it moderates it, regresses it toward the mean.” It does not discard intuition, and Kahneman denies that experience teaches regression.

questions.q: Which of these earlier ideas from 'Thinking, Fast and Slow' does the chapter 'Taming Intuitive Predictions' explicitly draw on?
options: Regression to the mean, as in golf scores on successive days
Base rates in the Tom W problem
The law of small numbers
Loss aversion in choices between gambles
The endowment effect
questions.explain: The chapter reuses the golf example and formula from the regression chapter, the Tom W base-rate procedure, and the law of small numbers for Kim. Loss aversion and the endowment effect belong to the later part on choices.

questions.q: Why is 'Taming Intuitive Predictions' a fitting chapter to close Part II on heuristics and biases and lead into Part III on overconfidence?
questions.a: It gathers earlier ideas, substitution, intensity matching, WYSIATI, base rates, the law of small numbers and regression, to show how they combine to make intuitive predictions nonregressive and too extreme, and offers a practical correction. It also stresses that intuitive predictions are overconfident because confidence comes from the coherence of a story, which sets up Part III's theme. The next chapter, The Illusion of Understanding, opens that part on overconfidence.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman's chapter on the illusion of understanding open Part 3, titled "Overconfidence"?
options: Because believing we understand the past leads us to think the future is knowable
Because it summarizes the heuristics catalogued throughout Part 2
Because it introduces the two systems that the rest of the book relies on
Because it begins the book's treatment of how people value gains and losses
questions.explain: The chapter argues that the sense of having understood the past feeds the further illusion that we can predict and control the future, which is the overconfidence Part 3 explores. The two systems were introduced in Part 1, and gains and losses belong to Part 4, "Choices".

questions.q: In Kahneman's chapter on the illusion of understanding, what does Nassim Taleb's term "narrative fallacy" describe?
options: Our habit of trusting statistics over vivid personal stories
How flawed stories of the past shape our views of the world and expectations for the future
The tendency of storytellers to exaggerate events in order to entertain listeners
The way experts deliberately invent explanations to protect their reputations
questions.explain: Taleb, in The Black Swan, used the term for how flawed accounts of the past shape both our view of the world and what we expect next. It is not about deliberate deception; Kahneman says such fallacies arise inevitably from our continuous attempt to make sense of the world.

questions.q: In The Black Swan, Nassim Taleb introduced the notion of a ____ to describe how flawed stories of the past shape our views of the world and our expectations for the future.
questions.explain: Kahneman borrows Taleb's term narrative fallacy and notes that such fallacies arise inevitably from our continuous attempt to make sense of the world.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman, following Taleb, list as features of the explanatory stories people find compelling?
options: They are simple
They are concrete rather than abstract
They give a larger role to talent, stupidity and intentions than to luck
They give luck its proper weight alongside skill
They dwell on the many events that failed to happen
questions.explain: Compelling stories are simple, concrete, and credit talent, stupidity and intentions over luck. They focus on a few striking events that happened, not on the countless events that did not, and they downplay luck rather than weighting it properly.

questions.q: In Kahneman's account of the narrative fallacy, sort each item by whether compelling stories emphasize it or neglect it.

items.t: A few striking events that happened
Talent and intentions of the actors
Concrete details
The role of luck
Countless events that failed to happen
The many ways the outcome could have differed

questions.explain: Good stories are concrete and credit talent and intentions for a few striking events. They leave out luck and nonevents, and Kahneman notes that the human mind does not deal well with nonevents.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says the halo effect helps keep explanatory narratives simple and coherent by exaggerating the consistency of our evaluations of people.
questions.explain: The halo effect makes us match all of a person's qualities to one significant attribute, so that good people seem to do only good things and bad people seem all bad. This exaggerated consistency makes stories tidy.

questions.q: Kahneman writes that if we think a baseball pitcher is handsome and athletic, we are likely to rate him better at throwing the ball too, an example of the ____.
questions.explain: The halo effect inclines us to match our view of all of a person's qualities to our judgment of one particularly significant attribute. It can also be negative, leading us to underrate a player we find ugly.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, why is the statement that Hitler loved dogs and little children shocking no matter how often you hear it?
options: Because it is historically doubtful and contradicts the known record
Because it is told so rarely that it never becomes familiar
Because any trace of kindness in someone so evil violates the expectations set up by the halo effect
Because System 2 refuses to process information about historical figures
questions.explain: The halo effect makes us expect bad people to be bad in every respect, so a kind trait breaks the coherence of the story. Kahneman adds that inconsistencies reduce the ease of our thoughts and the clarity of our feelings.

questions.q: Put the events of Kahneman's brief Google story in the order he tells them.
items: Two Stanford graduate students devise a superior way of searching the Internet
They seek and obtain funding to start a company
A year after founding, they offer to sell for less than $1 million and the buyer declines
The company becomes one of the most valuable stocks in America
questions.explain: Kahneman tells the tale blandly in this order to show how a compelling narrative fosters an illusion of inevitability, with one lucky incident, the failed sale, making it even more compelling.

questions.q: True or false: In Kahneman's Google story, the founders were willing to sell the company for less than $1 million a year after founding it, but the buyer refused because the price was too low.
questions.explain: The buyer said the price was too high, not too low. Kahneman uses this lucky escape to show how mentioning one lucky incident makes it easier to underestimate the many other ways luck shaped the outcome.

questions.q: In Kahneman's Google story, what is the effect of mentioning the single lucky incident in which a buyer turned down the chance to buy the company?
options: It makes readers appropriately cautious about drawing lessons from the story
It shows that the founders' success owed nothing to skill
It reminds readers that luck matters, so they estimate its role accurately
It makes it easier to underestimate the multitude of ways luck affected the outcome
questions.explain: Naming one lucky moment makes the story more compelling while implying that luck played only that one part. Kahneman says it actually makes it easier to underestimate the many other ways luck mattered.

questions.q: Kahneman writes that the ultimate test of an explanation is whether it would have made the event ____ in advance.
questions.explain: No story of Google's success meets this test, because no story can include the myriad of events that would have caused a different outcome.

questions.q: In Kahneman's comparison of a skilled rafter with Google's founders, sort each description by whom it fits.

items.t: Has gone down rapids hundreds of times
Has learned to read the water and anticipate obstacles
Has learned tiny adjustments of posture that keep him upright
Had few opportunities to learn how to create a giant company
Faced hidden rocks such as a brilliant innovation by a competing firm

questions.explain: Both stories are thrilling because of constant risk, but the rafter's skill is built on many repetitions, while there are few chances to learn how to build a giant company. Kahneman concludes that luck played a bigger role in the Google story than in its telling.

questions.q: A friend has won a large prize in a contest where she guessed a number that was drawn at random, and she wants to write a guide on how to win such contests. By Kahneman's reasoning in his chapter on the illusion of understanding, how much is there to learn from her success?
options: Very little, because the more luck was involved, the less there is to be learned
A great deal, because any winning strategy reveals a general lesson
A great deal, as long as her story is told in enough detail
Very little, but only because she has not yet won a second time
questions.explain: Kahneman says “the more luck was involved, the less there is to be learned.” A detailed story would only add a false sense of understanding, which is the illusion the chapter warns about.

questions.q: Kahneman explains that you build the best possible story from the information available to you and believe it if it is a good story, an instance of the powerful ____ rule.
accept: what you see is all there is
questions.explain: WYSIATI means dealing with the limited information you have as if it were all there is to know. This is why a coherent story feels true even when much is missing.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman argues that it is easier to construct a coherent story when you know little, because there are fewer pieces to fit into the puzzle.
questions.explain: Kahneman calls this paradoxical: having fewer facts makes coherence easier. He concludes that our conviction that the world makes sense rests on our almost unlimited ability to ignore our ignorance.

questions.q: What does Kahneman mean when he says our comforting conviction that the world makes sense rests on "our almost unlimited ability to ignore our ignorance"?
questions.a: Because of WYSIATI, we treat the limited information we have as if it were all there is to know and build the best story we can from it. Since a coherent story is easier to construct when we know little, our ignorance does not shake our confidence; we simply leave out what we do not know. The feeling that the world makes sense therefore comes from ignoring gaps, not from real understanding.

questions.q: In Kahneman's discussion of people who say they knew the 2008 financial crisis was inevitable, which word does he say should be removed from our vocabulary when discussing major events?
options: Inevitable
Crisis
Knew
Before
questions.explain: Kahneman objects to the word knew. Some people thought a crisis would come, but they could not know it, because something can be known only if it is both true and knowable.

questions.q: In Kahneman's discussion of the 2008 financial crisis, what leads him to infer that the crisis was not knowable in advance?
options: Official economic forecasts at the time contained no warnings
Many intelligent and well-informed people keenly interested in the economy did not believe a catastrophe was imminent
The few people who predicted it could not agree on its timing
The crisis was triggered by a single unforeseeable event
questions.explain: Kahneman reasons that if so many informed people did not expect a catastrophe, the crisis could not be conclusively shown in advance, so it was not knowable. Those who thought it would happen could not show it at the time.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman object to people saying they "knew" the 2008 financial crisis was inevitable, and what is the real harm in that language?
questions.a: We should use know only when what was known is true and can be shown to be true; those who thought a crisis was coming could not conclusively show it at the time, so they did not know it. The harm is not mainly that some people get undeserved credit for prescience. The language implies that the world is more knowable than it is, which helps perpetuate a pernicious illusion.

questions.q: Which of these words does Kahneman say are, in common usage, reserved for past thoughts that turned out to be true?
options: Know
Intuition
Premonition
Guess
Hope
questions.explain: Kahneman notes that know, intuition and premonition are applied only to beliefs that proved true, which is why "I had a premonition that the marriage would not last, but I was wrong" sounds odd. Guesses and hopes are routinely described as wrong.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what is the core of the illusion of understanding, and what does he say we must do to think clearly about the future?
questions.a: The core of the illusion is that we believe we understand the past, which implies that the future should also be knowable, when in fact we understand the past less than we think. Words like know, intuition and premonition reinforce it because they are reserved for past thoughts that turned out to be true. To think clearly about the future, we need to clean up the language we use to label the beliefs we had in the past.

questions.q: After an election, a colleague claims he knew all along that she would win. Before the vote he had said she was the likelier winner, while many well-informed observers expected her to lose. How would Kahneman, in his chapter on the illusion of understanding, prefer the colleague describe his earlier belief?
options: As knowledge, since his prediction turned out to be true
As an intuition, since intuitions can be trusted after the fact
As luck, since he had no reasons at all for his view
As something he thought, since it could not have been shown to be true at the time
questions.explain: Kahneman says we can know something only if it is both true and knowable; a belief that could not be conclusively shown at the time was a thought, not knowledge. Calling it an intuition would not help, since that word is also reserved for past thoughts that turned out true.

questions.q: A reader finishes a detailed biography of a famous company founder and feels she now understands what makes businesses succeed. Using Kahneman's chapter on the illusion of understanding, explain why her feeling is likely illusory.
questions.a: The ultimate test of an explanation is whether it would have made the outcome predictable in advance, and no success story can meet it because no story can include the countless events that would have caused a different result. Because the founder's key decisions turned out well, the story exaggerates skill and underestimates luck, and the halo effect lends the hero an aura of invincibility. The more luck was involved, the less there is to be learned.

questions.q: Kahneman describes the mind that makes up narratives about the past as a ____ organ.
questions.explain: When an unpredicted event occurs, this sense-making organ immediately adjusts our view of the world to accommodate the surprise.

questions.q: In Kahneman's example of a football game between two teams with the same record, what happens after one team trashes the other?
options: We conclude that the result was a fluke and keep our earlier view
We remember that we always expected the winner to dominate, but our view of the future is unchanged
We become more uncertain about which team is stronger
Our revised model of the world sees the winner as much stronger, altering our view of past and future
questions.explain: The sense-making mind immediately adjusts to the surprise, so the winning team now seems much stronger and both the past and the future look different. Kahneman says learning from surprises is reasonable but can have dangerous consequences.

questions.q: Put the steps of the attitude-change studies Kahneman describes in order.
items: The experimenter measures attitudes on a topic such as the death penalty
Participants see or hear a persuasive pro or con message
The experimenter measures attitudes again
Participants report the opinion they held beforehand
questions.explain: The last step turns out to be surprisingly difficult: asked for their former beliefs, people retrieve their current ones, and many cannot believe they ever felt differently.

questions.q: Kahneman says that when people asked to reconstruct their former beliefs retrieve their current ones instead, this is an instance of ____.
questions.explain: Reporting a current belief in place of a past one is substitution: an easier question is answered in place of the one asked, and many people cannot believe they ever felt differently.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, how does our imperfect ability to reconstruct past beliefs lead to hindsight bias?
questions.a: Once we adopt a new view of the world, we immediately lose much of our ability to recall what we believed before our mind changed. Because we cannot reconstruct our earlier state of knowledge, we inevitably underestimate how surprised we were by past events. The result is the "I-knew-it-all-along" effect, in which we revise the history of our beliefs in light of what actually happened.

questions.q: Kahneman calls the "I-knew-it-all-along" effect, first demonstrated by Baruch Fischhoff, ____.
questions.explain: Fischhoff showed the effect as a student in Jerusalem, and Kahneman explains that it follows from our inability to reconstruct past beliefs.

questions.q: Match each person in Kahneman's chapter on the illusion of understanding to the idea or claim associated with them.
pairs: Nassim Taleb
Introduced the notion of a narrative fallacy
Baruch Fischhoff
First demonstrated the I-knew-it-all-along effect
Ben Bradlee
Said the CIA director should have gone straight to the president
Philip Rosenzweig
Showed business writing exaggerates the impact of leadership
Jim Collins and Jerry I. Porras
Compared eighteen pairs of competing companies
questions.explain: Taleb supplies the chapter's opening concept, Fischhoff the classic hindsight study, Bradlee a vivid case of hindsight about 9/11, and Rosenzweig the critique of books such as Collins and Porras's Built to Last.

questions.q: Put the steps of Fischhoff and Beyth's study of Nixon's 1972 trips in order, as Kahneman describes them.
items: Respondents assign probabilities to fifteen possible outcomes of Nixon's diplomacy
Nixon visits China and Russia
The same people are asked to recall the probabilities they originally assigned
Recalled probabilities turn out inflated for events that occurred
questions.explain: The survey was done before the trips and the recall afterwards. People exaggerated the probabilities they had assigned to events that happened and recalled having thought unrealized events unlikely.

questions.q: True or false: In Fischhoff and Beyth's Nixon study, people recalled having assigned lower probabilities than they really had to events that actually occurred.
questions.explain: The direction is the reverse: if an event had occurred, people exaggerated the probability they had assigned to it. They recalled events that did not happen as ones they had always considered unlikely.

questions.q: Which of these findings about hindsight bias does Kahneman report from Fischhoff and Beyth's work and later experiments?
options: People exaggerated the probability they had assigned to events that occurred
People recalled unrealized events as ones they had always considered unlikely
People overstated the accuracy of predictions made by others as well as their own
People recalled their original probabilities accurately once told the outcome
The bias appeared only for events of little public interest
questions.explain: All three distortions point the same way, toward believing the outcome was foreseen. Kahneman notes similar results for events that gripped public attention, such as the O. J. Simpson trial and the Clinton impeachment, so the bias is not limited to minor events.

questions.q: Kahneman says that judging a decision by whether its result was good or bad, rather than by whether the process was sound, is ____.
questions.explain: Outcome bias makes it almost impossible to evaluate a decision properly, in terms of the beliefs that were reasonable when the decision was made.

questions.q: In Kahneman's example of a low-risk surgery in which an unpredictable accident killed the patient, what is a jury likely to believe afterwards?
options: That the operation was actually risky and the doctor should have known better
That the accident was unpredictable and the doctor acted reasonably
That the hospital rather than the doctor was responsible
That the patient knowingly accepted the risk
questions.explain: Hindsight leads observers to judge the decision by its outcome rather than by the process, so a reasonable choice looks negligent after a bad result. This is the outcome bias.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say hindsight does to decision makers who act as agents for others, such as physicians, financial advisers and CEOs?
options: We blame them for good decisions that worked out badly
We give them too little credit for successful moves that seem obvious only afterwards
We judge them by the beliefs that were reasonable at the time
We make their prudent actions look even more prudent afterwards
questions.explain: Kahneman says actions that seemed prudent in foresight can look irresponsibly negligent in hindsight, which is the opposite of looking more prudent. Judging by the beliefs reasonable at the time is what hindsight prevents.

questions.q: A financial adviser recommended a well-diversified fund that later fell sharply in a sudden market crash nobody predicted. Her client says she should have seen it coming. Which of Kahneman's images captures the client's error?
options: The adviser was a rafter who had not run enough rapids
The handwriting on the wall was written in invisible ink that became legible only afterward
The adviser was a lucky gambler crowned with a halo of prescience
The client is ignoring base rates in favour of a vivid story
questions.explain: Kahneman says clients blame agents for not seeing the handwriting on the wall, forgetting that it was written in invisible ink that became legible only afterward. The lucky-gambler image applies to reckless risk takers who won, not to a sound decision that turned out badly.

questions.q: True or false: In the Duluth study Kahneman describes, 24% of people given only the evidence available at the time thought the city should hire a flood monitor, compared with 56% of those told that debris had caused a flood.
questions.explain: The second group judged more harshly even though they were explicitly instructed not to let hindsight distort their judgment, showing how strong the bias is.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that the milder the consequences of an event, the greater the hindsight bias.
questions.explain: Kahneman says the reverse: the worse the consequence, the greater the hindsight bias. In a catastrophe such as 9/11 we are especially ready to believe officials were negligent or blind.

questions.q: Explain why Kahneman treats Ben Bradlee's comment about the July 10, 2001 CIA report on al-Qaeda as an example of hindsight bias.
questions.a: George Tenet took the intelligence to National Security Adviser Condoleezza Rice rather than to President Bush, and Bradlee later said it was elementary that a story that would dominate history should go straight to the president. But on July 10, no one knew, or could have known, that this tidbit would dominate history. Bradlee judged the decision using knowledge of the outcome, and because the consequence was catastrophic the hindsight bias was especially strong.

questions.q: In Kahneman's account of the social costs of hindsight, sort each effect by whom it mainly concerns.
groups: Decision makers who expect hindsight scrutiny
Reckless risk takers whose gambles paid off

items.t: Are driven to bureaucratic solutions
Become extremely reluctant to take risks
Order more tests and refer more cases to specialists
Are never punished for having taken too much risk
Are credited with flair and foresight
Are crowned with a halo of prescience and boldness

questions.explain: Hindsight and outcome bias generally foster risk aversion, as with physicians facing malpractice suits. But they also bring undeserved rewards to lucky gamblers, while the sensible people who doubted them look timid.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman call increased accountability "a mixed blessing"?
questions.a: Because adherence to standard operating procedures is hard to second-guess, decision makers who expect hindsight scrutiny turn to bureaucratic solutions and become extremely reluctant to take risks. As malpractice litigation grew, physicians ordered more tests, referred more cases to specialists and applied conventional treatments even when they were unlikely to help. These actions protected the physicians more than they benefited the patients, creating potential conflicts of interest.

questions.q: In Kahneman's discussion of recipes for success, what further illusion does the illusion of having understood the past feed?
options: The illusion that luck averages out over time
The illusion that experts are always overconfident
The illusion that one can predict and control the future
The illusion that other people's judgments are biased but one's own are not
questions.explain: The sense-making machinery of System 1 makes the world seem tidy and predictable, and believing we understand the past feeds the belief that we can predict and control the future. Kahneman says these illusions are comforting because they reduce anxiety about uncertainty.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, why are the illusions of understanding comforting, and how do many business books exploit this?
questions.a: The illusions reduce the anxiety we would feel if we fully acknowledged the uncertainties of existence. We all need the reassuring message that actions have appropriate consequences and that success will reward wisdom and courage. Many business books are tailor-made to satisfy this need by offering clear stories about the determinants of success and failure, however illusory.

questions.q: Kahneman says a very generous estimate of the correlation between the success of a firm and the quality of its CEO might be as high as ____.
questions.explain: Kahneman says this indicates 30% overlap, and it means the stronger CEO leads the more successful firm in only about 60% of comparable pairs.

questions.q: In Kahneman's thought experiment comparing pairs of similar firms, how often would a correlation of .30 between CEO quality and firm success find the stronger CEO leading the more successful firm?
options: About 30% of the pairs
About 50% of the pairs
About 60% of the pairs
About 90% of the pairs
questions.explain: A correlation of .30 implies the stronger CEO leads the stronger firm in about 60% of pairs, a mere 10 percentage points above the 50% expected if luck alone decided. It does not mean 30% of pairs.

questions.q: Match each condition in Kahneman's paired-firms thought experiment to its outcome.
pairs: Perfect correlation of 1 between CEO quality and success
Stronger CEO leads the more successful firm in 100% of pairs
Success determined entirely by factors the CEO does not control
More successful firm led by the weaker CEO 50% of the time
Correlation of .30
Stronger CEO leads the stronger firm in about 60% of pairs
Odds of success implied by a correlation of .30
Improved from 1:1 to 3:2
questions.explain: Kahneman uses these benchmarks to show that a generous .30 correlation yields only a modest edge over chance, though he stresses that moving from 1:1 to 3:2 is still a significant advantage.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that improving the odds of success from 1:1 to 3:2 is a trivial advantage in business.
questions.explain: Kahneman says it is a very significant advantage, both at the racetrack and in business. His point is that most business writers would not find such a modest edge impressive enough to celebrate.

questions.q: In Kahneman's discussion of CEOs, what should you conclude if you expected the stronger CEO to lead the more successful firm far more often than about 60% of the time, and why do business books rarely report this figure?
questions.a: If you expected a higher value, as most of us do, you should take it as a sign that you are prone to overestimate the predictability of the world you live in. Business books avoid such figures because readers would not line up to buy a book about leaders who, on average, do somewhat better than chance. Consumers hunger for a clear message about the determinants of success and failure, and need stories that offer a sense of understanding, however illusory.

questions.q: Which of these are the two popular genres of business writing that Philip Rosenzweig, in The Halo Effect, says meet the demand for illusory certainty?
options: Histories of the rise and fall of particular individuals and companies
Analyses of differences between successful and less successful firms
Statistical studies of the role of luck in markets
Memoirs written by failed entrepreneurs
Textbooks on accounting and finance
questions.explain: Rosenzweig concludes that both genres consistently exaggerate the impact of leadership style and management practices on firm outcomes, so their message is rarely useful.

questions.q: In Kahneman's halo-effect example about how experts describe the same chief executive, sort each description by when it is likely to be applied.

items.t: Flexible
Methodical
Decisive
Confused
Rigid
Authoritarian

questions.explain: The same executive and the same behaviors are described in opposite terms depending on how the firm is doing, and both descriptions sound right at the time. The halo from the firm's results drives the evaluation.

questions.q: Put the steps of Kahneman's halo-effect scenario about a chief executive's reputation in order.
items: The company is thriving
Experts describe the CEO as flexible, methodical and decisive
A year passes and things go sour
The same CEO is described as confused, rigid and authoritarian
questions.explain: Kahneman uses this sequence to show that the CEO's reputation follows the firm's results, so we get the causal relationship backward.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, how does the halo effect lead us to get the causal relationship between a CEO and a failing firm backward?
options: We believe the CEO is rigid because of his past training, when he is actually flexible
We believe the firm fails because the CEO is rigid, when the CEO appears rigid because the firm is failing
We believe the firm fails because of bad luck, when the CEO's rigidity is really to blame
We believe the board chose a rigid CEO, when the CEO chose a rigid board
questions.explain: Kahneman says we are prone to believe the firm fails because its CEO is rigid, when the truth is that the CEO appears rigid because the firm is failing. Blaming bad luck is the opposite of the error he describes.

questions.q: Explain how, according to Kahneman, the halo effect gives birth to illusions of understanding in judgments about business leaders.
questions.a: Experts judging a chief executive know whether the company has recently been thriving or failing, and that knowledge generates a halo. The same person and behaviors are called flexible and methodical when things go well and rigid and confused when they go badly, and both labels sound right at the time. We then reverse cause and effect, believing the firm fails because the CEO is rigid when the CEO only appears rigid because the firm is failing.

questions.q: Which of these are the basic messages of Built to Last and similar books that Kahneman says are overstated?
options: Good managerial practices can be identified
Good practices will be rewarded by good results
Luck largely determines which firms succeed
Regular patterns among successful firms are probably mirages
CEOs have only a modest effect on firm performance
questions.explain: Kahneman says both of these messages are overstated, because comparing more and less successful firms is to a significant extent comparing more and less lucky firms. The other statements reflect his own view, not the books' messages.

questions.q: Match each study Kahneman cites in his chapter on the illusion of understanding to its finding.
pairs: Fischhoff and Beyth's Nixon survey
People exaggerated the probability they had assigned to events that occurred
The Duluth flood-monitor study
24% favored hiring a monitor without hindsight, 56% with it
Attitude-change studies on topics such as the death penalty
People reported their current opinion as their former one
Follow-up on the firms in Built to Last
The gap in profitability and stock returns shrank to almost nothing
Study of Fortune's "Most Admired Companies"
Worst-rated firms later earned much higher stock returns
questions.explain: Each study shows a facet of the illusion of understanding: distorted memories of past beliefs, judgments warped by outcomes, and business patterns that fade because they were largely luck.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, why did the gap between the outstanding and less successful firms studied in Built to Last shrink to almost nothing after the study?
options: The successful firms became complacent while the others tried harder
The less successful firms copied the practices described in the book
Market conditions changed in ways that favored weaker firms
The original gap was due in good part to luck, so it regressed to the mean
questions.explain: Kahneman warns that causal stories such as complacency are the wrong way to think about it. Luck contributed to both the success of the top firms and the lag of the rest, so the average gap had to shrink.

questions.q: Kahneman says the shrinking gap between successful and less successful firms reflects a statistical fact of life already encountered in the book: ____.
questions.explain: Because the original gap was due in good part to luck, the average gap must shrink; no causal story about complacency or effort is needed.

questions.q: In Kahneman's discussion of why the performance gap between top firms and others shrinks, sort each explanation by whether it is the tempting causal story or Kahneman's account.

items.t: The successful firms became complacent
The less successful firms tried harder
The original gap was due in good part to luck
Regression to the mean

questions.explain: Kahneman says looking for causes here is the wrong way to think: luck contributed to both the top firms' success and the others' lag, so the gap must shrink.

questions.q: A sports magazine features the league's top-scoring team, praising its training regime. The next season, the team's results are merely average. Applying Kahneman's reasoning about business success stories, what is the best explanation?
options: The players became complacent after the magazine's praise
The original lead was partly luck, so regression to the mean was to be expected
Rival teams copied the training regime and caught up
The magazine's coverage distracted the coaches
questions.explain: Kahneman says that when an original gap is due in good part to luck, it must shrink, and inventing causes such as complacency is the wrong way to think about it.

questions.q: Put the steps of Kahneman's argument in his section on recipes for success in the order he presents them.
items: System 1's sense-making makes the world seem tidy and predictable
Research shows CEOs influence firm performance, but far less than the press suggests
Rosenzweig shows business writing exaggerates the impact of leadership
The advantage of the firms in Built to Last fades after the study
questions.explain: Kahneman moves from the psychological source of the illusion, to the modest real effect of CEOs, to the halo-driven business literature, and finally to the regression that undermines its lessons.

questions.q: Match each term from Kahneman's chapter on the illusion of understanding to its meaning.
pairs: Narrative fallacy
Flawed stories of the past that shape our views and expectations
Hindsight bias
The "I-knew-it-all-along" effect
Outcome bias
Judging a decision by its result rather than by its process
WYSIATI
Treating the limited information you have as all there is to know
Halo effect
Matching all of a person's qualities to one significant attribute
questions.explain: These are the chapter's key tools, and the closing "Speaking of Hindsight" remarks use several of them, such as narrative fallacy, outcome bias and halo effect.

questions.q: In Kahneman's closing remarks on hindsight, someone says, "She has no evidence for saying that the firm is badly managed. All she knows is that its stock has gone down." How does the speaker label the error?
options: As an outcome bias, part hindsight and part halo effect
As regression to the mean, part luck and part skill
As a narrative fallacy based on too little information
As substitution of a current belief for a past one
questions.explain: The remark calls inferring bad management from a falling stock an outcome bias, part hindsight and part halo effect, matching the chapter's account of how firm results color judgments of leaders.

questions.q: Put the parts of Kahneman's chapter on the illusion of understanding in the order they appear.
items: The narrative fallacy and the misuse of the word know
The Social Costs of Hindsight
Recipes for Success
Speaking of Hindsight
questions.explain: The chapter moves from how we build stories about the past, to the costs of hindsight for judging decision makers, to the business books that sell illusory lessons, and closes with sample remarks.

questions.q: Match each chapter number to its title from the table of contents of Thinking, Fast and Slow.
pairs: Chapter 17
Regression to the Mean
Chapter 18
Taming Intuitive Predictions
Chapter 19
The Illusion of Understanding
Chapter 20
The Illusion of Validity
questions.explain: Chapters 17 and 18 close Part 2 on heuristics and biases; Chapter 19 opens Part 3, "Overconfidence", and Chapter 20 continues it with a second illusion.

questions.q: Which of these ideas from earlier in the book does Kahneman draw on in his chapter on the illusion of understanding?
options: The halo effect
WYSIATI
Regression to the mean
Prospect theory
The endowment effect
questions.explain: The chapter explicitly reuses the halo effect, WYSIATI and regression to the mean. Prospect theory and the endowment effect belong to Part 4, "Choices", which comes later.

questions.q: How does Kahneman's chapter on the illusion of understanding build on the earlier chapter on regression to the mean?
questions.a: The chapter uses regression to the mean to explain why the advantage of the firms celebrated in Built to Last and In Search of Excellence shrank after the studies. Because the original gap was due in good part to luck, it had to shrink, so causal stories such as complacency are the wrong way to think about it. The chapter also recalls that the correlation coefficient was defined earlier, in relation to regression to the mean, by the extent to which two measures share common factors.

questions.q: What does the title "The Illusion of Understanding" signal about the argument of the chapter it heads?
questions.a: It signals that our sense of understanding the past is largely false: we build coherent stories that exaggerate skill and ignore luck and nonevents, and hindsight makes past events seem as if they were predictable. The title prepares the larger point of Part 3, that believing we understand the past implies the future should be knowable, when in fact we understand the past less than we believe. It also sets up the next chapter's parallel title, "The Illusion of Validity".

questions.q: In the opening of the chapter on the illusion of validity, sort each factor by whether it drives the subjective confidence System 1 produces or counts for little.

items.t: The coherence of the story constructed
The evidence at hand (WYSIATI)
The ease of processing the information
The amount of evidence
The quality of the evidence

questions.explain: Because of WYSIATI and confidence by coherence, only the evidence at hand and the coherence of the story count. The amount and quality of evidence count for little, because “poor evidence can make a very good story.”

questions.q: In the opening of the chapter on the illusion of validity, Kahneman writes that because of confidence by ____, the subjective confidence we have in our opinions reflects the coherence of the story System 1 and System 2 have constructed.
questions.explain: Confidence by coherence means our confidence tracks how well the story hangs together, not how much good evidence supports it.

questions.q: Put the steps of the opening argument of the chapter on the illusion of validity in Kahneman's order.
items: System 1 jumps to conclusions from little evidence
Because of WYSIATI, only the evidence at hand counts
Confidence reflects the coherence of the story constructed
Poor evidence can still make a very good story
Our confidence is preposterous, yet also essential
questions.explain: The opening moves from System 1's quick conclusions, through WYSIATI and confidence by coherence, to the point that weak evidence can yield a good story, and ends by calling our confidence both preposterous and essential.

questions.q: In the opening of the chapter on the illusion of validity, what does Kahneman mean when he says System 1 is not designed to know the size of its jumps, and why is our confidence both preposterous and essential?
questions.a: System 1 jumps to conclusions from little evidence but has no built-in sense of how far it has leapt beyond the evidence. Because of WYSIATI, only the evidence at hand counts, and confidence reflects how coherent the resulting story is, not how much or how good the evidence is. Considering how little we know, such confidence is preposterous, yet we could not function without it, so it is also essential.

questions.q: In the Israeli Army's leaderless group challenge, what did the eight candidates have to do?
options: Get a long log and every man over a six-foot wall without touching it
Build a bridge across a ditch using only ropes and planks
Carry a wounded comrade across an obstacle field in record time
Agree on a leader and then march the group through a forest
questions.explain: The candidates had to haul a long log to a wall about six feet high and get the whole group over without the log touching the ground or the wall and without anyone touching the wall.

questions.q: Match each detail of Kahneman's army officer-selection story to its description.
pairs: The candidates
Eight strangers with insignia removed and only numbered tags
The wall
About six feet high, to be crossed without anyone touching it
The feedback sessions
Every few months, compared assessments with commanders' opinions
The test methods
Developed by the British Army in World War II
questions.explain: These are the facts of the story: eight anonymous candidates, a six-foot wall, periodic feedback from the officer-training school, and methods borrowed from the British Army.

questions.q: Put the stages of a common solution to the leaderless group challenge in order.
items: The group lifts the long log from the ground
Several men crawl over the pole held at an angle like a fishing rod
The last man jumps up at the pole held by the others
He shinnies along the pole and leaps to the other side
questions.explain: Kahneman describes the team holding the pole at an angle so that men can cross; the hardest moment is the last man, who must jump at the pole and shinny along it, where failure was common.

questions.q: In Kahneman's army story, the officer-selection test conducted on an obstacle field was called the “____ challenge.”
questions.explain: The “leaderless group challenge” put eight strangers without rank insignia in front of a wall to see who emerged as a leader.

questions.q: Which of these describe how Kahneman and his colleague experienced their predictions about soldiers in the leaderless group challenge?
options: A single score usually came to mind
They rarely experienced doubts
They felt no need to moderate their forecasts
They often formed conflicting impressions of a candidate
They hedged each forecast with wide ranges
questions.explain: Because their impressions were coherent and clear, “A single score usually came to mind and we rarely experienced doubts or formed conflicting impressions.” They felt no need to moderate or equivocate.

questions.q: True or false: In Kahneman's army feedback sessions, the evaluators learned that their forecasts of success at officer school were no better at all than blind guesses.
questions.explain: Their ability to predict was negligible, but the forecasts were “better than blind guesses, but not by much.”

questions.q: True or false: After learning that their predictions were nearly useless, the army evaluators found it had very little effect on the confidence they felt in their judgments about individual candidates.
questions.explain: The dismal truth had no effect on how they evaluated candidates and very little effect on their confidence in their predictions about individuals.

questions.q: In describing the illusion of validity, which illusion does Kahneman say his army experience reminded him of?
options: The gorilla experiment, in which a visible event is missed
The Müller-Lyer illusion, in which equal lines look unequal
The bat-and-ball puzzle, in which an easy answer is wrong
The Linda problem, in which a detailed story seems likelier
questions.explain: Just as we know the Müller-Lyer lines are equal yet still see them as different, the evaluators knew their predictions were poor yet still felt each one was valid.

questions.q: Struck by the analogy with a visual illusion, Kahneman coined a term for knowing that predictions fail in general while still feeling each specific prediction is valid: the ____.
questions.explain: He named the experience the illusion of validity, which he calls his first cognitive illusion.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman describes the illusion of validity, discovered while evaluating army candidates, as his first cognitive illusion.
questions.explain: He writes simply that he had discovered his first cognitive illusion.

questions.q: Match each idea from earlier in the book to how it shows up in Kahneman's army officer-selection story.
pairs: Representativeness
Judging officer potential by how much a man looked like a leader at the wall
Nonregressive prediction
Predicting outright failure or stardom from weak evidence
WYSIATI
No way to represent ignorance of factors that would decide later performance
Base-rate neglect
Knowing the general failure rate yet ignoring it for each individual
