questions.explain: Kahneman says the story contains substitution and representativeness, completely nonregressive predictions, WYSIATI, and the same reluctance to infer the particular from the general that Nisbett and Borgida found.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say were illustrated by the army evaluators' predictions?
options: The representativeness heuristic
Completely nonregressive prediction
WYSIATI
Loss aversion
The endowment effect
questions.explain: He names substitution and representativeness, nonregressive predictions and WYSIATI. Ideas about gains and losses, such as loss aversion, play no part in the story.

questions.q: Kahneman compares the army evaluators' reaction to their poor record with which earlier study?
options: Mischel's studies of children resisting a marshmallow
Meehl's comparison of clinicians with simple formulas
Nisbett and Borgida's study of students and a helping experiment
Tversky's study of the hot hand in basketball shooting
questions.explain: Nisbett and Borgida's students believed the statistics on how few people helped a stranger having a seizure, yet the base rates did not affect their judgment of individuals, just as the evaluators' general knowledge did not affect individual cases.

questions.q: Kahneman concludes from the army story and the Nisbett and Borgida study that people are often reluctant to infer the particular from the ____.
questions.explain: Knowing a general rule, such as that predictions fail, does not change judgments of specific cases.

questions.q: In Kahneman's army story, sort each item by whether it was something the evaluators knew as a general fact or something they felt about specific candidates.

items.t: Our predictions are little better than random guesses
Our forecasts are largely useless
Feedback shows our ability to predict is negligible
This one will never make it
He will be a star
This man's true nature has revealed itself

questions.explain: The evaluators accepted the statistics about their failure, yet each specific candidate still produced a definite, confident impression. That gap is the illusion of validity.

questions.q: What was remarkable about how Kahneman and his fellow army evaluators responded to the evidence that their predictions were poor?
questions.a: The global evidence of failure should have shaken their confidence and made them moderate their predictions, but it did neither. The next day they again watched candidates at the wall and saw their true natures revealed as clearly as before. They knew as a general fact that their predictions were little better than random, yet felt and acted as if each specific prediction was valid.

questions.q: Why did the army evaluators find it easy to give each soldier a definite score after the leaderless group challenge?
questions.a: Their multiple observations of each candidate converged on a coherent story, so they felt they had already seen each man's leadership skills. The soldier who led the team over the wall seemed to be a leader, and predicting anything else seemed inconsistent with the evidence before their eyes. The coherence of the impression produced complete confidence, despite weak evidence from one hour in an artificial situation.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what is subjective confidence, and what does a declaration of high confidence actually tell you?
questions.a: Subjective confidence is not a reasoned evaluation of the probability that a judgment is correct. It is a feeling that reflects the coherence of the information and the cognitive ease of processing it. A declaration of high confidence mainly tells you that the person has constructed a coherent story in his mind, not that the story is true, whereas admissions of uncertainty deserve to be taken seriously.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman advises that declarations of high confidence deserve more weight than admissions of uncertainty.
questions.explain: It is the reverse: “It is wise to take admissions of uncertainty seriously,” while high confidence mainly signals a coherent story.

questions.q: Kahneman writes that confidence is a ____ which reflects the coherence of the information and the cognitive ease of processing it.
questions.explain: Confidence is a feeling, not a reasoned judgment of probability.

questions.q: A hiring manager knows that job interviews predict later performance poorly, yet after each interview she feels certain she knows how the candidate will do. Which idea from Kahneman best explains this?
options: The planning fallacy
An availability cascade
Loss aversion
The illusion of validity
questions.explain: Knowing that predictions in general fail while still feeling that each specific prediction is valid is exactly the illusion of validity from the army story. The planning fallacy concerns optimistic forecasts of one's own projects, not this gap between general knowledge and individual judgments.

questions.q: Put the events of Kahneman's army officer-selection story in order.
items: Watch candidates attempt the leaderless group challenge
Give each candidate a confident numerical score
Learn in feedback sessions that predictive ability was negligible
Evaluate the next batch with undiminished confidence
Coin the term illusion of validity
questions.explain: The evaluators formed confident scores, learned they could barely predict, carried on exactly as before with new candidates, and Kahneman named the experience the illusion of validity.

questions.q: When Kahneman asked a senior Wall Street investment manager who buys a stock when he sells it, what did the manager indicate?
options: Someone else very much like himself
Mostly small investors who knew less than he did
A computer program that traded automatically
A government fund that stabilized prices
questions.explain: He waved toward the window, indicating a buyer much like himself. This raised Kahneman's puzzle of what the seller thinks he knows that the buyer does not.

questions.q: What is the central idea of Burton Malkiel's A Random Walk Down Wall Street, as Kahneman presents it?
options: Prices swing randomly, so clever traders can profit from the swings
A stock's price incorporates all available knowledge about the company
Professional investors always beat individual investors over time
Stock prices follow recognizable patterns that careful study reveals
questions.explain: Malkiel's idea is that a stock's price already incorporates all available knowledge and the best predictions, so no one can expect to gain or lose by trading if all assets are correctly priced.

questions.q: What puzzle about the stock market does Kahneman say has hardened since his visit to a Wall Street firm?
questions.a: Billions of shares change hands daily, and most buyers and sellers know they have the same information; they trade because they have different opinions about whether the price will rise or fall. The puzzle is why both buyers and sellers think the current price is wrong and that they know better than the market. For most of them that belief is an illusion, so a major industry appears to be built largely on an illusion of skill.

questions.q: Put the steps of Terry Odean's study of individual investors in order.
items: Collect trading records of 10,000 brokerage accounts over seven years
Find cases where an investor sold one stock and soon bought another
Compare the two stocks' returns over the following year
Find that the stocks sold beat the stocks bought by 3.2 points a year
questions.explain: Odean used the records to find sell-then-buy switches, which revealed the investor's belief that the new stock would do better, and then checked one-year returns. The stocks sold did better.

questions.q: Kahneman concludes from Odean's research that for most individual investors, taking a ____ and doing nothing would have been a better policy than acting on the ideas that came to mind.
questions.explain: Because the stocks they sold beat the ones they bought, doing nothing, such as taking a shower, would have served them better.

questions.q: In Barber and Odean's research on investing, sort each group or choice by whether it did better or worse.

items.t: Stocks that individual investors sold
Stocks that individual investors bought
Investors who traded the least
The most active traders
Women investors
Men investors
Recent winners in the short run
Recent losers in the short run

questions.explain: Stocks sold beat stocks bought; the least active traders earned the most; women, who acted on useless ideas less often, beat men; and recent winners tend to beat recent losers in the short run.

questions.q: Match each publication mentioned by Kahneman to its main point.
pairs: Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth
The most active traders had the poorest results
Boys Will Be Boys
Men acted on useless ideas more often than women
Expert Political Judgment
Pundits did worse than assigning equal probabilities
The Black Swan
Coherent stories of the past hide the limits of forecasting
questions.explain: The first two are Barber and Odean papers on individual investors, the third is Tetlock's study of pundits, and the fourth is Taleb's book on narratives of the past.

questions.q: Which of these mistakes do individual investors make, according to Barber and Odean's research?
options: Selling recent winners to lock in gains
Hanging on to their losers
Flocking to companies that are in the news
Responding to news more selectively than professionals
Trading too rarely to profit from price changes
questions.explain: Individuals sell the wrong stocks, winners, while keeping losers, and buy the wrong ones, companies in the news. It is professionals who are more selective in responding to news.

questions.q: In what sense does Kahneman say finance professionals earn the label “smart money,” and in what sense do they still lack skill?
questions.a: Professionals are on the other side of individual investors' trades and take advantage of amateurs' mistakes, such as selling winners and buying stocks in the news, so they extract considerable wealth from amateurs. But few if any stock pickers can beat the market consistently year after year. They fail the basic test of skill, persistent achievement, since the year-to-year correlation of fund results is barely above zero.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what is the diagnostic for the existence of any skill?
options: The amount of training and effort a person invests
The confidence experts feel in their own judgments
The consistency of individual differences in achievement
A single outstanding result in a demanding year
questions.explain: If differences are due to luck, rankings vary erratically and the year-to-year correlation is zero; skill shows up as stable rankings. Training and confidence do not prove skill, as stock pickers show.

questions.q: Kahneman writes that the diagnostic for the existence of any skill is the ____ of individual differences in achievement.
questions.explain: Skill is confirmed when the same individuals keep doing better, which is why he speaks of persistent achievement.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give as examples where the persistence of individual differences confirms skill?
options: Golfers
Orthodontists
Speedy toll collectors
Mutual fund managers
Wealth advisers at the firm he visited
questions.explain: He lists golfers, car salespeople, orthodontists and speedy toll collectors. Fund managers and the wealth advisers fail this test, since their rankings barely persist.

questions.q: Kahneman says that for a large majority of fund managers, the selection of stocks is more like rolling ____ than like playing poker.
questions.explain: Over fifty years of research shows fund results are mostly luck, a roll of the dice, rather than a game where skill wins over time.

questions.q: True or false: According to Kahneman, typically at least two out of every three mutual funds underperform the overall market in any given year.
questions.explain: He states this directly, adding that the year-to-year correlation between fund outcomes is barely higher than zero.

questions.q: Using Kahneman's logic for detecting skill, sort each observation by whether it points to luck or to skill.

items.t: Rankings vary erratically from year to year
Year-to-year correlation of results near zero
A mutual fund's success in a single year
Rankings stay stable across many years
A golfer who keeps finishing near the top
A car salesperson with consistently high sales

questions.explain: Skill shows itself as persistence of individual differences. A single good year or rankings that reshuffle each year are what luck produces.

questions.q: Which of these were features of the wealth-adviser data Kahneman analysed before speaking to an investment firm?
options: About twenty-five anonymous advisers
Eight consecutive years of results
Each yearly score mainly determined the adviser's bonus
Several hundred advisers identified by name
A single year of results for each adviser
questions.explain: The spreadsheet covered some twenty-five anonymous advisers over eight consecutive years, and each year's score was the main determinant of the adviser's year-end bonus.

questions.q: Put the steps of Kahneman's analysis of the wealth advisers in order.
items: Obtain eight years of results for about twenty-five advisers
Rank the advisers by performance in each year
Compute 28 correlations between pairs of years
Find the average correlation is .01
Tell the executives over dinner
Report the findings to the advisers the next morning
questions.explain: He ranked advisers each year, correlated every pair of years, found essentially zero persistence, and then presented this to the executives and, the next morning, to the advisers.

questions.q: What was the average of the 28 year-to-year correlations Kahneman computed for the wealth advisers' rankings?
options: .30, a modest but real sign of skill
.50, a strong sign of skill
-.40, a reversal from year to year
.01, in other words zero
questions.explain: The average was .01, which is zero; the results resembled a dice-rolling contest, not a game of skill.

questions.q: True or false: When Kahneman and Thaler asked the firm's top executives to guess the year-to-year correlation of advisers' rankings, the executives expected it to be zero.
questions.explain: They smiled and said “not very high” or that performance fluctuates, but no one expected the average correlation to be zero.

questions.q: Which of these describe how the investment firm reacted when Kahneman and Thaler showed it was rewarding luck as if it were skill?
options: The executives showed no sign of disbelieving them
The findings were quickly swept under the rug
The advisers' response was bland
The executives disputed the analysis of their data
The firm redesigned its bonus system
questions.explain: The news should have been shocking but was not; there was no sign of disbelief, the advisers were equally bland, and Kahneman had no doubt life went on just as before.

questions.q: Why, according to Kahneman, were his findings about luck not absorbed by the investment firm?
questions.a: The illusion of skill is not only an individual aberration but is deeply ingrained in the culture of the industry. Facts that challenge basic assumptions and threaten people's livelihood and self-esteem are simply not absorbed; the mind does not digest them. Statistical studies of performance provide base-rate information that people ignore when it clashes with their personal experience of exercising careful judgment.

questions.q: What did Kahneman think, but not say, when an executive told him “I have done very well for the firm and no one can take that away from me”?
questions.a: He thought that he had taken it away from the executive that very morning. If the executive's success was due mostly to chance, as the near-zero correlations showed, then he was entitled to little credit for it. The exchange shows how the firm rewarded luck as if it were skill.

questions.q: An investor sells a stock that has risen since she bought it, to lock in the gain, and buys shares of a company that has been all over the news. What does Barber and Odean's research suggest?
options: She has probably sold the wrong stock and bought the wrong one
She is copying the selective strategy of professional investors
She has reduced her risk without changing her expected return
She is acting on information the market has not yet priced in
questions.explain: Recent winners tend to outperform recent losers in the short run, so selling winners is a mistake, and flocking to companies in the news is how individuals buy the wrong stocks. Professionals are more selective about news.

questions.q: Match each person to their role in Kahneman's discussion of stock-picking skill.
pairs: Terry Odean
Compared returns of stocks investors sold and bought
Burton Malkiel
Argued prices incorporate all available knowledge
Richard Thaler
Had dinner with Kahneman and the firm's top executives before the seminar
Brad Barber
Co-authored studies showing active traders did worst
questions.explain: Odean ran the original brokerage study, Malkiel wrote A Random Walk Down Wall Street, Thaler joined Kahneman for dinner with the firm's executives the evening before the seminar, and Barber worked with Odean on the later papers.

questions.section: What Supports the Illusions of Skill and Validity?
questions.q: Why does Kahneman say cognitive illusions can be more stubborn than visual illusions?
options: Visual illusions fade with practice, while cognitive ones grow stronger
Learning about Müller-Lyer changes behavior, but learning of low test validity did not
Cognitive illusions cannot be measured, while visual illusions can
Visual illusions affect only System 1, while cognitive ones affect only System 2
questions.explain: Knowing about the Müller-Lyer illusion does not change what you see but does change what you report. The army evaluators accepted their low validity intellectually, but it had no impact on their feelings or actions.

questions.section: What Supports the Illusions of Skill and Validity?
questions.q: In Kahneman's comparison of visual and cognitive illusions, sort each item by whether it was changed or left unchanged by learning the truth.

items.t: What you report about the length of Müller-Lyer lines
Whether you trust your impression of lines with fins
How the Müller-Lyer lines look to you
The army evaluators' feelings of confidence
The army evaluators' later actions with new candidates

questions.explain: With the visual illusion, knowledge changes behavior though not perception. With the illusion of validity, knowledge changed neither feelings nor actions.

questions.section: What Supports the Illusions of Skill and Validity?
questions.q: What does Kahneman call the most potent psychological cause of the illusion of skill in finance?
options: Stock pickers are paid regardless of how their picks perform
Stock pickers lack access to good economic data
Stock pickers really are exercising high-level skills
Stock pickers rarely see their own past results
questions.explain: They consult data, examine balance sheets and evaluate management, which is serious work, so they have the valid experience of using real skills. That experience feeds the illusion that they can beat the market.

questions.section: What Supports the Illusions of Skill and Validity?
questions.q: Kahneman says traders lack the skill to judge whether information is already in a stock's price, but they appear to be ignorant of their ____.
questions.explain: They are “ignorant of their ignorance”: unaware that their real business skill does not answer the crucial pricing question.

questions.section: What Supports the Illusions of Skill and Validity?
questions.q: Why does Kahneman say skill in evaluating a firm's business prospects is not enough for successful stock trading?
questions.a: In trading, the key question is whether the information about the firm is already incorporated in the price of its stock. Traders can evaluate income statements, management and competition, but they apparently lack the skill to answer that crucial question. Because the evaluation work feels like real skill, they do not notice that it misses the point.

questions.section: What Supports the Illusions of Skill and Validity?
questions.q: True or false: Kahneman concludes that our understanding of cognitive ease and associative coherence locates subjective confidence firmly in System 2.
questions.explain: He locates subjective confidence firmly in System 1; traders' confidence, like the cadet evaluators', is a feeling, not a judgment.

questions.section: What Supports the Illusions of Skill and Validity?
questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say support the illusions of skill and validity in the financial world?
options: Stock pickers really do exercise high-level skills
A professional culture of like-minded believers
Confidence that arises from cognitive ease and coherence
No access to statistics on their own performance
Pay that is unrelated to yearly results
questions.explain: He cites the genuine high-level skills involved, confidence as a System 1 feeling, and a powerful professional culture. The firm he visited did have performance data and did tie bonuses to yearly results.

questions.section: What Supports the Illusions of Skill and Validity?
questions.q: How does professional culture help sustain the illusions of validity and skill, according to Kahneman?
questions.a: People can maintain an unshakable faith in any proposition, however absurd, when they are sustained by a community of like-minded believers. The financial community has such a culture. So it is not surprising that many people in that world believe they are among the chosen few who can do what others cannot.

questions.section: What Supports the Illusions of Skill and Validity?
questions.q: A young analyst spends weeks studying a company's balance sheets, management and competitors and becomes confident he can beat the market with its stock. What crucial question does Kahneman say he has probably not answered?
options: Whether the company's managers are honest and capable
Whether the company's competitors are growing faster
Whether the economy as a whole will expand next year
Whether his information is already incorporated in the stock's price
questions.explain: Evaluating management and competitors is genuine skill, but trading success depends on whether that information is already reflected in the price, which traders apparently cannot judge.

questions.q: What point does Kahneman take from Nassim Taleb's The Black Swan in discussing pundits?
options: Coherent narratives of the past make it hard to accept limits of forecasting
Rare events are easy to predict once experts study them closely
Forecasting improves as soon as people learn about hindsight bias
Markets are efficient, so stories about them do not matter
questions.explain: Our tendency to construct and believe coherent narratives of the past makes it difficult to accept the limits of our forecasting ability; everything makes sense in hindsight.

questions.q: Kahneman writes that the illusion that we understand the past fosters ____ in our ability to predict the future.
questions.explain: Because the past seems easy to explain, we feel what makes sense today was predictable yesterday, which inflates confidence in forecasts.

questions.q: Match each image or example from Kahneman's discussion of pundits to the point it makes.
pairs: The march of history
Implies order and direction, unlike a random stroll
The embryo that became Hitler
Large historical events can hinge on luck
Dart-throwing monkeys
Experts did worse than spreading choices evenly
Two hedgehogs on television
Opinionated, clear views make a good show
questions.explain: The march image suggests order, the fertilized eggs show the role of luck, the monkeys stand for an even spread of probabilities, and dueling hedgehogs are what producers love.

questions.q: What does Kahneman's example of the eggs that became Hitler, Stalin and Mao Zedong illustrate?
options: Great men always arise when history needs them
Large historical events are determined partly by luck
The twentieth century would have been similar without them
Long-term developments are predictable from social movements
questions.explain: Each embryo had a fifty-fifty chance of being female, and these chance events had momentous consequences, which “makes a joke of the idea that long-term developments are predictable.”

questions.q: Kahneman calculates that, compounding three fifty-fifty events, there was a probability of ____ of a twentieth century without Hitler, Stalin and Mao Zedong.
questions.explain: Three independent fifty-fifty chances compound to one-eighth, showing how much of history rests on luck.

questions.q: In Philip Tetlock's twenty-year study, how did the experts' predictions compare with simply assigning equal probabilities to the three possible outcomes?
options: The experts did slightly better than equal probabilities
The experts did much better, but only in their own regions
The experts did worse than equal probabilities
The experts did exactly as well as equal probabilities
questions.explain: The results were devastating: experts did worse than if they had spread probability evenly, worse than dart-throwing monkeys.

questions.q: Match each number to what it describes in Philip Tetlock's study of expert predictions.
pairs: People who made a living commenting on political and economic trends
More than 80,000
Predictions gathered
Three
Outcomes rated in each case: status quo, more, or less
Twenty years
Length of the landmark study
questions.explain: Tetlock interviewed 284 professional commentators, gathered over 80,000 predictions over twenty years, and asked them to rate three alternative outcomes each time.

questions.q: True or false: In Tetlock's study, experts were significantly better than nonspecialists at predicting events in the region they knew best.
questions.explain: Even in the region they knew best, experts were not significantly better than nonspecialists.

questions.q: According to Tetlock's findings as Kahneman reports them, why are the forecasters with the most knowledge often less reliable?
options: They have less time to follow current events
They are pressured by employers to hide their real views
They focus on distant regions they know little about
They develop an enhanced illusion of skill and become overconfident
questions.explain: The person who acquires more knowledge develops an enhanced illusion of skill and becomes unrealistically overconfident; predictive returns to knowledge diminish quickly.

questions.q: Which of these did Tetlock find about expert forecasters, as Kahneman reports?
options: The more famous the forecaster, the more flamboyant the forecasts
Experts in demand were more overconfident than colleagues out of the limelight
Foxes scored best, though still very poorly
Top journal contributors read emerging situations far better than journalists
The most knowledgeable experts were always the most reliable
questions.explain: Tetlock found fame went with flamboyance and overconfidence, and that foxes scored best. He saw no reason to think top academics read situations better than attentive newspaper readers.

questions.q: Which of these excuses did Tetlock's experts use when compelled to admit they had been wrong?
options: They had been wrong only in their timing
An unforeseeable event had intervened
They had been wrong but for the right reasons
The questions they were asked had been unfair
The data they were given had been falsified
questions.explain: Experts resisted admitting error and had excuses ready: wrong timing, an unforeseeable event, or being wrong for the right reasons.

questions.q: Sort each description by whether it fits Tetlock's hedgehogs or his foxes.

items.t: Know one big thing and have a theory about the world
Say a failed prediction was off only on timing
Opinionated and clear, which television producers love
Especially reluctant to admit error
See reality emerging from many agents and blind luck
Scored best in Tetlock's study
Less likely to be invited to television debates
Complex thinkers who reject one big driving force

questions.explain: Hedgehogs fit events into one coherent framework and are confident and stubborn; foxes are complex thinkers who allow for luck and many forces, and they forecast best.

questions.q: Tetlock borrowed his terms for two styles of thinking from Isaiah Berlin's essay on Tolstoy, titled The Hedgehog and the ____.
questions.explain: Hedgehogs know one big thing; foxes are complex thinkers who see many interacting forces.

questions.q: What does Tetlock mean when he says experts are led astray not by what they believe but by how they think?
questions.a: Accuracy depended on thinking style rather than on particular views. Hedgehogs know one big thing, explain events within a coherent framework, are confident and are especially reluctant to admit error. Foxes recognize that reality emerges from many agents and forces, including blind luck, and they scored best, though their performance was still very poor.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say the role of luck in the births of Hitler, Stalin and Mao undermines the idea that history is predictable?
questions.a: Before each egg was fertilized there was a fifty-fifty chance the embryo would be female, so there was a one-eighth chance of a twentieth century without all three. It is impossible to argue history would have been roughly the same without them. Such momentous chance events show that large historical events are shaped by luck, which makes long-term prediction a joke, even though the march-of-history image suggests order.

questions.q: A television commentator explains every world event with one grand theory, scorns opponents, and calls each failed forecast “very nearly right.” In Tetlock's terms, the commentator is a:
options: Hedgehog
Fox
Specialist
Nonspecialist
questions.explain: Hedgehogs have one theory about the world, are impatient with those who disagree, and treat failed predictions as off only on timing or very nearly right.

questions.q: Put the steps of Kahneman's argument about the illusions of pundits in order.
items: The past is easy to explain, so the future seems predictable
History is shaped by luck, as the eggs of three villains show
Tetlock's experts did worse than equal probabilities
More knowledge brings an enhanced illusion of skill
Hedgehogs fare worse than foxes
questions.explain: Kahneman starts with Taleb's point about narratives, shows luck in history, presents Tetlock's devastating results and the knowledge paradox, and ends with the hedgehog-fox distinction.

questions.section: It is Not the Experts’ Fault—the World is Difficult
questions.q: What does Kahneman call the first lesson of the chapter on the illusion of validity?
options: People who predict the future make many errors
Errors of prediction are inevitable because the world is unpredictable
Experts are lazy and should be held to higher standards
Prediction becomes accurate once experts admit uncertainty
questions.explain: That predictors make many errors goes without saying; the first lesson is that errors are inevitable because the world is unpredictable, which is not the experts' fault.

questions.section: It is Not the Experts’ Fault—the World is Difficult
questions.q: True or false: In the chapter on the illusion of validity, Kahneman says that low subjective confidence could be more informative than high confidence.
questions.explain: His second lesson is that high subjective confidence is not to be trusted as an indicator of accuracy, and he adds that low confidence could be more informative.

questions.section: It is Not the Experts’ Fault—the World is Difficult
questions.q: Kahneman does not deny the validity of all tests: if a test predicts an important outcome with a validity of .20 or .30, he says the test should be ____.
questions.explain: Modestly valid tests are worth using, but “you should not expect more.”

questions.section: It is Not the Experts’ Fault—the World is Difficult
questions.q: Sort each forecast by whether Kahneman says it can be made with fair accuracy or should not be expected to succeed.

items.t: Short-term trends
Achievements from previous achievements
Behavior from previous behavior
Combat performance from an obstacle field
Stock prices more accurately than the market
Pundits' long-term forecasts

questions.explain: Short-term trends and future behavior from past behavior can be predicted with fair accuracy, but not officer performance from the wall, beating the market, or long-term punditry.

questions.section: It is Not the Experts’ Fault—the World is Difficult
questions.q: Why does Kahneman say officer performance in training and combat should not be expected to be predictable from behavior on an obstacle field?
questions.a: Behavior both on the test and in the real world is determined by many factors specific to the particular situation. Remove one highly assertive member from a group of eight and everyone else's personality will appear to change; let a sniper's bullet move a few centimeters and an officer's performance is transformed. So errors of prediction are inevitable because the world is unpredictable, not because the evaluators were at fault.

questions.section: It is Not the Experts’ Fault—the World is Difficult
questions.q: A school's entrance test predicts later success with a validity of about .25, and a board member wants to drop it as nearly useless. What would Kahneman advise?
options: Drop it and rely on interviews, which feel more informative
Keep using it and treat its scores as precise forecasts
Keep using it, but expect no more than its modest accuracy
Drop it, since only tests above .50 deserve to be used
questions.explain: He says a test with validity of .20 or .30 for an important outcome should be used, but one should not expect more. Swapping it for confident impressions would invite the illusion of validity.

questions.q: Match each remark from Kahneman's examples of speaking of illusory skill to the idea it names.
pairs: How can he be so confident in this case when the illness is mostly unpredictable?
Illusion of validity
What makes him believe that he is smarter than the market?
Illusion of skill
She has a theory that explains everything.
Hedgehog thinking
Not whether the experts are well trained, but whether their world is predictable
The world is difficult, not the experts' fault
questions.explain: Each remark applies one of the chapter's ideas: confidence despite a known unpredictable record, believing one can beat the market, a single all-explaining theory, and the predictability of the environment.

questions.q: Kahneman offers the remark “The question is not whether these experts are well trained. It is whether their world is predictable.” Which lesson of the chapter does this express?
options: Experts' errors come mainly from poor training
Well-trained experts are immune to the illusion of validity
Foxes are better trained than hedgehogs
Prediction errors are inevitable when the world is unpredictable
questions.explain: The remark echoes the point that it is not the experts' fault: the world is difficult, so even skilled people cannot predict an unpredictable environment.

questions.q: One of Kahneman's examples of speaking of illusory skill says that she has a coherent story that explains all she knows, and the ____ makes her feel good.
questions.explain: The remark points to confidence by coherence: a coherent story produces good feelings and confidence, whatever its truth.

questions.q: A doctor knows that the course of a certain illness is mostly unpredictable, yet he is very confident about how it will develop in one patient. Using Kahneman's ideas, how would you describe what is happening?
questions.a: This sounds like an illusion of validity: the doctor knows the general record of unpredictability, but that knowledge does not affect his confidence in the specific case, just as the army evaluators kept feeling sure about each candidate. His confidence is a feeling that reflects the coherence of the story he has built about this patient, not a reasoned estimate that the story is true.

questions.q: Why does the chapter on the illusion of validity belong in Part 3 of the book, titled “Overconfidence”?
options: It shows confidence persisting in judgments known to be poorly valid
It shows how losses loom larger than gains in decisions
It shows how memory distorts our evaluation of experiences
It shows how anchors bias numerical estimates
questions.explain: The chapter shows evaluators, stock pickers and pundits remaining confident despite evidence that their predictions are little better than chance, a central form of overconfidence.

questions.q: Put these chapters of Part 3, “Overconfidence,” in the book's order.
items: The Illusion of Understanding
The Illusion of Validity
Intuitions vs. Formulas
Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
The Outside View
The Engine of Capitalism
questions.explain: Part 3 runs from chapter 19, The Illusion of Understanding, through chapter 20, The Illusion of Validity, to chapters on formulas, expert intuition, the outside view and optimism.

questions.q: Put the sections of the chapter on the illusion of validity in order.
items: The Illusion of Validity
The Illusion of Stock-picking Skill
What Supports the Illusions of Skill and Validity?
The Illusions of Pundits
It is Not the Experts’ Fault—the World is Difficult
questions.explain: The chapter starts with the army story, extends the illusion to finance, explains what sustains it, turns to pundits, and closes with the lessons about an unpredictable world.

questions.q: How does the chapter on the illusion of validity link back to the previous chapter, “The Illusion of Understanding”?
options: It argues that understanding the past makes forecasts accurate
It notes that the illusion of understanding the past fosters overconfidence in predicting
It abandons the idea of narratives to focus on numbers
It shows that hindsight improves expert judgment
questions.explain: The section on pundits states that “The illusion that we understand the past fosters overconfidence in our ability to predict the future,” connecting the two illusions.

questions.q: How does the end of the chapter on the illusion of validity prepare for the next chapter, “Intuitions vs. Formulas”?
options: It claims all tests are worthless, so intuition must decide
It concludes that experts' intuition is always trustworthy
It says confidence is no guide to accuracy and modestly valid tests should be used
It argues that formulas are what make pundits overconfident
questions.explain: Having shown that confident intuitive judgments can be nearly worthless, Kahneman says tests with validity of .20 or .30 should be used, which sets up a comparison of intuitive judgment with formulas.

questions.q: What does the chapter title “The Illusion of Validity” signal, and why did Kahneman choose the word “illusion”?
questions.a: The title names the feeling that one's judgments are valid even when one knows they are not. Kahneman chose “illusion” because his army experience resembled the Müller-Lyer illusion, in which we know the lines are equal yet still see them as different. Likewise, the evaluators knew their predictions were little better than random but kept feeling that each one was valid.

questions.q: How does the chapter on the illusion of validity draw together themes from earlier in the book?
questions.a: Kahneman says the army story contains substitution and the representativeness heuristic, completely nonregressive predictions, and WYSIATI. The evaluators' indifference to their failure rate mirrors Nisbett and Borgida's finding that people are reluctant to infer the particular from the general, a form of base-rate neglect. Confidence is explained through cognitive ease and associative coherence, which locate it in System 1.

questions.q: Kahneman says clinical psychologists who rejected Meehl's findings were in the grip of an illusion of skill. Which chapter title from just before Intuitions vs. Formulas names a closely related illusion?
options: The Illusion of Validity
The Outside View
Regression to the Mean
The Engine of Capitalism
questions.explain: Intuitions vs. Formulas directly follows The Illusion of Validity, and its clinicians, confident in long-term predictions they cannot make, are another case of that illusion. The Outside View and The Engine of Capitalism come later in Part 3.

questions.q: In the book's table of contents, Intuitions vs. Formulas belongs to Part 3, which is titled ____.
questions.explain: Part 3, Overconfidence, runs from The Illusion of Understanding through The Engine of Capitalism. The chapter's experts, who trust judgments that simple formulas beat, are a study in overconfidence.

questions.q: True or false: In the book's table of contents, the chapter that immediately follows Intuitions vs. Formulas asks when expert intuition can be trusted.
questions.explain: Chapter 22 is Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It? It picks up the question left open when Kahneman warns against both blindly trusting and dismissing intuition.

questions.q: Put these chapters of Part 3, Overconfidence, in the order they appear in the book.
items: The Illusion of Understanding
The Illusion of Validity
Intuitions vs. Formulas
Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
The Outside View
The Engine of Capitalism
questions.explain: Intuitions vs. Formulas is the third chapter of Part 3, between the illusion of validity and the question of when expert intuition can be trusted.

questions.q: How does Intuitions vs. Formulas move Part 3's argument about overconfidence forward from the chapter on the illusion of validity?
options: It shows that experts' summary judgments improve when they are given more information
It turns from biases in judgment to how people choose between risky gambles
It gives hard evidence that in uncertain domains simple formulas match or beat confident experts
It argues that experts' overconfidence disappears with long professional experience
questions.explain: The chapter supplies the Meehl evidence: across about two hundred studies, algorithms matched or beat experts in low-validity environments. The idea that experience removes overconfidence runs against its account of clinicians who cannot see the limits of their skill.

questions.q: What does the title Intuitions vs. Formulas lead a reader to expect, and how does Kahneman's own army story keep the chapter from being a simple victory for formulas?
questions.a: The title frames a contest between clinical judgment and statistical rules, and most of the chapter reports Meehl's finding that formulas win or tie. But in his army interview, the interviewers' 'close your eyes' rating predicted as well as the six trait scores, so Kahneman concludes that intuition adds value after disciplined collection of facts. His lesson is “do not simply trust intuitive judgment—your own or that of others—but do not dismiss it, either,” which prepares the next chapter on when intuition can be trusted.

questions.q: Why does the order of sections in Intuitions vs. Formulas (the evidence, The Hostility to Algorithms, Learning from Meehl, Do It Yourself) make an effective argument?
questions.a: Kahneman first lays out the evidence that simple formulas match or beat experts, then explains why people resist that evidence, from the illusion of skill to the preference for the natural. He next shows the idea working in his own life, in the Israeli army interview system. He ends by turning it into a procedure readers can use themselves, such as hiring a sales representative by scoring six traits.

questions.q: In Meehl's typical study of counselors predicting freshmen's grades, what information did the statistical algorithm use?
options: A forty-five-minute interview and a personal statement
Several aptitude tests and a four-page personal statement
High school grades and one aptitude test
High school grades and the counselors' interview ratings
questions.explain: The formula used only a fraction of the counselors' information: high school grades and one aptitude test. The interview and the four-page personal statement were available only to the counselors.

questions.q: In Meehl's typical study, how many of the 14 trained counselors did the simple formula outpredict on freshmen's end-of-year grades?
questions.explain: The formula was more accurate than 11 of the 14 counselors, despite using much less information than they had.

questions.q: Of the roughly two hundred studies comparing clinical and statistical prediction, why does Kahneman count a draw as a win for the formulas?
options: Because a draw means experts were relying on the formula anyway
Because statistical rules are normally much less expensive than expert judgment
Because draws only occurred in domains with high predictability
Because the experts in drawn studies were usually inexperienced
questions.explain: A tie is “tantamount to a win for the statistical rules,” because the rules cost much less to use than expert judgment. About 60% of studies favored algorithms outright, and no exception was convincingly documented.

questions.q: Which three features of the weather did Orley Ashenfelter's formula use to predict the price of a Bordeaux wine?
options: Spring rainfall, summer sunshine hours and harvest temperature
Winter frost days, spring rainfall and summer humidity
Summer temperature, harvest temperature and spring rainfall
Average summer temperature, rain at harvest-time and the previous winter's rainfall
questions.explain: The formula used the average temperature over the summer growing season, the amount of rain at harvest-time and total rainfall during the previous winter. Wet springs are mentioned only as raising quantity without much effect on quality.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, which economic idea does Ashenfelter's wine-price formula challenge?
options: That prices should reflect all the available information, including the weather
That investors buy wine, like art, expecting its value to appreciate
That scarce goods become more valuable as supply falls
That experts' opinions help shape the early price of a wine
questions.explain: Because the formula forecasts future prices much better than current prices of young wines do, it challenges the theory that prices already reflect all available information. The idea that investors buy wine expecting appreciation is the reason forecasting matters, not something challenged.

questions.q: A formula predicts very accurately whether patients will show up for their appointments. In which case would Meehl's broken-leg rule justify setting the formula aside?
options: The receptionist has a gut feeling the patient seems unreliable
The patient was admitted to hospital this morning after an accident
The doctor has met the patient several times and likes her
The patient sounded cheerful when she booked the appointment
questions.explain: The broken-leg rule allows overriding a formula only for information that is rare and decisive, like learning the person broke a leg today. Hunches and personal impressions are exactly the kind of additional information that usually makes overruling the formula wrong.

questions.q: How often do experienced radiologists contradict themselves when they evaluate the same chest X-ray as normal or abnormal on separate occasions?
options: About 2% of the time
About 50% of the time
About 5% of the time
About 20% of the time
questions.explain: Radiologists contradict themselves 20% of the time, and a review of 41 studies suggests this level of inconsistency is typical among professionals.

questions.q: To what does Kahneman attribute the widespread inconsistency of professionals' summary judgments?
options: Lack of training in the relevant statistical methods
The extreme context dependency of System 1
Deliberate attempts to vary judgments to avoid boredom
Fatigue from reviewing too many cases in a day
questions.explain: He says the inconsistency is probably due to System 1's extreme context dependency: unnoticed stimuli, like a cool breeze or the time since a meal break, shift judgments without our knowing.

questions.q: What did Robyn Dawes observe about multiple regression in "The Robust Beauty of Improper Linear Models in Decision Making"?
options: It is the only reliable way to build a prediction formula
It works well only when experts choose the predictors
Its complex weighting adds little or no value over equal weights
It is less accurate than an expert's global judgment
questions.explain: Dawes found that combining standardized valid predictors with equal weights does about as well on new cases as the optimal regression formula. Later work found equal weights often superior because they are not affected by accidents of sampling.

questions.q: In the Apgar score, what did a baby's total of 8 or above usually indicate?
options: That the baby was in good shape: pink, squirming and crying
That the baby needed immediate intervention
That the baby should be rescored after another hour
That the baby had a pulse below 100
questions.explain: A score of 8 or above meant a baby likely pink, squirming, crying and grimacing, with a pulse of 100 or more. A score of 4 or below signaled the need for immediate intervention.

questions.q: What two reasons does Kahneman give for why expert judgment is inferior to simple algorithms?
questions.a: First, experts try to be clever, think outside the box and consider complex combinations of features, and complexity more often than not reduces validity; they even overrule a formula's score when given it, and are usually wrong. Second, humans are incorrigibly inconsistent in summary judgments of complex information, often giving different answers to the same case. Because “Unreliable judgments cannot be valid predictors of anything,” this inconsistency destroys predictive validity.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman conjecture that conducting interviews may lower the accuracy of medical school admissions?
questions.a: If the interviewers also make the final decision, they will be overconfident in their intuitions. They will give too much weight to their personal impressions from the interview and too little to other sources of information, which lowers validity. The same logic applies to wine experts, whose ability to taste young wine almost certainly makes their forecasts worse, and who cannot match a formula's consistency anyway.

questions.q: What practical implication does Kahneman draw from the success of equal-weighting formulas?
questions.a: Because equal weights work about as well as optimally weighted regression, useful algorithms can be built without any prior statistical research. Simple formulas based on existing statistics or common sense, like Dawes's marital-stability formula, often predict important outcomes well. An algorithm made “on the back of an envelope” is often good enough to compete with an optimal formula and to beat expert judgment, from stock picking to medical treatment choices.

questions.q: How did Virginia Apgar's score change the way delivery rooms judged newborns, and why did it matter?
questions.a: Before 1953, physicians and midwives used clinical judgment and focused on different cues, so danger signs were often missed and many newborns died. Apgar rated five signs (heart rate, respiration, reflex, muscle tone and color) as 0, 1 or 2 one minute after birth and summed them. This gave delivery rooms consistent standards for spotting babies in trouble, and the formula is credited with an important contribution to reducing infant mortality.

questions.q: Why is inconsistency so damaging to prediction in the low-validity environments studied by Meehl and his followers, and how do formulas avoid it?
questions.a: Human judgments fluctuate with unnoticed influences like priming, mood or the time since a meal break, so the same case can get different answers, and we never know it happened. When predictability is already poor, this added noise destroys whatever predictive validity there was. Formulas do not suffer from this: “Given the same input, they always return the same answer.”

questions.q: Kahneman calls domains such as cancer longevity, credit risk and football results, which entail significant uncertainty and unpredictability, "____ environments."
questions.explain: These are “low-validity environments,” and in every one the accuracy of experts was matched or exceeded by a simple algorithm.

questions.q: Meehl's thought experiment, in which it is proper to ignore a moviegoing formula on learning that the person broke a leg today, gave its name to the "____ rule."
questions.explain: The broken-leg rule makes the point that information justifying an override is very rare as well as decisive.

questions.q: Robyn Dawes's famous article argued for the robust beauty of ____ linear models, which weight predictors equally instead of optimally.
questions.explain: Dawes's improper linear models give equal weights to standardized predictors instead of optimal regression weights, yet predict new cases about as well.

questions.q: Dawes showed that marital stability is well predicted by the formula: frequency of lovemaking minus frequency of ____.
questions.explain: This back-of-the-envelope formula illustrates that common-sense equal-weight rules can predict important outcomes. Kahneman adds that you do not want your result to be a negative number.

questions.q: The dominant statistical practice in the social sciences for assigning weights to predictors, built into conventional software, is called ____.
questions.explain: Multiple regression finds the optimal weighted combination of predictors in the original sample, but Dawes found that its complexity adds little or no value over equal weights.

questions.q: Kahneman calls a new example of a formula outperforming experts, such as Ashenfelter's wine-price formula, a "Meehl ____."
questions.explain: Ashenfelter's formula is described as a new example of a “Meehl pattern,” in which a simple statistical rule beats the experts whose opinions shape early prices.

questions.q: Which of these outcomes does Kahneman list among the domains where a simple algorithm matched or exceeded the accuracy of experts?
options: The longevity of cancer patients
The winners of football games
The future prices of Bordeaux wine
The results of national elections
The literary quality of novels
questions.explain: Cancer longevity, football winners and Bordeaux prices all appear in Kahneman's list of low-validity domains. National elections and literary quality are not among the outcomes he names.

questions.q: Which of these did the counselors in Meehl's typical grade-prediction study have that the statistical formula did not use?
options: A forty-five-minute interview with each student
A four-page personal statement
The student's high school grades
A score on one aptitude test
questions.explain: The counselors interviewed each student and read a personal statement, while the formula used only high school grades and one aptitude test. The extra information did not make the counselors more accurate.

questions.q: Which of these outcomes did Meehl report formulas predicting with results similar to the grade-prediction study, in his original review?
options: Violations of parole
Success in pilot training
Criminal recidivism
The outcome of chess matches
The price of fine art
questions.explain: Meehl reported generally similar results for parole violations, pilot-training success and criminal recidivism. Chess matches and art prices are not among his examples.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give as reasons that human experts do worse than prediction formulas?
options: They consider complex combinations of features, which usually reduces validity
They give different answers when judging the same information twice
They overrule a formula's score with additional case information, and are usually wrong
They have far less information about each case than the formula does
They are generally less intelligent than the statisticians who build formulas
questions.explain: Complexity, inconsistency and unwarranted overriding are all reasons Kahneman gives. Experts in fact often have more information than the formula, as the counselors did, and intelligence is not the issue.

questions.q: True or false: About 60% of the roughly two hundred studies comparing clinical and statistical prediction showed significantly better accuracy for the algorithms.
questions.explain: About 60% favored the algorithms significantly, and the rest were draws. No exception favoring experts has been convincingly documented.

questions.q: True or false: Ashenfelter's weather formula forecasts the future prices of Bordeaux wines less accurately than the current prices of young wines do.
questions.explain: The reverse is true: his formula forecasts future prices much more accurately than the current prices of young wines, with a correlation with actual prices above .90.

questions.q: True or false: Several studies found that human decision makers outperform a prediction formula once they are given the score the formula suggests.
questions.explain: The studies found decision makers remained inferior to the formula even when given its score. They felt entitled to overrule it with additional information but were wrong more often than not.

questions.q: True or false: According to the wine example in Intuitions vs. Formulas, the best Bordeaux wines are produced when the summer is cool and wet.
questions.explain: The best wines come when the summer is warm and dry, which is why Kahneman calls the Bordeaux industry a likely beneficiary of global warming.

questions.q: Put these steps in the opening of Intuitions vs. Formulas in the order Kahneman presents them.
items: Meehl's review of 20 studies of clinical vs. statistical prediction
Ashenfelter's weather formula for Bordeaux wine prices
Why experts are inferior: complexity and inconsistency
The conclusion that final decisions should be left to formulas
Dawes's finding that equal-weight formulas do as well
The Apgar score for newborns
questions.explain: The opening moves from Meehl's evidence and a vivid wine example to the reasons behind it, draws the conclusion for decisions, then shows with Dawes and Apgar that simple formulas are easy to build and use.

questions.q: Put these events in the story of the Apgar score in order.
items: Practitioners judge newborns by different cues, often missing danger signs
A medical resident asks Apgar over breakfast how she would assess a newborn
Apgar jots down five variables, each scored 0, 1 or 2
Apgar begins rating infants one minute after birth
Delivery rooms gain consistent standards for babies in trouble
questions.explain: Apgar's score replaced inconsistent clinical judgment with a simple rule that began as a breakfast answer to a resident's question and became standard in every delivery room.

questions.q: Match each person to the contribution described in Intuitions vs. Formulas.
pairs: Paul Meehl
Reviewed studies of clinical vs. statistical prediction
Orley Ashenfelter
Predicted Bordeaux wine prices from the weather
Robyn Dawes
Showed equal-weight improper linear models work well
Virginia Apgar
Created a five-sign score for assessing newborns
Atul Gawande
Wrote A Checklist Manifesto on checklists and simple rules
questions.explain: Each person illustrates the power of simple rules: Meehl's review started the field, Ashenfelter and Apgar applied formulas, Dawes showed weights hardly matter, and Gawande collected checklist examples.

questions.q: Match each term from Intuitions vs. Formulas to its meaning.
pairs: Low-validity environment
A domain with significant uncertainty and unpredictability
Broken-leg rule
Override a formula only for rare, decisive information
Multiple regression
Algorithm finding optimal weights for predictors
Improper linear model
Formula combining standardized predictors with equal weights
questions.explain: These terms carry the chapter's argument: in low-validity environments formulas win, overrides need broken-leg evidence, and equal weights do about as well as regression.

questions.q: Match each piece of evidence to what it shows about the inconsistency of human judgment.
pairs: Radiologists reading chest X-rays
Contradict themselves 20% of the time on the same picture
101 independent auditors
Showed similar inconsistency rating internal corporate audits
Review of 41 studies of professionals
Such inconsistency is typical, even within a few minutes
Parole judges
Parole chances change with time since the last food break
questions.explain: All four show that human summary judgments vary with circumstances, while a formula given the same input always returns the same answer.

questions.q: Sort each description by whether Kahneman applies it to expert judgment or to a prediction formula.

items.t: Tries to be clever and weigh complex combinations of features
Can shift with something as small as a cool breeze
Contradicts itself when shown the same case twice
Always returns the same answer for the same input
Can be built on the back of an envelope
With equal weights, is not affected by accidents of sampling

questions.explain: Complexity and context-driven inconsistency are Kahneman's two reasons experts lose, while consistency and simplicity are the formula's strengths.

questions.q: Sort these signs by whether they describe a newborn with an Apgar score of 8 or above or one with a score of 4 or below.

items.t: Pink
Squirming and crying
Pulse of 100 or more
Bluish
Flaccid and passive
Slow or weak pulse

questions.explain: A high score marked a baby in good shape, while a score of 4 or below marked one in need of immediate intervention.

questions.q: Sort these by whether they were inputs to Ashenfelter's formula for predicting Bordeaux wine prices.

items.t: Average summer growing-season temperature
Amount of rain at harvest-time
Total rainfall during the previous winter
Experts' tasting of the young wine
The current market price of the young wine

questions.explain: The formula used only three weather features. Kahneman suggests tasting probably makes experts' forecasts worse, and current prices of young wines predict less well than the formula.

questions.q: Why, according to Kahneman, do clinicians' everyday experiences seem to contradict Meehl's evidence of clinical inferiority?
options: Their correct hunches are short-term predictions within therapy sessions, unlike the long-term predictions they fail at
Their patients tell them that formulas have made serious mistakes in the past
Their long-term predictions are usually confirmed by follow-up studies years later
Their training teaches them that statistical studies are unreliable
questions.explain: Many of their in-session hunches are confirmed, showing real clinical skill, but those are short-term predictions. The tasks they fail at involve long-term predictions about a patient's future.

questions.q: Why, according to Kahneman, have clinicians never had the opportunity to learn long-term prediction properly?
options: Because formulas have always made those predictions for them
Because their training programs do not teach statistics
Because patients rarely return for therapy after the first session
Because they would have to wait years for feedback
questions.explain: In-session hunches get instantaneous feedback, but long-term predictions would require waiting years to learn whether they were right, so the skill cannot be learned properly.

questions.q: In the organic apple example, what did most people do after being told the two apples taste the same and are equally nutritious and healthful?
options: Became indifferent between the two apples
Still preferred the organic apple
Switched to the commercially grown apple
Asked to taste both before choosing
questions.explain: A majority still preferred the organic fruit, illustrating the strong preference for the natural over the artificial that underlies aversion to algorithms.

questions.q: How, according to The New York Times as quoted by Kahneman, did French wine circles respond to Ashenfelter's formula?
options: With grateful enthusiasm for an improved forecasting tool
With polite skepticism and calls for further study
Somewhere between violent and hysterical
With quiet adoption by the major wine merchants
questions.explain: The response ranged “somewhere between violent and hysterical,” although one might have expected wine lovers to be grateful for a demonstrably better forecast.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman expect hostility to algorithms to soften over time?
options: Because formulas will soon become perfectly accurate
Because clinicians will be retrained in statistics
Because laws will require their use in medicine
Because algorithms are playing an expanding role in everyday life
questions.explain: As people get used to software recommendations, automated credit limits, simple health guidelines and sports formulas, the discomfort with Meehl's pattern should eventually fade.

questions.q: Why is it, in Kahneman's view, easy to sympathize with clinicians who rejected Meehl's research?
questions.a: Clinicians have many hunches in every therapy session that are confirmed, so their experience shows them real clinical skill. But that skill concerns short-term predictions with instant feedback, while they fail at long-term predictions they never had the chance to learn. The line between what they can and cannot do is not obvious to them: they know they are skilled, but not the boundaries of their skill, so a mechanical formula beating them seems obviously wrong.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say the rational argument that it is unethical to ignore a better algorithm runs into a stubborn psychological reality?
questions.a: Meehl and others argue that if an algorithm makes fewer mistakes, relying on intuition for important decisions is unethical. But for most people the cause of a mistake matters: a child dying because an algorithm erred is more poignant than the same tragedy caused by human error. That difference in emotional intensity is readily translated into a moral preference for human judgment, especially when decisions are consequential.

questions.q: How do the examples of John Henry, Kasparov versus Deep Blue, and the organic apple illustrate the roots of hostility to algorithms?
questions.a: When a human competes with a machine, our sympathies lie with our fellow human. Kahneman roots the aversion to algorithms in a strong preference for the natural over the synthetic or artificial. Most people still prefer the organic apple even when told it is identical to the commercial one, and beer sells better labeled "All Natural," so it is unsurprising that people resist mechanical rules deciding about humans.

questions.q: Kahneman says that clinical psychologists who responded to Meehl with hostility and disbelief were in the grip of an illusion of ____ about their long-term predictions.
questions.explain: They were “in the grip of an illusion of skill” because their real short-term skill led them to believe they could make long-term predictions too.

questions.q: Meehl and other proponents of algorithms argued that it is ____ to rely on intuitive judgments for important decisions if an available algorithm will make fewer mistakes.
questions.explain: Their argument is rational and compelling, but it collides with the feeling that the cause of a mistake matters.

questions.q: Kahneman roots the aversion to algorithms making decisions about humans in the strong preference many people have for the ____ over the synthetic or artificial.
questions.explain: The preference for the natural shows in the organic apple study and in beer sold with "All Natural" labels.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman cite as everyday uses of algorithms that should soften hostility to them?
options: Software recommendations for books or music
Decisions about credit limits
Choosing when to punt on fourth down
Jury verdicts in criminal trials
Picking a holiday destination
questions.explain: Recommendations, credit limits and sports decisions such as punting on fourth down are among Kahneman's examples. Jury verdicts and picking a holiday destination are not among his examples.

questions.q: Which of these help explain why clinicians do not know the boundaries of their own skill?
options: Many of their in-session hunches are confirmed
Their long-term predictions give them no timely feedback
The line between what they do well and badly is not obvious
Formulas predict patients' long-term futures almost perfectly
They rarely make any predictions during therapy sessions
questions.explain: Confirmed short-term hunches, years-delayed feedback and a blurry boundary combine to hide clinicians' limits. Even the best formulas do only modestly well at long-term prediction, and clinicians make many predictions in sessions.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says the prejudice against algorithms softens when the decisions involved are consequential.
questions.explain: The opposite: the prejudice against algorithms is magnified when decisions are consequential, as in Meehl's description of clinicians' horror at a treatable case misclassified by an equation.

questions.q: True or false: One oenophile scoffed that predicting wine prices with Ashenfelter's formula was like judging movies without actually seeing them.
questions.explain: This scoff, along with calling the findings “ludicrous and absurd,” illustrates the deep resistance to the demystification of expertise.

questions.q: Put these steps of the argument in The Hostility to Algorithms in the order Kahneman presents them.
items: Clinicians' confirmed hunches seem to prove their skill
Those hunches are short-term; the failures are long-term predictions
The debate's moral dimension and the clinicians' labels for each method
The preference for the natural, as in the organic apple
The violent reaction of the wine community to Ashenfelter
The expanding role of algorithms should soften hostility
questions.explain: The section explains the clinicians' illusion first, then widens to general human attitudes and examples of resistance, and ends on a hopeful note about algorithms becoming familiar.

questions.q: Match each example from The Hostility to Algorithms to the point it illustrates.
pairs: John Henry and Garry Kasparov
In human versus machine contests, we side with the human
The organic apple
People prefer the natural even when told it is identical
"All Natural" beer labels
Natural claims on labels increase sales
A child dying from an algorithm's error
The cause of a mistake affects how bad it feels
Automated credit-limit decisions
Algorithmic decisions are coming to be taken for granted
questions.explain: Each example supports Kahneman's account of why people resist algorithms and why that resistance may fade.

questions.q: Sort these words by whether, according to Meehl, they were used to describe the statistical method or the clinical method.

items.t: Mechanical
Atomistic
Rigid
Pedantic
Holistic
Sympathetic
Configural
Rich

questions.explain: Critics called the statistical method cold words like mechanical and rigid, while proponents praised the clinical method as holistic and rich, showing the debate's moral dimension.

questions.q: Why did Kahneman conclude that the Israeli army's original interview had failed?
options: It took far too long for each recruit
It let interviewers explore what they found most interesting, the dynamics of the recruit's mental life
It relied entirely on psychometric tests and never met the recruit
It was run by officers with no interest in dealing with people
questions.explain: He concluded it failed at least in part because interviewers pursued the interviewee's mental dynamics instead of gathering specific facts about his life in his normal environment.

questions.q: Why did Kahneman have interviewers ask standardized factual questions and rate the six traits in a fixed sequence?
options: To shorten the interview to under ten minutes
To let interviewers form a richer general impression
To make the interviews more interesting for recruits
To combat the halo effect from favorable first impressions
questions.explain: Factual questions and a fixed order, each trait scored before moving on, were precautions against the halo effect, in which early favorable impressions influence later judgments.

questions.q: What was the big surprise in the results of Kahneman's new army interview?
options: The "close your eyes" intuitive rating predicted as well as the sum of the six trait ratings
The new procedure predicted no better than the old one
The six trait ratings predicted soldiers' performance almost perfectly
The commanding officers refused to evaluate the soldiers
questions.explain: The intuitive rating made after the structured interview did just as well as the sum of the six ratings. The new procedure was a substantial improvement but far from perfect.

questions.q: How did Kahneman finally combine the "close your eyes" rating with the six trait ratings?
options: He used only the six trait ratings and discarded the intuitive score
He let the interviewer's intuitive score override the trait ratings
He gave the intuitive rating the same weight as the sum of the six trait ratings
He averaged the six ratings and ignored the intuitive score when they disagreed
questions.explain: He set a formula giving the “close your eyes” evaluation the same weight as the sum of the six trait ratings, so intuition counted but only inside a fixed rule.

questions.q: What lesson did Kahneman draw from the success of the "close your eyes" rating in his army interview?
questions.a: He learned that intuition adds value even in the much-derided selection interview, but only after a disciplined collection of objective information and disciplined scoring of separate traits. So he gave the intuitive rating equal weight with the sum of the six traits. His more general lesson was “do not simply trust intuitive judgment—your own or that of others—but do not dismiss it, either.”

questions.q: Why did the army interviewers come close to mutiny, and how did Kahneman resolve it?
questions.a: The bright young interviewers were displeased to be told, by someone hardly older, to switch off their intuition and ask only boring factual questions; one complained that he was turning them into robots. Kahneman compromised: they had to carry out the interview exactly as instructed, then close their eyes, imagine the recruit as a soldier and give a score from 1 to 5. That compromise unexpectedly produced a useful predictor.

questions.q: Which two lessons from Meehl's book did Kahneman apply when redesigning the army interview?
questions.a: First, interviewers should use their limited time to gather as much specific information as possible about the recruit's life in his normal environment, rather than exploring his mental dynamics. Second, interviewers' global evaluations should no longer determine the final decision, because statistical summaries of separately evaluated attributes achieve higher validity. So interviewers scored six traits separately and a standard formula computed the fitness score.

questions.q: One of Kahneman's army interviewers, told to switch off intuition and ask only factual questions, complained that Kahneman was turning them into ____.
questions.explain: The complaint led to the compromise of a final “close your eyes” rating after the structured interview.

questions.q: Kahneman's standardized, factual interview questions were meant to combat the ____ effect, where favorable first impressions influence later judgments.
questions.explain: Rating one trait at a time in a fixed sequence was a further precaution against halos.

questions.q: Kahneman told the army interviewers that their function was to provide reliable measurements and to leave the predictive ____ to him.
questions.explain: By predictive validity he meant the formula he would devise to combine their separate ratings, so interviewers did not need to predict the recruit's future adjustment.

questions.q: Which of these were among the personality traits Kahneman listed for his army interview?
options: Responsibility
Sociability
Masculine pride
Creativity
Intelligence
questions.explain: Kahneman names responsibility, sociability and masculine pride among his six traits. Creativity and intelligence are not among the traits he mentions.

questions.q: Which of these kinds of factual questions about a recruit's life before enlistment did Kahneman's interview include?
options: The number of different jobs he had held
How regular and punctual he had been in work or studies
The frequency of his interactions with friends
What he dreamed about at night
How he felt about his parents
questions.explain: The questions aimed to measure each trait as objectively as possible from facts, such as jobs held, punctuality and contact with friends, not from the recruit's inner life.

questions.q: True or false: When Kahneman visited his old army base some forty-five years later, the Psychological Unit had dropped the "close your eyes" step from its interviews.
questions.explain: The current practice had not changed much from his design, and the commanding officer ended her description by saying they still tell interviewers to close their eyes.

questions.q: Put the steps of Kahneman's redesigned army interview in order.
items: Ask factual questions about the recruit's past for one trait
Rate that trait on a five-point scale
Move on to the next trait in the fixed sequence
After all six traits, close your eyes and give a 1-to-5 score
Combine the ratings with a standard formula
questions.explain: Interviewers gathered facts and scored each trait in a fixed order to prevent halos, gave the intuitive rating last, and left the final prediction to the formula.

questions.q: Put these events from Kahneman's army interview story in chronological order.
items: Meehl's "little book" appears
Kahneman, aged twenty-one, is assigned to set up an interview system
Several hundred interviews are conducted by the new method
Commanding officers' evaluations of the soldiers are collected
Kahneman wins a Nobel Prize in economics
On a visit to the base, he hears "And then we tell them, 'Close your eyes.'"
questions.explain: Meehl's book appeared a year before Kahneman's 1955 assignment; results came months after the interviews, and the base visit followed his Nobel Prize some forty-five years later.

questions.q: Match each phrase from Kahneman's army story to what it refers to.
pairs: "Completely useless"
The army's original interview procedure
"Moderately useful"
The new procedure summing six trait ratings
"Close your eyes"
An intuitive 1-to-5 score given after the structured interview
"Reliable measurements"
The interviewers' only task under the new method
questions.explain: Kahneman moved the army from a “completely useless” interview to a “moderately useful” one, keeping a disciplined place for intuition at the end.

questions.q: Sort these features by whether they belonged to the army's original interview or to Kahneman's redesigned one.

items.t: Cover a range of topics and form a general impression
Explore the dynamics of the recruit's mental life
Interviewer's global evaluation drives the decision
Score six traits separately on a five-point scale
Ask factual questions about life before enlistment
