Final score computed by a standard formula

questions.explain: Following Meehl, Kahneman replaced global impressions with separately scored facts and a mechanical combination.

questions.q: In Kahneman's advice for hiring a sales representative, why should you not do a "close your eyes" rating at the end?
options: Because intuition never adds any value in interviews
Because you are in charge of the final decision
Because it takes too much time after six traits
Because candidates may notice and feel uncomfortable
questions.explain: Kahneman says that because you are in charge of the final decision, you should not do a “close your eyes.” His army interviewers did not make the final decision, and their intuition was given only a fixed weight in a formula.

questions.q: Describe the procedure Kahneman recommends for hiring a sales representative.
questions.a: Choose a few traits that are prerequisites for success, about six, as independent as possible and assessable reliably by a few factual questions. List the questions for each trait and decide how to score it on a 1 to 5 scale, knowing what "very weak" and "very strong" mean. Collect information one trait at a time, scoring each before moving on, add up the six scores, and hire the candidate with the highest total.

questions.q: What does Kahneman mean when he tells a hiring manager to resist the wish to "invent broken legs"?
questions.a: Meehl's broken-leg rule allows overriding a formula only for rare and decisive information. A manager who likes another candidate better will be tempted to find reasons, framed as special information, to overrule the scores. Kahneman asks you to firmly resolve to hire the candidate with the highest final score, because inventing such exceptions brings back the intuitive judgment the procedure is meant to discipline.

questions.q: In Kahneman's hiring procedure, he advises not overdoing the number of traits and says that ____ dimensions is a good number.
questions.explain: Six dimensions mirrors his army interview, and the traits should be as independent as possible from each other.

questions.q: Which of these qualities should the traits in Kahneman's hiring procedure have?
options: They are prerequisites for success in the position
They are as independent as possible from each other
They can be assessed reliably with a few factual questions
They are as numerous as possible, to capture the whole person
They overlap, so that each trait checks the others
questions.explain: Kahneman wants a few independent, reliably assessable prerequisites for success. He explicitly warns against overdoing the number, and independence rules out overlapping traits.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman estimates that preparing traits, questions and scoring rules for a structured hiring interview takes about half an hour.
questions.explain: He calls it a small investment that can make a significant difference in the quality of the people you hire.

questions.q: Put the steps of Kahneman's do-it-yourself hiring procedure in order.
items: Select about six independent traits needed for the job
Write factual questions and a 1-to-5 scoring scheme for each trait
Interview, scoring one trait at a time
Add up the six scores for each candidate
Hire the candidate with the highest total
questions.explain: Preparation comes first, halo effects are avoided by scoring trait by trait, and the final choice is made mechanically by the total score.

questions.q: Match each hiring pitfall to the remedy Kahneman recommends.
pairs: Halo effects from early impressions
Collect information one trait at a time
Liking a lower-scoring candidate better
Hire the candidate with the highest score anyway
Vague, inconsistent scoring
Define in advance what very weak and very strong mean
Walking into the interview unprepared
Spend half an hour choosing traits and questions
questions.explain: Each remedy replaces an intuitive habit with a bit of discipline, which Kahneman says the procedure requires more than effort.

questions.q: Sort these hiring behaviors by whether Kahneman recommends them or warns against them.

items.t: Score each trait before moving to the next
Add up the six scores to evaluate each candidate
Resolve in advance to hire the top scorer
Skip around between traits
Choose by "I looked into his eyes and liked what I saw"
Switch to the candidate you like better

questions.explain: Kahneman promises that the disciplined procedure is much more likely to find the best candidate than an unprepared, overall intuitive judgment.

questions.q: Match each remark from Speaking of Judges vs. Formulas to the idea from Intuitions vs. Formulas that it applies.
pairs: "Whenever we can replace human judgment by a formula, we should at least consider it."
Formulas match or beat experts in low-validity domains
"He thinks his judgments are complex and subtle, but a simple combination of scores could probably do better."
Complexity usually reduces validity; simple combinations work better
"Let's decide in advance what weight to give to the data we have on the candidates' past performance."
Interviewers overweight personal impressions unless weights are fixed
questions.explain: The remarks condense the chapter: consider formulas, distrust claims of subtle complexity, and fix weights before interview impressions take over.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: In Kahneman's account of academic controversies, why did he turn to adversarial collaborations instead of the usual critique, reply and rejoinder?
questions.a: Kahneman found hostile exchanges a waste of time: replies rarely concede anything and rejoinders almost never admit the critique was wrong, so he never found them instructive. In an adversarial collaboration, scholars who disagree on the science agree to write a jointly authored paper on their differences, sometimes doing research together with an arbiter moderating tense cases.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Sort these features into a hostile journal exchange or an adversarial collaboration, as Kahneman describes them.

items.t: Replies rarely concede anything to a biting critique
Exercises in sarcasm for beginners and advanced sarcasm
A failure to respond can be read as conceding error
Opponents write a jointly authored paper on their differences
Opponents sometimes conduct research together
In tense cases, an arbiter moderates the research

questions.explain: Kahneman found hostile exchanges uninstructive because neither side concedes anything, so he sought adversarial collaborations in which opponents work on their differences together.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Put the stages of a typical scientific journal controversy, as Kahneman describes it, in order.
items: Original research is published
Someone publishes a critique of it
The original author replies
The critic writes a rejoinder
questions.explain: Kahneman says such exchanges often begin with a critique of another's research, followed by a reply and a rejoinder, and he found them rarely instructive.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: When scholars who disagree on the science agree to write a jointly authored paper on their differences, Kahneman calls it an ____ collaboration.
questions.explain: Kahneman engaged in a few adversarial collaborations as an alternative to hostile exchanges; his most satisfying one was with Gary Klein.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Which of these describe the Naturalistic Decision Making (NDM) scholars led by Gary Klein?
options: They mostly work in organizations, studying how experts work
They reject the focus on biases in the heuristics and biases approach
They are deeply skeptical of rigid algorithms replacing human judgment
They rely mainly on artificial laboratory experiments
They count Paul Meehl among their heroes
questions.explain: NDMers study real experts at work, reject the bias-focused approach and distrust algorithms. They criticize artificial experiments rather than relying on them, and Kahneman notes that Meehl is not among their heroes.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: True or false: Naturalistic Decision Making scholars are deeply skeptical about the value of using rigid algorithms to replace human judgment.
questions.explain: Kahneman says NDMers are deeply skeptical about replacing human judgment with rigid algorithms, which is why Paul Meehl is not among their heroes.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: In the collaboration between Kahneman and Gary Klein, what specific question did they set out to answer?
options: Whether intuition is ever better than a statistical formula
When you can trust an experienced professional who claims to have an intuition
Why professional controversies bring out the worst in academics
How many hours of practice an expert needs to become reliable
questions.explain: They aimed to map the boundary between the marvels and flaws of intuition by asking when an experienced professional's claimed intuition can be trusted. The hours-of-practice figure comes from chess research, not from their question.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Why did Kahneman invite Gary Klein, a leader of a group that disliked his work, to collaborate on the question of expert intuition?
questions.a: Kahneman had never believed that intuition is always misguided, and he had long admired Klein's studies of expertise in firefighters and his book Sources of Power. He invited Klein to join an effort to map the boundary that separates the marvels of intuition from its flaws, expecting Klein to be more trusting and himself more skeptical.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Put these events in the story of Kahneman and Klein's adversarial collaboration in chronological order.
items: Kahneman first reads a draft of Klein's paper on firefighters
Kahneman invites Klein to map the boundary between intuition's marvels and flaws
They spend seven or eight years in discussions and drafts
They publish a joint article titled A Failure to Disagree
questions.explain: Kahneman had admired Klein's firefighter work since the 1970s, later invited him to the project, and after seven or eight years of arguments and drafts they published their joint article.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Kahneman and Klein's joint article was titled Conditions for Intuitive Expertise: A Failure to ____.
questions.explain: The title tells the story: they found no real issues on which they disagreed, though Kahneman adds that they did not really agree either.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: In the kouros story that opens Malcolm Gladwell's Blink, how did several art experts react to the statue?
options: They proved it was a fake by testing the marble
They praised it as a magnificent example of a striding boy
They disagreed sharply and asked for a systematic study
They felt in their gut it was a fake but could not say why
questions.explain: The experts had strong visceral reactions that the statue was fake without being able to articulate what made them uneasy, which Kahneman calls the very definition of intuition.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: What did Kahneman and Klein conclude about a systematic search for the cue that guided the art experts in the kouros story?
options: It would have been pointless, because intuition cannot be explained
It would have shown that the experts were simply lucky
It was needed and, done properly, would probably have succeeded
It would have damaged the experts' intuitive ability
questions.explain: Many readers took the story to imply that searching for the cue would fail, but Klein and Kahneman both rejected that, believing a proper inquiry, which Klein knows how to conduct, would probably have succeeded.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: In the kouros story, the art experts knew the sculpture was a fake without knowing how they knew, which Kahneman calls the very definition of ____.
questions.explain: Knowing something without knowing how you know it is how Kahneman defines intuition when he discusses the kouros example from Blink.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: True or false: According to Kahneman, Malcolm Gladwell himself holds an almost magical view of expert intuition.
questions.explain: Many readers of the kouros story were drawn to a magical view of intuition, but Kahneman says Gladwell does not hold that position, since a later chapter of Blink describes a massive failure of intuition.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Why does Kahneman treat the election of President Harding, described in Blink, as a failure of intuition?
questions.a: Harding's only qualification was that he perfectly looked the part: square jawed and tall, the image of a strong and decisive leader. Voters chose someone who looked decisive without any other reason to believe he was, so the intuitive prediction of his performance arose from substituting one question for another. Kahneman adds that such an intuition is likely to be held with confidence.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say about the intuitive judgment that led Americans to elect President Harding?
options: Harding's only qualification was that he looked the part
He was square jawed and tall, the image of a decisive leader
Voters had solid evidence of his decisiveness in office
The prediction arose from substituting one question for another
Experts had carefully assessed his record before the vote
questions.explain: Kahneman stresses that people voted for someone who looked strong and decisive without any other reason to believe he was; the judgment came from substitution, not from evidence or expert assessment.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: According to Kahneman, how should a reader of Thinking, Fast and Slow expect an intuition like the one that elected President Harding to be held?
options: With confidence
With hesitation
With open doubt
With indifference
questions.explain: Because the Harding intuition arose from substitution, Kahneman says a reader of his book should expect it to be held with confidence, even though it was not based on any evidence about his ability.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Which of these shaped Kahneman's early thinking about intuition, in contrast to Klein's?
options: Observing the illusion of validity in himself
Reading Paul Meehl's demonstrations of the inferiority of clinical prediction
Following fireground commanders as they fought fires
Interviewing firefighting leaders about their decisions
Studying how chess masters acquire skill
questions.explain: Kahneman's thinking was formed by the illusion of validity he saw in himself and by Meehl's work; Klein's views came from his field studies of fireground commanders.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: In Klein's studies of fireground commanders, what did the commanders usually do when making a decision?
options: Compared a pair of options side by side
Listed every option and scored each one
Waited for orders from a higher authority
Generated only a single option, which was all they needed
questions.explain: The initial hypothesis was that commanders would restrict themselves to a pair of options, but that proved wrong: they usually generated a single plausible option drawn from their repertoire of patterns.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Put the steps fireground commanders followed, according to Klein's description, in order.
items: Identify a plausible option from a repertoire of patterns
Mentally simulate the option to see if it will work
Modify the option if it has shortcomings
Turn to the next most plausible option if it cannot easily be modified
questions.explain: Commanders began with the most plausible course of action, tested it by mental simulation, implemented or modified it, and only moved on to another when it could not easily be fixed.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Klein turned his description of fireground commanders into a theory he called the ____ decision (RPD) model.
questions.explain: The recognition-primed decision model applies to firefighters but also to expertise in other domains, including chess.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: In Klein's recognition-primed decision model, sort each part of the process into System 1 or System 2.

items.t: A tentative plan comes to mind
Associative memory supplies the plan automatically
The plan is mentally simulated
A deliberate check of whether the plan will work

questions.explain: Kahneman says a plan comes to mind by an automatic function of associative memory, which is System 1, and is then deliberately simulated to check that it will work, which is an operation of System 2.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Match each person to the idea or work the chapter on expert intuition links to them.
pairs: Gary Klein
Recognition-primed decision model, from studying fireground commanders
Herbert Simon
Intuition is nothing more and nothing less than recognition
Paul Meehl
Showed the inferiority of clinical prediction
Malcolm Gladwell
Wrote Blink, which opens with the kouros story
Robin Hogarth
Described wicked environments that teach the wrong lessons
questions.explain: Klein's RPD model builds on Simon's view of intuition as recognition, while Meehl, Gladwell and Hogarth supply the clinical prediction research, the kouros story and the idea of wicked environments.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: According to Kahneman, which scholar is perhaps the only one admired as a hero and founding figure by all the competing tribes in the study of decision making?
options: Paul Meehl
Gary Klein
Herbert Simon
Robin Hogarth
questions.explain: Klein's model of intuition as pattern recognition develops ideas from Herbert Simon, whom Kahneman describes as admired by all the competing clans. Meehl, by contrast, is not among the NDM group's heroes.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Herbert Simon's definition of intuition ends: Intuition is nothing more and nothing less than ____.
questions.explain: Simon's statement reduces the apparent magic of intuition to the everyday experience of memory: a cue gives access to stored information that provides the answer.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Put the steps in Herbert Simon's definition of intuition in order.
items: The situation provides a cue
The cue gives the expert access to information stored in memory
The information provides the answer
questions.explain: Simon wrote: “The situation has provided a cue; this cue has given the expert access to information stored in memory, and the information provides the answer.”

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: How does Kahneman use the example of recognizing your friend Peter to explain the moral of Herbert Simon's definition of intuition?
questions.a: We marvel at the firefighter who knows the danger intuitively without knowing how he knows, yet we also do not know how we immediately recognize our friend Peter when we enter a room. The moral is that knowing without knowing is not a distinctive feature of intuition; it is the norm of mental life.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: A veteran mechanic hears a car engine, instantly thinks of a worn belt, and then pictures whether that fault would explain every symptom before fixing it. Which idea from the chapter on expert intuition best describes this?
options: The recognition-primed decision model
The illusion of validity
A wicked environment
Emotional learning from a single experience
questions.explain: Like Klein's fireground commanders, the mechanic recognizes a plausible option from experience (System 1) and then mentally simulates it to check it (System 2), which is the recognition-primed decision model.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Explain how Klein's recognition-primed decision model involves both System 1 and System 2.
questions.a: In the first phase, a tentative plan comes to mind by an automatic function of associative memory, which is System 1. In the next phase, the plan is deliberately simulated in the mind to check whether it will work, which is an operation of System 2. If the plan fails the check, it is modified or the next plausible option is tried.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: According to Kahneman, how quickly can a fear-based intuition be acquired?
options: Only after years of repeated exposure
Often from a single experience
Only after formal instruction
Only during early childhood
questions.explain: We have inherited a great facility to learn when to be afraid, and Kahneman says one experience is often sufficient to establish a long-term aversion and fear.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Match each example from the chapter on expert intuition to the kind of quick emotional learning it illustrates.
pairs: A single dubious dish at a restaurant
A lasting reluctance to return there
The ramp to the San Francisco airport
Tension at a spot where an unpleasant event once occurred
Pavlov's dogs and the bell
A learned hope that food is coming
A young platoon commander in a narrowing ravine
Fear learned by words rather than experience
questions.explain: Each example shows how little repetition emotional learning needs, whether the lesson comes from one bad meal, one road-rage incident, conditioning, or training.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Kahneman says that what Pavlov's dogs learned when the bell signaled food can be described as a learned ____.
questions.explain: Pavlov's dogs learned a hope; Kahneman adds that learned fears are even more easily acquired.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says learned fears are acquired even more easily than learned hopes such as those of Pavlov's dogs.
questions.explain: After describing Pavlov's dogs as learning a hope, Kahneman notes that learned fears are even more easily acquired.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: When you feel uneasy in a place without any conscious memory of a triggering event, and a bad experience follows, what does Kahneman say you will call that unease in hindsight?
options: A coincidence
A bias
An intuition
A learned hope
questions.explain: Kahneman says that in hindsight you will label such unease an intuition if it is followed by a bad experience, a mode of emotional learning close to Pavlov's conditioning.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: True or false: According to Kahneman, fear can be learned only through direct personal experience.
questions.explain: Kahneman says fear can also be learned quite easily by words; the platoon commander with no combat experience tenses up in a ravine because he was taught it favors an ambush.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Why does Kahneman say expertise in complex tasks such as high-level chess or firefighting develops slowly, while emotional learning can be quick?
questions.a: Emotional learning such as fear needs little repetition and can come from a single experience or from words. Expertise in a complex domain is slow and intricate because it is not a single skill but a large collection of miniskills; a chess master, for example, must become familiar with thousands of configurations of pieces.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Studies of chess masters cited by Kahneman found that at least ____ hours of dedicated practice are required to reach the highest levels of performance.
questions.explain: Kahneman reports at least 10,000 hours of dedicated practice, about 6 years of playing chess 5 hours a day.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Sort these examples from the chapter on expert intuition by how the intuition is acquired.

items.t: Reluctance to return to a restaurant after one bad dish
A platoon commander tensing up in a narrowing ravine
Unease at a spot where an unpleasant event occurred
Understanding a complex chess position at a glance
Professional basketball skill
A fireground commander's expertise

questions.explain: Emotional learning may be quick, but Kahneman says expertise in complex tasks such as chess, basketball or firefighting is intricate and slow because it is a large collection of miniskills.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: In Kahneman's comparison of learning chess to learning to read, match each element of reading to its counterpart in chess.
pairs: Letters
Recurrent patterns of interacting pieces
A long word or a sentence
A chess position
Pronouncing a word never seen before
Dealing with a chess word never encountered
questions.explain: Kahneman says recurrent patterns of interacting pieces play the role of letters, and a chess position is a long word or a sentence; experts in both can handle new combinations of familiar elements.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Put the stages of learning to read, as Kahneman describes them in comparing reading to chess, in order from beginner to expert.
items: Working hard to recognize individual letters
Assembling letters into syllables and words
Perceiving entire clauses
Correctly pronouncing a word never seen before
questions.explain: A first grader works on letters and assembles them into syllables and words; a good adult reader perceives whole clauses, and an expert reader can even assemble familiar elements to read a new word.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: According to Kahneman, why is acquiring expertise in chess harder and slower than learning to read?
questions.a: There are many more letters in the alphabet of chess, and its words consist of many letters. After thousands of hours of practice, however, chess masters can read a situation at a glance, and the few moves that come to mind are almost always strong and sometimes creative.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Why, according to Kahneman, can a skilled reader read the opening stanza of Lewis Carroll's Jabberwocky with perfect rhythm and intonation on first sight?
options: Expert readers can assemble familiar elements into a new pattern
Nonsense poems are easier to read than ordinary text
Most readers have memorized the poem in childhood
The rhythm of the poem is marked by the printer
questions.explain: An expert reader has acquired the ability to assemble familiar elements in a new pattern and so can recognize and pronounce words never seen before, just as a chess master handles new configurations.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: According to Kahneman, what was partly responsible for his initial disagreement with Klein about trusting expert intuition?
options: They used different statistical methods
They had different experts in mind
They disagreed on how intuitive skill is acquired
They defined System 1 differently
questions.explain: Klein had spent time with fireground commanders and nurses with real expertise, while Kahneman thought of clinicians, stock pickers and political forecasters. They had quickly agreed on how intuitive skill is acquired.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Sort these positions into Gary Klein's starting view or Kahneman's starting view about trusting experts who claim an intuition.

items.t: A default attitude of trust and respect toward experts
True experts know the limits of their knowledge
Spent much time with fireground commanders and clinical nurses
A default attitude of skepticism toward experts
Many pseudo-experts have no idea they do not know what they are doing
Subjective confidence is commonly too high and often uninformative

questions.explain: Klein's trust came from working with professionals who have real expertise; Kahneman's skepticism came from clinicians, stock pickers and forecasters, and from the illusion of validity.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: True or false: Klein was more willing than Kahneman to trust experts who claim an intuition because, he said, true experts know the limits of their knowledge.
questions.explain: Klein told Kahneman that true experts know the limits of their knowledge; Kahneman countered that many pseudo-experts suffer from the illusion of validity.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Kahneman traces people's confidence in a belief to two related impressions: cognitive ease and ____.
questions.explain: We are confident when our story comes easily to mind with no contradiction or competing scenario, but ease and coherence do not guarantee that the belief is true.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Which of these did Kahneman and Klein come to agree on in their collaboration on expert intuition?
options: The confidence people have in their intuitions is not a reliable guide to their validity
Intuitions are likely to be skilled when the environment is regular and there is a chance to learn it
The nature of intuitive skill and how it is acquired
The occasional failures of algorithms are mainly opportunities to improve them
The word bias is a fair description of most expert judgment
questions.explain: The two agreed on the nature and acquisition of skill, on the unreliability of confidence, and on the conditions for skilled intuition. Seeing algorithm failures as chances to improve them is Kahneman's own taste, and Klein still winces at the word bias.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Which of these are the two basic conditions for acquiring a skill, according to Kahneman and Klein?
options: An environment that is sufficiently regular to be predictable
An opportunity to learn its regularities through prolonged practice
High subjective confidence in one's judgments
The ability to name the cues one is using
Formal training from a recognized institution
questions.explain: When the environment is regular and there is prolonged practice to learn it, intuitions are likely to be skilled. Confidence is not a guide, and Klein's experts often use cues their System 2 has not learned to name.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Kahneman says that stock pickers and political scientists who make long-term forecasts operate in a ____ environment.
questions.explain: Their failures reflect the basic unpredictability of the events they try to forecast, unlike chess, bridge or firefighting, which have regularities that can support skill.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Match each term from the chapter on expert intuition to its meaning.
pairs: Naturalistic Decision Making
Study of how experts work in real organizations
Adversarial collaboration
Opponents jointly write a paper on their differences
Wicked environment
A setting where professionals learn the wrong lessons from experience
Zero-validity environment
A setting where events are basically unpredictable
Illusion of validity
Pseudo-experts not knowing they do not know what they are doing
questions.explain: These terms frame the debate: NDM is Klein's school, adversarial collaboration is how the two worked, and wicked and zero-validity environments are where intuition cannot be trusted despite the illusion of validity.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: What is a wicked environment, and how does the story of the early twentieth-century physician who predicted typhoid illustrate it?
questions.a: Robin Hogarth described wicked environments as ones in which professionals are likely to learn the wrong lessons from experience. The physician tested his hunches by palpating patients' tongues without washing his hands, so he spread the disease himself. When patient after patient became ill, he developed a sense of clinical infallibility, though his accurate predictions had nothing to do with professional intuition.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Put the events in the story of the typhoid-predicting physician, borrowed by Robin Hogarth from Lewis Thomas, in order.
items: The physician has an intuition that a patient is about to develop typhoid
He tests the hunch by palpating the patient's tongue
He moves to the next patient without washing his hands
Patient after patient becomes ill
He develops a sense of clinical infallibility
questions.explain: The physician's predictions came true because he was spreading the disease, so the environment taught him the wrong lesson about his own skill.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: According to Kahneman, why did the clinicians in Paul Meehl's studies perform poorly, and how do we know their failure was not due to lack of talent?
questions.a: Meehl's clinicians were not inept; they were assigned tasks with no simple solution, in low-validity situations that did not allow high accuracy. We know this because the best statistical algorithms, though more accurate than the clinicians, were never very accurate, and the studies never produced a smoking gun case in which clinicians missed a highly valid cue the algorithm detected.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Which of these are the reasons Kahneman gives for why statistical algorithms greatly outdo humans in noisy environments?
options: They are more likely to detect weakly valid cues
They maintain a modest level of accuracy by using such cues consistently
They regularly find strong cues that human observers miss entirely
They can process cases faster than human judges
They are immune to the influence of the environment
questions.explain: Algorithms win by detecting weak cues and applying them consistently. Kahneman says missing a strong cue is unlikely for humans, because if a strong predictive cue exists, human observers will find it given a decent opportunity.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Sort these domains according to Kahneman's account of whether their environment can support skilled intuition.

items.t: Chess
Bridge and poker
Firefighting
Nursing
Picking stocks
Long-term political forecasting
The clinical predictions studied by Meehl

questions.explain: Chess is an extreme regular environment and bridge, poker, nursing and firefighting have orderly regularities; stock picking and long-term political forecasting are zero-validity, and Meehl's clinicians worked in low-validity situations.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: For what does Kahneman think it is fair to blame professionals who forecast in an unpredictable world, and what does he say about their intuitive hits?
questions.a: It is wrong to blame anyone for failing to forecast accurately in an unpredictable world, but it is fair to blame professionals for believing they can succeed in an impossible task. Claims of correct intuitions in such situations are self-delusional at best, and in the absence of valid cues, intuitive hits are due either to luck or to lies.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Kahneman's rule: intuition cannot be trusted in the absence of stable ____ in the environment.
questions.explain: Kahneman says that if you are surprised by this conclusion, you still have a lingering belief that intuition is magic.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: A friend boasts that her gut feeling has picked next year's winning stocks three years in a row. Applying the chapter on expert intuition, what best explains her success?
options: Highly valid cues that her System 1 has learned to use
Prolonged practice in a regular environment
Accurate feedback that sharpened her skill
Luck, since stock picking offers no valid cues
questions.explain: Kahneman places stock picking in a zero-validity environment, and in the absence of valid cues intuitive hits are due either to luck or to lies, not to skill.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: In Kahneman's example of learning to brake on curves, why are the conditions for learning ideal?
options: The rules of braking can be learned from a manual
You receive immediate and unambiguous feedback at every bend
Every curve is exactly the same as the last
An instructor corrects every mistake you make
questions.explain: Each turn gives the mild reward of a comfortable curve or the mild punishment of difficulty handling the car, and the variability of curves prepares you for any curve you meet.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: According to Kahneman, why is skill harder to acquire by sheer experience for a harbor pilot maneuvering large ships than for a driver taking curves?
options: The harbor pilot's situations are less regular
Harbor pilots get less practice than drivers
Feedback on actions comes only after a long delay
Harbor pilots receive no training at all
questions.explain: Kahneman says the harbor pilot's situations are no less regular than driving, so the difficulty is the long delay between actions and outcomes, not irregularity.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Kahneman says that whether professionals can develop intuitive expertise depends essentially on the quality and speed of ____, as well as sufficient opportunity to practice.
questions.explain: Driving gives fast, clear feedback while harbor piloting gives slow feedback; that difference governs how easily skill can be learned by experience.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Sort these tasks from the chapter on expert intuition by the kind of feedback the professional receives.

items.t: A driver braking on a curve
An anesthesiologist acting during surgery
A psychotherapist watching a patient's immediate reaction
A radiologist making a diagnosis
A harbor pilot maneuvering a large ship
A psychotherapist choosing a general treatment approach

questions.explain: Drivers, anesthesiologists and therapists reading immediate reactions see results quickly; radiologists learn little about their accuracy, harbor pilots face long delays, and therapists rarely see long-term outcomes.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: True or false: According to Kahneman, radiologists are in a better position than anesthesiologists to develop useful intuitive skills.
questions.explain: It is the reverse: anesthesiologists see the effects of their actions quickly, while radiologists obtain little information about the accuracy of their diagnoses or the pathologies they miss.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Match each professional in the chapter on expert intuition to the feedback conditions Kahneman describes.
pairs: Anesthesiologist
The effects of actions are likely to be quickly evident
Radiologist
Little information about the accuracy of diagnoses
Harbor pilot
Long delay between actions and noticeable outcomes
Driver on a curve
Immediate and unambiguous feedback at every bend
questions.explain: Kahneman uses these cases to show that the quality and speed of feedback, not the regularity of the task alone, decide whether intuitive skill can develop.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: According to Kahneman, what intuitive skills can psychotherapists develop, and what can they not learn from experience?
questions.a: Psychotherapists observe patients' immediate reactions to what they say, so they can develop the intuitive skill to find the words and tone that calm anger, forge confidence or focus attention. They cannot learn which general treatment approach suits different patients, because feedback on long-term outcomes is sparse, delayed or usually nonexistent, and too ambiguous to support learning.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Which of these describe the feedback psychotherapists receive about their patients' long-term outcomes, according to Kahneman?
options: Sparse
Delayed
Immediate
Unambiguous
Plentiful
questions.explain: Kahneman says this feedback is sparse, delayed or usually nonexistent, and too ambiguous to support learning, the opposite of the immediate reactions therapists see in a session.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: How does Kahneman explain why experts are often overconfident at the end of his discussion of feedback and practice?
options: Experts do not recognize the limits of their professional skill
Experts deliberately exaggerate to win clients
Experts receive too much feedback to process
Experts ignore regular environments
questions.explain: Clinical psychologists, stock pickers and pundits have skills in some tasks but have not learned which tasks their intuition will betray them in; these unrecognized limits help explain overconfidence.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Kahneman says short-term anticipation and long-term ____ are different tasks, and a therapist has had the chance to learn only the first.
questions.explain: A therapist skilled at anticipating what a patient will say next may wrongly conclude she can also predict how the patient will do next year.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Why does Kahneman say an experienced psychotherapist who reads her patients well is not justified in concluding she can predict how a patient will do next year?
options: Short-term anticipation and long-term forecasting are different tasks
Therapists are poorly trained in reading patients
Patients rarely react to what therapists say
Long-term outcomes are recorded too precisely to need intuition
questions.explain: The therapist has had ample chance to learn what a patient will say next but no adequate chance to learn long-term outcomes, so her skill in one task does not carry over to the other.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: A sommelier with superb tasting skill claims her palate also tells her which new wineries will be commercial successes in ten years. Applying the chapter on expert intuition, what is the best response?
options: Trust her, since true experts know the limits of their knowledge
Trust her, since her confidence reflects long experience
Accept it, because tasting and forecasting use the same cues
Doubt it, because skill in one task does not extend to a different task
questions.explain: Kahneman says expertise is a collection of skills, and skill at a short-term task does not justify confidence in long-term forecasting, which the expert has had no adequate opportunity to learn.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Why does Kahneman say the same professional can be highly expert in some tasks of her domain while remaining a novice in others?
questions.a: Expertise is not a single skill but a collection of skills, and some aspects of any professional's tasks are much easier to learn than others. Surgeons can be more proficient in some operations than others; chess is an exception, because by the time players become experts they have seen almost everything.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: In Kahneman's comparison with judging whether a work of art is genuine, how should you evaluate an expert's intuition?
options: Look closely at the judgment itself
Focus on its provenance rather than the piece itself
Ask the expert how confident she feels
Compare it with the judgments of other experts
questions.explain: As with art, you do better by focusing on provenance, meaning whether the environment was regular and the judge had a chance to learn it, than by examining the intuition itself.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: According to Kahneman and Klein's final conclusion, under what conditions can you trust someone's intuitions?
questions.a: You can trust intuitions when the environment is sufficiently regular and the judge has had a chance to learn its regularities. Then associative machinery will recognize situations and generate quick and accurate predictions and decisions. Even in a regular environment, you should check whether there was an adequate opportunity to learn the cues.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: True or false: Kahneman notes that a talented chess youngster, on the way to near perfection, makes some mistakes with great confidence.
questions.explain: Skill does not become perfect all at once, so even in a regular environment you should consider whether there was an adequate opportunity to learn the cues.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: According to Kahneman, what happens to judgment in a less regular, or low-validity, environment?
options: System 2 takes over and judgment slows down
People refuse to give an answer
System 1 answers by substitution, creating coherence where there is none
Experts become aware of the limits of their skill
questions.explain: In low-validity environments the heuristics of judgment are invoked: System 1 answers a difficult question by substituting an easier one, and the answer may pass System 2's lax review.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: An investor feels sure a start-up will thrive, but her judgment is really driven by how energetic and capable its founder seems. Which process from the chapter on expert intuition does this illustrate?
options: Substitution of an easier question
Recognition of a valid cue
Learning from rapid feedback
Emotional learning from words
questions.explain: Kahneman gives the same kind of example: forecasting a company's commercial future while your evaluation is dominated by impressions of its executives' energy and competence, which is substitution.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Because judgments that answer the wrong question can also be made with high confidence, Kahneman says subjective confidence is not a good ____ of accuracy.
questions.explain: A substituted answer that is the only one coming to mind can feel just like a valid expert judgment, so confidence cannot tell them apart.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Why can a judgment produced by substitution feel as convincing as a valid expert judgment, according to Kahneman?
questions.a: Substitution occurs automatically, so you often do not know the origin of a judgment that your System 2 endorses and adopts. If it is the only judgment that comes to mind, it may be subjectively undistinguishable from valid judgments made with expert confidence. This is why judgments that answer the wrong question can also be made with high confidence.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Which of these did Kahneman and Klein know from the outset would end up on the valid side of the boundary of intuitive expertise?
options: Fireground commanders
Pediatric nurses
Stock pickers
Pundits
The specialties studied by Meehl
questions.explain: Kahneman says the contours of the solution were apparent from the beginning: fireground commanders and pediatric nurses on one side, and Meehl's specialties, stock pickers and pundits on the other.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Why does Kahneman say it took him and Klein years to reach a conclusion whose contours were apparent from the beginning?
questions.a: It took long discussions, endless drafts and hundreds of e-mails negotiating over words, and they almost gave up more than once. Kahneman says this is what always happens when a project ends reasonably well: once you understand the main conclusion, it seems it was always obvious.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Sort these attitudes into those Kahneman attributes to Gary Klein and those he attributes to himself after their collaboration.

items.t: Still winces when the word bias is mentioned
Enjoys stories of algorithms leading to absurd decisions
Views occasional failures of algorithms as opportunities to improve them
Enjoys the comeuppance of arrogant experts in zero-validity situations

questions.explain: Kahneman says their attitudes, emotions and tastes changed remarkably little over the years, showing most clearly in what each finds amusing and interesting.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: True or false: Kahneman reports that his and Klein's attitudes, emotions and tastes converged substantially over the years of their collaboration.
questions.explain: Kahneman says these attitudes, emotions and tastes changed remarkably little, even though the two reached joint solutions on almost all the substantive issues.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Match each situation to the verdict on intuition that follows from Kahneman and Klein's conclusions.
pairs: Regular environment and ample chance to learn its cues
Intuitions are likely to be skilled and can be trusted
Regular environment but little chance yet to learn the cues
Some mistakes may be made with great confidence
Low-validity environment
Heuristics and substitution produce plausible answers
Zero-validity environment
Intuitive hits are due to luck or lies
questions.explain: Trust depends on the regularity of the environment and the judge's learning history, not on how confident the judge feels.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: How does Kahneman weigh the outcome of his collaboration with Klein at the end of the chapter on expert intuition?
options: Their emotional differences made the agreement worthless
They should have published separate articles instead
Klein finally accepted that intuition is usually wrong
Their intellectual agreement matters more than lasting emotional differences
questions.explain: Although their attitudes and tastes barely changed, Kahneman concludes that finding as much intellectual agreement as they did is surely more important than the emotional differences that remained.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Match each remark from Speaking of Expert Intuition to the idea it applies.
pairs: How much practice has she had?
Prolonged practice is needed to learn regularities
Is the environment of start-ups regular enough to justify an intuition against the base rates?
Skill requires a sufficiently regular environment
She is very confident, but confidence is a poor index of accuracy
Confidence is not a reliable guide to validity
How quick and how clear was the feedback he received?
The quality and speed of feedback decide whether skill can develop
questions.explain: Each remark turns one of the chapter's conditions for trusting intuition into a practical question about an expert.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Which of these questions does the chapter on expert intuition suggest asking before trusting someone's intuitive judgment?
options: How much practice has this person had at this particular task?
Is the environment regular enough to justify the intuition?
How quick and how clear was the feedback on past judgments?
How confident does the person feel?
How eloquently can the person explain the judgment?
questions.explain: The chapter's sample remarks focus on practice, regularity and feedback; subjective confidence is called a poor index of accuracy, and Klein's experts often cannot name their cues.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: One of the chapter's sample remarks: She is very confident in her decision, but subjective confidence is a poor ____ of the accuracy of a judgment.
questions.explain: The remark applies the principle that the confidence people have in their intuitions is not a reliable guide to their validity.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Put these chapters of Part III, Overconfidence, in the order they appear in the book.
items: The Illusion of Understanding
The Illusion of Validity
Intuitions vs. Formulas
Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
The Outside View
questions.explain: Chapter 22 on expert intuition follows chapters on the illusions of understanding and validity and on Meehl's formulas, and comes just before The Outside View.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Why does the chapter Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It? come right after Intuitions vs. Formulas?
options: It repeats Meehl's case with new statistical data
It introduces the two systems for the first time
After the case for formulas, it asks when intuition can still be trusted
It begins the book's discussion of choices and risk
questions.explain: Having shown that formulas often beat clinicians, Kahneman turns to Klein's view of expert intuition to work out the conditions under which intuition deserves trust, rather than dismissing it altogether.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: What does the title Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It? signal about the chapter's argument?
questions.a: The title asks when, not whether, expert intuition can be trusted, signalling that Kahneman, who had never believed intuition is always misguided, aims to map the boundary between its marvels and its flaws. The answer turns out to depend on the environment and the expert's chance to learn it, not on the expert's confidence.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Match each chapter of Part III, Overconfidence, to its central concern as reflected in the chapter on expert intuition.
pairs: The Illusion of Validity
Confidence that persists without real predictive skill
Intuitions vs. Formulas
Meehl's finding that clinical prediction is inferior
Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
Conditions under which intuitive expertise is valid
The Outside View
The next chapter after expert intuition in Part III
questions.explain: The expert intuition chapter draws on the illusion of validity and on Meehl's clinicians from the two chapters before it, then leads into The Outside View.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: Put the sections of the chapter Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It? in the order they appear.
items: Marvels and Flaws
Intuition as Recognition
Acquiring Skill
The Environment of Skill
Feedback and Practice
Evaluating Validity
questions.explain: The chapter moves from examples of intuition's successes and failures, to what intuition is and how it is learned, to the conditions that make it valid and how to judge it.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: How does the chapter on expert intuition connect to the earlier chapter The Illusion of Validity?
options: It shows that the illusion of validity affects only amateurs
It explains pseudo-experts' confidence as the illusion of validity
It argues that the illusion of validity has been overcome
It replaces the illusion of validity with the planning fallacy
questions.explain: Kahneman argues against Klein that many pseudo-experts do not know they do not know what they are doing, which he names the illusion of validity, and says his own thinking was formed by seeing it in himself.

questions.unitTitle: Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
questions.q: True or false: The chapter Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It? belongs to Part III of the book, titled Overconfidence.
questions.explain: The table of contents places chapters 19 to 24, including the chapter on expert intuition, in Part III, Overconfidence.

questions.q: In Kahneman's curriculum-team story, when each member privately wrote down how long it would take to submit a finished draft of the textbook, what did the estimates look like?
options: Narrowly centered around two years, from one and a half to two and a half years
Widely spread, from six months to more than ten years
Centered around seven years, matching the experience of other teams
Centered around five years, with Seymour Fox as the most pessimistic
questions.explain: The estimates were tightly clustered around two years, ranging from one and a half to two and a half years. Seven to ten years was the outside-view figure Seymour gave later, not the team's own estimate.

questions.q: In the curriculum-team story, what fraction of comparable teams did Seymour Fox estimate had never finished their textbook projects?
options: About 10%
About 25%
About 40%
About 75%
questions.explain: Seymour estimated that about 40% of the teams at a comparable stage ended up failing to finish the job, a possibility the team had never considered.

questions.q: Why did Kahneman ask his curriculum team to write down their estimates confidentially instead of discussing them openly first?
options: Because open discussion would have taken too much of the Friday meeting
Because collecting each person's judgment privately makes better use of the group's knowledge than open discussion
Because he wanted to test whether Seymour Fox would contradict the rest of the group
Because the Ministry of Education required anonymous forecasts from its teams
questions.explain: Kahneman was following a procedure the team planned to teach: the proper way to elicit information from a group is to collect each judgment confidentially, which makes better use of the knowledge available than open discussion.

questions.q: In the curriculum-team story, what was surprising about Seymour Fox's own first estimate of the project's length?
options: It was far more pessimistic than anyone else's estimate
It was based on careful statistics about other curriculum teams
It was the only estimate that turned out to be accurate
It sat well within the group's optimistic consensus, despite what he knew about other teams
questions.explain: Seymour's prior estimate was well within the optimistic consensus; until Kahneman prompted him, there was no connection in his mind between his knowledge of other teams and his forecast for this one.

questions.q: True or false: When Kahneman asked Seymour Fox to compare the curriculum team's skills and resources with those of similar teams, Seymour ranked the team somewhat above average.
questions.explain: Seymour said the team was below average, though not by much, which meant the forecast was even slightly worse than the already grim baseline.

questions.q: True or false: The curriculum textbook was completed eight years after the Friday exercise, and by then the Ministry of Education's enthusiasm had waned and the book was never used.
questions.explain: The book was eventually completed eight years later, after Kahneman had left the team; the Ministry's initial enthusiasm had faded and the text was never used.

questions.q: Put the steps of the Friday afternoon exercise with the curriculum team in the order they happened.
items: Each member privately writes an estimate of the time to finish the draft
Kahneman asks Seymour Fox to recall similar teams at a comparable stage
Seymour reveals that about 40% of such teams never finished
Seymour says those that finished took seven to ten years
Seymour ranks the team slightly below average
The team carries on as if nothing had happened
questions.explain: The private estimates came first; then Kahneman's questions drew out the failure rate, the completion times and the team's ranking, after which the team briefly debated and carried on.

questions.q: Put these events in the history of Kahneman's curriculum project in the order they happened.
items: The team meets every Friday for about a year and writes a couple of chapters
The team estimates it will finish in about two years
Seymour Fox's statistics are noted and set aside
Kahneman leaves Israel and the team
The book is completed eight years after the exercise
The book is never used by the Ministry of Education
questions.explain: After a year of progress came the optimistic estimates and the ignored outside view; the team went on without Kahneman, finished eight years later, and the waning Ministry never used the book.

questions.q: Which of these are among the three lessons Kahneman says he eventually learned from the curriculum-team episode?
options: The distinction between the inside view and the outside view
That the team's two-year forecasts exhibited a planning fallacy
Irrational perseverance in failing to abandon the project
That regression to the mean explained the team's early progress
That hindsight bias made the project look easier than it was
questions.explain: Kahneman names three lessons: the inside versus outside view distinction, the planning fallacy in the two-year forecasts, and irrational perseverance. Regression and hindsight are ideas from other chapters, not lessons he draws here.

questions.q: Kahneman calls the third lesson of the curriculum story, the folly of failing to abandon the project that day, ____.
questions.explain: He was slowest to accept this lesson: “Facing a choice, we gave up rationality rather than give up the enterprise.”

questions.q: In the curriculum story, Kahneman says that what the team heard from Seymour Fox was ____ information, from which they should have inferred a causal story about how hard the task was.
questions.explain: Seymour's statistics were base-rate information, and like base rates usually are, they were noted and promptly set aside.

questions.q: In the curriculum story, why did Seymour Fox's statistics about other teams fail to change the team's plans, and what should the team have concluded from them?
questions.a: The statistics were base-rate information, and they conflicted with the team's direct experience of good progress and a reasonable-looking plan, so the new forecast seemed unreal. The team should have inferred a causal story: if so many teams failed and the rest took so long, writing a curriculum was much harder than they thought. Instead the statistics were treated as base rates normally are, “noted and promptly set aside.”

questions.q: What does Kahneman mean when he says that in the curriculum project the team gave up rationality rather than give up the enterprise?
questions.a: After hearing that comparable projects failed 40% of the time and took at least seven years, none of the team would rationally have agreed to start such a project, so they should have quit that day. But the warning gave no immediately compelling reason to stop, and after brief debate they carried on as if nothing had happened. Kahneman calls this irrational perseverance: keeping the project alive at the cost of abandoning sound reasoning.

questions.q: In the curriculum-team story, match each number to what it described.
pairs: About two years
The team's own private estimates of time to finish
About 40%
Share of comparable teams that never finished
Seven to ten years
Time taken by comparable teams that did finish
Eight years
Time it actually took to complete the book
questions.explain: The two-year figure was the team's inside view; 40% and seven to ten years were Seymour's outside view; eight years was the actual outcome.

questions.q: In the curriculum-team story, sort each figure or belief by whether it came from the team's own forecast or from Seymour Fox's knowledge of similar teams.

items.t: Finish in about two years
Low end of one and a half years
No thought that the project might fail
About 40% of teams never finished
No team finished in less than seven years
No team took more than ten years

questions.explain: The two-year estimates and the unexamined assumption of success were the team's inside view; the failure rate and the seven-to-ten-year range came from Seymour's memory of other teams.

questions.q: How does Kahneman define a baseline prediction in his discussion of the outside view?
options: The prediction you make about a case if you know nothing except the category it belongs to
The most optimistic forecast that a planning team can reasonably defend
The average of the confidential estimates collected from a group
The forecast an expert makes from the particular details of a case
questions.explain: A baseline prediction is what you would predict knowing only the category a case belongs to; it should be the anchor for later adjustments. Forecasting from the case's particular details is the inside view.

questions.q: In Kahneman's example of guessing the height of a woman who lives in New York City, what should happen to the estimate when you learn that her son is the starting center of his high school basketball team?
options: You should ignore the new fact because the baseline is always more reliable
You should start from the son's height instead of the city average
You should adjust away from the city average in the appropriate direction
You should replace the estimate with the average height of basketball players
questions.explain: The baseline is the average height of women in the city, and case-specific information justifies adjusting away from that mean in the appropriate direction, not discarding the baseline.

questions.q: How does Kahneman connect the curriculum team's neglect of Seymour Fox's statistics to Nisbett and Borgida's experiment on teaching psychology?
options: In both, people relied on statistics and ignored vivid personal impressions
In both, pallid statistical information was discarded when it clashed with impressions of an individual case
In both, people refused to listen because the statistics came from a non-expert
In both, people used the statistics but adjusted them too little
questions.explain: Nisbett and Borgida's students neglected the results they had just learned when predicting individual cases from bland interviews; likewise, “Pallid” statistical information is routinely discarded when it conflicts with personal impressions.

questions.q: When Kahneman asked his cousin, a distinguished lawyer, about the probability of a defendant winning in cases like the one at hand, how did the cousin respond?
options: He gave a precise figure from his firm's records
He said such statistics were available only to judges
He said the base rate was irrelevant because juries are unpredictable
He answered that every case is unique and found the question inappropriate
questions.explain: The cousin's answer that every case is unique, with a look suggesting the question was superficial, illustrates how preference for the inside view can carry moral overtones.

questions.q: Maya estimates that her thesis will take four months because she has written two chapters in five weeks and has eight to go, and she never asks how long other students' theses took. In Kahneman's terms, what is she doing?
options: Taking the outside view
Making a baseline prediction
Using reference class forecasting
Taking the inside view
questions.explain: Extrapolating from her own plan and progress while ignoring the record of similar cases is the inside view, exactly what the curriculum team did with the chapters they had already written.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman argues that the spectacular accuracy of Seymour Fox's outside-view forecast is strong evidence for the validity of the outside view.
questions.explain: Kahneman calls the accuracy a fluke that should not count as evidence; the case for the outside view rests on general grounds, that a properly chosen reference class shows where the ballpark is.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that, like the participants in the Tom W experiment, Seymour Fox knew the relevant base rate but did not think of applying it.
questions.explain: Seymour had all the knowledge needed to estimate the reference-class statistics, but his first forecast was based on the team's particular circumstances, just as Tom W participants neglected base rates they knew.

questions.q: In the outside-view discussion, Kahneman says the ____ prediction should be the anchor for further adjustments.
questions.explain: The baseline prediction, made from the category alone, is the starting point; case-specific information is then used to adjust it.

questions.q: Kahneman says the main problem with the curriculum team's forecast was failing to allow for what Donald Rumsfeld called the “____.”
questions.explain: Divorces, illnesses and crises of coordination with bureaucracies could not be foreseen, yet such events slowed the work and caused long stretches of little progress.

questions.q: When Kahneman asked Seymour Fox about other teams, Seymour estimated the base rate of success in that ____: 40% failure and seven to ten years for completion.
questions.explain: Directing attention away from the specific team and toward a class of similar cases is what produces the outside view.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give as reasons why the curriculum team's extrapolation from its early progress was a mistake?
options: The first chapters written were probably easier than the others
The team's commitment was probably at its peak at that time
Unforeseeable events such as illnesses and bureaucratic crises would slow the work
The team members lacked the expertise to write a textbook
The Ministry of Education had secretly shortened the deadline
questions.explain: Kahneman cites easier early chapters, peak commitment and above all the unknown unknowns. He never says the team lacked expertise; it included an expert in curriculum development.

questions.q: On what grounds does Kahneman say the case for the outside view should be made, given that its accuracy in the curriculum story was a fluke?
questions.a: The argument should be made on general grounds rather than on one lucky hit. If the reference class is properly chosen, the outside view indicates where the ballpark is. It may also reveal, as it did for the curriculum team, that inside-view forecasts are not even close to that ballpark.

questions.q: How does the preference for the inside view show up in the professions of law and medicine, according to Kahneman?
questions.a: The preference sometimes carries moral overtones: Kahneman's lawyer cousin replied that every case is unique and treated a question about the reference class as inappropriate and superficial. A proud emphasis on the uniqueness of cases is also common in medicine, despite advances in evidence-based medicine. The remaining ambivalence there is expressed as concern about the impersonality of procedures guided by statistics and checklists.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman find it noteworthy that the curriculum team members did not feel they needed information about other teams before making their guesses?
questions.a: Even though they could not have produced a reasonable baseline prediction themselves, they felt no need for one, and Kahneman's request for the outside view surprised everyone, including him. He says this is a common pattern: people who have information about an individual case rarely feel the need to know the statistics of the class to which the case belongs. The inside view feels complete, so the missing statistics are not missed.

questions.q: What does the discrepancy between Seymour Fox's two judgments reveal, according to Kahneman?
questions.a: Seymour had in his head all the knowledge needed to estimate the statistics of an appropriate reference class, yet he reached his first estimate without using it. That inside-view forecast was not an adjustment from a baseline prediction, because the baseline never came to his mind; it was based on the team's particular circumstances. Like participants in the Tom W experiment, he knew the base rate but did not think of applying it.

questions.q: Sort each way of forecasting the curriculum project into the inside view or the outside view.

items.t: Counting the chapters left to write
Timing how long the first two chapters took
Adding a few months as a margin of error
Recalling how long similar teams took to finish
Estimating the failure rate of comparable projects
Starting from the category the project belongs to

questions.explain: The inside view focuses on the specific case and extrapolates from its plan; the outside view looks at a class of similar cases and starts from its statistics.

questions.q: Match each term from Kahneman's chapter on the outside view to its meaning.
pairs: Inside view
Forecasting from the specific circumstances and plan of one's own case
Outside view
Forecasting from what happened in a class of similar cases
Baseline prediction
What you predict knowing only the category a case belongs to
Unknown unknowns
Unforeseeable events that derail a plan
questions.explain: The inside view uses the particulars of the case; the outside view uses a reference class; the baseline is the category-only prediction; unknown unknowns are events no one can anticipate.

questions.q: Which of these are the two features Kahneman and Tversky used to define the planning fallacy?
options: Plans and forecasts that are unrealistically close to best-case scenarios
Plans and forecasts that could be improved by consulting the statistics of similar cases
Plans and forecasts that are deliberately inflated to secure extra budget
Plans and forecasts that are overly pessimistic about the odds of success
Plans and forecasts made by people with no relevant expertise
questions.explain: The planning fallacy is defined by forecasts near the best case that could be improved with statistics of similar cases. It is about optimism, not pessimism or padding.

questions.q: What did the 2005 study of rail projects undertaken worldwide between 1969 and 1998 find about the forecasts over those thirty years?
options: Forecasts improved steadily once passenger shortfalls were publicized
Forecasts did not improve, even though the shortfalls were widely publicized
Forecasts became too pessimistic after early projects failed
Forecasts were accurate for passengers but not for costs
questions.explain: Passenger numbers were overestimated in more than 90% of cases and forecasts did not improve over thirty years: “As more evidence accumulated, the experts did not become more reliant on it.”

questions.q: Besides the optimism of planners, what other cause of overruns does Kahneman identify in kitchen renovations and weapon systems?
options: Customers fail to imagine how much their wishes will escalate, and contractors profit from the additions
Contractors are legally required to bid below their true costs
Materials prices rise faster than any planner could forecast
Clients deliberately underreport their budgets to get lower bids
questions.explain: Contractors admit, though not to clients, that they make most of their profit on additions to the original plan, reflecting customers' inability to imagine how their wishes will grow.

questions.q: When authors of unrealistic plans are driven by the desire to get those plans approved, who does Kahneman say bears the greatest responsibility for avoiding the planning fallacy?
options: The contractors who carry out the work
The customers who keep adding requests
The decision makers who approve the plan
The independent auditors who review costs afterward
questions.explain: Planners know projects are rarely abandoned merely because of overruns, so the burden falls on the approvers; if they do not recognize the need for an outside view, they commit a planning fallacy.

questions.q: Kahneman and Tversky coined the term ____ to describe plans and forecasts that are unrealistically close to best-case scenarios.
questions.explain: The planning fallacy also has a second feature: such forecasts could be improved by consulting the statistics of similar cases.

questions.q: Put the cost figures for the Scottish Parliament building in Edinburgh in the order they appeared, from first estimate to final cost.
items: Up to £40 million (1997 estimate)
£109 million (1999 budget)
£195 million (2000 cost cap)
£241 million (2001 final cost estimate)
Roughly £431 million (completed in 2004)
questions.explain: The budget grew at almost every stage, from an estimate of up to £40 million in 1997 to an ultimate cost of roughly £431 million in 2004.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say errors in the initial budget of a project are not always innocent, and what follows for those who approve plans?
questions.a: Authors of unrealistic plans are often driven by the desire to get the plan approved by their superiors or a client. They are supported by the knowledge that projects are rarely abandoned unfinished merely because of cost or time overruns. So the greatest responsibility for avoiding the planning fallacy lies with the decision makers who approve the plan; if they do not recognize the need for an outside view, they commit a planning fallacy themselves.

questions.q: A software team says a new feature will take two weeks because they can picture every step of the work, and nobody checks how long similar features took. Using Kahneman's ideas, why is this forecast likely to be wrong?
questions.a: The team is committing the planning fallacy: its forecast is close to a best-case scenario built from the inside view of its own plan. It cannot foresee the unknown unknowns, and although each possible problem is improbable, there are many ways for any plan to fail, so the chance that something goes wrong is high. Consulting the statistics of similar features, the outside view, would improve the forecast.

questions.q: Kahneman says errors in initial budgets are not always innocent. Sort each source of overruns by whether it is an honest failure to foresee or is driven by the wish to get the plan approved.
groups: Driven by the wish to get approval

items.t: Planners imagining a best-case scenario
Customers not imagining how their wishes will escalate
Unforeseeable events like illnesses and bureaucratic delays
Presenting a low budget so superiors will sign off
Counting on projects rarely being abandoned for overruns

questions.explain: Optimism, escalating wishes and unknown unknowns are honest errors; deliberately low plans backed by the knowledge that overrun projects are rarely abandoned are not innocent.

questions.q: Match each example of the planning fallacy in Kahneman's chapter to its figures.
pairs: Scottish Parliament building
