Estimated up to £40 million, finished at roughly £431 million
Rail projects 1969 to 1998
Passengers overestimated by 106% on average, costs over by 45%
American kitchen remodels (2002 survey)
Expected $18,658 on average, paid $38,769
questions.explain: Each case shows forecasts close to the best case: a public building, transport projects worldwide, and private home renovations.

questions.q: According to Bent Flyvbjerg's summary quoted by Kahneman, what is perhaps the major source of error in forecasting?
options: Relying on too many statistical databases instead of expert judgment
Failing to collect estimates confidentially from team members
The tendency to underweight or ignore distributional information
Political interference by the authorities that commission projects
questions.explain: Flyvbjerg says the prevalent tendency to underweight or ignore distributional information is perhaps the major source of error, and using that information from similar ventures, the outside view, is the cure.

questions.q: What does Kahneman say a well-run organization should do about executives who present overly optimistic plans while competing for resources?
options: Reward precise execution and penalize failing to anticipate difficulties, even the unknown unknowns
Always add a large budget reserve to every plan it approves
Let executives revise their forecasts freely once a project is under way
Reward the executives whose plans promise the highest returns
questions.explain: A well-run organization rewards precise execution and penalizes planners for failing to anticipate difficulties, including those they could not have anticipated. Budget reserves, by contrast, often become self-fulfilling: “A budget reserve is to contractors as red meat is to lions, and they will devour it.”

questions.q: Put the steps of reference class forecasting, as Kahneman describes Flyvbjerg's method, in the correct order.
items: Identify an appropriate reference class
Obtain the statistics of the reference class
Use the statistics to generate a baseline prediction
Adjust the baseline using specific information about the case
questions.explain: The method mirrors the remedy for base-rate neglect: start from the class and its statistics, form a baseline, and only then adjust for reasons to expect more or less optimistic bias in this case.

questions.q: Kahneman says the treatment for the planning fallacy has acquired a technical name: ____.
questions.explain: Flyvbjerg applied reference class forecasting to transportation projects in several countries, using a large database of plans and outcomes.

questions.q: The Danish planning expert whose summary of forecasting error Kahneman quotes, and who applied reference class forecasting to transportation projects, is Bent ____.
questions.explain: Bent Flyvbjerg, at Oxford University, argued that using distributional information from similar ventures, the outside view, is the cure for the planning fallacy.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say the large database used in Flyvbjerg's reference class forecasting provides?
options: Information on both plans and outcomes for hundreds of projects worldwide
Statistics about likely overruns of cost and time
Information about the likely underperformance of different types of projects
Personality profiles of the managers who led each project
Guaranteed fixed prices from contractors for new projects
questions.explain: The database holds plans and outcomes for hundreds of projects and yields statistics on likely cost and time overruns and underperformance; it says nothing about managers' personalities or guaranteed prices.

questions.q: Match each person to their role in Kahneman's chapter on the outside view.
pairs: Seymour Fox
Curriculum expert who knew the history of similar teams
Bent Flyvbjerg
Planning expert who applied reference class forecasting
Dan Lovallo
Coauthor of a theory linking optimistic bias to risk taking
Donald Rumsfeld
Coined the phrase unknown unknowns
Nisbett and Borgida
Showed students ignore statistics when judging individuals
questions.explain: Each person illustrates a different part of the chapter: the outside view in the story, its cure, its link to risk taking, its blind spot, and its neglect.

questions.q: Your friend estimates that remodeling her bathroom will cost $10,000 based on her own detailed plan. Following the method Kahneman describes from Flyvbjerg, how should she forecast instead?
questions.a: She should first identify an appropriate reference class, such as bathroom or home renovations, and obtain its statistics, for example the percentage by which such jobs typically exceed their budgets. She uses those statistics to generate a baseline prediction. Only then should she adjust the baseline using specific information about her project, if there are particular reasons to expect the optimistic bias to be more or less pronounced than usual.

questions.q: Sort each forecasting habit by whether it belongs to Flyvbjerg's reference class forecasting or to the inside view it is meant to correct.

items.t: Finding projects of the same type
Checking the average percentage of budget overrun
Adjusting the baseline only for specific reasons
Extrapolating from progress so far
Building the forecast from one's own detailed plan
Treating the project as unique

questions.explain: Reference class forecasting starts from similar projects and their statistics; the inside view starts from the case at hand and its plan.

questions.q: What alternative to the standard rational model of risk taking did Kahneman sketch with Dan Lovallo?
options: People take risks only when the odds are clearly favorable
People avoid risky projects because losses loom larger than gains
People often take on risky projects because they are overly optimistic about the odds
People take risks mainly to signal confidence to their superiors
questions.explain: In the rational model people accept risks because the odds are favorable; Kahneman and Lovallo proposed that the optimistic bias is a significant source of risk taking.

questions.q: Almost fifteen years after first reporting on the planning fallacy with Amos, Kahneman returned to the topic with Dan ____.
questions.explain: With Dan Lovallo, Kahneman sketched a theory of decision making in which optimistic bias is a significant source of risk taking.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman suggest the idea that people take risks because they are overly optimistic may help explain?
options: Why people litigate
Why people start wars
Why people open small businesses
Why people buy insurance
Why people save for retirement
questions.explain: Kahneman says the idea probably contributes to explaining why people litigate, start wars and open small businesses. Buying insurance and saving are cautious choices, not the result of optimism about the odds.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says executives in the grip of the planning fallacy overestimate costs and underestimate benefits.
questions.explain: The direction is the reverse: they overestimate benefits and underestimate costs, spinning scenarios of success while overlooking the potential for mistakes.

questions.q: How does Kahneman and Lovallo's view of risk taking differ from the standard rational model of economics?
questions.a: In the rational model, people take risks because the odds are favorable: they accept some chance of costly failure because the chance of success is sufficient. Kahneman and Lovallo argued that executives forecasting risky projects fall victim to the planning fallacy and decide based on delusional optimism rather than a rational weighting of gains, losses and probabilities. As a result they pursue initiatives unlikely to come in on budget or on time, to deliver the expected returns, or even to be completed.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it fits the standard rational model of risk taking or Kahneman and Lovallo's account of risk taking.

items.t: Risks are taken because the odds are favorable
Possible failure is accepted because success is likely enough
Gains, losses and probabilities are weighed rationally
Decisions rest on delusional optimism
Benefits are overestimated and costs underestimated
Scenarios of success crowd out possible mistakes

questions.explain: The rational model assumes accurate weighing of odds; Kahneman and Lovallo say optimistic bias distorts the odds people believe they face.

questions.q: Looking back on the curriculum story, how did Kahneman come to describe his own role?
options: Clever questioner and astute psychologist
Innocent bystander misled by an expert
The one team member who wanted to quit
Chief dunce and inept leader
questions.explain: For years he told the story with himself as the clever questioner; only recently did he realize that, as the leader responsible for the project, he had played the roles of chief dunce and inept leader.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that after hearing Seymour Fox's statistical summary, he himself remained in the grip of the planning fallacy for years.
questions.explain: He says he was cured of the planning fallacy as soon as he heard Seymour's summary; his failure was not forcing a discussion of whether to quit.

questions.q: Kahneman says the curriculum team's reluctance to abandon a project in which it had already invested a great deal of effort was an instance of the ____.
questions.explain: He notes that he will look more closely at the sunk-cost fallacy in the next part of the book.

questions.q: Kahneman describes the curriculum team's state after hearing the outside view as a form of ____, an unwillingness to think about what had happened.
questions.explain: The team carried on without any further attempt at rational planning, which Kahneman calls particularly troubling for a team dedicated to teaching rationality.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give as reasons the curriculum team carried on after hearing Seymour Fox's statistics?
options: They had already invested a great deal of effort
Giving up would have been embarrassing, especially for Kahneman
There was no crisis, only new facts about people they did not know
The Ministry of Education insisted that they continue
Seymour Fox argued that the team would beat the odds
questions.explain: Sunk costs, embarrassment and the absence of a crisis made it easy to go on. The Ministry did not insist, and Seymour actually ranked the team below average.

questions.q: Why was it so easy for the curriculum team to keep going after hearing the outside view, according to Kahneman?
questions.a: Nobody pressed for a discussion, and the team tacitly agreed to go on without an explicit forecast, which was easy because they had never made one. They had already invested a lot of effort, giving up would have been embarrassing, and there was no crisis to force a change of direction, only facts about other people. As Kahneman puts it, “The outside view was much easier to ignore than bad news in our own effort.”

questions.q: Why did Kahneman change his mind about the main point of the curriculum story?
questions.a: For many years he thought the main point was what he had learned about Seymour: that his forecast ignored what he knew about similar projects, with Kahneman cast as the clever questioner. He later realized the project was his initiative, so it was his responsibility to make sure major problems were discussed, and he failed that test. Although cured of the planning fallacy, he let the team carry on without discussion or rational planning.

questions.q: What is Kahneman's final conclusion about his own habit of looking for the outside view?
questions.a: He hopes he is wiser today and says he has acquired a habit of looking for the outside view. But he admits it will never be the natural thing to do. The pull of the inside view remains, so the outside view must be sought deliberately.

questions.q: Put these stages in the development of Kahneman's thinking about the curriculum story in chronological order.
items: The Friday exercise with the curriculum team
First reporting the planning fallacy with Amos
Sketching a theory of optimism and risk taking with Dan Lovallo
Realizing he had played the role of chief dunce and inept leader
questions.explain: The exercise came first; he later reported the planning fallacy with Amos, returned to it with Lovallo almost fifteen years later, and only recently saw his own failure as leader.

questions.q: A colleague is weighing a malpractice claim by an individual against a surgeon. Following Kahneman's advice on the outside view, which question should she ask first?
options: How sympathetic will the jury find this particular plaintiff?
How many claims like this one succeed in court or settle, and for what amounts?
How confident is the plaintiff's lawyer about winning?
What unusual details make this case different from all others?
questions.explain: Kahneman suggests starting from a baseline prediction for malpractice claims against surgeons, then asking whether this case is stronger or weaker than similar claims.

questions.q: Match each remark from Kahneman's examples of speaking about the outside view to the idea it names.
pairs: He should forget about his own case and look at other cases
Inside view
She is assuming a best-case scenario and cannot foresee every way to fail
Planning fallacy
We are investing more because we do not want to admit failure
Sunk-cost fallacy
What would we predict knowing only that this is a malpractice claim?
Baseline prediction
questions.explain: Each remark applies one of the chapter's key ideas to an everyday conversation.

questions.q: Why does a chapter on the outside view and the planning fallacy fit in Part 3 of the book, titled Overconfidence?
options: The inside view yields overconfident, optimistic forecasts
Because it shows that experts are always more accurate than statistical formulas
Because it explains how people weigh gains and losses when making choices
Because it describes the two selves that experience and remember events
questions.explain: The planning fallacy is a form of overconfidence: forecasts close to the best case made without consulting how similar projects turned out. Gains and losses belong to Part 4, and the two selves to Part 5.

questions.q: How does the chapter on the outside view prepare for the next chapter, The Engine of Capitalism?
options: It introduces prospect theory, which the next chapter applies to markets
It argues that entrepreneurs are usually too cautious about risk
It proposes that optimistic bias drives risk taking, such as opening small businesses
It shows that expert intuition is reliable in regular environments
questions.explain: Kahneman says he will return to the idea that people take risks because they are overly optimistic, and that it helps explain why people open small businesses, a natural lead-in to a chapter on optimism and capitalism.

questions.q: Put the sections of the chapter The Outside View in the order they appear.
items: Drawn to the Inside View
The Planning Fallacy
Mitigating the Planning Fallacy
Decisions and Errors
Failing a Test
Speaking of the Outside View
questions.explain: After the curriculum story, the chapter explains the pull of the inside view, defines and illustrates the planning fallacy, offers its cure, links it to risk taking, and discusses Kahneman's own failure, before the closing “Speaking of” section.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says the sunk-cost fallacy, which kept his curriculum team going, will be looked at more closely in the next part of the book.
questions.explain: In discussing his failure as team leader, he calls the decision to continue an instance of the sunk-cost fallacy and says it will be examined more closely in the next part of the book, on choices.

questions.q: Which of these ideas from earlier chapters does Kahneman draw on in the chapter on the outside view?
options: WYSIATI, forecasting from the information in front of you
The Tom W experiment, in which a known base rate went unused
Nisbett and Borgida's finding that students ignored statistics they had learned
The endowment effect in trading mugs
The fourfold pattern of risk attitudes
questions.explain: WYSIATI, Tom W and Nisbett and Borgida's experiment come from earlier chapters and are cited here. The endowment effect and the fourfold pattern belong to later chapters on choices.

questions.q: Match each idea from an earlier chapter to how the chapter on the outside view uses it.
pairs: WYSIATI (Chapter 7)
The team forecast only from the information in front of them
Tom W experiment (Chapter 14)
Seymour knew the base rate but did not think of applying it
Nisbett and Borgida (Chapter 16)
Pallid statistics are discarded in favor of impressions of a case
Taming Intuitive Predictions (Chapter 18)
The baseline prediction is the anchor for adjustments
questions.explain: The outside view chapter applies earlier lessons on WYSIATI, base-rate neglect and corrected prediction to forecasting real projects.

questions.q: Put the sections of Kahneman's chapter The Engine of Capitalism in the order they appear.
items: Optimists
Entrepreneurial Delusions
Competition Neglect
Overconfidence
The Premortem: a Partial Remedy
questions.explain: The chapter moves from who optimists are, to the costs of entrepreneurial optimism, to its cognitive roots (competition neglect and overconfidence), and ends with a partial remedy, the premortem.

questions.q: The Engine of Capitalism is the last chapter of the part of Thinking, Fast and Slow titled ____.
questions.explain: Chapter 24 closes Part 3, Overconfidence; the next chapter, Bernoulli's Errors, opens Part 4, Choices.

questions.q: What does the title of Kahneman's chapter The Engine of Capitalism refer to?
options: The rational calculation of odds by successful business founders
The optimistic risk taking of entrepreneurs that drives economic dynamism
The government loans that keep failing small businesses afloat
The stock market's ability to punish overconfident executives
questions.explain: Kahneman argues that the optimistic risk taking of entrepreneurs contributes to the economic dynamism of a capitalist society, even though most risk takers end up disappointed. Rational calculation of odds is exactly what optimists fail to do.

questions.q: How does Kahneman's chapter The Engine of Capitalism build on the preceding chapter, The Outside View?
questions.a: Chapter 23 described the planning fallacy and the remedy of taking the outside view. Chapter 24 opens by calling the planning fallacy “only one of the manifestations of a pervasive optimistic bias” and widens the lens to optimism in general. Its examples, such as the new restaurant owner, show people ignoring base rates; the idea of adopting the outside view probably did not occur to the restaurant owner.

questions.q: Which of these ideas from earlier in Thinking, Fast and Slow does Kahneman use to explain optimism in The Engine of Capitalism?
options: WYSIATI (what you see is all there is)
Answering an easier question (substitution)
The planning fallacy
The endowment effect
The peak-end rule
questions.explain: The chapter explains competition neglect and overconfidence through WYSIATI and substitution, and calls the planning fallacy one form of optimistic bias. The endowment effect and the peak-end rule belong to later parts of the book.

questions.q: Put these chapters of Part 3 of Thinking, Fast and Slow (Overconfidence) in the book's order.
items: The Illusion of Understanding
The Illusion of Validity
Intuitions vs. Formulas
Expert Intuition: When Can We Trust It?
The Outside View
The Engine of Capitalism
questions.explain: Part 3 runs from chapter 19, The Illusion of Understanding, to chapter 24, The Engine of Capitalism, which ends the part before Part 4, Choices.

questions.q: In The Engine of Capitalism, which bias does Kahneman say may well be the most significant of the cognitive biases in its consequences for decisions?
options: The anchoring effect
The availability heuristic
The hindsight bias
The optimistic bias
questions.explain: Kahneman writes that, in terms of its consequences for decisions, the optimistic bias may well be the most significant of the cognitive biases. The other biases are real but not singled out this way here.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman describes the planning fallacy as only one manifestation of a more pervasive optimistic bias.
questions.explain: The chapter opens by placing the planning fallacy inside a broader optimistic bias: we see the world as more benign, ourselves as more capable, and our goals as more achievable than they are.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, why should a person who is temperamentally optimistic be both happy and wary?
questions.a: Optimistic bias is both a blessing and a risk. Optimists tend to be happier, healthier and more resilient, but the same bias makes them see the world as more benign and their goals as more achievable than they are, and exaggerate their ability to forecast the future. That optimistic overconfidence can lead to costly decisions.

questions.q: Which of these benefits does Kahneman attribute to optimists in The Engine of Capitalism?
options: They are resilient in adapting to failures and hardships
Their immune system is stronger
They forecast the future more accurately than others
Their chances of clinical depression are reduced
They are more cautious about taking risks
questions.explain: Kahneman lists resilience, a stronger immune system, reduced depression, better health and longer life among optimism's blessings. He does not credit optimists with accurate forecasts or caution; the chapter argues the opposite.

questions.q: Kahneman writes that an optimistic attitude is largely ____ and is part of a general disposition for well-being.
questions.explain: He says an optimistic attitude is largely inherited, which is why he suggests that one wish for a child might seriously be optimism.

questions.q: In The Engine of Capitalism, what did a study find about people who exaggerate their expected life span beyond actuarial predictions?
options: They are more likely to remarry after divorce
They are less likely to bet on individual stocks
They work fewer hours than others
They are more pessimistic about future income
questions.explain: These optimists work longer hours, expect higher future income, bet more on individual stocks, and are more likely to remarry after divorce, the “triumph of hope over experience.”

questions.q: Kahneman describes a study of people who exaggerate their expected life span beyond actuarial predictions. Sort these into what the study found and what it did not find.

items.t: They work longer hours
They are more optimistic about their future income
They are more prone to bet on individual stocks
They work fewer hours than others
They are less likely to remarry after divorce
They avoid betting on individual stocks

questions.explain: The life-span optimists worked longer, expected more income, bet more on individual stocks, and were more likely to remarry after divorce. Each wrong item reverses one of these findings.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says the blessings of optimism are offered mainly to people who are strongly biased toward the positive.
questions.explain: The blessings go only to people who are mildly biased and can accentuate the positive without losing track of reality, not to the strongly biased.

questions.q: What hypothesis does Kahneman propose about the people who have the greatest influence on others' lives, and how does he reach it?
questions.a: Influential people such as inventors, entrepreneurs and leaders got where they are by seeking challenges and taking risks; they are talented and luckier than they acknowledge, and probably optimistic by temperament. Their successes confirm their faith in their judgment and control, and others' admiration reinforces their self-confidence. So he hypothesizes that the most influential people are likely to be optimistic and overconfident, and to take more risks than they realize.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, why do optimistic entrepreneurs often believe they are prudent even when they are not?
options: Because they carefully research the odds first
Because they are betting with other people's money
Because they misread the risks they face
Because they deliberately hide risks from investors
questions.explain: Risk takers usually underestimate the odds and do not put enough effort into finding out what the odds are, so they feel prudent while misreading the risks. Kahneman later rejects the idea that they bet recklessly because the money is someone else's.

questions.q: Sort these effects of optimism described by Kahneman into benefits and costs.

items.t: Resilience in the face of setbacks
Helps obtain resources from others
Raises the morale of employees
Inventors doubling their losses after a hopeless grade
Overpaying in value-destroying mergers
Taking risks one would avoid if one knew the odds

questions.explain: Optimism helps implementation through resilience, mood, and the ability to rally resources and staff. Its costs show up in decisions: persisting with doomed inventions, overpaying in acquisitions, and taking risks without knowing the odds.

questions.q: In Kahneman's survey of American entrepreneurs, their average estimate of the chances of success for any business like theirs was ____, almost double the true value.
questions.explain: Entrepreneurs estimated 60% on average, while the true chance that a small US business survives five years is about 35%.

questions.q: Match each figure from Kahneman's chapter The Engine of Capitalism to what it measured.
pairs: Chance that a small US business survives five years
Entrepreneurs rating their own odds of success at 7 out of 10 or higher
Entrepreneurs who said their chance of failing was zero
Inventors who kept developing after being told their project was hopeless
Rate of surprises in the CFOs' 80% confidence intervals
questions.explain: These numbers show the gap between optimistic beliefs and reality: entrepreneurs rate their own ventures far above the base rate, and forecasters are surprised far more often than their confidence implies.

questions.q: What point does Kahneman make with the example of a woman who has just opened an Italian restaurant?
questions.a: We would not expect her to underestimate her prospects or her ability, so the direction of the bias is unsurprising. The real question is whether she would still have invested money and time if she had learned the odds (60% of new restaurants are out of business after three years) or paid attention to them. Adopting the outside view probably never occurred to her.

questions.q: In Thomas Åstebro's studies, what did the Canadian Inventor's Assistance Program provide to inventors for a small fee?
options: Start-up loans for the most promising inventions
An objective assessment of the commercial prospects of their idea
Patent protection for their inventions
Training in optimistic thinking to help them persist
questions.explain: The program rated each invention on 37 criteria, such as need for the product and cost of production, and summarized the result as a letter grade predicting commercial success or failure.

questions.q: Put these events from Thomas Åstebro's studies of inventors in order.
items: Analysts rate the invention on 37 criteria
The invention receives a grade that predicts failure
About half of the inventors quit
The persistent 47% continue development
The persistent inventors double their initial losses before giving up
questions.explain: Inventors received a letter grade from careful ratings; after a failing grade about half quit, but 47% kept going and on average doubled their initial losses before stopping.

questions.q: Which of these describe the inventors in Åstebro's studies who kept going after receiving a grade that predicted failure?
options: They made up about 47% of those told their project was hopeless
Most of them eventually reached commercial success
They tended to score high on a personality measure of optimism
They tended to score low on a measure of optimism
On average they doubled their initial losses
questions.explain: Persistence after discouraging advice was common among inventors high in optimism, and it was costly: they doubled their losses. Of 411 projects given the lowest grade, none was successful, so the idea that most persisters succeeded is wrong.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman reports that, given the same qualifications, people achieve higher average returns by selling their skills to employers than by setting out on their own.
questions.explain: He notes that the financial benefits of self-employment are mediocre, one more sign that optimism is widespread, stubborn and costly.

questions.q: From the evidence on entrepreneurs and inventors, Kahneman concludes that optimism is widespread, stubborn, and ____.
questions.explain: The evidence suggests that optimism is widespread, stubborn, and costly: persisting inventors doubled their losses and self-employment pays less than employment.

questions.q: In The Engine of Capitalism, what does the hubris hypothesis explain?
options: Why entrepreneurs quit after receiving bad news
Why the stock market rewards firms that make acquisitions
Why film studios avoid releasing movies on the same day
Misguided acquisitions by executives who are less competent than they think
questions.explain: Leaders sometimes make huge bets on mergers, believing they can manage another company better than its owners. The hubris hypothesis says the acquiring executives are simply less competent than they think. The market usually downgrades, not rewards, the acquiring firm.

questions.q: How did the economists Ulrike Malmendier and Geoffrey Tate identify optimistic CEOs?
options: By the amount of company stock the CEOs owned personally
By the CEOs' scores on a personality test
By how often the CEOs gave press interviews
By the size of the CEOs' salaries
questions.explain: Optimistic CEOs were identified by how much company stock they personally held; these leaders took excessive risks and were more likely to undertake value-destroying mergers.

questions.q: True or false: Malmendier and Tate found that highly optimistic CEOs preferred to issue equity rather than assume debt.
questions.explain: The reverse: highly optimistic CEOs assumed debt rather than issue equity, one of the excessive risks they took.

questions.q: Kahneman says the Malmendier and Tate findings exonerate overconfident CEOs from one accusation while convicting them of another. Explain.
questions.a: Because optimistic CEOs were identified by the large amount of company stock they owned, they were not making unsound bets because they were gambling with other people's money. On the contrary, they took greater risks when they personally had more at stake. What convicts them is overconfidence: they overpaid for targets and undertook value-destroying mergers.

questions.q: Which of these did Malmendier and Tate find after CEOs won prestigious press awards?
options: Their firms subsequently underperformed in stock and operating performance
Their compensation increased
Their firms' stock outperformed the market
They spent more time on outside activities such as writing books
They spent more time managing their own company
questions.explain: The authors found that firms with award-winning CEOs subsequently underperform while CEO pay rises and CEOs turn to outside activities like books and outside boards. Celebrity status compounds the damage of overconfidence.

questions.q: What does Kahneman's story of the young couple who bought a motel on Vancouver Island illustrate?
questions.a: The former schoolteachers had used their life savings to buy a deserted motel cheaply “because six or seven previous owners had failed to make a go of it,” and planned to borrow to add a restaurant. They felt no need to explain why they would succeed where others had failed. The story shows the common thread of boldness and optimism, and neglect of base rates, that links businesspeople from motel owners to superstar CEOs.

questions.q: What policy problem does Marta Coelho raise about entrepreneurial optimism, and why does Kahneman find it hard to answer?
questions.a: Optimistic risk taking contributes to economic dynamism, yet founders of small businesses ask the government to support decisions that are most likely to end badly, such as loans to people who will probably bankrupt themselves in a few years. Behavioral economists are comfortable with libertarian paternalistic procedures that help people save more, but whether and how government should support small business has no equally satisfying answer.

questions.q: Kahneman lists ways the System 1 feature WYSIATI feeds entrepreneurial optimism. Match each focus to the bias it produces.
pairs: Focusing on our goal, anchoring on our plan, neglecting base rates
The planning fallacy
Focusing on what we want to do and can do
Neglect of the plans and skills of others
Focusing on the causal role of skill, neglecting luck
An illusion of control
Focusing on what we know, neglecting what we do not know
Overconfidence in our beliefs
questions.explain: Kahneman says emotion is only part of the story; in each case WYSIATI makes us attend to what is in front of us and neglect what is missing, whether base rates, competitors, luck or unknown information.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says the interpretation of the finding that 90% of drivers believe they are better than average has shifted from a cognitive bias to self-aggrandizement.
questions.explain: The shift went the other way: the finding used to be read as self-aggrandizement and is now interpreted as a cognitive bias.

questions.q: Using the questions Are you a good driver? and Are you better than average as a driver?, explain Kahneman's cognitive account of the above-average effect.
questions.a: The first question is easy and most drivers quickly say yes. The second is hard because it requires assessing the average quality of drivers, so people answer the easier question instead. They compare themselves to the average without ever thinking about the average, which produces the above-average effect.

questions.q: What evidence does Kahneman give for the cognitive, rather than self-aggrandizing, interpretation of the above-average effect?
options: People refuse to rate themselves on any task at all
People rate themselves above average on every task
On tasks they find difficult, people readily rate themselves below average
Only people with high self-esteem show the effect
questions.explain: When asked about something difficult, such as starting conversations with strangers, people readily rate themselves below average. That fits substitution of an easy question, not a general wish to feel superior.

questions.q: Kahneman concludes that people tend to be overly optimistic about their relative standing on any activity in which they do ____ well.
questions.explain: Because people answer how good they are rather than how they compare with the average, they overrate their standing on activities they do moderately well, and underrate it on difficult ones.

questions.q: Priya is a decent home cook. Asked whether she cooks better than the average person, she quickly says yes. How would Kahneman explain her answer?
options: She carefully estimated the skill of the average cook
She answered the easier question of whether she is a good cook
She is a pessimist hiding her true opinion
She took the outside view of typical cooks
questions.explain: Like drivers, she compares herself to the average without thinking about the average, substituting an easy question for a hard one. Estimating the average cook's skill is exactly the step people skip.

questions.q: When Kahneman asked founders of start-ups how much of their outcome would depend on what they do in their firm, the answer was never less than ____.
questions.explain: Even founders unsure of success thought their fate was almost entirely in their own hands, never answering less than 80%.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say start-up founders are wrong to believe their outcome depends almost entirely on what they do?
questions.a: The outcome of a start-up depends as much on the achievements of its competitors and on changes in the market as on its own efforts. Because of WYSIATI, entrepreneurs focus on what they know best: their plans and actions and immediate threats and opportunities such as funding. They know less about competitors, so they imagine a future in which the competition plays little part.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, which of these do start-up founders naturally focus on, and which do they tend to neglect?

items.t: Their own plans and actions
The availability of funding
The most immediate threats and opportunities
The achievements of competitors
Changes in the market

questions.explain: WYSIATI leads founders to focus on what they know best, their own plans and immediate concerns, and to neglect competitors and market changes, which matter as much to the outcome.

questions.q: Why did the chairman of Disney Studios say so many big-budget movies are released on the same days?
options: Audiences are largest on holidays, so it is a sound bet
Studios agree in advance to split the audience
Distributors require release on fixed dates
Hubris: studios think only about their own business
questions.explain: He answered, “Hubris. Hubris.” Studios think about their own good story and marketing departments and do not consider that everybody else is thinking the same way.

questions.q: Colin Camerer and Dan Lovallo coined the concept of ____ and illustrated it with a quote from the chairman of Disney Studios.
questions.explain: Competition neglect is the failure to consider what competitors will do; the Disney chairman's account of crowded holiday release dates is their illustration.

questions.q: How does Kahneman interpret the Disney chairman's answer about crowded movie release dates?
options: Competition was simply not part of the decision; an easier question replaced a hard one
Executives believed their studio was superior to all rivals
Executives knew the competition but chose to fight it
Executives were betting with other people's money
questions.explain: Kahneman notes the answer shows no arrogance or conceit of superiority. The executives asked whether they had a good film and a good organization to market it, instead of how many people would see the film given what others will do.

questions.q: Kahneman describes hard questions that people replace with easier ones. Sort each question into the one that needs an answer or the easier one actually answered.

items.t: Considering what others will do, how many people will see our film?
Do we have a good film and a good organization to market it?
Are you better than average as a driver?
Are you a good driver?

questions.explain: In both the above-average effect and competition neglect, WYSIATI and substitution swap a question that requires knowledge of others for one about oneself that is easy to answer.

questions.q: Kahneman says the consequence of competition neglect is ____: more competitors enter a market than it can profitably sustain.
questions.explain: With excess entry the average outcome for entrants is a loss, though the effect on the economy as a whole could well be positive.

questions.q: Put these steps in the chain Kahneman describes, from competition neglect to its effect on the economy, in order.
items: Entrants neglect the plans of competitors
More competitors enter than the market can sustain
The typical entrant suffers a loss
Failed firms signal new markets to more qualified competitors
questions.explain: Competition neglect leads to excess entry and an average loss for entrants, but failed firms can benefit the economy by revealing new markets; Dosi and Lovallo call them optimistic martyrs.

questions.q: Which of these System 1 processes does Kahneman say produce both competition neglect and the above-average effect?
options: Regression to the mean
WYSIATI
Loss aversion
Substitution of an easier question
The anchoring effect
questions.explain: Kahneman names WYSIATI and substitution as the familiar System 1 processes behind both effects. Loss aversion and regression to the mean are discussed elsewhere in the book.

questions.q: In the Duke University survey of chief financial officers, what was the correlation between their forecasts of S&P returns and the true values?
options: Moderately positive
Close to perfect
Slightly less than zero
Strongly negative
questions.explain: Across 11,600 forecasts the correlation was slightly less than zero: when CFOs said the market would go down, it was slightly more likely to go up. The truly bad news was that they did not seem to know their forecasts were worthless.

questions.q: In the Duke CFO study, the range between a value the forecaster is 90% sure is too high and one 90% sure is too low is called an 80% ____.
questions.explain: Outcomes outside an 80% confidence interval are labeled surprises, and someone setting such intervals should expect about 20% surprises.

questions.q: In the Duke CFO study, how often did outcomes fall outside the CFOs' 80% confidence intervals?
options: 20% of the time, exactly as expected
67% of the time, more than three times the expected rate
10% of the time, half the expected rate
40% of the time, double the expected rate
questions.explain: Well-calibrated 80% intervals should produce about 20% surprises; the CFOs had 67%, showing gross overconfidence about forecasting the market.

questions.q: Put these steps of the Duke study of CFO forecasts in order.
items: CFOs give a best guess of next year's S&P return
They add values they are 90% sure are too high and too low
Actual returns are compared with their intervals
Surprises are found to occur 67% of the time
Researchers calculate the interval that would cut surprises to 20%
questions.explain: The CFOs' intervals were checked against outcomes, revealing far too many surprises; the authors then calculated how wide the intervals should have been, between -10% and +30%.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman call overconfidence another manifestation of WYSIATI?
questions.a: When we estimate a quantity, we rely on the information that comes to mind and construct a coherent story in which the estimate makes sense. We cannot allow for information that does not come to mind, perhaps because we never knew it. So our confidence reflects the story we can build, not the limits of our knowledge, and our intervals are too narrow.

questions.q: According to the Duke study, how did a confidence interval that properly reflected the CFOs' knowledge compare with the intervals they actually gave?
options: It was about the same width
It was half as wide
It was slightly narrower but shifted upward
It was more than 4 times wider
questions.explain: To keep surprises at 20%, the CFOs should have said year after year that the S&P return would be between -10% and +30%, an interval more than 4 times wider than theirs, reflecting their ignorance.

questions.q: Why, according to Kahneman, would a truthful CFO be unlikely to state the wide confidence interval that matches his real knowledge?
questions.a: A CFO who said the S&P return would probably fall between -10% and +30% could expect to be laughed out of the room. A wide interval is a confession of ignorance, which is not socially acceptable for someone paid to be knowledgeable about finance, so executives would be penalized for admitting how little they know. Kahneman recalls President Truman asking for a “one-armed economist” who would take a clear stand.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman cite as evidence that overconfidence among professionals is common and socially rewarded?
options: The most overconfident experts were the most likely to be invited on news shows
Clinicians completely certain of a diagnosis were wrong 40% of the time
Patients generally prefer doctors who openly disclose uncertainty
Appearing unsure is seen as a weakness in clinicians
Experts who admit ignorance are usually promoted over confident rivals
questions.explain: Tetlock found overconfident experts in demand on television, and an ICU autopsy study found certain clinicians wrong 40% of the time, with uncertainty treated as weakness. Kahneman says experts who admit ignorance may be replaced by more confident competitors, not promoted.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says risk takers in the economic domain have an unusual appetite for gambles on high stakes.
questions.explain: He says there is no evidence of an unusual appetite for high-stakes gambles; risk takers are merely less aware of risks than more timid people are.

questions.q: Kahneman and Dan Lovallo coined the phrase bold forecasts and ____ decisions to describe the background of risk taking.
questions.explain: People are not seeking big gambles; they make bold, optimistic forecasts that make risky choices look safe, so even timid decision makers take large risks.

questions.q: Match each person cited in Kahneman's chapter The Engine of Capitalism to the contribution described.
pairs: Martin Seligman
Optimistic explanation style that builds resilience
Philip Tetlock
Overconfident experts most likely to appear on news shows
Nassim Taleb
Underrating uncertainty leads agents to take risks they should avoid
Thomas Åstebro
Studies of inventors who persist after bad news
Gary Klein
Proposed the premortem
questions.explain: Each researcher supplies one piece of the chapter's case: Åstebro on costly persistence, Taleb and Tetlock on rewarded overconfidence, Seligman on resilience, and Klein on a remedy.

questions.q: After a job interview goes badly, which thought best fits what Martin Seligman calls an optimistic explanation style?
options: The interviewer was clearly having a bad day
I am simply bad at interviews
I should calculate the base rate of job offers
I will never find a job in this field
questions.explain: The optimistic style takes credit for successes but little blame for failures, defending one's self-image, like the insurance salesperson who thinks the homemaker was awful rather than that he is inept.

questions.q: Kahneman says emotional, cognitive and social factors support exaggerated optimism. Sort these into cognitive factors and social pressures.

items.t: Anchoring on our plan and neglecting base rates
Building a coherent story from information that comes to mind
Replacing a hard question with an easier one
A CFO stating a wide interval being laughed out of the room
Clinicians who appear unsure being seen as weak
Overconfident experts being invited onto news shows

questions.explain: The cognitive factors are System 1 features such as WYSIATI and substitution; the social factors are the rewards for appearing confident and penalties for admitting ignorance.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman reports that attempts to train people to state confidence intervals reflecting their imprecision have produced only a few reports of modest success.
questions.explain: He says he is not optimistic about training; a few cases, like Royal Dutch Shell geologists, showed modest improvement.

questions.q: What helped geologists at Royal Dutch Shell become less overconfident in assessing drilling sites?
options: Being paid bonuses for accurate predictions
Working in larger teams with a strong leader
Training with multiple past cases whose outcomes were known
Relying more on their intuitive first impressions
questions.explain: Shell's geologists improved after training on past cases with known outcomes, an often cited example of modest success against overconfidence.

questions.q: Kahneman writes that subjective confidence is determined by the ____ of the story one has constructed, not by the quality and amount of the supporting information.
questions.explain: This is the main obstacle to curing overconfidence: it comes from features of System 1 that can be tamed but not vanquished.

questions.q: How does Kahneman describe Gary Klein, who proposed the premortem?
options: A statistician who champions algorithms over intuition
His adversarial collaborator, who generally defends intuitive decision making
A CEO who invented the method at Davos
An economist who studied optimistic CEOs
questions.explain: Klein generally defends intuition against claims of bias and is typically hostile to algorithms, which makes his contribution of a debiasing procedure notable. The CEO at Davos only praised the idea.

questions.q: Put the steps of Gary Klein's premortem procedure in order.
items: The organization has almost reached an important decision
Knowledgeable people gather before formal commitment
They imagine the plan was implemented and the outcome was a disaster
Each writes a brief history of that disaster
questions.explain: The premortem happens before the organization formally commits; participants imagine a year in the future after a disaster and take 5 to 10 minutes to write its history.

questions.q: Which of these are advantages of the premortem according to Kahneman?
options: It guarantees complete protection against nasty surprises
It overcomes the groupthink that sets in once a decision seems made
It legitimizes doubts
It removes the need to consult knowledgeable people
It unleashes the imagination of knowledgeable individuals in a needed direction
questions.explain: The premortem counters groupthink, legitimizes doubts and directs imagination toward threats. Kahneman says it is not a panacea and does not provide complete protection.

questions.q: How does doubt get suppressed as a team converges on a decision, and how does the premortem counter this?
questions.a: As a team converges, especially once the leader tips her hand, public doubts are gradually suppressed and come to be treated as evidence of flawed loyalty, so only supporters have a voice and the group grows overconfident. The premortem legitimizes doubts and encourages even supporters to search for threats they had not considered.

questions.q: A product team is about to commit to a launch plan, and the manager wants to run a premortem. What should she ask the team to do?
options: Imagine the launch succeeded and list the reasons why
Vote anonymously on whether to go ahead
Estimate the probability that the launch succeeds
Imagine the launch a year later was a disaster and write its history
questions.explain: Klein's premise is to imagine the plan was implemented and the outcome was a disaster, then write a brief history of that disaster. Imagining success would reinforce the optimism the premortem is meant to tame.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman present the premortem as only a partial remedy for overconfident optimism?
questions.a: Overconfidence comes from features of System 1, mainly that confidence follows the coherence of a story, which can be tamed but not vanquished. The premortem is not a panacea and does not provide complete protection against nasty surprises, but it goes some way toward reducing the damage of plans subject to WYSIATI and uncritical optimism. Kahneman thinks organizations may tame optimism better than individuals can.

questions.q: Match each comment from Kahneman's Speaking of Optimism to the idea it expresses.
pairs: They seriously underestimate the obstacles.
Illusion of control
They seem to believe they know more than they actually do know.
Overconfidence
Someone may come up with a threat we have neglected.
The premortem
They seem to suffer from an acute case of competitor neglect.
Competition neglect
questions.explain: Each comment applies a concept from the chapter: underestimating obstacles reflects an illusion of control, believing one knows more reflects overconfidence, and searching for a neglected threat is the purpose of a premortem.

questions.q: Match each example from Kahneman's chapter The Engine of Capitalism to the idea it illustrates.
pairs: Vancouver Island motel bought after six or seven owners failed
Bold optimism that ignores base rates
Disney Studios releasing big films on the same holiday weekends
Competition neglect
Royal Dutch Shell geologists
Training on known past cases reduces overconfidence
Cold-call insurance salespeople
Teaching an optimistic explanation style
Duke survey of chief financial officers
Overconfident forecasting of the stock market
questions.explain: The chapter uses concrete cases to anchor its ideas: the motel and Disney show neglect of base rates and rivals, the CFOs show overconfidence, and Shell and Seligman's salespeople show partial remedies and resilience.

questions.q: Match each term from Kahneman's chapter The Engine of Capitalism to its meaning.
pairs: Hubris hypothesis
Acquiring executives are less competent than they think
Excess entry
More competitors enter a market than it can profitably sustain
Optimistic martyrs
Failed firms that signal new markets to more qualified competitors
Above-average effect
Most people rate themselves better than average
Premortem
Imagining a future failure of a plan and writing its history
questions.explain: These terms name the ways optimism plays out in markets and one tool for taming it. Optimistic martyrs, a term from Dosi and Lovallo, are good for the economy but bad for their investors.

questions.q: Dev opens a café on a street that already has five cafés, reasoning that his coffee is excellent and his staff are friendly. Which idea from Kahneman's chapter best describes his thinking?
options: Competition neglect
Loss aversion
Regression to the mean
The optimistic explanation style
questions.explain: Like the Disney executives, Dev asks whether he has a good product and team, not how many customers he will get given what the other cafés do. The optimistic explanation style concerns how people explain failures, not how they plan.

questions.q: Put the chapters at the start of Part 4 of Thinking, Fast and Slow, together with the chapter just before it, in book order.
items: The Engine of Capitalism
Bernoulli’s Errors
Prospect Theory
The Endowment Effect
questions.explain: The Engine of Capitalism closes Part 3, Overconfidence. Bernoulli’s Errors opens Part 4, Choices, and is followed by Prospect Theory and then The Endowment Effect.

questions.q: Put the steps of Kahneman's argument in the chapter Bernoulli’s Errors in the order they appear.
items: Frey's essay reveals the gap between Econs and Humans
Kahneman and Tversky begin studying choices between simple gambles
Fechner's psychophysics relates physical quantities to subjective experience
Bernoulli explains risk aversion with the utility of wealth
Jack and Jill and Anthony and Betty expose the missing reference point
Theory-induced blindness explains why the flaw went unnoticed
questions.explain: The chapter starts with the Econs-versus-Humans contrast and the gamble research, goes back to Fechner and then to Bernoulli, shows Bernoulli's flaw with two pairs of examples, and ends by asking why no one noticed it.

questions.q: The chapter after Bernoulli’s Errors, which presents the theory Kahneman and Tversky built to fix Bernoulli's flaw, is titled ____.
questions.explain: Bernoulli’s Errors shows what expected utility theory leaves out, especially the reference point; the next chapter, Prospect Theory, presents the model that adds it.

questions.q: What does the title of Kahneman's chapter Bernoulli’s Errors signal about its argument?
options: That a brilliant, long-lived theory of the utility of wealth has a hidden flaw
That gamblers in Bernoulli's time made systematic betting errors
That economists misread Bernoulli and drew the wrong conclusions from him
That Bernoulli made arithmetic mistakes in his table of utilities
questions.explain: Kahneman praises Bernoulli's essay as brilliant and lasting, then argues it is seriously flawed because it ignores reference points. The errors are in the theory's tacit assumptions, not in its arithmetic.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter Bernoulli’s Errors opens the part of Thinking, Fast and Slow titled Overconfidence.
questions.explain: Bernoulli’s Errors opens Part 4, Choices. Overconfidence is Part 3, which ends with The Engine of Capitalism.

questions.q: Why does Bernoulli’s Errors make a fitting opening for Part 4, Choices, of Thinking, Fast and Slow?
questions.a: It moves the book from judgment to decision making by introducing the rational-agent model and its foundation, expected utility theory. It shows the flaw in Bernoulli's utility of wealth, its missing reference point, which sets up prospect theory in the next chapter. It also contrasts Econs with Humans who have a System 1, linking the new topic to the earlier parts of the book.

questions.q: According to the first sentence of Bruno Frey's essay, which Kahneman can still recite, how does economic theory describe its agent?
options: Intuitive, cooperative, and guided by habit
Rational, selfish, and with tastes that do not change
Rational, altruistic, and open to persuasion
Emotional, generous, and easily swayed by framing
questions.explain: The sentence reads “The agent of economic theory is rational, selfish, and his tastes do not change.” To a psychologist, all three assumptions looked false.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman reports that Bruno Frey vividly remembers writing the essay that Amos Tversky showed him.
questions.explain: It is the other way round: Frey barely recalls writing the piece, while Kahneman remembers its dark red cover and can still recite its first sentence.

questions.q: The behavioral economist Richard Thaler dubbed the two different species studied by economists and psychologists Econs and ____.
questions.explain: Econs are the rational, selfish agents with stable tastes of economic theory; Humans are the people psychologists know, who have a System 1.

questions.q: In Kahneman's contrast between Econs and Humans, what do Humans have that makes them less consistent and logical than Econs?
options: Perfectly stable tastes that prevent them from adapting
A complete set of axioms of rationality
A System 1, with a view of the world limited to the information available at the moment
A stronger System 2 that overrules their feelings
questions.explain: Humans have a System 1, and their view of the world is limited by what is available at a given moment (WYSIATI), so they cannot be as consistent as Econs.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say are true of the Humans that psychologists know, as opposed to Econs?
options: They are sometimes generous and willing to contribute to their group
They often have little idea of what they will like next year or even tomorrow
Their view of the world is limited by the information available at a given moment
Their tastes are stable over time
They are completely selfish
questions.explain: Humans can be generous, have poor knowledge of their future tastes, and suffer from WYSIATI. Stable tastes and complete selfishness are the assumptions about Econs that psychologists reject.

questions.q: Sort these traits into those Kahneman attributes to Econs and those he attributes to Humans.

items.t: Fully rational
Selfish
Tastes do not change
Have a System 1
Often willing to contribute to their group
Unsure what they will like tomorrow

questions.explain: Frey's sentence defines the Econ as rational, selfish, and with stable tastes. Kahneman's Humans have a System 1, are sometimes generous, and are poor at predicting their own future tastes.

questions.q: Why did the first sentence of Bruno Frey's essay astonish Kahneman, and what did it lead to?
questions.a: The sentence described the economic agent as rational, selfish, and with unchanging tastes, while to a psychologist it is self-evident that people are none of these. Kahneman realized the economists next door were effectively studying a different species, Econs rather than Humans. This opened a conversation across disciplines, and soon Amos Tversky proposed that they study decision making, a conversation that came to define Kahneman's career.

questions.q: What specific question did Kahneman and Tversky set out to answer when they began studying decision making?
options: How framing changes people's moral judgments
How experts should choose investments to maximize wealth
Why people misjudge the frequency of events
What rules govern people's choices between simple gambles and between gambles and sure things
questions.explain: Their subject was people's attitudes to risky options, and the question was what rules govern choices between simple gambles and between gambles and sure things.

questions.q: Kahneman writes that simple gambles are to students of decision making what the ____ is to geneticists.
questions.explain: Like the fruit fly in genetics, choices between simple gambles are a simple model sharing important features with the more complex decisions researchers want to understand.

questions.q: Which of these reasons does Kahneman give for why decision theorists study choices between simple gambles?
options: Such choices share important features with more complex real decisions
The consequences of real choices are never certain
It is what other decision theorists do
Most people gamble regularly in everyday life
Gambles are the only choices that obey the axioms of rationality
questions.explain: Gambles model the uncertainty in every significant choice, and Kahneman adds wryly that the main reason is that other decision theorists study them. He makes no claim that people gamble often or that only gambles obey the axioms.

questions.q: What does the apple and banana example illustrate in Kahneman's account of expected utility theory?
options: An elementary rule (axiom) of rationality: preferring an apple implies preferring a 10% chance of an apple to a 10% chance of a banana
That probabilities are overweighted when outcomes are vivid
That the utility of food is logarithmic
That people often reverse their preferences between fruits
questions.explain: Expected utility theory is a logic of choice built on axioms of rationality. The example states one: if you prefer an apple to a banana, you also prefer the same chance of an apple to the same chance of a banana.

questions.q: Who, according to Kahneman, derived the theory of rational choice between gambles from a few axioms?
options: Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman
John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern
Daniel Bernoulli and Gustav Fechner
Richard Thaler and Bruno Frey
questions.explain: The mathematician John von Neumann and the economist Oskar Morgenstern derived expected utility theory from axioms. Bernoulli and Fechner came earlier with psychophysical ideas, and Thaler and Frey appear for other reasons.

questions.q: Which of these were the two roles in which economists adopted expected utility theory, according to Kahneman?
options: As a logic that prescribes how decisions should be made
As a description of how Econs make choices
As a description of how Humans actually make risky choices
As a model of how System 1 generates intuitions
questions.explain: Economists used the theory both prescriptively and as a description of Econs. Kahneman and Tversky, as psychologists, set out to learn how Humans actually choose, without assuming rationality.

questions.q: How did Kahneman and Tversky's approach to risky choice differ from the way economists used expected utility theory?
questions.a: Economists treated expected utility theory both as a logic prescribing how decisions should be made and as a description of how Econs choose. Kahneman and Tversky, as psychologists, wanted to learn how Humans actually make risky choices, without assuming anything about their rationality. Their resulting model, prospect theory, was purely descriptive and aimed to document and explain systematic violations of the axioms.

questions.q: When Kahneman and Tversky compared a coin toss to win $100 with getting $46 for sure, what were they trying to find?
options: The option with the higher expected value
The choice a perfectly rational agent would make
The intuitive choice, the one that appeared immediately tempting
The answer economists would predict
questions.explain: They were not looking for the most rational or advantageous choice but for the intuitive one. Both would have picked the sure $46.

questions.q: Put the steps of Kahneman and Tversky's informal method for studying their own intuitive preferences in order.
items: Invent a simple decision problem
Ask themselves how they would choose
Note when they confidently agreed on a choice
Assume most people would share that preference and move on
Verify the hunch later with real subjects
questions.explain: By playing both experimenters and subjects they moved fast: they invented problems, checked their own choices, treated confident agreement as evidence, and verified later.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman reports that when he and Tversky confidently agreed on a choice, their belief that most people would share it turned out almost always correct.
questions.explain: He writes that they believed most people would share their preference, “almost always correctly, as it turned out,” though they knew they would need to verify later.

questions.q: Why could Kahneman and Tversky move quickly in their early study of risky choice, and what was the catch?
questions.a: They spent hours inventing simple decision problems and asking how they themselves would choose, looking for the immediately tempting option rather than the rational one. When they confidently agreed, they assumed most people would share the preference, which turned out to be almost always correct. Playing both experimenters and subjects made them fast, but they knew their hunches would have to be verified with real data later.

questions.q: What was the most important way the 1979 essay Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk departed from utility theory?
options: It rejected the use of gambles as research tools
It replaced probabilities with frequencies
It prescribed better rules for rational investors
It was purely descriptive, not prescriptive
questions.explain: Prospect theory was modeled closely on utility theory but was purely descriptive, documenting and explaining systematic violations of rationality axioms in choices between gambles.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman describes prospect theory as a purely descriptive model rather than a logic of how people should choose.
questions.explain: Unlike expected utility theory, which economists used prescriptively, prospect theory aimed only to document and explain how people actually violate the axioms.

questions.q: Why, according to Kahneman, did he and Tversky submit their prospect theory essay to Econometrica?
options: Econometrica was where the best papers on decision making had been published
Their economist colleagues required it
They wanted to change economics and chose the venue for maximum impact
A psychology journal had rejected the paper
questions.explain: Their choice was not guided by a wish to influence economics; Econometrica simply was where the best decision-making papers had appeared. Kahneman calls this lucky, since the same paper in a psychology journal would likely have had little impact on economics.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say about the publication of prospect theory and related work?
options: It turned out to be the most significant work he and Tversky ever did
Two years later they published an account of framing effects in Science
The same paper in a psychological journal would likely have had little impact on economics
It was first published in a psychological journal
It was written within a year of starting the research
questions.explain: Prospect theory became their most significant work, the framing paper followed in Science, and the Econometrica venue mattered. It took five years to complete and appeared in an economics journal.

questions.q: True or false: Two years after prospect theory, Kahneman and Tversky published their account of framing effects in Econometrica.
questions.explain: The framing paper appeared in Science. Econometrica was the venue for the prospect theory essay itself.

questions.q: Kahneman defines ____ effects as the large changes of preferences sometimes caused by inconsequential variations in the wording of a choice problem.
questions.explain: Kahneman and Tversky published their account of framing effects in Science two years after prospect theory.

questions.q: Put these events in Kahneman and Tversky's work on decision making in chronological order.
items: Tversky shows Kahneman Bruno Frey's essay
They decide to make decision making their next project
They spend five years establishing facts about risky choices
They publish prospect theory in Econometrica
They publish an account of framing effects in Science
questions.explain: The Frey essay prompted the project; five years of work produced the prospect theory essay; the framing paper followed two years later.

questions.q: How did Kahneman and Tversky construct prospect theory from their observations?
questions.a: In their first five years studying decisions they established a dozen facts about choices between risky options, several of which flatly contradicted expected utility theory. They then built a theory that modified expected utility theory just enough to explain their collection of observations. That theory was prospect theory, closely modeled on utility theory but purely descriptive.

questions.q: The field of psychology founded and named by Gustav Fechner, which relates subjective experience to physical quantities, is called ____.
questions.explain: Fechner sought psychophysical laws relating the subjective quantity in the mind to the objective quantity in the material world; Kahneman and Tversky worked in its spirit.

questions.q: Match each physical quantity in Kahneman's account of Fechner's psychophysics to the subjective experience it produces.
pairs: Energy of a light
Brightness
Frequency of a tone
Pitch
Amount of money
Value
questions.explain: Fechner was obsessed with how variations in a physical quantity cause variations in a subjective experience, such as brightness, pitch, or value.

questions.q: Fechner proposed that for many dimensions the function relating stimulus intensity to psychological intensity is ____.
questions.explain: A logarithmic function means that increasing stimulus intensity by a given factor always adds the same increment on the psychological scale.

questions.q: Under Fechner's logarithmic law, if raising a sound from 10 to 100 units of energy raises psychological intensity by 4 units, what does raising it from 100 to 1,000 units do?
options: Raises psychological intensity by 40 units
Raises psychological intensity by 4 units
Raises psychological intensity by 0.4 units
Leaves psychological intensity unchanged
questions.explain: Each tenfold increase in the stimulus yields the same increment on the psychological scale, so the second tenfold increase also adds 4 units.

questions.q: Explain Fechner's logarithmic law and the example Kahneman uses to illustrate it.
questions.a: Fechner proposed that for many dimensions the relation between the physical stimulus and the psychological experience is logarithmic: increasing the stimulus by a given factor, such as times 10, always yields the same increment in subjective intensity. If raising a sound's energy from 10 to 100 units adds 4 units of psychological intensity, raising it from 100 to 1,000 adds another 4 units.

questions.q: Match each person to the contribution Kahneman credits them with in the chapter Bernoulli’s Errors.
pairs: Bruno Frey
Essay on the psychological assumptions of economic theory
Richard Thaler
Dubbed the two species Econs and Humans
Gustav Fechner
Founded psychophysics and proposed logarithmic laws
Daniel Bernoulli
Related the utility of money to wealth in 1738
Daniel Gilbert
Observed that disbelieving is hard work
questions.explain: Frey's essay started the conversation, Thaler named Econs and Humans, Fechner founded psychophysics, Bernoulli anticipated him with the utility of wealth, and Gilbert's observation helps explain theory-induced blindness.

questions.q: According to Bernoulli, a gift of 10 ducats to someone who already has 100 ducats has the same utility as which gift?
options: 100 ducats to someone who has 1,000 ducats
10 ducats to someone who has 200 ducats
20 ducats to someone who has 200 ducats
20 ducats to someone who has 100 ducats
questions.explain: The psychological response to a change in wealth is inversely proportional to initial wealth, so a 10% gift has the same utility at any level: 10 of 100 equals 20 of 200.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says Daniel Bernoulli anticipated Fechner's psychophysical reasoning by about one hundred years.
questions.explain: Bernoulli wrote in 1738, and Kahneman says that “One hundred years before Fechner, Bernoulli invented psychophysics to explain this aversion to risk.”

questions.q: If utility is a logarithmic function of wealth, as Bernoulli concluded, which pair of distances is psychologically equal?
options: From $100,000 to $1 million, and from $1 million to $1.9 million
From $1 million to $2 million, and from $9 million to $10 million
From $10 million to $100 million, and from $100 million to $110 million
From $100,000 to $1 million, and from $10 million to $100 million
questions.explain: Under a logarithmic function each tenfold increase covers the same psychological distance, so $100,000 to $1 million equals $10 million to $100 million.

questions.q: Before Bernoulli, mathematicians assumed gambles are assessed by their ____: a weighted average of the possible outcomes, each weighted by its probability.
questions.explain: For example, an 80% chance to win $100 and 20% chance to win $10 has an expected value of $82.

questions.q: Kahneman defines ____ as the common preference for a sure thing over a favorable gamble of equal or slightly higher expected value.
questions.explain: Bernoulli proposed that the diminishing marginal value of wealth explains this risk aversion.

questions.q: According to Kahneman's account of Bernoulli, what does a risk-averse decision maker do when offered a gamble or a sure amount?
options: Accepts a sure thing that is less than the expected value, in effect paying a premium to avoid uncertainty
Takes the gamble whenever its expected value exceeds the sure amount
Demands a sure amount well above the gamble's expected value
Chooses at random when the two values are close
questions.explain: A risk-averse person will choose a sure thing worth less than the gamble's expected value, paying a premium to avoid the uncertainty.

questions.q: How did Bernoulli use psychophysics to explain why people dislike risk?
questions.a: Bernoulli argued that people's choices are based not on dollar values but on the psychological values of outcomes, their utilities. Because wealth has diminishing marginal utility, each added amount of money adds less utility than the last. The psychological value of a gamble is the average of the utilities of its outcomes weighted by their probabilities, which falls below the utility of a sure thing of equal expected value, so a decision maker with this utility function is risk averse.

questions.q: Put the steps in order for evaluating a gamble the way Bernoulli proposed.
items: List the possible outcomes in wealth
Convert each outcome to its utility
Weight each utility by its probability
Add the weighted utilities
Compare the total with the utility of the sure thing
questions.explain: Bernoulli's expected utility is the average of the utilities of the outcomes, each weighted by its probability, not the weighted average of the dollar outcomes.

questions.q: In Bernoulli's table, equal chances to have 1 million or 7 million have a utility of 42, while 4 million for sure has a utility of 60. Why does the sure thing win even though both are worth 4 million in expected ducats?
options: Because people round down uncertain amounts
Because utility rises 60 units from 1 to 4 million but only 24 units from 4 to 7 million
Because Bernoulli assumed people overweight small probabilities
Because the gamble's expected value is actually lower
questions.explain: Diminishing utility of wealth makes the upside of the gamble worth far less than the downside costs, so the gamble's utility (84/2 = 42) is below the sure thing's 60.

questions.q: Sort these ideas into the approach mathematicians used before Bernoulli and Bernoulli's own approach to evaluating gambles.

items.t: Weight each dollar outcome by its probability
A gamble worth $82 should beat $80 for sure
Choices depend on the psychological values of outcomes
Average the utilities of outcomes, weighted by probability
Diminishing marginal value of wealth explains risk aversion

questions.explain: Before Bernoulli, gambles were assessed by expected value. Bernoulli replaced dollar values with utilities, which explains why people prefer a sure thing to a slightly better gamble.

questions.q: Bernoulli called his new concept of expected utility “____.”
questions.explain: He applied this moral expectation to questions such as how much a St. Petersburg merchant would pay to insure a spice shipment from Amsterdam.

questions.q: How did Bernoulli's utility function explain insurance, according to Kahneman?
options: Insurance companies exploit people's ignorance of expected value
Merchants buy insurance because ships are rarely lost
Losing 1 million costs a person with 3 million far more utility than a person with 10 million, so the poorer one pays to transfer risk to the richer one
Rich people fear losses more and so buy insurance from the poor
questions.explain: Losing 1 million cuts utility by 4 points for someone with 10 million but by 18 points for someone with 3 million, so the poorer man will happily pay a premium to the richer one.

questions.q: Using Bernoulli's table, explain why poor people buy insurance and richer people sell it to them.
questions.a: Because of the diminishing utility of wealth, the same loss hurts more when you have less. Losing 1 million costs someone with 10 million only 4 utility points (100 to 96), but costs someone with 3 million 18 points (48 to 30). The poorer man will therefore happily pay a premium to transfer the risk to the richer one, “which is what insurance is about.”

questions.q: Which of these could Bernoulli's utility theory explain, according to Kahneman?
options: Why most people prefer a sure thing to a gamble of equal expected value
Why poor people buy insurance from richer people
Why people pay only a few ducats for the St. Petersburg gamble
Why Jack, who rose to 5 million, is happier than Jill, who fell to 5 million
Why Betty prefers the gamble to a sure 2 million
questions.explain: Diminishing utility of wealth explains risk aversion, insurance, and the St. Petersburg paradox. Jack and Jill and Betty's risk seeking require a reference point, which Bernoulli's model lacks.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, where are the errors of a theory usually found?
options: In the way later scholars misapply it
In its mathematical derivations
In the data its authors chose to report
In what it ignores or tacitly assumes rather than what it asserts explicitly
questions.explain: Kahneman writes that the errors of a theory “hide in what it ignores or tacitly assumes,” and Bernoulli's tacit assumption is that only current wealth matters.

questions.q: Match each person in Kahneman's examples against Bernoulli to how they see their situation.
pairs: Jack
