Elated, having risen from 1 million to 5 million
Jill
Despondent, having fallen from 9 million to 5 million
Anthony
Sees the options as gains from 1 million
Betty
Sees the options as losses from 4 million
questions.explain: Jack and Jill have the same wealth but different histories; Anthony and Betty face the same possible states of wealth but different reference points. In both pairs the reference point, not wealth itself, shapes the experience.

questions.q: How does the story of Jack and Jill show that Bernoulli's theory is wrong?
questions.a: Today Jack and Jill each have 5 million, but yesterday Jack had 1 million and Jill had 9 million. Bernoulli's theory says utility depends on wealth, so they should be equally happy, yet obviously Jack is elated and Jill despondent. Their happiness is determined by the recent change in wealth relative to their different reference points, which the theory ignores.

questions.q: Two friends each check their retirement accounts and see a balance of $50,000. Last month one had $30,000 and the other had $80,000. What does Kahneman's account of Jack and Jill predict?
options: The one who rose from $30,000 will feel much better than the one who fell from $80,000
The one who fell will feel better because they were once richer
Neither will care, since the change is small relative to lifetime wealth
Both will feel equally satisfied because their wealth is the same
questions.explain: As with Jack and Jill, happiness depends on the change from each person's reference point, not on the current amount. Bernoulli's theory wrongly predicts equal satisfaction.

questions.q: Kahneman says the happiness Jack and Jill experience is determined by the recent change in their wealth, relative to the states of wealth that define their ____.
questions.explain: Jack's reference point is 1 million and Jill's is 9 million, so the same 5 million is a gain for him and a loss for her.

questions.q: Which of these examples does Kahneman use to show that reference dependence is ubiquitous in sensation and perception?
options: A sound feels loud or faint depending on whether a whisper or a roar preceded it
A gray patch looks dark or light depending on its background
The utility of an amount of wealth depends on a reference amount
A tone's pitch is fixed by its frequency alone
Brightness depends only on the absolute energy of a light
questions.explain: Kahneman argues you must know the reference sound, the background, or the reference wealth to predict experience. Saying experience depends only on the absolute stimulus is exactly the view he rejects.

questions.q: In the Anthony and Betty example, why are the two likely to choose differently even though they face the same states of wealth?
questions.a: Both choose between a gamble of 1 or 4 million and a sure 2 million, so Bernoulli predicts the same choice. But Anthony currently has 1 million and sees the sure thing as doubling his wealth, while Betty has 4 million and sees it as losing half. Anthony thinks in gains and is risk averse; Betty thinks in losses and is likely to take her chances on the gamble.

questions.q: Sort these thoughts into Anthony's view and Betty's view of the choice between a sure 2 million and equal chances of 1 or 4 million.

items.t: The sure thing doubles my wealth
The gamble may quadruple my wealth or gain nothing
I will probably take the sure thing
The sure thing loses half my wealth
The gamble may lose three-quarters of my wealth or nothing
I will probably take my chances on the gamble

questions.explain: Anthony thinks in gains and is risk averse; Betty thinks in losses and, like others facing very bad options, is likely to gamble.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, in whom is Betty's risk-seeking preference for the gamble often observed?
options: Retirees protecting their savings
Entrepreneurs and generals when all their options are bad
Insurance companies pricing policies
Students choosing between simple gambles in experiments
questions.explain: Bernoulli's model can explain Anthony's risk aversion but not Betty's risk seeking, which Kahneman says is often seen in entrepreneurs and generals when every option is bad.

questions.q: True or false: In Kahneman's Anthony and Betty example, Betty, who currently owns 4 million, is more likely than Anthony to choose the sure 2 million.
questions.explain: Betty sees the sure 2 million as losing half her wealth, so she is the one more likely to take her chances on the gamble; Anthony sees the sure thing as doubling his wealth.

questions.q: Kahneman calls the scholarly weakness of finding it extraordinarily difficult to notice a theory's flaws once you have accepted it and used it as a tool ____.
questions.explain: Theory-induced blindness is his explanation for why Bernoulli's flawed utility concept survived obvious counterexamples for so long.

questions.q: Put the stages of theory-induced blindness, as Kahneman describes it, in order.
items: Accept a theory and use it as a tool in your thinking
Come upon an observation that does not fit the model
Assume there must be a good explanation you are missing
Give the theory the benefit of the doubt, trusting the experts who accepted it
questions.explain: Once the theory is a tool, a misfit observation is explained away as something you are missing, and trust in the expert community keeps the theory in place.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman include in his description of theory-induced blindness?
options: Once you use a theory as a tool, it is extraordinarily difficult to notice its flaws
You assume a misfit observation has a good explanation you are missing
You trust the community of experts who have accepted the theory
You actively search for counterexamples to test the theory
You abandon the theory as soon as one observation contradicts it
questions.explain: Theory-induced blindness means explaining away anomalies and deferring to experts. Actively seeking counterexamples or dropping the theory at the first anomaly is the opposite.

questions.q: How does Kahneman explain why Bernoulli's flawed conception of utility survived for almost 300 years?
questions.a: He attributes it to theory-induced blindness: once a theory is accepted and used as a tool, it is extraordinarily difficult to notice its flaws. Scholars who noticed stories like Jack and Jill casually assumed there was a good explanation they were missing and trusted the experts, rather than concluding that utility depends on the history of wealth, not only on present wealth. As Daniel Gilbert observed, disbelieving is hard work, and System 2 is easily tired.

questions.q: Sort these cases into those Kahneman would describe as risk averse and those he would describe as risk seeking.

items.t: Choosing $46 for sure over a coin toss to win $100
Anthony choosing a sure 2 million from a base of 1 million
A wife suing for alimony who can only gain and would like to settle
Betty gambling rather than accept a sure loss of half her wealth
A general taking a gamble when all his options are bad
A husband facing only bad options who prefers to go to court

questions.explain: People choosing among gains tend to take the sure thing; people facing only bad options or losses tend to gamble, which Bernoulli's model cannot explain.

questions.q: Match each example from the opening of the chapter Bernoulli’s Errors to the point Kahneman uses it to make.
pairs: Simple gambles compared to the fruit fly
Gambles are a simple model sharing features with complex decisions
A neighbor's son taking up the tuba after you buy an apartment
Even ostensibly sure outcomes are uncertain
Preferring an apple implies preferring a 10% chance of an apple
An axiom of rationality in expected utility theory
A coin toss to win $100 versus $46 for sure
The intuitive choice is the immediately tempting sure thing
questions.explain: Each example serves the case for studying risky choice: gambles as a model organism, the uncertainty of real choices, the axioms of expected utility theory, and Kahneman and Tversky's search for intuitive preferences.

questions.q: Sort these descriptions into those that fit expected utility theory as economists used it and those that fit Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory.

items.t: Prescribes how decisions should be made
Describes how Econs make choices
Derived from axioms by von Neumann and Morgenstern
Purely descriptive
Documents and explains systematic violations of the axioms
Built from a dozen facts about how people choose between risky options

questions.explain: Economists used expected utility theory both prescriptively and as a description of Econs. Prospect theory modified it just enough to describe how Humans actually choose, including their violations of the axioms.

questions.q: Match each term from the chapter Bernoulli’s Errors to its meaning.
pairs: Expected value
Average of a gamble's dollar outcomes, each weighted by its probability
Expected utility
Average of the utilities of the outcomes, each weighted by its probability
Risk aversion
Preferring a sure thing to a favorable gamble of equal or slightly higher expected value
Reference point
The prior state against which a change in wealth is experienced
Theory-induced blindness
Difficulty noticing a theory's flaws once you use it as a tool
questions.explain: Bernoulli replaced expected value with expected utility to explain risk aversion; Kahneman argues the theory missed the reference point and survived because of theory-induced blindness.

questions.q: Match each remark from the end of the chapter Bernoulli’s Errors to the idea it applies.
pairs: A $20,000 bonus pleased him three years ago, but his salary has since risen 20%
He now needs a higher bonus to get the same utility
Both candidates accept the same salary offer, but she currently earns much more
Different reference points mean they will not be equally satisfied
She would settle the alimony case, but he prefers to go to court
Those who can only gain are risk averse; those facing bad options take risks
questions.explain: The remarks apply proportional utility, reference dependence, and the contrast between Anthony's risk aversion and Betty's risk seeking to everyday cases.

questions.q: Two job candidates both accept the same salary offer, but one currently earns much more than the other. What does the chapter Bernoulli’s Errors suggest?
options: Satisfaction will depend only on the size of the company
Both will be equally satisfied because the offer is identical
The candidate with the higher current salary will be less satisfied with the offer
The candidate with the higher current salary will be more satisfied
questions.explain: Because their reference points differ, the same salary is a smaller gain, or even a loss, for the candidate who already earns more, so they will not be equally satisfied.

questions.q: In the alimony example at the end of the chapter Bernoulli’s Errors, why does the wife want to settle while the husband prefers to go to court?
questions.a: The wife can only gain from the case, so like Anthony she evaluates her options as gains and is risk averse, preferring a sure settlement. The husband faces options that are all bad, so like Betty he thinks in losses and would rather take the risk of going to court. Their attitudes to risk follow from their different reference points, not from their final states of wealth.

questions.q: Why would an employee who was delighted with a $20,000 bonus three years ago need a larger bonus now to feel the same way, according to the chapter Bernoulli’s Errors?
questions.a: His salary has risen by 20% since then, so his reference point has moved up. Following Bernoulli's insight that we judge changes in proportion to what we already have, the same $20,000 is now a smaller relative gain and yields less utility. To produce the same psychological response, the bonus must grow along with his salary.

questions.q: In the opening of the Prospect Theory chapter, what puzzled Kahneman about the experiments he read about in Amos Tversky's book?
options: They measured the utility of wealth by having people gamble on changes of a few pennies
They measured risk attitudes only among professional traders and bankers
They offered people gambles with millions of dollars at stake
They asked people directly how wealthy they felt rather than offering gambles
questions.explain: The scholars measured the utility of wealth by modifying wealth within a range of less than a dollar. Kahneman doubted that people evaluate gambles by such tiny differences in total wealth.

questions.q: In the Prospect Theory chapter, which economist had earlier proposed attaching utilities to changes of wealth rather than to states of wealth?
options: Daniel Bernoulli
Harry Markowitz
Matthew Rabin
Richard Thaler
questions.explain: Amos remembered that Harry Markowitz, later a Nobel laureate for his work on finance, had proposed this idea about a quarter of a century earlier, though it had attracted little attention. Bernoulli is the author of the states-of-wealth view being rejected.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what combination of factors led him and Tversky to their breakthrough of defining outcomes as gains and losses?
options: Extensive training in economics and a large research grant
A mathematical proof showing utility theory was internally inconsistent
Knowledge of perception together with ignorance about decision theory
Field data from investors who had lost large sums in the markets
questions.explain: Kahneman writes that knowledge of perception and ignorance about decision theory both contributed. He did not know enough about utility theory to be blinded by respect for it.

questions.q: In the Prospect Theory chapter, how does Kahneman say you can tell that you have made a theoretical advance?
options: Other scholars immediately accept your new idea
Your new theory turns out to be simpler than the old one
You can derive the old theory as a special case of the new one
You can no longer reconstruct why you failed for so long to see the obvious
questions.explain: After overcoming theory-induced blindness, the rejected idea seemed not only false but absurd. Kahneman notes “You know you have made a theoretical advance when you can no longer reconstruct why you failed for so long to see the obvious.”

questions.q: In utility theory as described in the Prospect Theory chapter, how may the utilities of a gain and a loss of the same size differ?
options: Only in their sign, plus or minus
Losses must always weigh about twice as much
Gains must always weigh more than losses
They differ according to the decision maker's mood
questions.explain: Utility theory assesses both as differences between utilities of two states of wealth, so they can differ only in sign. There is no way to represent the fact that losing $500 hurts more than winning $500 pleases.

questions.q: In Problem 2 of the Prospect Theory chapter (lose $900 for sure OR a 90% chance to lose $1,000), what do most people choose, and why?
options: The sure loss, because people are risk averse in all situations
The gamble, because losing $900 feels like much more than 90% of the pain of losing $1,000
The sure loss, because the expected loss of the gamble is larger
The gamble, because people overestimate their chance of winning in general
questions.explain: Most people are risk seeking here. The negative value of losing $900 is much more than 90% of the negative value of losing $1,000, so the sure loss is very aversive.

questions.q: In Problems 3 and 4 of the Prospect Theory chapter, why should Bernoulli's theory predict the same choice in both problems?
options: Both problems have the same expected value of zero
Both problems offer a sure loss against a larger probable loss
In both, the final states of wealth on offer are the same: richer by $1,500 for sure, or a 50-50 chance of richer by $1,000 or $2,000
In both, the gift is large enough to change the respondent's attitude to risk
questions.explain: In terms of final states of wealth, the only thing that matters for Bernoulli, the two problems are identical. Yet most people take the sure thing in Problem 3 and the gamble in Problem 4.

questions.q: In Problems 3 and 4 of the Prospect Theory chapter, what explains why being $1,500 richer is attractive in one problem and unattractive in the other?
options: People are confused by the arithmetic in the second problem
The gift in Problem 4 is taxed while the gift in Problem 3 is not
People ignore probabilities when the stakes are large
The reference point is $1,000 above current wealth in Problem 3 and $2,000 above it in Problem 4
questions.explain: The gift is absorbed into the reference point. Richer by $1,500 is therefore a gain of $500 in Problem 3 and a loss of $500 in Problem 4.

questions.q: According to the Prospect Theory chapter, what is the 'moving part' that Bernoulli's theory lacks?
options: The reference point, the earlier state relative to which gains and losses are evaluated
The probability of each outcome
The decision maker's total current wealth
The expected value of the gamble
questions.explain: Kahneman says Bernoulli's theory is too simple and lacks a moving part. In prospect theory you need to know not only the state of wealth but also the reference state; wealth and probability were already in Bernoulli's model.

questions.q: In the Prospect Theory chapter, why does Kahneman say prospect theory's greater complexity had to be justified?
options: Because economists refuse to accept any psychological theory
Because in science complexity is a cost that must be repaid with new and interesting predictions
Because complex theories cannot be tested experimentally
Because the two-systems model already explained the same facts
questions.explain: Complexity is considered a cost in science, justified only by a sufficiently rich set of new predictions of facts the existing theory cannot explain. That was the challenge he and Amos had to meet.

questions.q: In the Prospect Theory chapter, the three-bowls-of-water demonstration illustrates which principle?
options: Loss aversion
Diminishing sensitivity
Evaluation relative to a neutral reference point
The utility of states of wealth
questions.explain: After one hand sits in cold water and the other in warm, the room-temperature bowl feels hot to one hand and cold to the other. Evaluation depends on the adaptation level, not on the absolute temperature.

questions.q: According to the Prospect Theory chapter, in Figure 10 what does the abrupt change in the slope of the value function at the reference point represent?
options: Diminishing sensitivity for gains
Risk seeking for gains
The utility of total wealth
Loss aversion: a stronger response to losses than to corresponding gains
questions.explain: The S-shape represents diminishing sensitivity, while the asymmetry, with the slope changing abruptly at the reference point, represents loss aversion.

questions.q: In the Prospect Theory chapter, why did Kahneman find it implausible to study the utility of wealth through gambles over a few pennies?
questions.a: The experiments modified wealth within a range of less than a dollar, as if people evaluated gambles by tiny differences in their total wealth. Psychophysics suggested that to study the subjective value of wealth you should ask about wealth itself, not about changes of wealth. The realization led him and Amos to attach value to changes, that is, to gains and losses, rather than to states of wealth.

questions.q: How does Kahneman describe overcoming theory-induced blindness in the Prospect Theory chapter, and what example shows the old view was absurd?
questions.a: Once they adopted gains and losses as outcomes, the idea they had rejected seemed not only false but absurd. They were amused to realize they could not even assess their own current wealth within tens of thousands of dollars, so deriving attitudes to small changes from the utility of wealth seemed indefensible.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say, in the Prospect Theory chapter, that differences between gains and losses were never studied by utility theorists?
questions.a: In utility theory, a gain and a loss are both differences between the utilities of two states of wealth and may differ only in sign. Because the dominant theory assumed the distinction did not matter, there was no point in examining it. This is a case of theory-induced blindness: the theory could not represent the obvious fact that losing $500 hurts more than winning $500 pleases.

questions.q: Explain, using Problems 1 and 2 of the Prospect Theory chapter, why people are risk averse for gains but risk seeking for losses.
questions.a: In Problem 1 the value of a sure $900 is more than 90% of the value of $1,000, so people take the sure gain. In Problem 2 the mirror image holds: the negative value of losing $900 is much more than 90% of the negative value of losing $1,000, so the sure loss is very aversive and people gamble. Kahneman adds that the weighting of probabilities (90% versus 100%) also contributes to both choices.

questions.q: Why were Problems 3 and 4 in the Prospect Theory chapter a decisive counterexample to Bernoulli's theory?
questions.a: In terms of final wealth the two problems are identical: a sure $1,500 more or a 50-50 chance of $1,000 or $2,000 more. If only the utility of wealth mattered, they should yield the same choice, yet most people take the sure thing in Problem 3 and the gamble in Problem 4. The difference comes from the reference point, which includes the gift, so the same final wealth is a gain in one problem and a loss in the other.

questions.q: According to the Prospect Theory chapter, why do people barely notice the $1,000 or $2,000 they were 'given' before choosing in Problems 3 and 4?
questions.a: The gift is included in the reference point, and reference points are generally ignored. People's attitudes to risk would not change if their net worth were a few thousand dollars higher or lower. They simply like winning and dislike losing, and their attitudes are not derived from evaluating their wealth.

questions.q: Kahneman says the three cognitive features at the heart of prospect theory are operating characteristics of System 1. What are they, and why does he connect them to System 1?
questions.a: The three features are evaluation relative to a neutral reference point, diminishing sensitivity, and loss aversion. They play an essential role in evaluating financial outcomes, and they are common to many automatic processes of perception, judgment, and emotion, which is why they belong to System 1. He notes that he and Amos were not using the two-systems model when they built the theory.

questions.q: What is the evolutionary explanation Kahneman offers for loss aversion in the Prospect Theory chapter?
questions.a: The asymmetry between the power of positive and negative expectations or experiences has an evolutionary history. Organisms that treat threats as more urgent than opportunities have a better chance to survive and reproduce, so losses come to loom larger than gains.

questions.q: In prospect theory, outcomes are defined as gains and losses rather than as states of ____.
questions.explain: Following Markowitz, Kahneman and Tversky attached value to changes of wealth instead of to total wealth, as Bernoulli had.

questions.q: Kahneman calls the failure to notice the flaws in a theory one has accepted ____.
questions.explain: Theory-induced blindness explains why the obvious difference between gains and losses was neither expected nor studied by utility theorists.

questions.q: In Problem 1 (get $900 for sure OR a 90% chance to get $1,000), the great majority of people are risk ____.
questions.explain: Most people take the sure $900, because its subjective value is more than 90% of the value of $1,000. This choice would not have surprised Bernoulli.

questions.q: Kahneman notes that the neutral reference point is sometimes referred to as an ____.
questions.explain: Evaluation is relative to an adaptation level, as the three-bowls demonstration shows: the same water feels warm to one hand and cold to the other.

questions.q: For financial outcomes, the usual reference point is the ____, though it can also be an expected outcome or one you feel entitled to.
questions.explain: The status quo is the default reference point, but an expected result or an entitlement, such as the raise colleagues received, can also serve.

questions.q: The principle that the subjective difference between $900 and $1,000 is much smaller than between $100 and $200 is called diminishing ____.
questions.explain: Diminishing sensitivity applies to both sensory dimensions and changes of wealth, like a weak light that matters a lot in a dark room but not in a bright one.

questions.q: In prospect theory, the value function in Figure 10 has an ____ shape, which represents diminishing sensitivity for both gains and losses.
questions.explain: The S-shaped curve flattens as gains or losses grow larger, showing diminishing sensitivity in both directions.

questions.q: Which of these are the three cognitive features Kahneman places at the heart of prospect theory?
options: Evaluation relative to a neutral reference point
Diminishing sensitivity
Loss aversion
Evaluation of final states of wealth
Overweighting of base rates
questions.explain: The three principles are the reference point, diminishing sensitivity, and loss aversion. Evaluating final states of wealth is Bernoulli's approach, which prospect theory rejects.

questions.q: Which of these can serve as the reference point for a financial outcome, according to the Prospect Theory chapter?
options: The status quo
The outcome you expect
The outcome you feel entitled to, such as the bonus your colleagues receive
The highest outcome you could possibly imagine
Your total lifetime wealth
questions.explain: Kahneman lists the status quo, an expected outcome, and an outcome you feel entitled to. Total wealth is what Bernoulli used, not a reference point.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman use in the Prospect Theory chapter to illustrate diminishing sensitivity?
options: A weak light turned on in a dark room versus a brightly lit room
The difference between $100 and $200 compared with $900 and $1,000
Three bowls of water at different temperatures
A coin toss to lose $100 or win $150
questions.explain: Both the light example and the dollar comparison show that the same increment matters less as the level rises. The bowls illustrate the reference point, and the coin toss illustrates loss aversion.

questions.q: Which of these describe how the value function in Figure 10 of the Prospect Theory chapter differs from Bernoulli's model?
options: Gains and losses, not states of wealth, are the carriers of value
It has two distinct parts on either side of a neutral reference point
Losses produce a stronger response than corresponding gains
Value depends only on the final state of wealth
questions.explain: In prospect theory gains and losses carry value, the graph is split at a reference point, and the slope is steeper for losses. Dependence on final wealth alone is Bernoulli's view.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says he expected Tversky to explain why the penny-gamble experiments made sense, but Tversky instead saw the relevance of modern psychophysics at once.
questions.explain: Kahneman reported his puzzlement as a vague thought, fully expecting to be set straight. Instead, the relevance of modern psychophysics was immediately obvious to Amos.

questions.q: True or false: According to Kahneman, he and Tversky were the first to notice that people become risk seeking when all their options are bad.
questions.explain: Kahneman says they were not the first to notice this; theory-induced blindness meant that earlier observations were ignored because the dominant theory could not accommodate them.

questions.q: True or false: In Problem 3 of the Prospect Theory chapter (given $1,000, then a 50% chance to win $1,000 OR $500 for sure), a large majority of respondents preferred the gamble.
questions.explain: In Problem 3 a large majority preferred the sure thing. It was in Problem 4, framed as losses after a $2,000 gift, that most preferred the gamble.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says the three features at the heart of prospect theory are operating characteristics of System 2.
questions.explain: He says they should be seen as operating characteristics of System 1, since they are common to many automatic processes of perception, judgment, and emotion.

questions.q: Put the steps of how Kahneman and Tversky arrived at the gains-and-losses idea in the order the Prospect Theory chapter tells them.
items: Kahneman reads about penny-gamble experiments in Amos's book
Kahneman reports his puzzlement to Amos as a vague thought
Amos recalls Markowitz's theory of utilities for changes of wealth
They decide to define outcomes as gains and losses
Amos asks, 'How about losses?' and they find risk seeking
questions.explain: The puzzle over penny gambles led to Markowitz's idea and the decision to use gains and losses. Only later did Amos's casual question about losses reveal risk seeking.

questions.q: Put the steps of the three-bowls-of-water demonstration in the Prospect Theory chapter in order.
items: Fill the left bowl with ice water, the right with warm, the middle at room temperature
Immerse your hands in the cold and warm water for about a minute
Dip both hands in the middle bowl
Feel the same water as heat in one hand and cold in the other
questions.explain: The demonstration shows that evaluation is relative to an adaptation level: identical water feels different depending on what each hand was used to.

questions.q: Put the steps of Kahneman's argument from Problems 3 and 4 in order.
items: Show that both problems offer the same final states of wealth
Observe that most choose the sure thing in Problem 3 and the gamble in Problem 4
Conclude that this is a decisive counterexample to Bernoulli's theory
Identify the reference point as the missing variable
questions.explain: The identical final states lead to the prediction of the same choice; the different choices refute it, and the reference point explains why.

questions.q: Put the three principles of prospect theory in the order Kahneman presents them in the chapter.
items: Evaluation relative to a neutral reference point
Diminishing sensitivity
Loss aversion
questions.explain: Kahneman first presents the reference point (the bowls of water), then diminishing sensitivity (the light), then loss aversion, called 'the third principle'.

questions.q: Match each person to their role in the Prospect Theory chapter.
pairs: Harry Markowitz
Proposed attaching utilities to changes of wealth
Amos Tversky
Casually asked, 'How about losses?'
Daniel Bernoulli
Model in which states of wealth carry value
Daniel Kahneman
Puzzled by penny gambles used to measure utility of wealth
questions.explain: Markowitz's overlooked idea, Amos's question, and Kahneman's puzzlement led to prospect theory, which replaced Bernoulli's states-of-wealth model.

questions.q: Match each principle of prospect theory to the illustration Kahneman gives for it.
pairs: Reference point
Same water feels hot to one hand and cold to the other
Diminishing sensitivity
A weak light has a large effect only in a dark room
Loss aversion
Organisms that treat threats as more urgent survive better
questions.explain: Each principle is drawn from perception or evolution: adaptation level for the reference point, light intensity for diminishing sensitivity, and survival for loss aversion.

questions.q: Match each feature of the value function in Figure 10 to what it represents.
pairs: Two parts left and right of a neutral point
Outcomes are gains or losses relative to a reference point
S-shaped curve
Diminishing sensitivity for gains and losses
Steeper slope on the loss side
Loss aversion
questions.explain: Kahneman says if prospect theory had a flag, this image would be drawn on it: the reference point, the S-shape, and the asymmetry capture the three principles.

questions.q: Sort each choice by whether it is the majority's risk-averse or risk-seeking choice in the Prospect Theory chapter.

items.t: Problem 1: get $900 for sure
Problem 2: 90% chance to lose $1,000
Problem 3: get $500 for sure
Problem 4: 50% chance to lose $1,000

questions.explain: People take the sure thing when outcomes are gains (Problems 1 and 3) and gamble when outcomes are losses (Problems 2 and 4).

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it describes Bernoulli's utility theory or prospect theory.

items.t: States of wealth are the carriers of value
Gains and losses are the carriers of value
You need to know only the state of wealth
You also need to know the reference state
Gains and losses differ only in sign
Losses loom larger than gains

questions.explain: Prospect theory adds the reference point and loss aversion, making it more complex but able to predict facts utility theory cannot explain.

questions.q: Using the Prospect Theory chapter's idea of the reference point, sort each outcome by whether it would be felt as a gain or a loss.

items.t: You get a 3% raise when you expected none
You get a 3% raise when all your colleagues got 6%
You find $20 on the street
Your expected bonus is cut in half

questions.explain: Outcomes better than the reference point are gains and those below it are losses. The reference point can be the status quo, an expectation, or what colleagues received.

questions.q: Sort each example by the principle of prospect theory it illustrates.

items.t: The jump from $100 to $200 feels bigger than from $900 to $1,000
A weak light is barely noticed in a bright room
Room-temperature water feels warm after a hand was in ice water
Richer by $1,500 is a gain in Problem 3 but a loss in Problem 4

questions.explain: Diminishing sensitivity concerns the shrinking impact of increments; the reference point concerns what an outcome is compared with.

questions.q: In the Loss Aversion section, what is a 'mixed' prospect?
options: An option with both a risk of loss and an opportunity for gain
A choice between two sure gains
A choice between a sure loss and a larger probable loss
A gamble whose probabilities are unknown
questions.explain: Mixed options involve both a possible loss and a possible gain, as faced by investors, lawyers, generals, and politicians. A sure loss against a probable larger loss is a 'bad' choice, not a mixed one.

questions.q: In Problem 5 (lose $100 on tails, win $150 on heads), how do most people respond?
options: They accept it, because the expected value is positive
They reject it, because the fear of losing $100 is more intense than the hope of gaining $150
They accept it, because people are risk seeking for gains
They are indifferent, because the amounts are small
questions.explain: Although the expected value is positive, most people dislike the gamble. The rejection is an act of System 2, but the critical inputs are emotional responses from System 1.

questions.q: According to the Loss Aversion section, in what range has the 'loss aversion ratio' usually been estimated?
options: 3 to 5
questions.explain: The ratio is usually in the range of 1.5 to 2.5; for many people the smallest gain that balances an equal chance to lose $100 is about $200.

questions.q: According to the Loss Aversion section, what happened when experiment participants were told to 'think like a trader'?
options: They became more loss averse and more anxious
They refused to take part in any gambles
Their choices became random
They became less loss averse and their emotional reaction to losses was sharply reduced
questions.explain: Professional risk takers are more tolerant of losses, probably because they do not react emotionally to every fluctuation. Instructing people to think like a trader reduced both loss aversion and physiological arousal.

questions.q: According to the Loss Aversion section, what happens to the loss aversion coefficient when a possible loss is potentially ruinous?
options: It falls to 1, making people indifferent to risk
It stays the same as for small stakes
It turns negative, so people seek the risk
It becomes very large and may even be infinite
questions.explain: If a loss threatens ruin or your lifestyle, the coefficient may be infinite: there are risks you will not accept regardless of how many millions you might win.

questions.q: In the Loss Aversion section, how does Kahneman reconcile the claims that loss aversion causes risk aversion and diminishing sensitivity causes risk seeking?
options: One applies to experts and the other to novices
Loss aversion governs mixed gambles, while diminishing sensitivity governs choices where all options are bad
One applies to small stakes and the other to large stakes
Loss aversion disappears whenever probabilities are high
questions.explain: There is no contradiction. In mixed gambles the loss looms about twice as large as the gain; in bad choices the bending of the curve makes a sure loss of $900 hurt more than 90% of a $1,000 loss.

questions.q: What did Matthew Rabin's theorem, described in the Loss Aversion section, show?
options: That loss aversion disappears when stakes are large
That expected utility theory explains small-stakes risk aversion well
That rejecting a favorable small-stakes gamble commits a utility maximizer to absurd risk aversion for some larger gamble
That traders are more loss averse than ordinary people
questions.explain: Rabin proved in 2000 that explaining loss aversion by the utility of wealth is absurd and doomed to fail: someone who rejects lose $100/win $200 would also have to reject lose $200/win $20,000.

questions.q: In the Loss Aversion section, how can you measure your own loss aversion, and what do typical answers show?
questions.a: Ask yourself the smallest gain needed to balance an equal chance to lose $100. For many people the answer is about $200, twice the loss, and experiments estimate the loss aversion ratio at usually 1.5 to 2.5. The ratio is an average; some people are much more loss averse than others.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say there is no contradiction between extreme risk aversion in mixed gambles and risk seeking in bad choices?
questions.a: In mixed gambles, where both a gain and a loss are possible, loss aversion makes the possible loss loom about twice as large as the gain, as the slopes of the value function show. In bad choices, where a sure loss is compared with a larger probable loss, diminishing sensitivity bends the curve so that losing $900 hurts more than 90% as much as losing $1,000. Kahneman calls these two insights the essence of prospect theory.

questions.q: In the Loss Aversion section, why does Kahneman call the 250-year neglect of small-stakes loss aversion a striking example of theory-induced blindness?
questions.a: People show considerable loss aversion even when the amount at risk is minuscule relative to their wealth, which attitudes to states of wealth cannot plausibly explain. Yet this obvious flaw in Bernoulli's theory failed to attract scholarly notice for more than 250 years, until Matthew Rabin proved in 2000 that explaining such loss aversion by the utility of wealth is doomed to fail.

questions.q: In Problem 5 of the Loss Aversion section, what are the roles of System 1 and System 2 in rejecting the coin-toss gamble?
questions.a: The decision to reject the gamble to lose $100 or win $150 is an act of System 2. But the critical inputs are emotional responses generated by System 1: for most people the fear of losing $100 is more intense than the hope of gaining $150.

questions.q: Kahneman and Tversky summarized many observations with the phrase 'losses loom ____ than gains.'
questions.explain: From responses to gambles like Problem 5, they concluded that “losses loom larger than gains” and that people are loss averse.

questions.q: In a 50-50 gamble to lose $10, if the smallest gain you need is exactly $10, you are ____ to risk.
questions.explain: A required gain of $10 means you are indifferent to risk; less than $10 means you seek risk, and more than $10 means you are loss averse.

questions.q: Kahneman notes that professional risk takers in the ____ markets are more tolerant of losses than other people.
questions.explain: They are probably more tolerant because they do not respond emotionally to every fluctuation.

questions.q: Rabin and Thaler, recalling a Monty Python sketch, wrote that expected utility is an ____.
questions.explain: Echoing the dead-parrot sketch's “this is an ex-parrot,” they declared expected utility an ex-hypothesis, which many economists saw as near blasphemy.

questions.q: Rabin and Thaler noted that the gamble of a 50% chance to lose $200 and a 50% chance to win $20,000 has an expected return of ____.
questions.explain: The gamble has an expected return of $9,900 with zero chance of losing more than $200, so rejecting it would be absurd.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give as examples of people facing mixed prospects?
options: Investors evaluating a start-up
Lawyers wondering whether to file a lawsuit
Politicians deciding whether to run for office
Someone choosing between two sure gains of different sizes
Someone choosing between a sure loss and a larger probable loss
questions.explain: Investors, lawyers, generals, and politicians all face both possible victory and defeat. Two sure gains, or a sure loss against a probable loss, are not mixed prospects.

questions.q: Which of these statements about the loss aversion ratio are made in the Loss Aversion section?
options: For many people it is about 2
Some people are much more loss averse than others
It tends to increase as stakes rise, but not dramatically
It is exactly the same for everyone
It is always below 1 for professional traders
questions.explain: The ratio averages about 2 with individual variation, and it rises modestly with stakes. Traders are more tolerant of losses, but the book does not say their ratio falls below 1.

questions.q: Which of these would show that a person is loss averse in a 50-50 gamble to lose $10?
options: Requiring a possible gain of $20
Requiring a possible gain of $15
Requiring a possible gain of $10
Requiring a possible gain of $5
questions.explain: Any required gain above $10 shows loss aversion. Exactly $10 shows indifference to risk, and less than $10 shows risk seeking.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says the rejection of the coin-toss gamble in Problem 5 is an act of System 2, though its critical inputs come from System 1.
questions.explain: System 2 makes the decision, but it relies on the emotional responses System 1 generates, in which the fear of loss outweighs the hope of gain.

questions.q: True or false: According to the Loss Aversion section, loss aversion appears only when the amount at risk is large relative to a person's wealth.
questions.explain: Figure 10 shows an abrupt change in slope because there is considerable loss aversion even when the amount at risk is minuscule relative to wealth.

questions.q: True or false: Many economists saw Rabin and Thaler's 'ex-hypothesis' remark as little short of blasphemy.
questions.explain: Kahneman reports that many economists reacted this way, though he thinks the blindness it mocked was a legitimate target for humorous comment.

questions.q: Put the steps of Rabin's argument, as told in the Loss Aversion section, in order.
items: Most people reject a 50-50 gamble to lose $100 or win $200
Utility theory implies they must also reject lose $200 or win $20,000
No one in their right mind would reject the larger gamble
Rabin and Thaler conclude expected utility is an 'ex-hypothesis'
questions.explain: Rabin starts from a common small-stakes rejection, derives an absurd implication under utility theory, and concludes the theory fails to explain loss aversion.

questions.q: Match each smallest acceptable gain in a 50-50 gamble to lose $10 with what it reveals.
pairs: Exactly $10
Indifferent to risk
Less than $10
Risk seeking
More than $10
Loss averse
questions.explain: Kahneman's self-test compares the required gain with the possible loss: equal means indifferent, lower means risk seeking, higher means loss averse.

questions.q: Match each item from the Loss Aversion section to its description.
pairs: Matthew Rabin, 2000
Proved loss aversion cannot be explained by the utility of wealth
Expected return of the lose $200 or win $20,000 gamble
Monty Python
Sketch about returning a dead parrot
Think like a trader
Instruction that reduced loss aversion and arousal
questions.explain: Rabin's proof, Rabin and Thaler's comment on the larger gamble, the dead-parrot joke, and the trader instruction are all part of the section's case.

questions.q: Sort each situation by whether it is a mixed prospect or a bad choice in which all options are losses.

items.t: Coin toss: lose $100 on tails, win $150 on heads
A general considering an offensive that could bring victory or defeat
Lose $900 for sure OR 90% chance to lose $1,000
Lose $500 for sure OR 50% chance to lose $1,000

questions.explain: In mixed prospects loss aversion produces risk aversion; in choices where every option is a loss, diminishing sensitivity produces risk seeking.

questions.q: According to the Blind Spots section, why does Kahneman think it is reasonable to leave prospect theory out of introductory economics texts?
options: Because basic economic concepts are best taught assuming Econs, and the failures of rationality are often irrelevant to economic predictions
Because prospect theory has been disproved
Because prospect theory applies only to psychologists' laboratory gambles
Because economists have never heard of prospect theory
questions.explain: Basic economic tools are hard to grasp even with simplified assumptions, and questioning them early would be confusing. Also, the predictions of economic theory often work well despite the failures prospect theory describes.

questions.q: In the Blind Spots section, what assumption of prospect theory leads to absurd consequences?
options: That losses loom larger than gains
That the reference point, usually the status quo, has a value of zero
That sensitivity diminishes with larger amounts
That people evaluate gains and losses rather than wealth
questions.explain: Assigning zero to winning nothing makes sense for unlikely or small gambles but not when a large win was highly probable. Kahneman uses this to show prospect theory's own blind spot.

questions.q: Among the prospects in the Blind Spots section, why is winning nothing in the 90% chance to win $1 million very different from winning nothing in the one-in-a-million chance?
options: Because the expected value of the one-in-a-million chance is higher
Because the second gamble involves a possible loss
Because the high probability of a big win sets up a tentative new reference point, so winning nothing feels like a large loss
Because people do not understand small probabilities
questions.explain: Like an informally promised raise, a likely large win shifts expectations. Relative to them, winning nothing is intensely disappointing, but prospect theory still assigns it zero.

questions.q: In the Blind Spots section, what does Kahneman say, in simple words, prospect theory cannot deal with?
options: Loss aversion
Small probabilities
Changes in wealth
Disappointment
questions.explain: Prospect theory does not allow the value of an outcome such as winning nothing to change with what was expected. In simple words, it cannot deal with disappointment.

questions.q: In the Blind Spots section, why did regret and disappointment theories have less influence than prospect theory?
options: They made few striking predictions that distinguished them from the simpler prospect theory
Regret and disappointment turned out not to be real emotions
They were too simple to explain any data
They were proposed only by economists
questions.explain: The emotions are real and anticipated, but regret theories added complexity without striking new predictions. Prospect theory's complexity was accepted because it predicted what utility theory could not.

questions.q: In the Blind Spots section, explain why prospect theory cannot handle the case of failing to win in a 90% chance to win $1 million.
questions.a: Prospect theory assigns the reference point, winning nothing, a value of zero in every gamble. But a 90% chance of a large sum sets up a tentative new reference point, like a salary increase that has been promised informally, so winning nothing is experienced as a large loss. Because the theory does not let the value of an outcome change with expectations, it cannot deal with disappointment.

questions.q: Using Problems 6 and 7 in the Blind Spots section, explain what regret is and why both prospect theory and utility theory miss it.
questions.a: Both theories assume each option is evaluated separately and independently and the highest-valued one is chosen. But losing the 90% gamble for $1 million hurts more when you spurned a sure $150,000 (Problem 7) than a sure $50 (Problem 6), because you would regret the 'greedy' decision. In regret, the experience of an outcome depends on an option you could have adopted but did not.

questions.q: What lesson about how scientific theories succeed does Kahneman draw at the end of the Blind Spots section?
questions.a: Richer and more realistic assumptions are not enough; scientists treat theories as a bag of working tools and will not carry a heavier bag unless the new tools are very useful. Prospect theory was accepted not because it is 'true' but because its additions, notably the reference point and loss aversion, yielded new predictions that turned out to be true. Kahneman adds, “We were lucky.”

questions.q: Kahneman admits that theory-induced blindness to prospect theory's own ____ helped it become accepted as the main alternative to utility theory.
questions.explain: Theory-induced blindness is not restricted to expected utility theory; prospect theory has flaws of its own that its supporters overlooked.

questions.q: In ____, the experience of an outcome depends on an option you could have adopted but did not.
questions.explain: Regret is why losing the gamble in Problem 7 hurts more: you turned down a sure $150,000.

questions.q: Kahneman says scientists use theories as a bag of working ____.
questions.explain: They will not take on a heavier bag unless the new tools are very useful, which is why richer assumptions alone do not make a theory successful.

questions.q: Which of these prospects in the Blind Spots section involve an outcome of winning nothing that is reasonably treated as a nonevent with zero value?
options: One chance in a million to win $1 million
10% chance to win $12 and 90% chance to win nothing
90% chance to win $1 million and 10% chance to win nothing
An informally promised salary increase that never arrives
questions.explain: Winning nothing is a nonevent in the first two cases. When a $1 million win was 90% likely, failing to win is intensely disappointing, just as a promised raise that never comes is felt as a loss.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman identify as blind spots of prospect theory?
options: It cannot deal with disappointment
It does not allow for regret
It assumes the reference point always has a value of zero
It ignores loss aversion
It treats states of wealth as the carriers of value
questions.explain: Disappointment, regret, and the zero value of the reference point are the flaws Kahneman names. Loss aversion is central to prospect theory, and states of wealth belong to Bernoulli's model.

questions.q: True or false: According to Kahneman, most introductory economics textbooks feature prospect theory and loss aversion in their indexes.
questions.explain: You are unlikely to find these terms in the index of an introductory economics text, even though most graduate students have heard of them.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says prospect theory was accepted because its added concepts yielded new predictions that turned out to be true, not because it is 'true'.
questions.explain: Concepts like the reference point and loss aversion were worth the trouble because they produced correct new predictions.

questions.q: Put the steps of Kahneman's argument in the Blind Spots section in order.
items: Explain why introductory economics texts reasonably leave prospect theory out
Admit that prospect theory has its own theory-induced blindness
Show that it cannot deal with disappointment
Show that it does not allow for regret
Explain why regret theories still had less influence
questions.explain: Kahneman seeks balance: he defends economics texts, admits prospect theory's flaws (disappointment, then regret), and ends by explaining why prospect theory still won out.

questions.q: Match each term from the Blind Spots section to its meaning.
pairs: Disappointment
Winning nothing feels like a loss when a big win was expected
Regret
Pain depends on an option you could have chosen but did not
Reference point value
Assumed to be zero, usually the status quo
Theory-induced blindness
Failing to see the flaws of a theory you have accepted
questions.explain: These terms explain where prospect theory falls short and why its flaws went unnoticed.

questions.q: Sort each phenomenon by whether prospect theory, as described in the Prospect Theory chapter, can represent it.

items.t: Losses looming larger than gains
Risk seeking when all options are bad
Different choices in Problems 3 and 4
Disappointment at failing to win a 90% chance of $1 million
Regret over spurning a sure $150,000

questions.explain: Prospect theory explains loss aversion and reference effects, but it cannot deal with disappointment or regret.

questions.q: In the Speaking of Prospect Theory examples, why does Kahneman say someone who weighs losses about twice as much as gains is behaving normally?
options: Because the loss aversion ratio is usually in the range of 1.5 to 2.5
Because people are indifferent to risk on average
Because traders have taught people to think this way
Because the utility of wealth doubles as wealth increases
questions.explain: A ratio of about 2 falls in the typical 1.5 to 2.5 range, so the speaker says “He weighs losses about twice as much as gains, which is normal.”

questions.q: True or false: One Speaking of Prospect Theory example says a very wealthy woman's emotional response to trivial gains and losses makes no sense in terms of her wealth.
questions.explain: The example reflects the chapter's point that reactions to small gains and losses are not derived from the utility of wealth.

questions.q: In the Speaking of Prospect Theory examples, a man is said to suffer from extreme loss ____, which makes him turn down very favorable opportunities.
questions.explain: Extreme loss aversion leads people to reject gambles with clearly positive expected value, as in the chapter's coin-toss problem.

questions.q: Why would the remark 'Considering her vast wealth, her emotional response to trivial gains and losses makes no sense' be puzzling only from Bernoulli's point of view?
questions.a: In Bernoulli's theory, small changes should matter little to a very wealthy person because utility depends on states of wealth. Prospect theory holds that people simply like winning and dislike losing relative to a reference point, regardless of total wealth. So strong reactions to trivial gains and losses are exactly what prospect theory expects.

questions.q: In the structure of Part 4, how does the Prospect Theory chapter relate to the preceding chapter, Bernoulli's Errors?
options: It repeats Bernoulli's model without criticism
It abandons the topic of risky choice to discuss happiness
It offers the alternative that fixes the error, adding the reference point that Bernoulli's model lacked
It presents Bernoulli's original experiments in detail
questions.explain: Bernoulli's Errors showed, through stories like Anthony and Betty, that the utility of wealth ignores reference points. The Prospect Theory chapter supplies the missing variable and builds a new theory around gains and losses.

questions.q: How does the Prospect Theory chapter build on the idea of theory-induced blindness introduced in Bernoulli's Errors, and how does it turn the idea back on itself?
questions.a: Bernoulli's Errors named theory-induced blindness as the reason obvious flaws in utility theory survived for centuries. The Prospect Theory chapter uses it to explain why gains-versus-losses differences and small-stakes loss aversion went unstudied. In the Blind Spots section, Kahneman admits that theory-induced blindness to prospect theory's own flaws, such as ignoring disappointment and regret, helped it gain acceptance.

questions.q: Why does it make sense that the Prospect Theory chapter ends with a section on its own blind spots, right before Part 4 continues with The Endowment Effect?
questions.a: After extolling prospect theory and criticizing utility theory in Part 4 so far, Kahneman says it is time for balance and shows what the theory cannot handle, namely disappointment and regret. This keeps the reader from treating prospect theory as simply 'true': it was accepted because the reference point and loss aversion yielded true predictions. The following chapters of Part 4, such as The Endowment Effect and Bad Events, can then apply those useful tools.

questions.q: Which of these ideas from Bernoulli's Errors does the Prospect Theory chapter rely on?
options: Theory-induced blindness
The story of Anthony and Betty
The distinction between Econs and Humans
The mood heuristic for happiness
The illusion of validity
questions.explain: The chapter refers back to theory-induced blindness, says Anthony and Betty's story had the same structure as Problems 3 and 4, and contrasts Econs and Humans. The mood heuristic and the illusion of validity come from earlier parts of the book.

questions.q: Put these chapters of Part 4, Choices, in the order they appear in the book.
items: Bernoulli's Errors
Prospect Theory
The Endowment Effect
Bad Events
The Fourfold Pattern
questions.explain: Part 4 opens with Bernoulli's Errors, presents prospect theory in chapter 26, and continues with chapters 27 to 29.

questions.q: Put the parts of the Prospect Theory chapter in the order they appear.
items: Problems 1 to 4 and the three principles of the value function
Loss Aversion
Blind Spots of Prospect Theory
Speaking of Prospect Theory
questions.explain: The chapter first builds the theory and its value function, then examines loss aversion, then turns to the theory's weaknesses, and closes with sample sentences.

questions.q: Match each element of the Prospect Theory chapter to the earlier idea it connects to.
pairs: Problems 3 and 4
Similar structure to Anthony and Betty's story
Three principles as features of System 1
The two-systems model of Part 1
Humans of prospect theory
Thaler's contrast with Econs
250 years of unnoticed flaws
Theory-induced blindness
questions.explain: The chapter ties prospect theory back to earlier material: the reference-point stories, the two systems, Econs versus Humans, and theory-induced blindness.

questions.q: Match each part of the Prospect Theory chapter to its role in the chapter's argument.
pairs: Opening problems
Show risk aversion for gains and risk seeking for losses
Figure 10
Pictures the three principles in one value function
Loss Aversion
Measures loss aversion and shows Rabin's critique of utility theory
Blind Spots
Gives balance by admitting what the theory cannot explain
questions.explain: The chapter moves from evidence to the value function, then to loss aversion in depth, then to the theory's limits.

questions.q: Sort these chapter titles by whether they belong to Part 4 (Choices) or to another part of the book.

items.t: Bernoulli's Errors
The Endowment Effect
Risk Policies
The Outside View
The Engine of Capitalism
Two Selves

questions.explain: Part 4 runs from Bernoulli's Errors to Frames and Reality. The Outside View and The Engine of Capitalism close Part 3, and Two Selves opens Part 5.

questions.q: In The Endowment Effect, what does each indifference curve on the economist's indifference map connect?
options: Combinations of income and vacation days that are equally desirable, having the same utility
Combinations of income and vacation days that a worker currently holds under a contract
Combinations of income and vacation days that employers are most willing to offer
Combinations of income and vacation days that maximize total wealth over a lifetime
questions.explain: Each indifference curve joins combinations of the two goods that have the same utility, so a person does not care where on the curve they are. The curves say nothing about the worker's current situation, which is exactly the omission Kahneman criticizes.

questions.q: In The Endowment Effect, the convex shape of indifference curves indicates diminishing marginal ____: each added day of leisure is worth less than the one before.
questions.explain: The convexity reflects diminishing marginal utility: the more leisure or income you already have, the less you care about an extra unit of it.

questions.q: In The Endowment Effect, what does Kahneman say is missing from the standard indifference map?
options: Any indication of how income is taxed at different levels of salary
Any indication of how much the employer values the worker's time
An indication of the individual's current income and leisure, the reference point
An indication of the probabilities attached to each combination of goods
questions.explain: The figure does not show where the person currently is, their status quo, and so invites the belief that the reference point does not matter. Kahneman insists that it does.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman describes the omission of the reference point from the indifference map as a surprising case of theory-induced blindness.
questions.explain: He calls it a surprising case of theory-induced blindness, because the reference point so obviously matters in everyday cases such as labor negotiations and job changes.

questions.q: Kahneman says that by leaving out the reference point, the indifference map repeats Bernoulli's ____ all over again.
questions.explain: Like Bernoulli's representation of outcomes as states of wealth, the indifference map assumes utility depends only on the present situation and ignores where the person started.

questions.q: In The Endowment Effect, what does Kahneman say both sides in labor negotiations understand to be the reference point?
options: The average wage paid across the whole industry
The existing contract, relative to which concessions are demanded
The wage the union would ideally like to achieve
The lowest wage that the law allows the employer to pay
questions.explain: Negotiations focus on mutual demands for concessions relative to the existing contract. Because of loss aversion, making those concessions hurts.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman offer as everyday evidence that the reference point matters, in contrast to the indifference map?
options: Labor negotiations focus on concessions relative to the existing contract
People considering a new job code its features as pluses or minuses relative to the current one
Unemployed workers' minimal acceptable wage averages 90% of their previous wage
Workers' evaluation of a possible job is independent of the terms of their current job
People's tastes for income and leisure stay fixed no matter where they start
questions.explain: Negotiations, job changes and the wage demands of the unemployed all show evaluation relative to a starting point. The idea that a job is judged independently of the current one is the unrealistic assumption of the indifference map, not evidence against it.

questions.q: True or false: In The Endowment Effect, the minimal wage that unemployed workers would accept averages 90% of their previous wage and drops by more than half over a year.
questions.explain: The minimal acceptable wage averages 90% of the previous wage and drops by less than 10% over a year. The point is that changes for the worse are hard to accept.

questions.q: In The Endowment Effect, why does Kahneman use the experience of changing jobs or locations to show that the reference point matters?
questions.a: When you change jobs or locations, or even consider it, the features of the new place are coded as pluses or minuses relative to where you are now. You may also notice that the disadvantages loom larger than the advantages, which is loss aversion at work. So evaluation depends on the current situation, which the indifference map leaves out.

questions.q: Kahneman calls Albert and Ben "____ twins" because they have identical tastes and identical starting jobs.
questions.explain: Albert and Ben are hedonic twins: identical tastes and identical starting jobs with little income and little leisure, so any later difference in preferences must come from their different reference points.

questions.q: In the story of Albert and Ben, how do the twins decide who gets the raise and who gets the extra vacation?
options: Their manager assigns each the position that suits his tastes
Each bids for the position he values more highly
The older twin chooses first and takes the raise
Being indifferent between the two positions, they toss a coin
questions.explain: Both twins find the two positions equally attractive, so they toss a coin. Albert gets the $10,000 raise and Ben gets the extra day of paid vacation each month.

questions.q: Put the events of Kahneman's Albert and Ben story in order.
items: The twins hold identical starting jobs with little income and leisure
The firm offers a raise and an extra vacation day each month
A coin toss gives Albert the raise and Ben the leisure
The twins get accustomed to their new positions
The company invites them to switch jobs
Both twins prefer to remain as they are
questions.explain: The coin toss and the period of getting used to the positions set new reference points. When switching is offered, loss aversion makes each twin keep his current job.

questions.q: In the story of Albert and Ben, once Albert has taken position A, how is the option of moving to position B structured for him?
options: 12 extra days of vacation together with a $10,000 salary cut
12 extra days of vacation with no change in his salary
A $10,000 raise in exchange for giving up 12 vacation days
No gain and no loss, exactly as it looked at the start
questions.explain: Taking A changes Albert's reference point, so B now means gaining vacation and losing $10,000. Staying at A is the option with no gain and no loss.

questions.q: Match each option in the Albert and Ben story to how it is framed relative to the twin's reference point.
pairs: Albert, from the starting job, goes to A
A gain: a raise of $10,000
Albert, already at A, stays at A
No gain and no loss
Albert, already at A, moves to B
A gain of 12 vacation days plus a $10,000 salary cut
Ben, already at B, moves to A
A gain in income plus the loss of now-precious leisure
questions.explain: The same positions are coded differently once the reference point has moved. A switch always involves a loss, and losses outweigh the matching gains.

questions.q: In the story of Albert and Ben, why does Albert refuse to switch to position B even though he was once indifferent between A and B?
questions.a: Taking position A changed Albert's reference point, so moving to B now means 12 extra vacation days combined with a $10,000 salary cut. Because of loss aversion, the salary cut hurts more than the equal-sized gain in leisure pleases him. The disadvantage of moving outweighs the advantage, so he stays at A.

questions.q: In The Endowment Effect, Kahneman says that the twins' preference for the ____ is a consequence of loss aversion.
questions.explain: Prospect theory predicts both twins will stay where they are; this preference for the status quo follows from loss aversion.

questions.q: Sort each claim about Albert and Ben by which view makes it.

items.t: Preferences are stable over time
The twins need little or no incentive to switch
Utility depends only on the present situation
Tastes vary with the reference point
Both twins will definitely prefer to stay as they are
The disadvantages of a change loom larger than its advantages

questions.explain: The standard theory treats positions A and B as equally attractive regardless of history. Prospect theory says each twin's new position becomes his reference point, and loss aversion biases him toward it.

questions.q: Which of these are the two aspects of choice that, according to Kahneman, the Albert and Ben example shows the standard model of indifference curves does not predict?
options: Tastes are not fixed; they vary with the reference point
The disadvantages of a change loom larger than its advantages, favoring the status quo
People never prefer to change their situation once settled
Leisure is always valued more highly than income
Preferences are stable over time
questions.explain: Kahneman names exactly these two: tastes shift with the reference point, and disadvantages loom larger than advantages. He explicitly denies that loss aversion means people never change their situation.

questions.q: True or false: According to Kahneman, loss aversion implies that people never prefer to change their situation.
questions.explain: The benefits of an opportunity may exceed even overweighted losses. Loss aversion implies only that choices are strongly biased in favor of the reference situation, and toward small rather than large changes.

questions.q: Sort each outcome by how it is coded relative to the person's reference point, as described in The Endowment Effect.

items.t: Albert at A: 12 extra vacation days from moving to B
Ben at B: extra income from moving to A
A shopper: a drop in the price of eggs
Albert at A: a $10,000 salary cut from moving to B
Ben at B: giving up leisure by moving to A
A shopper: a rise in the price of orange juice

questions.explain: Outcomes are coded as changes from where the person stands. Price increases are losses relative to the reference price, and their effect on purchases is about twice that of price drops.

questions.q: What mistaken assumption does Kahneman say conventional indifference maps share with Bernoulli's representation of outcomes as states of wealth?
questions.a: Both assume that your utility for a state of affairs depends only on that state and is not affected by your history. The past and the terms of your current situation are treated as irrelevant. Kahneman counts correcting this mistake as one of the achievements of behavioral economics.

questions.q: Maya is weighing a job offer in a new city. She lists its features as better or worse than her current town, and the things she would give up weigh on her more than the things she would gain. Which idea from The Endowment Effect best explains her thinking?
options: Diminishing marginal utility of income at higher salaries
Indifference between any two points on the same curve
Evaluation relative to a reference point, with loss aversion
The equal weighting of advantages and disadvantages by Econs
questions.explain: Kahneman says the features of a new place are coded as pluses or minuses relative to where you are, and that disadvantages loom larger than advantages. Equal weighting is what the standard model assumes, not what people do.

questions.q: In The Endowment Effect, what were Professor R's buying and selling limits for a bottle of good wine?
options: He would pay up to $100 but would sell for anything above $35
He would pay up to $35 but would sell only at $100 or more
He would buy and sell at the same price of about $50
He would never buy at auctions but would sell for $35
questions.explain: Professor R would not pay more than $35 at auction but refused to sell even at $100; between those prices he would neither buy nor sell. In Kahneman's words, “Owning the good appeared to increase its value.”

questions.q: Why is Professor R's wine behavior inconsistent with standard economic theory?
questions.a: Economic theory expects the professor to have a single value for the bottle, say $50. He should then sell for any amount above $50 and pay any amount up to $50, so his just-acceptable selling and buying prices should be identical. Instead his minimum selling price ($100) was far higher than his maximum buying price ($35).

questions.q: Richard Thaler called the gap between Professor R's buying and selling prices the ____ effect.
questions.explain: Thaler found many examples of what he called the endowment effect, especially for goods that are not regularly traded.

questions.q: In Kahneman's concert ticket example, you bought a ticket for $200, would have paid up to $500, and are now offered $3,000 but refuse. What does this reveal?
options: Your lowest selling price is above $3,000 while your maximum buying price is $500
Your lowest selling price and your maximum buying price are both about $500
You value the ticket at $200 because that is what you paid for it
You expect that other fans will soon offer you even more than $3,000
questions.explain: Refusing $3,000 means your selling price exceeds it, though you would never have paid more than $500. That gap between selling and buying prices is the endowment effect.

questions.q: How did prospect theory explain Professor R's reluctance to sell his wine?
questions.a: Prospect theory abandons the idea that the professor has a unique utility for owning the bottle; willingness to buy or sell depends on whether he owns it now. If he owns it, he considers the pain of giving it up; if not, the pleasure of getting it. Because of loss aversion the value function is steeper for losses, so giving up the bottle hurts more than getting an equally good one pleases.

questions.q: Explaining the endowment effect, Kahneman reminds readers that the slope of the value function is steeper in the negative ____: the response to a loss is stronger than the response to a gain.
questions.explain: The loss-averse value function from prospect theory is steeper for losses than for gains, which is why giving up a good hurts more than acquiring it pleases.

questions.q: Put the steps of Richard Thaler's path to explaining the endowment effect in the order Kahneman tells them.
items: As a Rochester graduate student, he collects behavior the rational model cannot explain
He observes Professor R's reluctance to sell his wine
He obtains an early draft of prospect theory at a conference
He spends a year at Stanford with Amos and Kahneman
A Russell Sage grant lets him spend a year with Kahneman in Vancouver
questions.explain: Thaler's collection of anomalies came first; reading prospect theory gave him the explanation; then came collaboration at Stanford and, seven years later, in Vancouver with Jack Knetsch.

questions.q: Put the steps of Kahneman's explanation of Professor R's wine puzzle in order.
items: Professor R will not pay over $35 but will not sell for $100
Standard theory says he should have a single value for the bottle
Prospect theory says his reference point is whether he owns it now
Loss aversion makes giving it up hurt more than getting it pleases
questions.explain: The observed gap contradicts the single-value theory; prospect theory resolves it by making the reference point depend on ownership and applying loss aversion.

questions.q: Match each person in The Endowment Effect to his role.
pairs: Richard Thaler
Collected economic anomalies and named the endowment effect
Richard Rosett (Professor R)
Wine lover who would buy at $35 but not sell at $100
Jack Knetsch
Vancouver economist who ran the pen and chocolate experiment
Vernon Smith
Founder of experimental economics, known for token markets
John List
Studied trading at baseball card conventions
questions.explain: Thaler supplied the puzzle, Professor R the example, Smith the market method, Knetsch the collaboration and simple gift experiment, and List the evidence that trading experience removes the effect.

questions.q: Which of these exchanges does Kahneman say involve no loss aversion?
options: Changing a $5 bill for five singles
A shoe merchant handing over shoes for money
A shopper paying for shoes from a shoe budget
Professor R selling a bottle from his collection
A Super Bowl ticket holder selling at a high price
questions.explain: Routine commercial exchanges involve goods and money held for exchange, so neither side feels a loss. Wine and Super Bowl tickets are held for use, which is where reluctance to sell appears.

questions.q: In The Endowment Effect, what example does Kahneman give to show that the endowment effect is not universal?
options: A collector refusing to sell a rare coin he inherited
A family refusing to sell a house below its purchase price
Handing over five singles in exchange for a $5 bill
A fan refusing to sell a sold-out concert ticket
questions.explain: When someone asks you to change a $5 bill for five singles, you feel no sense of loss. The other examples are cases where reluctance to give something up does appear.

questions.q: Sort each item by how Kahneman says it is held.

items.t: Shoes in a merchant's stock
Money you budgeted for buying shoes
A $5 bill you swap for five singles
A bottle of wine in a collection
A Super Bowl ticket
Your leisure time
The standard of living your income supports

questions.explain: Goods held for exchange are meant to be traded for other goods, so giving them up is not a loss. Goods held for use are to be consumed or enjoyed, and leisure and living standards are not intended for sale.

questions.q: Kahneman says wine and Super Bowl tickets, unlike a merchant's shoes, are held "for ____", to be consumed or otherwise enjoyed.
questions.explain: The distinction is between goods held for exchange and goods held for use; the endowment effect appears for goods held for use.

questions.q: Why, according to Kahneman, does neither side feel a loss when you buy a pair of shoes from a merchant?
questions.a: For the merchant, the shoes have always been a cumbersome proxy for the money he hoped to collect from a customer. For you, the money was effectively a proxy for the shoes you intended to buy. Both shoes and money are held for exchange, so the trade is no different from changing a $5 bill for five singles.

questions.q: In Vernon Smith's token markets, what does economic theory predict if half the participants are randomly assigned tokens?
options: Almost none of the tokens will change hands
All of the tokens will end up with the experimenter
Every token will change hands at least twice
Half of the tokens will change hands
questions.explain: With random assignment, about half the owners value their token less than some non-owner does, so theory predicts half the tokens will trade. Smith's results matched such predictions closely.

questions.q: True or false: In Vernon Smith's token markets, tokens ended up with those who could get the most money for them, and theory correctly predicted both the final price and the number of trades.
questions.explain: Kahneman likens the regularity to a physics demonstration: low-value owners sell at a profit to those who value the token more, and theory predicts the price and the number of tokens that change hands.

questions.q: Put the steps of the mugs experiment by Knetsch, Thaler and Kahneman in order.
items: Several rounds of trading tokens replicate Smith's finding
Mugs are distributed randomly to half the participants
