Sellers keep their mugs while Buyers look at a neighbor's mug
Everyone indicates the price at which they would trade
Prices and trades are compared with standard theory's predictions
questions.explain: The token rounds confirmed that the market worked for goods with no use value; the mug market then tested a good people expected to use.

questions.q: What were the results of the mugs market run by Knetsch, Thaler and Kahneman?
options: Selling prices were about double buying prices, and trades were under half the predicted number
Selling and buying prices were equal, and trades matched the predicted number exactly
Buying prices were about double selling prices, and trades exceeded the prediction
Selling prices were slightly higher, but trades still matched the predicted number
questions.explain: The average selling price was about double the average buying price, and estimated trades were less than half of the prediction. “The magic of the market did not work for a good that the owners expected to use.”

questions.q: Sort each result by whether it matched or contradicted the predictions of standard economic theory.

items.t: The number of token trades in Smith-style markets
The final price at which token markets settled
Shoppers buying more eggs when prices drop
Mug trades falling below half the predicted number
Mug Sellers asking about double what Buyers offered
Price increases affecting purchases twice as much as price drops

questions.explain: Theory works for tokens, which have no use value, and gets the direction of price responses right. It fails for goods held for use and for the asymmetric size of the response to price increases.

questions.q: Match each group in the mugs experiment with Choosers to the average value it set on the mug.
pairs: Sellers
Choosers
Buyers
questions.explain: Sellers, who owned the mug, valued it at more than twice what Choosers and Buyers did, while Choosers and Buyers set similar values.

questions.q: In the mugs experiment, why does Kahneman find the gap between Sellers and Choosers remarkable?
questions.a: Sellers and Choosers actually face the same choice: both can go home with either a mug or money, and the long-term effects are identical. The only difference is the emotion of the moment. Sellers set a much higher price because of their reluctance to give up an object they already own, which is loss aversion.

questions.q: True or false: In the mugs experiment, Buyers set much lower cash values than Choosers because Buyers had to pay for the mug with their own money.
questions.explain: Buyers ($2.87) and Choosers ($3.12) set similar values even though only Buyers had to pay. Kahneman takes this as a sign that Buyers do not experience spending money on the mug as a loss.

questions.q: What does Kahneman conclude from the fact that Buyers and Choosers set similar values on the mug?
questions.a: Buyers had to pay for the mug while it was free for Choosers, yet their cash values were similar. This is what you would expect if Buyers do not experience spending money on the mug as a loss. Brain imaging supports this: buying activates pain-related regions only when prices seem too high.

questions.q: How does Kahneman connect the high prices set by mug Sellers to babies and to System 1?
questions.a: The Sellers' high prices reflect a reluctance to give up an object they already own. The same reluctance is seen in babies who hold on fiercely to a toy and become agitated when it is taken away. Kahneman concludes that “Loss aversion is built into the automatic evaluations of System 1.”

questions.q: Which of these findings from brain imaging does Kahneman report in discussing the endowment effect?
options: Selling goods one would normally use activates regions associated with disgust and pain
Buying activates those regions only when prices are perceived as too high
Buying at especially low prices is a pleasurable event
Buying any good always activates regions associated with pain
Selling tokens activates the same regions as selling mugs
questions.explain: Selling goods held for use registers like pain or disgust, while buying does so only when the price seems to exceed exchange value. The claim that buying always hurts contradicts the finding that low prices give pleasure.

questions.q: The roughly 2:1 ratio of Sellers' to Choosers' values for the mug is very close to the loss aversion ____ in risky choice.
questions.explain: Kahneman notes this is what you would expect if the same value function for gains and losses of money applies to both riskless and risky decisions.

questions.q: In The Endowment Effect, what pattern do households show in response to price changes for goods such as eggs, orange juice or fish?
options: They ignore price changes entirely and buy the same amounts
Price drops affect their purchases about twice as much as price increases
Price increases and price drops affect their purchases equally
Price increases affect their purchases about twice as much as price drops
questions.explain: Customers buy more when prices drop and less when they rise, as economists predict, but price increases, which are losses relative to the reference price, have about twice the effect.

questions.q: In Jack Knetsch's pen and chocolate experiment, what proportion of participants traded their gift for the alternative?
options: About half, as standard theory would predict
About 48%, similar to experienced traders
About 90%, once they saw the alternative
Only about 10%
questions.explain: Only about 10% exchanged their gift; those who got the pen kept the pen and those who got the chocolate kept the chocolate. The 48% figure belongs to experienced traders in List's later replication.

questions.q: Which of these were features of Jack Knetsch's pen and chocolate experiment?
options: The gift was a reward for filling out a questionnaire
The gift remained in front of participants for the duration of the experiment
Only about 10% of participants exchanged their gift
Participants paid for their gift with their own money
Most participants who received chocolate switched to the pen
questions.explain: Participants received the gift for a questionnaire and kept it in front of them, and very few traded. No one paid for the gift, and chocolate recipients did not budge either.

questions.q: In the study of Boston condo owners during a downturn, what did owners with a high reference point (a high buying price) do?
options: They set lower prices so they could sell their units quickly
They set higher prices, took longer to sell, and eventually received more money
They set the same prices as other owners, as rational agents would
They withdrew their units from the market until prices recovered fully
questions.explain: Facing larger losses relative to what they had paid, these owners set higher prices, spent longer trying to sell, and eventually received more. For a rational agent the buying price would be irrelevant.

questions.q: Kahneman says that for a rational agent, the price paid for a home is irrelevant ____; only the current market value matters.
questions.explain: For a rational agent the buying price is irrelevant history, but Humans in a down market treat it as a reference point.

questions.q: Which of these did Boston condo owners who had bought at higher prices do during the downturn, compared with owners of similar units?
options: Set a higher price on their dwelling
Spend a longer time trying to sell
Eventually receive more money
Accept the current market value immediately
Sell faster than other owners
questions.explain: A higher reference point meant higher losses, so these owners held out for more, took longer, and eventually got more. Accepting market value at once is what a rational agent would do.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say the endowment effect can be eliminated in some situations?
questions.a: Reference points are labile, especially in unusual laboratory situations, so changing the reference point can remove the effect. No endowment effect is expected when owners view their goods as carriers of value for future exchanges, as is common in routine commerce and financial markets. Experienced traders and subtle manipulations of possession both make the effect disappear.

questions.q: Put the steps of John List's experiment at a baseball card convention in order.
items: A notice invites people to take a short survey
Volunteers receive a mug or chocolate bar at random
As they leave, each is offered a trade for the other gift
Trading rates of inexperienced and experienced traders are compared
questions.explain: The design replicated Knetsch's gift experiment; the new element was comparing people with and without trading experience.

questions.q: In John List's experiment at baseball card conventions, how often did inexperienced and experienced traders exchange their gift?
options: 10% of inexperienced and 18% of experienced traders
48% of inexperienced and 18% of experienced traders
18% of inexperienced and 48% of experienced traders
About half of both groups
questions.explain: Only 18% of inexperienced traders exchanged, but 48% of experienced traders did, showing no trace of an endowment effect where trading was the norm.

questions.q: Which of these did John List find in his studies at baseball card conventions?
options: Novice traders were reluctant to part with the cards they owned
That reluctance eventually disappeared with trading experience
Trading experience also affected the endowment effect for new goods like mugs
Experienced traders were the most reluctant to exchange their gifts
Participants chose which gift they received at the start
questions.explain: List found experience removed reluctance to trade, even for new goods such as a mug or chocolate. The gifts were assigned at random, and experienced traders traded most.

questions.q: Match each percentage to what it describes in The Endowment Effect.
pairs: Participants in Knetsch's pen and chocolate study who exchanged gifts
Inexperienced traders in List's study who exchanged gifts
Experienced traders in List's study who exchanged gifts
Unemployed workers' minimal acceptable wage relative to their previous wage
questions.explain: Low trading rates signal an endowment effect; the experienced traders' 48% is close to what standard theory predicts. The 90% figure shows how hard it is to accept a change for the worse.

questions.q: True or false: Jack Knetsch found that participants displayed an endowment effect only if they had physical possession of the good for a while before trading was mentioned.
questions.explain: This subtle manipulation made the effect disappear, a result reflecting the variables social psychologists expect to matter.

questions.q: What question does Kahneman say veteran traders have learned to ask, and why does it remove the endowment effect?
questions.a: Veteran traders ask “How much do I want to have that mug, compared with other things I could have instead?” This is the question Econs ask. With it, the asymmetry between the pleasure of getting and the pain of giving up becomes irrelevant, so there is no endowment effect.

questions.q: Kahneman says that veteran traders ask the question that ____ ask, so the asymmetry between getting and giving up becomes irrelevant.
questions.explain: Comparing the mug with other things one could have instead is how Econs think, and it leaves no room for an endowment effect.

questions.q: In The Endowment Effect, how does prospect theory describe being poor?
options: Having less money than one's neighbors
Having no reference point at all
Being indifferent between gaining and giving up
Living below one's reference point
questions.explain: Being poor means living below one's reference point, always in the losses. Indifference between gaining and giving up describes traders, which Kahneman explicitly says the poor are not.

questions.q: Why are the poor not expected to show the endowment effect, and how does their situation differ from that of traders?
questions.a: The poor live below their reference point, so small amounts of money are perceived as a reduced loss, not a gain, and they remain on the steep limb of the value function. Like traders they think in terms of what else money could buy, but unlike traders they are not indifferent to gaining and giving up. All their choices are between losses: money spent on one good is the loss of another.

questions.q: Kahneman sums up decision making under poverty this way: for the poor, costs are ____.
questions.explain: Every choice the poor make is between losses, because money spent on one good is the loss of another good they could have bought. “For the poor, costs are losses.”

questions.q: Sort each description by whether Kahneman applies it to experienced traders or to the poor.

items.t: Indifferent to the difference between gaining and giving up
Their reluctance to trade disappears with experience
View goods as carriers of value for future exchanges
All their choices are between losses
Small amounts of money received feel like a reduced loss
Always remain on the steep limb of the value function

questions.explain: Both groups lack an endowment effect, but for different reasons: traders treat goods as exchangeable, while the poor are always in the losses.

questions.q: True or false: In the mugs study, the gap between buying and selling prices is much larger among English students than among American students.
questions.explain: The direction is reversed: prices diverge substantially among American students, while the differences are much smaller among English students.

questions.q: What possible explanation does Kahneman suggest for the different results of the mugs study in the United States and the UK?
options: Cultural differences in attitudes toward spending money on whims and minor luxuries
Differences in the price of mugs between the two countries
English students having more trading experience at conventions
American students being poorer and therefore always in the losses
questions.explain: He suggests there may be cultural differences in attitudes to money, especially toward spending on whims such as a decorated mug, and adds that much remains to be learned.

questions.q: Sort each case by whether it shows an endowment effect or Kahneman expects no endowment effect.

items.t: Professor R and his wine
Novice traders holding their baseball cards
American students selling mugs
Pen recipients in Knetsch's experiment
Experienced traders at card conventions
A merchant selling shoes
Traders in Smith's token markets
Someone changing a $5 bill for singles

questions.explain: The effect appears for goods held for use by people without trading experience. It vanishes when goods are held for exchange or traders have learned to compare a good with alternatives.

questions.q: An antiques dealer happily sells a vase he likes at a fair price, while a collector who owns the same vase refuses even a generous offer. Which idea from The Endowment Effect best explains the difference?
options: The collector is poor and therefore always in the losses
The dealer holds the vase for exchange, while the collector holds it for use
The dealer suffers from loss aversion, but the collector does not
The collector values the vase less than the dealer does
questions.explain: Kahneman expects no endowment effect when owners view goods as carriers of value for future exchanges, as dealers and experienced traders do. The collector, like Professor R with his wine, holds the good for use and feels giving it up as a loss.

questions.q: Match each remark from Speaking of the Endowment Effect to the idea it illustrates.
pairs: She no longer wanted to trade offices a day after the announcement
The endowment effect from newly owning something
Negotiations go nowhere because concessions are hard to make
Losses loom larger than gains in bargaining
When they raised their prices, demand dried up
Price increases are losses relative to the reference price
He hates selling his house for less than he paid
Loss aversion relative to the purchase price
He is a miser who treats any dollar he spends as a loss
Experiencing spending itself as a loss
questions.explain: Each remark applies the chapter's ideas: ownership shifts the reference point, concessions are losses, price rises weigh about twice as much as drops, purchase price acts as a reference point, and some people feel all spending as a loss.

questions.q: A colleague did not care which of two parking spots she was assigned, but a day after getting one she refuses to swap it for the other. Which idea does Kahneman's Speaking example about two offices use for this?
options: Diminishing marginal utility
Theory-induced blindness
The endowment effect
Thinking like a trader
questions.explain: Once she owns the spot, it becomes her reference point and giving it up feels like a loss. Thinking like a trader would remove this reluctance, not cause it.

questions.q: Using the chapter's ideas, explain the Speaking remark that negotiations are going nowhere because both sides find it difficult to make concessions even when they can get something in return.
questions.a: In negotiations the existing contract is the reference point, and each concession is coded as a loss relative to it. Because losses loom larger than gains, what each side gives up feels bigger than an equal gain it receives in return. So both sides resist trades that would look fair to an Econ.

questions.q: Match each idea from The Endowment Effect to the example Kahneman uses for it.
pairs: Theory-induced blindness
Textbook indifference maps that omit the reference point
Endowment effect
Professor R refusing to sell wine he would not buy at that price
Goods held for exchange
The shoes a merchant hands over for money
Status quo bias
Albert and Ben both keeping the positions the coin gave them
questions.explain: Each idea is anchored in an example: the indifference map shows how an elegant model hides the reference point, Professor R shows ownership raising value, shoes show routine exchange without loss, and the twins show loss aversion favoring the status quo.

questions.q: Match each study discussed in Thinking Like a Trader to its finding.
pairs: Boston condo market in a downturn
Owners who paid more set higher prices and waited longer to sell
List at baseball card conventions
Trading experience removed the endowment effect
Knetsch's possession manipulation
The effect appeared only after holding the good for a while
Mugs study in the US and the UK
The price gap was much smaller among English students
questions.explain: These studies show reference points at work in real markets and the conditions under which the endowment effect shrinks or disappears.

questions.q: Which of these remarks in Speaking of the Endowment Effect explicitly name loss aversion, or losses looming larger than gains, as the cause?
options: He just hates the idea of selling his house for less money than he paid for it
These negotiations are going nowhere because both sides find it difficult to make concessions
She didn't care which of the two offices she would get, but a day later would not trade
When they raised their prices, demand dried up
questions.explain: The house remark ends with loss aversion at work, and the negotiation remark with losses looming larger than gains. The office remark is labeled as the endowment effect, and the price remark names no cause.

questions.q: Why does The Endowment Effect come right after the chapter Prospect Theory?
options: It drops prospect theory and returns to Bernoulli's utility theory
It applies prospect theory's reference point and loss aversion to riskless choices
It introduces probability weighting before the value function is explained
It moves on from economics to the study of memory and experience
questions.explain: The chapter uses the loss-averse value function from the previous chapter to explain riskless puzzles like Professor R's wine and the mugs, calling this the first application of prospect theory to an economic puzzle.

questions.q: Put these chapters of Part 4, Choices, in the order they appear in the book.
items: Bernoulli's Errors
Prospect Theory
The Endowment Effect
Bad Events
The Fourfold Pattern
questions.explain: The Endowment Effect follows the critique of Bernoulli and the presentation of prospect theory, and precedes Bad Events and The Fourfold Pattern.

questions.q: Put the topics of The Endowment Effect in the order the chapter presents them.
items: The indifference map and its missing reference point
Professor R's wine and Thaler's discovery
The mugs experiments and the Choosers
Trading experience and decision making under poverty
Remarks for speaking about the endowment effect
questions.explain: The chapter moves from a theoretical critique, to the original puzzle, to experimental evidence, to the conditions under which the effect disappears, and ends with everyday remarks.

questions.q: How does the opening of The Endowment Effect link back to the earlier chapter on Bernoulli's errors?
questions.a: Kahneman argues that the textbook indifference map omits the reference point, which he calls Bernoulli's error all over again. Both the indifference map and Bernoulli's representation of outcomes as states of wealth assume utility depends only on the current state, not on history. The chapter thus extends the earlier critique from risky choices about wealth to riskless choices between goods like income and leisure.

questions.q: True or false: The Endowment Effect extends the value function of prospect theory, first developed for risky choice, to riskless decisions such as trading mugs.
questions.explain: Kahneman notes that the 2:1 ratio in the mugs study matches the loss aversion coefficient in risky choice, as expected if the same value function applies to both riskless and risky decisions.

questions.q: The Endowment Effect is a chapter in Part 4 of the book, titled "____".
questions.explain: Part 4, Choices, runs from Bernoulli's Errors through the chapters on prospect theory, the endowment effect, bad events and risk.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman call it odd that loss aversion is psychology's most significant contribution to behavioral economics?
options: Because economists had already proved loss aversion decades earlier
Because the idea that losses loom larger than gains surprises no one
Because loss aversion appears only in laboratory gambles, not real life
Because psychologists had long rejected the idea of reference points
questions.explain: The idea is so familiar that Kahneman and Tversky joked they were studying a subject their grandmothers knew a great deal about. What is new is not the idea but its embedding in a broader model and its specific predictions.

questions.q: True or false: In the opening of Bad Events, Kahneman lists as a consequence of loss aversion that professional golfers putt more accurately for a birdie than for par.
questions.explain: The direction is reversed: golfers putt more accurately for par than for a birdie, because missing par is a loss while missing a birdie is only a foregone gain.

questions.q: In Bad Events, Kahneman says that today we know more about loss aversion than our grandmothers did. What is it that we now know?
questions.a: We can embed loss aversion in the broader two-systems model of the mind, within a biological and psychological view in which negativity and escape dominate positivity and approach. We can also trace its consequences in surprisingly diverse observations, such as compensation rules for goods lost in transport, the failure of large reforms, and golfers' putting. Even a clever grandmother who found the general idea obvious would have been surprised by these specific predictions.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman list at the start of Bad Events as surprisingly diverse consequences of loss aversion?
options: Only out-of-pocket losses are compensated when goods are lost in transport
Attempts at large-scale reforms very often fail
Professional golfers putt more accurately for par than for a birdie
Investors buy more lottery tickets after a losing week
Bargaining over an expanding pie is harder than over a shrinking one
questions.explain: These three are the opening's examples. The lottery idea is not in the chapter, and the chapter says the reverse about pies: bargaining over a shrinking pie is the hard case because it allocates losses.

questions.q: Kahneman places loss aversion within a biological and psychological view in which negativity and escape dominate positivity and ____.
questions.explain: The two pairs are negativity and escape versus positivity and approach; the first pair dominates, which is the broader frame for loss aversion.

questions.q: In the brain-scanner study with pictures of terrified eyes shown for under 2/100 of a second and then masked, what did the scans reveal?
options: The visual cortex registered the eyes but the emotional centers did not
Observers consciously recognized fear but showed no bodily reaction
The amygdala responded intensely though observers never knew they had seen eyes
Happy eyes produced a stronger response than terrified ones
questions.explain: None of the observers consciously knew they had seen eyes, yet the amygdala, the brain's threat center, responded strongly to the threatening picture. The happy eyes were described as not nearly as exciting.

questions.q: Kahneman describes the amygdala as having a primary role as the ____ center of the brain, although it is also active in other emotional states.
questions.explain: The amygdala is called the brain's “threat center”, which is why its intense response to unseen terrified eyes shows that part of the brain detected danger.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, how did information about the masked threatening eyes probably reach the emotional part of the brain?
options: Through slow deliberate processing by System 2
Through conscious recognition followed by appraisal
Through the visual cortex after a delay of several seconds
Through a superfast channel that bypasses the visual cortex
questions.explain: The threat information probably traveled by a superfast neural channel feeding directly into an emotion-processing area, bypassing the visual cortex that supports the conscious experience of seeing. That is why no awareness was needed.

questions.q: True or false: Some experimenters report that an angry face pops out of a crowd of happy faces, but a single happy face does not stand out in an angry crowd.
questions.explain: This is the asymmetry Kahneman reports: the same threat circuit makes angry faces processed faster and more efficiently than happy faces.

questions.q: According to Bad Events, why do the brains of humans and other animals give priority to bad news, and is there a matching mechanism for good news?
questions.a: A mechanism that shaves a few hundredths of a second from the time needed to detect a predator improves an animal's odds of living long enough to reproduce, and the automatic operations of System 1 reflect this evolutionary history. No comparably rapid mechanism for recognizing good news has been detected. We are alerted to opportunities to mate or feed, but threats are privileged above opportunities, as they should be.

questions.q: The psychologist Paul Rozin observed that a single ____ will completely wreck the appeal of a bowl of cherries, while a cherry does nothing for a bowl of them.
questions.explain: Rozin's image shows how the negative trumps the positive: one bad element spoils the whole, while one good element improves nothing.

questions.q: Following Paul Rozin, Kahneman presents loss aversion as one of many manifestations of a broad negativity ____.
questions.explain: Negativity dominance is the general principle that the negative trumps the positive in many ways; loss aversion is only one case of it.

questions.q: According to John Gottman, as cited in Bad Events, what does a stable relationship require?
options: Good interactions outnumbering bad ones by at least 2 to 1
Good interactions outnumbering bad ones by at least 5 to 1
An equal number of good and bad interactions
Seeking the positive more than avoiding the negative
questions.explain: Gottman estimated a ratio of at least 5 to 1, and observed that long-term success depends far more on avoiding the negative than on seeking the positive, the reverse of the last idea.

questions.q: Which of these are claims from the summary in the paper Bad Is Stronger Than Good, as quoted by Kahneman?
options: Bad feedback has more impact than good feedback
Bad information is processed more thoroughly than good information
Bad impressions are quicker to form and harder to disconfirm than good ones
Good stereotypes are more resistant to disconfirmation than bad ones
The self is more motivated to pursue good self-definitions than avoid bad ones
questions.explain: The summary says bad emotions, parents and feedback have more impact, bad information is processed more thoroughly, and bad impressions and stereotypes form faster and resist disconfirmation. The two wrong options reverse that, including the claim about self-definitions, where avoiding bad ones motivates more.

questions.q: In Bad Events, what does the example of finding shelter behind a rock on a cold, rainy night illustrate, according to the biologist Michel Cabanac?
questions.a: Cabanac would call that moment intensely pleasurable, because pleasure normally indicates the direction of a biologically significant improvement of circumstances. The example shows that, apart from a few hardwired distinctions like pain and sweetness, the boundary between good and bad is a reference point that changes over time and depends on immediate circumstances. The relief does not last: you soon shiver again and are driven to seek better shelter.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether, according to Bad Events, it gets more priority or impact, or less.

items.t: An angry face in a crowd of happy faces
A happy face in a crowd of angry faces
Words such as war and crime
Words such as peace and love
A single cockroach in a bowl of cherries
A single cherry in a bowl of cockroaches
Bad feedback
Good feedback

questions.explain: Each pair shows negativity dominance: the bad member pops out, attracts attention faster, spoils the whole or has more impact, while the good member does not.

questions.q: Match each researcher cited in Bad Events to the observation Kahneman attributes to them.
pairs: Paul Rozin
A single cockroach wrecks a bowl of cherries
John Gottman
Stable relationships need good interactions to outnumber bad ones at least 5 to 1
Michel Cabanac
Pleasure signals the direction of a biologically significant improvement
questions.explain: Rozin is the disgust expert behind the cherries image, Gottman is the expert on marital relations, and Cabanac is the biologist whose view explains the pleasure of the sheltering rock.

questions.q: Match each stimulus described in Bad Events to the finding about it.
pairs: Masked pictures of terrified eyes
The amygdala responds although viewers are unaware of them
Schematic angry faces
Processed faster and more efficiently than happy faces
Bad words such as war and crime
Attract attention faster than happy words
A sentence stating an opinion you strongly oppose
Registered as a threat in under a quarter of a second
questions.explain: All four show the brain responding quickly to threats, even purely symbolic ones such as words and disagreeable opinions, which System 1 treats as threatening.

questions.q: Put the steps of the masked-eyes brain-scanner study, as Kahneman describes it, in order.
items: A picture of eyes is shown to a person in a scanner
The picture disappears after less than 2/100 of a second
Visual noise immediately masks the picture
The amygdala responds intensely to the unseen terrified eyes
questions.explain: The brief exposure and the mask of random dark and bright squares kept the eyes out of awareness, so the amygdala's response showed the brain registering a threat without conscious seeing.

questions.q: A colleague you have been friendly with for years makes one cutting public remark about you, and the friendship suddenly feels damaged, while a stranger's kind gesture that day barely registers. Which idea from Bad Events best explains this?
options: The endowment effect for owned goods
Diminishing sensitivity to large gains
Negativity dominance in the social domain
Regression to the mean in impressions
questions.explain: Kahneman notes that a friendship that may take years to develop can be ruined by a single action, one of the striking social asymmetries showing that bad is stronger than good.

questions.q: Kahneman defines loss aversion as the relative strength of two ____: we are driven more strongly to avoid losses than to achieve gains.
questions.explain: Loss aversion compares two motives, avoiding losses and achieving gains, and says the first is stronger.

questions.q: True or false: When a goal serves as the reference point, Kahneman says the aversion to failing to reach the goal is much stronger than the desire to exceed it.
questions.explain: Not achieving a goal is a loss and exceeding it is a gain, so, as negativity dominance predicts, the two motives are not equally powerful.

questions.q: According to Bad Events, what goal typically controls the effort of New York cabdrivers?
options: A target income for the year
A fixed number of hours behind the wheel
A target income for the month
A daily target of earnings
questions.explain: Drivers may have monthly or yearly targets, but the goal that controls their effort is typically a daily earnings target, and that is what produces the behavior on rainy and mild days.

questions.q: In Bad Events, how do economic logic and loss aversion make opposite predictions about how long New York cabdrivers work on rainy days and on pleasant days?
questions.a: On rainy days cabs fill quickly, so economic logic says drivers should work many hours then and take leisure on mild days, when leisure is cheaper to buy. Loss aversion with a fixed daily target predicts the opposite: drivers reach the target quickly in the rain and go home early, but work many more hours on mild days when pickings are slim, because falling short of the daily goal is a loss.

questions.q: A delivery driver sets a goal of earning 200 dollars a day. On a busy day she reaches it by early afternoon and stops; on slow days she works late into the night. What does Bad Events say about behavior like this?
options: It fits loss aversion with a daily goal but violates economic logic
It is what economic logic recommends for maximizing income
It shows that people care only about yearly income
It shows that reference points have no effect on effort
questions.explain: This mirrors the cabdrivers: short-term goals are things people strive to reach but not to exceed, so they ease off once the goal is met, with results that sometimes violate economic logic.

questions.q: Devin Pope and Maurice Schweitzer reasoned that golf provides a perfect example of a reference point, namely ____.
questions.explain: Every hole has a par number that provides the baseline for good but not outstanding performance, so strokes above and below it are losses and gains.

questions.q: Match each golf outcome to how Bad Events classifies it.
pairs: Par
The baseline for good but not outstanding performance
Birdie
One stroke under par, a gain
Bogey
One stroke over par, a loss
Missing a birdie putt
A foregone gain rather than a loss
questions.explain: Par is the reference point; a birdie is a gain and a bogey a loss, so failing to make par is a loss, while missing a birdie putt only forgoes a gain.

questions.q: In the Pope and Schweitzer study of professional golfers, how large was the difference in success rate between putting for par and putting for a birdie?
questions.explain: The difference was 3.6%, which Kahneman says is not trivial: putting for birdies as well as for par would have been worth about one stroke per tournament for Tiger Woods.

questions.q: True or false: Bad Events widens loss aversion beyond money, presenting it as one manifestation of a broad negativity dominance that also shapes goals, negotiations and judgments of fairness.
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the brain's priority for threats to goals as reference points, defending the status quo and fairness rules, all as expressions of the same asymmetry between bad and good.

questions.q: Put the steps of the Pope and Schweitzer golf study, as Kahneman describes it, in order.
items: Identify par as the reference point for each hole
Predict from loss aversion that players try harder putting for par
Analyze more than 2.5 million putts
Find more success for par than birdie at every distance
Estimate what the gap cost Tiger Woods per season
questions.explain: The study started from a theoretical concept, derived a precise prediction, tested it on millions of putts, confirmed it at every distance, and then showed its cost: about one stroke and almost $1 million a season for Tiger Woods.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what does the study of putts for par and birdie illustrate about the value of a theoretical concept?
questions.a: It shows the power of a theoretical concept as an aid to thinking. No one would have thought it worthwhile to spend months analyzing putts for par and birdie, but the idea of loss aversion, which surprises no one except perhaps some economists, generated a precise and nonintuitive hypothesis. That hypothesis led to a finding that surprised everyone, including professional golfers.

questions.q: Which of these does Bad Events say about why professional golfers putt better for par than for a birdie?
options: They do not consciously decide to slack off on birdie putts
Their intense aversion to a bogey apparently adds extra concentration
They consciously save effort on birdie putts to rest for later holes
The effect disappears for top players such as Tiger Woods
The effect appears only on long, difficult putts
questions.explain: Kahneman says these fierce competitors do not consciously slack off; aversion to a bogey seems to sharpen focus. The effect held at every distance and applied to Tiger Woods too.

questions.q: Sort each outcome by whether, relative to the reference point, Bad Events treats it as a gain or a loss.

items.t: A golfer scores a birdie
A golfer scores a bogey
Exceeding a goal you set
Not achieving a goal you set
A cabdriver earning beyond the daily target
A cabdriver falling short of the daily target

questions.explain: A reference point can be a goal: falling short of it is a loss and going beyond it is a gain. In golf, par plays that role, so a birdie is a gain and a bogey a loss.

questions.q: Sort each behavior by whether it is what economic logic implies or what Bad Events reports people actually do because of reference points.

items.t: Cabdrivers work many hours on rainy days
Cabdrivers go home early on rainy days
Golfers putt equally well for birdie and for par
Golfers putt better for par than for birdie
Cabdrivers take leisure on mild days
Cabdrivers work longer on mild days

questions.explain: Economic logic says to work when fares are plentiful and to treat every stroke alike, but daily targets and par act as reference points, so falling short is a loss that drives extra effort.

questions.q: According to Bad Events, why does loss aversion make renegotiating an existing contract difficult?
options: Because each side forgets what the original terms were
Because each concession hurts the giver more than it pleases the receiver
Because negotiators value gains more than they fear losses
Because neither side is influenced by the existing terms
questions.explain: The existing terms are the reference point, so any change is a concession: a loss to the side that gives it and a gain to the other, and losses weigh more. Each side therefore values its own concessions more than the other side does.

questions.q: Kahneman says negotiations over a shrinking ____ are especially difficult because they require an allocation of losses.
questions.explain: Bargaining over a shrinking pie divides losses, which loom large; people are much more easygoing when they bargain over an expanding pie, which divides gains.

questions.q: According to Bad Events, why do negotiators often pretend an intense attachment to some good that they actually plan to give away?
questions.a: Many messages in bargaining are attempts to communicate a reference point and provide an anchor to the other side, and they are not always sincere. A negotiator may treat something, such as missiles of a particular type in arms talks, as a bargaining chip. Because negotiators follow a norm of reciprocity, a concession presented as painful calls for an equally painful, and perhaps equally inauthentic, concession from the other side.

questions.q: Because negotiators are influenced by a norm of ____, a concession presented as painful calls for an equally painful concession from the other side.
questions.explain: The norm of reciprocity is why faking the pain of a concession can pay: it obliges the other side to give up something that feels as costly.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman reports a biologist's observation that when a territory holder is challenged by a rival, the challenger almost always wins.
questions.explain: It is the owner who almost always wins, usually within seconds. Animals, including people, fight harder to prevent losses than to achieve gains, which explains the success of defenders.

questions.q: In Bad Events, what typically happens to an institutional reform plan with many winners and some losers when the affected parties have political influence?
options: Potential winners organize and push the reform through as planned
Both sides lose interest and the status quo is kept by default
The reform becomes cheaper and more effective than first planned
Potential losers fight harder and the reform ends up costlier and less effective
questions.explain: Potential losers are more active and determined than potential winners, so the outcome is biased in their favor and becomes more expensive and less effective than initially planned.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give as examples of grandfather clauses that protect current stakeholders in reforms?
options: Reducing the existing workforce by attrition rather than dismissals
Applying cuts in salaries and benefits only to future workers
Raising every current employee's pay to win support for the reform
Cutting the pay of current and future workers by the same amount
questions.explain: Grandfather clauses spare those who already have something to lose. Equal cuts for everyone would impose losses on current workers, which is exactly what such clauses avoid.

questions.q: Kahneman calls loss aversion a powerful conservative force. According to Bad Events, what good does this conservatism do in individual lives?
questions.a: Loss aversion favors minimal changes from the status quo in the lives of both institutions and individuals. For individuals, this conservatism helps keep us stable in our neighborhood, our marriage and our job. Kahneman calls it “the gravitational force that holds our life together near the reference point.”

questions.q: A city proposes a transit plan that would slightly benefit many residents but would take parking spaces from a few shop owners. Based on Bad Events, what is the most likely outcome?
options: The shop owners campaign hard and the plan is diluted or made costlier
The many residents campaign hard and the plan passes unchanged
Nobody campaigns, because the net benefit is positive
The shop owners accept the loss because the plan helps more people
questions.explain: Potential losers are more active and determined than potential winners, so reforms with an overall improvement are typically biased toward the losers and end up more expensive and less effective.

questions.q: Sort each negotiation by whether, in the terms of Bad Events, the parties are allocating losses or allocating gains.

items.t: Departments dividing a budget cut
Partners dividing an unexpected windfall
Renegotiating a contract to reduce benefits
Sharing profits from a growing market
Countries agreeing which weapons each will give up
Dividing the proceeds of a new joint venture

questions.explain: A shrinking pie forces an allocation of losses, which makes agreement difficult, while people are much more easygoing when bargaining over an expanding pie.

questions.q: Put in order how, according to Bad Events, a typical institutional reform plays out when the affected parties have political influence.
items: The plan is conceived with many winners, some losers and an overall improvement
Potential losers become more active and determined than potential winners
The outcome is biased in favor of the potential losers
The reform ends up more expensive and less effective than planned
questions.explain: Because losses loom larger than gains, the few who stand to lose fight harder than the many who stand to gain, which explains why reforms are watered down, often with grandfather clauses.

questions.q: In the fairness studies, the existing wage, price or rent sets a reference point that has the nature of an ____ that must not be infringed.
questions.explain: The reference transaction works as an entitlement: it is unfair for a firm to impose losses relative to it unless it must do so to protect its own entitlement.

questions.q: Why did 82% of respondents rate as unfair a hardware store raising the price of snow shovels from $15 to $20 the morning after a snowstorm?
options: They saw the old price as a reference point and the rise as a loss imposed simply because the store could
They believed the store's costs had not changed since the previous week
They thought snow shovels should be given away during emergencies
They misunderstood how supply and demand set prices
questions.explain: The standard economic model says raising the price when demand rises is appropriate, but respondents treated the pre-blizzard price as the reference point. Exploiting market power to impose losses on others is unacceptable by the public's rules of fairness.

questions.q: True or false: Most respondents judged it acceptable for a hardware store to raise its snow shovel price after a large snowstorm because demand had increased.
questions.explain: 82% rated the price rise Unfair or Very Unfair. Only the standard economic model treats it as appropriate.

questions.q: Sort each action by how most respondents in the fairness surveys described in Bad Events judged it.

items.t: Cutting a current employee's wage from $9 to $7 because unemployment rose
Paying a replacement worker $7 after the current employee leaves
Raising the price of snow shovels after a snowstorm
Reducing workers' wages when the firm's profitability is falling
Not sharing savings from lower production costs
Breaking an informal contract to impose a loss in order to raise profit

questions.explain: Imposing losses on workers or customers relative to the reference transaction just to increase profit is unfair. A firm may protect its own profit, need not share a bonanza, and owes no entitlement to a new worker.

questions.q: In the photocopy shop survey, why was paying a replacement worker $7 an hour judged acceptable when cutting the current worker's wage to $7 was not?
options: Because the replacement worker had less experience
Because the entitlement to the $9 reference wage is personal to the current worker
Because the shop's profits had fallen in the meantime
Because the replacement worker agreed to the lower wage in writing
questions.explain: The current worker has a right to keep his wage even if the market would allow a cut, but the replacement has no entitlement to the previous worker's reference wage. The shop's business was still satisfactory, so falling profits were not the reason.

questions.q: What did Kahneman, Thaler and Knetsch mean by dual entitlements in their fairness research?
questions.a: The rules of fairness give entitlements both to the firm and to the individuals it deals with. Customers and workers are entitled to their reference price or wage, so a firm may not impose losses on them simply to increase profit. The firm in turn is entitled to retain its current profit, so when it faces a threat of loss it may pass the loss on to others, and it is not even expected to absorb part of it.

questions.q: True or false: Respondents in the fairness surveys branded a firm as unfair if it did not share savings from lower production costs with its customers or workers.
questions.explain: Respondents liked a generous firm better, but they did not brand as unfair a firm that did not share a bonanza. Indignation was reserved for firms that imposed losses on others to increase profit.

questions.q: Match each fairness-survey scenario to how respondents judged it.
pairs: Snow shovel price raised from $15 to $20 after a storm
82% rated it Unfair or Very Unfair
Current employee's wage cut from $9 to $7
83% rated it Unfair or Very Unfair
Replacement worker hired at $7 an hour
73% rated it Acceptable
questions.explain: The two cases that impose a loss on an existing customer or worker drew large majorities calling them unfair, while the replacement case, where no one loses a reference wage, was judged acceptable.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what is the important task for students of economic fairness?
questions.a: The task is not to identify ideal behavior. It is to find the line that separates acceptable conduct from actions that invite opprobrium and punishment. In the surveys, that line ran between failing to share gains, which was tolerated, and exploiting power to impose losses on others in order to increase profit, which provoked indignation.

questions.q: Which of these were reasons Kahneman and his colleagues were not optimistic when they submitted their fairness research to the American Economic Review?
options: It challenged the accepted view that economic behavior is ruled by self-interest
It relied on survey responses, which economists generally have little respect for
Its questionnaires had to include a mention of fish
Its data had been collected by unemployed professionals
It claimed fairness was economically insignificant
questions.explain: The worries were the challenge to accepted wisdom that fairness is irrelevant and the reliance on survey evidence. The fish requirement and the interviewers were details of how the data were collected, and the article argued that fairness matters, not that it is insignificant.

questions.q: Which of these does Bad Events report from more recent research on the economic significance of fairness?
options: Employers who violate rules of fairness are punished by reduced productivity
Merchants who follow unfair pricing policies can expect to lose sales
Customers who saw a lower catalog price for a recent purchase cut future purchases by 15%
Fairness concerns turned out to have negligible economic effects
The customers who reacted most strongly were those who bought the fewest items
questions.explain: Later research showed fairness concerns are economically significant, as the authors had suspected but not proved. In the catalog study, the strongest reactions came from customers who bought more items at higher prices, not fewer.

questions.q: In the catalog study described in Bad Events, why did customers reduce their future purchases after seeing a lower price for a product they had recently bought?
options: They assumed the product's quality had dropped
They could no longer afford to buy as many items
They switched to waiting for further price cuts
They took the lower price as the reference point and felt they had lost by overpaying
questions.explain: Customers perceived the new lower price as the reference point and thought they had sustained a loss by paying more than appropriate. Their purchases fell by 15%, an average loss of $90 per customer.

questions.q: Neuroeconomists found that punishing one stranger for behaving unfairly to another is accompanied by increased activity in the brain's ____ centers.
questions.explain: This altruistic punishment lights up the “pleasure centers” of the brain, suggesting that maintaining the social order and the rules of fairness is its own reward.

questions.q: What asymmetry does Kahneman find in altruistic punishment, and why does he think such punishment matters for societies?
questions.a: Strangers who observe unfair behavior often join in punishing it, and this altruistic punishment is accompanied by increased activity in the brain's pleasure centers, so maintaining fairness is its own reward. Kahneman suggests it could well be the glue that holds societies together. But our brains are not designed to reward generosity as reliably as they punish meanness, which is another marked asymmetry between losses and gains.

questions.q: In the study by David Cohen and Jack Knetsch, how does the law typically treat a merchant whose goods were lost in transit?
options: He may be compensated for costs actually incurred, but not for lost profits
He may be compensated for lost profits, but not for costs incurred
He is compensated equally for costs incurred and lost profits
He is compensated only if he can show the carrier acted unfairly
questions.explain: Cohen and Knetsch found a sharp legal distinction between actual losses and foregone gains: incurred costs are compensated, lost profits usually are not.

questions.q: Kahneman says the familiar rule that ____ is nine-tenths of the law confirms the moral status of the reference point.
questions.explain: Possession marks the reference point; the legal rule favoring the possessor reflects the same entitlement that loss aversion creates.

questions.q: What provocative point does Eyal Zamir make about the law's distinction between restoring losses and compensating for foregone gains?
questions.a: Zamir argues that the distinction may be justified by the asymmetrical effects of losses and foregone gains on individual well-being. If people who lose suffer more than people who merely fail to gain, they may also deserve more protection from the law. The legal asymmetry would then mirror loss aversion itself.

questions.q: Put these events in the history of the fairness research described in Bad Events in order.
items: The authors write a new questionnaire every week for a telephone survey program
They find that the public's fairness rules distinguish sharply between losses and gains
They submit their report to the American Economic Review
The editor sends it to two economists not bound by the usual conventions
Later research shows fairness concerns are economically significant
questions.explain: The surveys came out of the year in Vancouver; the findings challenged economic orthodoxy, the editor sent it to two economists not bound by the usual conventions, who proved very friendly reviewers, and the article's conclusions have stood the test of time, with later work confirming the economic weight of fairness.

questions.q: Match each researcher or group to the contribution Bad Events attributes to them.
pairs: Kahneman, Thaler and Knetsch
Surveys showing fairness rules based on dual entitlements
David Cohen and Jack Knetsch
Legal decisions separating actual losses from foregone gains
Eyal Zamir
Legal asymmetry may be justified by effects on well-being
Neuroeconomists
Altruistic punishment activates the brain's pleasure centers
questions.explain: Each finding extends loss aversion and entitlements beyond individual choice, into public judgments of fairness, the practice of law, legal theory and brain research.

questions.q: A small manufacturer's profits are falling because of a downturn, and it trims its workers' wages slightly. According to the fairness surveys in Bad Events, how would most people judge this?
options: As unfair, because workers are entitled to their reference wage in all cases
As not unfair, because a firm may pass on a threatened loss to protect its profit
As unfair unless the owner first gives up all of his own profit
As acceptable only if the firm also cuts its prices to customers
questions.explain: A substantial majority thought it not unfair to cut wages when profitability is falling. The firm's own entitlement is to keep its current profit, and it is not even expected to absorb part of the loss.

questions.q: Match each remark from the Speaking of Losses examples to the idea it expresses.
pairs: This reform will not pass
Potential losers fight harder than potential winners
Each thinks the other's concessions are less painful
The asymmetry of concessions in negotiation
The pie is actually expanding
Allocating gains is easier than allocating losses
Tenants object to a rent rise
Current terms feel like an entitlement
Clients accept a price hike after costs rose
The firm's entitlement to stay profitable
questions.explain: The remarks apply the chapter's main ideas: reform resistance, concessions as losses, shrinking versus expanding pies, and the dual entitlements of customers and firms.

questions.q: In one Speaking of Losses example, rental prices nearby have gone up, but tenants think it unfair for their landlord to raise their rent too. According to the chapter, why?
options: They believe the landlord's costs have fallen
They expect rents to drop again soon
They do not know that market rents have risen
They feel entitled to their current terms
questions.explain: The existing rent is the reference transaction and has the nature of an entitlement, so a rise imposed simply because the market allows it feels like an unfair loss, as in the snow shovel case.

questions.q: Using the ideas of Bad Events, explain why someone might predict of a proposed reform that it will not pass.
questions.a: A reform defines winners and losers relative to the status quo, which is the reference point. Because losses loom larger than gains, those who stand to lose will fight harder than those who stand to gain. If the losers have political influence, the outcome is biased in their favor, so the reform is blocked or ends up costlier and less effective than planned.

questions.q: Put the sections of Bad Events in the order they appear in the chapter.
items: Negativity Dominance
Goals Are Reference Points
Defending the Status Quo
Loss Aversion in the Law
Speaking of Losses
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the biology of bad news, to goals as reference points, to negotiations and reform, to fairness and the law, and closes with its usual set of example remarks.

questions.q: What does the title Bad Events signal about the chapter's scope compared with the narrower idea of loss aversion?
options: That it focuses on statistical errors in predicting disasters
That it is limited to monetary losses in gambles
That losses are one case of a broader dominance of bad over good
That it argues bad events are rarer than people think
questions.explain: The chapter treats loss aversion as one manifestation of a broad negativity dominance, covering threats, emotions, relationships, goals, negotiations and fairness, not only monetary gambles.

questions.q: Put these chapters of Part 4, Choices, in the order they appear in the book.
items: Prospect Theory
The Endowment Effect
Bad Events
The Fourfold Pattern
Rare Events
questions.explain: Bad Events comes after The Endowment Effect and before The Fourfold Pattern, in the middle of the part on how people make choices.

questions.q: How does Bad Events build on the two chapters before it, Prospect Theory and The Endowment Effect?
questions.a: Those chapters establish that people evaluate outcomes as gains and losses relative to a reference point and that losses loom larger than gains, including in reluctance to give up owned goods. Bad Events widens the frame: it grounds loss aversion in a biological negativity dominance and in System 1, shows that goals and the status quo serve as reference points, and traces the asymmetry into negotiations, reform, public fairness rules and the law.

questions.q: Which of these ideas from earlier in the book does Bad Events draw on?
options: The automatic operations of System 1
The word vomit evoking attenuated reactions to the real thing
Anchors as reference points communicated in negotiation
Regression to the mean in flight instruction
The law of small numbers in kidney cancer rates
questions.explain: The chapter ties threat detection to System 1, recalls the vomit example to explain symbolic threats, and describes negotiators providing an anchor to the other side. Regression and small-sample examples do not appear in it.

questions.q: In the opening of the chapter on the fourfold pattern, which mental system does Kahneman say usually assigns weights to the characteristics of a complex object, such as a car or a son-in-law?
options: System 1, often without our awareness
System 2, through deliberate calculation
Both systems equally, in strict alternation
Neither system; weights come from explicit rules
questions.explain: Kahneman says the weighting happens whether or not you are aware of it and is an operation of System 1. It is sometimes conscious, but most often you are just an observer of the global evaluation System 1 delivers.

questions.q: Kahneman says that the weighting of characteristics in a global evaluation, whether of a car or of an uncertain prospect, is an operation of ____.
questions.explain: The weighting occurs whether or not we notice it, which marks it as an automatic System 1 operation rather than deliberate System 2 work.

questions.q: Which of these characteristics does Kahneman name as features that may get more or less weight in your overall evaluation of a car?
options: Gas economy
Comfort
Appearance
Resale price
Safety record
questions.explain: Kahneman lists gas economy, comfort and appearance as the car features that might be weighted. Resale price and safety record are plausible features but are not the examples he gives.

questions.q: In the opening of the chapter on the fourfold pattern, why does Kahneman say that you are usually “just an observer” of your own evaluation of an uncertain prospect?
questions.a: Any global evaluation assigns weights to features or outcomes, and for uncertain prospects the weights go to the possible outcomes. The weights are correlated with probabilities, but the weighting is an operation of System 1 that happens whether or not you are aware of it. It is sometimes conscious and deliberate, but most often System 1 delivers the overall evaluation and you simply receive it.

questions.q: In the chapter on the fourfold pattern, what is the expected value of the gamble “20% chance to win $1,000 and 75% chance to win $100”?
questions.explain: Expected value averages the outcomes weighted by their probabilities: 20% of $1,000 is $200 and 75% of $100 is $75, giving $275.

questions.q: In the chapter on the fourfold pattern, the ____ of a gamble is defined as the average of its outcomes, each weighted by its probability.
questions.explain: Before Bernoulli, gambles were assessed by their expected value, the probability-weighted average of their outcomes.

questions.q: The rule that weights each outcome of a gamble by its probability, which Bernoulli retained but applied to psychological value, is known as the ____.
questions.explain: Bernoulli kept the probability weighting, called the expectation principle, but averaged the utilities of the outcomes instead of their dollar values.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what did Bernoulli change about the way gambles were assessed in the pre-Bernoulli days?
options: He replaced probabilities with decision weights that differ from them
He abandoned probability weighting in favor of the best outcome
He kept weighting by probability but applied it to the utility of outcomes
He applied values to gains and losses rather than to wealth
questions.explain: Bernoulli retained the expectation principle but applied it to the psychological value of outcomes. Replacing probabilities with decision weights and valuing gains and losses are prospect theory ideas, not Bernoulli's.

questions.q: Which of these improvements in the chance of receiving $1 million does Kahneman say everyone agrees are more impressive than the others?
options: From 0 to 5%
From 5% to 10%
From 60% to 65%
From 95% to 100%
questions.explain: Kahneman says 0 to 5% and 95% to 100% are qualitative changes, creating a possibility or a certainty, while 5% to 10% and 60% to 65% are only quantitative improvements.

questions.q: Kahneman calls the change in the chance of winning $1 million from 0 to 5% a qualitative change. Why?
options: It doubles the probability of winning, so value doubles too
It produces the largest gain in expected value of any change
It removes all remaining doubt about the outcome
It creates a possibility, a hope of winning, that did not exist before
questions.explain: Going from 0 to 5% creates a hope of winning that did not exist earlier. Doubling the probability describes the move from 5% to 10%, which Kahneman says does not double psychological value.

questions.q: In the chapter on the fourfold pattern, the large psychological impact of improving a chance from 0 to 5% illustrates the ____, which makes highly unlikely outcomes weigh more than they deserve.
questions.explain: The possibility effect causes highly unlikely outcomes to be weighted disproportionately, which is why lottery buyers pay far more than expected value.

questions.q: In the chapter on the fourfold pattern, the large impact of improving a chance from 95% to 100% is called the ____.
questions.explain: Outcomes that are almost certain are given less weight than their probability justifies, so reaching full certainty has an outsized impact: the certainty effect.

questions.q: In Kahneman's example of the contested $1 million inheritance, a risk-adjustment company offers $910,000 for a case you have a 95% chance to win. Which effect makes the offer tempting?
options: The certainty effect
The possibility effect
The endowment effect
The halo effect
questions.explain: The offer is $40,000 below the $950,000 expected value, yet it is tempting because a sure thing is valued above a 95% chance. Kahneman says the structured settlements industry profits from exactly this certainty effect.

questions.q: True or false: According to Kahneman, the possibility effect means that outcomes that are almost certain are given more weight than their probability justifies.
questions.explain: The possibility effect concerns improbable outcomes, which are overweighted. Almost-certain outcomes are underweighted relative to certainty, which is the certainty effect.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that overweighting of small probabilities increases the attractiveness of both gambles and insurance policies.
questions.explain: Overweighting small chances makes a long-shot gamble more attractive, and overweighting small risks makes people pay more than expected value to remove them through insurance.

questions.q: In the chapter on the fourfold pattern, how does the example of four 5% improvements in the chance of winning $1 million show that the expectation principle is poor psychology?
questions.a: The expectation principle says utility should rise by exactly 5% of the value of $1 million in each case. In fact, 0 to 5% and 95% to 100% feel far more impressive than 5% to 10% or 60% to 65%, because they create a possibility or a certainty. So decision weights are not identical to probabilities: improbable outcomes are overweighted and nearly certain outcomes are underweighted relative to certainty.

questions.q: Explain how the possibility effect and the certainty effect appear in the domain of losses, using Kahneman's surgery example.
questions.a: When a loved one goes into surgery, a 5% risk of amputation feels much more than half as bad as a 10% risk, because small risks are overweighted, so people pay far more than expected value to remove them altogether. At the other end, the difference between a 95% risk of disaster and certain disaster feels even greater, because the sliver of hope that everything could still be okay looms very large.

questions.q: In the chapter on the fourfold pattern, what was von Neumann and Morgenstern's argument for the expectation principle, and why does Kahneman say it makes “the plot thicken”?
questions.a: In 1944 von Neumann and Morgenstern derived the expectation principle from axioms of rational choice, proving that any weighting of outcomes not strictly proportional to probability leads to inconsistencies. This placed expected utility theory at the core of the rational agent model. The plot thickens because the expectation principle is poor psychology, yet a decision maker who wishes to be rational must conform to it.

questions.q: Who, according to Kahneman, proved in 1944 that any weighting of uncertain outcomes not strictly proportional to probability leads to inconsistencies?
options: Maurice Allais
John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern
Daniel Bernoulli
Jimmie Savage
questions.explain: Kahneman credits von Neumann and Morgenstern's axiomatic version of utility theory with this proof. Allais later challenged the theory, and Bernoulli's work came much earlier.

questions.q: Match each term from the chapter on the fourfold pattern to its meaning.
pairs: Expected value
The average of a gamble's outcomes, each weighted by its probability
Expectation principle
The rule that outcomes should be weighted in proportion to their probability
Possibility effect
Highly unlikely outcomes are weighted more than they deserve
Certainty effect
Almost certain outcomes are weighted less than their probability justifies
questions.explain: Expected value and the expectation principle describe the rational weighting rule; the possibility and certainty effects describe how real decision weights depart from it at the two ends of the probability scale.

questions.q: Match each improvement in the chance of winning $1 million to Kahneman's description of it.
pairs: From 0 to 5%
A qualitative change that creates a hope of winning
From 5% to 10%
Doubles the probability but does not double psychological value
From 95% to 100%
A qualitative change that removes all doubt
questions.explain: The two ends of the scale bring qualitative changes, possibility and certainty, while a move in the low middle is only a quantitative improvement.

questions.q: Put these steps of Kahneman's argument about changing chances in the order he presents them.
items: The expected value of a gamble weights each outcome by its probability
Bernoulli applies the same weighting to the utility of outcomes
Examples of 5% improvements show that weights do not match probabilities
Von Neumann and Morgenstern show a rational agent must follow the expectation principle
questions.explain: Kahneman starts with the expectation rule, notes Bernoulli's version, shows it is poor psychology through the possibility and certainty effects, and then notes the axiomatic argument that rationality requires it.

questions.q: In Kahneman's simplified version of Allais's problem A (61% chance to win $520,000 OR 63% chance to win $500,000), which option do most people prefer?
options: The 63% chance to win $500,000
They are evenly split between the two
The 61% chance to win $520,000
Neither; most refuse to choose
questions.explain: In problem A almost everybody prefers the left-hand option, because the difference in prize size is more impressive than the small difference in the chance of winning.

questions.q: Sort the options in Kahneman's simplified Allais problems by whether most people prefer or reject them.

items.t: 61% chance to win $520,000
63% chance to win $500,000
98% chance to win $520,000
100% chance to win $500,000

questions.explain: Most people take the larger prize in problem A but the sure $500,000 in problem B. The switch is inconsistent, because problem B's urns are just improved versions of problem A's.

questions.q: What did Maurice Allais intend to show the distinguished economists at the 1952 Paris meeting?
options: That they overweighted small probabilities when buying lottery tickets
That they were more loss averse than ordinary people
That they valued outcomes in terms of final wealth rather than changes
That they were susceptible to a certainty effect and so violated expected utility theory
questions.explain: Kahneman says Allais intended to show his guests were susceptible to a certainty effect, violating expected utility theory and the axioms of rational choice beneath it.

questions.q: In Kahneman's urn explanation of the Allais problems, how are the urns of problem B related to the urns of problem A?
options: Each is a better version of A, with 37 white marbles replaced by red winning ones
Each is a worse version of A, with 37 red marbles replaced by white ones
The urns are identical, but the prizes are larger
Only the right-hand urn is changed, by adding 2 red marbles
questions.explain: Both urns improve by 37 red winning marbles, and the left-hand urn improves more because its red marbles win $520,000. So preferring left in A but right in B makes no logical sense.

questions.q: Which of these people does Kahneman name as attending the 1952 Paris meeting on the economics of risk?
options: Paul Samuelson
Milton Friedman
Jimmie Savage
Daniel Bernoulli
Chris Guthrie
questions.explain: Kahneman lists Samuelson, Arrow, Friedman and the statistician Savage among the American guests. Bernoulli lived centuries earlier, and Guthrie is the legal scholar whose work comes later in the chapter.

questions.q: True or false: According to Kahneman, the economists at the Paris meeting did not notice that their preferences violated utility theory until Allais pointed it out as the meeting was about to end.
questions.explain: Allais drew attention to the violation only near the end, intending the announcement as a bombshell about the world's leading decision theorists.

questions.q: True or false: According to Kahneman, after Allais's demonstration in Paris, his audience abandoned “the American school” and adopted his alternative logic of choice.
questions.explain: Allais hoped for this but was sorely disappointed. Economists mostly treated the problem as an anomaly and kept using expected utility theory.

questions.q: Allais hoped the economists in Paris would give up the approach he rather contemptuously labeled “the ____ school.”
questions.explain: Allais wanted his audience to abandon what he called the American school and adopt his own logic of choice, but he was to be sorely disappointed.

questions.q: Sort these reactions to Allais's paradox by who Kahneman says had them.

items.t: Noted the problem as an anomaly
Kept using expected utility theory as if nothing had happened
Mostly ignored the Allais problem
Took Allais's challenge very seriously
Tried to bend the rules of rational choice to permit the Allais pattern

questions.explain: Kahneman contrasts economists who mostly ignored the problem with decision theorists, a mixed group of statisticians, economists, philosophers and psychologists, who took it seriously and often tried to rationalize it.

questions.q: How did Kahneman and Tversky respond to Allais's paradox, according to the chapter on the fourfold pattern?
options: They bent the rules of rational choice so that the Allais pattern became permissible
They kept utility theory as a logic of rational choice but dropped the idea that people are perfectly rational
They rejected utility theory even as a standard of rational choice
They argued the paradox disappears when stakes are modest
questions.explain: Unlike most decision theorists, who tried to make the Allais pattern rational, they retained utility theory as logic but set out to describe the choices people actually make, rational or not.

questions.q: Kahneman says that in prospect theory, ____ would not be identical to probabilities.
questions.explain: Prospect theory was designed to describe actual choices, so the weights attached to outcomes were allowed to differ from their probabilities.

questions.q: Using the urn of 100 marbles, explain why preferring the left option in Allais problem A and the right option in problem B is a logical error, and what psychological explanation Kahneman gives.
questions.a: Problem B's urns are problem A's urns with 37 white marbles replaced by red winning marbles in each. The left urn improves more, since each red marble there wins $520,000 rather than $500,000, so a preference for the left in A should carry over to B. The switch is explained by the certainty effect: the 2% gap between 98% and 100% is far more impressive than the same gap between 61% and 63%.

questions.q: How did Kahneman and Tversky's response to Allais's paradox differ from that of most decision theorists, including Allais himself?
questions.a: Most decision theorists kept their belief in human rationality and tried to bend the rules of rational choice so the Allais pattern would become permissible, without convincing results. Kahneman and Tversky instead kept utility theory as the logic of rational choice and abandoned the assumption that people are perfectly rational choosers. They set out to build a psychological theory describing the choices people actually make, in which decision weights are not identical to probabilities.

questions.q: Put these events from the chapter on the fourfold pattern in chronological order.
items: Von Neumann and Morgenstern publish their axiomatic utility theory
Allais poses his puzzle at the Paris meeting on the economics of risk
Amos introduces Kahneman to von Neumann and Morgenstern's work
Kahneman and Tversky publish prospect theory
Kahneman and Tversky measure decision weights for gambles with modest stakes
questions.explain: The theory came in 1944, the Paris meeting in 1952, Amos's introduction about thirty years after the theory, then prospect theory, and the decision weight study many years after prospect theory was published.

questions.q: Put these events of the 1952 Paris meeting and its aftermath in the order Kahneman describes them.
items: Allais presents his choice questions to the distinguished audience
The economists state preferences that seem comfortable to them
As the meeting ends, Allais reveals that their preferences violate utility theory
Most economists note the problem as an anomaly and carry on
questions.explain: Allais saved his bombshell for the end of the meeting, and its reception disappointed him: most economists filed it away as an anomaly.

questions.q: In Kahneman and Tversky's table of decision weights for gains, what decision weight corresponds to a 2% chance of winning?
questions.explain: The weight for a 2% chance is 8.1, so the rare event is overweighted by a factor of about 4 compared with the weight of 2 that rational choice would require.

questions.q: Match each probability of winning to the decision weight Kahneman reports for it.
pairs: About 71
questions.explain: Low probabilities get weights above their value (possibility effect) and high probabilities get weights below their value (certainty effect).

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman report about the decision weights in his table for gains?
options: They equal the probabilities at 0 and at 100
A 2% chance has a decision weight of 8.1
They are higher than the probabilities across the whole scale
They are proportional to probabilities between 5% and 95%
