questions.explain: Weights match probabilities only at the extremes and depart sharply near them. They are not higher everywhere, since high probabilities are underweighted, and the 5% to 95% range maps to a compressed range of weights.

questions.q: Kahneman notes that probabilities from 5% to 95% map to decision weights from only 13.2 to 79.3. What does this show?
options: Oversensitivity to intermediate probabilities
That decision weights equal probabilities in the middle range
That the possibility effect disappears for gains
Inadequate sensitivity to intermediate probabilities
questions.explain: The range of weights is about two-thirds as large as rationally expected, so the possibility and certainty effects at the ends are accompanied by too little sensitivity in the middle.

questions.q: True or false: According to Kahneman, neuroscientists have found that the brain's response to changes in the probability of winning a prize is strikingly similar to the decision weights estimated from choices.
questions.explain: Kahneman reports that brain regions responding to probability changes behave much like the decision weights inferred from people's choices.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that people readily distinguish a cancer risk of 0.001% from a cancer risk of 0.00001%.
questions.explain: People are almost completely insensitive to variations among small probabilities, even though these two risks would mean 3,000 versus 30 cancers in the United States.

questions.q: What does Kahneman's table of decision weights for gains show at the extremes of the probability scale and close to them?
questions.a: Decision weights equal probabilities at the extremes: 0 for an impossible outcome and 100 for a sure thing. Near these points they depart sharply. At the low end a 2% chance gets a weight of 8.1, an overweighting by a factor of 4 (the possibility effect), and at the high end a 2% risk of not winning drops the weight from 100 to 87.1 (the certainty effect, which is even more striking).

questions.q: Using his 1% examples, explain the asymmetry Kahneman describes between the possibility effect and the certainty effect.
questions.a: Compare a 1% chance to win $1 million with being almost certain to win it but facing a 1% chance of not winning, with the outcome known tomorrow in both cases. The anxiety of the second situation is more salient than the hope in the first, so the certainty effect is stronger. The same holds for surgery: the faint hope in an almost certainly fatal operation grips us more intensely than the fear of a 1% risk.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman treat probabilities below 1% or above 99% as a special case?
questions.a: Very rare events are sometimes ignored altogether, effectively getting a decision weight of zero, as when we spend little time worrying about nuclear meltdowns. But when such an event becomes the focus of attention, it gets much more weight than its probability deserves. People are also almost completely insensitive to differences among small probabilities, such as a cancer risk of 0.001% versus 0.00001%.

questions.q: Kahneman says that because of the possibility effect, reducing a worrying risk is not adequate: to eliminate the worry, the probability must be brought down to ____.
questions.explain: Worry is not proportional to probability, so only removing the risk completely makes the worry go away.

questions.q: In the insect spray study, parents were asked about a spray causing 15 poisonings per 10,000 bottles. How much more were they willing to pay to eliminate the risk completely than to reduce it to 5?
options: More than three times as much ($8.09 versus $2.38)
About the same amount ($2.38 versus $2.10)
About half as much ($1.20 versus $2.38)
Exactly 1.5 times as much, in line with the risk reduced
questions.explain: Parents paid $2.38 to cut the risk by two-thirds but $8.09 to eliminate it, a certainty premium that fits the psychology of worry but not the rational model.

questions.q: In the insect spray study, parents were willing to pay a ____ premium to eliminate a risk completely, which fits the psychology of worry but not the rational model.
questions.explain: The extra amount paid for complete elimination is a certainty premium; parents even paid it separately for each of the two risks.

questions.q: What did the insect spray study of parents reveal about how people value the elimination of risk, and why is this inconsistent with the rational model?
questions.a: Parents would pay an extra $2.38 to cut poisonings from 15 to 5 per 10,000 bottles, but $8.09, more than three times as much, to eliminate the risk entirely. They treated inhalation and child poisoning as separate worries and paid a certainty premium to eliminate either one. Paying so much for the last bit of risk reflects the psychology of worry, not a value proportional to the risk removed.

questions.q: Put these elements of the insect spray study in the order Kahneman presents them.
items: Parents are told their $10 spray causes 15 poisonings of each kind per 10,000 bottles
Parents learn of a pricier spray that cuts each risk to 5 per 10,000
Parents say they would pay $2.38 more for the safer spray
Comparison shows they would pay $8.09 to eliminate the risk completely
questions.explain: The study sets up the current risk, offers a reduction, records willingness to pay, and then contrasts it with the much larger amount paid for complete elimination.

questions.q: A homeowner learns that a filter would cut a radon risk from 4 in 10,000 to 1 in 10,000 and shrugs, but would pay several times more for a system that removes the risk entirely. Which idea from Kahneman's discussion of decision weights explains this?
options: Decision weights equal probabilities for small risks
Worry is not proportional to probability, so only elimination removes it
Diminishing sensitivity makes large risks feel smaller
The expectation principle favors paying for full elimination
questions.explain: Like the parents in the insect spray study, the homeowner pays a certainty premium: the decision weight reflects worry, and reducing a risk does not end the worry the way eliminating it does.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, which two conclusions of prospect theory together explained the fourfold pattern?
options: People are loss averse, and they prefer the status quo
People use the expectation principle, and they value final wealth
People value gains and losses rather than wealth, and decision weights differ from probabilities
People overweight vivid outcomes, and they neglect base rates
questions.explain: Kahneman says neither idea was entirely new, but combining reference-dependent values with decision weights that differ from probabilities explained the distinctive fourfold pattern.

questions.q: In the fourfold pattern, choices are said to be ____ if the sure thing is preferred to a gamble with the same expected value.
questions.explain: Preferring the sure thing is risk averse; preferring the gamble is risk seeking.

questions.q: Sort these cells of the fourfold pattern by the risk attitude most people show in them.

items.t: 95% chance to win $10,000
95% chance to lose $10,000
5% chance to win $10,000
5% chance to lose $10,000

questions.explain: People are risk averse for likely gains and unlikely losses, and risk seeking for unlikely gains (lotteries) and likely losses (desperate gambles).

questions.q: Which of these cells of the fourfold pattern are ones where most people are risk seeking?
options: High probability of a gain (top left)
High probability of a loss (top right)
Low probability of a gain (bottom left)
Low probability of a loss (bottom right)
questions.explain: Risk seeking appears in the top right, where people gamble to avoid a sure loss, and in the bottom left, where lotteries are bought. The other two cells show risk aversion.

questions.q: Which cell of the fourfold pattern does Kahneman say was new and unexpected to him and Tversky?
options: Top left: a high probability of a gain
Bottom left: a low probability of a gain
Bottom right: a low probability of a loss
Top right: a high probability of a loss
questions.explain: Three cells were familiar. The top right, risk seeking in the face of likely losses, initially surprised them because they were used to thinking in terms of risk aversion.

questions.q: In Kahneman's fourfold pattern, what does the bottom right cell (low probability of a large loss) explain?
options: Why people buy insurance at more than expected value
Why people buy lottery tickets
Why people take desperate gambles to avoid a sure loss
Why plaintiffs with strong cases accept settlements
questions.explain: Overweighting a small chance of disaster makes people risk averse here, paying more than expected value for insurance, which is how insurers cover costs and make profits.

questions.q: Kahneman says that people who buy insurance get more than protection against an unlikely disaster: they eliminate a worry and purchase ____.
questions.explain: In the bottom right cell, the extra price paid above expected value buys relief from worry as well as protection.

questions.q: Kahneman explains that a sure loss is very aversive partly because of ____: the reaction to losing $900 is more than 90% as intense as the reaction to losing $1,000.
questions.explain: Diminishing sensitivity makes a sure $900 loss feel almost as bad as a $1,000 loss, which pushes people toward gambling when facing losses.

questions.q: Which of these are the reasons Kahneman gives for risk seeking when choosing between a sure loss and a gamble with a high probability of a larger loss?
options: Diminishing sensitivity makes the sure loss more aversive
The decision weight for a 90% probability is only about 71
The small chance of a large win is overweighted
The endowment effect raises the value of the money at stake
questions.explain: Kahneman names diminishing sensitivity and the certainty effect, which underweights the 90% chance of losing. Overweighting a small chance of winning belongs to the bottom left cell, not the top right.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what happens to the two factors (the value function's shape and decision weights) in the bottom row of the fourfold pattern?
options: They pull in the same direction, both favoring risk aversion
They pull in opposite directions, and overweighting of low probabilities wins
They cancel exactly, leaving people indifferent to risk
They pull in opposite directions, and diminishing sensitivity wins
questions.explain: In the top row both factors push the same way. In the bottom row, diminishing sensitivity still favors risk aversion for gains and risk seeking for losses, but overweighting of low probabilities overcomes it, producing gambling for gains and caution for losses.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that he and Tversky were the first to observe risk seeking with negative prospects.
questions.explain: At least two authors had already reported risk seeking with losses but had not made much of it. Kahneman and Tversky's contribution was a framework that made the finding easy to interpret.

questions.q: Kahneman says that what people acquire with a lottery ticket is more than a chance to win; it is the right to ____ pleasantly of winning.
questions.explain: In the bottom left cell, the possibility effect makes even a minuscule chance valuable, and the ticket buys “the right to dream pleasantly of winning.”

questions.q: Which of these situations does Kahneman place in the top right cell of the fourfold pattern, where people facing very bad options take desperate gambles?
options: Businesses losing ground to a superior technology wasting their remaining assets
People buying lottery tickets for a huge top prize
The losing side in a war fighting long after defeat is certain
Homeowners buying insurance against an unlikely disaster
questions.explain: Both the failing business and the losing side in a war accept a high chance of making things worse for a small hope of avoiding a large loss. Lotteries and insurance belong to the bottom row.

questions.q: Sort these examples from the chapter by whether they illustrate mainly the possibility effect or the certainty effect.

items.t: Buying lottery tickets for a minuscule chance at a huge prize
Paying far more than expected value to eliminate a small risk
A 2% chance getting a decision weight of 8.1
The structured settlements industry
Preferring $500,000 for sure over a 98% chance at $520,000
Being tempted by $910,000 for a case you have a 95% chance to win

questions.explain: The possibility effect overweights unlikely outcomes, as in lotteries and insurance. The certainty effect makes a sure thing worth more than a near-certainty, as in structured settlements and Allais's problem B.

questions.q: Sort these examples from the chapter by whether they involve the domain of gains or the domain of losses.

items.t: Buying a lottery ticket
A plaintiff with a strong case weighing a settlement
A plaintiff filing a frivolous claim for a large sum
Buying insurance
A business wasting assets trying to catch up with a superior technology
A defendant with a weak case weighing a settlement

questions.explain: Lotteries and plaintiffs' claims are chances to gain; insurance, failing businesses and defendants facing payment are about avoiding losses.

questions.q: Sort these situations by which row of the fourfold pattern they belong to.

items.t: A plaintiff with a 95% chance to win in court
A defendant whose trial is going poorly
A lottery ticket buyer
An insurance buyer
A plaintiff with a flimsy case and a large claim
A business almost certain to lose to a superior rival

questions.explain: The top row covers likely outcomes, such as strong cases and nearly certain defeat. The bottom row covers long shots and unlikely disasters, such as lotteries, insurance and frivolous suits.

questions.q: Sort these from the chapter by whether the outcome is overweighted or underweighted relative to its probability.

items.t: A 2% chance to win a prize
A 5% risk that amputation will be needed
A 98% chance to win a prize
A 95% chance to win a court case
A small chance of a large loss in a frivolous suit
A 90% probability of losing

questions.explain: Improbable outcomes are overweighted (the possibility effect), and outcomes that are almost certain are underweighted relative to certainty (the certainty effect).

questions.q: Match each cell of the fourfold pattern to the example Kahneman links with it.
pairs: High probability of a gain
A plaintiff with a strong case accepting a settlement
High probability of a loss
A failing business spending its last assets to catch up
Low probability of a gain
Buying a lottery ticket
Low probability of a loss
Buying insurance
questions.explain: Each cell pairs a probability level with gains or losses; Kahneman ties each to a familiar behavior, from cautious settlement to desperate gambling.

questions.q: A project manager whose project is almost certain to fail keeps pouring money into it, hoping for a small chance of complete rescue rather than accepting a smaller sure loss now. Which cell of Kahneman's fourfold pattern describes this?
options: Top left: risk aversion for a likely gain
Bottom left: risk seeking for an unlikely gain
Top right: risk seeking in the face of a likely loss
Bottom right: risk aversion for an unlikely loss
questions.explain: This is the top right cell, where accepting the large sure loss is too painful and hope of relief too enticing, so people refuse to cut their losses.

questions.q: A shopper pays a high price for an extended warranty that protects against a rare but expensive breakdown. Which cell of Kahneman's fourfold pattern explains this behavior?
options: Top right: risk seeking for a high probability of a loss
Bottom left: risk seeking for a low probability of a gain
Top left: risk aversion for a high probability of a gain
Bottom right: risk aversion for a low probability of a large loss
questions.explain: Like insurance, the warranty is bought at more than expected value because a small chance of a large loss is overweighted, and it buys peace of mind.

questions.q: Explain the two reasons Kahneman gives for risk seeking when people choose between a sure loss and a gamble with a high probability of a larger loss.
questions.a: First, diminishing sensitivity: the reaction to a $900 loss is more than 90% as intense as the reaction to a $1,000 loss, so the sure loss is very aversive. Second, and perhaps more powerful, the decision weight for a 90% probability is only about 71, so the certainty effect makes the gamble less aversive. Together these make the gamble attractive; the same two factors favor the sure thing when outcomes are gains.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say that many unfortunate human situations unfold in the top right cell of the fourfold pattern?
questions.a: In the top right cell, people facing very bad options take desperate gambles, accepting a high chance of making things worse for a small hope of avoiding a large loss. The sure loss is too painful and the hope of complete relief too enticing for them to cut their losses. Kahneman says “Risk taking of this kind often turns manageable failures into disasters,” as when businesses chase a superior technology or losing sides fight on in war.

questions.q: Describe the four cells of the fourfold pattern and the typical risk attitude in each.
questions.a: With a high probability of a gain (top left), people are risk averse and accept less than expected value for a sure gain, as Bernoulli described. With a high probability of a loss (top right), they are risk seeking and gamble to avoid a sure loss. With a low probability of a gain (bottom left), they are risk seeking and buy lottery tickets, and with a low probability of a loss (bottom right), they are risk averse and buy insurance.

questions.q: Put these steps in Kahneman and Tversky's discovery of risk seeking for losses in the order Kahneman describes them.
items: They expected risk aversion everywhere except for lotteries
They looked at their own choices for bad options
They realized they were as risk seeking for losses as risk averse for gains
They used their framework to identify two reasons for the effect
questions.explain: Their habit of thinking in terms of risk aversion was overturned when they examined bad options, and their framework then made the finding easy to interpret, a milestone in their thinking.

questions.section: Gambling in the Shadow of the Law
questions.q: Who does Kahneman credit with applying the fourfold pattern to plaintiffs and defendants negotiating a settlement in a civil suit?
options: Chris Guthrie
Maurice Allais
Jimmie Savage
Milton Friedman
questions.explain: Kahneman calls Chris Guthrie's application of the fourfold pattern to civil suits compelling. Allais, Savage and Friedman appear earlier in the chapter, at the Paris meeting.

questions.section: Gambling in the Shadow of the Law
questions.q: Which of these emotions does Kahneman say push a plaintiff with a strong case (95% chance to win) toward accepting a settlement?
options: The attraction of a sure and substantial gain
Fear of intense disappointment and regret if the case is lost
Hope of a large win against long odds
Repugnance at accepting a sure loss
questions.explain: Both emotions push the strong-case plaintiff toward caution. Hope against long odds fits the frivolous plaintiff, and repugnance at a sure loss fits the defendant with a weak case.

questions.section: Gambling in the Shadow of the Law
questions.q: Match each party in Kahneman's civil suit examples to the cell of the fourfold pattern it occupies.
pairs: Plaintiff with a strong case
Top left: likely gain, risk averse
Defendant with a weak case
Top right: likely loss, risk seeking
Plaintiff with a frivolous claim
Bottom left: unlikely gain, risk seeking
Defendant facing a frivolous claim
Bottom right: unlikely loss, risk averse
questions.explain: Strong cases put both parties in the top row; frivolous suits put them in the bottom row, where the roles reverse.

questions.section: Gambling in the Shadow of the Law
questions.q: In Kahneman's account of a strong case, who holds the stronger hand when a risk-averse plaintiff faces a risk-seeking defendant?
options: The plaintiff, so the defendant pays more than the expected outcome
The defendant, so the plaintiff settles for less than the expected outcome
Neither, so settlements match the expected outcome
The judge, who sets the settlement amount
questions.explain: The risk-seeking defendant is willing to fight on, so the cautious plaintiff should settle for less than the statistically expected outcome of the trial, a prediction confirmed by experiments and real negotiations.

questions.section: Gambling in the Shadow of the Law
questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says the prediction that strong-case plaintiffs settle for less than the expected outcome was confirmed by experiments with law students and judges and by analyses of actual negotiations.
questions.explain: The chapter reports confirmation from experiments with law students and practicing judges and from analyses of negotiations in the shadow of civil trials.

questions.section: Gambling in the Shadow of the Law
questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that plaintiffs with frivolous claims are likely to obtain a less generous settlement than the statistics of the situation justify.
questions.explain: Frivolous plaintiffs overweight their small chance and bargain boldly, while defendants buy insurance against a bad verdict, so such plaintiffs get a more generous settlement than the statistics justify.

questions.section: Gambling in the Shadow of the Law
questions.q: Which of these describe the defendant facing a frivolous lawsuit, according to Kahneman?
options: Faces a small risk of a very bad outcome
Treats settling as buying insurance against a bad verdict
Is likely to be risk averse
Is likely to be risk seeking
Holds the stronger bargaining hand
questions.explain: The frivolous suit is a nuisance with a small risk of a large loss, which is overweighted, so the defendant wants to be safe. Risk seeking and the stronger hand belong to the weak-case defendant in the top row.

questions.section: Gambling in the Shadow of the Law
questions.q: Kahneman calls a lawsuit in which a plaintiff with a flimsy case files a large claim that is most likely to fail ____ litigation.
questions.explain: In frivolous litigation the plaintiff holds a lottery ticket for a large prize, and the negotiation takes place in the bottom row of the fourfold pattern.

questions.section: Gambling in the Shadow of the Law
questions.q: In Kahneman's example, the City of New York faces 200 frivolous suits a year, each with a 5% chance of costing $1 million, and each could be settled for $100,000. What happens under each policy?
options: Litigating all costs about $20 million; settling all costs $10 million
Both policies cost about $10 million
Litigating all costs about $10 million; settling all costs $20 million
Litigating all costs about $1 million; settling all costs $2 million
questions.explain: Going to trial, the city loses about 10 cases at $1 million each, $10 million in all, while settling 200 cases at $100,000 costs $20 million. Paying a premium to avoid a small risk is costly in the long run.

questions.section: Gambling in the Shadow of the Law
questions.q: Put the steps of Kahneman's City of New York example in the order he presents them.
items: The city faces 200 frivolous suits a year, each with a 5% chance of costing $1 million
The city weighs a policy of settling every case against a policy of going to trial
Litigating all cases would lose about 10, costing $10 million
Settling every case for $100,000 would cost $20 million
Paying a premium to avoid a small risk of a large loss is costly in the long run
questions.explain: Kahneman sets up the many similar cases, compares the two policies, and draws the general lesson about systematic deviations from expected value.

questions.section: Gambling in the Shadow of the Law
questions.q: Why does Kahneman expect a defendant with a weak case to hold the stronger hand in negotiating with a plaintiff who has a strong case?
questions.a: The plaintiff, with a 95% chance to win, is in the top left cell: the attraction of a sure gain and fear of regret make him risk averse. The defendant faces a high probability of loss, the top right cell: the settlement is almost as painful as the worst outcome and there is still hope of winning, so he is risk seeking. A risk-seeking defendant facing a risk-averse plaintiff can hold out, so the plaintiff tends to settle for less than the statistically expected outcome.

questions.section: Gambling in the Shadow of the Law
questions.q: How does frivolous litigation reverse the positions of plaintiff and defendant compared with a strong case, according to Kahneman?
questions.a: In a frivolous suit the plaintiff has a small chance to win a very large amount, so the claim is like a lottery ticket and overweighting that chance makes him bold. The defendant faces a small risk of a very bad verdict, and overweighting it makes settlement feel like buying insurance. Now the plaintiff gambles and the defendant wants safety, so frivolous plaintiffs get more generous settlements than the statistics justify.

questions.section: Gambling in the Shadow of the Law
questions.q: What lesson does Kahneman draw from the City of New York example about the long-run cost of the choices in the fourfold pattern?
questions.a: Individual decisions in the fourfold pattern are not obviously unreasonable, but deviations from expected value add up. If the city settles all 200 frivolous suits it pays $20 million, compared with about $10 million if it litigates them all. Taking the long view of many similar decisions shows that systematic deviations from expected value, whether risk averse or risk seeking, are costly, and consistent overweighting of improbable outcomes leads to inferior outcomes.

questions.section: Gambling in the Shadow of the Law
questions.q: Using the fourfold pattern, sort these parties by whether they are likely to play safe or to gamble.
groups: Likely to play safe and settle
Likely to gamble or bargain aggressively

items.t: A plaintiff with a 95% chance of winning a large claim
A defendant whose trial is going badly
A plaintiff with a flimsy case and a huge claim
A company facing a frivolous suit with a small risk of a large verdict
A tenant offered $45,000 now on a near-certain $50,000 claim
A shop owner facing near-certain bankruptcy who bets everything on a risky expansion

questions.explain: People play safe with likely gains and unlikely losses, and gamble with likely losses and unlikely gains, whether in court or in everyday life.

questions.q: Match each person to the role Kahneman gives them in the chapter on the fourfold pattern.
pairs: Maurice Allais
Posed a puzzle at the 1952 Paris meeting showing a certainty effect
Von Neumann and Morgenstern
Derived the expectation principle from axioms of rational choice
Amos Tversky
Called rationalizers of utility violations lawyers for the misguided
Chris Guthrie
Applied the fourfold pattern to settlements in civil suits
questions.explain: These four figures trace the chapter's story, from the axiomatic theory and Allais's challenge to Tversky's impatience with rationalizers and Guthrie's legal application.

questions.q: Match each row of each cell in Kahneman's fourfold pattern figure to what it shows.
pairs: Top row
An illustrative prospect, such as a 95% chance to win $10,000
Second row
The focal emotion the prospect evokes
Third row
How most people choose between the gamble and its expected value for sure
Fourth row
Expected attitudes of a defendant and a plaintiff discussing a settlement
questions.explain: Kahneman explains that each cell lists a prospect, its focal emotion, the typical risk attitude, and the corresponding stance in civil litigation.

questions.q: Sort these claims by whether they belong to expected utility theory or to Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory.

items.t: Outcomes should be weighted strictly in proportion to probability
Its axioms define what a rational choice is
The Allais pattern of choices violates its rules
Decision weights are not identical to probabilities
People attach values to gains and losses rather than to wealth
It describes the choices people make, whether or not they are rational

questions.explain: Expected utility theory is a logic of rational choice built on the expectation principle; prospect theory is a psychological description built on reference-dependent values and decision weights.

questions.q: Match each remark from the chapter's closing examples to the idea it illustrates.
pairs: He is tempted to settle this frivolous claim to avoid a freak loss.
Overweighting of small probabilities
We never let our vacations hang on a last-minute deal.
Willingness to pay a lot for certainty
They will not cut their losses so long as there is a chance of breaking even.
Risk seeking in the losses
They know the risk of a gas explosion is minuscule, but they want it mitigated.
The possibility effect and peace of mind
questions.explain: Each closing remark applies one of the chapter's ideas: overweighting rare losses, the certainty effect, risk seeking for losses, and the possibility effect.

questions.q: Which of these closing remarks from the chapter on the fourfold pattern illustrate the overweighting of small probabilities?
options: Tempted to settle a frivolous claim to avoid a freak loss
Wanting a minuscule gas explosion risk mitigated
Refusing to cut losses while there is a chance of breaking even
Never letting vacations hang on a last-minute deal
questions.explain: Settling to avoid a freak loss and mitigating a minuscule explosion risk both overweight unlikely losses. Refusing to cut losses is risk seeking in losses, and the vacation remark is about paying for certainty.

questions.q: One closing remark says a person tempted to settle a frivolous claim to avoid a freak loss would be better off not yielding. Why, according to the chapter?
options: Frivolous claims never succeed in court
Settling would reveal he is risk seeking
The plaintiff is sure to drop the claim soon
He is likely to face many similar problems, and settling them all is costly in the long run
questions.explain: As in the City of New York example, someone facing many similar decisions does better by not paying a premium to avoid each small risk of a large loss.

questions.q: One closing remark describes people who will not cut their losses while there is a chance of breaking even as showing ____ in the losses.
questions.explain: Refusing a sure loss while any hope of breaking even remains is the top right cell of the fourfold pattern.

questions.q: Put these sections of the chapter on the fourfold pattern in the order they appear.
items: Changing Chances
Allais’s Paradox
Decision Weights
The Fourfold Pattern
Gambling in the Shadow of the Law
questions.explain: The chapter moves from why probabilities are not weighted linearly, to a historic challenge to expected utility, to measured decision weights, to the pattern itself and its legal application.

questions.q: Put these chapters of Part 4, “Choices,” in the order they appear in the book.
items: Prospect Theory
The Endowment Effect
Bad Events
The Fourfold Pattern
Rare Events
Risk Policies
questions.explain: The fourfold pattern comes after the chapters on prospect theory, the endowment effect and bad events, and just before Rare Events and Risk Policies.

questions.q: True or false: In the book's table of contents, the chapter on the fourfold pattern sits in Part 4, “Choices,” between “Bad Events” and “Rare Events.”
questions.explain: Chapter 28 is Bad Events, Chapter 29 is The Fourfold Pattern, and Chapter 30 is Rare Events, all within Part 4.

questions.q: Kahneman calls the fourfold pattern of preferences one of the core achievements of ____, the theory he and Tversky built.
questions.explain: The fourfold pattern combines prospect theory's two key ideas, valuing gains and losses and decision weights that differ from probabilities.

questions.q: Why does the chapter on the fourfold pattern begin by revisiting Bernoulli and the expectation principle?
options: To show that weighting outcomes by probability, kept since Bernoulli, misdescribes how people treat chances
To defend Bernoulli's theory against the criticisms of earlier chapters
To introduce loss aversion for the first time
To show that utility should be measured in final wealth
questions.explain: Earlier chapters criticized Bernoulli's view of values; this chapter turns to his other legacy, weighting by probability, and shows that real decision weights depart from it.

questions.q: The chapter after the fourfold pattern is titled “Rare Events.” Which idea from the chapter on the fourfold pattern does that title most directly pick up?
options: How plaintiffs and defendants bargain over settlements
How very unlikely events are sometimes ignored and sometimes heavily overweighted
How the expected value of a gamble is calculated
How Allais's audience reacted at the Paris meeting
questions.explain: The chapter flags very rare events as a special case, ignored or overweighted depending on attention, which is the natural topic for a chapter called Rare Events.

questions.q: How does the chapter on the fourfold pattern build on the earlier chapters of Part 4 and set up the chapter that follows it?
questions.a: Earlier chapters of Part 4 introduced prospect theory's idea that people value gains and losses rather than wealth, and examined losses and loss aversion. This chapter adds the second key idea, that decision weights differ from probabilities, and combines the two to produce the fourfold pattern. It ends by flagging very rare events as a special case, sometimes ignored and sometimes overweighted, which leads into the next chapter, Rare Events.

questions.q: What does the title “The Fourfold Pattern” signal about how the chapter organizes its argument?
questions.a: The title points to a two-by-two grid: outcomes are either gains or losses, and either highly probable or improbable. Each of the four cells shows a typical attitude to risk, risk averse for likely gains and unlikely losses and risk seeking for likely losses and unlikely gains. The sections leading up to it supply the ingredients, especially the possibility and certainty effects, and the legal section then applies the grid to civil suits.

questions.q: During the period of bus bombings in Israel, how did Kahneman's own behavior change while driving a rented car?
options: He disliked stopping next to a bus at a red light and drove away faster
He stopped renting cars and took taxis to avoid all public roads
He calculated the exact risk and found it large enough to justify caution
He felt no change at all, because he knew the risk was negligible
questions.explain: Kahneman was chagrined to find that he avoided stopping beside buses and pulled away quickly when the light changed, even though he knew the risk was negligible. His knowledge of the low risk did not prevent the behavior.

questions.q: In Kahneman's example of two cities warned about suicide bombers, one told of two bombers and one told of a single bomber, what point is he making?
options: Residents correctly feel twice as safe when the risk is halved
The emotion is insensitive to the exact level of probability
People ignore threats unless more than one attacker is reported
System 2 reliably corrects the fear once numbers are given
questions.explain: Although the risk in the second city is lower by half, residents would hardly feel much safer. Kahneman says the emotion is not only disproportionate to the probability but also insensitive to its exact level.

questions.q: Why did Kahneman avoid stopping next to buses in Israel even though he knew the risk was negligible?
questions.a: His avoidance was not driven by a rational concern for survival but by the experience of the moment: being next to a bus made him think of bombs, and those thoughts were unpleasant. He was avoiding buses because he wanted to think of something else. In effect he was assigning an inordinately high decision weight to a minuscule probability.

questions.q: How does Kahneman compare the psychology of buying a high-prize lottery ticket with the psychology of avoiding buses during a terrorism campaign?
questions.a: In both cases a vivid possibility is shared by the community and reinforced by conversation. Buying a ticket is immediately rewarded by pleasant fantasies, just as avoiding a bus is immediately rewarded by relief from fear. In both cases the actual probability is inconsequential and only possibility matters.

questions.q: Kahneman says terrorism is so effective because it induces an availability ____: a vivid image of death, reinforced by media attention and conversation, becomes highly accessible.
questions.explain: An availability cascade makes the image of death and damage highly accessible, especially when tied to a specific situation like the sight of a bus. The emotional arousal it produces is automatic and prompts protective action.

questions.q: Of both terrorism and high-prize lotteries, Kahneman says the actual probability is inconsequential; only ____ matters.
questions.explain: Kahneman writes that in both cases “the actual probability is inconsequential; only possibility matters.” The mere chance of the outcome drives the feeling, not its size.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says his avoidance of buses in Israel was motivated by a rational concern for survival.
questions.explain: He says the opposite: he was more likely to be hurt in a driving accident than by stopping near a bus, and his avoidance was driven by the unpleasant thoughts the bus evoked, not by rational concern for survival.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says the psychology of high-prize lotteries is similar to the psychology of terrorism.
questions.explain: Both involve a vivid possibility shared by the community and an immediate emotional reward, pleasant fantasies for the lottery and relief from fear for bus avoidance.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say influence fluency, availability and judgments of probability, and so account for our excessive response to the rare events we do not ignore?
options: Emotion
Vividness
Careful calculation of expected value
Loss aversion
Regression to the mean
questions.explain: Kahneman says his view of decision weights was shaped by research on the role of emotions and vividness, which influence fluency, availability and probability judgments. Expected-value calculation is what this overweighting departs from, not its cause.

questions.q: Put in order the steps by which Kahneman says terrorism produces protective behavior.
items: A vivid image of death and damage is reinforced by media and conversation
The image becomes highly accessible, linked to a situation such as a bus
Associative, automatic emotional arousal follows
An impulse for protective action arises
questions.explain: The availability cascade makes the image accessible; the emotional arousal it triggers is automatic and uncontrolled; and that arousal produces an impulse for protective action, which System 2 knowledge cannot switch off.

questions.q: Match each number to what it describes in Kahneman's account of bus bombings in Israel (December 2001 to September 2004).
pairs: Total number of bus bombings in the period
Total number of fatalities caused by the bombings
1.3 million
Approximate number of daily bus riders in Israel
questions.explain: These figures show that for any single traveler the risk was tiny, even though the public avoided buses as much as they could.

questions.q: Sort each feature into the case Kahneman links it to: terrorism (bus bombings) or high-prize lotteries.

items.t: Avoiding a bus is rewarded by relief from fear
Buying a ticket is rewarded by pleasant fantasies
A vivid image of death and damage
The thrilling possibility of winning the big prize
Scanning neighbors for packages or bulky clothes
Stores in New York City doing good business

questions.explain: Kahneman pairs the two cases because both run on vivid possibility and immediate emotional reward; one rewards avoidance with relief, the other rewards purchase with fantasy.

questions.q: Kahneman asks two questions: your judgment of the probability that the next US president will be a third-party candidate, and how much you would pay for a bet paying $1,000 if that happens. What does the second question ask you to do?
options: Estimate the probability of the event a second time, in dollars
Calculate the exact expected value of the bet before answering
Put a decision weight on the unlikely event by placing a bet on it
Imagine the event as impossible and price the bet at zero
questions.explain: The first question asks you to assess a probability; the second invites you to put a decision weight on the same event by betting on it. The two are related but distinct.

questions.q: When you think about the unlikely victory of a third-party candidate, why does Kahneman say you do not simply imagine the Fairy of the West installing a third-party president?
options: System 2 rejects every scenario that could make the event true
You retrieve evidence against the event rather than for it
Your mind assigns the event a probability of zero by default
Your biased search still looks for a plausible scenario
questions.explain: The associative system works in confirmatory mode, selectively retrieving evidence that would make the statement true. The process is biased, but it is not fantasy: it seeks a plausible scenario, and the ease with which one comes to mind sets the judgment.

questions.q: Asked the probability that a baby born in your local hospital will be released within three days, what does Kahneman say your mind most likely focuses on?
options: The medical problems that might keep the baby from going home
The baby going home on schedule, which is the event named
The exact national statistics on hospital stays
The cost of the hospital stay for the parents
questions.explain: When the target event is very likely, you focus on its alternative. The unusual event of a problem becomes focal, availability is evoked, and because you are in confirmatory mode your estimate of problems is probably too high.

questions.q: In Craig Fox's study, basketball fans estimated the probability that each of the eight playoff teams would win. What did their eight judgments add up to?
questions.explain: Each team in turn became the focal event, and confirmatory imagination built a victory for it, so the eight judgments summed to 240% rather than the logically required 100%.

questions.q: A friend planning to open a bakery can easily picture it thriving but has only a vague sense of the many ways it could fail. By Kahneman's account, what is the friend most likely to do?
options: Underestimate success, because failure is easier to imagine
Judge the odds correctly, because the plan is specific
Both overestimate the chance of success and overweight that estimate in deciding
Overestimate failure, because failures have many routes
questions.explain: Kahneman says successful execution of a plan is specific and easy to imagine, while failure is diffuse because there are innumerable ways for things to go wrong. Entrepreneurs are prone both to overestimate their chances and to overweight their estimates.

questions.q: Kahneman's first oversimplified answer is that people ____ the probabilities of unlikely events.
questions.explain: The two simple answers are that people overestimate the probabilities of unlikely events and overweight unlikely events in their decisions. The first concerns judgment, the second choice.

questions.q: Kahneman says your judgment of the probability of a third-party victory was ultimately determined by the cognitive ease, or ____, with which a plausible scenario came to mind.
questions.explain: Cognitive ease and fluency are the same idea here: the easier a plausible scenario is to construct, the higher the judged probability.

questions.q: Kahneman says the probability of a rare event is most likely to be overestimated when the alternative is not fully ____.
questions.explain: In Fox's study the focal team's victory was well defined, while the alternative, one of seven other teams winning, was diffuse and less evocative, so the focal event was overestimated.

questions.q: Which of these psychological mechanisms does Kahneman say are involved in both overestimation and overweighting of unlikely events?
options: Focused attention
Confirmation bias
Cognitive ease
Loss aversion
Regression to the mean
questions.explain: Kahneman says overestimation and overweighting are distinct phenomena but share the same mechanisms: focused attention, confirmation bias and cognitive ease. Loss aversion concerns the asymmetry of gains and losses, not rare events.

questions.q: Which of these did the basketball fans in Craig Fox's study do?
options: Overestimated the probability of whichever team they were asked about
Assigned cash equivalents to bets that summed to more than the payoff
Gave probabilities for the eight teams that summed to exactly 100%
Refused to bet on teams they considered weak
questions.explain: The fans both overestimated the probability of the focal teams and were much too willing to bet on them. Their eight probability judgments summed to 240%, not 100%.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says overestimation and overweighting of unlikely events are a single phenomenon with one name.
questions.explain: He says they are distinct phenomena, one about judging probability and one about weighting in decisions, although the same psychological mechanisms are involved in both.

questions.q: True or false: In Craig Fox's study, when the same fans judged whether the NBA winner would come from the Eastern or the Western conference, their two probabilities added up to 100%.
questions.explain: The absurd total disappeared in this question because the focal event and its alternative were equally specific.

questions.q: Put the steps of Craig Fox's basketball study, as Kahneman reports it, in order.
items: Fans estimate the chance that each of the eight teams will win
The eight probability judgments are found to add up to 240%
The same judges are asked whether the winner will be from the Eastern or Western conference
Those two judgments add up to 100%
questions.explain: The overestimation appears when each team in turn is focal against a diffuse alternative, and vanishes when the focal event and its alternative are equally specific.

questions.q: Match each figure from Craig Fox's betting task to what it represents.
pairs: The payoff for winning any one of the bets
The sum of cash equivalents for bets on all eight teams
The guaranteed loss for someone taking all eight bets
The sum of probability judgments for the eight teams
questions.explain: Fans knew there were only eight teams and that betting on all of them could not return more than $160, yet they valued the eight bets at $287, showing overweighting as well as overestimation.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning as Kahneman uses it in discussing unlikely events.
pairs: Overestimation
Judging the probability of an unlikely event as too high
Overweighting
Giving an unlikely event too much weight in a decision
Focal event
The event attention is drawn to and imagination tries to make true
Confirmatory mode
Selectively retrieving evidence and images that make a statement true
questions.explain: Overestimation is about judgment and overweighting about choice; both grow when an event becomes focal and memory works in confirmatory mode.

questions.q: Sort each event into whether it is the specific, easy-to-imagine focal event or the diffuse alternative, as Kahneman describes them.

items.t: The Chicago Bulls win the playoffs
One of the other seven teams wins
A project is carried out successfully as planned
One of the innumerable ways a project could go wrong
The Lakers win the tournament
Some team other than the Lakers wins

questions.explain: A focal event is well defined and easy to construct; its alternative is diffuse and less evocative, which is why the focal event's probability is overestimated.

questions.q: Sort each task into whether it asks for a judgment of probability or a decision weight.

items.t: Estimating the chance that a third-party candidate wins the presidency
Saying how much you would pay for a $1,000 bet on a third-party win
Fans estimating each team's chance of winning the playoffs
Fans stating a cash equivalent for a bet paying $160
Estimating the chance a newborn is released within three days

questions.explain: Judging how likely an event is differs from betting on it; the second assigns a decision weight. Fox studied both and found errors in each.

questions.q: Why did the probability judgments of Craig Fox's basketball fans for the eight teams add up to far more than 100%?
questions.a: Each team in turn became the focal event, and the fan's memory and imagination, working in confirmatory mode, tried to construct a victory for that team. The alternative, one of the other seven teams winning, was diffuse and less evocative. Since all eight teams were very good, it was possible to imagine any of them winning, so each was overestimated and the total reached 240%.

questions.q: How does Kahneman say the findings on overestimation and overweighting shed light on the planning fallacy and optimism?
questions.a: The successful execution of a plan is specific and easy to imagine, while failure is diffuse because there are innumerable ways for things to go wrong. Success therefore becomes the focal event and is overestimated. Entrepreneurs and their investors are prone both to overestimate their chances and to overweight their estimates.

questions.q: Using the third-party presidential candidate example, explain the difference between overestimating an unlikely event and overweighting it.
questions.a: Overestimating is a judgment error: answering the question about the probability that a third-party candidate wins with a number that is too high. Overweighting is a decision error: paying too much for a bet that returns $1,000 if that candidate wins, giving the event too large a decision weight. The two are distinct but driven by the same mechanisms of focused attention, confirmation bias and cognitive ease.

questions.q: What did the University of Chicago article "Money, Kisses, and Electric Shocks" find about the valuation of gambles?
options: It was more sensitive to probability when the outcomes were emotional
It was equally sensitive to probability for cash and emotional outcomes
It depended only on the size of the cash prize, not on probability
It was much less sensitive to probability when the outcomes were emotional
questions.explain: Gambles on outcomes such as kissing a favorite movie star or a painful shock were valued with much less regard to probability than gambles on cash. The tempting reverse reading gets the direction of the effect wrong.

questions.q: What did the Princeton team argue about the low sensitivity to probability found for emotional outcomes?
options: It is normal, and gambles on money are the exception because they have a definite expected value
It is caused by the intensity of emotion the outcomes evoke
It disappears once people are told the outcomes are fictitious
It shows that people cannot perceive probabilities above 50%
questions.explain: The Princeton team challenged the Chicago conclusion that affect-laden imagery was the cause. They said sensitivity is relatively high only for money gambles, which have a definite expected value.

questions.q: Why is it easier to name a cash equivalent for an 84% chance to win $59 than for an 84% chance to receive a dozen red roses in a glass vase?
options: Roses provoke strong emotions that block any thought about value
The quick sense that the money bet is worth about $50 gives a helpful anchor
People compute the exact expected value of money bets to the cent
Most people have no idea that roses can be bought for money
questions.explain: You do not compute the exact expected value ($49.56), but a vague estimate near $50 anchors your search for an equally attractive cash amount. No such anchor exists for the roses.

questions.q: The Princeton team compared willingness to pay to avoid a chance of painting someone's three-bedroom apartment with a chance of cleaning three dormitory bathroom stalls after a weekend of use. What did they find?
options: The more disgusting chore received far greater decision weight
People were more sensitive to probability for the bathroom chore
The decision weights for the two outcomes did not differ
Neither chore produced any willingness to pay to avoid it
questions.explain: The bathroom chore is surely more emotional, yet the decision weights were the same. Kahneman concludes that the intensity of emotion is not what makes people insensitive to probability.

questions.q: Kahneman predicts that a 21% (or 84%) chance to receive a large blue cardboard envelope containing $59 next Monday morning will be evaluated differently from a plain chance to receive $59. What is his prediction?
options: There will be more sensitivity to probability for the blue envelope
The envelope will be valued at less than $59 at any probability
The two will be valued identically, since the money is the same
There will be less sensitivity to probability for the blue envelope
questions.explain: His hypothesis is that adding irrelevant but vivid details disrupts calculation. The envelope evokes a richer, more fluent representation than an abstract sum, which reduces the role of probability.

questions.q: In an experiment Kahneman cites, the decision weight was 71.2 for a 90% chance and 18.6 for a 10% chance; the ratio of weights was only 3.83 instead of 9.0, showing insufficient ____ to probability.
questions.explain: In utility theory the weights would equal the probabilities, so the ratio would be 9. In prospect theory, variations of probability have less effect on decision weights.

questions.q: The Chicago team proposed that affect-laden ____ overwhelmed the response to probability.
questions.explain: The Chicago team explained the insensitivity to probability by “affect-laden imagery.” The Princeton team later challenged this conclusion.

questions.q: Kahneman says cognitive ease contributes to the ____ effect as well: when you hold a vivid image of an event, the possibility of its not occurring is also represented vividly and overweighted.
questions.explain: A vivid outcome enhances both the possibility effect and the certainty effect, leaving little room for decision weights to change between chances of 21% and 84%.

questions.q: Which of these findings does Kahneman cite as evidence that insensitivity to probability is not caused by the intensity of emotion?
options: Decision weights did not differ between painting an apartment and cleaning dirty bathroom stalls
Adding the price of the roses ($59) did not make evaluations sensitive to probability
Fear of an impending electric shock was essentially uncorrelated with its probability
Gambles on kissing a movie star were less sensitive to probability than cash gambles
questions.explain: The chores comparison and the roses-with-price result undercut the emotion explanation. The shock and kisses findings were the original evidence that seemed to point toward emotion as the cause.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that in both utility theory and prospect theory, decision weights depend only on probability, not on the outcome.
questions.explain: Both theories predict that the decision weight for a 90% chance is the same for winning $100, receiving roses or getting a shock. Kahneman says this prediction turns out to be wrong.

questions.q: True or false: Researchers using physiological measures such as heart rate found that fear of an impending electric shock rose steadily with the probability of receiving it.
questions.explain: They found the fear was essentially uncorrelated with the probability; the mere possibility of a shock triggered the full-blown fear response.

questions.q: Put in order the steps of Kahneman's argument about vivid outcomes.
items: The Chicago team finds emotional outcomes insensitive to probability
The Princeton team argues that money gambles are the exception
The chores comparison shows emotional intensity is not the answer
Stating the roses' cash value fails to restore sensitivity to probability
Kahneman concludes that a vivid representation of the outcome reduces the role of probability
questions.explain: The argument moves from an emotion explanation, through the Princeton challenge and two experiments that rule out emotion, to Kahneman's own vividness hypothesis.

questions.q: Match each source to the view of probability and decision weights it holds in Kahneman's account.
pairs: Utility theory
Decision weights are the same as probabilities
The Chicago team
Affect-laden imagery overwhelms the response to probability
The Princeton team
Money gambles are the exception because they have a definite expected value
Kahneman
A rich, vivid representation of the outcome reduces the role of probability
questions.explain: Each view revises the one before: utility theory equates weight and probability, the Chicago team blames emotion, the Princeton team points to expected value, and Kahneman points to vividness.

questions.q: Sort each gamble by whether the evidence or prediction Kahneman describes makes its valuation relatively sensitive or relatively insensitive to probability.

items.t: 84% or 21% chance to win $59
84% or 21% chance to receive a dozen red roses
Chance to win roses with their value of $59 stated
Chance of a painful but not dangerous electric shock
Chance to receive a blue cardboard envelope containing $59
Chance to receive $59 next Monday

questions.explain: Plain cash gambles have a definite expected value and stay relatively sensitive to probability. Vivid outcomes, emotional or not, reduce that sensitivity, even when a price is attached.

questions.q: According to the Princeton team, why are gambles on money relatively sensitive to probability while gambles on other outcomes are not?
questions.a: Money gambles have a definite expected value, so even a vague estimate of it provides an anchor for finding an equally attractive cash amount. For an 84% chance to win $59 you quickly sense the bet is worth about $50. No such anchor exists for outcomes like roses, so those evaluations are harder and less sensitive to probability.

questions.q: What story does Kahneman think is told by the finding that stating the roses' value ($59) did not make evaluations sensitive to probability?
questions.a: He believes that a rich and vivid representation of the outcome, whether or not it is emotional, reduces the role of probability in evaluating an uncertain prospect. People who thought of the prize as roses did not use the price as an anchor. This led him to predict that adding irrelevant but vivid details even to a money outcome would disrupt calculation.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say that a vivid outcome leaves little room for decision weights to change between chances of 21% and 84%?
questions.a: A vivid image of the outcome exists in your mind even if you know its probability is low, which enhances the possibility effect. At the same time the possibility of its not occurring is also represented vividly and overweighted, which enhances the certainty effect. The combination of the two flattens decision weights across the middle range of probabilities.

questions.q: Urn A contains 10 marbles, 1 of them red; urn B contains 100 marbles, 8 of them red; red wins a prize. What does Kahneman report about students' choices?
options: About 30% to 40% choose urn B, which has more winning marbles but a lower chance
Nearly all students choose urn A, which gives the better chance
About 30% to 40% choose urn A, the urn with fewer marbles in total
Most students say the two urns offer exactly the same chance
questions.explain: Urn A gives a 10% chance and urn B 8%, yet a sizable minority choose B because it has more winning marbles. Seymour Epstein saw this as the superficial processing of System 1.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say that "One of 100,000 vaccinated children will be permanently disabled" affects the mind differently from "a 0.001% risk of permanent disability"?
options: It states a larger risk than the percentage version does
It calls up the image of an individual disabled child while the others fade into the background
It is harder to understand, so people distrust the vaccine
It invites people to calculate the risk more carefully
questions.explain: The two statements describe the same risk. The frequency version evokes one disabled child, and the 99,999 safely vaccinated children fade away, which is why low probabilities weigh more in frequency formats.

questions.q: People judged "a disease that kills 1,286 people out of every 10,000" as more dangerous than "a disease that kills 24.14% of the population." What makes this result striking?
options: The two diseases have exactly the same risk
The first disease's risk is about twice as large as the second's
The first disease's risk is only about half as large as the second's
Participants saw both descriptions side by side
questions.explain: 1,286 out of 10,000 is about 12.9%, roughly half of 24.14%, yet the frequency format made it seem more threatening. Participants saw only one formulation, as in most of life.

questions.q: Forensic psychologists and psychiatrists decided whether to discharge Mr. Jones, a patient with a history of violence, given an expert risk assessment in one of two formats. What happened?
options: Those given the probability format were almost twice as likely to deny discharge
Experienced professionals were unaffected by the format
Both groups denied discharge at about the same rate of 41%
Those given the frequency format were almost twice as likely to deny discharge
questions.explain: With the frequency format (10 of every 100 similar patients) the professionals denied discharge 41% of the time, compared to 21% with the probability format. The more vivid description produced a higher decision weight for the same probability.

questions.q: A city council member wants residents to take a rare but serious flood risk more seriously. Following Kahneman's account of format effects, which wording would most raise its weight?
options: "In a typical year, 1 of every 2,000 homes here will be flooded"
"The annual flood probability per home is 0.05%"
"The flood risk here is statistically negligible"
"The likelihood of flooding is about five hundredths of a percent"
questions.explain: Low-probability events are weighted much more heavily when stated as relative frequencies (how many) than as abstract chances or probabilities (how likely), because a frequency brings to mind an individual case.

questions.q: Following Paul Slovic, Kahneman calls the bias in which people choose the urn with more winning marbles rather than the better chance denominator ____.
questions.explain: If your attention is drawn to the winning marbles, you do not assess the nonwinning marbles with the same care. That is denominator neglect.

questions.q: Seymour Epstein, who argued that the urn results show superficial processing, calls System 1 the ____ system.
questions.explain: Epstein's experiential system corresponds to Kahneman's System 1, whose superficial processing leads many to pick the urn with more winners.

questions.q: Kahneman notes that the format effect would shrink if people compared two formulations directly, but life is usually a ____ experiment, in which you see only one formulation at a time.
questions.explain: Direct comparison calls for System 2. In real life you see one version, and it would take an exceptionally active System 2 to generate alternative formulations and notice they feel different.

questions.q: Which of these statements about the study of the disease that "kills 1,286 people out of every 10,000" are correct according to Kahneman?
options: It was judged more dangerous than a disease that kills 24.14% of the population
Its risk is only about half as large as 24.14%
It was judged more dangerous than a disease that kills 24.4 out of 100
Participants compared both formulations side by side before answering
The effect disappeared when the numbers were stated as percentages
questions.explain: All three comparisons show denominator neglect in frequency formats. The study did not use a direct comparison; Kahneman says such a comparison, which calls on System 2, would probably reduce the effect.

questions.q: Which of these reasons does Kahneman give for low-probability events weighing more when stated as frequencies?
options: The frequency calls up the image of an individual case
System 1 is much better at dealing with individuals than categories
Frequencies are more precise than percentages
People find it easier to compute expected values from frequencies
questions.explain: A frequency such as one child in 100,000 brings up one vivid individual while the rest fade, and System 1 deals better with individuals than categories. The point is vividness, not precision or calculation.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says low-probability events are weighted much more heavily when stated as "chances," "risk" or "probability" than when described as relative frequencies.
questions.explain: He says the reverse: low-probability events weigh much more when described as relative frequencies (how many) than in abstract terms of how likely.

questions.q: True or false: In the Mr. Jones discharge experiment, professionals who saw the risk stated as a frequency (10 of every 100 similar patients) were almost twice as likely to deny discharge as those who saw it stated as a 10% probability.
questions.explain: They denied discharge 41% of the time compared to 21% in the probability format, showing that experienced professionals are not immune to format.

questions.q: Put these three disease descriptions from Kahneman's account in order of their actual risk, from lowest to highest.
items: Kills 1,286 people out of every 10,000
Kills 24.14% of the population
Kills 24.4 out of 100
questions.explain: 1,286 out of 10,000 is about 12.9%, the smallest risk, yet it was judged more dangerous than either of the others, which is denominator neglect at work.

questions.q: Match each abstract statement of risk to its frequency version from Kahneman's examples.
pairs: A 0.001% risk of permanent disability from a vaccine
One of 100,000 vaccinated children will be permanently disabled
A 10% probability that patients like Mr. Jones commit violence
Of every 100 patients like Mr. Jones, 10 commit violence
A 0.1% chance of a false DNA match
A false match occurs in 1 of 1,000 capital cases
questions.explain: Each pair states the same risk, but the frequency version evokes an individual case and so receives a higher decision weight.

questions.q: Match each person to their role in Kahneman's discussion of vivid probabilities.
pairs: Seymour Epstein
Saw the urn choices as superficial processing by the experiential system
Paul Slovic
Gave the bias its name and showed how advocates exploit risk formats
A defense attorney
Prefers 1 of 1,000 cases to cast doubt on DNA evidence
A prosecutor
Prefers the abstract frame, hoping to fill jurors' minds with decimals
questions.explain: Epstein interpreted the urn results, Slovic named denominator neglect and documented manipulation, and the courtroom example shows each side choosing the format that serves it.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it uses a frequency format or an abstract probability format.

items.t: One of 100,000 vaccinated children will be permanently disabled
A vaccine carries a 0.001% risk of permanent disability
Of every 100 patients similar to Mr. Jones, 10 commit violence
Patients similar to Mr. Jones have a 10% probability of violence
A false match occurs in 1 of 1,000 capital cases
The chance of a false match is 0.1%

questions.explain: Frequency formats say how many out of how many and evoke individual cases; abstract formats speak of chances, risk or probability and weigh less.

questions.q: Sort each description into the urn it applies to in the marble experiment Kahneman describes.

items.t: Gives a 10% chance of winning
Gives an 8% chance of winning
Offers the better chance of winning
Contains the larger number of winning marbles
Chosen by 30% to 40% of students despite worse odds
Pictured by Kahneman as a single red marble on a vague white background

questions.explain: Urn A is the better choice, but urn B's eight vivid winning marbles create a more hopeful feeling and attract many students.

questions.q: How does vivid imagery contribute to denominator neglect in the two-urn experiment, as Kahneman experiences it?
questions.a: When he thinks of the small urn he sees a single red marble on a vaguely defined background of white marbles; for the large urn he sees eight winning red marbles on an indistinct background, which feels more hopeful. The distinctive vividness of the winning marbles increases the decision weight of winning and enhances the possibility effect. Attention to the winners means the nonwinning marbles are not assessed with the same care.

questions.q: How would a defense attorney and a prosecutor each present the risk of a false DNA match, according to Kahneman, and why?
questions.a: A good defense attorney says that a false match occurs in 1 of 1,000 capital cases rather than that the chance is 0.1%. This invites jurors to imagine the man before them being wrongly convicted because of flawed DNA evidence, so it more easily passes the threshold of reasonable doubt. The prosecutor favors the abstract frame, hoping to fill the jurors' minds with decimal points.

questions.q: What does the example of advocates describing homicides by seriously mentally ill people show about the format of risk information?
questions.a: The same fact can be stated as about 1,000 homicides a year, as 1,000 out of 273,000,000 Americans, as an annual likelihood of about 0.00036%, or in comparison with deaths from suicide and laryngeal cancer. Each format produces a different feeling of danger. Slovic notes that the advocates chose the frightening format openly, hoping fear would bring more funding for mental health services, which shows the power of format creates opportunities for manipulation.

questions.q: In experiments on choice from experience, where participants learn the outcomes of two buttons over many trials, what happens to rare outcomes?
options: Rare outcomes are overweighted, just as in choice from description
Overweighting is never observed, and underweighting is common
Rare outcomes are weighted exactly by their probabilities
Rare outcomes are overweighted only when they are losses
questions.explain: Choice from description yields the possibility effect predicted by prospect theory, but in sharp contrast choice from experience never shows overweighting, and underweighting is common.

questions.q: What does Kahneman say there is general agreement on as one major cause of the underweighting of rare events?
options: People experience the rare event too often to notice it
Rare events are always described in abstract percentages
Many people never experience the rare event at all
People are unable to remember any event older than a year
questions.explain: Most Californians have never experienced a major earthquake, and in 2007 no banker had personally experienced a devastating financial crisis. Without experience of the event, it receives less weight than it deserves.

questions.q: Ralph Hertwig and Ido Erev say that chances of rare events receive less impact than they deserve. What example do they point to?
options: The public's panic over bus bombings in Israel
The overpricing of lottery tickets in New York City
The basketball fans' bets on all eight teams
The public's tepid response to long-term environmental threats
questions.explain: Hertwig and Erev point to the tepid response to long-term environmental threats as an example of neglect. The bus bombings and lotteries illustrate overweighting, the opposite error.

questions.q: Adele is consistently fairly helpful; Brian is usually a bit less helpful but has occasionally been extremely generous. Which colleague does Kahneman think you will approach with a complicated question, and why?
options: Adele, because your global impression of each is biased toward typical and recent instances
Brian, because the rare generous episode is overweighted by a possibility effect
Brian, because System 1 always seeks the highest possible payoff
Adele, because System 2 calculates that her expected help is larger
questions.explain: Kahneman finds the global-impression view far more plausible in a two-system mind. Unless Brian's rare generosity comes to mind explicitly, it will not be overweighted, so the pooled impression favors Adele.

questions.q: Two coffee shops are near your office. One is reliably decent; the other is usually a little worse but now and then makes a superb cup. With no particular episode in mind, which does Kahneman's account predict you will tend to choose?
options: The other shop, since the rare superb cup is overweighted
The reliably decent shop, since rare superb cups are pooled into a typical impression
Whichever shop has the higher calculated expected quality
Each shop equally often, since the expected values match
questions.explain: Like the restaurant and the Adele and Brian examples, repeated experience forms a global impression biased toward typical instances. A rare event is overweighted only if it comes to mind explicitly.

questions.q: Kahneman contrasts choices from description, analyzed in prospect theory, with choices from ____, in which people learn outcomes by observing many trials.
questions.explain: In choice from experience a participant sees the consequences of pressing each button over many trials; in choice from description she reads a verbal statement such as “5% to win $12.”

questions.q: Kahneman says that as the two buttons in a choice-from-experience experiment generate outcomes over time, they develop integrated "____" to which emotional responses are attached.
questions.explain: Like Adele and Brian, the buttons come to have global representations, and the choice compares the approach or avoid tendencies attached to them rather than weighting each outcome.

questions.q: Kahneman concludes that a rare event is overweighted if it specifically attracts attention, and when there is no overweighting, there will be ____.
questions.explain: Rare events tend to be either overweighted or neglected; Kahneman writes that “when there is no overweighting, there will be neglect.”

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say enhance the salience of an unlikely event?
options: The mere mention of the event
The event's vividness
The format in which its probability is described
Having observed many trials in which it did not occur
A larger expected value
questions.explain: Salience is enhanced by mere mention, vividness and probability format. Repeated experience without the event tends to produce underweighting instead.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman list as contributing to the overweighting of rare events?
options: Vivid images, such as the roses
Concrete representations, such as 1 of 1,000
Explicit reminders, as in choice from description
Repeated experience in which the event never occurs
Abstract statements of probability in decimals
questions.explain: Kahneman lists obsessive concerns, vivid images, concrete representations and explicit reminders. Experience without the event and abstract decimals lead toward neglect rather than overweighting.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says the bias toward overestimating and overweighting salient events is an absolute rule with no exceptions.
questions.explain: He says it is not an absolute rule, though it is large and robust. Exceptions include an erroneous theory that makes an event seem impossible and an inability to imagine how an outcome could come about.

questions.q: Put in order the steps of a typical choice-from-experience experiment as Kahneman describes it.
items: The participant faces two buttons, each paying a reward or nothing at random
She presses the buttons over many trials and observes the outcomes
On the critical trial she chooses one of the two buttons
She earns the outcome produced on that trial
questions.explain: The participant learns the buttons' outcomes through experience rather than description, and only the critical trial counts for her earnings.

questions.q: Put in order Kahneman's account of how System 1 decides which colleague, Adele or Brian, to approach.
items: Good and bad experiences with each colleague are pooled
System 1 forms a global representation of each, with an emotional attitude
The tendencies to approach or avoid each colleague are compared
You knock on the door of the colleague with the more favorable impression
questions.explain: Kahneman says nothing beyond a comparison of the approach and avoid tendencies is needed to decide; the rare event is not weighted separately unless it comes to mind explicitly.

questions.q: Match each example to the point it illustrates in Kahneman's discussion of choice from experience.
pairs: Most Californians
Have never experienced a major earthquake
Bankers in 2007
Had never personally experienced a devastating financial crisis
A usually good restaurant
Variable outcomes from the same source, occasionally brilliant or awful
Hertwig and Erev
Note that rare events such as housing bubbles bursting receive too little impact
questions.explain: These examples show that underweighting of rare events in real life often arises because people have never experienced the rare event.

questions.q: Match each factor that contributes to overweighting with the example Kahneman pairs it with in his conclusion.
pairs: Obsessive concerns
The bus in Jerusalem
Vivid images
The roses
Concrete representations
Explicit reminders
Choice from description
questions.explain: Kahneman's conclusion gathers the chapter's cases: each factor draws separate attention to the rare event and so raises its decision weight.

questions.q: Sort each feature into choice from description or choice from experience.

items.t: Reading a verbal statement such as "5% to win $12" before choosing
Pressing buttons over many trials and observing the outcomes
Rare outcomes are overweighted relative to their probability
Underweighting of rare outcomes is common
The prospects are analyzed in prospect theory
Many participants never see the rare outcome

questions.explain: Description draws explicit attention to each outcome and produces the possibility effect; experience pools outcomes into an impression, and rare events are often never seen.

questions.q: Describe Kahneman's two possible views of the choice between asking Adele or Brian for help, and explain which he finds more plausible.
questions.a: One view treats it as a choice between two gambles: Adele is closer to a sure thing, while Brian offers a low probability of a very good outcome, which a possibility effect would overweight, favoring Brian.
