The other view treats it as a choice between global impressions, in which good and bad experiences are pooled and biased toward typical and recent instances, favoring Adele. In a two-system mind the second is far more plausible, since System 1 forms global representations with approach or avoid tendencies, and the rare event is not overweighted unless it comes to mind explicitly.

questions.q: What exceptions does Kahneman acknowledge to the rule that focusing on an event raises its judged probability and weight?
questions.a: Focusing on an event does not raise its probability when an erroneous theory makes the event appear impossible even when you think about it. It also fails when an inability to imagine how an outcome might come about leaves you convinced it will not happen. Kahneman says the bias toward overestimating and overweighting salient events is not absolute, but it is large and robust.

questions.q: Why is a rare event almost guaranteed to be overweighted when prospects are described explicitly, as in "99% chance to win $1,000, and 1% chance to win nothing"?
questions.a: A rare event is overweighted if it specifically attracts attention, and an explicit description effectively guarantees it separate attention. The rare outcome is named on its own, so it cannot be pooled into a global impression as happens in choice from experience. This is why choice from description shows a possibility effect while choice from experience does not.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say his conclusions about rare probabilities are not good news for the residents of our planet?
questions.a: When it comes to rare probabilities, the mind is not designed to get things quite right: rare events are either overweighted when they attract attention or neglected when they do not. Events that no one has yet experienced receive no vivid image or explicit reminder, so they tend to be neglected. A planet that may be exposed to such unprecedented events is therefore poorly protected by our intuitions.

questions.q: Someone says: "We shouldn't focus on a single scenario, or we will overestimate its probability. Let's set up specific alternatives and make the probabilities add up to 100%." Which finding is this advice drawing on?
options: The finding that money gambles have a definite expected value
The finding that experienced professionals are swayed by risk format
Fox's finding that judgments summed to 100% when the alternatives were equally specific
The finding that people never overweight rare events from experience
questions.explain: In Fox's study, judging each team against a diffuse alternative inflated the total to 240%, while equally specific alternatives (East versus West) produced judgments that added up to 100%.

questions.q: True or false: In one of Kahneman's sample remarks, someone says that describing a risk as "1 death per 1,000" counts on denominator neglect to make people worry.
questions.explain: The frequency format evokes an individual death and makes the risk feel larger, which is what those who want people worried are counting on.

questions.q: Put in order the stages of what Kahneman's sample remark calls "the familiar disaster cycle."
items: Exaggeration
Overweighting
Neglect
questions.explain: The remark reads “Begin by exaggeration and overweighting, then neglect sets in.” A vivid disaster is first overestimated and overweighted, then forgotten.

questions.q: Chapter 30, "Rare Events," follows "The Fourfold Pattern." How does it build on that chapter?
options: It abandons decision weights and returns to Bernoulli's utility theory
It introduces the two selves that experience and remember outcomes
It drops probability to focus on the endowment effect for goods
It explains when and why unlikely events are overweighted or ignored, refining decision weights
questions.explain: The fourfold pattern rests on the overweighting of unlikely outcomes. This chapter asks what psychological mechanisms produce that overweighting and under what conditions rare events are neglected instead.

questions.q: Kahneman explains the fear of buses in Israel as an availability cascade. Which earlier part of the book does this connect the chapter to?
options: Part II, Heuristics and Biases, including "Availability, Emotion, and Risk"
Part III, Overconfidence, including "The Engine of Capitalism"
Part V, Two Selves, which comes after the Choices chapters
Part IV's "Keeping Score," which comes after this chapter
questions.explain: The availability heuristic and availability cascades belong to Part II. Chapter 30 brings these System 1 mechanisms into the Part IV discussion of choices and decision weights.

questions.q: How does Chapter 30 refine the original formulation of prospect theory?
questions.a: The original prospect theory argued that highly unlikely events are either ignored or overweighted, but it did not specify when each happens or offer a psychological interpretation. Chapter 30 supplies both, drawing on research on emotion and vividness: rare events are overweighted when they specifically attract attention through vivid images, concrete frequencies, obsessive concerns or explicit description. When they do not, as often in choice from experience, they are neglected.

questions.q: Why does a chapter on rare events belong in Part IV, "Choices," rather than only among the heuristics of Part II?
questions.a: The chapter is about decision weights, the way probabilities are translated into weights in risky choices, which is the core of prospect theory in Part IV. It uses System 1 mechanisms from Part II, such as availability, cognitive ease and confirmation bias, but applies them to explain overweighting in bets, gambles and real decisions. It thus connects judgment of probabilities to how we actually choose.

questions.q: Chapter 30, "Rare Events," belongs to Part IV of the book, whose title is ____.
questions.explain: Part IV, Choices, runs from Bernoulli's Errors through Frames and Reality and develops prospect theory and its consequences for decisions.

questions.q: Which of these ideas from earlier in the book does Chapter 30 draw on?
options: The planning fallacy and optimism
The availability heuristic
The possibility and certainty effects
The peak-end rule for remembered experiences
The two selves of experience and memory
questions.explain: The chapter links focal-event overestimation to the planning fallacy, uses availability to explain scenario-based judgments, and speaks of enhanced possibility and certainty effects. The two selves belong to Part V, which comes later.

questions.q: Which of these chapters belong to Part IV, "Choices," alongside "Rare Events"?
options: Prospect Theory
Bad Events
Risk Policies
The Outside View
Availability, Emotion, and Risk
questions.explain: Prospect Theory, Bad Events and Risk Policies are in Part IV. The Outside View is in Part III, Overconfidence, and Availability, Emotion, and Risk is in Part II, Heuristics and Biases.

questions.q: Put these chapters of Part IV in the order they appear in the book.
items: Prospect Theory
The Endowment Effect
Bad Events
The Fourfold Pattern
Rare Events
Risk Policies
questions.explain: Rare Events comes right after The Fourfold Pattern, which it refines, and right before Risk Policies, which turns to how to handle risky choices more broadly.

questions.q: In the paired decisions that open the Risk Policies chapter (sure gain of $240 vs a 25% chance of $1,000; sure loss of $750 vs a 75% chance of losing $1,000), which combination did 73% of respondents choose?
options: The sure gain and the gamble for losses (A and D)
The gamble for gains and the sure loss (B and C)
The sure gain and the sure loss (A and C)
Both gambles (B and D)
questions.explain: People were risk averse for gains, taking the sure $240, and risk seeking for losses, taking the gamble over the sure $750 loss. Only 3% chose the combination of the gamble for gains and the sure loss, which later turns out to be the better package.

questions.q: True or false: In Kahneman and Tversky's original study of the paired decisions, the combination of options that dominates the others was chosen by only 3% of respondents.
questions.explain: The dominant option BC is the combination of the two options most people rejected, and only 3% favored it, while 73% preferred the inferior combination AD.

questions.q: When one option is unequivocally better than another, as option BC is better than option AD in the paired-decisions problem, Kahneman says that BC ____ AD.
questions.explain: Kahneman calls this dominance, “the technical term for one option being unequivocally better than another.”

questions.q: In the paired-decisions problem, why did most respondents fail to notice that their two choices added up to an inferior package?
options: They believed the two decisions would never be paid out together
They never worked out the four combinations, which would have taken laborious paper-and-pencil work
They computed the combinations but misjudged the probabilities
They were told to treat each decision as the only one they would ever make
questions.explain: Each separate preference felt intuitively compelling, and combining the two problems is a laborious exercise, so people simply did not do it. They were in fact asked to examine both options before choosing, not to treat each in isolation.

questions.q: In the paired-decisions problem that opens the Risk Policies chapter, what role does System 1 play in people's choices?
questions.a: System 1 produces an immediate emotional evaluation: attraction to the sure gain and aversion to the sure loss. This reaction comes before the effortful and optional System 2 computation of the gambles' expected values. Most people's choices follow these System 1 predilections, so they take the sure gain and gamble to avoid the sure loss.

questions.q: Match each option in the paired-decisions problem to its expected value as given in the Risk Policies chapter.
pairs: Gamble B: 25% chance to gain $1,000
Gain of $250
Gamble D: 75% chance to lose $1,000
Loss of $750
Combined option AD
Combined option BC
questions.explain: Gamble B is worth $250 on average and gamble D a loss of $750. Combining the choices most people made (A and D) gives a package that is worse in every outcome than combining the rejected choices (B and C).

questions.q: Put the steps of the paired-decisions demonstration in the Risk Policies chapter in the order Kahneman presents them.
items: Make separate choices in decision i and decision ii
Note that most people pick the sure gain and the gamble for losses
Face a single choice between combined options AD and BC
Recognize that BC dominates AD
Realize BC combines the two options most people rejected
questions.explain: Kahneman first has the reader make the two choices separately, then presents the combined problem, which is easy, and finally reveals that the obvious winner is the combination most people had turned down.

questions.q: Sort each choice or attitude from the Risk Policies chapter by whether it is risk averse or risk seeking.

items.t: Taking a sure gain of $240 over a 25% chance of $1,000
Taking a 75% chance to lose $1,000 over a sure loss of $750
Paying a premium to obtain a sure gain rather than face a gamble
Paying a premium in expected value to avoid a sure loss
Division managers refusing an equal chance to lose capital or earn double
Gambling in the domain of losses

questions.explain: Kahneman notes people tend to be risk averse in the domain of gains and risk seeking in the domain of losses, and that holding both attitudes at once is costly.

questions.q: Treating decisions i and ii as a sequence of two simple decisions, considered separately, is what Kahneman calls ____ framing.
questions.explain: Narrow framing means considering the decisions one at a time; broad framing treats them as a single comprehensive decision with four options.

questions.q: Treating several decisions as a single comprehensive decision, such as one choice with four options in the paired-decisions problem, is called ____ framing.
questions.explain: Broad framing considers all combinations together and is superior, or at least not inferior, whenever several decisions are contemplated together.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman argues that broad framing is superior to narrow framing in some cases but can be inferior when several decisions are contemplated together.
questions.explain: He says broad framing will be superior, “or at least not inferior,” in every case in which several decisions are to be contemplated together.

questions.q: How does Kahneman describe the logical consistency of Human preferences after the paired-decisions problem?
options: As a goal people reach with enough practice
As something System 2 reliably enforces
As a hopeless mirage
As a property guaranteed by loss aversion
questions.explain: He says the example helps us see the logical consistency of Human preferences for what it is, “a hopeless mirage,” because any simple choice can be decomposed into choices that yield inconsistent preferences.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say it is costly to be risk averse for gains and risk seeking for losses at the same time?
questions.a: Risk aversion for gains makes you pay a premium to get a sure gain rather than gamble, and risk seeking for losses makes you pay a premium in expected value to avoid a sure loss. Both payments come out of the same pocket. When you face both kinds of problems at once, these discrepant attitudes are unlikely to be optimal, as the dominated choice in the paired-decisions problem shows.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give as reasons Humans are narrow framers who cannot achieve logical consistency?
options: They are susceptible to WYSIATI
They are averse to mental effort
Their preferences are automatically set to be coherent
They tend to make decisions as problems arise
They always compute all combinations but forget them
questions.explain: Because of WYSIATI and aversion to mental effort, people decide as problems arise, even when told to consider them jointly. Automatically coherent preferences belong to the rational-agent model, not to Humans.

questions.q: Sort each description of the paired-decisions problem by whether it reflects narrow framing or broad framing.

items.t: A sequence of two simple decisions considered separately
A single comprehensive decision with four options
Choosing the sure gain, then gambling on the losses
Considering all four combinations of choices together
Five binary choices made one after another
One choice among 32 combined options

questions.explain: Narrow framing handles each decision on its own; broad framing combines them into one choice among all combinations, which is how a rational agent would decide.

questions.q: When 5 simple binary decisions are considered together, Kahneman says the broad frame consists of a single choice with ____ options.
questions.explain: Five binary decisions give 32 combinations. Narrow framing yields just one of those 32, which is possible but not very likely to be the best.

questions.q: In Samuelson's problem, how did his friend respond to the coin-toss offer?
options: He accepted one bet but refused to play 100 times
He accepted one bet and asked for 100 more
He refused both one bet and 100 bets
He refused one bet but offered to play if allowed 100 such bets
questions.explain: The friend said he would feel the $100 loss more than the $200 gain, but added, “I’ll take you on if you promise to let me make 100 such bets.”

questions.q: Why did Rabin and Thaler argue that Samuelson's proof about repeated gambles exposes a problem with utility theory?
questions.a: They pointed out that one hundred of the 50–50 lose $100/gain $200 bets has an expected return of $5,000 with only a 1/2,300 chance of losing any money. Rejecting such a package is foolish. If utility theory can be consistent with such a foolish preference under any circumstances, something must be wrong with it as a model of rational choice.

questions.q: According to Rabin and Thaler, the aggregated gamble of one hundred 50–50 lose $100/gain $200 bets has an expected return of $____.
questions.explain: Rabin and Thaler noted the bundle has an expected return of $5,000, with only a 1/2,300 chance of losing any money and a 1/62,000 chance of losing more than $1,000.

questions.q: In Kahneman's analysis of Samuelson's problem, how does Sam express his aversion to losses before computing the value of the bet?
options: He multiplies each loss by a factor of 2
He ignores outcomes with less than a 25% chance
He halves each possible gain
He adds a fixed fee to every bet
questions.explain: Sam rewrites the bet by doubling each loss, reflecting that losing a dollar feels twice as intense as winning one, and then computes the expected value.

questions.q: Match each version of Sam's coin-toss bet to its value after losses are doubled, as shown in Kahneman's table.
pairs: One toss
Two tosses
Three tosses
Five tosses (cash equivalent)
questions.explain: A single toss is worth nothing to Sam, but bundling raises the loss-weighted value to $50 for two tosses, $112.50 for three, and a cash equivalent of $203.125 for five.

questions.q: In Sam's two-toss bundle, why is the compound gamble worth something to him even though each single toss is worth nothing?
options: Loss aversion weakens after the first toss
The extreme outcomes cancel out and the intermediate outcome of one loss and one gain is positive
The probability of losing rises but the size of the loss falls
The second toss pays twice as much as the first
questions.explain: Losing 200 and winning 400 are equally likely and cancel when losses are doubled, while the one-loss-one-gain outcome nets a positive $100, so the bundle is worth $50 to Sam.

questions.q: True or false: In Kahneman's analysis of Sam, aggregating favorable gambles works because Sam gradually becomes less averse to losses.
questions.explain: Kahneman stresses that Sam never wavers in his aversion to losses. Aggregation instead rapidly reduces the probability of losing, so loss aversion has less impact on his preferences.

questions.q: Which of these figures does Kahneman give for Sam being offered five bundled coin-toss gambles?
options: An expected value of $250
A probability of losing anything of 18.75%
A cash equivalent of $203.125
A probability of losing anything of 25%
An expected value of $500
questions.explain: With five gambles, the expected value is $250, the chance of losing anything is 18.75%, and Sam's cash equivalent is $203.125. A 25% chance of losing belongs to the two-toss bundle.

questions.q: The mantra Kahneman offers to control your emotional response to losing a small favorable gamble is: you win a few, you ____ a few.
questions.explain: The mantra “you win a few, you lose a few” helps you see each small gamble as part of a bundle, bringing you closer to economic rationality.

questions.q: In his sermon to Sam, what does Kahneman mean by asking, “Are you on your deathbed?”
questions.a: He is reminding Sam that a single small favorable gamble is not the last one he will ever face. Over a lifetime he will have many opportunities to consider attractive gambles with stakes that are small relative to his wealth. Seeing each as part of a bundle of small gambles, rather than in isolation, would do him a large financial favor.

questions.q: Which of these are qualifications Kahneman attaches to the mantra “you win a few, you lose a few”?
options: The gambles must be genuinely independent of each other
The possible loss must not make you worry about your total wealth
It should not be applied to long shots with a very small chance of winning
It applies best to several investments in the same industry
It works only for gambles played exactly once
questions.explain: Kahneman warns that the mantra does not apply to investments in the same industry, which would all go bad together, nor to losses that threaten your wealth or to long shots.

questions.q: Sort each situation by whether Kahneman's mantra “you win a few, you lose a few” applies or does not apply.

items.t: Many independent small bets with positive expected value
Small risks whose stakes are tiny relative to your wealth
Several investments in the same industry
A loss you would take as bad news about your economic future
Repeated long-shot bets with a very small chance of winning
Turning down extended warranties on many unrelated products

questions.explain: The mantra fits small, independent, favorable risks. It fails for correlated investments, for losses that threaten your wealth, and for long shots.

questions.q: In the experiment on thinking like a trader described in the Risk Policies chapter, what did broad-framing instructions do to the students?
options: They increased the emotional reaction to losses and reduced risk taking
They had no effect on emotions but increased risk taking
They blunted the emotional reaction to losses and increased willingness to take risks
They reduced risk taking but made students happier with gains
questions.explain: Measured partly by skin conductance, broad framing blunted the emotional reaction to losses and increased willingness to take risks, compared with being told to make each decision as if it were the only one.

questions.q: True or false: In the trader experiment, students in the broad-framing condition were told to imagine themselves as a trader and treat each decision as one of many that sum to a portfolio.
questions.explain: Broad-framing instructions included “imagine yourself as a trader” and treating the choice as one of many monetary decisions; narrow-framing students were told to decide as if each choice were the only one.

questions.q: In the trader experiment, emotional responses to gains and losses were assessed by physiological measures, including changes in the electrical conductance of the ____ used in lie detection.
questions.explain: The experimenters measured changes in skin conductance, the same signal used in lie detection, to track emotional reactions.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, how often is it enough for individual investors to check how their investments are doing?
options: Every day
Once a week
Once a month
Once a quarter
questions.explain: He says once a quarter is enough, and may be more than enough, because following daily fluctuations means the pain of frequent small losses exceeds the pleasure of equally frequent small gains.

questions.q: Which of these benefits does Kahneman attribute to investors who get aggregated feedback and check their portfolios less often?
options: Improved emotional quality of life
Less useless churning of the portfolio
Being less risk averse and likely ending up richer
Avoiding all losses
Greater loss aversion after bad news
questions.explain: Less frequent exposure to short-term outcomes improves emotional life, decisions and outcomes, and reduces churning. Increased loss aversion is the typical short-term reaction to bad news, which these investors encounter less often.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman call the combination of loss aversion and narrow framing “a costly curse,” and how can individual investors escape it?
questions.a: Loss aversion makes each small loss feel more painful than an equal gain feels good, and narrow framing makes people evaluate every small outcome on its own, so they reject favorable risks and suffer from daily fluctuations. Investors can escape by checking their investments less often, for example once a quarter. Aggregated feedback brings bad news less often, reduces loss aversion and churning, and improves both emotional life and outcomes.

questions.q: Maya checks her retirement fund every morning and feels upset on down days, often moving money around. Based on the Risk Policies chapter, what would most improve her situation?
options: Checking far less often, such as once a quarter
Moving everything into one industry fund
Checking more often to catch losses early
Treating each day's result as the only one that matters
questions.explain: Kahneman says closely following daily fluctuations is a losing proposition. Checking less often reduces the pain of frequent small losses, useless churning and loss aversion, and improves outcomes.

questions.q: A freelancer is offered many small, unrelated projects, each with a good expected payoff and a small chance of losing a modest fee. According to the Risk Policies chapter, how should she view each offer?
options: As a long shot to be avoided
As part of a bundle of small gambles: you win a few, you lose a few
As a decision to make as if it were the only one
As a threat to her total wealth
questions.explain: Small, independent, favorable risks are exactly where Kahneman's mantra applies. Seeing each offer as part of a bundle controls the emotional response to the occasional loss.

questions.q: An investor puts all his savings into several small companies in the same industry, telling himself “you win a few, you lose a few.” Using the Risk Policies chapter, explain why this reasoning is misapplied.
questions.a: Kahneman says the mantra works only when the gambles are genuinely independent of each other. It does not apply to multiple investments in the same industry, which would all go bad together. Putting all his savings at stake also means a loss could threaten his total wealth, another condition under which the mantra should not be used.

questions.q: Put the steps of Kahneman's discussion of Samuelson's problem in the order he presents them.
items: Samuelson's friend refuses one bet but would accept 100
Samuelson proves a utility maximizer who rejects one gamble should reject many
Rabin and Thaler show the 100-bet bundle is overwhelmingly attractive
Kahneman models Sam's loss aversion by doubling losses
Kahneman offers Sam a sermon and the mantra
An experiment shows thinking like a trader blunts reactions to losses
questions.explain: The section runs from the anecdote and Samuelson's proof, through Rabin and Thaler's critique, to the worked Sam example, the practical mantra, and finally experimental evidence for broad framing.

questions.q: Instead of constructing a preference every time they face a risky choice, Kahneman says decision makers would do better by having a risk ____ that they routinely apply.
questions.explain: A risk policy, such as never buying extended warranties, is a broad frame applied whenever a relevant problem arises.

questions.q: Match each remedy or bias discussed in the Risk Policies chapter with its description.
pairs: Outside view
A broad frame for thinking about plans
Risk policy
A broad frame embedding one risky choice in a set of similar choices
Planning fallacy
Exaggerated optimism
Loss aversion
Exaggerated caution
questions.explain: Kahneman pairs the outside view against the exaggerated optimism of the planning fallacy, and the risk policy against the exaggerated caution induced by loss aversion.

questions.q: How does Kahneman describe the relationship between the planning fallacy and loss aversion?
options: They reinforce each other, doubling the risk taken
They are the same bias seen from two angles
They oppose each other: optimism counters loss aversion's paralysis and loss aversion counters optimistic folly
Loss aversion causes the planning fallacy
questions.explain: The two biases oppose each other. Exaggerated optimism protects against the paralyzing effects of loss aversion, and loss aversion protects against the follies of overconfident optimism.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman concludes that because optimism and loss aversion oppose each other, organizations should leave both biases in place so they cancel out.
questions.explain: He notes there is no guarantee the biases cancel in every situation, and says an organization that could eliminate both should do so: “The combination of the outside view with a risk policy should be the goal.”

questions.q: How does a risk policy help a person cope with the occasional loss it leaves them exposed to, as in the insurance examples?
questions.a: With a policy such as always taking the highest deductible, you expect occasionally to lose the whole deductible or to have an uninsured product fail. The key is that you can reduce or eliminate the pain of that occasional loss by thinking that the policy that left you exposed will almost certainly be financially advantageous over the long run. The policy is a broad frame, so no single loss is judged on its own.

questions.q: In Richard Thaler's story about the 25 division managers, how did the CEO respond to the risky gamble the managers had all refused?
options: He agreed that none of them should take it
He wanted only the most experienced managers to take it
He proposed buying insurance against the losses
He said he would like all of them to accept their risks
questions.explain: Without hesitation the CEO said, “I would like all of them to accept their risks,” because his broad frame covered all 25 bets.

questions.q: Why did the CEO in Thaler's story see the managers' risky gamble so differently from the managers themselves?
questions.a: Each manager viewed the gamble narrowly, as a single bet that could lose a large part of the capital he or she controlled, and loss aversion made them refuse. The CEO naturally adopted a broad frame that encompassed all 25 bets. Like Sam facing 100 coin tosses, he could count on statistical aggregation to reduce the overall risk.

questions.q: Sort each item from the Risk Policies chapter by whether it is a remedy for bias or a bias it addresses.

items.t: The outside view
A risk policy
Exaggerated optimism of the planning fallacy
Exaggerated caution induced by loss aversion
Checking investments only once a quarter
Narrow framing of each risky choice

questions.explain: The outside view, risk policies and less frequent checking are broad frames; the planning fallacy, loss aversion and narrow framing are the biases they counter.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman describe as broad frames in the Risk Policies chapter?
options: The outside view
A risk policy
Considering each risky choice as if it were the only one
The CEO's view of all 25 managers' bets
Checking each stock every day
questions.explain: The outside view, a risk policy and the CEO's view across 25 bets all embed one decision in a larger set. Treating each choice as the only one and daily checking are forms of narrow framing.

questions.q: Match each person in the Risk Policies chapter with what the chapter credits to them.
pairs: Paul Samuelson
Proved that rejecting one gamble implies rejecting many, under specific conditions
Rabin and Thaler
Showed the 100-bet bundle has only a 1/2,300 chance of losing money
Richard Thaler
Asked 25 division managers to consider a risky option
The company's CEO
Wanted all the division managers to accept their risks
questions.explain: Samuelson supplied the proof, Rabin and Thaler exposed how absurd it is to reject the bundle, and Thaler's conversation with managers and their CEO illustrates narrow versus broad framing in an organization.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give as familiar examples of risk policies?
options: Always take the highest possible deductible when purchasing insurance
Never buy extended warranties
Always choose the lowest possible deductible
Re-evaluate every insurance purchase on its own merits
Buy an extended warranty on every expensive product
questions.explain: His two familiar examples are taking the highest possible deductible and never buying extended warranties. Re-evaluating each purchase separately is the narrow framing a policy is meant to replace.

questions.q: In the Speaking of Risk Policies examples, what reason does a speaker give for evaluating a portfolio only once a quarter?
options: Too much loss aversion to make sensible decisions in the face of daily price fluctuations
Quarterly reports are more accurate than daily prices
Trading costs are lower on a quarterly schedule
A financial adviser required it
questions.explain: The speaker says, “I am too loss averse to make sensible decisions in the face of daily price fluctuations,” echoing the chapter's advice that aggregated feedback improves decisions.

questions.q: True or false: In the Speaking of Risk Policies examples, a speaker notes that because each executive is loss averse in his or her domain, the organization is not taking enough risk.
questions.explain: The speaker says the result of each executive's natural loss aversion is that the organization is not taking enough risk, as in Thaler's story of the 25 division managers.

questions.q: How does the Risk Policies chapter build on the earlier chapter The Outside View?
options: It rejects the outside view as a remedy for optimism
It presents risk policies as a broad frame for risky choices, analogous to the outside view for plans
It shows that the outside view causes loss aversion
It replaces the outside view with narrow framing
questions.explain: Kahneman explicitly links the two: the outside view is a broad frame for thinking about plans, and a risk policy is a broad frame for risky choices, so combining them should be the goal.

questions.q: Put these chapters of Part 4 (Choices) in the order they appear in the book.
items: Prospect Theory
The Fourfold Pattern
Rare Events
Risk Policies
Keeping Score
questions.explain: Risk Policies comes after Rare Events and before Keeping Score in Part 4, building on the earlier treatment of prospect theory and risk attitudes.

questions.q: Put the main sections of the Risk Policies chapter in the order they appear.
items: The paired decisions i and ii
Broad or Narrow?
Samuelson’s Problem
Risk Policies
Speaking of Risk Policies
questions.explain: The chapter moves from a demonstration of inconsistent choices, to the concepts of narrow and broad framing, to Samuelson's repeated gamble, and finally to risk policies as a practical remedy.

questions.q: What does the title Risk Policies signal about the chapter's place in Kahneman's discussion of choices?
questions.a: After earlier chapters describe how loss aversion and the fourfold pattern shape single risky choices, the title signals a practical remedy. Instead of constructing a preference each time a risky choice arises, a decision maker can adopt a risk policy, a broad frame that embeds each choice in a set of similar choices. The chapter thus shifts from describing biases in individual decisions to how broad framing can counter the cost of loss aversion.

questions.q: At the start of Kahneman's chapter on keeping score, what does he say money mainly represents for everyone except the very poor?
options: Points on a scale of self-regard and achievement
A guarantee of survival and basic security
A store of utility measured by total wealth
A signal used mainly to impress other people
questions.explain: Kahneman writes that for the billionaire and the experimental participant alike, money “is a proxy for points on a scale of self-regard and achievement.” Only for the very poor does income coincide with survival.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman name, in opening his chapter on keeping score, as results of the emotional score we keep in our heads?
options: Refusing to cut losses when doing so would admit failure
Being biased against actions that could lead to regret
Drawing a sharp distinction between omission and commission
Overweighting rare events when they are vividly described
Preferring sure gains over favorable gambles in every case
questions.explain: The chapter opens by listing three consequences of mental score-keeping: refusing to cut losses, bias against regret-prone actions, and an illusory omission/commission distinction. Overweighting vivid rare events belongs to the earlier discussion of rare events, not to this list.

questions.q: Kahneman says the ultimate currency that rewards or punishes us is often ____, a form of mental self-dealing.
questions.explain: He describes the reward and punishment currency as often emotional, which is why he calls it mental self-dealing that creates conflicts of interest for agents of organizations.

questions.q: Why, according to Kahneman, does emotional score-keeping create conflicts of interest when a person acts as an agent for an organization?
questions.a: The rewards and punishments that really move us are often emotional, a form of mental self-dealing kept in our own mental accounts. When an individual acts for an organization, what protects his own emotional score (for example, avoiding admitting a failure) can differ from what is best for the organization, so his incentives and the organization's interests come apart.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman calls the distinction people draw between omission and commission illusory, and says it arises because the sense of responsibility is greater for doing than for not doing.
questions.explain: He says we draw “an illusory but sharp distinction between omission and commission” because responsibility feels greater for acting than for not acting.

questions.q: Kahneman says that for Humans, mental accounts are a form of ____ framing that keeps things manageable by a finite mind.
questions.explain: Mental accounts split outcomes into separate pots rather than taking a comprehensive view, which is narrow framing. Econs, by contrast, have a comprehensive view of outcomes.

questions.q: True or false: According to Kahneman, the Econs of the rational-agent model rely on mental accounting to keep their finances under control.
questions.explain: Kahneman says Econs do not resort to mental accounting; they have a comprehensive view of outcomes and are driven by external incentives. Mental accounts are a Human device.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give as examples of using mental accounts for self-control?
options: Making a household budget
Limiting the daily consumption of espressos
Keeping savings while carrying credit card debt
Selling stocks that have gained in value
Buying tickets to a basketball game
questions.explain: Budgets and espresso limits are his examples of accounts used for self-control, and keeping savings while holding credit card debt is how we often pay for self-control. Selling winners and buying game tickets are examples of mental accounting distorting choices, not of self-control.

questions.q: In Kahneman's discussion of mental accounts, what does the finding that professional golfers putt better to avoid a bogey than to achieve a birdie suggest?
options: The best golfers keep only one account for the whole round
The best golfers keep a separate account for each hole
Golfers care more about birdies than about par
Golfers stop keeping score once they lead a tournament
questions.explain: Kahneman concludes that the best golfers create a separate account for each hole rather than maintaining only a single account for their overall success.

questions.q: In Thaler's example of two fans and a blizzard, why is the fan who paid for his ticket more likely to drive to the game?
questions.a: Both fans have opened a mental account for the game, and missing it closes the account with a negative balance. For the fan who paid, the closing balance is more negative because he is out of pocket as well as deprived of the game, so staying home feels worse and he is more motivated to drive. These are tacit calculations of emotional balance made by System 1.

questions.q: Put in order the steps of Kahneman's mental-accounting explanation of the blizzard example.
items: Both fans open a mental account for the game
A blizzard threatens to make them miss it
Missing the game would close the account at a loss
The buyer's closing balance would be worse, since he is also out of pocket
The buyer is more motivated to drive into the storm
questions.explain: The explanation builds from the shared account, through the threat of closing it negatively, to the larger loss for the buyer, which is why he is the one who braves the blizzard.

questions.q: In Thaler's blizzard example, an Econ would see the price of the already purchased ticket as ____ and would not care whether he bought it or got it from a friend.
questions.explain: Because the ticket has been paid for and cannot be returned, its cost is sunk, and an Econ would ignore how he came by it.

questions.q: In the blizzard example, what question does Kahneman say System 2 would have to ask in order to behave rationally?
options: How much did I pay for this ticket compared to my friend?
What is the probability that the game will be canceled?
Would I still drive into this storm if the ticket had been free?
Would my friend think less of me if I stayed at home?
questions.explain: To implement rational behavior, System 2 would have to raise the counterfactual of having gotten the ticket free from a friend. Kahneman notes it takes an active and disciplined mind to raise such a difficult question.

questions.q: Finance research has documented a massive preference for selling winning stocks rather than losing ones, a bias labeled the ____.
questions.explain: Kahneman calls the disposition effect an opaque label for the preference for selling winners over losers, and treats it as an instance of narrow framing.

questions.q: In Kahneman's stock example, you must sell either Blueberry Tiles (up $5,000) or Tiffany Motors (down $5,000). If you care about your wealth, which should you sell?
options: Blueberry Tiles, the winner
Either one, since the purchase price does not matter
Half of each, to balance gains and losses
Tiffany Motors, the loser
questions.explain: Kahneman says a person who cares about wealth rather than immediate emotions will sell the loser and keep the winner. The idea that it makes no difference is exactly what he rejects.

questions.q: Which of these reasons does Kahneman give for selling the losing stock rather than the winning one?
options: In the United States, realizing losses reduces your taxes
Stocks that recently gained tend to keep gaining for a short while
The losing stock is likely to recover its value soon
The purchase price is irrelevant to any rational decision
Selling a winner records a success for your investing record
questions.explain: He cites the tax advantage of realizing losses and the market anomaly that recent gainers keep gaining briefly. The pleasure of recording a success is the emotional reason people sell winners, and he explicitly says purchase price does matter.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, in which month do American investors sell more losing stocks, showing that taxes are on their mind?
options: December
January
April
June
questions.explain: Investors sell more losers in December, when taxes are on their mind, even though the tax advantage is available all year; for the other 11 months mental accounting prevails.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says Amos was right to dismiss the stocks' buying prices as irrelevant when a financial adviser asked for them.
questions.explain: Kahneman says Amos was wrong on this point: the purchase price does matter and should be considered even by Econs, mainly because of taxes.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say the disposition effect is a costly bias, and why do American investors sell more losers in December?
questions.a: Whether to sell winners or losers has a clear answer: selling losers reduces taxes, selling winners exposes you to taxes, and recent winners tend to keep gaining briefly, worth an expected 3.4% extra after-tax return in his example. Investors know about the tax rule but act on it mainly in December, when taxes are on their mind; for the other 11 months mental accounting prevails over financial common sense.

questions.q: The decision to invest additional resources in a losing account when better investments are available is called the ____.
questions.explain: Kahneman defines the sunk-cost fallacy this way and notes that driving into the blizzard because one paid for tickets is a sunk-cost error.

questions.q: In Kahneman's example of a company that has spent $50 million on a lagging project, what does a company afflicted by sunk costs typically do?
options: Moves the money to the more promising new project
Invests $60 million more in the failing project
Cancels both projects to limit further losses
Waits for better forecasts before deciding anything
questions.explain: All too often such a company drives into the blizzard, throwing good money after bad rather than closing the account of a costly failure.

questions.q: Kahneman places the choice faced by a company with large sunk costs in which cell of the fourfold pattern?
options: A sure gain versus a favorable gamble
A small chance of a large gain
A sure loss versus an unfavorable gamble
A small chance of a large loss
questions.explain: He puts it in the top-right cell, where the choice is between a sure loss and an unfavorable gamble, and the gamble is often unwisely preferred.

questions.q: When an executive's personal incentives to continue a failing project conflict with the interests of the firm, Kahneman calls this a familiar type of the ____.
questions.explain: In the presence of sunk costs the manager's incentives are misaligned with the firm and its shareholders, which is what is known as the agency problem.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say escalation of commitment to a failing project may be a mistake for the firm but not for the executive who owns it?
questions.a: Canceling the project would leave a permanent stain on the executive's record. His personal interests may be best served by gambling further with the organization's resources, hoping to recoup the original investment or at least postpone the day of reckoning, even though the firm would do better to cut its losses.

questions.q: Why do boards often replace a CEO who is reluctant to cut losses, according to Kahneman, even if they do not think the successor is more competent?
questions.a: The board knows the old CEO is encumbered by prior decisions and the mental accounts attached to them. The new CEO does not carry those mental accounts, so she is better able to ignore the sunk costs of past investments when evaluating current opportunities.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say the sunk-cost fallacy keeps people in for too long?
options: Poor jobs
Unhappy marriages
Unpromising research projects
Diversified stock portfolios
Long-term savings plans
questions.explain: Kahneman lists poor jobs, unhappy marriages and unpromising research projects, and mentions young scientists struggling to salvage doomed projects.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman reports evidence that graduate students in economics and business are more willing than others to walk away from a failing project.
questions.explain: The sunk-cost fallacy is taught as a mistake in these fields, apparently to good effect, which suggests the fallacy can be overcome in some contexts.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it describes an Econ or a Human, as Kahneman uses the terms.

items.t: Has a comprehensive view of outcomes
Is interested only in future consequences of investments
Does not care whether the ticket was bought or a gift
Uses mental accounts as a form of narrow framing
Wants to close every stock account as a gain
Feels more driven to brave the blizzard after paying

questions.explain: Econs ignore sunk costs and view outcomes comprehensively; Humans keep separate mental accounts and feel the emotional balance of closing them.

questions.q: What do mental accounts do for Humans, and why does Kahneman count them as narrow framing?
questions.a: We sort money into accounts such as spending money, general savings and earmarked savings, and use accounts for self-control, which keeps things under control and manageable by a finite mind. But each account is evaluated separately rather than as part of a comprehensive view of outcomes, which is narrow framing; that is why the results are sometimes helpful and sometimes foolish.

questions.q: Match each situation to the idea Kahneman uses it to illustrate.
pairs: A fan who paid drives into a blizzard to see the game
Sunk-cost error
An investor sells the winning stock to fund a wedding
Disposition effect
An executive keeps funding a floundering project to protect his record
Agency problem
A golfer treats each hole as its own scorecard
A separate mental account per hole
A household keeps savings while carrying credit card debt
Paying for self-control
questions.explain: Each example shows mental accounting at work: sunk costs, closing accounts as gains, misaligned incentives, separate accounts, and self-control accounts.

questions.q: Maya paid $90 for a nonrefundable concert ticket. On the night, a heavy storm hits and she would rather stay home, but she goes anyway, saying she paid for it. How would Kahneman describe her choice?
options: A rational choice, since the ticket cost is lost if unused
An example of the disposition effect in action
An example of the precautionary principle
A sunk-cost error driven by mental accounting
questions.explain: Like the fan who drives into the blizzard, she is trying to avoid closing a mental account with a negative balance. An Econ would treat the $90 as sunk and decide only on the future benefits.

questions.q: Raj needs cash in March and owns two equal, stable stocks, one up $3,000 and one down $3,000. Following Kahneman's analysis, what will most investors do, and what should Raj do?
options: Most sell the winner; Raj should sell the loser
Most sell the loser; Raj should sell the winner
Most sell the winner; Raj should sell the winner
Most sell the loser; Raj should sell the loser
questions.explain: The disposition effect makes most investors sell winners, especially outside December, but the tax advantage and the short-term momentum of winners favor selling the loser.

questions.q: Put in order Kahneman's account of the company stuck with a failing project.
items: The company has spent $50 million on a project
The project falls behind and forecasts worsen
Another $60 million is needed to give it a chance
A new project promises higher returns for the same money
The company often keeps funding the failing project
questions.explain: The example sets up the sunk investment, the bad news, the further outlay, the better alternative, and finally the sunk-cost choice of throwing good money after bad.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it is a reason to sell the losing stock (Tiffany Motors) or the emotional reason investors sell the winning stock (Blueberry Tiles).
groups: Emotional pull to sell the winner

items.t: Realizing losses reduces your taxes
Recent winners tend to keep gaining for a while
An expected 3.4% after-tax extra return
Closing an account with a gain feels like a success
Avoiding adding a failure to your investing record
Enjoying a sense of investment prowess

questions.explain: Taxes, momentum and expected return favor selling the loser; the pleasure of a recorded success and the pain of a recorded failure push people toward selling the winner.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether Kahneman links it to System 1 or System 2.

items.t: Tacit calculations of emotional balance in the blizzard case
The moral intuition behind enhanced loss aversion
Asking whether you would drive if the ticket had been free
Experienced investors resisting the disposition effect

questions.explain: Kahneman says the emotional balance is computed by System 1 without deliberation and that enhanced loss aversion originates in System 1, while the counterfactual question and experienced investors' resistance reflect System 2.

questions.q: Kahneman describes regret as an emotion and also as a ____ that we administer to ourselves.
questions.explain: He opens the discussion by saying regret is an emotion and also a punishment we administer to ourselves; fear of it shapes many decisions.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, when is regret most intense?
options: When the financial loss involved is very large
When you can most easily imagine having done otherwise
When other people blame you for the outcome
When the outcome was entirely beyond your control
questions.explain: He writes that intense regret is what you experience “when you can most easily imagine yourself doing something other than what you did.”

questions.q: Kahneman calls regret one of the ____ emotions, triggered by the availability of alternatives to reality.
questions.explain: Regret is a counterfactual emotion: it depends on how easily an alternative to what actually happened comes to mind.

questions.q: Why are stories of passengers who should not have been on a crashed plane so poignant, according to Kahneman?
questions.a: They involve unusual events, such as getting a seat at the last moment or being transferred from another airline, and unusual events are easier than normal ones to undo in imagination. Associative memory holds a picture of the normal world, so an abnormal event draws attention and activates the idea of what would normally have happened.

questions.q: Put in order Kahneman's account of how an abnormal event produces strong counterfactual feelings.
items: An unusual event occurs, such as a last-minute seat change
The abnormal event attracts attention
It activates the idea of what would have been normal
The normal alternative is easy to imagine, intensifying regret
questions.explain: Associative memory represents the normal world; an abnormal event draws attention and calls up the normal alternative, which makes the outcome easy to undo in imagination.

questions.q: True or false: In the hitchhiker study, most respondents said Mr. Brown, who rarely picks up hitchhikers, would be criticized more severely by others.
questions.explain: For criticism by others, 77% chose Mr. Smith, who often picks up hitchhikers. Mr. Brown was chosen by 88% as the one who would feel more regret.

questions.q: Sort each judgment by which man it applies to in the hitchhiker study.

items.t: Expected by most to feel greater regret
Acted out of character this one time
Tempting to call him unlucky
Expected by most to be criticized more severely
Seen as habitually taking unreasonable risks
Tempting to say he deserved his fate

questions.explain: Regret follows what each man usually does, so Mr. Brown feels it more; blame follows conventional norms of reasonable behavior, so observers blame Mr. Smith.

questions.q: How does Kahneman explain why regret and blame point at different men in the hitchhiker example?
questions.a: Both regret and blame come from comparison to a norm, but the norms differ. Regret follows a person's own habits, so Mr. Brown, for whom picking up a hitchhiker was abnormal, is expected to kick himself; blame follows conventional norms of reasonable behavior, so observers criticize Mr. Smith for habitually taking risks.

questions.q: In Kahneman's example, Paul kept stock A instead of switching to B, and George switched from B to A; both would be $1,200 better off with B. Who do most people say feels greater regret, and why?
options: Paul, because he failed to act on his idea
Paul, because he considered the switch for longer
George, because he got there by acting
Neither, because their situations are identical
questions.explain: 92% said George. Their situations are objectively identical, but people expect stronger emotions to outcomes produced by action than to the same outcomes produced by inaction.

questions.q: Kahneman says the key is not the difference between commission and omission but the distinction between ____ options and actions that deviate from them.
questions.explain: When you deviate from the default you can easily imagine the norm, and a bad outcome then produces painful emotions. That is why failing to greet a colleague can also cause regret or blame.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman treat as departures from the default option, and so as natural candidates for regret or blame?
options: Selling a stock you own
Failing to greet a coworker in the morning
A coach keeping the same lineup after a bad loss
Holding on to a stock you own
Greeting a colleague when you meet
questions.explain: The default for a stock is to keep it, and the default with a colleague is to greet him, so selling and not greeting are departures. After a bad loss, the coach's default is to make a change, so doing nothing is the departure.

questions.q: In the blackjack simulation where players were asked either whether they wished to hit or whether they wished to stand, what did Kahneman report?
options: Hitting always brought more regret than standing
Standing always brought more regret than hitting
Players felt equal regret whatever they answered
Saying yes brought more regret after a bad outcome, whichever question was asked
questions.explain: Regardless of the question, saying yes was associated with more regret than saying no when the outcome was bad, because the question implies a default of not wishing to act.

questions.q: What does the blackjack study show about default options, according to Kahneman?
questions.a: Whether players were asked if they wished to hit or to stand, saying yes was followed by more regret than saying no after a bad outcome. The question itself suggests a default response, roughly that one has no strong wish to act, and it is departing from that default, not the content of the action, that produces regret.

questions.q: Match each decision maker to how anticipated regret or evaluation shapes their behavior in Kahneman's account.
pairs: Consumers reminded they may feel regret
Lean toward brand names over generics
Fund managers near the end of the year
Clear out unconventional, questionable stocks
A physician weighing an unusual treatment
Faces risk of regret, blame and litigation
A coach whose team lost badly
Expected to change personnel or strategy
questions.explain: Kahneman uses each case to show that the asymmetry in the risk of regret favors conventional choices, except where action itself is the default, as for the losing coach.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say the potential benefit to a physician who dares an unusual treatment is smaller than the potential cost?
options: Success is generally a more normal outcome than failure
Unusual treatments rarely help gravely ill patients
Patients usually refuse unconventional treatments
Courts rarely hear cases about standard treatments
questions.explain: A good outcome adds to the daring physician's reputation, but because success is the more normal outcome, the gain is smaller than the regret and blame that would follow failure, when the abnormal choice is easy to undo.

questions.q: Lena always drives to work on the highway; today she took back roads and was stuck for an hour behind an accident. Her colleague Omar always takes those back roads and was stuck in the same jam. Using Kahneman's analysis, who is likely to feel more regret?
options: Omar, because his route is generally riskier
Lena, because she departed from her usual habit
Both equally, because the outcome was identical
Neither, because nobody could foresee the accident
questions.explain: As with Mr. Brown and the hitchhiker, regret follows what a person usually does. Lena's choice was abnormal for her and is easy to undo in imagination.

questions.q: What broad pattern does the Paul and George example illustrate, and how does Kahneman extend it?
questions.a: People expect stronger emotional reactions, including regret, to an outcome produced by action than to the same outcome produced by inaction. The same holds for gambling, where people expect to be happier if they gamble and win than if they refrain and get the same amount; the asymmetry is at least as strong for losses and applies to blame as well as regret.

questions.q: Kahneman says losses weigh about twice as much as gains in several contexts. In what kind of situation does he say the loss-aversion coefficient may be much higher?
options: Small everyday purchases made with cash
Gambles offered repeatedly over many trials
Aspects of life more important than money, such as health
Choices made by professional traders
questions.explain: He notes you may be more loss averse for aspects of life more important than money, such as health, especially when selling them could make you responsible for an awful outcome.

questions.q: Put in order the steps of Thaler's disease and vaccine questions as Kahneman presents them.
items: You learn you have a 1 in 1,000 chance of a fatal disease
You state the most you would pay for a vaccine
You are asked to volunteer for a 1 in 1,000 exposure
You state the least you would accept to volunteer
Volunteer fees turn out far higher, about 50 to 1
questions.explain: The first question sets a buying price for safety, the variation sets a selling price for the same risk, and the comparison shows the selling price far exceeds the buying price.

questions.q: Kahneman says one reason volunteers demand so much in Thaler's disease question is that you are not supposed to sell your ____.
questions.explain: Selling health is not considered a legitimate transaction, and reluctance to engage in it shows up as a higher price.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give as reasons for the extremely high price people demand to volunteer for a 1 in 1,000 disease risk?
options: Selling your health is not considered a legitimate transaction
You would be responsible for the outcome if it were bad
The chance of disease is higher for volunteers than for others
People cannot understand a probability of 1 in 1,000
Volunteers expect to receive the vaccine afterwards
questions.explain: Kahneman names two features: the transaction is seen as illegitimate, and, perhaps most important, you would be responsible for a bad outcome. The risk is the same 1 in 1,000 in both versions, and volunteers are not allowed to buy the vaccine.

questions.q: Why does responsibility make people demand so much to accept a small health risk in Thaler's volunteer question?
questions.a: If you woke up with fatal symptoms after volunteering, you would feel far more regret than if you had simply been exposed, because you could have rejected the idea of selling your health without even considering the price. You could have stayed with the default and done nothing, and that counterfactual would haunt you, so the selling price rises far above the buying price.

questions.q: True or false: In the insecticide survey, the minority of parents who named an acceptable discount demanded more than they were willing to pay for a much larger safety improvement.
questions.explain: The minority who accepted a discount demanded significantly more than they were willing to pay for a far larger improvement in safety.

questions.q: Put in order the insecticide survey of parents as Kahneman describes it.
items: Parents imagine an insecticide with a risk of 15 per 10,000 bottles
A cheaper product raises the risk to 16 per 10,000
Parents name the discount that would make them switch
More than two-thirds refuse to switch at any price
questions.explain: The survey sets a baseline risk, offers a slightly riskier cheaper product, asks for the required discount, and finds most parents reject the trade outright.

questions.q: Kahneman calls the refusal to accept any increase in risk to a child in exchange for money a ____ tradeoff.
questions.explain: He says the taboo tradeoff against accepting any increase in risk is not an efficient way to use the safety budget.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman call parents' refusal to trade a tiny increase in insecticide risk for money incoherent and potentially damaging?
questions.a: Even loving parents have finite time and money for their child's safety; the keeping-my-child-safe mental account has a limited budget. Money saved by accepting a minute increase in pesticide risk could reduce other dangers, such as buying a safer car seat or covers for electric sockets, so the taboo tradeoff wastes the safety budget and may be driven more by fear of regret than by the child's safety.

questions.q: What does Kahneman suggest may really motivate parents' refusal to accept any added insecticide risk for a discount?
options: A careful estimate of the child's total risk
Distrust of the manufacturer's statistics
A belief that cheaper products are always worse
A selfish fear of regret
questions.explain: He suggests the resistance may be motivated more by a selfish fear of regret than by a wish to optimize the child's safety, since a parent who made the trade would picture the regret and shame if harm occurred.

questions.q: The doctrine that prohibits any action that might cause harm, widely accepted in Europe, is called the ____.
questions.explain: In regulation, the precautionary principle puts the entire burden of proving safety on anyone whose actions might harm people or the environment.

questions.q: What does Kahneman report as Cass Sunstein's main point about the precautionary principle?
options: It is costly, and paralyzing when interpreted strictly
It is the most efficient way to manage risk
It has been adopted mainly in the United States
It applies only to environmental questions
questions.explain: Sunstein points out that the principle is costly and, interpreted strictly, can be paralyzing, listing many valuable innovations that would not have passed the test.

questions.q: Which of these innovations does Kahneman quote Cass Sunstein as listing among those that would not have passed a strict precautionary test?
options: Airplanes
Antibiotics
X-rays
Nuclear power
The internet
Electric lighting
questions.explain: Sunstein's list includes airplanes, antibiotics and X-rays, along with items such as air conditioning, automobiles and the smallpox vaccine. Nuclear power, the internet and electric lighting are not on it.

questions.q: How does Kahneman sum up the conflict between loss-averse moral attitudes and efficient risk management?
questions.a: The strong version of the precautionary principle is untenable, yet enhanced loss aversion is embedded in a strong, widely shared moral intuition that originates in System 1. So the dilemma between intensely loss-averse moral attitudes and efficient risk management has no simple and compelling solution.

questions.q: To what does Kahneman compare susceptibility to regret when asking whether it is reasonable to let anticipated regret influence choices?
options: Susceptibility to optical illusions
Susceptibility to fainting spells
A habit that can easily be broken
An error that training removes
questions.explain: He says susceptibility to regret, like susceptibility to fainting spells, is a fact of life to which one must adjust, not something to deny.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman recommend as ways to inoculate yourself against regret?
options: Be explicit about the anticipation of regret before deciding
Do what you can to preclude hindsight
Be either very thorough or completely casual on long-term decisions
Think about a decision a little, but not too much
Avoid making any decisions with long-term consequences
questions.explain: Kahneman recommends being explicit about anticipated regret and preventing hindsight, and his own policy is to be very thorough or completely casual. Thinking a little is what he warns against, since it lets you later say you almost made a better choice.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman try to be either very thorough or completely casual when making a decision with long-term consequences?
questions.a: Regret and hindsight bias come together, so anything that prevents hindsight helps. Hindsight is worst when you think a little, just enough to tell yourself later that you almost made a better choice; being thorough or completely casual avoids that half-considered alternative.

questions.q: Daniel Gilbert and his colleagues argue that people underestimate the power of their psychological defenses, which they call the psychological ____ system.
questions.explain: Because of the psychological immune system, they argue, regret will hurt less than people now think.

questions.q: True or false: Daniel Gilbert and his colleagues claim that people generally anticipate more regret than they will actually experience.
questions.explain: Gilbert and colleagues say people underestimate their psychological defenses, so regret will hurt less than they now think and should not get too much weight.

questions.q: Before choosing a risky but promising job, Ana writes down exactly how she would feel if it failed, and decides to take it anyway. According to Kahneman, how is this likely to affect her if things go badly?
options: She will probably feel more regret
It will make her more prone to hindsight
She will probably feel less regret
It will have no effect on her regret
questions.explain: Kahneman says being explicit about anticipated regret is perhaps the most useful precaution: if you remember that you considered regret carefully before deciding, you are likely to experience less of it.

questions.q: Is it reasonable to let your choices be influenced by the anticipation of regret? Summarize Kahneman's balanced answer.
questions.a: Regret and moral responsibility are costly to Humans and absent in Econs, but they are real emotions, so the fact that Econs lack them may not be relevant. Like fainting spells, regret is a fact of life to adjust to; a rich and cautious investor may afford a portfolio that minimizes expected regret. Still, Gilbert's work suggests regret will hurt less than we expect, so it should not get too much weight.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say are harmed by the self-administered emotional punishments we experience as we score our lives?
options: The wealth of individuals
The soundness of policy
The welfare of society
The accuracy of memory
The speed of System 1
questions.explain: He says these intangible outcomes lead to actions detrimental to the wealth of individuals, the soundness of policy, and the welfare of society.

questions.q: Match each number to the finding it belongs to in Kahneman's chapter on keeping score.
pairs: Respondents who said Mr. Brown would feel more regret
Respondents who said Mr. Smith would be criticized more
Respondents who said George would feel more regret
About 50 to 1
Typical ratio of selling price to buying price for disease risk
More than two-thirds
Parents who would not buy the riskier insecticide at any price
questions.explain: These figures come from the hitchhiker, Paul and George, Thaler vaccine and insecticide studies, each showing how regret, blame and responsibility shape choices.

questions.q: Match each person to the idea Kahneman credits to them in his chapter on keeping score.
pairs: Richard Thaler
Analogies between accounting and mental accounts
Amos Tversky
Questioned why an adviser wanted stock buying prices
Cass Sunstein
The precautionary principle is costly and can paralyze
Daniel Gilbert
The psychological immune system softens regret
Two Dutch psychologists
A vivid description of the feeling of regret
questions.explain: Thaler originated mental accounting and the vaccine question, Amos asked the adviser about purchase prices, Sunstein criticized the precautionary principle, Gilbert proposed the psychological immune system, and the Dutch psychologists described regret's emotional state.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning as Kahneman uses it.
pairs: Disposition effect
Preference for selling winning stocks rather than losers
Sunk-cost fallacy
Investing more in a losing account despite better options
Agency problem
A manager's incentives misaligned with the firm's goals
Precautionary principle
Prohibiting any action that might cause harm
Counterfactual emotion
A feeling triggered by imagining alternatives to reality
questions.explain: These are the chapter's defined terms for mental accounting errors, organizational conflicts, risk regulation and regret.

questions.q: Sort each action by whether Kahneman would treat it as staying with the default or departing from it.

items.t: Keeping a stock you already own
Greeting a colleague in the morning
A coach changing strategy after a bad loss
Selling a stock you own
Failing to greet a coworker
A physician choosing an unusual treatment

questions.explain: Kahneman says the default for a stock is not to sell and for a colleague is to greet; for a losing coach, change is the default. Departures from defaults are natural candidates for regret or blame.

questions.q: Match each remark to the idea Kahneman's chapter on keeping score uses it to illustrate.
pairs: He keeps separate accounts for cash and credit purchases
Mental accounting; money is money
We are holding the stock to avoid closing the account at a loss
Disposition effect
We never try another dish at that restaurant
Avoiding regret by sticking with the default
I could not bring myself to buy the cheaper car seat
Taboo tradeoff
questions.explain: These paraphrase the chapter's closing remarks, each applying one of its ideas: mental accounts, the disposition effect, regret aversion, and the taboo tradeoff.

questions.q: Put the parts of Kahneman's chapter Keeping Score in the order they appear.
items: Money as a proxy for points of self-regard
Mental Accounts
Regret
Responsibility
Speaking of Keeping Score
questions.explain: The chapter opens with money as a score, then moves from mental accounts and sunk costs, to regret and defaults, to responsibility and taboo tradeoffs, and closes with sample remarks.

questions.q: Put these chapters from Part IV, Choices, in the order they appear in the book.
items: The Fourfold Pattern
Rare Events
Risk Policies
Keeping Score
Reversals
Frames and Reality
questions.explain: In the table of contents, Keeping Score is chapter 32, following Risk Policies (31) and followed by Reversals (33) and Frames and Reality (34).

questions.q: What does the title Keeping Score signal about the chapter's main theme?
options: We should track every expense to become more rational
Experts keep better records than ordinary people do
Economic models measure utility precisely
We tally emotional rewards and punishments in mental accounts
questions.explain: The chapter argues that money and outcomes are points we keep score of in our heads, and these emotional scores shape preferences, regret and responsibility.

questions.q: How does Keeping Score build on the preceding chapter, Risk Policies?
options: It shows mental accounts as another form of narrow framing
It replaces narrow framing with a theory of broad framing
It drops framing to focus on statistical prediction
It argues that Humans are by nature broad framers
questions.explain: Risk Policies contrasted broad framing with the narrow framing Humans naturally use. Keeping Score presents mental accounts, such as an account for each share bought, as a form of narrow framing.

questions.q: True or false: Keeping Score recalls an earlier finding that professional golfers putt more successfully when working to achieve a birdie than to avoid a bogey.
questions.explain: The earlier finding was the reverse: golfers putt more successfully when working to avoid a bogey than to achieve a birdie, which Kahneman reads as keeping a separate account for each hole.

questions.q: Match each Part IV chapter to an idea it contributes to the argument about choices.
pairs: The Endowment Effect
Reluctance to give up what one owns
The Fourfold Pattern
Risk seeking when choosing between a sure loss and a gamble
Risk Policies
Broad framing of many small gambles together
Keeping Score
Mental accounts, regret and responsibility
Reversals
Judgments that change between joint and single evaluation
questions.explain: Keeping Score draws on loss aversion and the fourfold pattern and extends the framing theme of Risk Policies, before Reversals turns to joint versus single evaluation.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it belongs to chapter 31, Risk Policies, or chapter 32, Keeping Score.

items.t: A pair of concurrent decisions between sure things and gambles
Samuelson's friend and the repeated coin-toss gamble
Evaluating gambles with a broad frame
The disposition effect in selling stocks
The hitchhiker study of regret and blame
Thaler's disease and vaccine question

questions.explain: Risk Policies treats concurrent decisions, Samuelson's gamble and broad framing; Keeping Score turns to mental accounts, regret and responsibility.

questions.q: In Dale Miller and Cathy McFarland's between-subjects study of a man shot during a store robbery, how did the store's identity affect the compensation awarded?
options: He was awarded a much larger sum when shot in a store he rarely visited than in his regular store
He was awarded a much larger sum when shot in his regular store than in a store he rarely visited
Awards were the same in both versions, because participants judged only the crippling injury
Awards were higher in both versions than when participants saw the two scenarios side by side
questions.explain: Participants who saw only one scenario gave more when he was shot in the unfamiliar store, because the thought “if only he had shopped at his regular store …” comes readily to mind. Equal awards are what people endorse only when they see both scenarios together.

questions.q: Put in order the steps by which, in single evaluation, the burglary victim shot in the unfamiliar store ends up with a larger award.
items: The victim is shot in a store he rarely visits
The thought 'if only he had shopped at his regular store' comes to mind
A counterfactual feeling of poignancy is evoked
Substitution and intensity matching map the feeling onto money
A larger dollar award is assigned
questions.explain: Kahneman explains that the readily available counterfactual thought evokes poignancy, and the System 1 mechanisms of substitution and intensity matching translate the strength of that emotion onto a monetary scale.

questions.q: In the burglary scenarios, Kahneman calls poignancy a counterfactual feeling and a close cousin of ____.
questions.explain: Kahneman writes that poignancy is “a close cousin of regret”: both are counterfactual feelings evoked by how easily an alternative outcome comes to mind.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say about judging the two burglary scenarios in joint evaluation?
options: You can apply a rule and compare the two scenarios explicitly
Thinking is slow and System 2 is involved
Almost everyone agrees compensation should be the same in both
The poignancy of the unfamiliar store justifies a higher award
Most people decide that location is a legitimate factor
questions.explain: Joint evaluation lets people examine their moral principles, and for most people location is not a relevant factor, so they award the same amount. The idea that poignancy justifies more is what single evaluation produces, not what people endorse on reflection.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that we normally experience life in the within-subject mode, where contrasting alternatives are available to change our minds.
questions.explain: He says we normally experience life in the between-subjects mode, where contrasting alternatives that might change your mind are absent, and WYSIATI applies.

questions.q: Using the burglary scenarios, explain why Kahneman concludes that the moral intuitions that come to mind in different situations are not internally consistent.
questions.a: When people see both scenarios together, almost everyone endorses the principle that poignancy is not a legitimate consideration for compensation. But that principle becomes relevant only when the scenarios are seen together, and life is usually lived in the between-subjects mode where the contrasting case is absent (WYSIATI).
