So the beliefs we endorse when we reflect about morality do not necessarily govern our emotional reactions to single cases.

questions.q: In Miller and McFarland's ____ experiment on the burglary victim, each participant saw only one scenario and assigned a dollar value to it.
questions.explain: A between-subjects design gives each participant only one scenario, which is single evaluation; seeing both scenarios together is the within-subject, joint-evaluation mode.

questions.q: Which of these System 1 mechanisms does Kahneman say translate the emotional reaction to the burglary story into a large difference in dollar awards?
options: Substitution
Intensity matching
Loss aversion
Regression to the mean
The planning fallacy
questions.explain: Kahneman names “substitution and intensity matching” as the mechanisms that carry the strength of the emotional reaction onto a monetary scale. Loss aversion and the other ideas are from elsewhere in the book.

questions.q: Match each term from the reversals chapter to its meaning.
pairs: Joint evaluation
Considering two options at the same time and comparing them
Single evaluation
Judging one option on its own, without the alternative in view
Poignancy
A counterfactual feeling evoked by an easy 'if only' thought
Preference reversal
Ranking options one way when judged together and another way when judged alone
questions.explain: Joint evaluation is explicit comparison, single evaluation sees one case alone, poignancy is the counterfactual feeling in the burglary case, and a preference reversal is the inconsistency between the two modes.

questions.q: In the burglary compensation case, why does the store where the man was shot change the award in single evaluation but not in joint evaluation?
questions.a: In single evaluation, the unusual store evokes poignancy because 'if only he had shopped at his regular store' comes readily to mind, and System 1 converts that emotion into dollars by substitution and intensity matching. In joint evaluation, the explicit comparison engages System 2, which examines moral principles and recognizes that location is not a relevant factor, so the two cases get the same award.

questions.q: Who reported the preference reversals between bets that attracted the attention of economists?
options: David Grether and Charles Plott, two respected economists
Sarah Lichtenstein and Paul Slovic, two psychologists
Dale Miller and Cathy McFarland, two psychologists
Christopher Hsee and Cass Sunstein, at Chicago
questions.explain: Lichtenstein and Slovic, who did their graduate work at Michigan at the same time as Amos, reported the reversals. Grether and Plott were the economists who later tried to discredit those findings.

questions.q: In Lichtenstein and Slovic's experiment with Bet A (11/36 to win $160) and Bet B (35/36 to win $40), what preference reversal appears?
options: People choose A over B, but set a higher selling price on B than on A
People choose A over B, and also set a higher selling price on A
People choose B over A, but set a higher selling price on A than on B
People choose B over A, and also set a higher selling price on B
questions.explain: Safety prevails in choice, so B is more popular, yet when people imagine owning just one bet they set a higher value on A. Consistent preferences in both tasks would not be a reversal.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, why do people set a higher selling price on the risky Bet A than on the safe Bet B?
options: They realize that A has the higher expected value once they calculate it carefully
They are negotiating with a buyer and want to leave room to bargain down
They feel loss aversion more strongly for B because it is almost certain to win
The prize that can be won is salient, and their valuation is anchored on it
questions.explain: Kahneman says the prize is salient in the pricing task and the evaluation of the bet is anchored on that value, so A with its $160 prize gets the higher price. He stresses that you are not negotiating with anyone.

questions.q: Kahneman says the emotional reactions of System 1 mostly determine single evaluation, while the comparison in joint evaluation involves a careful, effortful assessment that calls for ____.
questions.explain: Kahneman writes that the comparison that occurs in joint evaluation “always involves a more careful and effortful assessment, which calls for System 2.”

questions.q: True or false: Grether and Plott said openly that their series of experiments was designed to discredit the psychologists' work as applied to economics.
questions.explain: Their unusually dramatic introductory paragraph said the experiments were “designed to discredit the psychologists’ works as applied to economics.” In the end their results supported the psychologists.

questions.q: True or false: Of the thirteen theories Grether and Plott tested to explain the preference reversals, the only one left standing was that the psychologists were right.
questions.explain: After carefully designed tests, including the patronizing hypothesis that the results were due to psychologists running the experiment, only one hypothesis survived: the psychologists were right.

questions.q: What effect does Kahneman say Grether and Plott's report had?
options: It led economists to abandon the rational-agent model within a few years
It had little direct effect on economists' convictions but made them more willing to take psychological research seriously
It convinced psychologists that their findings had been caused by flawed experimental methods
It was ignored by economists because it appeared in a psychology journal
questions.explain: Kahneman says the report had little direct effect on economists' convictions, probably including Grether and Plott's own, but it greatly advanced the conversation across the disciplines. It appeared in the American Economic Review, not a psychology journal.

questions.q: Which of these describe the bewildered participant in Sarah Lichtenstein's classic 1968 interview?
options: He chose one bet over another
He was then willing to pay money to exchange the chosen bet for the rejected one
He went through the cycle repeatedly
He spotted his inconsistency at once and corrected it
He refused to set any selling prices on the bets
questions.explain: The participant chose one bet, then paid to swap it for the one he had rejected, and repeated the cycle. Kahneman notes participants are unaware of the inconsistency, so the idea that he corrected it at once is wrong.

questions.q: Put in order the history of how preference reversals entered economics.
items: Lichtenstein and Slovic report preference reversals between bets
Grether and Plott publish experiments aiming to discredit the findings
Grether and Plott test thirteen possible explanations
Only one hypothesis survives: the psychologists were right
Economists become more willing to take psychological research seriously
questions.explain: The psychologists' finding came first; Grether and Plott then set out to discredit it, tested thirteen theories, were left only with the psychologists being right, and the main effect was greater openness among economists to psychology.

questions.q: Why were preference reversals a challenge to the rational-agent model and economic theory?
questions.a: Rational Econs would not be susceptible to preference reversals, because their preferences should not change with the way options are presented. The reversals show choice depending on whether options are evaluated together or apart. Grether and Plott admitted the surviving explanation was the least satisfactory for standard preference theory because “it allows individual choice to depend on the context in which the choices are made,” violating the coherence doctrine.

questions.q: Why, according to Kahneman, did Grether and Plott's confirmation of preference reversals not cause anguished soul-searching among economists?
options: Economists found a flaw in the bets that explained the results away
The finding concerned only gambling, which economists considered unimportant
Theoretical beliefs are robust, and one embarrassing finding is not enough to make established theories seriously questioned
Psychologists themselves soon withdrew their claims about the reversals
questions.explain: Kahneman says this is not how social science works, in psychology or economics: theoretical beliefs are robust and it takes much more than one embarrassing finding to shake an established theory.

questions.q: Sort each feature into the bet it belongs to in Lichtenstein and Slovic's experiment.

items.t: 11/36 chance to win $160
35/36 chance to win $40
High probability of losing $15
1/36 chance to lose $10
The more popular choice
Given the higher selling price

questions.explain: Bet A is the risky bet with a small chance of a large prize and a high chance of losing; Bet B is the almost certain modest win. People choose B but price A higher.

questions.q: Kahneman says that rational ____ would surely not be susceptible to preference reversals, which is why the phenomenon challenged economic theory.
questions.explain: Econs are the rational agents of economic theory. Their preferences would be coherent across choice and pricing, so reversals challenge the model built on them.

questions.q: Maya picks a guaranteed $500 bonus over a 1-in-4 chance at $3,000. Later, asked separately the lowest price at which she would sell each option, she names a higher price for the gamble. Which idea from the reversals chapter best explains this?
options: Choosing between the options made safety salient, while pricing each alone anchored her on the prize
She is negotiating, so she inflates the price of whichever option she likes less
Loss aversion makes her overvalue whichever option she happens to own
She has learned from experience that gambles are usually underpriced
questions.explain: This mirrors Lichtenstein and Slovic's bets: joint evaluation brings out the difference in safety, while single evaluation of a selling price is anchored on the salient prize, producing a preference reversal.

questions.q: Match each researcher or pair to their contribution in the reversals chapter.
pairs: Lichtenstein and Slovic
Reported preference reversals between safe and risky bets
Grether and Plott
Economists who tried to discredit the reversals and ended up confirming them
Miller and McFarland
Designed the burglary victim compensation scenarios
Christopher Hsee
Proposed the evaluability hypothesis using secondhand music dictionaries
Cass Sunstein
Compared administrative penalties across U.S. government agencies
questions.explain: Each name is tied to one study in the chapter: the bets, the economists' replication, the burglary scenarios, the dictionaries and the agency penalties.

questions.q: Sort each process from the reversals chapter by whether Kahneman attributes it mainly to System 1 or System 2.

items.t: Emotional reactions that drive single evaluation
The careful comparison made in joint evaluation
Intensity matching a feeling onto a dollar scale
Automatic evaluation on the good-bad dimension
Examining moral principles about which factors matter
Retrieving the height norm for a child's age

questions.explain: Kahneman assigns automatic emotional reactions, norm retrieval and intensity matching to System 1, and the effortful comparison and reflection on principles in joint evaluation to System 2.

questions.q: In Kahneman's example, John is 6 and 5 feet tall, and Jim is 16 and 5 feet 1 inch tall. How are they judged?
options: Alone, Jim seems very tall and John not; asked directly, you say John is as tall as Jim
Alone, both seem average for their age; asked directly, you say Jim is taller
Alone, John seems very tall and Jim not; asked directly, you say John is not as tall as Jim
Alone, John seems very short and Jim very tall; asked directly, you cannot answer
questions.explain: In single evaluation each boy is compared to the norm for his age, so John seems very tall and Jim does not; the direct comparison correctly says John is not as tall. Kahneman notes there is little ambiguity here.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that a restaurant meal matching the height of a 5-foot John would be much more expensive if John were 16 than if he were 6.
questions.explain: It is the reverse: a 5-foot 16-year-old is short for his age, so the matching meal would be much less expensive than for a 5-foot 6-year-old, who is very tall.

questions.q: Kahneman says judgments and preferences are coherent within ____ but potentially incoherent when the objects evaluated belong to different ones.
questions.explain: Our world is broken into categories with norms, such as six-year-old boys or tables, and coherence holds within a category but can break down across them.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say there is no preference reversal when you compare apples and peaches?
options: Both evoke fruit, so they are compared to the same norm in single as well as joint evaluation
People have no real preference between fruits, so any answer is equally stable
Apples and peaches are cheap, so the comparison does not engage System 1
Most people have tasted both often, so experience overrides intuition
questions.explain: Different fruits are compared to the same norm and implicitly compared to each other even in single evaluation, so you recover the same ranking either way.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give as reasons there is no stable answer to whether you like apples or steak more?
options: Apples and steak are not natural substitutes
They do not fill the same need
You rarely say either one will do just as well as the other
Steak is much more expensive than apples
Apples and steak are compared to the same norm
questions.explain: Kahneman says you sometimes want steak and sometimes an apple, because they are not substitutes and fill different needs. Being compared to the same norm is what makes apples versus peaches stable, the opposite case.

questions.q: Sort each comparison by whether Kahneman's account predicts a stable preference or a possible reversal between single and joint evaluation.

items.t: Apples vs. peaches
Steak vs. stew
Apples vs. steak
Dolphins vs. farmworkers
Dolphins vs. carp as species to protect

questions.explain: Items in the same category share a norm and are implicitly compared even when judged alone; items from different categories each recruit their own norm, so single and joint evaluation can disagree.

questions.q: In the dolphin fundraising appeal, how does Kahneman say the dolphin fares in your automatic System 1 evaluation?
options: It ranks low because pollution threats feel abstract and distant
It ranks low compared with public-health causes involving people
It has no rank, because dollar values cannot be compared across causes
It ranks highly among the species to which it is spontaneously compared
questions.explain: Projects to preserve endangered species come to mind, and the dolphin is much more charming than ferrets, snails or carp, so it has a highly favorable rank in that set.

questions.q: Kahneman says that evaluation on the ____ dimension is an automatic operation of System 1, which gave you a crude impression of the dolphin's rank among species.
questions.explain: The automatic GOOD–BAD evaluation ranks the dolphin among the species that come to mind, before any dollar question is answered.

questions.q: Put in order how Kahneman says you arrive at a dollar contribution for the dolphin appeal.
items: Related causes such as endangered species come to mind
The dolphin gets a crude, favorable rank among those species
The hard dollar question is replaced by how much you like dolphins
The intensity of liking is mapped onto your scale of contributions
A specific number of dollars is produced
questions.explain: Associations come first, then automatic good-bad ranking; substitution replaces the dollar question with liking, and intensity matching moves from 'like a lot' to 'fairly large contribution' and then to a number.

questions.q: Sort each outcome in the dolphins versus farmworkers appeals by whether it occurs in single or joint evaluation.

items.t: Dolphins attract somewhat larger contributions
The dolphin is compared with other endangered species
Skin cancer is compared with other public-health issues
The human vs. animal feature becomes salient
A solid preference for helping the farmworkers

questions.explain: Alone, each cause is ranked within its own category, which favors dolphins. Together, the decisive fact that farmworkers are human stands out and people give substantially more to them.

questions.q: In the dolphins and farmworkers appeals, why did the fact that farmworkers are human and dolphins are not play no role in single evaluation?
questions.a: In single evaluation each cause recruits its own category as a norm. All the causes activated by the dolphin appeal were other species, so 'not human' did not stand out, and all public-health issues involve humans, so 'human' did not stand out either. The narrow framing let dolphins get a higher intensity score; only when the two are seen together does the human vs. animal feature become salient and decisive.

questions.q: Which of these are true of Christopher Hsee's two secondhand music dictionaries?
options: Both were published in 1993
Dictionary B has 20,000 entries
Dictionary A is like new
Dictionary A has more entries than dictionary B
Dictionary B was published more recently
questions.explain: Both date from 1993; A has 10,000 entries and is like new, while B has 20,000 entries and a torn cover. So the claims that A has more entries or that B is newer are wrong.

questions.q: According to Hsee's evaluability hypothesis, why is dictionary A valued more highly in single evaluation?
options: Buyers believe a torn cover signals that many pages are missing
The number of entries is not evaluable on its own, so it gets no weight
Buyers anchor on the year of publication, which favors dictionary A
Buyers expect a dictionary in perfect condition to have been cared for
questions.explain: Alone, a number like 10,000 or 20,000 entries means little, so condition dominates. In joint evaluation B is obviously superior on entries, and entries matter far more than the cover.

questions.q: Christopher Hsee's music dictionary example illustrates his ____ hypothesis: an attribute gets no weight in single evaluation if its values cannot be judged on their own.
questions.explain: Hsee's evaluability hypothesis says numbers that are not “evaluable” on their own are ignored in single evaluation but become decisive in joint evaluation.

questions.q: True or false: In Hsee's experiment, dictionary B, with 20,000 entries and a torn cover, is valued more highly in single evaluation.
questions.explain: In single evaluation dictionary A, which is like new, is valued more highly; the preference changes to B only in joint evaluation, when the number of entries becomes evaluable.

questions.q: Explain Hsee's evaluability hypothesis using the secondhand music dictionaries.
questions.a: Dictionary A has 10,000 entries and is like new; dictionary B has 20,000 entries but a torn cover. Seen alone, A is valued more because the number of entries is not evaluable on its own and gets no weight, while condition is easy to judge. Seen together, it is immediately obvious that B is superior on entries and that entries matter far more than the cover, so the preference reverses.

questions.q: Priya reads a single job offer listing a 4% employer pension contribution and gives the number little thought. Later she sees three offers side by side with 1%, 4% and 9% and the figure suddenly seems important. Which idea from the reversals chapter fits best?
options: Poignancy: the counterfactual 'if only' thought makes the offer feel worse
Anchoring on the prize: the highest number sets her valuation
Hsee's evaluability hypothesis: the attribute becomes evaluable only in comparison
Loss aversion: the low offers feel like losses relative to the high one
questions.explain: Like the number of dictionary entries, a pension percentage means little on its own and gets no weight in single evaluation; joint evaluation makes it evaluable and important.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman warn against concluding that single and joint evaluations are always inconsistent or that judgments are completely chaotic?
questions.a: Our world is broken into categories for which we have norms, such as six-year-old boys or tables. Within a category, items are compared to the same norm and implicitly to each other even in single evaluation, so preferences such as apples versus peaches are coherent. Incoherence arises when the objects being evaluated belong to different categories, as with apples and steak or dolphins and farmworkers.

questions.q: Match each example from the reversals chapter to what it illustrates.
pairs: John and Jim's heights
Each object is judged against the norm of its own category
Apples vs. peaches
Items in the same category give the same ranking alone or together
Dolphins vs. farmworkers
A decisive feature becomes salient only when causes are seen together
Hsee's music dictionaries
An attribute that cannot be judged alone gets no weight
Bets A and B
Pricing a bet alone is anchored on its prize
questions.explain: Each example shows a different source of the gap between single and joint evaluation, or, for apples and peaches, why there is no gap within a category.

questions.q: Which of these help explain why the dolphin appeal drew somewhat larger contributions than the farmworker appeal in single evaluation?
options: The dolphin ranks highly among the species it is compared with
Skin cancer in farmworkers ranks fairly low among public-health issues
Intensity matching turns the strength of the reaction into dollars
People judge dolphins to be more important than humans
The dolphin fund was described as more efficient
questions.explain: Each cause is ranked within its own category and the intensity is matched to a dollar amount. People do not think dolphins matter more than humans: in joint evaluation they clearly prefer the farmworkers.

questions.q: Put in order the procedure in the mock-jury experiment on punitive damages.
items: Mock jurors are recruited from Texas jury rolls
Each juror assesses one case of a pair on its own
The juror is shown the paired case
The juror compares the two cases in joint evaluation
questions.explain: Jurors first made a single evaluation of one case, then saw its partner and compared them; half started with the physical-injury case and half with the financial-loss case.

questions.q: In the mock-jury study, which case received higher punitive damages in single evaluation, and why?
options: The burned child, because sympathy for an individual victim dominated
The burned child, because negligence toward a child evokes outrage
Both received about the same, because each juror judged only one case
The defrauded bank, because the size of the financial loss provided a high anchor
questions.explain: Alone, jurors gave more to the bank, presumably because the $10 million loss was a high anchor. Sympathy for the child prevailed only when the cases were seen together.

questions.q: What happened to the awards in the mock-jury study when jurors considered the burned child and the defrauded bank together?
options: The award to the child rose to surpass the bank's, while the bank's stayed anchored on its loss
The award to the bank fell sharply, while the child's stayed the same
Both awards rose, but the bank still received more than the child
Both awards fell, because jurors became more cautious when comparing
questions.explain: In joint evaluation the bank's award remained anchored on its loss, but the child's award increased, reflecting outrage at negligence that injures a child, until it exceeded the bank's.

questions.q: Averaging over several pairs of cases in the mock-jury study, awards to victims of personal injury were more than ____ as large in joint evaluation as in single evaluation.
questions.explain: Kahneman reports that personal-injury awards were more than twice as large in joint than in single evaluation.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman reports that jurors assessing punitive damages are encouraged to compare the case before them with other cases, so the legal system favors joint evaluation.
questions.explain: Cass Sunstein told him jurors are explicitly prohibited from considering other cases; the legal system, contrary to psychological common sense, favors single evaluation.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman report about Cass Sunstein's comparison of penalties across U.S. government agencies?
options: Within an agency, more serious harms are punished more severely
Penalty sizes across agencies reflect politics and history more than fairness
A serious worker-safety violation is capped below a Wild Bird Conservation Act fine
The system of penalties is coherent both within and across agencies
All agencies set fines using one shared formula
questions.explain: Sunstein found penalties sensible within categories but varying across agencies; the worker-safety cap of $7,000 versus up to $25,000 under the Wild Bird Conservation Act shows the global incoherence.

questions.q: Kahneman concludes that the system of administrative penalties is coherent within agencies but incoherent ____.
questions.explain: The fines make sense next to other penalties set by the same agency, but look odd when compared across agencies; the absurdity shows only in a broad frame.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman presume comparative judgments are more stable than single evaluations, and what exception does he note?
questions.a: Rationality is generally served by broader frames, and joint evaluation is broader than single evaluation; the comparison necessarily involves System 2, while single evaluations often reflect the intensity of System 1's emotional responses. The exception is when someone who controls what you see has a vested interest in what you choose, as salespeople who manipulate the context in which customers see a good can profoundly influence preferences.

questions.q: In the mock-jury study, why did the jurors who saw the burned child's case alone give an award that later looked inadequate?
questions.a: Seeing the case alone, they made an offer that matched the intensity of their feelings about it. They could not anticipate that this award would look inadequate next to a large award to a financial institution anchored on a $10 million loss. Only in joint evaluation did the outrage at negligence injuring a child push the child's award above the bank's.

questions.q: Sort each observation from the mock-jury study by whether it belongs to single or joint evaluation.

items.t: The bank receives higher damages than the child
The award matches the intensity of feeling about one case
Sympathy for the individual victim prevails over anchoring
The child's award rises above the bank's
Personal-injury awards are more than twice as large

questions.explain: Alone, the bank's loss acts as a high anchor and each award matches feelings about that case; together, sympathy for the child wins and personal-injury awards more than double.

questions.q: At a store, a salesperson places a deliberately overpriced, poorly featured model right next to the one they want you to buy. What does Kahneman's discussion of reversals advise?
options: Trust the comparison, since joint evaluation always yields the more rational choice
Be wary of joint evaluation when someone who controls what you see has a vested interest
Ignore the comparison and rely on your emotional reaction to each item alone
Assume that the more expensive item is the better one, since price reflects quality
questions.explain: Kahneman says joint evaluation is usually broader and more stable, but you should be wary of it when the person choosing the context profits from your choice, as salespeople learn to do.

questions.q: Order the occupational safety and health violations in Sunstein's study from largest penalty to smallest.
items: Repeated violations
Violations that are both willful and serious
Failures to do the required record-keeping
questions.explain: Sunstein reported that the largest penalties are for repeated violations, the next for willful and serious ones, and the least for record-keeping failures, showing coherence within the category.

questions.q: Match each case from the unjust reversals discussion to its detail.
pairs: Serious worker-safety violation
Fine capped at $7,000
Wild Bird Conservation Act violation
Fine of up to $25,000
Bank harmed by another bank's dealings
Loss of $10 million
Child burned while playing with matches
Pajamas not made adequately fire resistant
questions.explain: The two fines show global incoherence across agencies; the bank and the burned child are the paired cases in the mock-jury study.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say the legal system's handling of punitive damages runs contrary to psychological common sense?
questions.a: An institution that wants thoughtful judgments should give judges a broad context for assessing individual cases, because comparative judgment involves System 2 and is more stable. Yet jurors assessing punitive damages are explicitly prohibited from considering other cases, so the system favors single evaluation, which often reflects the intensity of System 1's emotional responses, as in the low award to the burned child judged alone.

questions.q: Match each remark from the reversals chapter's closing quotes to the idea it expresses.
pairs: BTU units meant nothing until I saw how air conditioners vary
An attribute becomes evaluable only in joint evaluation
An outstanding speech compared to her other speeches
The judgment used the wrong comparison norm
Broaden the frame
Broader frames tend to produce more reasonable decisions
Seeing cases in isolation
Single evaluation is guided by emotional System 1 reactions
questions.explain: The quotes apply the chapter's lessons: evaluability, category norms, the value of broad frames, and System 1's role in single evaluation.

questions.q: One of the closing remarks says: “You say this was an outstanding speech because you compared it to her other speeches. Compared to others, she was still inferior.” What mistake does it point out?
questions.a: The speech was judged against the norm of the speaker's own category, her other speeches, much as a 5-foot John looks very tall against six-year-olds. Within that category it ranked high, but compared with other speakers' work it was inferior. The judgment depends on which context of comparison the object recruits, which is why single evaluation can mislead.

questions.q: A closing remark in the reversals chapter says that it is often the case that when you broaden the ____, you reach more reasonable decisions.
questions.explain: Kahneman's theme is that broader, more comprehensive frames, such as joint evaluation, generally serve rationality.

questions.q: What does the title "Reversals" signal about the main finding of Chapter 33?
options: People's preferences reverse over time as they gain experience with a choice
Gains and losses reverse their effect when the reference point shifts
The same options can be ranked one way in joint evaluation and the opposite way in single evaluation
Economists reversed their theories once psychologists challenged them
questions.explain: The chapter is about preference reversals between single and joint evaluation, in bets, donations, dictionaries and legal awards. Kahneman explicitly says economists' convictions changed little.

questions.q: How does Chapter 33's statement that rationality is generally served by broader and more comprehensive frames connect to the rest of Part 4, "Choices"?
options: It introduces broad framing for the first time, to be developed in Part 5
It contradicts earlier chapters that recommended evaluating each choice on its own merits
It is unrelated to framing and concerns only memory for past events
It extends earlier chapters' case for broad frames, now applied to judging options together rather than one at a time
questions.explain: Kahneman writes “As we have seen, rationality is generally served by broader and more comprehensive frames,” referring back to earlier chapters in Part 4, and applies that idea to joint versus single evaluation.

questions.q: Put the parts of Chapter 33, "Reversals," in the order they appear.
items: The burglary victim compensation scenarios
Challenging Economics: preference reversals between bets
Categories: norms, dolphins and Hsee's dictionaries
Unjust Reversals: juries and agency penalties
Speaking of Reversals
questions.explain: The chapter opens with the burglary scenarios, then traces the economic history, explains reversals through categories, applies them to the legal system, and closes with sample remarks.

questions.q: True or false: Chapter 33, "Reversals," falls in Part 4, "Choices," coming after "Keeping Score" and before "Frames and Reality."
questions.explain: The table of contents places Reversals as chapter 33 in Part 4, between chapter 32, Keeping Score, and chapter 34, Frames and Reality.

questions.q: How does Chapter 33 fit the larger argument of Part 4, "Choices," about the rational-agent model?
questions.a: Part 4 contrasts how real people choose with how rational Econs would. Chapter 33 adds preference reversals: the same people rank options differently depending on whether they evaluate them alone or together, which Econs would never do. Grether and Plott's failed attempt to discredit the finding shows it is a genuine violation of the coherence doctrine, since choice depends on the context in which choices are made.

questions.q: Why is Chapter 33, "Reversals," a natural lead-in to the next chapter, "Frames and Reality"?
questions.a: Chapter 33 shows that preferences depend on the frame in which options are seen: single evaluation is a narrow frame dominated by System 1's emotional reactions, while joint evaluation is a broader frame engaging System 2. It ends by stressing that broadening the frame leads to more reasonable decisions. The next chapter's title signals that the book continues with how the framing of a choice, rather than its substance, shapes what people decide.

questions.q: In the World Cup example, why are "Italy won" and "France lost" interchangeable for the purpose of logical reasoning?
options: They have identical truth conditions: if one is true, the other is true
They evoke the same associations in System 1 when heard
Both sentences describe the outcome from a neutral reference point
Both sentences are equally easy to process and so feel equally true
questions.explain: Logically the two sentences designate the same state of the world, so their truth conditions are identical. The idea that they evoke the same associations is exactly what Kahneman denies.

questions.q: In the World Cup example, what is the second sense of meaning in which "Italy won" and "France lost" differ?
options: What a sentence would mean to an Econ choosing between states of the world
What happens in your associative machinery while you understand the sentence
The emotional intensity the speaker intended when choosing the words
The truth conditions the sentence has under a different reference point
questions.explain: In this sense meaning is how System 1 reacts: the associations a sentence brings to mind. "France lost" calls up the French team and what it did to lose, which "Italy won" does not.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what does the sentence "France lost" evoke that "Italy won" does not?
options: Thoughts of the Italian players and the tactics that won them the final
A feeling that the result was unfair to the Italian team
Thoughts of the French team and what it did to lose, including Zidane's head butt
A sense of how improbable the result was before the match
questions.explain: "France lost" directs attention to the French team and its failure, including the memorable head butt by Zidane, while "Italy won" directs attention to the Italian team and how it won.

questions.q: Econs' beliefs and preferences are ____: the objects of their choices are states of the world, unaffected by the words used to describe them.
questions.explain: Kahneman describes Econs as reality-bound; Humans, whose System 1 responds to wording, are not.

questions.q: Sort each description according to whether it fits Econs or Humans as Kahneman describes them in the opening of Frames and Reality.

items.t: Treat "Italy won" and "France lost" as having the same meaning
Choose among states of the world, not descriptions
Hold preferences that are reality-bound
React differently to logically equivalent statements
Have choices shaped by the associations words evoke
Cannot be as reliably rational as the other group

questions.explain: Econs are reality-bound and judge by truth conditions. Humans respond to the associations System 1 attaches to words, which makes it impossible for them to be as reliably rational as Econs.

questions.q: Using the World Cup example, explain the two senses in which "Italy won" and "France lost" can be said to have the same or different meanings, and why this matters for rationality.
questions.a: In the logical sense the sentences mean the same thing, because they have identical truth conditions and designate the same state of the world; this is how reality-bound Econs understand them. In another sense, meaning is what happens in the associative machinery of System 1, and here the sentences differ: one evokes the Italian team winning, the other the French team losing, including Zidane's head butt. Because logically equivalent statements evoke different reactions, Humans cannot be as reliably rational as Econs.

questions.q: Kahneman and Tversky applied the label ____ to the unjustified influences of formulation on beliefs and preferences.
questions.explain: Framing effects are influences of wording that should not matter, because the state of the world described is the same.

questions.q: Kahneman compares accepting a gamble with a 10% chance to win $95 and a 90% chance to lose $5 with paying $5 for a lottery with a 10% chance to win $100. Which version attracts more positive answers, and why?
options: The gamble version, because the possible prize of $95 is stated directly rather than hidden
The lottery version, because $100 is a larger and rounder prize than $95
Neither, because most people see that the two problems are identical and answer the same
The lottery version, because a bad outcome is more acceptable as the cost of a losing ticket than as a lost gamble
questions.explain: The two problems leave you richer by $95 or poorer by $5 either way, yet the lottery framing wins because losses evoke stronger negative feelings than costs. The idea that people notice the identity is what reality-bound preferences would predict, but such individuals are rare.

questions.q: True or false: In Kahneman's two equivalent problems, more people accept the gamble described as a 10% chance to win $95 and a 90% chance to lose $5 than agree to pay $5 for a lottery ticket with a 10% chance to win $100.
questions.explain: It is the other way around: the lottery version attracts many more positive answers, because paying for a losing ticket feels like a cost while losing a gamble feels like a loss.

questions.q: When Richard Thaler was a graduate student, he pinned a card on his board that said COSTS ARE NOT ____.
questions.explain: Thaler's slogan captures the idea that people feel costs much less painfully than losses, which shaped the lottery version of Kahneman and Tversky's framing problem.

questions.q: True or false: In Thaler's gas-station example, the credit-card lobby preferred that any price difference be labeled a credit surcharge rather than a cash discount.
questions.explain: The lobby wanted the label cash discount, because people more readily forgo a discount than pay a surcharge. “The two may be economically equivalent, but they are not emotionally equivalent.”

questions.q: Explain why people are more willing to pay $5 for a lottery ticket with a 10% chance to win $100 than to accept a gamble with a 10% chance to win $95 and a 90% chance to lose $5, and what this shows about choices.
questions.a: The two problems are identical: either way you end up $95 richer or $5 poorer, so a reality-bound person would answer both the same way. But a bad outcome is more acceptable when framed as the cost of a ticket that did not win than as losing a gamble, because losses evoke stronger negative feelings than costs. The lesson is that “Choices are not reality-bound because System 1 is not reality-bound.”

questions.q: Put the stages of one trial in the University College London framing experiment in order.
items: The subject imagines she has received an amount of money, such as £50
She chooses between a sure option, framed as KEEP or LOSE, and a gamble on a wheel of chance
Researchers later sort trials by whether the choice conformed to the frame
questions.explain: Each trial began with an imagined endowment, then offered a sure outcome framed as KEEP or LOSE against a gamble; afterwards trials were separated into frame-conforming and non-conforming categories for the brain analysis.

questions.q: In the University College London framing experiment, where the subject imagines receiving £50, what is the sure outcome offered against the gamble?
options: The expected value of the gamble, framed either as KEEP £20 or as LOSE £30
Half the endowment, framed either as KEEP £25 or as LOSE £25
The full endowment, framed either as KEEP £50 or as LOSE nothing
The expected value of the gamble, always framed as a gain of £20
questions.explain: The sure outcome was simply the gamble's expected value, a gain of £20, and the same outcome was presented in two frames: KEEP £20 or LOSE £30.

questions.q: True or false: In the University College London KEEP–LOSE experiment, every one of the 20 subjects showed a framing effect.
questions.explain: All 20 subjects were more likely to choose the sure thing in the KEEP frame and the gamble in the LOSE frame, though they differed greatly in how susceptible they were.

questions.q: The University College London researchers ranked their 20 subjects by how little they were swayed by the KEEP and LOSE frames and called the ranking the ____ index.
questions.explain: Subjects who mostly made the same choice regardless of the frame, as a reality-bound individual should, ranked high on what the authors strikingly labeled the rationality index.

questions.q: In the KEEP–LOSE brain study, a region commonly associated with emotional arousal, the ____, was most likely to be active when subjects' choices conformed to the frame.
questions.explain: The amygdala is accessed very rapidly by emotional stimuli and is a likely suspect for involvement in System 1.

questions.q: In the KEEP–LOSE brain study, a region associated with conflict and self-control, the ____, was more active when subjects chose the sure thing in spite of its being labeled LOSE.
questions.explain: Activity in the anterior cingulate suggests that resisting the inclination of System 1 involves conflict.

questions.q: Match each brain finding from the KEEP–LOSE framing study to when it occurred.
pairs: Amygdala (emotional arousal)
Most active when choices conformed to the frame
Anterior cingulate (conflict, self-control)
More active when subjects chose the sure thing despite the LOSE label
Frontal area combining emotion and reasoning
Enhanced in the subjects least susceptible to framing
questions.explain: The three findings link frame-conforming choices to emotion, resisting the frame to conflict, and rationality to a region that combines emotion and reasoning.

questions.q: True or false: In the KEEP–LOSE brain study, the most "rational" subjects were those who showed the strongest neural evidence of conflict.
questions.explain: Remarkably, the rational subjects were not those with the strongest evidence of conflict; they showed enhanced activity in a frontal area that combines emotion and reasoning and were often reality-bound with little conflict.

questions.q: Which of these were findings of the University College London framing study that combined choices with brain recordings?
options: The amygdala was most likely to be active when choices conformed to the frame
The anterior cingulate was more active when subjects resisted the frame
The least frame-susceptible subjects showed enhanced activity in a frontal area combining emotion and reasoning
The most rational subjects showed the strongest neural evidence of conflict
About half the subjects showed no framing effect at all
questions.explain: The study's three main findings concerned the amygdala, the anterior cingulate and a frontal area. The rational subjects did not show the most conflict, and every one of the 20 subjects showed some framing effect.

questions.q: What does Kahneman say the KEEP–LOSE brain-imaging study illustrates well?
options: That framing effects disappear once subjects have seen many trials
How the emotion evoked by a word can leak into the final choice
That rational decisions require suppressing all emotion
That the amygdala carries out the work of System 2
questions.explain: By joining observed choices with neural mapping, the study shows emotion triggered by words like KEEP and LOSE leaking into decisions. The most rational subjects used a region that combines emotion and reasoning, so suppressing all emotion is not the lesson.

questions.q: Describe the three main brain findings of the University College London KEEP–LOSE study and what they suggest about System 1 and framing.
questions.a: The amygdala, linked to emotional arousal, was most active when choices conformed to the frame, as expected if the words KEEP and LOSE produce an immediate tendency to approach or avoid the sure thing; it is a likely suspect for System 1. The anterior cingulate, linked to conflict and self-control, was more active when subjects resisted the frame, so resisting System 1 involves conflict. The least frame-susceptible subjects showed enhanced activity in a frontal area that combines emotion and reasoning, and were often reality-bound with little conflict.

questions.q: In Amos Tversky's lung-cancer study at Harvard Medical School, what share of physicians chose surgery when its short-term outcome was described as a one-month survival rate of 90%?
questions.explain: In the survival frame 84% of physicians chose surgery, while in the frame of 10% mortality in the first month, 50% favored radiation instead.

questions.q: True or false: In the lung-cancer framing study, physicians were less susceptible to the survival–mortality framing effect than hospital patients and business-school graduate students.
questions.explain: Physicians were just as susceptible as medically unsophisticated people. “Medical training is, evidently, no defense against the power of framing.”

questions.q: What did the survival–mortality lung-cancer experiment show, and why does Kahneman consider the physicians' result important?
questions.a: Physicians were told the same short-term outcome of surgery either as a 90% one-month survival rate or as 10% mortality in the first month; 84% chose surgery in the survival frame, while 50% favored radiation in the mortality frame. The descriptions are transparently equivalent, but System 1 reacts to emotional words: survival is good and mortality is frightening. Physicians were just as susceptible as patients and business students, so medical training offers no defense against framing.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give as differences between the KEEP–LOSE brain study and the survival–mortality physician study?
options: Brain-study participants met both frames over many trials
Physicians in the survival frame had no reason to suspect that a mortality frame would change their choice
Brain-study participants had a chance to adopt a common frame, such as translating LOSE amounts into KEEP equivalents
The physician study measured outcomes in money rather than lives
Only the physician study showed any framing effect
questions.explain: Repeated trials let alert brain-study subjects notice the frames and simplify by translating into one frame, while the physicians saw a single frame and had no cue to reframe. Both studies found framing effects, and the physician study concerned survival, not money.

questions.q: Why, according to Kahneman, do most people rarely discover that their preferences are frame-bound rather than reality-bound?
options: System 1 automatically translates every problem into a common frame
People usually see both frames and notice the inconsistency themselves
Frames only affect trivial decisions that people never revisit
Reframing takes effort and a lazy System 2 usually accepts problems as they are framed
questions.explain: Unless there is an obvious reason, people passively accept the frame offered, so they never see how a different description would have changed their choice. “Reframing is effortful and System 2 is normally lazy.”

questions.q: Why could some participants in the KEEP–LOSE brain study partly escape the framing effect, while physicians in the survival–mortality study could not?
questions.a: The brain-study participants faced many trials with both frames, giving them an opportunity to recognize the distracting effects of the frames and adopt a common frame, for example translating LOSE amounts into their KEEP equivalents; this took intelligence and an alert System 2, and the few who managed it were probably among the most rational. The physicians saw only one frame and had no reason to suspect that a different description would change their choice. Because reframing is effortful and System 2 is lazy, most people passively accept problems as framed.

questions.q: A doctor tells one patient that a procedure has a 95% survival rate and tells another that it carries a 5% risk of death. Based on the lung-cancer framing study, what would Kahneman predict?
options: The first patient is more likely to agree, because survival sounds encouraging and death sounds frightening
Both patients will decide the same way, since the statistics are logically equivalent
The second patient is more likely to agree, because the small number 5% feels reassuring
Only patients without medical knowledge will be affected by the wording
questions.explain: System 1 is rarely indifferent to emotional words, so the survival frame favors the procedure. Expertise does not help either: physicians were just as susceptible as patients.

questions.q: Sort each description from Frames and Reality by whether it is the more appealing or the less appealing frame of the same outcome.

items.t: KEEP £20
LOSE £30
One-month survival rate of 90%
10% mortality in the first month
Paying $5 for a lottery ticket that does not win
Losing $5 on a gamble
Cash discount
Credit surcharge

questions.explain: In each pair the outcomes are identical, but words framing an outcome as a gain, a survival or a cost feel better than words framing it as a loss, a death or a surcharge.

questions.q: Sort each choice by whether it conforms to the frame or resists the frame, as defined in the KEEP–LOSE brain study.

items.t: Choosing the sure thing labeled KEEP
Choosing the gamble when the sure thing is labeled LOSE
Choosing the sure thing even though it is labeled LOSE
Choosing the gamble when the sure thing is labeled KEEP

questions.explain: Trials were split by whether the choice followed the frame (sure thing for KEEP, gamble for LOSE) or went against it; the amygdala was linked to conforming and the anterior cingulate to resisting.

questions.q: What did Richard Thaler's account of the gas-station pricing debate show about the difference between economic and emotional equivalence?
questions.a: When gas stations might be allowed to charge different prices for cash and credit, the credit-card lobby's fallback was that any difference be labeled a cash discount rather than a credit surcharge. Their psychology was sound: people more readily forgo a discount than pay a surcharge, in line with Thaler's slogan that costs are not losses. “The two may be economically equivalent, but they are not emotionally equivalent.”

questions.q: Which of these are pairs that Kahneman presents as two descriptions of the same outcome that feel different?
options: A cash discount versus a credit surcharge
KEEP £20 versus LOSE £30 out of £50
A one-month survival rate of 90% versus 10% mortality in the first month
Program A versus Program B in the lives-saved version of the Asian disease problem
Adam's 12 mpg car versus his new 14 mpg car
questions.explain: Each correct pair describes one objective outcome in two ways. Programs A and B are genuinely different options, a sure thing and a gamble, and Adam's two cars really differ in fuel use.

questions.q: Match each term from Frames and Reality to its meaning.
pairs: Framing effects
Unjustified influences of formulation on beliefs and preferences
Reality-bound
Preferences about states of the world, unaffected by the words describing them
Rationality index
A ranking of subjects by how little framing swayed their choices
Neuroeconomics
The study of what a person's brain does while he makes decisions
Opt-out form
Form under which people are donors unless they check a box
questions.explain: These terms frame the chapter: framing effects violate reality-bound preferences, the rationality index and neuroeconomics come from the brain study, and the opt-out form drives high organ donation.

questions.q: In the Asian disease problem, which program does a substantial majority choose when the options are described as 200 people saved for sure versus a one-third chance of saving all 600?
options: Program B, the gamble with a one-third chance of saving 600
Program A, the certain option of saving 200 people
Neither, since respondents split evenly between the two
Program B, because its expected outcome is clearly larger
questions.explain: In the lives-saved frame most respondents prefer the sure thing over the gamble. The expected outcomes are in fact equal, so the idea that the gamble is better on average is wrong.

questions.q: Match each program in the Asian disease problem to how its outcome was described.
pairs: Program A
200 people will be saved
Program B
One-third chance 600 saved, two-thirds chance no one saved
Program A′
400 people will die
Program B′
One-third chance nobody dies, two-thirds chance 600 die
questions.explain: A and A′ have identical consequences, as do B and B′; only the wording, lives saved versus lives lost, differs.

questions.q: In the lives-lost version of the Asian disease problem, a large majority choose the gamble, showing that people tend to be risk ____ when both outcomes are negative.
questions.explain: As in prospect theory, people are risk averse when outcomes are good and risk seeking when both outcomes are bad, and the disease problem shows the same rule for lives.

questions.q: What does Kahneman say the Asian disease problem adds to what was already known about choices between gambles and sure things?
options: People become risk neutral when lives rather than money are at stake
Risk seeking for losses disappears when the stakes are high enough
The same pattern of risk aversion for gains and risk seeking for losses holds when outcomes are lives rather than money
Professionals reverse the usual pattern and prefer gambles for gains
questions.explain: These conclusions were well established for money; the disease problem shows the rule applies to lives saved or lost, and that risk attitudes are not reality-bound.

questions.q: Explain how the Asian disease problem fits prospect theory and what it reveals about risk attitudes.
questions.a: Programs A and A′ have identical consequences, as do B and B′, yet most people choose the sure option when outcomes are described as lives saved and the gamble when they are described as deaths. This fits prospect theory: people are risk averse when outcomes are good and risk seeking when both outcomes are negative. The problem extends this rule from money to lives and shows that risk-averse and risk-seeking preferences are not reality-bound, since preferences between the same objective outcomes reverse with different formulations.

questions.q: Which of these groups does Kahneman report as susceptible to framing effects in Frames and Reality?
options: Physicians given lung-cancer treatment statistics
Public-health professionals given the Asian disease problem
Hospital patients and business-school graduate students given the lung-cancer statistics
Econs choosing between states of the world
questions.explain: Physicians, public-health officials, patients and students were all swayed by framing. Econs are by definition reality-bound and unaffected by the words used.

questions.q: Put the steps of the Asian disease framing demonstration, as Kahneman describes it, in order.
items: A person chooses to save 200 lives for sure in the lives-saved version
The same person chooses to gamble rather than accept 400 deaths in the lives-lost version
The person is shown that the two choices were inconsistent and asked to decide
The usual answer is embarrassed silence
questions.explain: The demonstration elicits contradictory choices across frames, then confronts the person with the inconsistency, which usually leaves them speechless because System 2 has no independent moral intuition.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman find it even more troubling than the framing effect itself when people are confronted with their inconsistent Asian disease choices?
questions.a: When told that they saved 200 lives for sure in one version but gambled rather than accept 400 deaths in the other, people usually respond with embarrassed silence. The intuitions behind the original choices came from System 1 and had no more moral basis than preferring to keep £20 over losing £30: saving lives for certainty feels good and deaths feel bad. Most people find that their System 2 has no moral intuitions of its own to settle the real question, so the intuitions turn out to be empty.

questions.q: True or false: Thomas Schelling's book Choice and Consequence, which contains Kahneman's favorite example of a framing effect, was written before Kahneman and Tversky's work on framing was published.
questions.explain: Schelling wrote the book before their framing work appeared, and framing was not his main concern; the example came from his teaching at the Kennedy School.

questions.q: Put the steps of Thomas Schelling's child-exemption lesson at the Kennedy School in order.
items: He explained that each child earns a standard exemption regardless of income
He asked whether the exemption should be larger for the rich, and students rejected it
He pointed out that taking a childless family as the default is arbitrary
He asked whether the childless poor should pay as large a surcharge as the childless rich, and students rejected it
He showed that the students could not logically reject both proposals
questions.explain: Schelling first elicited a rejection in the exemption frame, then rewrote the tax code around a two-child default to elicit an equally vehement rejection, and finally showed the two rejections contradict each other.

questions.q: In Schelling's child-exemption problem, what immediate response does Kahneman say System 1 delivers to any question about rich and poor?
options: Treat rich and poor families exactly the same
Reward families who have more children
Follow whatever the current tax law already says
When in doubt, favor the poor
questions.explain: System 1 applies a simple moral rule to favor the poor, but the rule gives contradictory answers to the same problem depending on how it is framed.

questions.q: Explain why Schelling's students could not logically reject both of his tax proposals.
questions.a: The difference in tax between a childless family and a family with two children can be described as a reduction for having children, with a childless default, or as a surcharge for being childless, with a two-child default. If you want the poor to get at least as large a benefit as the rich for having children, then you must want the poor to pay at least as large a penalty as the rich for being childless. Rejecting both a bigger exemption for the rich and an equal surcharge for the childless poor is therefore contradictory; the System 1 rule to favor the poor gives opposite answers depending on the frame.

questions.q: Kahneman says the moral intuitions in Schelling's tax problem depend on an arbitrary ____ point and are not about the real problem.
questions.explain: Whether the default family is childless or has two children is arbitrary, yet that reference point decides whether the difference looks like a benefit or a penalty.

questions.q: What stark message about the nature of framing does Kahneman draw from Schelling's problem, the Asian disease problem and the lung-cancer study?
options: There is no underlying preference that the frame masks or distorts; preferences are about framed problems
Frames distort a true underlying preference that careful thought can recover
Framing effects vanish when the stakes involve lives or moral questions
Moral intuitions are reliable once both frames are presented together
questions.explain: Kahneman rejects the idea that framing is an intervention hiding a real preference. “Our preferences are about framed problems, and our moral intuitions are about descriptions, not about substance.”

questions.q: Which of these conclusions does Kahneman draw from Schelling's child-exemption problem?
options: Our moral feelings are attached to frames rather than to reality itself
People have no compelling moral intuitions about how much tax individual families should pay
Framing masks a true underlying preference about the tax code
System 2 supplies clear moral intuitions once the frames are compared
questions.explain: Kahneman concludes that intuitions about rich and poor depend on an arbitrary reference point and say nothing about the real question of how to fill the tax-code matrix. He denies that any underlying preference is masked, and finds that people are left dumbfounded.

questions.q: What does Kahneman mean when he says that framing should not be viewed as an intervention that masks or distorts an underlying preference?
questions.a: The usual view treats a frame as a distortion layered on top of a real preference that could be uncovered. Kahneman argues that in Schelling's tax problem, the Asian disease problem and the surgery-versus-radiation study there is no underlying preference at all: when people see both frames they are dumbfounded and have no intuition about the actual states of the world. Our moral feelings are attached to descriptions of reality rather than to reality itself, so our preferences are about framed problems.

questions.q: Sort each choice by whether it shows risk aversion or risk seeking, as Kahneman describes the responses in Frames and Reality.

items.t: Most people choosing Program A when outcomes are framed as lives saved
Most people choosing Program B′ when outcomes are framed as deaths
Choosing the sure thing when it is labeled KEEP
Accepting the gamble when the sure thing is labeled LOSE
Preferences when the outcomes are good
Preferences when both outcomes are negative

questions.explain: Gain frames such as lives saved and KEEP favor the sure thing; loss frames such as deaths and LOSE favor the gamble, matching prospect theory's pattern.

questions.q: A charity asks donors to choose between a sure program and an equivalent gamble. Half the donors see the sure program described as protecting 300 of 900 families; the other half see it described as leaving 600 of 900 families homeless. Based on the Asian disease problem, which result would Kahneman expect?
options: Donors favor the sure program under both descriptions
Donors favor the sure program in the protecting description and the gamble in the homeless description
Donors favor the gamble under both descriptions
Donors choose the same way because the outcomes are identical
questions.explain: Framing outcomes as saved makes people risk averse, while framing the same outcomes as lost makes them risk seeking, so preferences reverse with formulation.

questions.q: In the lost theater tickets problem, why do most respondents think the woman who lost her tickets will go home without seeing the show?
options: She is now poorer overall and can no longer afford two more tickets
Losing the tickets is treated as a small reduction in general wealth
The lost tickets are posted to the account for that play, so the show's cost seems to have doubled
She worries that the theater will refuse to sell her replacement tickets
questions.explain: Lost tickets are naturally charged to the mental account associated with the play, making it appear to cost twice as much. Lost cash, by contrast, is charged to a general revenue account and seems only a small reduction in wealth.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman name as the explanation for the different answers to the lost-tickets and lost-cash theater problems?
options: Mental accounting
The sunk-cost fallacy
The anchoring effect
Regression to the mean
The availability heuristic
questions.explain: The two frames evoke different mental accounts, and treating the lost tickets as part of the play's cost ignores that the loss is sunk.

questions.q: In the lost theater tickets problem, lost cash is charged to a ____ account, so it seems only a small reduction in disposable wealth.
questions.explain: Because lost cash is not tied to the play, the theater patron simply feels slightly poorer, and most respondents think she will still buy tickets.

questions.q: Kahneman says the lost-cash frame is better because the loss, even if tickets were lost, is ____ and should be ignored.
questions.explain: History is irrelevant; only the options she has now and their consequences matter, and either way she is simply less wealthy than before.

questions.q: What advice does Kahneman say he would give the theater patron who lost her tickets?
options: Go home, since paying twice for the same play is more than it is worth
Buy only one new ticket to split the loss evenly
Ask the theater to replace the tickets before deciding anything
Ask whether she would have bought tickets after losing the same amount of cash, and if so, buy new ones
questions.explain: Kahneman recommends adopting the better frame of lost cash, which treats the loss as sunk. The idea that the show now costs double is exactly the mental-accounting error he wants her to avoid.

questions.q: In the lost theater tickets problem, why is the lost-cash frame better than the lost-tickets frame, and what general lesson does Kahneman draw?
questions.a: Lost tickets are posted to the account for the play, so its cost seems to have doubled, while lost cash goes to a general revenue account and seems only a small reduction in wealth. The cash frame is better because whatever was lost is sunk, and sunk costs should be ignored: only the options she has now matter, and she is simply less wealthy than before. The general lesson is that “Broader frames and inclusive accounts generally lead to more rational decisions.”

questions.q: True or false: In the MPG Illusion example, Beth, who switches from a 30 mpg car to a 40 mpg car, saves more gas than Adam, who switches from 12 mpg to 14 mpg, when both drive the same distance.
questions.explain: Over 10,000 miles Adam saves 119 gallons and Beth only 83. The mpg frame makes Beth's change feel larger, which is the illusion.

questions.q: Order these yearly fuel figures from the MPG Illusion example (10,000 miles of driving) from the most gallons to the fewest.
items: Adam's old 12 mpg car: 833 gallons
Adam's new 14 mpg car: 714 gallons
Beth's old 30 mpg car: 333 gallons
Beth's new 40 mpg car: 250 gallons
questions.explain: The small mpg gain on Adam's gas-guzzler removes 119 gallons, more than the 83 gallons saved by Beth's larger mpg gain, because fuel used depends on gallons per mile.

questions.q: Kahneman says the misleading miles-per-gallon frame should be replaced by the ____ frame.
questions.explain: Gallons per mile (or liters per 100 kilometers, used in most other countries) tracks fuel consumed directly, so it gives the right intuitions to car buyers and policy makers.

questions.q: Which of these statements about the MPG Illusion are made in Frames and Reality?
options: The miles-per-gallon frame misleads policy makers as well as car buyers
Raising a gas-guzzler from 12 to 14 mpg saves more fuel than raising a car from 30 to 40 mpg over the same distance
The 2013 fuel economy sticker shows gallons-per-mile information in large print
Larrick and Soll published The MPG Illusion in Science magazine in 2008
Most car buyers ignore gas mileage when choosing a car
questions.explain: Larrick and Soll's 2008 Science article showed the mpg frame misleads both buyers and policy makers. On the 2013 sticker the gallons-per-mile figure is in small print, and most buyers do list gas mileage as a factor.

questions.q: True or false: On the fuel economy and environment sticker for new cars starting in 2013, the gallons-per-mile information appears in small print alongside the familiar mpg information in large print.
questions.explain: Kahneman regrets that the correct formulation is in small print but calls the move a step in the right direction.

questions.q: What does Kahneman say about the five-year interval between the publication of The MPG Illusion and the new fuel economy sticker?
options: It is probably a speed record for a significant application of psychological science to public policy
It shows how slowly governments respond to psychological research
It was delayed by the car industry's lobbying against the change
It proves the rational-agent model guides public policy
questions.explain: Kahneman, noting Cass Sunstein's role at the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, presents the partial correction as remarkably fast for psychology reaching policy.

questions.q: Match each person to their role in Frames and Reality.
pairs: Richard Thaler
Kept a card reading COSTS ARE NOT LOSSES and described the cash-discount debate
Thomas Schelling
Taught a class on child exemptions in the tax code
Larrick and Soll
Identified the MPG Illusion in Science magazine
Cass Sunstein
Ran the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs under President Obama
Amos Tversky
Ran the lung-cancer framing study with physicians at Harvard Medical School
questions.explain: Each person contributed one example: Thaler on costs versus losses, Schelling on tax frames, Larrick and Soll on fuel frames, Sunstein on the sticker policy, and Tversky on survival versus mortality.

questions.q: Match each country to its organ donation rate as reported in the 2003 article Kahneman cites.
pairs: Austria
Close to 100%
Germany
Sweden
Denmark
questions.explain: Neighboring, culturally similar countries showed startling differences, which Kahneman traces to opt-out versus opt-in forms.

questions.q: Order these countries by their organ donation rate, as reported in the article Kahneman cites, from highest to lowest.
items: Austria
Sweden
Germany
Denmark
questions.explain: Austria was close to 100% and Sweden 86%, both opt-out countries, while Germany was 12% and Denmark 4%, both opt-in countries.

questions.q: The high organ-donation countries use an ____ form, in which people are considered willing donors unless they check a box.
questions.explain: In opt-out countries people must act to avoid donating; in low-donation opt-in countries they must check a box to become donors.

questions.q: Kahneman says the best single predictor of whether people will donate their organs is the designation of the ____ option, adopted without checking a box.
questions.explain: Whatever happens when people do nothing is what most of them end up with, which is why opt-out and opt-in forms produce such different rates.

questions.q: Sort these items by whether they belong to high organ-donation or low organ-donation countries in Kahneman's comparison.

items.t: Austria
Sweden
Germany
Denmark
People are donors unless they check a box
People must check a box to become donors

questions.explain: Austria and Sweden use opt-out forms and have very high rates; Germany and Denmark use opt-in forms and have low rates.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that, unlike other framing effects traced to System 1, the organ donation effect is best explained by the laziness of System 2.
questions.explain: People unprepared for the question must make the effort to think about checking the box, so many simply accept the default.

questions.q: What is Kahneman's imagined organ donation form, with 2 + 2 in one box and 13 × 37 in the other, meant to illustrate?
options: That people refuse to donate when the form looks like a test
That the effort required to choose an option would sway the donation rate, as System 2 laziness predicts
That System 1 can solve simple arithmetic but not moral questions
That donation decisions depend mainly on intelligence
questions.explain: If people must solve a problem in the box for their choice, the easier box would win; this dramatizes how the default works by sparing a lazy System 2 any effort.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman explain the organ donation framing effect by the laziness of System 2 rather than by System 1, and what policy conclusion follows?
questions.a: People who have already decided will check whichever box they want, but those unprepared for the question would have to make the effort of thinking about it, so most simply accept the default; the best single predictor of donation is which option is the default. Kahneman dramatizes this with a form requiring 2 + 2 in one box and 13 × 37 in the other. Once the role of formulation is acknowledged, anyone who believes a large supply of organs is good for society cannot be neutral between an opt-out form yielding almost 100% donations and an opt-in form yielding 4%.

questions.q: Sort each formulation by whether Kahneman treats it as the better frame or the worse frame in the section on good frames.

items.t: Gallons per mile
Miles per gallon
Treating a loss as lost cash from general revenue
Treating a loss as lost tickets charged to the play
Opt-out organ donation form
Opt-in organ donation form

questions.explain: Gallons per mile gives correct fuel intuitions, the general-revenue frame treats the loss as sunk, and the opt-out form yields far more donations for those who value organ supply.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, why does the organ donation case count as a point against the rational-agent theory?
options: It shows people donate only when they gain financially
It shows that donation rates depend on national culture
An important choice is controlled by an inconsequential feature of the situation, which the theory says cannot happen
It shows that people always choose the option requiring the least effort, as the theory predicts
questions.explain: A real theory asserts that certain events are impossible; the formulation of a form determining a significant choice is such an impossible event for the rational-agent model, so observing it falsifies the theory.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say about believers in the rational-agent model?
options: They take it for granted that the formulation of a choice cannot determine preferences on significant problems
They are not interested in investigating framing problems, which often leaves us with inferior outcomes
Their model survived the evidence against it, as theories can long after being falsified
They are trained to be sensitive to the power of inconsequential factors
questions.explain: Believers assume formulation cannot matter and so do not investigate it, and their theory has survived conclusive evidence. It is the skeptics who are trained to be sensitive to inconsequential factors.

questions.q: What does Kahneman say about how a scientific theory should be tested, and how does this bear on the rational-agent model and the debate over human rationality?
questions.a: A theory worthy of the name asserts that certain events are impossible, and when an impossible event is observed the theory is falsified; for the rational-agent model, important choices controlled by inconsequential features such as a form's default are such events. Theories can survive long after conclusive evidence falsifies them, and the rational-agent model has. The debate matters in the real world: believers take for granted that formulation cannot determine significant preferences and do not investigate, leaving inferior outcomes, while skeptics are trained to notice the power of inconsequential factors.

questions.q: Match each example from Frames and Reality to the idea it illustrates.
pairs: Lost theater tickets versus lost cash
Mental accounting and the sunk-cost fallacy
Opt-out versus opt-in donation forms
The power of the default option
Asian disease problem
Risk aversion for gains and risk seeking for losses, applied to lives
Schelling's child exemption
Moral intuitions that depend on an arbitrary reference point
Italy won versus France lost
Same truth conditions, different associations
questions.explain: Each example isolates one way description, rather than reality, drives judgment and choice.

questions.q: A company's retirement plan enrolls new employees automatically unless they tick a box to leave. Another company requires employees to tick a box to join. Based on Kahneman's organ donation discussion, what should we expect?
options: Enrollment will be similar, since the choice matters to employees
More will enroll at the second company, because joining actively builds commitment
Enrollment will depend mainly on the employees' cultural background
Far more employees will be enrolled at the first company, because most accept the default
questions.explain: As with organ donation, whichever option happens without checking a box is the best predictor of what people end up with, because a lazy System 2 often avoids the effort of deciding.

questions.q: Match each remark from the Speaking of Frames and Reality section to the idea it applies.
pairs: They will feel better if they frame the outcome as money kept rather than lost
Emotional framing of the same outcome as KEEP rather than LOSE
Imagine we did not own it; how much would we think it is worth?
Reframing by changing the reference point
Charge the loss to your mental account of general revenue
Using a broader mental account for a loss
Their list would shrink if they asked you to check a box to opt in
The power of the default option
questions.explain: Each remark applies an idea from the chapter: KEEP–LOSE framing, reference points, inclusive mental accounts and defaults.

questions.q: Which of these pieces of advice are given in the Speaking of Frames and Reality section?
options: Frame an outcome in terms of how much money was kept rather than lost
Reframe a problem by imagining you did not own the item
Charge a loss to your mental account of general revenue
Post a loss to the specific account where it occurred
Always choose the sure option when outcomes are framed as losses
questions.explain: The section recommends frames that make losses easier to bear and decisions more rational. Posting a loss to a specific account is the narrow framing the lost-tickets example warns against.
