questions.q: A website pre-ticks a box so that you stay on its mailing list unless you uncheck it. Using Kahneman's discussion of frames, explain why the website does this.
questions.a: Whichever option takes effect without checking a box is the default, and Kahneman calls the default the best single predictor of what people end up with, as in the organ donation forms. Most people have not decided in advance and a lazy System 2 avoids the effort of deciding, so they accept the default. As the chapter's closing remark puts it, the list would shrink if the site asked people to check a box to opt in.

questions.q: Frames and Reality is the last chapter of Part 4, Choices. What role does it play at that point in the book?
options: It shows that preferences attach to descriptions rather than to states of the world, a final point against the rational-agent model
It introduces the distinction between the experiencing self and the remembering self
It presents Bernoulli's utility theory as the basis for prospect theory
It explains how overconfident experts mispredict the outcomes of their choices
questions.explain: Part 4 builds the case that Humans are not Econs, and this chapter closes it by showing that framing alone reverses preferences, counting against the rational-agent theory. The experiencing and remembering selves belong to Part 5, which begins with Two Selves.

questions.q: What does the title Frames and Reality signal about the chapter's argument?
options: That good frames always reveal reality, so framing effects can be eliminated
That reality-bound Econs choose among states of the world, while Humans respond to the frames that describe them
That reality is socially constructed and no description is better than another
That frames matter only for money, while reality governs choices about lives
questions.explain: The chapter contrasts the description of an outcome with the outcome itself. It also argues that some frames are better than others and that framing affects choices about lives, so the other readings contradict it.

questions.q: Put the main sections of Frames and Reality in the order they appear.
items: Emotional Framing
Empty Intuitions
Good Frames
Speaking of Frames and Reality
questions.explain: The chapter moves from how emotional words sway choices, to the emptiness of the intuitions behind them, to which frames are better and what follows for policy and the rational-agent model.

questions.q: Put these chapters in the order they appear in Thinking, Fast and Slow.
items: Keeping Score
Reversals
Frames and Reality
Two Selves
questions.explain: Frames and Reality follows Keeping Score and Reversals at the end of Part 4, Choices, and is followed by Two Selves, which opens Part 5.

questions.q: How does Frames and Reality build on earlier chapters of Part 4, Choices, and why does it make a fitting end to that part?
questions.a: Earlier chapters of Part 4 developed prospect theory, with reference points, loss aversion and the different treatment of gains and losses, and examined mental accounting and preference reversals. Frames and Reality draws on these ideas: the Asian disease problem applies prospect theory's risk attitudes to lives, and the lost-tickets problem uses mental accounting and sunk costs. It ends the part by concluding that preferences are about framed problems rather than reality and that this counts against the rational-agent theory, before Part 5 turns to the two selves.

questions.q: In the opening of the Two Selves chapter, Bentham's famous sentence names which two 'sovereign masters' governing mankind?
options: Pain and pleasure
Reason and passion
Gain and loss
Memory and experience
questions.explain: Bentham opened his book by saying nature placed mankind under “two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure.” Gain and loss belong to prospect theory, and memory versus experience is Kahneman's own later distinction.

questions.q: In the Two Selves chapter, what did Bentham apologize for in an awkward footnote?
options: Claiming that pleasure could be measured precisely
Using the word utility for experiences of pain and pleasure
Ignoring the role of memory in moral choices
Borrowing the word utility from the economists
questions.explain: Bentham said he could not find a better word than utility for these experiences. The idea that he borrowed the term from economists reverses the history: economists later used the same word for something else.

questions.q: In the Two Selves chapter, Kahneman calls Bentham's meaning of utility, the pain and pleasure actually felt, ____.
questions.explain: To distinguish Bentham's interpretation from the economists' usage, Kahneman labels it experienced utility.

questions.q: In the Two Selves chapter, the economists' meaning of utility as “wantability” is what Kahneman calls ____.
questions.explain: For the last hundred years economists and decision theorists have used utility to mean wantability, which Kahneman calls decision utility.

questions.q: True or false: According to the Two Selves chapter, expected utility theory is mainly a theory about hedonic experiences.
questions.explain: Expected utility theory is about the rules of rationality that should govern decision utilities; Kahneman says it has nothing at all to say about hedonic experiences.

questions.q: In the Two Selves chapter, under what condition would experienced utility and decision utility coincide, and how is this assumption tied to the idea of rational economic agents?
questions.a: The two utilities coincide if people want what they will enjoy and enjoy what they chose for themselves. This assumption of coincidence is implicit in the idea that economic agents are rational: rational agents are expected to know their present and future tastes and to make good decisions that maximize those interests.

questions.q: In Kahneman's injections puzzle, where each daily injection hurts equally, how do people value reducing planned injections from 20 to 18 versus from 6 to 4?
options: They would pay the same for both cuts
They would pay more for the cut from 20 to 18
They would pay more for the cut from 6 to 4
They would refuse to pay for either cut
questions.explain: Cutting 6 to 4 removes a third of the injections, 20 to 18 only a tenth, so people pay more for the first. Equal payment is what experienced utility would justify, but it is not what people do.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman did not collect data on the injections puzzle because he considered the outcome evident.
questions.explain: Kahneman says he did not collect data because the outcome was evident, and invites readers to verify their own preference.

questions.q: In the injections puzzle, why does Kahneman call it absurd to pay more to go from 6 to 4 injections than from 20 to 18?
questions.a: The pain is the same every day with no adaptation, so both reductions spare exactly the same amount of pain: two injections. A decision maker who pays different amounts for the same gain in experienced utility is making a mistake. The puzzle suggests experienced utility can serve as the criterion by which a decision should be judged.

questions.q: According to the Two Selves chapter, what is the only basis traditional decision theory has for judging a decision to be wrong?
options: Its failure to maximize experienced pleasure
Its conflict with the decision maker's memories
Its departure from expert advice
Its inconsistency with other preferences
questions.explain: Kahneman notes that in decision theory the only basis for calling a decision wrong is inconsistency with other preferences. The injections puzzle pointed to a new standard, experienced utility, which decision theory did not use.

questions.q: In the injections puzzle, the experienced utility of equally painful injections can be measured simply by counting the ____.
questions.explain: Because each injection hurts the same, the total pain is proportional to their number, so counting the injections measures experienced utility.

questions.q: A patient pays $50 to cut a course of identically painful treatments from 6 to 4, but only $10 to cut a different course from 20 to 18. How would Kahneman's injections puzzle judge this?
options: As a mistake, since both cuts spare the same amount of pain
As rational, since a third is a bigger share than a tenth
As reasonable, since pain adapts over a long course
As a framing effect that cannot be called wrong
questions.explain: Both cuts remove two equally painful treatments, so experienced utility is the same; paying different amounts for the same gain is a mistake. The share argument is exactly the intuition Kahneman calls absurd, and the puzzle assumes no adaptation.

questions.q: Which of these are part of Kahneman's injections puzzle as he describes it?
options: The pain of each injection is the same from day to day
There is no adaptation to the pain
It compares cutting 20 to 18 with cutting 6 to 4
Kahneman tested it on a large sample of patients
The injections become less painful as the course goes on
questions.explain: The puzzle assumes one equally painful injection a day with no adaptation and compares two reductions of two injections. Kahneman collected no data, and diminishing pain would contradict the puzzle's setup.

questions.q: Francis Edgeworth imagined an instrument, the ____, that would measure the level of pleasure or pain a person experiences at each moment.
questions.explain: Edgeworth's imaginary hedonimeter was analogous to devices in weather stations, recording pleasure or pain over time.

questions.q: In Edgeworth's conception described in the Two Selves chapter, how is the total pleasure or pain of an episode measured, and what role does time play?
questions.a: Momentary pleasure or pain is plotted as a function of time, and the total experienced utility of an episode is the “area under the curve.” Time is critical: if Helen stays on the beach for 40 minutes instead of 20 with the same enjoyment, the total doubles, just as doubling injections makes a course twice as bad.

questions.q: In the colonoscopy study, why does Kahneman say patient B clearly suffered more than patient A by the hedonimeter measure?
options: B reported a much higher peak level of pain
B's procedure lasted much longer, so the area under the curve was larger
B's pain ended at a much worse moment
B rated the total amount of pain higher afterward
questions.explain: B spent at least as much time as A at every level of pain and the key factor was that B's procedure lasted much longer. Both had the same peak, and it was A, not B, whose procedure ended badly.

questions.q: In the colonoscopy study, patients A and B both had a worst rating of 8, while A's last rating was 7 and B's was 1. What was patient A's peak-end average?
questions.explain: The peak-end average is the mean of the worst moment and the end: (8 + 7) / 2 = 7.5 for A. The figure 4.5 belongs to patient B.

questions.q: In the colonoscopy study, the ____ rule says the global retrospective rating is well predicted by the average of pain at the worst moment and at the end.
questions.explain: The peak-end rule was one of the two findings from the statistical analysis of the patients' retrospective ratings.

questions.q: In the colonoscopy study, the finding that the length of the procedure had no effect whatsoever on ratings of total pain is called ____.
questions.explain: Duration neglect was the second finding: retrospective ratings ignored how long the procedure lasted.

questions.q: True or false: In the colonoscopy study, longer procedures led patients to give higher ratings of the total amount of pain.
questions.explain: The duration of the procedure had no effect whatsoever on ratings of total pain; this is duration neglect.

questions.q: True or false: In the colonoscopy study, patient A kept a worse memory of the procedure than patient B, even though B's procedure was much longer.
questions.explain: A's procedure ended at a bad moment, giving a peak-end average of 7.5 against B's 4.5, so A retained a much worse memory despite B's larger area under the curve.

questions.q: Why does the Two Selves chapter call hedonimeter totals 'duration-weighted'?
options: They give the most weight to the final moments of an episode
They weight each moment by how well it is remembered
They count only the moments of the most intense pain
They give equal weight to every moment, so longer pain counts for more
questions.explain: Computing the area under the curve weights all moments equally, so two minutes at level 9 is twice as bad as one minute. Weighting the end or the peak describes retrospective assessments, not hedonimeter totals.

questions.q: Which of these did the statistical analysis of the colonoscopy patients' retrospective ratings reveal?
options: Ratings were well predicted by the average of the worst and final pain
The length of the procedure had no effect on ratings of total pain
Patients' ratings closely reproduced their hedonimeter totals
Longer procedures were remembered as more painful
questions.explain: The two findings were the peak-end rule and duration neglect. Despite wording meant to encourage it, patients did not reproduce the integral of their reported pain.

questions.q: Which of these does the Two Selves chapter say a physician should do if the objective is to reduce patients' memory of pain?
options: Lower the peak intensity of pain
Give gradual rather than abrupt relief so the end is mild
Conduct the procedure as swiftly as possible
End the procedure abruptly at its most painful point
questions.explain: To improve the memory, lowering the peak could matter more than shortening the procedure, and gradual relief may help if the end is mild. Speed is the recommendation only when the goal is to reduce pain actually experienced.

questions.q: In the colonoscopy study, why does Kahneman say there is “an embarrassment of riches,” and what dilemma does this create for the physician?
questions.a: There are two measures of experienced utility, the hedonimeter total and the retrospective assessment, and they are systematically different: one is duration-weighted, the other ignores duration and weights the peak and the end. The physician must choose between reducing the memory of pain, for example by lowering the peak or providing gradual relief, and reducing the pain actually experienced by working swiftly even if that leaves an awful memory.

questions.q: Asked whether a physician should aim to reduce patients' memory of pain or the pain they actually experience, what does Kahneman say most people choose?
options: Reducing the memory of pain
Reducing the pain actually experienced
Splitting the difference equally
Letting each patient decide during the procedure
questions.explain: Kahneman's impression, without a proper survey, is that a strong majority come down in favor of reducing the memory of pain.

questions.q: In the Two Selves chapter, the ____ is the self that answers the question “Does it hurt now?”
questions.explain: The experiencing self answers about the present moment, while the remembering self answers “How was it, on the whole?”

questions.q: What does the anecdote about the scratched symphony recording illustrate in the Two Selves chapter?
questions.a: A listener said a shocking sound near the end “ruined the whole experience,” but only the memory was ruined. The experiencing self had already enjoyed some 40 minutes of musical bliss that the bad ending could not undo. The anecdote shows how hard it is to distinguish memories from experiences.

questions.q: What does Kahneman mean by “the tyranny of the remembering self”?
questions.a: The experiencing self has no voice, while the remembering self, though sometimes wrong, keeps score, governs what we learn from living, and makes the decisions. As a result we learn to maximize the qualities of our future memories, not necessarily of our future experience. Confusing experience with its memory is a compelling cognitive illusion that makes us believe a past experience can be ruined.

questions.q: Kahneman calls the remembering self's control over what we learn and decide the ____ of the remembering self.
questions.explain: Because the remembering self keeps score and makes decisions while the experiencing self has no voice, Kahneman calls this the tyranny of the remembering self.

questions.q: Which of these does the Two Selves chapter attribute to the remembering self?
options: It keeps score
It governs what we learn from living
It makes the decisions
It answers the question “Does it hurt now?”
It is the self that has no voice
questions.explain: The remembering self keeps score, governs learning and makes decisions. Answering “Does it hurt now?” and having no voice describe the experiencing self.

questions.q: A family's two-week holiday is mostly delightful, but the last day is ruined by a cancelled flight and hours stuck at the airport. Afterward they describe the trip as a disaster. Which idea from the Two Selves chapter best explains this?
options: Diminishing sensitivity to longer stays
The remembering self weights the end heavily and neglects duration
Loss aversion when comparing holidays to staying home
The experiencing self overriding memory
questions.explain: As with the scratched symphony, a bad ending dominates the memory while the many good days are neglected. Diminishing sensitivity explains the injections puzzle, not a ruined ending, and the experiencing self has no voice in such judgments.

questions.q: Sort each description into the self it belongs to in the Two Selves chapter.

items.t: Answers “Does it hurt now?”
Answers “How was it, on the whole?”
Has no voice
Makes the decisions
Lived through 40 minutes of musical bliss
Gave the scratched symphony a failing grade

questions.explain: The experiencing self lives through moments but has no voice; the remembering self evaluates whole episodes, keeps score and chooses.

questions.q: Sort each feature by the measure of experienced utility it describes in the colonoscopy study.

items.t: Computed by an observer from reports of moments
Assigns equal weight to all moments
Area under the curve
Insensitive to duration
Weights the peak and the end heavily
The patient's rating after the procedure

questions.explain: Hedonimeter totals are duration-weighted sums of momentary reports; retrospective assessments ignore duration and are dominated by two singular moments.

questions.q: Put the steps of the colonoscopy study in order.
items: Patients report their pain every 60 seconds
The procedure ends
Patients rate the total amount of pain they experienced
Analysis shows ratings follow the peak-end rule and neglect duration
questions.explain: Momentary reports were collected during the procedure, the global rating came afterward, and the statistical analysis then revealed the peak-end rule and duration neglect.

questions.q: Match each fact from the colonoscopy study to its value.
pairs: Length of patient A's procedure
8 minutes
Length of patient B's procedure
24 minutes
Patient A's peak-end average
Patient B's peak-end average
Shortest procedure among the 154 patients
4 minutes
questions.explain: A's short procedure ended at pain 7, giving a worse peak-end average than B's long procedure that ended at 1; procedures ranged from 4 to 69 minutes.

questions.q: Match each person to their role in the Two Selves chapter.
pairs: Jeremy Bentham
Called pain and pleasure mankind's two sovereign masters
Francis Edgeworth
Imagined the hedonimeter
Don Redelmeier
Physician who carried out the colonoscopy study
Christopher Hsee
Showed that adding broken dishes lowered a set's value
Amos
Worked with Kahneman on prospect theory when the injections puzzle arose
questions.explain: Bentham supplied the original meaning of experienced utility, Edgeworth its measurement, Redelmeier the colonoscopy data, and Hsee an earlier less-is-more result.

questions.q: Kahneman calls the experiment in which participants hold a hand in painfully cold water the ____ situation.
questions.explain: Its ugly technical name is cold-pressor, but Kahneman calls it the cold-hand situation.

questions.q: Put the events of the cold-hand experiment in order, as a participant experienced them.
items: Told there will be three cold-hand trials
Endure the first episode with one hand
Wait seven minutes, then endure the second episode with the other hand
Wait seven minutes more
Choose which experience to repeat as the third trial
questions.explain: Participants had the short and long episodes, each with a different hand, separated by seven minutes, and seven minutes after the second trial chose which one to repeat.

questions.q: Match each detail of the cold-hand experiment to its value.
pairs: Length of the short episode
60 seconds
Length of the long episode
90 seconds
Water temperature in the first minute
14° Celsius
Rise in temperature in the final phase
Roughly 1°
Share who chose to repeat the long episode
questions.explain: The long episode added 30 seconds of slightly warmer water to the identical 60-second short episode; 80% of those who felt the pain diminish chose to repeat it.

questions.q: In the cold-hand experiment, what happened during the extra 30 seconds of the long episode?
options: The water was made colder to raise the peak pain
The participant was offered a warm towel
Slightly warmer water raised the temperature by about 1°
The experimenter told the participant to keep still
questions.explain: A valve let in slightly warmer water so pain decreased slightly. The warm towel came only after removal, and the experimenter said nothing at the 60-second mark.

questions.q: Sort each feature into the cold-hand episode it describes.

items.t: Lasted 60 seconds
Lasted 90 seconds
Experimenter said to remove the hand at the 60-second mark
Ended with slightly warmer water
Left the worse memory
Was worse for the experiencing self

questions.explain: The long episode contained the whole short one plus 30 seconds of slightly reduced pain, so it was objectively worse but, by the peak-end rule, left the better memory.

questions.q: Which of these were features of the design of the cold-hand experiment?
options: Half had the short trial with the left hand and half with the right
Half began with the short trial and half with the long
Participants were told the truth that there would be only two trials
Participants recorded their pain continuously with their free hand
Participants were asked whether they preferred 90 seconds or only the first part of it
questions.explain: Hand and order were counterbalanced and pain was recorded continuously via keyboard arrows. Participants were told there would be three trials, and the researchers deliberately did not ask the 90-seconds-versus-first-part question.

questions.q: True or false: In the cold-hand experiment, participants who chose to repeat the long episode did not know which episode had been longer.
questions.explain: The subjects knew quite well which exposure was longer, since the researchers asked them, but they did not use that knowledge in choosing.

questions.q: Why did most participants in the cold-hand experiment choose to repeat the longer episode, and does Kahneman think they were masochists?
questions.a: They were not masochists; they “simply made a mistake.” They followed a simple rule of intuitive choice, picking the option they disliked least, and rules of memory, the peak-end rule and duration neglect, made the long episode the less aversive memory. Asked directly whether they preferred 90 seconds or only its first part, they would certainly have chosen the short option.

questions.q: According to the Two Selves chapter, what conflict was the cold-hand experiment designed to create?
options: Between System 1 and System 2 judgments of pain
Between gains and losses in the choice of trials
Between the left and right hands' sensitivity to cold
Between the experiencing and remembering selves, and between experienced and decision utility
questions.explain: The experiment set the experiencing self's interest against the remembering self's memory, and experienced utility against decision utility. Kahneman says the two selves do not correspond to the two systems, and the hands were counterbalanced.

questions.q: A clinic wants patients to be willing to come back for a second uncomfortable procedure. Based on the Two Selves chapter, which change would most improve their memory of the first one?
options: Add a period of milder discomfort at the end before stopping
Shorten the procedure even if the final minute is the worst
Tell patients in advance exactly how long it will last
Spread the same discomfort evenly over a longer time
questions.explain: As in the cold-hand experiment, a milder ending lowers the peak-end average and duration is neglected, so the memory improves. Shortening it while ending at the worst moment leaves an awful memory, as with patient A.

questions.q: In the Two Selves chapter, why does Kahneman say the cold-hand results are another example of the less-is-more effect seen with Hsee's dishes and Linda?
questions.a: The same operating feature of System 1 explains all three: “System 1 represents sets by averages, norms, and prototypes, not by sums.” Each cold-hand episode is a set of moments that the remembering self stores as a prototypical moment shaped by the peak and the end, so adding a milder phase improves the average even though it adds to the sum, just as adding broken dishes lowered the set's value.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman explain by System 1 representing sets by averages, norms and prototypes rather than sums?
options: Preferring the longer cold-hand episode
Valuing a set of 24 dishes more than a larger set that includes broken dishes
Judging Linda more likely a feminist bank teller than a bank teller
A squirrel tracking the total amount of food it has stored
Paying more to cut injections from 6 to 4 than from 20 to 18
questions.explain: Kahneman says the similarity among the cold-hand, Hsee and Linda cases is not accidental. A squirrel's food store is an example of memory storing integrals, and the injections puzzle reflects diminishing sensitivity.

questions.q: Sort each item by how the Two Selves chapter says it is represented.
groups: As an average or prototypical moment

items.t: An observer's area under the curve of reported pain
A squirrel's knowledge of its total stored food
The remembering self's memory of a cold-hand episode
System 1's view of a set of dishes
A hedonimeter total
Linda as a prototype

questions.explain: Sums integrate over time or quantity; System 1 and the remembering self store a representative moment or prototype instead.

questions.q: In the Two Selves chapter, what does the example of a squirrel storing food show?
options: Animals, unlike humans, neglect duration completely
Evolution can make memory store integrals when the total matters
Squirrels show the peak-end rule for pleasure
Memory always represents sets by their average
questions.explain: Kahneman says it matters for a squirrel to know its total stored food, so memory surely stores integrals in some cases. The integral of pain or pleasure over time may be less biologically significant.

questions.q: In the rat experiment where a light signaled an upcoming electric shock, what was the main finding?
options: Longer shocks produced proportionally greater fear
Rats failed to learn that the light predicted a shock
The shock's duration had little or no effect on the rats' fear
Fear depended mainly on how the shock ended
questions.explain: Rats quickly learned to fear the light, but only the painful intensity of the stimulus mattered, not its duration, showing duration neglect in animals.

questions.q: Put the steps of the rat fear experiment described in the Two Selves chapter in order.
items: A light comes on
An electric shock is soon delivered
The rats learn to fear the light
Their fear is measured by physiological responses
questions.explain: The light's onset signaled a shock; after learning, fear of the light was measured physiologically, revealing that shock duration had little effect.

questions.q: Which of these findings about rats are reported in the Two Selves chapter?
options: Fear of a signaled shock depends on its intensity, not its duration
Some rats able to stimulate pleasure areas of the brain will starve rather than stop
Up to a point, longer bursts of pleasurable stimulation do not increase eagerness
Rats remember the total amount of pain they receive over time
Rats prefer longer shocks that end mildly
questions.explain: Rats show duration neglect for both pain and pleasure, and brain stimulation can be so pleasurable they forgo food. Nothing in the chapter says rats track pain totals or prefer longer shocks.

questions.q: Match each animal or earlier example in the Two Selves chapter to the lesson Kahneman draws from it.
pairs: A squirrel storing nuts
Memory can store integrals when totals matter
Rats fearing a light that signals shock
Fear depends on intensity, not shock duration
Rats pressing a lever for brain stimulation
Intense pleasure can matter more than food
Hsee's set of dishes
Adding items can lower a set's value
questions.explain: The animal cases show that duration neglect has a long evolutionary history, while Hsee's dishes show System 1 judging sets by averages rather than sums.

questions.q: What do the animal studies in the Two Selves chapter suggest about the origins of the remembering self's rules?
questions.a: Rats show duration neglect for both pleasure and pain: fear of a signaled shock depends on its intensity, and longer bursts of pleasurable brain stimulation do not increase the animals' eagerness. Although evolution can store integrals when totals matter, as for a squirrel's food, the integral of pain or pleasure may be less biologically significant. Kahneman concludes that “The rules that govern the remembering self of humans have a long evolutionary history.”

questions.q: In the Two Selves chapter, Kahneman says the discrepancy between decision and experience in the injections puzzle originated from diminishing ____.
questions.explain: The difference between 18 and 20 injections seems smaller than between 6 and 4 because of diminishing sensitivity.

questions.q: Put Kahneman's argument in the Biology vs. Rationality section in order.
items: Equally painful injections can be measured by counting them
A decision that departs from experienced utility is wrong
The same logic applies to choosing the 90-second cold-hand episode
Different mechanisms produce the same outcome: decisions not attuned to experience
This challenges the rational-agent model of consistent preferences
questions.explain: Kahneman moves from measurable experienced utility, to a standard for judging decisions, to both studies, and finally to the challenge for the rational-agent model.

questions.q: Match each case to the source of the mismatch between choice or judgment and experience that the Two Selves chapter identifies.
pairs: Injections puzzle
Diminishing sensitivity
Cold-hand experiment
Duration neglect and the peak-end rule
Scratched symphony
Confusing the memory with the experience
Linda problem
Judging a set by its prototype
questions.explain: Kahneman stresses that the mechanisms differ, diminishing sensitivity versus rules of memory, but the outcome is the same: a decision not correctly attuned to the experience.

questions.q: According to the Two Selves chapter, what preferences do people have about the duration of pain and pleasure, and how does memory serve them?
options: We care little about duration, and memory matches this
We want pain brief and pleasure long, and memory tracks totals
We want intense moments, and memory stores them faithfully
We want pain brief and pleasure long, but memory neglects duration
questions.explain: Kahneman says we want pain to be brief and pleasure to last, but memory evolved to represent the peak and the end. “A memory that neglects duration will not serve our preference for long pleasure and short pains.”

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say the cold-hand study is bad news for believers in the rationality of choice?
questions.a: It shows we cannot fully trust our preferences to reflect our interests, even when they rest on personal experience laid down within the last quarter of an hour. Tastes and decisions are shaped by memories, and memories can be wrong. This challenges the cornerstone of the rational-agent model, that humans have consistent preferences and know how to maximize them; “An inconsistency is built into the design of our minds.”

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it concerns the injections puzzle or the cold-hand experiment, as the Biology vs. Rationality section compares them.

items.t: Error comes from diminishing sensitivity
Error comes from duration neglect and the peak-end rule
A cut from 20 to 18 seems worth less than from 6 to 4
People choose to endure 90 seconds rather than 60
Kahneman collected no data
The memory was formed within a quarter of an hour

questions.explain: Kahneman says the two cases have different mechanisms but the same outcome: a decision that is not correctly attuned to the experience.

questions.q: Match each term from the Two Selves chapter to its meaning.
pairs: Experienced utility
Bentham's sense: the pain and pleasure actually felt
Decision utility
The economists' sense: wantability
Peak-end rule
Memory rated by the average of the worst moment and the end
Duration neglect
The length of an episode does not affect its remembered rating
Hedonimeter total
Area under the curve of momentary reports
questions.explain: These are the chapter's core terms: two meanings of utility and the two memory rules that make the remembering self diverge from the hedonimeter.

questions.q: Sort each item by which meaning of utility it belongs to in the Two Selves chapter.

items.t: Bentham's pain and pleasure
Wantability
The subject of expected utility theory
Measured by counting equally painful injections
What people reveal by which cold-hand trial they choose
Edgeworth's hedonimeter reading

questions.explain: Experienced utility is felt hedonic experience; decision utility is what people want and choose, the subject of decision theory.

questions.q: A friend says their ten-year relationship was a waste because the last few months were miserable. Using the Two Selves chapter, how would Kahneman respond?
questions.a: The friend is judging the relationship entirely from the perspective of the remembering self, which is dominated by the end and neglects duration. Like a symphony with a screeching sound at the end, “the fact that it ended badly does not mean it was all bad”: the experiencing self lived years of good moments that the bad ending cannot undo.

questions.q: In the Two Selves chapter's example remark about duration neglect, what mistake is the listener said to be making?
options: Giving equal weight to a good part that lasted ten times as long as the bad
Remembering only the good part and forgetting the bad
Giving the bad part more weight because losses loom larger
Judging the experience by its average moment
questions.explain: The remark says the listener gives the good and bad parts equal weight although the good part lasted ten times as long, a case of duration neglect.

questions.q: Why does the Two Selves chapter open Part 5 of the book?
options: It sums up the heuristics and biases covered in Part 2
It introduces the experiencing and remembering selves that the later chapters on stories and well-being build on
It completes the case for prospect theory begun in Part 4
It shows how experts can learn to trust their intuitions
questions.explain: Part 5 is titled Two Selves and continues with Life as a Story, Experienced Well-Being and Thinking About Life, all of which apply the distinction this chapter introduces.

questions.q: True or false: In the Two Selves chapter, Kahneman says the experiencing self and remembering self correspond to System 1 and System 2.
questions.explain: Kahneman explicitly says the two selves do not correspond to the two familiar systems, although he describes memory as a function of System 1.

questions.q: Put the chapters of Part 5, Two Selves, in order.
items: Two Selves
Life as a Story
Experienced Well-Being
Thinking About Life
questions.explain: Part 5 runs from chapter 35, Two Selves, through chapter 38, Thinking About Life, before the Conclusions.

questions.q: Put the main sections of the Two Selves chapter in order.
items: Experienced Utility
Experience and Memory
Which Self Should Count?
Biology vs. Rationality
questions.explain: The chapter defines experienced utility, separates experience from memory, tests which self governs choice, then draws the lesson for rationality.

questions.q: True or false: The Two Selves chapter presents the cold-hand preference as another example of the less-is-more effect seen earlier in the book with Linda.
questions.explain: Kahneman links the cold-hand result to Hsee's dishes and to Linda, the subject of the earlier chapter Linda: Less Is More, since System 1 represents sets by prototypes rather than sums.

questions.q: How does the Two Selves chapter connect to Part 4 of the book, Choices?
questions.a: Part 4 dealt with decision utility, the economists' wantability governed by expected utility theory and prospect theory. Kahneman formulated the injections puzzle while he and Amos were still working on prospect theory, and its error comes from diminishing sensitivity. The chapter turns from how people choose to whether choices serve experienced utility, extending Part 4's challenge to the rational-agent model.

questions.q: In Kahneman's reflection on Verdi's La Traviata, what did he realize he cared about as he walked home from the opera?
options: Whether Violetta would have lived to 28 rather than dying at 27
Whether the young lover would arrive before Violetta died
Whether the lovers' reunion lasted a week rather than 10 minutes
Whether Violetta's sacrifice had protected the sister's marriage
questions.explain: He cared intensely about the last 10 minutes and whether the lover arrived in time, while an extra year of her life or a longer reunion would not have moved him. As he puts it, “A story is about significant events and memorable moments, not about time passing.”

questions.q: Using La Traviata, explain what Kahneman means when he says that duration neglect is normal in a story, and how this connects to the remembering self.
questions.a: Kahneman did not care whether Violetta lived a year longer or whether the reunion lasted a week instead of 10 minutes, but it mattered enormously whether her lover arrived before she died. Stories are about significant events and memorable moments, so their length is neglected and the ending often defines their character. The same features appear in memories of colonoscopies, vacations, and films, because the remembering self works by composing stories and keeping them for future reference.

questions.q: Kahneman writes that in a story, ____ is normal, and the ending often defines its character.
questions.explain: A story is about significant events and memorable moments rather than time passing, so how long it lasts is largely ignored. This is the same duration neglect found in memories of colonoscopies and other episodes.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, caring for people often takes the form of concern for the quality of their ____, not for their feelings.
questions.explain: When we want an estranged mother and daughter to reconcile before the mother dies, it is not only about feelings: “it is the narrative of the mother’s life that we wish to improve.”

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give as examples of caring about the story of a person's life rather than about that person's experiences?
options: A colonoscopy patient whose procedure ended with a gentle final few minutes
A man who died believing in his wife's love, though she stayed only for his money
The news that Violetta died at age 27 rather than 28
A scientist whose important discovery was proved false after she died
Wanting to know whether an estranged mother and daughter reconciled before the mother's death
questions.explain: The deceived husband, the posthumously refuted scientist, and the estranged mother are all cases where we are moved by changes to a life's story, even when the person never experiences them. Violetta's exact age was something Kahneman said would not have moved him at all.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that we pity a man who died believing in his wife's love, after learning she stayed with him only for his money, even though he had lived a happy life.
questions.explain: The example shows we care about the narrative of a life, not only its experiences: “We pity the husband although he had lived a happy life.”

questions.q: Which of these were features of the fictitious life of Jen used by Ed Diener and his students?
options: She was a never-married woman with no children
She died after a long and painful illness
She died instantly and painlessly in an automobile accident
In one version, 5 extra years were added that were pleasant but less so than before
The extra years were described as deeply miserable
Her story was told through her own daily diary entries
questions.explain: Jen was childless and never married, and died instantly in a car accident; the added years were only slightly less happy than the rest. The idea that the extra years were miserable misses the point of the study, which is that even mildly happy years lowered the evaluation.

questions.q: In Diener's between-subjects study of Jen's life, what effect did doubling the length of her very happy life from 30 to 60 years have on judgments of its desirability and total happiness?
options: No effect whatsoever on either judgment
A large increase in both judgments
An increase in total happiness but not in desirability
A small decrease in both judgments
questions.explain: Doubling the duration had no effect at all, which is clear evidence of duration neglect in the evaluation of entire lives. Her life was represented by a typical slice of time rather than as a sum over time.

questions.q: Kahneman concludes from the Jen study that her life was represented by a ____ slice of time, not as a sequence of time slices.
questions.explain: Because a prototypical period stood for the whole life, Jen's total happiness was judged as the happiness of a typical period, not the sum of happiness over her lifetime.

questions.q: In the Jen study, adding 5 slightly happy years to a very happy life caused a substantial drop in evaluations of her total happiness. What does Kahneman say this less-is-more effect indicates?
options: That participants misread the length of Jen's life
That loss aversion makes any change to a life feel like a loss
That young participants judge lives more harshly than older ones
That an average, or prototype, has been substituted for a sum
questions.explain: If people summed happiness, extra happy years could only add to the total; the drop shows they judged the average, which falls when less happy years are added. The idea that only young people judge this way was tested and rejected when parents and older friends gave the same pattern.

questions.q: Explain why, in Diener's Jen study, adding 5 slightly happy years to a very happy life made people judge her total happiness as lower, and what this reveals about how lives are evaluated.
questions.a: People represented Jen's life by a prototypical slice of time rather than as a sequence of moments, so her total happiness was taken to be the happiness of a typical period, not the sum over her lifetime. Adding pleasant but less happy years lowered that average and also gave her life a worse ending, so the evaluation dropped. This less-is-more effect shows that an average has been substituted for a sum: in judging whole lives, as with brief episodes, peaks and ends matter but duration does not.

questions.q: True or false: When Diener's team ran the extra-5-years comparison within subjects, so that each participant made both judgments in immediate succession, the less-is-more effect disappeared.
questions.explain: Kahneman expected reasonable people to see that the added years could not make a life worse, but he admits he was wrong: the intuition that the disappointing extra years made the whole life worse was overwhelming.

questions.q: Put these steps in the Jen research into the order Kahneman describes them.
items: A between-subjects test shows doubling Jen's life has no effect
A less-is-more effect is found for 5 added slightly happy years
At Kahneman's urging, a within-subject version is run
Parents and older friends of students answer the same questions
questions.explain: The between-subjects results came first, with the less-is-more effect, then the within-subject test Kahneman pushed for, and finally the check with older participants, which ruled out the idea that the pattern reflected the folly of the young.

questions.q: Kahneman discusses the objection that 24 hours of labor is worse than 6, and that 6 days at a good resort beat 3. How does he reconcile these intuitions with duration neglect?
options: Duration matters for physical pain but not for pleasure
These cases are judged by the experiencing self, not the remembering self
Duration seems to matter only because the quality of the end changes with length
People learn from experience to count hours in these familiar situations
questions.explain: The mother is more depleted after 24 hours and the vacationer more rested after 6 days, so what is really being judged is the progressive change in experience and how the person feels at the end. The idea that duration matters for pain but not pleasure ignores that both examples receive the same explanation.

questions.q: Which of these changes does Kahneman say left his feelings about La Traviata, or the evaluation of a life in the studies he describes, unaffected?
options: Learning that the lovers had a week together rather than 10 minutes
The lover arriving too late to see Violetta before she died
Doubling the length of Jen's very happy life
Adding 5 slightly happy years to the end of Jen's life
questions.explain: A longer reunion and a doubled lifespan change only duration, which is neglected. A late arrival would have made it an altogether different story, and the added mildly happy years did lower evaluations of Jen's life.

questions.q: Sort these changes by whether, according to Kahneman, they alter how a story or life is evaluated.

items.t: Violetta's lover arriving too late
Violetta dying at 27 rather than 28
The lovers' reunion lasting a week rather than 10 minutes
Jen living 60 very happy years instead of 30
Adding 5 slightly happy years to the end of Jen's life
Learning that a dead man's wife stayed only for his money

questions.explain: Endings and significant events change the story, while sheer length is neglected. That is why a late arrival, a worse ending for Jen, or a revealed betrayal matter, but an extra year or a longer reunion do not.

questions.q: Match each example from the chapter to the idea Kahneman uses it to show.
pairs: Violetta's last 10 minutes
The ending often defines the character of a story
Jen living 30 or 60 years
Duration neglect in evaluating entire lives
5 slightly happy years added to Jen's life
An average has been substituted for a sum
Labor lasting 24 rather than 6 hours
The quality of the end changes with the episode's length
questions.explain: Each example illustrates a different face of the remembering self: endings dominate, duration is neglected, averages replace sums, and apparent effects of duration really reflect changes in how the episode ends.

questions.q: How does Kahneman answer the common objection that duration obviously matters because 24 hours of labor is worse than 6 hours, and 6 days at a good resort is better than 3?
questions.a: He agrees that duration seems to matter in these cases, but says this is only because the quality of the end changes with the length of the episode. The mother is more depleted and helpless after 24 hours than after 6, and the vacationer more refreshed after 6 days than after 3. What truly matters in intuitive assessment is the progressive deterioration or improvement of the experience and how the person feels at the end, so duration neglect still holds.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says resorts cater to the remembering self by helping people construct stories and collect memories, while tourism offers restorative relaxation.
questions.explain: He says the reverse: resorts offer restorative relaxation, while tourism is about helping people construct stories and collect memories.

questions.q: Kahneman writes that the tourist taking frenetic pictures does not view the scene as a moment to be savored but as a future ____ to be designed.
questions.explain: Picture taking serves the remembering self by storing memories, though it is not necessarily the best way for the experiencing self to enjoy a view.

questions.q: Sort these vacation behaviors by which self they mainly serve, according to Kahneman.

items.t: Frenetic picture taking at every sight
A relaxing week at a familiar resort
Calling the highlights of a trip memorable
Savoring a view without a camera
Trekking through the jungle for the story
Returning to a happy place when memories will be wiped

questions.explain: Collecting pictures, stories, and memorable highlights, and choosing painful adventures, serve the remembering self. Relaxation, savoring the moment, and maximizing pleasure for an amnesic traveler serve the experiencing self.

questions.q: Put the steps of Diener's spring-break study into the order in which they happened.
items: Students keep daily diaries rating each day of spring break
Students give a global rating of the vacation after it ends
Students say whether they intend to repeat the vacation
Analysis links intentions to the final evaluation
questions.explain: Daily evaluations during the break came first, then a global rating at the end, then the intention to repeat; the analysis showed that intentions depended entirely on the final evaluation.

questions.q: After a ten-day trip, Maya's daily journal is mostly cheerful, but a chaotic last two days leave her rating the trip poorly overall, and she decides never to go back. Which finding from the chapter does this illustrate?
options: Intentions to repeat a vacation are determined by the final evaluation, not the diaries
Tourists who take many pictures enjoy their trips less in real time
The value of a vacation falls sharply when its memories are erased
People care less about their experiencing self than about a stranger
questions.explain: In Diener's spring-break study, intentions for future vacations were entirely determined by the final evaluation, even when it did not match the experience recorded in the diaries. As in the cold-hand experiment, people choose by memory.

questions.q: What did Ed Diener's spring-break diary study show about which self chooses vacations, and why does this matter?
questions.a: Students recorded daily evaluations in diaries, gave a global rating at the end, and said whether they would repeat the vacation. Their intentions were entirely determined by the final evaluation, even when it did not accurately represent the experience recorded in the diaries. So it is the remembering self that chooses vacations: as in the cold-hand experiment, right or wrong, people choose by memory whether to repeat an experience.

questions.q: Which of these reactions does Kahneman report from people imagining a vacation whose photos would be destroyed and memories wiped by a potion?
options: Returning to a place where they had been happy before, to maximize pleasure
Not bothering to go at all
Refusing to send themselves to climb mountains or trek through the jungle
Paying more for it than for a normally memorable vacation
Choosing the most adventurous trip, since its pains would be forgotten
questions.explain: Kahneman's impression is that erasing memories greatly reduces a vacation's value, so people would not pay more. Some would maximize pleasure in a familiar place, some would skip it, and many would avoid painful adventures whose value lies in being memorable.

questions.q: In Kahneman's amnesic vacation thought experiment, why do many people say they would not send themselves or another amnesic to climb mountains or trek through the jungle?
options: Because amnesic travelers would be unable to find their way safely
Because such experiences are mostly painful in real time and gain value from being memorable
Because such trips are too expensive to justify without photographs
Because the peak moment of reaching the goal is always disappointing
questions.explain: These experiences are valued for the expectation that both the pain and the joy of reaching the goal will be memorable; without memory, only the real-time pain is left.

questions.q: In Kahneman's thought experiment about a painful operation followed by a drug that wipes out all memory of it, how does he say most people react?
options: They insist on full anesthesia regardless of the amnesia drug
They value the amnesia drug more than relief from the pain itself
They become anxious because they cannot predict the pain
They are remarkably indifferent to the pains of their experiencing self
questions.explain: His informal observation is that most people are remarkably indifferent; some don't care at all, and others feel pity for the suffering self but no more than they would for a stranger in pain.

questions.q: Kahneman concludes the painful-operation thought experiment by saying: I am my ____ self, and the experiencing self, who does my living, is like a stranger to me.
questions.explain: He identifies with the self that keeps score and makes choices, and feels for the suffering experiencing self only as he would for a stranger in pain.

questions.q: What do Kahneman's two amnesia thought experiments, the memory-erased vacation and the painful operation with an amnesia drug, reveal about our attitude to our experiencing self?
questions.a: Wiping out memories greatly reduces the value people place on a vacation, and some would not go at all, showing they care about their remembering self more than their experiencing self. Likewise, most people are remarkably indifferent to pain they will not remember. Kahneman concludes that we treat the experiencing self like a stranger: “I am my remembering self, and the experiencing self, who does my living, is like a stranger to me.”

questions.q: Match each scenario from the Amnesic Vacations discussion to what Kahneman takes it to show.
pairs: Vacation whose memories will be wiped
Eliminating memories greatly reduces the value of an experience
Painful operation with an amnesia drug
Most people are indifferent to pains they will not remember
Climbing mountains or jungle trekking
Painful experiences valued because they will be memorable
Frenetic picture taking by tourists
Storing memories is often an important goal of a vacation
questions.explain: Each scenario shows the remembering self's dominance: experiences are valued for the memories they leave, and pain without memory matters little to us.

questions.section: Speaking of Life as a Story
questions.q: In the closing remarks of Life as a Story, what does Kahneman say about an Alzheimer's patient?
options: Her remembering self still constructs vivid stories of her life
She no longer experiences pleasure or pain in the moment
She no longer maintains a narrative of her life, but her experiencing self still responds to beauty
Her evaluations of her life now depend on duration rather than endings
questions.explain: The remark separates the two selves: the narrative kept by the remembering self is gone, but the experiencing self “is still sensitive to beauty and gentleness.”

questions.section: Speaking of Life as a Story
questions.q: Match each closing remark from Life as a Story to the idea it applies.
pairs: He is protecting the narrative of a life of integrity
We care intensely that our own life is a good story
The lengths he went to for a one-night encounter
Total duration neglect
Put away the camera and enjoy the moment
A vacation devoted to constructing memories
She no longer maintains a narrative of her life
An experiencing self without a remembering self's story
questions.explain: The remarks apply the chapter's themes: life as a story, duration neglect, the tourist serving the remembering self, and the experiencing self that persists without a narrative.

questions.q: Life as a Story follows the chapter Two Selves in Part 5 of the book. How does it build on that earlier chapter?
options: It replaces the peak-end rule with a new rule for long episodes
It extends duration neglect and the peak-end rule from brief episodes to stories and whole lives
It introduces the experiencing self for the first time
It shows that the remembering self is accurate when judging entire lives
questions.explain: The chapter links its ideas to colonoscopies and the cold-hand experiment and then asks, through the Jen study, whether the same rules govern evaluations of entire lives; they do.

questions.q: Put these parts of the chapter Life as a Story into the order in which they appear.
items: Reflection on the ending of La Traviata
Caring about the stories of other people's lives
Diener's study of the fictitious Jen
Amnesic vacations and the painful operation
Speaking of Life as a Story
questions.explain: The chapter moves from an opera's ending, to life stories in general, to experimental evidence about whole lives, then to vacations and amnesia, and closes with sample remarks.

questions.q: What does the title Life as a Story signal, and how does the chapter fit between Two Selves and the following chapter, Experienced Well-Being?
questions.a: The title signals that the remembering self treats a whole life the way it treats a story: by its significant moments and its ending, neglecting its duration. The chapter carries the two-selves distinction and the findings about colonoscopies and the cold hand into evaluations of entire lives and choices such as vacations. By ending with the observation that we identify with the remembering self and treat the experiencing self like a stranger, it sets up the next chapter's turn to measuring the well-being of the experiencing self.

questions.q: In Kahneman's account of well-being research, the standard survey question "All things considered, how satisfied are you with your life as a whole these days?" is addressed to which self?
options: The remembering self, invited to think about one's life
The experiencing self, reporting how the present moment feels
System 1, producing a quick intuitive impression of mood
System 2, calculating an average of all past moments
questions.explain: Kahneman says the question is clearly addressed to the remembering self, which is invited to think about your life. That is exactly why, after his colonoscopy and cold-hand studies, he was suspicious of it as a measure of well-being.

questions.q: According to Kahneman's proposal, what would make it sensible to say "Helen was happy in the month of March"?
options: She rated her satisfaction with life highly when asked at the end of March
She spent most of her time in activities she would rather continue than stop
She remembered March as a month with several memorable peaks of joy
She spent most of March in a calm, neutral state with no strong feelings
questions.explain: Helen counts as happy if most of her time went to activities she would rather continue than stop, little to situations she wished to escape, and not too much to a neutral state. A high life-satisfaction rating or a fond memory reflects the remembering self, and a mostly neutral month is exactly what the definition warns against.

questions.q: In Kahneman's memory of crying as a child when his mother took him away from his toys and later from the swings, what did that resistance to interruption show?
options: That young children cannot yet judge what is good for them
That the remembering self distorts childhood experiences
That he had been having a good time with the toys and the swings
That the pain of an ending dominates the memory of an episode
questions.explain: Kahneman treats wanting to continue rather than stop as a mark of good experience: “The resistance to interruption was a sign I had been having a good time”. The same idea underlies flow, where interruptions are not welcome.

questions.q: Why did Kahneman's team develop the Day Reconstruction Method (DRM) instead of relying only on experience sampling?
options: Experience sampling could only measure physical pain, not emotions
Experience sampling depended on the remembering self and so was biased
Experience sampling could not record who the person was with
Experience sampling was expensive and burdensome, so a more practical method was needed
questions.explain: The book says experience sampling is expensive and burdensome, so the team built the DRM hoping it would approximate its results. Experience sampling does record activities and companions, and it captures the experiencing self in the moment rather than relying on memory.

questions.q: Using the U-index as Kahneman defines it, what is the U-index of a person who spends 3 hours of a 15-hour waking day in episodes where a negative feeling was rated higher than all the positive feelings?
questions.explain: The U-index is the percentage of time spent in an unpleasant state, and an episode is unpleasant when a negative feeling outranks all positive ones. Three of fifteen hours is 20%; 80% would be the share of time that was not unpleasant.

questions.q: In the closing remarks of the chapter on experienced well-being, what does Kahneman say the objective of policy should be?
options: To raise average life satisfaction scores on national surveys
To reduce human suffering, aiming for a lower U-index in society
To push household incomes above the satiation level
To increase educational attainment across the population
questions.explain: The remark reads: “The objective of policy should be to reduce human suffering.” It adds that dealing with depression and extreme poverty should be a priority; raising life satisfaction, education or income beyond satiation targets the remembering self rather than experience.

questions.q: What did the DRM studies reveal about how emotional pain is distributed across people?
options: Almost everyone spends a similar, moderate share of the day in distress
Distress is concentrated among the wealthy, who report higher stress
A small fraction of the population does most of the suffering
Unpleasant episodes are spread evenly across all activities
questions.explain: About half the participants went through an entire day without an unpleasant episode, while a significant minority suffered considerable distress for much of the day. Kahneman concludes that “a small fraction of the population does most of the suffering”.

questions.q: In the DRM study of American women in a Midwestern city, what did Kahneman call the biggest surprise?
options: Work was more unpleasant than the morning commute
Watching TV was as unpleasant as housework
Socializing was less enjoyable than working
Time spent with one's children was slightly less enjoyable than housework
questions.explain: The biggest surprise was that, for American women, time with their children was slightly less enjoyable than doing housework. The commute (29%) was actually worse than work (27%), and socializing (12%) was far better than work.

questions.q: A manager wants to improve employees' moment-to-moment mood at work. Based on Kahneman's DRM findings, which change is most likely to help?
options: Easing time pressure and giving people chances to socialize with coworkers
Improving the benefits package that drives overall job satisfaction
Giving everyone a more prestigious job title
Having the boss spend more time sitting with each employee
questions.explain: Mood at work is largely unaffected by factors behind general job satisfaction, such as benefits and status. What matters are situational factors: socializing with coworkers, noise, time pressure, and the immediate presence of a boss, which was among the worst situations in the first study.

questions.q: Maya always eats lunch while answering emails at her desk. Applying Kahneman's comparison of French and American women, why is she likely to get less pleasure from her meal?
options: Because eating alone always has a high U-index
Because pleasure depends on attention, and eating is not focal for her
Because her remembering self will forget the meal by evening
Because time pressure makes food taste worse
questions.explain: Kahneman says “Attention is key”: to enjoy eating you must notice you are doing it. American women, who often combined eating with other activities, had their pleasure diluted, while for Frenchwomen eating was twice as likely to be focal.

questions.q: According to the Gallup data in Kahneman's chapter on experienced well-being, how is educational attainment related to the two aspects of well-being?
options: It raises both life evaluation and experienced well-being
It raises experienced well-being but not life evaluation
It is associated with higher life evaluation but not greater experienced well-being
It has no association with either measure
questions.explain: More education goes with a higher evaluation of one's life but not with greater experienced well-being; in the United States the more educated even report higher stress. It is the book's example of something that affects evaluation more than experience.

questions.q: Sam already earns well above $75,000 a year in a high-cost city and then gets a large raise. According to the Gallup analysis Kahneman reports, what is the most likely effect?
options: Both his life satisfaction and his experienced well-being will rise
His experienced well-being will rise, but his life satisfaction will not
Neither his life satisfaction nor his experienced well-being will change
His life satisfaction may rise, but his experienced well-being will not improve on average
questions.explain: Beyond a satiation level of about $75,000 in high-cost areas, the average increase in experienced well-being was precisely zero, yet higher income kept bringing higher life satisfaction well beyond that point.

questions.q: Why does the chapter on experienced well-being follow the chapters on the two selves and "Life as a Story"?
options: Having shown the remembering self to be an unreliable witness, Kahneman turns to measuring the experiencing self directly
It explains the peak-end rule for the first time before it is applied to vacations
It returns to prospect theory to explain why people value income gains
It introduces System 1 and System 2 as the two selves
questions.explain: Kahneman says he came to well-being from the mistaken memories of colonoscopies and cold hands, and since the remembering self had not been a good witness he focused on the experiencing self. The peak-end rule and the two selves were already introduced in the preceding chapters.

questions.q: True or false: In the DRM studies, Frenchwomen spent more time with their children than American women did but enjoyed that time less.
questions.explain: It was the other way round: Frenchwomen spend less time with their children but enjoy it more, perhaps because they have more access to child care and spend less of the afternoon driving children to activities.

questions.q: True or false: According to the Gallup data, ill health has a much stronger adverse effect on life evaluation than on experienced well-being.
questions.explain: The direction is reversed. Ill health has a much stronger adverse effect on experienced well-being than on life evaluation, which is why a headache can make a person miserable.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman remarks that beyond the satiation level of income, you can buy more pleasurable experiences but will lose some of your ability to enjoy the less expensive ones.
questions.explain: This is one of the chapter's closing remarks. It echoes the suggestion that higher income is associated with a reduced ability to enjoy small pleasures, supported by the finding that priming students with wealth reduced the pleasure they showed eating chocolate.

questions.q: True or false: In the Midwestern DRM study, the U-index was about 6% higher on weekends than on weekdays.
questions.explain: The U-index was higher by about 6% on weekdays, mostly because on weekends people spend less time in activities they dislike and are free of the tension and stress of work.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman ends the chapter by concluding that life satisfaction is not a flawed measure of experienced well-being but something different altogether.
questions.explain: He reverses his earlier view: life satisfaction “is not a flawed measure of their experienced well-being, as I thought some years ago.” Evaluations of life and actual experience are related but different.

questions.q: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi calls a state of total absorption in a task, in which interruptions are not welcome, ____.
questions.explain: Flow is Kahneman's example of an experience one would rather continue than stop, as when artists create or people are enthralled by a film, a book, or a crossword puzzle.

questions.q: Kahneman proposed to measure Helen's objective happiness from a profile of moment-by-moment well-being, following Edgeworth's ____ method of a century earlier.
questions.explain: Edgeworth's hedonimeter imagines recording experienced well-being moment by moment, the same approach used to assess the two colonoscopy patients.

questions.q: In experience sampling, a method invented by ____, a person's cell phone beeps at random times and asks what they are doing, who they are with, and how they feel.
questions.explain: Csikszentmihalyi invented experience sampling, the closest practical alternative to a continuous record of experience, which is impossible because nobody can live normally while constantly reporting.

questions.q: The method in which participants relive the previous day in detail, break it into episodes like scenes in a film, and rate their feelings in each episode is called the ____.
questions.explain: The Day Reconstruction Method was developed as a cheaper alternative to experience sampling, drawing on evidence that people who retrieve a past situation in detail can relive its feelings.

questions.q: Because DRM participants reported when each episode began and ended, Kahneman's team could compute a ____ measure of feeling across the whole waking day, in which longer episodes counted more.
questions.explain: Weighting by duration is what the remembering self fails to do, so it makes the DRM summary a measure of the experiencing self rather than of memory.

questions.q: Kahneman called the percentage of time that an individual spends in an unpleasant state the ____.
questions.explain: The U-index's appeal is that it rests on an objective measurement of time rather than a rating scale, so a drop from 20% to 18% means total time in discomfort fell by a tenth.

questions.q: Kahneman suggests improving experience by switching time from ____, such as TV watching, to active forms of leisure such as socializing and exercise.
questions.explain: The feelings attached to different activities show that how time is used matters, and active leisure feels better than passive leisure.

questions.q: The household income of about $75,000 in high-cost areas, beyond which experienced well-being no longer increases, is called the ____.
questions.explain: Above the satiation level the average gain in experienced well-being was precisely zero, even though life satisfaction kept rising with income.

questions.q: Which of these activities had a lower U-index than child care (24%) for the American women in Kahneman's Midwestern DRM study?
options: Morning commute
Housework
Work
TV watching
Socializing
questions.explain: Housework (18%), TV watching (12%) and socializing (12%) were all less unpleasant than child care. The morning commute (29%) and work (27%) were the two most unpleasant activities on the list.

questions.q: Which of these are properties of the U-index as Kahneman describes it?
options: It is based on an objective measurement of time rather than a rating scale
It averages people's answers on a 0 to 10 happiness ladder
It can be computed for activities such as commuting or child care
A fall from 20% to 18% means total time in discomfort fell by a tenth
It can only be computed for whole countries, not individuals
questions.explain: The U-index is the share of time spent in an unpleasant state, so it can be computed for individuals, populations and activities, and changes in it translate directly into time. The 0 to 10 ladder belongs to the Cantril life-evaluation question, a measure of the remembering self.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman suggest as relatively efficient ways to reduce the U-index of society?
options: Higher pay for workers already above the satiation level
Improved transportation for the labor force
Availability of child care for working women
Expanded access to university education
Improved socializing opportunities for the elderly
questions.explain: Better transport cuts the misery of commuting, child care eases one of the more stressful parts of the day, and socializing is among the most pleasant activities. Income beyond satiation and more education raise life evaluation rather than experienced well-being.

questions.q: Which of these findings about severe poverty does Kahneman report from the Gallup data?
options: A headache raises sadness and worry from 38% to 70% among the poorest tenth
The beneficial effects of the weekend are smaller for the very poor
The very poor are less affected by loneliness than others
The very poor report a lower baseline of sadness and worry than others
questions.explain: Severe poverty amplifies other misfortunes: the poorest tenth have a higher baseline (38% versus 19%) and a much larger rise with a headache, and they gain less from weekends. Divorce and loneliness also hit them harder, not less.

questions.q: Which of these did the gigantic Gallup samples confirm as important in experienced well-being?
options: Situational factors
Educational attainment
Physical health
Social contact with friends or relatives
Income above the satiation level
questions.explain: The Gallup analyses confirmed the importance of situational factors, physical health and social contact; contact with friends or relatives was the second best predictor of a day's feelings. Education and income beyond satiation raise life evaluation rather than experience.

questions.q: Put the steps of measuring unpleasantness with the Day Reconstruction Method in order.
items: Participants relive the previous day and break it into episodes
They rate the intensity of each feeling in each episode on 0 to 6 scales
An episode is classed as unpleasant if a negative feeling outranks all positive ones
The percentage of time spent in unpleasant episodes gives the U-index
questions.explain: The DRM first reconstructs the day into episodes, then collects feeling ratings per episode; comparing negative and positive ratings identifies unpleasant episodes, and their share of time is the U-index.

questions.q: Put the chapters of Part V, "Two Selves", in the order they appear in the book.
items: Two Selves
Life as a Story
Experienced Well-Being
Thinking About Life
questions.explain: Part V moves from introducing the experiencing and remembering selves, to the remembering self's view of life as a story, to measuring the experiencing self, and finally to how people think about their lives as a whole.

questions.q: Order these activities from highest to lowest U-index, as measured for American women in a Midwestern city.
items: Morning commute
Work
Child care
Housework
Sex
questions.explain: The U-index was 29% for the morning commute, 27% for work, 24% for child care, 18% for housework and 5% for sex.

questions.q: Put the steps of the argument in Kahneman's chapter on experienced well-being in order.
items: Doubts that the standard life-satisfaction question measures well-being
Proposes judging Helen's happiness by how she spends her time
Develops the DRM and the U-index to measure the experiencing self
Uses Gallup data to compare experience with life evaluation
Concludes that life satisfaction is something else entirely
questions.explain: The chapter starts from suspicion of the remembering self's survey answer, builds measures of the experiencing self, then compares the two aspects of well-being and ends by revising Kahneman's earlier view.

questions.q: Match each person to their role in the chapter on experienced well-being.
pairs: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi
Named the state of flow and invented experience sampling
Edgeworth
Proposed the hedonimeter, a moment-by-moment record of well-being
Alan Krueger
Economist who led efforts to bring the method into national statistics
questions.explain: Csikszentmihalyi supplied both the concept of flow and the experience-sampling method, Edgeworth's hedonimeter inspired the moment-by-moment profile, and Krueger was the economist on Kahneman's team.

questions.q: Match each group of women in the DRM studies to the share of time they spent in an unpleasant state.
pairs: American women
About 19%
French women
About 16%
Danish women
About 14%
questions.explain: American women spent about 19% of their time in an unpleasant state, somewhat more than French (16%) or Danish (14%) women.

questions.q: Match each measure to what it records.
pairs: Experience sampling
Feelings reported when a phone beeps at random moments
Day Reconstruction Method
Feelings in each episode of the previous day, relived in detail
U-index
Percentage of time spent in an unpleasant state
Cantril ladder
Where a person places their life between worst (0) and best (10)
questions.explain: Experience sampling, the DRM and the U-index all target the experiencing self, while the Cantril Self-Anchoring Striving Scale used by Gallup is a life evaluation by the remembering self.

questions.q: Match each factor to its effect on well-being as reported from the Gallup data.
pairs: Educational attainment
Higher life evaluation, but not greater experienced well-being
Ill health
Much stronger harm to experience than to life evaluation
Religious participation
Helps positive affect and stress but not depression or worry
Income above about $75,000
Higher life satisfaction, zero gain in experienced well-being
questions.explain: These contrasts show that the two aspects of well-being respond differently to the same circumstances. Religion's benefits were mainly to positive affect and stress, with surprisingly no reduction in depression or worry.

questions.q: Sort these measures by which self they mainly assess.

items.t: Experience sampling
Day Reconstruction Method episode ratings
U-index
Gallup reports of emotions felt the previous day
How satisfied are you with your life as a whole?
Cantril ladder of best and worst possible life

questions.explain: Experience sampling, DRM ratings, the U-index and reports of yesterday's emotions capture how life feels as it is lived. Global life-satisfaction questions and the Cantril ladder ask for an evaluation, which Kahneman interprets as the satisfaction of the remembering self.
