questions.q: Sort these factors by which aspect of well-being they affect more, according to the Gallup data.

items.t: Ill health
Living with children
Religious participation
Educational attainment
Income beyond the satiation level

questions.explain: Ill health, children and religion matter more in the currency of daily feelings than in life evaluation. Education and income beyond about $75,000 raise evaluation without improving experience.

questions.q: Sort these feelings named in the chapter on experienced well-being into positive and negative emotions.

items.t: Engagement
Hope
Amusement
Shame
Loneliness
Anger

questions.explain: Kahneman stresses that a moment is not easily captured by a single happiness value: positive feelings include love, joy, engagement, hope and amusement, and negative ones include anger, shame, depression and loneliness.

questions.q: Sort these situations by how they fit Kahneman's definition of Helen being happy.

items.t: Being absorbed in a crossword puzzle
Being enthralled by a film
Playing so happily that being taken away brings tears
Being stuck in a situation she wishes to escape
Spending long stretches in a neutral state

questions.explain: Helen is happy if she spends most of her time in activities she would rather continue than stop, such as flow states, and little time in situations she wants to escape or in a neutral state, which matters because life is short.

questions.q: Why was Kahneman suspicious of global life satisfaction as a measure of well-being when he began studying the subject?
questions.a: The standard survey question about satisfaction with life as a whole is addressed to the remembering self. Kahneman came to well-being from studies of colonoscopies and cold hands, where the remembering self had produced mistaken memories, so it had not proved a good witness. He therefore chose to focus on the well-being of the experiencing self.

questions.q: Explain Kahneman's criterion for saying that "Helen was happy in the month of March" and why each part matters.
questions.a: Helen was happy if she spent most of her time in activities she would rather continue than stop, little time in situations she wished to escape, and not too much time in a neutral state. Wanting to continue, as in flow or Kahneman’s own childhood memory of crying when he was taken away from his toys, signals good experience. Neutral time counts against happiness “because life is short”.

questions.q: How does the Day Reconstruction Method work, and why did Kahneman's team believe it captured the experiencing self?
questions.a: Participants relive the previous day in detail, break it into episodes like scenes in a film, and then report for each episode what they were doing, who they were with, and how intensely they felt various feelings on 0 to 6 scales. The method relied on evidence that people who retrieve a past situation in detail can relive its feelings, and comparisons with experience sampling confirmed its validity. Episode times allowed a duration-weighted measure of the whole day.

questions.q: What did Kahneman learn from how unpleasant time is distributed across people in the DRM studies, and why does it matter for policy?
questions.a: About half the participants had an entire day with no unpleasant episode, while a significant minority were in considerable distress for much of the day. So “a small fraction of the population does most of the suffering”, through illness, temperament or misfortune. This is why reducing the U-index, especially by dealing with depression and extreme poverty, should be a priority of policy.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say that attention is key to experienced well-being? Use the eating example.
questions.a: Our emotional state is largely determined by what we attend to, and we normally focus on our current activity and immediate environment, so we draw pleasure and pain from what is happening if we attend to it. To enjoy eating you must notice that you are eating. Frenchwomen were twice as likely as American women to make eating focal, while Americans combined it with other activities and so diluted their pleasure. Exceptions occur when recurrent thoughts, such as love or grief, dominate experience.

questions.q: What answer does the Gallup research give to the question "Can money buy happiness?"
questions.a: The conclusion is that being poor makes one miserable, and being rich may enhance life satisfaction but does not, on average, improve experienced well-being. Severe poverty amplifies other misfortunes such as illness, divorce and loneliness. Beyond a satiation level of about $75,000 in high-cost areas, extra income added precisely zero to experienced well-being, though it kept raising life satisfaction.

questions.q: Why might the extra pleasures that a higher income can buy not show up in reports of emotional experience?
questions.a: Kahneman offers a plausible interpretation: “higher income is associated with a reduced ability to enjoy the small pleasures of life.” Suggestive evidence comes from a study in which students primed with the idea of wealth showed less pleasure on their faces while eating a chocolate bar. Gains from vacations or opera tickets may be offset by enjoying everyday pleasures less.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say the easiest way for an individual to increase happiness is to control their use of time?
questions.a: Few people can will themselves to have a sunnier disposition, but the use of time is one of the areas of life over which people have some control. Since mood depends mainly on the current situation and activity, people can arrange to spend less time commuting and more time doing things they enjoy with people they like. They can also switch from passive leisure like TV to active leisure such as socializing and exercise.

questions.q: How does the conclusion of the chapter on experienced well-being echo the colonoscopy studies of the earlier "Two Selves" chapter, and how does it revise Kahneman's starting position?
questions.a: Just as colonoscopy patients' memories differed from what they actually experienced, people's evaluations of their lives and their actual experience are related but different; income, education and health affect them differently. Kahneman began inclined to dismiss the remembering self as an error-prone witness, but he now concludes that life satisfaction is not a flawed measure of experienced well-being: “It is something else entirely.” Both selves have to be taken seriously.

questions.q: In Chapter 38, where do the data in Kahneman's Figure 16 on marriage and life satisfaction come from?
options: The German Socio-Economic Panel, which asked the same people every year
A one-time survey of newlyweds and divorced people in the United States
Day Reconstruction Method diaries kept by married and single women
A Gallup poll comparing happiness across married and unmarried adults
questions.explain: Clark, Diener, and Georgellis analyzed the German Socio-Economic Panel, in which the same respondents rated their life satisfaction every year and reported major changes in their lives. The DRM studies of women with and without a mate are a separate piece of evidence in the chapter.

questions.q: True or false: In Kahneman's account, a disposition for well-being is as heritable as height or intelligence, as shown by studies of twins separated at birth.
questions.explain: Kahneman gives the genetics of temperament as one reason for the low correlations between people's circumstances and their satisfaction with life. People who appear equally fortunate vary greatly in how happy they are.

questions.q: Kahneman, using a term from Daniel Gilbert and Timothy Wilson, says that for many people the decision to get married reflects a massive error of ____.
questions.explain: Couples expect marriage to make them happier or to preserve their bliss, and they do not believe the high rates of divorce and disappointment apply to them. That misprediction of future feelings is an error of affective forecasting.

questions.q: In Chapter 38, what alternative reading does Kahneman offer for the steep decline of life satisfaction after marriage shown in Figure 16?
options: The early joys of marriage disappear as married life becomes routine
Unhappy people are more likely than happy people to get married
The graph tracks how likely people are to think of their marriage when asked about life
Respondents grow tired of the yearly survey and answer more carelessly
questions.explain: Kahneman reads the graph through heuristics of judgment: “Attention is the key to the puzzle.” The salience of the marriage fades as its novelty wanes, so the curve may say little about happiness or adaptation; the routine-joys idea is the common interpretation he questions.

questions.q: In Norbert Schwarz's experiment described in Chapter 38, what happened when half the subjects found a dime on the copying machine before a life-satisfaction questionnaire?
options: Their reported satisfaction with life as a whole rose markedly
Their reported satisfaction rose only for questions about money
They became suspicious and gave more cautious, lower ratings
They reported more happiness these days but not more life satisfaction
questions.explain: The minor lucky incident caused a marked improvement in reported satisfaction with life as a whole. Kahneman uses it, with the dating study, to show that a mood heuristic can substitute for a global evaluation of life.

questions.q: In Chapter 38, the dime-on-the-copier experiment shows that a ____ is one way people answer life-satisfaction questions, letting current feelings stand in for the whole of life.
questions.explain: Finding a small coin lifted mood, and the mood was then reported as satisfaction with life as a whole. Kahneman calls this a mood heuristic.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say are likely to come to mind when you are quickly asked to evaluate your life?
options: Significant events in your recent past or near future
Recurrent concerns, such as the health of a spouse
Important achievements and painful failures
A careful weighting of every domain of your life
Long-run statistics on happiness in your country
questions.explain: Kahneman lists recent or coming events, recurrent concerns, and achievements and failures as things that come to mind. The quick score is set by a small sample of highly available ideas, not by a careful weighting of all the domains of life.

questions.q: Why, according to Kahneman in Chapter 38, should answers to global well-being questions such as "How satisfied are you with your life as a whole?" be taken with a grain of salt?
questions.a: Such questions are hard, yet people answer them in seconds, so most substitute an easier question; System 1 is at work. The dating question and the dime on the copier showed that irrelevant moods and recent prompts change the answer. Even without such accidents, the score is determined by a small sample of highly available ideas, not by a careful weighting of the domains of one's life.

questions.q: Explain how Kahneman reinterprets Figure 16, which shows life satisfaction rising around marriage and then falling steeply.
questions.a: The usual reading is adaptation: early joys fade as marriage becomes routine. Kahneman instead treats a life-satisfaction answer as a judgment built from whatever comes to mind. People recently married or about to marry are likely to think of it, and since marriage is voluntary they are happy with the thought, so the graph can be read as the likelihood of thinking about the marriage, which falls as its novelty wanes. On this reading the curve tells us little about happiness or about adaptation to marriage.

questions.q: Sort each statement about Figure 16 by which reading of the marriage graph it belongs to in Chapter 38.

items.t: The early joys of marriage disappear as experiences become routine
A tide of raised happiness lasts a few years and gradually recedes
The graph shows how likely people are to think of their marriage when asked
The salience of the marriage fades as its novelty wanes
People glad to be reminded of their marriage are not necessarily happier the rest of the time

questions.explain: The adaptation reading treats the curve as a real rise and fall in happiness. Kahneman's alternative says the curve reflects what comes to mind when people answer, so we cannot infer a receding tide of happiness from it.

questions.q: According to Chapter 38, why do Kahneman's DRM studies find no overall difference in experienced well-being between women who live with a mate and women who do not?
options: Marriage makes no real difference to how women spend their days
Women with a mate quickly adapt and stop noticing their partner
Women without a mate overstate their happiness in the diaries
Marriage changes some aspects of life for the better and others for the worse
questions.explain: Women with a mate spend more time making love but also more time on housework, cooking, and child care, and much less time with friends. The effects balance on average; the claim that marriage makes no difference is exactly what Kahneman denies.

questions.q: Which of these do women who have a mate spend more time doing, according to the DRM findings in Chapter 38?
options: Making love
Doing housework and preparing food
Caring for children
Spending time with friends
Spending time alone
questions.explain: Married women spend more time making love, doing housework, preparing food, and caring for children. They spend less time alone and much less time with friends.

questions.q: Kahneman says the correlation between marriage and well-being is low partly because of ____: the same situation may be good for some people and bad for others, and new circumstances have both benefits and costs.
questions.explain: Marriage improves some parts of life and worsens others, and suits some people more than others. These balancing effects keep the average correlation with well-being low.

questions.q: In Chapter 38, what does Kahneman give as one main reason for the low correlations between people's circumstances and their satisfaction with life?
options: People misreport their circumstances on surveys
Experienced happiness and life satisfaction are largely set by the genetics of temperament
Life circumstances change too often to be measured reliably
Most people's circumstances are nearly identical to one another
questions.explain: Kahneman says both experienced happiness and life satisfaction are largely determined by the genetics of temperament, so people who appear equally fortunate vary greatly in happiness. Balancing effects and differences in how much people care about money add to the picture.

questions.q: Give the reasons Kahneman offers for why people's life circumstances, such as marriage or income, correlate only weakly with their well-being.
questions.a: Both experienced happiness and life satisfaction are largely determined by the genetics of temperament; a disposition for well-being is as heritable as height or intelligence. Some circumstances, like marriage, have balancing effects: they are good for some people and bad for others, and bring both benefits and costs. For others, like high income, the effect is generally positive but varies because some people care much more about money than others.

questions.q: Which of these were measured in the study of about 12,000 people who started higher education at elite schools in 1976?
options: How important "being very well-off financially" was to them at age 17 or 18
Their income in 1995
A global measure of their life satisfaction
Their mood in each episode of a reconstructed day
Their scores on an intelligence test
questions.explain: Participants rated the financial goal on a 4-point scale as teenagers; about twenty years later they reported their 1995 income and their overall life satisfaction. Day-by-day mood belongs to the separate DRM method.

questions.q: Match each group or comparison in the elite-schools study to its finding.
pairs: Physicians and medical professionals, per scale point
Over $14,000 more job income in 1995 dollars
Nonworking married women, per scale point
Over $12,000 more household income
Money rated essential: high vs low income
Life satisfaction differed by .57 on a 5-point scale
Money rated not important: high vs low income
Life satisfaction differed by only .12
questions.explain: Each extra point on the money-importance scale predicted more income, for married women through the spouse's earnings. The effect of income on life satisfaction was much larger for those who had called being well-off financially essential.

questions.q: True or false: In the elite-schools study, the effect of income on life satisfaction was larger for people who had said at 18 that money was not important to them.
questions.explain: The effect was larger for those who had listed being well-off financially as essential: .57 point versus only .12 for those who said money was not important. People who wanted money and did not get it were significantly more dissatisfied.

questions.q: In the elite-schools study, which goal set at age 17 or 18 was the least promising for life satisfaction 20 years later?
options: Being very well-off financially
Raising a family
Becoming an authority in one's field
Becoming accomplished in a performing art
questions.explain: Kahneman reports that the least promising goal was “becoming accomplished in a performing art.” It illustrates his point that setting goals that are especially difficult to attain is one recipe for a dissatisfied adulthood.

questions.q: What did the elite-schools study reveal about the goals young people set for themselves, according to Kahneman?
questions.a: Goals make a large difference: many who rated being well-off financially as important at 18 had high incomes nineteen years later. The importance given to money also predicted how much income mattered to adult life satisfaction: those who wanted money and got it were more satisfied, and those who wanted it and did not were more dissatisfied. Setting goals that are especially hard to attain, such as becoming accomplished in a performing art, is a recipe for a dissatisfied adulthood.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman concludes in Chapter 38 that well-being should be defined by experienced well-being alone, ignoring how people evaluate their lives.
questions.explain: Kahneman says the elite-schools findings changed his mind: an exclusive focus on experienced well-being is not tenable because goals matter so much. He equally rejects a view that looks only at life evaluation.

questions.q: Kahneman concludes that we must accept the complexities of a ____, in which the well-being of both the experiencing self and the remembering self is considered.
questions.explain: Ignoring what people want is untenable, and so is ignoring how people feel as they live. Kahneman therefore settles on a hybrid view that considers both selves.

questions.q: Describe the hybrid view of well-being that Kahneman adopts at the end of the opening of Chapter 38, and why he rejects each of the two simpler views.
questions.a: An exclusive focus on experienced well-being is untenable because the goals people set are so important to what they do and how they feel; we cannot ignore what people want. But a concept that looks only at how people feel when they think about their life, ignoring how they feel as they live, is also untenable. So the well-being of both selves, experiencing and remembering, must be considered together.

questions.q: Priya is asked for a survey how satisfied she is with her life, a week after getting a long-awaited promotion. Based on Kahneman's account of life-satisfaction judgments, what is most likely to happen?
options: She will carefully weigh every domain of her life before answering
Her answer will be unaffected because promotions do not change happiness
The salient promotion will come to mind and lift her rating
She will rate her life lower because of the stress of a new role
questions.explain: Kahneman says a quick life evaluation is set by a small sample of highly available ideas, and recent significant events are among the first to come to mind. A fresh, welcome promotion will loom large in her answer, just as a recent marriage does.

questions.q: Put the steps of Norbert Schwarz's dime experiment, as Kahneman describes it, in order.
items: Subjects are invited to the lab to complete a life-satisfaction questionnaire
Before starting, they are asked to photocopy a sheet of paper
Half of them find a dime planted on the copying machine
They rate their satisfaction with life as a whole
Those who found the dime report markedly higher satisfaction
questions.explain: The photocopying errand came before the questionnaire, so the planted dime could lift mood just before the rating. The minor lucky incident raised reported satisfaction with life as a whole.

questions.q: Put the steps of Kahneman's argument in the opening of Chapter 38 in order.
items: Life satisfaction rises around marriage and then falls steeply
Life-satisfaction answers are judgments built by substitution
Marriage has no overall effect on experienced well-being in the DRM
Teenagers' goals predict their income and adult satisfaction
Well-being needs a hybrid view of both selves
questions.explain: Kahneman starts with Figure 16, reinterprets it as a heuristic judgment, shows that experienced well-being is balanced across marriage, turns to the lasting effects of goals, and ends by adopting a hybrid view.

questions.q: Match each researcher to the work Kahneman describes in Chapter 38.
pairs: Clark, Diener, and Georgellis
Life satisfaction around marriage in the German panel
Norbert Schwarz
The dime planted on the copying machine
David Schkade
With Kahneman, the happiness of Californians
Beruria Cohn
Estimates of time paraplegics spend in a bad mood
Gilbert and Wilson
The terms affective forecasting and miswanting
questions.explain: Each name is tied to one study or idea in the chapter. Gilbert and Wilson supplied the vocabulary of affective forecasting, miswanting, and focalism; the others ran or analyzed the studies listed.

questions.q: Match each study in the opening of Chapter 38 to what Kahneman takes it to show.
pairs: Students asked how many dates they had
One salient fact can stand in for a whole life
The German panel on marriage (Figure 16)
Salience of a marriage fades as its novelty wanes
DRM study of women with and without a mate
Gains and costs of marriage balance in daily experience
Elite-schools study of 12,000 people
Goals set at 18 shape income and later satisfaction
questions.explain: The dating study and the marriage graph show that quick life evaluations rest on what comes to mind. The DRM and elite-schools studies show that experience and goals must both be counted.

questions.q: Sort each finding from Chapter 38 by whether it concerns experienced well-being or life evaluation.

items.t: Women with and without a mate show no overall DRM difference
Colostomy patients' experience sampling matches healthy people
Paraplegics are in a fairly good mood most of the time within a month
Satisfaction ratings peak around the time of marriage
Finding a dime raises satisfaction with life as a whole
Colostomy patients would trade years of life to be rid of it

questions.explain: Moment-by-moment measures such as the DRM and experience sampling track the experiencing self. Answers to questions about one's life as a whole reflect the remembering self's evaluation, which is open to mood and focusing effects.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say that marriage, on average, does not change experienced well-being, even though it does make a difference to happiness?
questions.a: In the DRM studies, women who lived with a mate and women who did not showed no overall difference in experienced well-being. Women with a mate spend less time alone and much less with friends, and more time making love but also more time on housework, preparing food, and caring for children, which are relatively unpopular activities. Marriage changes some aspects of life for the better and others for the worse, and time with a husband is more pleasant for some than others, so the effects balance out on average.

questions.q: Kahneman says people evaluating their life use heuristics that are examples of both ____ and WYSIATI, as System 1 lets a small part of life stand for the whole.
questions.explain: Fast answers and mood effects show people are not examining their lives carefully. They answer an easier question in place of the hard one, which is substitution, and use only what comes to mind, which is WYSIATI.

questions.q: Which sentence does Kahneman use to sum up the focusing illusion?
options: Nothing in life is as important as you think it is when you are thinking about it
What you see is all there is, so you never ask what you might be missing
People care more about how an experience ends than about how long it lasts
Losses loom larger than gains when people think about changes in their life
questions.explain: Kahneman states the focusing illusion in one sentence: “Nothing in life is as important as you think it is when you are thinking about it.” The other sentences describe WYSIATI, the peak-end pattern, and loss aversion.

questions.q: Kahneman and Schkade traced the students' mistaken belief that Californians are happier to an exaggerated belief in the importance of climate, an error they described as a ____.
questions.explain: Students gave too much weight to climate and too little to the other determinants of well-being. Kahneman named this error the focusing illusion.

questions.q: Put in order the events that led to Kahneman's study of happiness in California.
items: A family debate about moving from California to Princeton
A workshop on the social science of global warming
Kahneman and David Schkade receive research funds
Students in California, Ohio, and Michigan are surveyed
The data show no difference in life satisfaction between regions
questions.explain: The idea began with the family debate, was sharpened at the global warming workshop, and was tested with Schkade's funded survey of students. The result showed Kahneman had won the family argument.

questions.q: What did Kahneman and Schkade find when they compared the life satisfaction of students in California and in the Midwest?
options: Californians were somewhat happier, mainly because of the climate
There was no difference whatsoever in life satisfaction
Midwesterners were happier because they had lower expectations
Californians were happier only during the winter months
questions.explain: Californians enjoyed their climate and Midwesterners despised theirs, but there was no difference whatsoever in life satisfaction. Climate was not an important determinant of well-being.

questions.q: True or false: In the Kahneman and Schkade study, Midwestern students reported lower life satisfaction than students in California.
questions.explain: There was no difference whatsoever between the life satisfaction of students in California and in the Midwest. The two groups differed only in how much they liked their climate.

questions.q: True or false: In the California study, students in both California and the Midwest shared the mistaken belief that Californians enjoy greater well-being.
questions.explain: Kahneman's wife was not alone: students in both regions believed Californians were happier. The error was traced to an exaggerated belief in the importance of climate.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it was found in Kahneman and Schkade's California study.

items.t: Californians enjoyed their climate
Midwesterners despised their climate
Students in both regions believed Californians were happier
Californians reported higher life satisfaction
Climate was an important determinant of well-being
Midwestern students believed they were the happier group

questions.explain: Attitudes to climate differed greatly, and both groups held the same mistaken belief about Californians. But life satisfaction did not differ, and climate was not an important determinant of well-being.

questions.q: Kahneman writes that the essence of the focusing illusion is ____, giving too much weight to the climate and too little to all the other determinants of well-being.
accept: what you see is all there is
questions.explain: Only the feature in focus, here climate, comes to mind, and the rest of life is left out of the judgment. That is WYSIATI, the tendency to treat what comes to mind as all there is.

questions.q: In Kahneman's car example, when you rate how much pleasure you get from your car, what narrower question do you actually answer?
options: How much did my car cost compared with other cars?
How much pleasure do I get from my car when I think about it?
How much do other people admire my car?
How much pleasure do I get from driving on an open road?
questions.explain: You get pleasure from your car mainly when you think about it, which is not often, even while driving. Substituting the narrower question makes you ignore how rarely you think about the car.

questions.q: In the car example, substituting the question about pleasure when you think about the car makes you ignore how rarely you think about it, a form of ____.
questions.explain: The share of time the car is actually on your mind drops out of the judgment. Kahneman calls this a form of duration neglect, which feeds the focusing illusion.

questions.q: Using Kahneman's car example, explain the difference between asking "How much pleasure do you get from your car?" and "When do you get pleasure from your car?"
questions.a: The first question gets an immediate answer based on how much you like the car. The second reveals that you get pleasure from it only when you think about it, which is rarely, even while driving, since your mood depends on whatever you are thinking about. Answering the narrower question in place of the broad one ignores how rarely the car is on your mind, a form of duration neglect, so you exaggerate the pleasure it brings, both for your current car and when you consider buying a new one.

questions.q: Why, according to Kahneman, are long-term Californians unlikely to think of the climate when asked to evaluate their life?
options: They secretly dislike the climate and avoid thinking of it
The climate changes too little from year to year to notice
Without a contrasting alternative in mind, the climate is not salient
They are too busy with outdoor activities to answer surveys
questions.explain: For a lifelong resident, living in California is “like having ten toes: nice, but not something one thinks much about.” Any aspect of life is more salient when a contrasting alternative is highly available, which is the case for newcomers.

questions.q: Kahneman describes a man who moved from Ohio to California for the better climate. Explain how the focusing illusion affects how happy he says he is in the years after the move.
questions.a: When asked about his life, he is likely to be reminded of the move and of the contrast between the two climates, a comparison that favors California. Attention to that aspect of life may distort its true weight in experience. Whether or not he is actually happier, he will report himself happier, because thoughts of the climate make him believe he is. So the focusing illusion can make people wrong about their present well-being, not just about others or their future.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman name as conditions to which there is no adaptation, because they keep drawing attention?
options: Chronic pain
Constant exposure to loud noise
Severe depression
Paraplegia
A recent marriage
Winning a lottery
questions.explain: Pain and noise are biologically set to attract attention, and depression is a self-reinforcing cycle of miserable thoughts. Paraplegia is explicitly not one of the exceptions: attention to it is withdrawn as it becomes familiar.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman reports that detailed observations show paraplegics are in a bad mood more than half of the time one month after their accident.
questions.explain: Detailed observations show paraplegics are in a fairly good mood more than half of the time as early as one month after the accident. Their mood is somber mainly when they think about their situation.

questions.q: Because adaptation consists largely of thinking less about a new situation, Kahneman says most long-term circumstances, including paraplegia and marriage, are ____ that one inhabits only when one attends to them.
questions.explain: Kahneman writes that “Adaptation to a new situation, whether good or bad, consists in large part of thinking less and less about it.” A circumstance affects mood mainly while it is attended to, which makes it a part-time state.

questions.q: Match each condition to Kahneman’s account of how attention to it behaves over time.
pairs: Chronic pain or loud noise
Biologically set to be signals that attract attention
Severe depression
A self-reinforcing cycle of miserable thoughts
Paraplegia
Attention is withdrawn as the situation becomes familiar
Lifelong residence in California
Nice, but rarely thought about without a contrast
questions.explain: Pain, noise, and depression keep capturing attention. Paraplegia gradually fades from attention as it becomes familiar. A long-familiar climate is nice but rarely thought about, like having ten toes.

questions.q: Sort these conditions by Kahneman's account of whether people adapt to them by thinking about them less over time.

items.t: Paraplegia
Marriage
Winning a lottery
Living in California for life
Chronic pain
Constant loud noise
Severe depression

questions.explain: Most long-term circumstances fade from attention as they become familiar, which is what adaptation mostly consists of. Pain and noise are signals built to attract attention, and depression feeds itself, so these are the exceptions.

questions.q: Match each group in Beruria Cohn's survey to its average estimate of the time paraplegics spend in a bad mood.
pairs: Knew a paraplegic; accident a month earlier
Did not know one; accident a month earlier
Knew a paraplegic; accident a year earlier
Did not know one; accident a year earlier
questions.explain: The groups agreed about recent paraplegics but differed sharply a year after the accident. Those who knew a paraplegic had seen attention withdraw from the condition; others did not forecast that adaptation.

questions.q: In Beruria Cohn's survey, why did people who knew a paraplegic give much lower estimates of bad mood a year after the accident than people who did not?
options: They had observed the gradual withdrawal of attention from the condition
They were reluctant to say bad things about someone they knew
They knew paraplegics whose injuries were less severe
They had been told the accident happened more recently
questions.explain: Kahneman says those who knew a paraplegic had seen attention gradually withdraw from the condition, while others did not forecast this adaptation. The same pattern appeared in judgments about lottery winners one month and one year after winning.

questions.q: What did Beruria Cohn's study of judgments about paraplegics show, and how does Kahneman explain it?
questions.a: Respondents estimated how much time paraplegics spend in a bad mood, a month or a year after the accident, and said whether they knew a paraplegic. For a month after, both groups said about 70 to 75%; for a year after, those who knew a paraplegic said 41% while others said 68%. Those who knew one had seen attention gradually withdraw from the condition, but others failed to forecast this adaptation; lottery winners showed the same pattern.

questions.q: Which of these are findings Kahneman reports from recent studies of colostomy patients?
options: Experience sampling shows no difference in experienced happiness from a healthy population
Patients would trade away years of life for a shorter life without the colostomy
Patients whose colostomy was reversed remember that time as awful
Experience sampling shows patients are unhappy most of the day
Patients rate their lives as highly as healthy people do
questions.explain: Experienced happiness matches that of healthy people, yet patients' evaluations of life are poor: they would give up years of life to be rid of the condition, and those reversed would give up even more not to return to it.

questions.q: What does Kahneman conclude from the gap between colostomy patients' experienced happiness and their evaluations of their lives?
options: The experiencing self suffers far more than the patients admit
Experience sampling cannot measure the mood of people who are ill
Patients adapt in their evaluations but not in their daily mood
The remembering self is subject to a massive focusing illusion
questions.explain: Kahneman writes that the remembering self is subject to a massive focusing illusion about a life the experiencing self endures quite comfortably. Daily mood is normal; it is the evaluation, not the experience, that is distorted.

questions.q: Sam has a chronic, burdensome condition but is cheerful through most of his day. Based on Kahneman's argument, how will Sam probably answer a question about his satisfaction with life?
options: He will rate it as high as his daily mood, since the two always match
He will rate it lower than his daily mood, because the question reminds him of other lives and his old one
He will rate it higher than his daily mood, to avoid sounding self-pitying
He will refuse to answer because the question is too broad
questions.explain: Kahneman expects the life satisfaction of people with chronic conditions to be low relative to their experienced well-being. A request to evaluate their lives inevitably reminds them of the lives of others and the life they used to lead.

questions.q: Explain the inconsistency Kahneman describes between colostomy patients' experienced well-being and their evaluations of their lives, and what it shows about the two selves.
questions.a: Experience sampling shows no difference in experienced happiness between colostomy patients and a healthy population. Yet the patients would trade away years of life for a shorter life without the colostomy, and those whose colostomy was reversed remember the time as awful and would give up even more life not to return to it. The remembering self is subject to a massive focusing illusion about a life the experiencing self endures quite comfortably.

questions.q: Daniel Gilbert and Timothy Wilson introduced the word ____ to describe bad choices that arise from errors of affective forecasting.
questions.explain: Kahneman says the word deserves to be in everyday language. The focusing illusion is a rich source of miswanting, especially about purchases and changed circumstances.

questions.q: Gilbert and Wilson's name for the focusing illusion is ____.
questions.explain: Kahneman notes that the focusing illusion, which Gilbert and Wilson call focalism, is a rich source of miswanting.

questions.q: Kahneman compares buying a comfortable new car with joining a weekly poker or book club. Which is people likely to overvalue in the long run, and why?
options: The club, because social events are exciting at first but grow dull
Both equally, because all novelties fade at the same rate
Neither, because people forecast long-term pleasure accurately
The car, because they will eventually pay little attention to it while driving
questions.explain: Both are novel at first, but you will always attend to the social interaction while the car fades from attention. By WYSIATI, people exaggerate the car's long-term benefits but not the club's.

questions.q: Using Kahneman's car-versus-club comparison, sort these choices by how the focusing illusion is likely to affect forecasts of their long-term value.

items.t: A comfortable new car
A fancy sports car
A larger house
Joining a weekly book club
Taking up tennis
Learning to play the cello

questions.explain: Goods that excite at first but fade from attention are overvalued, because time is neglected. Social and inherently attention-demanding activities keep their attention value, so people are not likely to make the same mistake about them.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman name as commitments people are not likely to overvalue, because they keep demanding attention over time?
options: Joining a group that meets weekly, such as a book club
Playing tennis
Learning to play the cello
Buying a comfortable new car
Moving to a place with a better climate
questions.explain: Social gatherings and inherently attention-demanding activities keep their attention value, so their benefits are not exaggerated. A new car and a better climate fade from attention and are the classic objects of the focusing illusion.

questions.q: Lena is about to pay extra for an apartment with a sea view, sure it will keep her happier for years. What would Kahneman most likely warn her about?
options: Loss aversion: she will regret the money more than she enjoys the view
The planning fallacy: the move will take longer than she expects
The focusing illusion: she will notice the view far less once it is familiar
The peak-end rule: she will remember only her last day there
questions.explain: Like the car or the California climate, a view is exciting at first and then fades from attention. The focusing illusion biases choices toward goods that are initially exciting, even if they will eventually lose their appeal.

questions.q: Your friend must choose between spending a bonus on a new car or joining a weekly club that meets to play music. Using Kahneman's idea of miswanting, explain which choice is more likely to be overvalued and why.
questions.a: Both choices will be novel and exciting at first. But your friend will eventually pay little attention to the car while driving, while the weekly club will keep demanding attention every time it meets. By WYSIATI and the focusing illusion, people exaggerate the long-term benefits of the car, a case of miswanting, because time is neglected and experiences that keep their attention value are appreciated less than they deserve.

questions.q: What is the focusing illusion, and how does Kahneman connect it to substitution and WYSIATI?
questions.a: The focusing illusion is the tendency for any aspect of life to which attention is directed to loom large in a global evaluation: “Nothing in life is as important as you think it is when you are thinking about it.” When evaluating life, System 1 substitutes a small part of it for the whole, which is substitution. It gives too much weight to the aspect in view, such as climate, and too little to all other determinants of well-being, which is WYSIATI.

questions.q: Put the topics of the section "The Focusing Illusion" in Chapter 38 in the order Kahneman presents them.
items: The California and Midwest student study
How much pleasure you get from your car
The man who moved from Ohio to California
How much time paraplegics spend in a bad mood
Colostomy patients' experience versus evaluation
Miswanting: a new car versus a weekly club
questions.explain: The section starts from the climate study and the car question, applies the idea to Californians and a newcomer, then to paraplegics and colostomy patients, and ends with Gilbert and Wilson's miswanting and the car-versus-club comparison.

questions.q: Kahneman calls the value of an episode for the experiencing self, the sum of the values of its moments, a ____.
questions.explain: It is logical to see the experiencing self's life as a series of moments, each with a value, whose sum is the hedonimeter total. But the mind does not represent episodes this way.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says that in storytelling mode an episode is represented by a few critical moments, especially the beginning, the peak, and the end.
questions.explain: In storytelling mode duration is neglected, and a few singular moments stand for the episode. Kahneman points back to the cold-hand situation and Violetta's story as examples.

questions.q: Sort these features by whether they describe the hedonimeter total or the remembering self's storytelling mode.

items.t: The value of an episode is the sum of its moments
Each moment of the experiencing self counts
A few critical moments stand for the episode
The beginning, peak, and end carry the weight
Duration is neglected

questions.explain: The hedonimeter total adds up every moment, so time counts in full. The remembering self tells stories built on a few critical moments and neglects duration.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what form of duration neglect appears in prospect theory?
options: Episodes are judged by their peak and end, not their length
Gains are weighted less than losses of the same size
Rare outcomes are given more weight than they deserve
A state is represented by the transition to it, ignoring how long it lasts
questions.explain: Decision utility for a lottery win corresponds to the anticipated reaction to the news of winning. The withdrawal of attention and other adaptations to the new state of wealth are neglected; peak and end belong to the storytelling mode instead.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say show the same focus on the transition to a new state and the same neglect of time and adaptation?
options: Decision utility for winning a lottery in prospect theory
Forecasts of the reaction to chronic diseases
The focusing illusion
The hedonimeter total of an episode
The life satisfaction of long-term Californians
questions.explain: Kahneman links prospect theory's lottery example, forecasts about chronic disease, and the focusing illusion as cases where a thin slice of time is considered. The hedonimeter total, by contrast, counts every moment.

questions.q: In "Time and Time Again," how does Kahneman argue that the mind fails to represent time properly?
questions.a: The experiencing self's life is logically a series of moments whose values sum to a hedonimeter total, but the remembering self tells stories and makes choices that do not represent time. In storytelling mode an episode is represented by a few critical moments such as the beginning, peak, and end, as in the cold-hand situation and Violetta's story. Prospect theory represents a state by the transition to it, and the same neglect of time and adaptation appears in forecasts of chronic disease and in the focusing illusion: “The mind is good with stories, but it does not appear to be well designed for the processing of time.”

questions.q: What does Kahneman say ten years of research have taught about the word happiness?
options: It has a simple meaning that surveys finally capture well
It does not have a simple meaning and should not be used as if it does
It should be replaced entirely by the term life satisfaction
It means the same as the hedonimeter total of a life
questions.explain: Kahneman says we have learned many new facts about happiness but also that the word does not have a simple meaning. Sometimes scientific progress leaves us more puzzled than before.

questions.q: Match each remark from "Speaking of Thinking About Life" to the idea it applies.
pairs: She thought a fancy car would make her happier, but it did not
An error of affective forecasting
His car broke down this morning; not a good day to ask about his job
Current mood colors global evaluations
She looks cheerful but says she is very unhappy
The question reminds her of a recent divorce
Buying a larger house may not make us happier in the long term
The focusing illusion
questions.explain: Each remark applies a chapter idea to everyday life: a mispredicted feeling, the mood heuristic, a salient recent event in life evaluation, and the focusing illusion.

questions.q: A coworker's car broke down on the way to work and he is in a foul mood. HR wants to ask him today how satisfied he is with his job. What would Kahneman advise?
options: Ask today, since bad moods make people more honest
Ask today, since job satisfaction is a stable judgment
Wait, since his foul mood will likely color his answer
Wait, since people only judge jobs well at the end of the week
questions.explain: Like the dime on the copier, an irrelevant event changes mood, and mood stands in for a global evaluation. The chapter's own remark says this is not a good day to ask him about his job satisfaction.

questions.q: True or false: Chapter 38, "Thinking About Life," is the last chapter of Part V, "Two Selves," and is followed directly by the book's Conclusions.
questions.explain: Part V runs from "Two Selves" through "Life as a Story" and "Experienced Well-Being" to "Thinking About Life." The Conclusions come next.

questions.q: Put the chapters of Part V, "Two Selves," and the unit that follows in their order in the book.
items: Two Selves
Life as a Story
Experienced Well-Being
Thinking About Life
Conclusions
questions.explain: Part V moves from the distinction between the two selves to stories, then measuring experience, then life evaluation in Chapter 38, before the Conclusions.

questions.q: How does the title "Thinking About Life" signal Chapter 38's place after "Experienced Well-Being"?
options: It shifts from how people feel as they live to how they judge their lives when asked
It shifts from decisions under risk to decisions about health
It returns to the two systems of thought introduced in Part I
It introduces a new self that replaces the remembering self
questions.explain: Chapter 37 measured the experiencing self through the DRM; Chapter 38 examines what happens when people think about and evaluate their life, the remembering self's judgment. It does not introduce a new self or return to Part I's framework as its subject.

questions.q: Put the parts of Chapter 38, "Thinking About Life," in their order.
items: Marriage, goals, and the heuristics of life evaluation
The Focusing Illusion
Time and Time Again
Speaking of Thinking About Life
questions.explain: The chapter opens with life-satisfaction judgments around marriage and the goals study, develops the focusing illusion, steps back to the role of time across Part V, and ends with its Speaking of remarks.

questions.q: Which of these earlier examples from the book does Kahneman explicitly recall in Chapter 38?
options: The students asked about their dates before rating their happiness
The cold-hand situation
Violetta's story
The Linda problem
The Asian disease problem
questions.explain: Kahneman recalls the dating study as an earlier example of substitution and cites the cold-hand situation and Violetta's story in "Time and Time Again" as cases of focus on singular moments. The Linda and Asian disease problems are not discussed.

questions.q: How does Chapter 38 draw together the themes of Part V, "Two Selves," before the book's Conclusions?
questions.a: It applies the distinction between the experiencing self and the remembering self to life evaluation, showing that judgments of life, as with colostomy patients and paraplegics, can diverge from experience through the focusing illusion. In "Time and Time Again" Kahneman notes that the role of time has been a refrain in this part, linking duration neglect in stories, prospect theory, and the focusing illusion. It ends with his hybrid view that the well-being of both selves must be considered, leaving the question of happiness more complex as the book moves to its Conclusions.

questions.q: Match each term from the book's three distinctions to how Kahneman describes it at the start of the Conclusions.
pairs: System 1
The intuitive character that does the fast thinking
System 2
The effortful, slower character that monitors System 1 within limited resources
Econs
The fictitious species that lives in the land of theory
Experiencing self
The self that does the living
Remembering self
The self that keeps score and makes the choices
questions.explain: The Conclusions open by recalling the two characters, the two species and the two selves. Humans, the other species, are the ones who act in the real world.

questions.q: In the Conclusions' summary of the two selves, the experiencing self does the living, while the remembering self keeps score and makes the ____.
questions.explain: Kahneman describes the remembering self as the one “which keeps score and makes the choices.” This is why its biases matter for decisions.

questions.q: What three distinctions does Kahneman say the book introduced, and how does he describe each pair at the start of the Conclusions?
questions.a: The two characters are the intuitive System 1, which does the fast thinking, and the effortful System 2, which does the slow thinking and monitors System 1 within its limited resources. The two species are the fictitious Econs of the land of theory and the Humans who act in the real world. The two selves are the experiencing self, which does the living, and the remembering self, which keeps score and makes the choices.

questions.q: In the cold-hand study, as Kahneman recalls it in the Conclusions, why did subjects choose to repeat the trial that involved more pain?
options: They left the choice to the remembering self, which preferred the trial that left the better memory
They believed the longer trial would build their tolerance for future cold exposure
Their experiencing self judged the longer trial as less painful moment by moment
They feared that refusing the longer trial would disappoint the experimenters
questions.explain: Subjects chose by the quality of the memory, and duration neglect plus the peak-end rule made the longer trial leave the better memory. The experiencing self actually suffered more in that trial.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says the choices cold-hand subjects made on their own behalf are fairly described as mistakes.
questions.explain: He writes that “The choices that people made on their own behalf are fairly described as mistakes.” An objective observer choosing for someone else would pick the short exposure.

questions.q: In the cold-hand study, the combination of duration neglect and the ____ rule led to choices that Kahneman calls manifestly absurd.
questions.explain: Duration neglect together with the peak-end rule made people prefer the trial with more pain because it ended better.

questions.q: Sort these by where Kahneman locates them in his discussion of the remembering self in the Conclusions.

items.t: Duration neglect
The peak-end rule
The remembering self as a construction
The belief that duration is important

questions.explain: The remembering self is a construction of System 2, but its evaluation rules, duration neglect and the peak-end rule, come from memory and System 1. They do not necessarily match System 2's values, which hold that duration matters.

questions.q: Kahneman writes that the central fact of our existence is that ____ is the ultimate finite resource, a reality the remembering self ignores.
questions.explain: Because time does matter, the remembering self's rules for evaluating the past are poor guides for decision making.

questions.q: Match each situation to how, according to the Conclusions, duration neglect and the peak-end rule bias our preferences about it.
pairs: A short period of intense joy
Favored over a long period of moderate happiness
A short period of intense but tolerable suffering
Feared more than a much longer period of moderate pain
A long period of mild unpleasantness
Accepted because the end will be better
A long happy period likely to end poorly
Given up as an opportunity
questions.explain: All four follow from ignoring duration and overweighting peaks and ends. The bias toward intense joy and its mirror image toward intense suffering are two sides of the same error.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, why does the common admonition “Don’t do it, you will regret it” sound wise?
options: Anticipated regret reliably predicts how the experiencing self will feel moment by moment
Anticipated regret is the verdict of the remembering self, and we tend to accept such judgments as final
Loss aversion makes the remembering self give extra weight to how long an outcome lasts
People who ignore anticipated regret usually report lower satisfaction with their lives
questions.explain: The advice sounds wise because it carries the remembering self's verdict, which we treat as conclusive. Kahneman warns that this perspective is not always correct, and an observer of the hedonimeter profile might advise differently.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say combine to make the remembering self yield distorted reflections of our actual experience?
options: Its reliance on statistical base rates
Its neglect of duration
Its tendency to weight every moment equally
Its exaggerated emphasis on peaks and ends
Its susceptibility to hindsight
questions.explain: Kahneman names neglect of duration, emphasis on peaks and ends, and susceptibility to hindsight. Weighting every moment equally is the opposite approach, the duration-weighted view.

questions.q: The ____-weighted conception of well-being treats all moments of life alike, memorable or not.
questions.explain: In contrast to the remembering self, the duration-weighted view counts every moment, though moments can gain weight by being dwelt on or by changing later experience.

questions.q: Match each example to how the duration-weighted view of well-being treats it, according to the Conclusions.
pairs: An hour spent practicing the violin
Gains weight by enhancing many later hours of playing or listening
A brief awful event that causes PTSD
Weighted by the total duration of the long-term misery it causes
Time spent dwelling on a memorable moment
Included in that moment's duration, adding to its weight
Sincerely saying a moment is meaningful
A prediction that can be false, and often is
questions.explain: In the duration-weighted perspective, a moment matters by how much time it actually affects, so its importance can be known only after the fact.

questions.q: In the duration-weighted perspective described in the Conclusions, how should a sincere statement that you will always remember a moment be treated?
options: As reliable evidence that the moment deserves extra weight
As a report from the experiencing self about the present moment
As a promise or prediction that can be false, and often is
As irrelevant, since memorable moments never receive extra weight
questions.explain: Whether a moment is memorable or meaningful can be determined only after the fact, and many things we vow to remember are forgotten ten years later. Memorable moments can gain weight, but only through the time actually spent dwelling on them.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman concludes that the logic of duration weighting is compelling enough to serve as a complete theory of well-being.
questions.explain: He calls the logic compelling but says it cannot be a complete theory, because individuals identify with their remembering self and care about their story.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman argue that neither a purely duration-weighted theory nor a theory based only on how people evaluate their lives can be sustained?
questions.a: A duration-weighted theory ignores that people identify with their remembering self and care about their story, and a theory of well-being that ignores what people want cannot be sustained. But a theory that looks only at what people think about their life ignores what actually happens in their lives. So both selves must be considered, because their interests do not always coincide.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman offer as possible guides for deciding how much to invest in treating conditions such as blindness, deafness, or kidney failure?
options: The intensity of patients' desire for relief and the sacrifices they would make
The price that drug companies charge for treatment
The suffering that patients actually experience
How many doctors specialize in each condition
How much people fear the conditions
questions.explain: Kahneman poses fear, actual suffering, and desire for relief as competing measures, and notes that rankings of conditions might differ depending on which is used. Prices and numbers of specialists are not among his measures.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say the question of which of the two selves matters more is not only a question for philosophers?
questions.a: It has implications for policy in domains such as medicine and welfare. For example, investment in treating conditions could follow how much people fear them, how much patients actually suffer, or how intensely patients want relief, and the ranking of conditions such as blindness and deafness may differ by measure. In his words, “No easy solution is in sight, but the issue is too important to be ignored.”

questions.q: At the end of his discussion of the two selves, what possibility for national statistics does Kahneman raise?
options: Replacing income statistics entirely with measures of overall life satisfaction
Recording each citizen's peak and end experiences of every year
Publishing a hedonimeter profile for every government program
An index of the amount of suffering in society, alongside measures of unemployment, disability, and income
questions.explain: He notes growing interest, among academics and European governments, in well-being measures to guide policy, and says a suffering index may someday join standard national statistics. Nothing is said about replacing income measures.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say the rules the remembering self uses to evaluate the past are poor guides for decision making?
questions.a: Duration neglect and the peak-end rule are features of memory that originate in System 1, and they do not match the values of System 2: we believe duration is important, but memory tells us it is not. Because time is the ultimate finite resource, rules that ignore it lead to bad choices, such as preferring brief intense joy over long moderate happiness.

questions.q: Sort these descriptions by which of the two selves they belong to, as described in the Conclusions.

items.t: Does the living
Keeps score
Makes the choices
Its interests favor choosing the shorter cold-hand trial
Delivers the verdict of anticipated regret
Is ignored by a theory that looks only at how people think about their lives

questions.explain: The experiencing self lives through each moment, so an observer protecting it picks the shorter exposure. The remembering self keeps score, makes choices, and voices anticipated regret.

questions.q: A friend says she would cancel a two-week holiday entirely if she knew the last day would be rainy and miserable. Which idea from the Conclusions best explains her reasoning?
options: Duration neglect favors giving up a long happy period if it is likely to have a poor ending
Loss aversion makes the cost of the trip loom larger than its pleasures
The planning fallacy makes her underestimate how long the trip will take
Narrow framing makes her consider each day of the trip separately
questions.explain: Kahneman notes that duration neglect, combined with the peak-end rule, favors giving up an opportunity for a long happy period if it is likely to end badly. Thirteen good days count for little in a memory dominated by the ending.

questions.q: For economists and decision theorists, what is the only test of rationality, according to Kahneman?
options: Whether a person's beliefs are generally in tune with reality
Whether a person's beliefs and preferences are internally consistent
Whether a person's preferences are in line with their interests and values
Whether it is possible to reason with the person
questions.explain: In this technical sense, “Rationality is logical coherence—reasonable or not.” Being in tune with reality and serving one's interests describe being reasonable in everyday speech.

questions.q: In the economists' sense of rationality, Kahneman says, a rational person can believe in ____ so long as all her other beliefs are consistent with their existence.
questions.explain: The example shows that rationality as coherence says nothing about whether beliefs are reasonable, only whether they fit together.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says his research with Amos demonstrated that human choices are irrational.
questions.explain: He cringes when the work is credited that way; the research only showed that Humans are not well described by the rational-agent model.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say the word irrational connotes?
options: Careful calculation
Stubborn resistance to reasonable argument
Impulsivity
Emotionality
Lack of warmth
questions.explain: Irrational is a strong word implying impulsivity, emotionality, and resistance to argument, which is why reasonable people should not be branded with it. Calculation and less warmth are what the word rational conveys.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman call the definition of rationality as coherence impossibly restrictive?
options: It forbids people from holding unusual beliefs, such as a belief in ghosts
It requires people always to act in their own long-term interest
It demands adherence to rules of logic that a finite mind is not able to implement
It allows only trained economists to judge whether a choice is rational
questions.explain: Coherence requires flawless logic that no finite mind can carry out, so reasonable people cannot meet it. Unusual beliefs are allowed under coherence as long as they are consistent.

questions.q: Sort these descriptions into Econs and Humans, as the Conclusions describe them.

items.t: Read and understand the fine print before signing
Make important decisions carefully, using all the information provided
Need no protection beyond disclosure of the relevant information
Cannot consistently avoid priming and WYSIATI
Need protection from firms that exploit their weaknesses
Usually sign contracts without reading them

questions.explain: Rational agents are assumed to process all information carefully, so disclosure is enough for them. Humans have the quirks of System 1 and a lazy System 2, which others can exploit.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what is faith in human rationality closely linked to in the Chicago school of economics?
options: A belief that governments should set helpful defaults for their citizens
A conviction that markets often fail to allocate goods efficiently
A view that intuitive thinking needs constant supervision by experts
An ideology in which it is unnecessary and even immoral to protect people against their choices
questions.explain: For the Chicago school, rational people should be free and responsible for themselves, a view captured in Milton Friedman's title Free to Choose. Setting defaults is the behavioral economists' idea, not theirs.

questions.q: Match each person to what the Conclusions associate with them.
pairs: Milton Friedman
Leading Chicago figure whose popular book was titled Free to Choose
Gary Becker
Co-author of A Theory of Rational Addiction
Shlomo Benartzi
Proposed Save More Tomorrow with Richard Thaler in 2003
Cass Sunstein
Became administrator of the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs
questions.explain: Friedman and Becker represent the Chicago school's faith in rationality, while Benartzi and Sunstein, both partners of Thaler, represent behavioral policy in practice.

questions.q: Put in order the approach to explaining odd behavior that Kahneman draws from Gary Becker's half-joking explanation of obesity.
items: Observe people acting in ways that seem odd
First examine whether they have a good reason for what they do
Invoke psychological interpretations only when the reasons become implausible
questions.explain: Kahneman calls this a valuable point even though Becker's obesity explanation, that people expect a cure for diabetes, is probably implausible.

questions.q: In the Conclusions, a motorcycle rider chooses to ride without a helmet. How does Kahneman say a libertarian would respond?
options: Support his right to do so, since in a nation of Econs government stays out of the way
Require a helmet by law, because he is a Human rather than an Econ
Make wearing a helmet the default and let him opt out
Charge him a fee to cover society's cost of his possible injuries
questions.explain: The libertarian position is to leave people free to choose unless their choices harm others. Making helmets a default is a nudge, the behavioral economists' approach.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say that for Chicago school economists freedom is free of charge, while for behavioral economists it is not?
questions.a: Chicago economists assume rational agents who do not make mistakes, so leaving them free costs nothing. Behavioral economists value freedom just as much, but they see that freedom has a cost, borne by individuals who make bad choices and by a society that feels obligated to help them. Whether to protect people against their mistakes is therefore a dilemma only for behavioral economists.

questions.q: Sort these positions by whether they belong to the Chicago school or to the behavioral economists, as described in the Conclusions.

items.t: Rational agents do not make mistakes
Disclosing the relevant information is protection enough
Elderly people who failed to save deserve little sympathy
Freedom has a cost borne by those who choose badly and by society
Firms should offer contracts simple enough for Humans to understand
Protecting people against their mistakes is a dilemma

questions.explain: Both sides value freedom; they differ on whether people make mistakes worth protecting against. The hard edge of the Chicago view gives little sympathy to those who did not save.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says Save More Tomorrow was sponsored in Congress by an unusual coalition that included extreme conservatives as well as liberals.
questions.explain: He uses this to show that libertarian paternalism appeals across a broad political spectrum.

questions.q: Thaler and Sunstein advocate libertarian ____, in which the state and other institutions may nudge people toward decisions that serve their long-term interests.
questions.explain: Libertarian paternalism is their answer to the dilemma of helping people decide well without curtailing their freedom.

questions.q: Thaler and Sunstein's term for the framing of an individual's decision, which has a huge effect on the outcome, is choice ____.
questions.explain: Choice architecture is the design of how a decision is presented, such as which choice is the default.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say it is difficult to argue that being automatically enrolled in a pension plan diminishes anyone's freedom?
options: Pension plans are required by law in most countries
People merely have to check a box to opt out
Most people would enroll anyway after reading the fine print
The plan's returns are guaranteed by the government
questions.explain: A default changes what happens if people do nothing but leaves every choice open, which is why it counts as a nudge rather than a mandate.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman give as psychological reasons that a default choice is so powerful?
options: Deviating from it is an act of commission that requires more effortful deliberation
Deviating from it takes on more responsibility and is more likely to evoke regret
The default is naturally perceived as the normal choice
People are legally penalized for leaving a default
Defaults are usually set by experts who have full information
questions.explain: Normality, effort, responsibility and regret are the forces that guide someone who is unsure what to do. Kahneman says nothing about expert-set defaults or penalties.

questions.q: According to Kahneman, what is a pernicious implication of the rational-agent model in its extreme form?
options: Firms are forced to write all their contracts in plain language
Governments must set default choices for every financial product
Customers are assumed to need no protection beyond disclosure of the relevant information
Customers are assumed to ignore everything they are told
questions.explain: Because an Econ can handle small print, the size of print and complexity of language are treated as irrelevant, leaving firms free to hide information in plain sight. Plain-language contracts are what Nudge recommends instead.

questions.q: Put in order how Save More Tomorrow works for an employee.
items: The employee signs on to the plan
The employee later receives a raise
The contribution to the saving plan rises by a fixed proportion
The higher saving rate continues automatically until the employee opts out
questions.explain: Saving rises only when pay rises, and the increase stays in place automatically unless the employee gives notice to stop.

questions.q: Match each feature of Save More Tomorrow to the psychological principle Kahneman says it uses.
pairs: Requiring no immediate change
Avoids the resistance to an immediate loss
Tying increased saving to pay raises
Turns losses into foregone gains, which are easier to bear
Automatic increases until opting out
Aligns the laziness of System 2 with long-term interests
questions.explain: The plan draws on loss aversion, framing, and the laziness of System 2, all without compelling anyone or using misdirection.

questions.q: By tying increased saving to pay raises, Save More Tomorrow turns losses into ____ gains, which are much easier to bear.
questions.explain: Money never received feels less painful to give up than money already in hand, an application of loss aversion.

questions.q: Britain's Behavioural Insight Team, which applies behavioral science to help the government reach its goals, is widely known as the ____ Unit.
questions.explain: Kahneman notes that Richard Thaler is an adviser to this team.

questions.q: Put these events from the Conclusions in chronological order.
items: Thaler and Benartzi propose Save More Tomorrow
Thaler and Sunstein publish Nudge
Sunstein is invited by President Obama to head the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs
The Office of Management and Budget's report describes the office's mission
questions.explain: Save More Tomorrow dates from 2003, Nudge from 2008, Sunstein's appointment was its storybook sequel, and the report is from 2010.

questions.q: Which of these behavioral applications does Kahneman say have been implemented in the United States?
options: Replacing the Food Pyramid with a Food Plate
Allowing 90% fat-free labels only if 10% fat is shown equally prominently
Mandatory helmet laws for motorcyclists
A ban on large sugary drinks
Automatic enrollment in health insurance
questions.explain: These informed and unintrusive measures help Humans decide without forcing them. Helmet laws and bans on sugary drinks are not among the applications listed as implemented; the helmet example appears only to illustrate the libertarian position.

questions.q: A gym contract hides an automatic renewal fee in tiny print deep inside the document. Which point from the Conclusions does this illustrate?
options: Libertarian paternalism forbids firms from offering automatic renewals of any kind
Customers who sign without reading are irrational in the strong sense of the word
Choice architecture works only when the default benefits the firm
Firms can exploit Humans, who usually sign without reading, by hiding important information in plain sight
questions.explain: Kahneman says Humans need protection from those who exploit the quirks of System 1 and the laziness of System 2, and that disclosure alone does not protect them. He rejects calling such people irrational.

questions.q: Explain why Kahneman holds up Save More Tomorrow as a model of libertarian paternalism.
questions.a: It raises employees' saving automatically whenever they get a raise, until they opt out, so no one is forced to do anything. It requires no immediate change, which avoids resistance to immediate losses; tying saving to raises turns losses into foregone gains; and automaticity aligns the laziness of System 2 with workers' long-term interests. It has improved the savings of millions without misdirection or artifice.

questions.q: What does Kahneman mean when he says Humans are not irrational yet often need help, and why is that claim controversial?
questions.a: Humans fail the economists' test of rationality as logical coherence, which no finite mind can meet, but that does not make them impulsive or unreasonable; they are simply not well described by the rational-agent model. They often need help from policies and institutions to judge and decide better. This is controversial because the Chicago school links faith in rationality to an ideology in which protecting people against their choices is unnecessary and even immoral.

questions.q: In the Conclusions, what does Kahneman say the phrase System 1 does X is a shortcut for?
options: X occurs automatically
X is performed by a specific region of the brain
X is done after deliberate reasoning
X is triggered by a strong emotion
questions.explain: He reminds readers that the two systems do not really exist in the brain or anywhere else; the language of systems is a helpful shorthand.

questions.q: Besides often endorsing or rationalizing System 1's ideas, what else does Kahneman credit System 2 with in the Conclusions?
options: Maintaining the rich model of the world in associative memory
Preventing many foolish thoughts and inappropriate impulses from overt expression
Producing skilled responses automatically as challenges arise
Signaling when intuitive answers have become unreliable
questions.explain: System 2 is not merely an apologist for System 1; it also blocks foolish thoughts and impulses. The model of the world and skilled responses belong to System 1, and no system gives a warning signal.

questions.q: Put in order how, according to Kahneman, System 2 ends up rationalizing a feeling generated by System 1.
items: Something about a project's leader reminds you of your beloved sister
You feel optimistic about the project
You are asked for an explanation
You search memory for presentable reasons and find some
You believe the story you made up
questions.explain: System 2 articulates judgments but often endorses feelings from System 1, and you never learn the real cause of your optimism.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say System 2 is not a paragon of rationality?
options: It is entirely controlled by the intuitions of System 1
It never engages in comparison, choice, or ordered reasoning
Its abilities are limited and so is the knowledge it has access to
It works properly only when arousal is low
questions.explain: We often make mistakes because System 2 simply does not know any better. Attention is in fact essential to comparison, choice and ordered reasoning.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says our errors in reasoning are always due to intrusive and incorrect intuitions from System 1.
questions.explain: He says the errors are not always due to intrusive intuitions: “Often we make mistakes because we (our System 2) do not know any better.”

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say that the many pages he devoted to System 1's errors are a poor indicator of the balance between its marvels and its flaws?
questions.a: System 1 is the origin of much that we do wrong, but it is also the origin of most of what we do right, which is most of what we do. Our thoughts and actions are routinely guided by System 1 and are generally on the mark. Its marvels include the rich model of the world in associative memory and the vast repertory of skills acquired through practice.
