questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say the model of the world maintained in associative memory does?
options: Sounds a warning when its own answers become unreliable
Computes exact answers to problems such as 17 × 24
Automatically searches for a causal interpretation of surprises and events
Distinguishes surprising from normal events in a fraction of a second
Immediately generates an idea of what was expected instead of a surprise
questions.explain: These are among the marvels of System 1. It gives no warning signal when it becomes unreliable, and a problem like 17 × 24 calls in System 2.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman say the acquisition of skills requires?
options: High general intelligence
Rapid and unequivocal feedback
Formal instruction from a recognized expert
An adequate opportunity to practice
A regular environment
questions.explain: When these three conditions are met, skill eventually develops and quick intuitive judgments will mostly be accurate. Intelligence and formal instruction are not on his list.

questions.q: A nurse with years of practice and quick, clear feedback instantly senses that a patient is deteriorating. What does the account of skill in the Conclusions suggest about this judgment?
options: It is a heuristic substitution, so it should be distrusted until checked
It is System 2 reasoning carried out too fast to be noticed
It cannot be trusted, because intuitive thinking never improves with study
It is skilled System 1 work, and under such conditions intuitions like this will mostly be accurate
questions.explain: With a regular environment, practice and rapid feedback, skill develops and the judgments that come quickly to mind will mostly be right. Kahneman's point that System 1 is not readily educable concerns biases, not skills learned through practice.

questions.q: In Kahneman's conception of heuristics, as restated in the Conclusions, how does a heuristic answer differ from the answer to the original question?
options: It is more accessible, computed more quickly and easily, but not necessarily simpler
It is always simpler and more frugal than the original question
It is random and rarely close to the correct answer
It is produced by System 2 when System 1 is dumbfounded
questions.explain: System 1 generates answers to related questions and may substitute one that comes to mind more easily. Such answers are often approximately correct, and sometimes quite wrong.

questions.q: Why, according to Kahneman, is it hard for System 2 to catch the errors of System 1?
options: System 1's errors arrive too slowly for System 2 to connect them to the question
System 1 gives no warning when it becomes unreliable, and skilled and heuristic answers both arrive quickly and confidently
System 2 can easily tell skilled from heuristic answers but chooses not to
System 1 deliberately hides its computations from System 2
questions.explain: System 2's only recourse is to slow down and build an answer itself, which it is reluctant to do because it is indolent. So many suggestions are endorsed with minimal checking, as in the bat-and-ball problem.

questions.q: Sort these descriptions by which system Kahneman assigns them to in the Conclusions.

items.t: Generates answers to related questions while searching for one
Holds the vast repertory of skills acquired through practice
Registers cognitive ease but gives no warning when unreliable
Is called in for a problem like 17 × 24
Articulates judgments and makes choices
Is reluctant to slow down because it is indolent

questions.explain: System 1 is fast, automatic and not limited by capacity. System 2 is attentive and deliberate but lazy, and it is who we think we are.

questions.q: Sort these into the operative features of System 1 and the biases or illusions Kahneman says they give rise to.

items.t: WYSIATI
Intensity matching
Associative coherence
Anchoring
Nonregressive predictions
Overconfidence

questions.explain: Kahneman says these operative features give rise to predictable biases and cognitive illusions, which is how System 1 acquires its bad reputation.

questions.q: Speaking from experience, Kahneman says System 1 is not readily ____.
questions.explain: Despite studying biases, his intuitions remain prone to overconfidence, extreme predictions and the planning fallacy; he has improved only at recognizing situations where errors are likely.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman says he has made much more progress in recognizing the errors of others than his own.
questions.explain: He admits his own intuitive thinking is as error-prone as ever, which is one reason the book is aimed at observers rather than decision makers.

questions.q: Put in order the steps of Kahneman's procedure for blocking errors that originate in System 1.
items: Recognize the signs that you are in a cognitive minefield
Slow down
Ask for reinforcement from System 2
questions.explain: He calls the procedure simple in principle, as with the Müller-Lyer illusion, but says it is least likely to be applied when it is needed most.

questions.q: Kahneman says it is much easier to identify a cognitive ____ when you watch others wander into it than when you are about to do so yourself.
questions.explain: Observers are less cognitively busy and more open to information than actors.

questions.q: Why did Kahneman write a book oriented to critics and gossipers rather than to decision makers?
questions.a: It is much easier to spot a cognitive minefield when you watch others wander into it than when you are about to enter it yourself. Observers are less cognitively busy and more open to information than actors, who are under stress and do not want more doubt. Sharper critics in turn help decision makers, who can imagine the voices of gossipers and critics better than they hear their own doubts.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say cognitive illusions are harder to guard against than the Müller-Lyer illusion?
questions.a: With the Müller-Lyer lines, the fins are a clear sign that you should not trust your impression of length. Cognitive illusions give no such sign: there is no warning bell, the voice of reason may be fainter than the loud voice of an erroneous intuition, and questioning your intuitions is unpleasant under the stress of a big decision. As he puts it, “More doubt is the last thing you want when you are in trouble.”

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman argues that organizations are better than individuals at avoiding errors because they naturally think more slowly and can impose orderly procedures.
questions.explain: Organizations can enforce checklists and exercises such as reference-class forecasting and the premortem, and encourage people to watch out for one another.

questions.q: Kahneman compares an organization to a factory that manufactures judgments and decisions. Match each stage of a factory's quality control to its counterpart in producing decisions.
pairs: Initial design
Framing of the problem to be solved
Fabrication
Collection of relevant information leading to a decision
Final inspection
Reflection and review
questions.explain: An organization seeking a better decision product should routinely look for improvements at each of these stages.

questions.q: Which of these does Kahneman mention as procedures or exercises that organizations can institute to avoid errors?
options: Reference-class forecasting
Deferring to the leader's confident intuition
Useful checklists
Wholesale reviews undertaken only after a disaster
The premortem
questions.explain: He recommends checklists and exercises such as reference-class forecasting and the premortem, and contrasts constant quality control with the wholesale reviews organizations usually conduct after disasters.

questions.q: For an organization seeking to improve its decision product, Kahneman says the operative concept is ____.
questions.explain: Constant quality control at every stage is his alternative to wholesale reviews of processes after disasters.

questions.q: Why does Kahneman say a richer vocabulary is essential to the skill of constructive criticism of judgments?
questions.a: Identifying judgment errors is a diagnostic task, like medicine, and needs a precise vocabulary. Just as a disease's name is a hook for everything known about its symptoms, causes and care, labels such as anchoring effects, narrow framing or excessive coherence bring together in memory everything we know about a bias, its causes, its effects and what can be done about it.

questions.q: How does Kahneman link more precise gossip at the watercooler to better decisions?
questions.a: Decision makers are sometimes better able to imagine the voices of present gossipers and future critics than to hear the hesitant voice of their own doubts. If that gossip is precise, it pushes them to choose more carefully. They will make better choices when they trust their critics to be sophisticated and fair, and when they expect their decision to be judged by how it was made, not only by how it turned out.

questions.q: A manager is about to approve a large project on a gut feeling and an attractive first estimate. Using the Conclusions, explain what she could do, alone and through her organization, to guard against System 1 errors.
questions.a: On her own she should recognize the signs of a cognitive minefield, for example that the first estimate may act as an anchor, then slow down and ask for reinforcement from System 2, though Kahneman warns this is hardest exactly when the stakes are high. Her organization can do better, because it thinks more slowly and can impose procedures such as checklists, reference-class forecasting and a premortem. A shared vocabulary of biases also lets colleagues watch out for one another.

questions.q: Put the sections of the Conclusions in the order Kahneman presents them.
items: Two Selves
Econs and Humans
Two Systems
questions.explain: He says he will consider the three distinctions in reverse order, so the most recent topic, the two selves, comes first and the two systems come last.

questions.q: Put these parts of the book in the order they appear in the table of contents.
items: Two Systems
Heuristics and Biases
Overconfidence
Choices
Two Selves
questions.explain: The book moves from the two systems through their biases and overconfidence to choices and finally the two selves, after which the Conclusions close the book.

questions.q: Match each topic the Conclusions draw on to the part of the book where it was developed, according to the table of contents.
pairs: The experiencing and remembering selves
Part V, Two Selves
Econs and Humans
Part IV, Choices
The automatic and effortful systems
Part I, Two Systems
Anchoring and nonregressive predictions
Part II, Heuristics and Biases
Overconfidence as a cognitive illusion
Part III, Overconfidence
questions.explain: The Conclusions gather threads from every part: the selves from Part V, the Econs-Humans contrast from the choices chapters of Part IV, and the systems and their biases from Parts I to III.

questions.q: True or false: The Conclusions revisit the book's three distinctions in the same order in which the book introduced them.
questions.explain: Kahneman says he considers applications of the three distinctions “taking them in reverse order,” starting with the two selves and ending with the two systems.

questions.q: Why does the Two Selves section come first in the Conclusions?
options: The two selves were the book's first and most basic distinction
Kahneman considers the two selves the least controversial distinction
Kahneman takes the three distinctions in reverse order, and the two selves came last, in Part V
Part V needed a summary because it was the shortest part of the book
questions.explain: The book ended Part V with Thinking About Life, so the Conclusions start from the most recent distinction and work back to the two systems, which opened the book.

questions.q: Given where it sits in the table of contents, what does the title Conclusions signal about this chapter's role?
options: It opens a sixth part devoted to new experiments on well-being
It is an appendix that reprints Kahneman and Tversky's original articles
It concludes only Part V and its discussion of the two selves
It follows Part V and closes the book by applying all three of its distinctions
questions.explain: The Conclusions come after the last chapter of Part V and draw on the two systems, Econs and Humans, and the two selves. The reprinted articles are the separate appendices that follow.

questions.q: How do the Conclusions tie together the whole book, and what role does each of the three sections play?
questions.a: The Conclusions apply the book's three distinctions, in reverse order of their introduction. Two Selves draws on Part V to ask which self should guide decisions and policy; Econs and Humans draws on the choices chapters to argue that Humans need help, as offered by libertarian paternalism; and Two Systems returns to Part I to restate how System 1 and System 2 work and how individuals and organizations can reduce errors. The book ends where it began, with the two systems and better gossip.
